title: Game-Theoretic Data Allocation for Expert Specialization and Routing
description:
arXiv:2611.25167v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can the allocation used to train experts also predict which expert will perform best on a prompt? Such a connection would make the intended division of labor inspectable before training and allow the allocation itself to guide inference. We introduce InflEns, a mixture of LoRA experts whose training weights and inference routes come from the same location game in a fixed prompt-trait space. Players choose positions to maximize their expected shares of the prompt distribution, without using expert losses. We utilize the game's kernel-general theoretical criterion for when co-located positions become locally unstable to separation. We evaluate InflEns on a corpus assembled from seven safety-related benchmarks, which demonstrates that the highest-share expert has the lowest held-out response negative log-likelihood (NLL) on approximately 90% of prompts across four kernels under a sharpened simplex representation, compared with approximately 15% after permuting allocations across prompts. We demonstrate that the method performs comparably to published learned gates without having to train an explicit gate on the experts. Because the router is fixed, we can trace harmful behavior to a single expert and retrain only that expert, which lowers HarmBench attack success from 0.51 to 0.02 while keeping instruction following. The game also gives us several controls over how the experts specialize, including the kernel choice and its parameters, the trait-space geometry, and the number of experts. Importantly, InflEns is a general framework that can be extended to any encoder and data distribution.

title: Open-Vocabulary Scene Text Recognition via Pseudo-Image Labeling and Margin Loss
description:
arXiv:2403.07518v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scene text recognition is an important and challenging task in computer vision. However, most prior works focus on recognizing pre-defined words, while there are various out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words in real-world applications.
  In this paper, we propose a novel open-vocabulary text recognition framework, Pseudo-OCR, to recognize OOV words. The key challenge in this task is the lack of OOV training data. To solve this problem, we first propose a pseudo label generation module that leverages character detection and image inpainting to produce substantial pseudo OOV training data from real-world images. Unlike previous synthetic data, our pseudo OOV data contains real characters and backgrounds to simulate real-world applications. Secondly, to reduce noises in pseudo data, we present a semantic checking mechanism to filter semantically meaningful data. Thirdly, we introduce a quality-aware margin loss to boost the training with pseudo data. Our loss includes a margin-based part to enhance the classification ability, and a quality-aware part to penalize low-quality samples in both real and pseudo data.
  Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art on eight datasets and achieves the first rank in the ICDAR2022 challenge.

title: How to fix 'Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404' (and find which page is asking for it)
description:
Scheduled broken-link and redirect checks that tell you the moment a link breaks — linkbruno.com

Open the console on almost any website and you'll eventually see it:

Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (Not Found)

It's a broken link, just not one a human clicked. The page asked the browser to fetch something (a script, a stylesheet, an image, a font, a JSON file, a source map), the browser requested it, and the server said it doesn't exist. Sometimes nothing visible breaks. Sometimes it's the reason the page has no styles, a button does nothing, or a font falls back to Times New Roman.

Here's how to track it down and fix it properly.

Step 1: get the exact URL that failed

The console line alone doesn't say much. Click through to the Network tab and reload with the tab open:

  1. Filter by status: type status-code:404 in the filter box (Chrome and Edge support this).
  2. Click the failing request. The Headers panel shows the full Request URL.
  3. The Initiator column (or tab) shows what asked for it: the HTML document, a CSS file, or a line of JavaScript.

The initiator is the important part. A 404 for /fonts/inter.woff2 initiated by main.css means the bug is a url() inside your stylesheet, not your HTML.

From the command line you can confirm it independently:

curl -sI https://www.example.com/assets/app.3f9a1c.js | head -1

Step 2: figure out why the URL is wrong

Compare the URL the browser requested with where the file actually lives. The difference almost always falls into one of these:

A relative path resolved against the wrong base. <script src="js/app.js"> on the page /blog/post-1/ requests /blog/post-1/js/app.js. It worked on the homepage and breaks on every nested page. The fix is a root-relative path (/js/app.js) or a correct <base href>. This is also the classic cause of "works locally, 404 in production" when the production site is served from a subfolder.

The app is deployed under a subpath, but the build doesn't know. If your site lives at example.com/docs/ but was built assuming /, every asset request misses the /docs prefix. Most build tools have a setting for this: base in Vite, basePath and assetPrefix in Next.js, publicPath in webpack, baseurl in Jekyll, baseURL in Hugo.

Hashed filenames from an old build. Modern builds produce files like app.3f9a1c.js. If an HTML page is cached (by a CDN, a service worker or the browser) and the deploy deleted the old hashes, the cached page asks for files that no longer exist. Keep the previous build's assets around for a while after each deploy, and make sure HTML is cached for much less time than hashed assets.

Case sensitivity. Logo.PNG on a Mac works as logo.png. On a Linux server it's a 404. Check the exact casing in the file system against the reference.

A source map that was never uploaded. A 404 for app.js.map only appears when DevTools is open, and it's harmless for users. Either deploy the maps or stop the build from adding //# sourceMappingURL comments.

favicon.ico. Browsers request /favicon.ico even if your HTML never mentions it. A 404 there is noise in logs and monitoring. Put a file there or declare an icon with <link rel="icon">.

One 404 in the console is easy to fix; the next deploy can add ten more on pages you never open. linkbruno.com checks your pages and the assets they load on a schedule, and tells you when an image, script or stylesheet starts returning 404.

Step 3: find every page with the same problem

The page where you noticed the error is rarely the only one. To find others, crawl the site and request every asset URL each page references. A quick shell version for a handful of pages:

for page in / /blog/ /pricing/; do
  curl -s "https://www.example.com$page" \
  | grep -oE '(src|href)="[^"#]+"' | cut -d'"' -f2 \
  | while read -r url; do
      case "$url" in http*) full="$url" ;; /*) full="https://www.example.com$url" ;; *) full="https://www.example.com$page$url" ;; esac
      code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "$full")
      [ "$code" = 404 ] && echo "$page -> $full"
    done
done

It's rough (it won't see assets loaded by JavaScript or referenced from CSS), but it catches the relative-path and subpath bugs quickly. For JavaScript-loaded resources, a headless browser test that listens for failed responses catches the rest:

page.on('response', r => { if (r.status() === 404) console.log(page.url(), '->', r.url()); });

Step 4: stop it shipping again

  • Fail the build on missing assets. Most bundlers already fail on a missing import. The risk is in paths written as plain strings in HTML, CSS or Markdown, so add a link check of the built output to CI.
  • Keep old hashed assets for a while. Upload new assets before switching HTML, and don't delete the previous release's assets in the same deploy.
  • Log 404s for asset paths separately. A 404 on /assets/ is a bug on your side; a 404 on /wp-login.php is a bot. Splitting them makes the real ones visible.
  • Check the live site after deploy, not just the build. CDN rules, rewrites and base paths only exist in production.

That last one is where a scheduled check helps: linkbruno.com watches the live site, so the 404s introduced by a CDN rule or a stale cache show up too, not just the ones a build would catch.

Related reading

  • Postmortem: the deploy deleted last week's JavaScript bundles, and cached pages kept asking for them
  • How to find and fix broken images on a website
  • How to fix net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT (when an ad blocker breaks your images, scripts and links)
  • The anatomy of a URL, and which part of it broke your link
  • When you delete a page on purpose, should it return 404 or 410? Let's argue about it

What's the strangest cause you've found for a console 404? Mine was a CSS file that referenced fonts with ../ and worked everywhere except the one page served from a deeper path.

title: Test-Time Compute: Why Spending More Compute at Inference Beats Training a Bigger Model
description:
For most of deep learning history, the recipe for a better model was simple: train a bigger one. More parameters, more data, more training compute, better results. That recipe still works, but it has a rival. Instead of spending compute once, up front, during training, you can spend it every time the model answers a question. Let the model think longer, try several answers, check its own work, and pick the best one. This is test-time compute, and in the last two years it has quietly become one of the most effective ways to improve a model you already have.

The intuition is older than the term. A student who spends ten minutes on a hard exam question usually does better than one who rushes the first answer that comes to mind. Language models behave the same way. A single greedy forward pass is the rushed answer. Given more time, the same model, with the same weights, can produce substantially better answers.

Two ways to spend compute at test time

Test-time compute comes in two flavours, and understanding the difference matters, because they scale differently and fail differently.

Sequential scaling makes one attempt longer. The model generates a chain of thought, revises it, backtracks from a dead end, and tries another approach inside a single long output. This is what "reasoning models" do when they produce thousands of tokens of internal deliberation before answering. The benefit is that later tokens can correct earlier ones: the model can notice a contradiction, re-derive a step, or verify a calculation.

Parallel scaling makes many attempts and selects among them. Sample N independent answers, then pick the best. The simplest selector is majority vote, known as self-consistency: if 32 samples mostly agree on an answer, that answer is probably right. A stronger selector is a verifier, a second model that scores each candidate. Best-of-N with a good verifier often beats majority vote, because the verifier can recognise a correct answer even when it is in the minority.

In practice the two combine. A common strong recipe is to generate many long chains of thought and then verify them, or to run a search procedure, such as beam search or Monte Carlo tree search, over the model's own reasoning steps.

Why it works: the maths of repeated tries

Suppose a model answers a given question correctly with probability p on a single attempt, and that attempts are roughly independent. The chance that at least one of N attempts is correct is:

1−(1−p)N

Even a modest p becomes a near-certainty as N grows. If p is 0.3, then N = 10 gives about a 97% chance that at least one sample is correct. This is the raw power behind parallel scaling. The hard part is not generating a correct answer somewhere in the pile; it is identifying it. That is why the verifier, not the sampler, is usually the bottleneck.

A useful way to think about the total compute budget is to split it between training and inference. Let C be the total compute available. Training a model of size M on D tokens costs roughly 6MD FLOPs, while answering one query with a model of size M costs roughly 2M FLOPs per generated token. Test-time compute shifts the balance: a smaller model, run for longer at inference, can match a larger model run once, at least on tasks where verification is easy.

This trade-off was made precise in a 2024 study by Snell and colleagues, who compared scaling test-time compute against scaling model parameters. On easy and medium-difficulty problems, scaling inference compute beat scaling parameters. On the hardest problems, the larger pretrained model still won, because a small model simply never samples a correct answer, no matter how many tries it gets. That asymmetry is the key result: test-time compute helps most where the base model is already close.

The verifier problem

Every selection method needs a way to judge candidates, and the choice of judge shapes everything.

Outcome verifiers check only the final answer. They are cheap and reliable when the answer is checkable, as in maths problems with a single numeric answer or code that can be run against tests. This is why test-time compute has shown its largest gains on maths and coding benchmarks.

Process verifiers score each intermediate step. They can catch a reasoning error early, before it poisons the rest of the chain, and they support search: keep the promising partial solutions, discard the rest. But they are expensive to train, because they need step-level labels, and a process verifier that is itself imperfect can systematically prefer fluent-looking but wrong reasoning.

Generative verifiers are just the same language model asked to critique its own output. This works better than it sounds, because judging is often easier than generating, but it inherits the model's blind spots. A model that cannot solve a problem usually cannot reliably tell a wrong solution from a right one either.

The practical consequence is a rule of thumb: test-time compute pays off when answers are verifiable. Maths, code, and formal logic are the sweet spots. Open-ended writing and judgement calls are not, because there is no reliable way to pick the best of N essays.

A minimal implementation

The simplest useful version of test-time compute is self-consistency with majority vote. It needs no extra model and no training. Here is the core idea in Python:

from collections import Counter

def self_consistent_answer(model, prompt, n=16, temperature=0.7):
    samples = [
        model.generate(prompt, temperature=temperature)
        for _ in range(n)
    ]
    answers = [extract_final_answer(s) for s in samples]
    most_common, count = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0]
    confidence = count / n
    return most_common, confidence

A few details matter. Sampling temperature must be high enough for diversity, but not so high that the answers degenerate; 0.6 to 0.8 is a common range. The extraction step must be reliable, since a vote is only as good as the parser that reads each sample. And the confidence estimate, the fraction of samples agreeing, is genuinely useful: it tells you when to spend more compute. If 15 of 16 samples agree, stop. If the vote is split 9 to 7, sample more, or escalate to a verifier.

Best-of-N adds a scoring step:

def best_of_n(model, verifier, prompt, n=16):
    samples = [model.generate(prompt, temperature=0.8) for _ in range(n)]
    scores = [verifier.score(prompt, s) for s in samples]
    return samples[scores.index(max(scores))]

The cost is N generations plus N verifier calls. When the verifier is much smaller than the generator, this is cheap. When the verifier is another large model call, the budget doubles, and you should ask whether the extra verification is worth more than extra samples.

When test-time compute fails

Test-time compute is not a free lunch, and its failure modes are worth naming.

Verification collapse. If the verifier is wrong, more samples make things worse, not better. Best-of-N optimises the verifier's score, and with enough samples it will find an answer that games the verifier while being wrong. This is reward hacking at inference time, and it gets worse as N grows. The fix is a better verifier or a cap on N, not more sampling.

The base model ceiling. If the model never produces a correct answer in N samples, selection cannot help. On problems far beyond the model's capability, test-time compute is wasted. The Snell study's finding, that pretraining wins on the hardest problems, is the formal version of this.

Cost and latency. Test-time compute converts a fixed training cost into a per-query cost. Generating 32 samples costs 32 times as much per answer. For a service answering millions of queries, that trade is often unaffordable, and a larger model run once may be cheaper. The economics depend on how many queries you expect to serve.

Diminishing returns. The curve 1−(1−p)N flattens fast. Going from 1 to 8 samples is usually a large gain; going from 32 to 128 is usually small. Adaptive compute, spending more only on hard or uncertain queries, captures most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

The takeaway

Test-time compute reframes the scaling question. Instead of asking how big a model you can afford to train, ask how much compute you can afford to spend on each answer. For verifiable tasks, and for models that are already close to the answer, spending compute at inference is often the cheaper and faster route to better performance. It does not replace pretraining, and it cannot rescue a model that is fundamentally out of its depth. But it is the reason the same model can look mediocre on a one-shot benchmark and impressive when you let it think.

title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.23824v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

title: Server-driven rendering eliminates client bundle bloat and streamlines web application data fetching
description:
React Server Components (RSC) represent a paradigm shift in React application architecture by allowing components to render exclusively on the server and stream serialized UI payloads to the client. This approach eliminates large dependency libraries from client JavaScript bundles, enables direct database access without separate REST or GraphQL API layers, and eliminates client-side data fetching waterfalls. However, Server Components cannot use browser APIs, React state hooks like useState, or event listeners like onClick, requiring developers to explicitly declare interactive UI elements as Client Components using the 'use client' directive.

Why This Matters

For years, single-page application (SPA) architectures forced developers to choose between heavy client-side JavaScript bundles and complex data fetching patterns. Traditional Client-Side Rendering (CSR) requires browsers to download massive JavaScript bundles before executing data requests, leading to slow Initial Page Loads and visual layout shifts. React Server Components solve this fundamental trade-off by keeping heavy dependencies on the server, running database queries alongside component rendering, and streaming minimal interactive code to the user browser.

Client-Side Bundles and Data Fetching Waterfalls

Before the introduction of Server Components, standard React applications relied on Client-Side Rendering (CSR) or Server-Side Rendering (SSR) through frameworks like Next.js Pages Router. While traditional SSR renders HTML on the server for the initial page load, it still requires the browser to download and hydrate the complete JavaScript bundle for every component on the page.

This traditional architecture introduces two primary friction points:

  • Heavy Client Bundles: Third-party libraries used for formatting dates, parsing markdown, or sanitizing HTML get shipped directly to the browser, increasing bundle size and parsing time.
  • Data Fetching Waterfalls: Parent components fetch data on the client, trigger a render, and then child components initiate their own nested network requests, causing sequential delays.

React Server Components address both issues by moving data fetching and heavy computational dependencies directly to the server infrastructure.

React Server Components Architecture: Server vs. Client Components

The core innovation of React Server Components lies in the explicit separation between server-side rendering logic and client-side interactivity. In an RSC architecture, components are Server Components by default.

Server Components vs. Client Components

Server Components execute only on the server or during build time. They never hydrate on the client and their code is never included in the browser JavaScript bundle.

Client Components are declared using the 'use client' directive at the top of a file. They are rendered on the server into HTML shells and then hydrated on the client to provide interactivity.

Feature / Capability Server Components Client Components
Execution Environment Server only (build time or request time) Server for HTML, Client for Hydration
Client Bundle Size Contribution Zero bytes Includes component code and imports
Direct Database / File System Access Supported directly Not supported (requires API endpoints)
React State and Lifecycle Hooks Not supported (no useState, useEffect) Fully supported
Event Listeners (onClick, onChange) Not supported Fully supported

The Flight Payload and Streaming

When a Server Component renders, React does not output raw HTML alone. Instead, it generates a JSON-like serialized data structure known as the RSC Payload (or Flight Payload). This stream contains:

  • The rendered UI tree structure.
  • Placeholders for Client Components and their prop data.
  • Props passed from Server Components to Client Components.

The browser receives this stream and progressively builds the DOM tree without losing active client state or resetting form inputs.

Definition: The RSC Payload (Flight Payload) is a compact, serialized representation of the Server Component tree sent over HTTP, allowing React to stream UI updates to the client dynamically.

Step-by-Step Practical Guide: Implementing RSC in Next.js App Router

Next.js App Router uses React Server Components by default. The following step-by-step example demonstrates how to fetch data directly inside a Server Component and pass reactive handlers to a Client Component.

Step 1: Create a Server Component for Direct Data Fetching

In Next.js App Router, files inside the app/ directory are Server Components by default. You can use async/await directly inside the component body.

// app/products/page.tsx (Server Component)
import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import AddToCartButton from '@/components/AddToCartButton';

interface Product {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  price: number;
}

export default async function ProductsPage() {
  // Direct database query without an extra API layer
  const products: Product[] = await db.product.findMany();

  return (
    <main className="p-6">
      <h1 className="text-2xl font-bold mb-4">Product Catalog</h1>
      <div className="grid grid-cols-3 gap-4">
        {products.map((product) => (
          <div key={product.id} className="border p-4 rounded shadow">
            <h2 className="text-lg font-semibold">{product.name}</h2>
            <p className="text-gray-600">${product.price.toFixed(2)}</p>
            {/* Passing data down to an interactive Client Component */}
            <AddToCartButton productId={product.id} />
          </div>
        ))}
      </div>
    </main>
  );
}

Step 2: Isolate Interactivity in a Client Component

Create a dedicated Client Component using the 'use client' directive to handle interactive state and click events.

// components/AddToCartButton.tsx (Client Component)
'use client';

import { useState } from 'react';

interface AddToCartButtonProps {
  productId: string;
}

export default function AddToCartButton({ productId }: AddToCartButtonProps) {
  const [isAdded, setIsAdded] = useState(false);

  const handleAddToCart = () => {
    setIsAdded(true);
    setTimeout(() => setIsAdded(false), 2000);
  };

  return (
    <button
      onClick={handleAddToCart}
      className="mt-2 px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 text-white rounded hover:bg-blue-700"
    >
      {isAdded ? 'Added to Cart!' : 'Add to Cart'}
    </button>
  );
}

Step 3: Handle Form Submissions with Server Actions

Server Actions allow Client Components or native HTML forms to invoke server-side functions without writing explicit API routes.

// app/actions.ts (Server Action)
'use server';

import { db } from '@/lib/db';
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache';

export async function createProduct(formData: FormData) {
  const name = formData.get('name') as string;
  const price = parseFloat(formData.get('price') as string);

  await db.product.create({
    data: { name, price },
  });

  revalidatePath('/products');
}

Real-World Scale, Performance Impact, and Ecosystem Adoption

Production deployments of React Server Components demonstrate measurable reductions in client bundle sizes and improved Core Web Vitals metrics.

Real-world performance benefits include:

  • Bundle Size Reductions: Enterprise applications migrating from Pages Router to App Router report significant reductions in initial JavaScript bundle size by leaving heavy rendering engines and markdown parsers on the server.
  • Elimination of Waterfall Latency: Consolidating nested data fetching into server-side parallel execution improves First Contentful Paint (FCP) and Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) scores.
  • Framework Adoption: React Server Components are fully integrated into Next.js App Router and are being adopted across frameworks such as Waku and Expo for React Native.

Trade-offs, Architectural Limitations, and Migration Challenges

Despite significant performance advantages, React Server Components introduce new architectural constraints and learning curves:

  • Third-Party Ecosystem Compatibility: Legacy React libraries that rely on React Context or DOM APIs without the 'use client' directive cannot be rendered directly inside Server Components.
  • Mental Model Shift: Developers must carefully plan where the server-client boundary sits to prevent unintentionally marking large subtrees with 'use client'.
  • Prop Serialization Restrictions: Props passed from Server Components to Client Components must be serializable JSON objects, preventing functions or complex class instances from crossing the boundary.
  • Vendor Lock-In and Server Infrastructure: Hosting RSC applications effectively requires server environments or edge runtimes capable of streaming responses, increasing infrastructure complexity compared to static SPA hosting.

Sources

  • React Documentation: React Server Components
  • Next.js Documentation: Server Components
  • React Server Components RFC
  • Vercel: Understanding React Server Components
  • Next.js Documentation: Server Actions and Mutations

title: INER: A communication protocol that separates client intentions from authoritative server events
description:
I've been developing a communication protocol called INER (Intention, Notification, Event, Response), originally designed for a multiplayer game I'm building in C++.

The problem I wanted to solve was how to organize communication between clients and servers without treating every message as a generic packet whose meaning is determined entirely by application code.

INER introduces four message types, two distinct roles, and a structured way to represent requests, results, and information.

The problem

Consider a multiplayer game where players can move, fire weapons, purchase items, and interact with the world.

These interactions don't all mean the same thing.

When a player tries to purchase an item, the client is requesting an operation. The server must evaluate whether that operation is allowed.

When the server informs players that an entity has moved, it's communicating an authoritative occurrence.

And when a client reports its FPS, it's simply providing information. It isn't requesting a change to the server's state.

All of this can be implemented with generic messages and custom handlers. However, developers still need conventions for distinguishing requests, results, and informational messages.

I wanted those distinctions to be part of the protocol itself.

Two roles: Authority and Obedient

INER defines two communicating roles:

Authority: Controls the application's internal state, evaluates requested operations, and communicates authoritative information.

Obedient: Requests operations from the Authority, sends informational messages, and receives authoritative events and results.

In a typical multiplayer game, the server acts as the Authority and the clients act as Obedients.

The important distinction is that an Obedient can request something, but the Authority decides whether it actually happens.

The four INER message types

  1. Intention (Obedient → Authority)

An Intention represents an action that the Obedient wants the Authority to perform.

Examples:

  • A player requests to move.
  • A player attempts to fire a weapon.
  • A player tries to use an item.
  • A client requests to join a match.

Sending an Intention doesn't mean the action has happened. The Authority must evaluate it.

Header:

  • "size" — 2 bytes.
  • "type_id" — 2 bytes.
  • "correlationId" — 2 bytes.

Payload: Variable-length data describing the requested operation.

For example, a movement Intention could contain the movement information that the server needs to evaluate.

The correlation identifier allows the corresponding Response to be associated with the original request.

  1. Notification (Obedient → Authority)

A Notification communicates information without requesting a change to the Authority's internal state.

Examples:

  • Reporting measured network latency.
  • Sending client FPS information.
  • Reporting client-side diagnostic data.

Unlike an Intention, a Notification doesn't request an operation or expect a Response.

Header:

  • "size" — 2 bytes.
  • "type_id" — 2 bytes.

Payload: Optional, containing application-defined information.

For example, a client could periodically send a Notification containing its measured latency.

This distinction prevents informational messages from being treated as operations requiring authorization.

  1. Event (Authority → Obedient)

An Event communicates an occurrence or state update from the Authority.

Examples:

  • A player joins the game.
  • An entity moves.
  • A projectile spawns.
  • A match begins.

An Event communicates something authoritative rather than requesting permission for it to happen.

Header:

  • "size" — 2 bytes.
  • "type_id" — 2 bytes.

Payload: Optional, containing information about the occurrence.

For example, after processing a player's movement, the server could send an Event informing relevant clients about the entity's new position.

Unlike a Response, an Event doesn't need to correspond to a particular Intention.

  1. Response (Authority → Obedient)

A Response communicates the result of a specific Intention.

For example, after receiving an Intention to fire a weapon, the server can respond according to the outcome of that operation.

INER defines four response statuses:

Approved (0): The requested operation was fully approved.

Example: A player requests to move, and the server accepts the movement.

Denied (1): The requested operation was rejected.

Example: A player attempts to fire a weapon without sufficient ammunition.

Partially Approved (2): The requested operation was only partially applied.

Example: A player requests an operation involving several items, but the server can fulfill only part of it.

Failure (3): An internal error occurred while processing the request.

Example: The server encounters an unexpected processing error.

A Failure doesn't necessarily mean the operation was denied. It means the Authority couldn't process it successfully.

Base Response header:

  • "size" — 2 bytes.
  • "correlationId" — 2 bytes.
  • "status" — 1 byte.

The base header occupies 5 bytes.

Denied and Partially Approved responses use an extended header containing an additional 2-byte "reasonCode", making it 7 bytes.

Payload rules:

  • Approved: No payload.
  • Denied: No payload in the recommended format; includes a reason code.
  • Partially Approved: May include an application-defined payload and includes a reason code.
  • Failure: No payload.

This allows the application to distinguish a rejected operation from an internal processing failure, or a completely approved operation from a partially applied one.

Binary message representation

INER uses compact binary headers.

Every message contains a header, followed by a payload when applicable.

The "size" field represents the total message size, including its header and payload.

For messages sent by the Obedient, the size is represented directly.

For messages sent by the Authority, the first field also encodes whether the message is an Event or a Response.

Its least significant bit distinguishes the two:

  • "0" identifies an Event.
  • "1" identifies a Response.

The remaining bits encode the message size.

This allows the receiving implementation to distinguish these message categories without introducing a separate message-category field.

Message types and payload formats are defined by the application using INER.

What does INER actually solve?

The objective isn't to replace TCP, UDP, or existing networking transports.

It's to provide consistent semantics for application-level communication.

INER helps distinguish:

  • What a client wants to happen.
  • What information a client wants to report.
  • What the authoritative server says happened.
  • What result the server produced when evaluating a request.

It also standardizes request correlation and the representation of different operation outcomes.

This doesn't eliminate application-specific logic.

For example, INER doesn't determine whether a player has enough ammunition to fire a weapon. That decision still belongs to the server.

The protocol simply provides a structured way to communicate the request and its outcome.

Independent of the transport

INER doesn't define sockets, connections, threads, or how messages are physically transmitted.

It defines their semantic structure.

I've implemented INER in LightnerX, my open-source C++17 networking library for multiplayer applications.

LightnerX uses Valve's GameNetworkingSockets for transport and provides components for connection management, message interpretation, callbacks, and message delivery.

The intention is to keep the communication model conceptually separate from the underlying network transport.

Source code: https://github.com/pietroth/LightnerX

Documentation: https://pietroth.github.io/LightnerX-docs/

I'm still developing and refining the project, and I'd appreciate technical feedback on the protocol's design.

Do you think explicitly distinguishing intentions, notifications, events, and responses at the protocol level provides useful architectural structure, or would you prefer a generic messaging system where all these conventions are implemented exclusively in application code?

title: PostgreSQL 19 removes the MultiXact members wall. Reclamation still waits for template0.
description:
Between May 10 and May 17, 2025, Metronome had four outages that each lasted over an hour. Their dashboards showed "less than 50% utilization" of the configured MultiXact ID threshold (autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age = 400 million) on an Aurora PostgreSQL 13.18 cluster of more than 30 TB. The limit they actually hit was MultiXact member space. In their words, "PostgreSQL does not expose metrics for member space consumption". (Metronome RCA)

Member space is addressed by a 32-bit offset in every release through 18. PostgreSQL 19 widens it to 64 bits (commit bd8d9c9bd: "This eliminates MultiXactOffset wraparound and the 2^32 limit on the total number of multixid members. Multixids are still limited to 2^31").

I rebuilt the failure from scratch on PostgreSQL 18.7 and on 19.0, released on 19 November 2026, with 19 RC2 as a cross-check. 19.0 reproduced every RC2 count I reran exactly. Short version:

  • The member-offset stop is gone in 19; the 2^31 MultiXact ID stop is not. In a fast-forwarded lab cluster 18.7 refused writes with multixact "members" limit exceeded; 19.0 went past 2^32 member offsets without an error (3/3 runs on each of 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0).
  • The burn rate did not change. Same members per lock and the same member bytes on disk; only the offsets area doubles (8 bytes per MultiXact instead of 4).
  • pg_upgrade to 19 keeps one member per MultiXact. How much that shrinks depends on your lock pattern; in my k=64 runs on 19.0 the whole pg_multixact directory went from 107 MB to 8.2 MB (13x), the same as on RC2.
  • Reclamation did not change, and it is cluster-wide. On a fresh cluster where template0 had never been frozen, none of VACUUM, VACUUM (FREEZE) or vacuumdb --all --freeze freed a byte of member space on 18.7, 19 RC2 or 19.0, because truncation waits for the oldest datminmxid of every database and vacuumdb skips template0. One idle session that had taken a row lock before the workload, in a different database, stopped reclamation for the whole cluster.

FACT marks what I measured, INTERPRETATION what I conclude from it, and "source" what I read in the PostgreSQL code. Everything was measured on one VM; see "Method and limits" and "Reproduce". Scripts and raw data: https://github.com/firfircelik/pg-multixact-lab

1. What a MultiXact member is

When one transaction locks a row, PostgreSQL writes that transaction's ID into the row's xmax. When a second transaction locks the same row while the first is still open (SELECT ... FOR SHARE, or the FOR KEY SHARE lock that a foreign-key check takes on the parent row), the row needs to point at a set of transactions. That set is a MultiXact. Its ID goes into xmax; the list of transaction IDs (the members) is appended to pg_multixact/members. MultiXacts are immutable: when a third locker arrives, PostgreSQL creates a new MultiXact and copies in every member that is still running (plus a committed updater, if there is one), then adds the newcomer (MultiXactIdExpand in multixact.c).

So while lockers overlap, every new locker pays for all the others again.

2. Growth: member cost is quadratic in overlap

Setup. One row; k sessions lock it one after another, all transactions stay open, then all commit. 1,000 such episodes per run, 6 values of k, two lock types (explicit FOR SHARE and an FK insert into a child table), 3 repetitions, 18.7 and 19 RC2, fresh cluster per run, shuffled order (72 runs), then the same 36 cells on 19.0 the day it shipped. 108 runs.

Theory. Locker 2 creates a MultiXact with 2 members, locker 3 one with 3, ..., locker k one with k. Per episode: k-1 MultiXacts and k(k+1)/2 - 1 members. Metronome's RCA gives the same example: "locking a row with 5 transactions creates 4 MultiXacts containing a total of 14 members".

Result (FACT). The MultiXact count matched the formula exactly in 108/108 runs. The member count matched exactly in 36/36 runs on 19 RC2 and 36/36 on 19.0 (every count and file size identical to RC2), and was formula + 1 in 36/36 runs on 18.7 (18.7 skips offset 0 on the first allocation).

overlapping lockers k MultiXacts / episode members / episode
2 1 2
8 7 35
32 31 527
64 63 2,079

Two more facts from the same runs:

  • Each member costs about 5.0 bytes in pg_multixact/members on both versions (2,079,000 members = 10,412,032 bytes = 10.4 MB). So 2^31 members, where 18.x starts aggressive anti-wraparound work, is about 10.7 GB (10 GiB), and the 2^32 stop is about 21.5 GB (20 GiB). The PostgreSQL 18 docs give the same scale: "about 10GB" and "about 20GB" (routine vacuuming, 18).
  • 19 (RC2 and 19.0) writes 8 bytes per MultiXact in pg_multixact/offsets instead of 4 (507,904 vs 253,952 bytes for 63,000 MultiXacts). Same member bytes; offsets double.

Source note: a backend reuses a cached MultiXact when it needs exactly the same member set again (mXactCacheGetBySet in multixact.c). Repeating the same few sessions in the same order is therefore cheap; damage needs fresh combinations, which is what concurrent short writers produce.

3. Growth under real concurrency: the pause inside your transaction

Setup. pgbench, 20 s per run, transaction = BEGIN; INSERT INTO child(parent_id) ...; [\sleep 5 ms]; COMMIT;. Factors: 8/32/64 clients, 1 or 16 hot parent rows, 0 or 5 ms pause inside the transaction, both versions, 3 reps. 72 runs, fsync off (see Method). One run (64 clients, 16 hot rows, 5 ms, 18.7, rep 1) followed a 286 s box suspension and ran at half speed; I voided it and reran it under the load rule (242,906 transactions, 4.53 members per transaction, in line with its siblings).

clients hot parents pause in txn members / committed txn (18.7, median, fsync off)
8 1 0 ms 3.0
64 1 0 ms 9.6
8 1 5 ms 7.7
64 1 5 ms 60.7
64 16 5 ms 4.6
64 16 0 ms 1.5

Durable commits (control, FACT). I repeated the two 64-client, 1-hot-row cells with fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes on (3 reps, both versions). With the 5 ms pause: 58.2 members per transaction on 18.7 and 58.3 on 19 RC2 (medians; fsync off: 60.7 and 60.6), at about 670k members/s. Without the pause: 20.8 and 21.4 (fsync off: 9.6 and 9.5), more than double. The pause cell is stable. The no-pause cell is not: commit latency itself keeps transactions open longer, which creates overlap (INTERPRETATION). Treat every number in this section as lab-relative.

FACT. With 64 clients and a 5 ms pause inside each transaction, each insert cost about 61 members. 19 RC2 was within run-to-run noise of 18.7 in every cell (one 19 RC2 run of the 64/1/5 ms cell was about 10% slower than its siblings; medians are reported). This grid, the cross-database grid (section 5) and the mitigations (section 7) ran on 18.7 and 19 RC2; nothing in multixact.c or ri_triggers.c changed between RC2 and 19.0.

INTERPRETATION. Each insert joins a MultiXact that already holds every other open inserter, so a pause inside the transaction (an HTTP call, a slow ORM flush, a sleep in a backfill) multiplies the cost. At the 741k members/s this box sustained with fsync off (about 670k with durable commits), an 18.x cluster would reach the 2^31 point in about 48 minutes and the 2^32 stop in about 1.6 hours if nothing reclaimed. Treat that as a ceiling for this box, not a production estimate; your rate is your transactions per second times members per transaction. The shape matches Metronome's description: a backfill with FK-heavy inserts on a few parent rows, running alongside other write-heavy jobs.

4. Reclamation: what actually frees member space

Two cluster-wide floors decide what can be released (source: multixact.c, vacuum.c):

  • Truncation floor. Member files are deleted only up to the minimum datminmxid over every database, template0 included.
  • Freezing floor. Vacuum cannot freeze MultiXacts newer than the oldest value in OldestMemberMXactId[] / OldestVisibleMXactId[]. A backend sets its entry when it first locks, updates or deletes a row in a transaction. The arrays have no database dimension.

Setup. k=32, 4,000 episodes in database app (124,000 MultiXacts, 2,108,000 members, 10,559,488 bytes = 10.6 MB of members). Then one of seven actions. 3 reps each on 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0, 63 runs. In the two "locker" arms a session in the same database app took a FOR SHARE lock before the workload and stayed idle in transaction.

action after the workload members after oldestMultiXid
nothing 10.6 MB 1
VACUUM parent 10.6 MB 1
VACUUM (FREEZE) parent 10.6 MB 1
vacuumdb --all --freeze 10.6 MB 1
same, with an idle-in-transaction locker 10.6 MB, also after the locker ended and vacuumdb ran again 1
autovacuum, autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age = 10000 0.86 MB (at most 1.65 MB in post-workload samples) 114,391 to 116,282
same, with an idle-in-transaction locker 10.6 MB for 120 s; 74 kB at the first poll (2 s) after it ended 1, then 124,001

Identical on 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0. Sizes are decimal (1 MB = 10^6 bytes, 1 kB = 10^3 bytes).

FACT (from pg_database). After vacuumdb --all --freeze, postgres, template1 and app moved to datminmxid 124,001. template0 stayed at 1, and so did oldestMultiXid.

Source. vacuumdb skips databases with datallowconn = false (vacuumdb.c), which is template0. Autovacuum does not check datallowconn and processes template0 once its MultiXact age passes the effective autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age. You can also do it by hand: ALTER DATABASE template0 ALLOW_CONNECTIONS true, VACUUM (FREEZE) in it, then set it back.

FACT (autovacuum arm). With the lab's 10,000 freeze age, the members directory was at most 1.65 MB in the samples taken right after the workload; there were no samples during it. All 9 runs ended at my 180 s poll limit with the oldest MultiXact about 8,000 to 10,000 behind the next one. At the end template0 held the lowest datminmxid in 5 of 9 runs, postgres in 2 (both 19 RC2), and template1 and app in one 19.0 run each. Two 19.0 runs in this section (one autovacuum, one autovacuum + locker) had a 7-minute box suspension inside the poll window. I kept them, flagged them and reran both: 0.86 MB, and 10.6 MB while pinned with 74 kB at the first poll after release, the same as every other run. INTERPRETATION: with a low freeze age, autovacuum keeps member space small during the workload, but template0 or another database still sets the floor.

INTERPRETATION. A fresh lab cluster is the extreme case: template0 had never been frozen. On a long-lived cluster template0 has been frozen before, but the rule is the same. Member files are released when the laggiest database, often template0, is processed. Manual VACUUM FREEZE on your hot table is necessary, not sufficient.

The blocker (FACT). In the "autovacuum + locker" arm, one session that took a FOR SHARE lock before the workload and went idle in transaction kept oldestMultiXid at 1 for the full 120 s while autovacuum was running. Vacuums meanwhile logged WARNING: cutoff for freezing multixacts is far in the past. In the lab that warning fired immediately because I set the freeze age to 10,000. At default settings (400 million, lowered on 18.x only once members pass 2^31) it fires only once the oldest MultiXact is past the effective freeze age, so treat it as a late alarm, not an early one.

5. Cross-database pinning

Metronome's RCA states that "even a single long-running transaction holding an old MultiXact alive prevents the vacuum from reclaiming newer, unused member spaces". It does not say whether that transaction must be in the same database. I tested that.

Setup. Same workload in app (k=32, 4,000 episodes), autovacuum on with autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age = 10000 so reclamation normally keeps up. Before the workload starts, a second session in a different database (other) opens one of four things. Poll for 90 s, release, poll 90 s. 5 arms, 3 reps, both versions, 30 runs.

session in database other, opened before the workload members after 90 s oldestMultiXid after release
none (control) 0.86 MB about 115,000 n/a
SELECT ... FOR SHARE on one of its own rows, then idle in transaction 10.6 MB 1 74 kB at the first poll (3 s)
open transaction with an assigned xid (pg_current_xact_id()), no row lock 0.60 to 0.86 MB about 115,000 same
REPEATABLE READ snapshot after a read, no row lock 0.60 to 0.86 MB about 115,000 same
row lock, but idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 10s 0.60 to 0.86 MB about 115,000 the timeout ended the session about 10 s in, during the workload

Identical on 18.7 and 19 RC2 (6/6 runs per arm).

FACT. A session that took a FOR SHARE row lock in another database before the workload pinned MultiXact reclamation for the whole cluster. A plain open xid or a repeatable-read snapshot in another database did not pin it in my runs. With the 10 s timeout the session was killed during the workload and member space never accumulated.

Source-based extension. MultiXactIdSetOldestMember is called when a transaction first locks, updates or deletes a row (heapam.c), and records the next MultiXact ID at that moment in a shared array with no database dimension. By that code, any row lock, UPDATE or DELETE sets the same pin, and the pin covers every MultiXact created after the session took it. I only measured FOR SHARE.

INTERPRETATION. On a shared cluster, a forgotten psql session in a reporting database that ran SELECT ... FOR SHARE (or, by the source, FOR UPDATE) and stayed open can stall member reclamation for the busy OLTP database next to it. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ended that in 6/6 runs. It does not cover prepared transactions, which keep their pin across restarts until COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED.

6. The danger zone: 18.7 vs 19 at the members stop

Reaching 2^32 real members takes about 21 GB and hours. I used a lab shortcut, so weigh the result accordingly:

  1. Pin the oldest MultiXact with an orphaned prepared transaction (prepared transactions survive restarts).
  2. Clean shutdown, then pg_resetwal -O moves the next member offset to 4,274,017,280, a segment boundary 20,897,664 members below the 18.7 stop point (2^32 - 52,352). The skipped range holds no data, but the server's limit arithmetic sees about 4.27 billion members in use.
  3. Run k=64 hot-row episodes on fresh rows until error, or until 24M members past 2^32.
18.7 (3 runs + 1 control) 19.0 (3 runs) 19 RC2 (3 runs)
outcome ERROR: multixact "members" limit exceeded after 20,897,624 members no error; next offset 4,319,755,280, past 2^32 same as 19.0
warnings before the error 31,729 occurrences of must be vacuumed before N more multixact members are used none of that kind none of that kind
vacuumdb --all --freeze while the pin is held (control) exit code 0, writes still failing n/a n/a
after ROLLBACK PREPARED + vacuumdb --all --freeze exit code 0, writes still failing, template0 datminmxid still 1 n/a n/a
writes back 12.2 to 15.3 s later in the 3 runs, 6.2 s in the control, once autovacuum had processed template0 n/a n/a

Details:

  • 18.7 stopped 40 members before the source-derived stop point (20,897,664): the next MultiXact needed 57 members and only 39 were left. The DETAIL line reads "This command would create a multixact with 57 members, but the remaining space is only enough for 39 members". After the first error the next offset still advanced by 35 members, so smaller MultiXacts kept being created. INTERPRETATION: small lockers keep working while the FK-heavy batch fails, which can make the incident look intermittent.
  • The warnings start 20 segments (1,047,040 members) before the stop and repeat for every new MultiXact. With k=64 that is about 1,047,040 / 2,079 x 63 = 31,728 MultiXacts, so the count depends on MultiXact size, not on time.
  • On 19, pg_get_multixact_stats() (new in 19, commit 97b101776) reported num_members = 4,319,755,279 and members_size of 21.6 GB, while the directory held 229 MB: only about 45.7 million members were really written, the rest is the fast-forward gap. On a real cluster that function is the metric Metronome said they did not have.

Fast-forward artifact. In the first runs on both versions the gap made MultiXact 1 look like it had about 4.27 billion members. Every VACUUM of the table holding it failed (18.7: invalid memory alloc request size; 19 RC2 and 19.0: MultiXact 1 has too many members), so those runs say nothing about vacuum behaviour under a pin. The control run fixed that: the gap sits behind MultiXact 2 on a table that is dropped before the test, all probes use fresh rows, and vacuumdb exit codes are recorded. The control logged 0 artifact errors and reproduced the same stop point, the same 31,729 warnings, and writes failing until template0 was processed.

7. Mitigations, measured

Setup. The worst cell from section 3 (64 clients, 1 hot parent, 5 ms pause inside the transaction) against four changes, one at a time. 20 s, 3 reps, both versions, 30 runs, fsync off. For a backfill of fixed size the useful metric is members per inserted row: total member cost = rows x members per row.

change members / row (18.7, median) rows / s members / s
baseline 59.7 12,076 721,155
cap the pool at 16 clients 14.9 2,979 44,489
no pause inside the transaction 10.6 71,299 750,496
10 child rows per transaction 6.1 118,457 727,444
spread over 16 hot parent keys 4.6 12,032 55,693

The baseline is a separate run set of the section 3 worst cell (59.7 here vs 60.7 there). 19 RC2 was within 1% of 18.7 on members per row in every arm; on members per second the largest gap was 2.05% (batch10: 727,444 vs 742,350).

FACT. Every change cut member cost per row by 4x to 13x in this lab. Batching and removing the pause also made the job faster, so the member rate stayed at about 0.72 to 0.75 million per second. Spreading the hot key was the only change that cut both cost per row and rate without costing throughput. The no-pause arm is the one most sensitive to fsync (in section 3 its members per transaction doubled with durable commits), so its advantage here is likely overstated; read all of these as lab-relative.

INTERPRETATION. A backfill of 100 million rows costs about 6.0 billion members at baseline and 0.6 billion batched. If reclamation is pinned, the batched job still reaches the stop after a similar wall-clock time; it just gets about 10x more rows done first. For a backfill: batch children per parent, keep slow work out of the transaction, and rate-limit on members, not on rows. On 18.x, next_multi_offset growth per minute is the number to throttle on.

8. Upgrading 18 to 19: pg_upgrade compacts member space

19 stores offsets as 64-bit, so pg_upgrade rewrites pg_multixact (multixact_rewrite.c at REL_19_0). It reads "only one member from each multixid: the one updating one, or if there was no update, arbitrarily the first locking xid", because lock-only members do not matter once no transaction can be running across the upgrade.

Setup. 18.7 cluster, k=64 hot-row episodes (1,000 / 10,000 / 30,000), no vacuum. The upgrade rewrites every MultiXact in the old cluster's [oldest, next) range; in these runs only the last MultiXact of each episode is still referenced by a row. pg_upgrade --link to 19 RC2 (and, for 10,000 episodes, to 19.0), then re-lock up to 2,000 of the old rows on 19 with 4 sessions (all 1,000 in the smallest run) and compare row counts and sums. 3 reps. Controls: 18.7 to 18.7 with 1,000 episodes, 18.7 to 19 RC2 with an empty cluster, and one 10,000-episode run with amcheck.

episodes members before (18.7) members before members after (19) members after pg_upgrade --link time
0 (control) 0 8 kB 0 8 kB 1.58 to 1.62 s
1,000 2,079,000 10.4 MB 63,000 0.32 MB 1.62 to 1.66 s
10,000 20,790,000 104 MB 630,000 3.2 MB 1.67 to 1.77 s
30,000 62,370,000 312 MB 1,890,000 9.5 MB 1.95 to 2.01 s
10,000, to 19.0 20,790,000 104 MB 630,000 3.2 MB 1.86 to 1.97 s

Rows without a version label are 18.7 to 19 RC2. All reps gave identical member counts and sizes, and 19.0 matched RC2 byte for byte (members 3,162,112 bytes, offsets 5,046,272 bytes, 10,010 rows matched after re-locking). The 19.0 upgrades took about 0.2 s longer than RC2 at the same size; I ran no 19.0 empty-cluster baseline and these runs were not load-gated, so I do not attribute that to the version.

FACT.

  • After the upgrade the member count equals the MultiXact count. For this workload that is a 33x reduction in members, which is (k+2)/2 at k=64, the members per MultiXact of a staircase episode. Your ratio is your own members per MultiXact; in my concurrent runs (section 3) the per-cell median ranged from 2.1 to 60.7.
  • The offsets area doubles (8 bytes per MultiXact), so the whole pg_multixact directory shrank less than members alone: 319.9 MB to 24.6 MB (13x) at 30,000 episodes on RC2, and 106.6 MB to 8.2 MB (13x) at 10,000 episodes on both RC2 and 19.0.
  • 18.7 to 18.7 kept all 2,079,001 members (1.55 to 1.58 s): the compaction comes from the 18 to 19 rewrite, not from pg_upgrade as such.
  • The rewrite added 0.0 to 0.4 s over the empty-cluster baseline, growing with size.
  • Re-locking worked and row counts and sums matched (1,010 / 10,010 / 30,010 rows). In the 10,000-episode control, amcheck (verify_heapam and bt_index_check) reported no corruption before the upgrade, after it, and after all 10,010 rows were re-locked by 4 sessions.

INTERPRETATION. If you are on 18.x with a large pg_multixact/members, the upgrade resets member usage to one per MultiXact in the retained range. It is not an emergency tool (it needs downtime and a clean shutdown), but it is worth knowing when you plan the 19 migration.

9. What I would do on Monday

Three monitoring queries (not benchmarked; on managed platforms, check privileges first):

-- Which database holds the MultiXact floor (template0 included)
SELECT datname, datallowconn, datminmxid, mxid_age(datminmxid) AS mxid_age
FROM pg_database ORDER BY mxid_age(datminmxid) DESC;

-- PostgreSQL 19+: returns NULLs unless the role has pg_read_all_stats
SELECT num_mxids, num_members, members_size, oldest_multixact FROM pg_get_multixact_stats();

-- Pinning candidates, cluster-wide (pg_stat_activity cannot show who holds a row lock)
SELECT pid, datname, usename, state, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, backend_xid, left(query, 80)
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state LIKE 'idle in transaction%' ORDER BY xact_start;
SELECT gid, database, owner, prepared FROM pg_prepared_xacts ORDER BY prepared;

The full set of seven queries, including per-table MultiXact age, member consumption since the last checkpoint and the members directory size, is in monitoring.sql.

On 18.x and earlier:

  1. Monitor member space, not just MultiXact age: the members directory size or next_multi_offset (about 5 bytes per member; 10.7 GB is the aggressive-vacuum point, 21.5 GB the stop), plus mxid_age(datminmxid) for every database including template0. [measured: sections 2, 4]
  2. Alert on long idle-in-transaction sessions and orphaned prepared transactions in every database, not just the busy one. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout; it does not end prepared transactions. [measured: section 5]
  3. Grep for cutoff for freezing multixacts is far in the past and must be vacuumed before ... multixact members. [source: vacuum.c, multixact.c; a late signal at default settings]
  4. Shape writes: no network calls or sleeps inside transactions that insert children of hot parents; batch children per transaction; spread hot keys. In my runs these cut members per row by 4x to 13x. [measured: section 7]
  5. Recovery order when it hits: end the pinning session or ROLLBACK PREPARED, then get every database including template0 past the old MultiXacts: wait for autovacuum, or temporarily ALTER DATABASE template0 ALLOW_CONNECTIONS true, run VACUUM (FREEZE) in it, and set it back. In my 18.7 runs autovacuum alone restored writes 6 to 15 s after the pin was released. [measured on 18.7: section 6; manual template0 path documented, not run]
symptom check action
multixact "members" limit exceeded (18.x) pg_prepared_xacts, idle-in-transaction sessions in every database end the pin, then freeze every database including template0
members directory keeps growing after VACUUM (FREEZE) mxid_age(datminmxid) per database the lowest database (often template0) needs processing
oldest_multi_xid does not move while autovacuum runs sessions open since before the growth started end them or set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
high member rate during a backfill members per inserted row batch, remove pauses inside transactions, spread hot keys

On 19:

  • The member-offset stop is gone, so a member blow-up turns from "writes rejected" into "disk keeps growing at about 5 bytes per member". MultiXact IDs are still limited to 2^31, and that wraparound stop still exists. Points 1 to 4 still apply, and pg_get_multixact_stats() makes point 1 a single query.
  • Member pressure no longer launches anti-wraparound vacuum in 19 (commit 6aa2cefe11). It only makes vacuums that run anyway freeze more aggressively, scaled linearly from 2,000,000,000 members (MULTIXACT_MEMBER_LOW_THRESHOLD) to 4,000,000,000 (MULTIXACT_MEMBER_HIGH_THRESHOLD). With autovacuum disabled, nothing comes to clean up members for you.
  • 19 raises the MultiXact and XID wraparound warning distance to 100 million (commit 48f11bfa0).

Method and limits

  • Native builds of 18.7, 19 RC2 and 19.0 from the official tarballs, sha256 verified; gcc 14.2, Debian, Linux 6.12, 8 vCPU (the hypervisor reports "Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor"), 15 GiB RAM, virtio disk of unknown media, single VM, no Docker.
  • fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes off; autovacuum off unless the arm says otherwise. These settings do not affect deterministic counts (sections 2, 4, 5, 6 and 8 member and MultiXact counts, bytes per member). They can affect concurrency-dependent results (sections 3 and 7: members per transaction or row, and every rate), because commit latency changes how long lockers overlap. The fsync-on control in section 3 shows how much.
  • Counts come from pg_controldata after CHECKPOINT, file sizes in pg_multixact/, and pg_get_multixact_stats() on 19. Sizes are decimal (MB = 10^6 bytes) unless marked GiB.
  • Fresh cluster per run, shuffled run order with recorded seeds, 3 repetitions. The cross-database, mitigation and upgrade grids, and the control runs, were added after the original protocol; the upgrade and limit runs used a fixed order.
  • A load and suspension rule (load average below 2 before each run, void and rerun if wall-clock time and VM uptime disagree by more than 5%) was applied to the control runs only. Earlier runs had no such gate; I voided one run that followed a suspension (section 3).
  • The VM was reset once during the study. One limit-test attempt was cut off and discarded (raw file kept); the reclamation results were restored from a checksummed backup written before the reset.
  • The members-limit test fast-forwards the counter with pg_resetwal. The limit logic is real; the 4 billion members are not.
  • PostgreSQL 19.0 (tarball on ftp.postgresql.org on 19 Nov 2026, sha256 a89fd70e...e692d verified) was built and rerun the same afternoon for sections 2, 4, 6 and 8. Sections 3, 5 and 7 and the fsync-on control are from 19 RC2 (released 2026-11-12); between RC2 and 19.0 nothing changed in multixact.c, ri_triggers.c or the pg_upgrade MultiXact code. The 19.0 limit runs took 196 to 214 s for the same 22,000 episodes that took 176 to 179 s on RC2; that is wall time on a shared, ungated box, not a measured version difference.

Reproduce

Everything above comes from Python scripts that build fresh clusters on unix sockets, run one cell, and append one JSON line per run. The layout is:

scripts/      lab.py (cluster harness), grid_*.py, limit_ff.py, upgrade_rewrite.py, controls.py, analyze.py
results/      one .jsonl per grid, results/controls/ for the control runs
PROTOCOL.md   design, seeds, deviations, load rule, reset timeline

To rerun on your own machine: clone the repo, build PostgreSQL 18.7 and 19.0 (and 19 RC2 for the comparison) into install/pg-<version> with scripts/build_pg.sh (it includes contrib/amcheck for the upgrade control), create a Python venv with psycopg and matplotlib, then run for example python scripts/grid_growth.py g1 18.7,19.0, the other grid_*.py scripts, and python scripts/analyze.py. PROTOCOL.md lists every grid, its seed and its arguments.

Scripts, raw JSONL, charts and PROTOCOL.md: https://github.com/firfircelik/pg-multixact-lab (MIT; snapshot used for this article: commit 45f8d9d). Build steps, tarball checksums and the per-grid commands are in its README.

Sources

All accessed 2026-11-19. Code links are pinned to tags REL_18_7 (f5c41f6681c9) and REL_19_0 (5c839a2a08b9).

  • 64-bit member offsets, commit bd8d9c9bd: https://git.postgresql.org/gitweb/?p=postgresql.git;a=commit;h=bd8d9c9bd
  • Member pressure no longer signals the autovacuum launcher, commit 6aa2cefe11: https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commit/6aa2cefe11841a6bff4dab65860c1a12a3e57146
  • pg_get_multixact_stats(), commit 97b101776: https://git.postgresql.org/gitweb/?p=postgresql.git;a=commit;h=97b101776
  • 100M warning limit, commit 48f11bfa0: https://git.postgresql.org/gitweb/?p=postgresql.git;a=commit;h=48f11bfa0
