title: Three of our four product demos bleed off the right edge of a phone on purpose, and that puts every price off screen
description:
Notifio's home page does not show screenshots of the desktop app. It shows four animated mockups that act out the app working: a rental site with new listings appearing, the tray app finding one, the alert email arriving, and an auto-reply being sent. I have written about how they are built and about what 997 lines of them cost.

What I had never done is look at them on a phone with a ruler. So I loaded all 38 pages of the site at 320, 360, 390 and 430 CSS pixels and measured every element's right edge against the viewport.

The site is fine. The demos are not. 

width   pages scrolling sideways   elements past the right edge   scrollable containers
 320            1 of 38                        112                         0
 360            0 of 38                         90                         0
 390            0 of 38                         85                         0
 430            0 of 38                         35                         0

No page has a horizontal scrollbar except one, which I will come back to. But "no horizontal scrollbar" is not the same as "nothing is off screen". It can also mean the overflow is clipped, and clipped is worse: a reader who scrolls sideways at least gets to see the content.

Here is the markup responsible. The comment above it reads "mobile: left + bottom padding, bleeds right", so this was a decision rather than an accident:

<div className={`w-full md:w-[560px] ...`}>
  <div className="overflow-hidden md:overflow-visible md:px-6 md:py-10">
    <div className="pl-6 pb-8 pt-0 md:pl-0 md:pb-0 min-w-[480px] md:min-w-0">
      {demo}
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

Three of the four demos render through that wrapper. A 480 pixel minimum width inside an overflow-hidden box means the mockup keeps its desktop proportions on a phone and runs off the edge, which is a reasonable visual idea: a window that continues past the screen reads as a real window rather than a squashed one.

Measured, it comes out like this:

viewport   mockup box        visible    lost
   320     x=17 → x=497      63.1%     177px
   390     x=17 → x=497      77.7%     107px
   430     x=17 → x=497      86.0%      67px
   540     x=17 → x=523     100.0%       0

The min-w-[480px] only bites while the available width is under about 504 pixels. Above that w-full wins and nothing is lost. Below it, which is every phone held in portrait, between a fifth and a third of each mockup is cut off and there is no way to see it: the parent is overflow-hidden, not overflow-x-auto, and across all 38 pages at all four widths there is not one horizontally scrollable container on the site.

What is in the missing 107 pixels

This is the part that turned a styling note into something worth fixing. I sampled the three mockups every three seconds for 18 seconds, so that the animation loops could not hide anything, and recorded the position of every price and every button at 390 pixels.

element                       left   right    at 390px
listings demo  €895/mo         420     467    off screen
               €1,150/mo       413     467    off screen
               €780/mo         421     467    off screen
               €1,650/mo       411     467    off screen
email demo     "View" button   ~410    467    off screen
               "Mon 09:15"     ~415    467    off screen
auto-reply     "Send"/"Sent"   408     467    off screen
hero demo      "Stop" button   282     336    visible

Every price in the mockup of a rental site is off screen. The call to action in the mockup of our alert email is off screen. The send button in the mockup of the auto-reply is off screen. They are all right-aligned inside a 480 pixel window, so they cluster at x=467 and the viewport ends at 390.

The page is selling one idea, which is that you find out about a listing before anybody else does. On a phone, the mockup of the listing has no price in it, and the two mockups of us acting on the listing have no visible action. The hero demo escapes because it is the one that is not in the bleed wrapper: it is 358 pixels wide at this viewport and its "Stop" button sits comfortably inside the screen.

The best detail is inside the email mockup, because part of it was already fixed. The macOS notification card that slides in over the mail window is positioned top-3 left-3 md:left-auto md:right-3: on a desktop it sits at the top right of the window, and under 768 pixels it jumps to the left edge instead.

notification card at 1280px    x=668 → x=888    visible
notification card at  390px    x=54  → x=274    visible
"View" button at      390px    x=410 → x=467    off screen

Both of those are in the same component. Somebody hit this problem once, solved it for the one element they were looking at with a single Tailwind prefix, and never asked what else in the same window was sitting at x=467. I know that, because I am somebody.

The one page that does scroll sideways, and the one word responsible

At 320 pixels, exactly one of the 38 pages has scrollWidth greater than clientWidth, by nine pixels: the ImmobilienScout24 alerts page. The cause is not a layout bug, it is a dictionary problem.

h1 text    "ImmobilienScout24 alerts when you are not paying for SuchenPlus"
font       Space Grotesk, 34px
column     272px  (320 viewport minus px-6 either side)
line box   304.8px wide, right edge at 328.8

"ImmobilienScout24" is one unbreakable word that renders 305 pixels wide at the h1 size, so it overhangs its own column by 33 and takes the document with it. It is the longest word on a site that names fifteen rental portals, and it is the only reason any page on the site scrolls horizontally at any width. Every other long name on the sites hub has a space or a hyphen in it: "WG-Gesucht", "Facebook Marketplace", "HousingAnywhere" at 15 characters is the runner-up and it fits.

The fixes, and why the obvious one does not work here

The textbook fix for a too-wide block on a phone is to let the reader swipe it:

.wrapper { overflow-x: auto; }

That does not work on this site, because of something in globals.css that I put there for unrelated reasons:

* {
  scrollbar-width: none;
  -ms-overflow-style: none;
}
*::-webkit-scrollbar {
  display: none;
}

Every scrollbar on the site is hidden. A swipeable mockup would be swipeable with no indication whatsoever that it is, which is a worse failure than clipping: at least clipping looks intentional. Making this fix work means exempting one container from that global rule, which is the kind of CSS exception that outlives the reason for it.

So, in the order I will actually do them:

  1. Mirror the layout under md. The right-hand column of each mockup is where the price, the View and the Send live. The left-hand column is descriptive text a reader can guess at. Bleeding the left and pinning the right costs nothing and saves everything worth seeing.
  2. Scale instead of clip. transform: scale(0.78) with transform-origin: top left fits a 500 pixel mockup into 390 and keeps all of it. The cost is honest: the 11 pixel labels inside become 8.6 pixel labels, which is too small to read but not too small to recognise as a price next to a room.
  3. overflow-wrap: anywhere on the h1s. Nine pixels of sideways scroll on one page is nearly nothing, but it is nothing shared with a page whose entire job is ranking for one long German brand name.

If you want to see it, the measurement needs no tools: open the home page on a phone, or pull a desktop window in to about 400 pixels wide, and scroll to the three mockups below the hero. Everything you can see there is deliberate, and so is everything you cannot. The same page at full width, and the download page it is trying to get you to, are what the mockups look like when nothing is missing.

title: I tested 9 name-matching methods on the OFAC sanctions list. Here's what I found.
description:
If you've ever built customer onboarding for a bank, a lender, a title company or a payments app, you've had to answer one question: is this person on the OFAC sanctions list?

The list is public. The hard part is the name. Customers type "Aymen Zawahri"; the list says "AL ZAWAHIRI, Dr. Ayman". An exact match misses it. A loose fuzzy match flags half your customers named John. And when a compliance analyst asks why a name was flagged, "the library returned 0.87" is not an answer.

I spent ten years building title and mortgage systems, including OFAC screening. This post walks through how I approached name matching in OfacMatch, an open-source screener, with the real numbers at each step. The ideas apply whatever language or library you use.

Why exact matching fails

The Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list has about 19,500 entries and many more aliases. Real names arrive with:

  • Spelling and transliteration differences: Mohammed, Muhammad, Mohamed
  • Different order: "DOE, John" on the list, "John Doe" in your form
  • Titles and particles: "Dr.", "AL", "BIN"
  • Typos: a missing or swapped letter
  • Extra or missing parts: a middle name the list doesn't have
  • Company suffixes: "EXAMPLE TRADING CO., LTD." versus "Example Trading LLC"

On my held-out test set, exact matching after cleaning up case and punctuation found only 35% of realistic variations of listed names. So you need fuzzy matching, and then you need to keep it from flagging everyone.

Step 1: normalize both names the same way

Before comparing anything, both names go through the same cleanup:

Step Example
Remove accents José Müller → JOSE MULLER
Upper case al-Zawahiri → AL-ZAWAHIRI
Drop apostrophes O'Neil → ONEIL
Other punctuation becomes a space AL-ZAWAHIRI → AL ZAWAHIRI
Remove honorifics Dr. Ayman → AYMAN
Turn LAST, First around (people) AL ZAWAHIRI, Ayman → AYMAN AL ZAWAHIRI
Drop legal forms (companies only) EXAMPLE TRADING CO., LTD. → EXAMPLE TRADING

Two details matter. Legal forms are removed for companies only, never for people. And legal forms are matched even with a one-letter typo ("COMPALY"), because real data is messy.

Step 2: OFAC already tells you how its own tool scores

OFAC publishes how its Sanctions List Search scores names, in its FAQ. It uses two techniques and reports the higher score:

  1. Whole name: Jaro-Winkler similarity of the full strings.
  2. Name parts: compare each part of the name separately, using Jaro-Winkler plus Soundex for parts that sound alike.

OfacMatch uses the same two techniques and the same 0 to 100 scale, so its scores read the way analysts are used to. (It doesn't reproduce OFAC's tool exactly: for example, it applies the Jaro-Winkler prefix bonus only when the base score is above 0.7, as in Winkler's original definition. I haven't yet measured how often the two agree.)

Step 3: score the name parts

Here's the name-parts method on a real pair: searched Aymen Zawahri, listed AL ZAWAHIRI, Dr. Ayman.

  1. Compare every searched part with every listed part using Jaro-Winkler.
  2. If two parts share a Soundex code, raise the score halfway toward 1: (similarity + 1) / 2.
  3. Pair parts greedily from the best pair down; each listed part is used once.
  4. Average the pair scores, weighted by the length of each searched part, so a short particle like "AL" counts less than "ZAWAHIRI".
Searched part Paired with Jaro-Winkler Sounds alike? Part score
AYMEN AYMAN 0.907 yes (A550) 0.953
ZAWAHRI ZAWAHIRI 0.946 yes (Z600) 0.973

Weighted average: (0.953 × 5 + 0.973 × 7) / 12 = 0.965. A small coverage adjustment (5% of the score depends on how much of the listed name was matched; "AL" wasn't) brings it to 95.8.

The whole-name Jaro-Winkler score for the same pair is only 84.5, because "AL" sits in the middle of the listed string. Taking the higher of the two gives 95.8. That's why the two-technique approach works: each one covers the other's blind spots.

Step 4: the false-positive trap, and a guard

"Take the higher of the two" has a problem. Try John Smith against a listed John Numbi:

Score
Whole name (Jaro-Winkler) 88.0
Name parts: JOHN ↔ JOHN 1.000
Name parts: SMITH ↔ NUMBI 0.467
Name parts total 70.4

Jaro-Winkler rewards a long shared prefix, and "JOHN " is a long shared prefix. So the whole-name score says 88, above a typical threshold of 85, for two names that only share a first name.

The fix is one rule:

The whole-name score can only raise the result when every searched part pairs with a listed part scoring at least 0.70.

SMITH ↔ NUMBI scores 0.467, so the whole-name score doesn't count, and the pair scores 70.4: not an alert.

On held-out ordinary names (common first names and surnames from many cultures), this guard cut alerts at a threshold of 85 from 53.0% to 37.5% for two-part names, and from 30.5% to 10.3% for three-part names. Recall on listed-name variations stayed at 100%.

Step 5: explain every score

Every score should come with its reasoning: which name or alias it hit, which technique won, and how each part paired. For the first example, that's the table in Step 3. A reviewer can read it and decide in seconds, and it goes straight into the audit record.

A score also isn't an identity check. "Ivan Hernandez" scores 100 against a listed "HERNANDEZ, Ivan" even if they're different people. So OfacMatch also takes an optional birth year and country, and flags a match whose listed birth year or country disagrees, rather than hiding it. That decision belongs to a person.

How I tested it

Tuning a matcher on the same names you test it on tells you nothing. So I split the work:

  • Development set: used while building and tuning.
  • Held-out set (a different random seed, entries and ordinary names never used in development): used once, for the numbers below.

The held-out set has 4,235 variations of 600 listed people and companies (typos, swapped letters, transliterations, reordering, missing middle names, changed company suffixes), plus 3,000 ordinary names for measuring false alerts. Results at a threshold of 85:

  • 100% of the 4,235 variations found
  • 99.6% of 2,160 harder variations found (wrong first letter like Kassim → Qassim, two wrong letters, nicknames like Aleksandr → Sasha, an initial instead of a first name, an extra middle name)
  • 37.5% of two-part ordinary names and 10.3% of three-part names raise an alert that a person must clear

I also compared eight standard methods on the same data: exact match, Levenshtein, Jaro-Winkler alone, RapidFuzz's token sort and token set ratios, Soundex parts, Monge-Elkan, and trigram TF-IDF. Different methods' scores mean different things, so the fair comparison fixes the alert rate and measures recall:

Method Recall when ≤ 1% of ordinary names alert Recall when ≤ 5% alert
Jaro-Winkler (whole name) 82.7% 85.4%
Levenshtein 85.5% 86.9%
Trigram TF-IDF cosine 93.3% 97.6%
Token sort ratio 95.2% 96.7%
Token set ratio 99.9% 100.0%
OfacMatch (default) 99.2% 100.0%

Token set ratio slightly beats OfacMatch at the strictest alert rate. It's a strong, simple baseline, and if you're building your own matcher it's a good place to start. What it doesn't give you is OFAC's 0-100 scale or a part-by-part explanation an analyst can check.

Full tables, the protocol and the code are in the repo, and there's a paper with the details.

Picking a threshold from data

There's no regulator-approved threshold. OFAC won't recommend one, and "set it to 85" isn't a policy. What you can do is measure the trade-off on data and write down why you chose your number. Here's the trade-off for OfacMatch on the held-out set:

Threshold Variations found Harder variations found Two-part ordinary names alerting Three-part ordinary names alerting
80 100.0% 99.9% 75.7% 51.0%
85 100.0% 99.6% 37.5% 10.3%
90 100.0% 98.4% 10.2% 2.2%
95 99.6% 83.4% 2.1% 0.0%

Three things stand out:

  • Short names drive the alerts. At 85, a two-part name is more than three times as likely to alert as a three-part name. A single global threshold treats them the same; collecting a birth year for every customer is what separates "Daniel Perez" from a listed "PEREZ ROJAS, Daniel".
  • Between 85 and 90, alerts drop by about three quarters while recall on ordinary variations holds. The cost is on the harder cases (99.6% → 98.4%), such as nicknames.
  • At 95, nickname-style variations are mostly missed (42% found). A high threshold looks efficient until someone types "Sasha" instead of "Aleksandr".

Your customers aren't my test set, so run the same kind of test on your own names. A missing birth year should never count against a match; it only means you have less to clear it with.

Try it

The fastest way is the browser page, which runs entirely client-side: krunalsolanki.github.io/ofac-match. Screen one name or a CSV of up to 10,000, and download an audit file.

From Python, run the self-hosted API and use the client:

docker run -p 8080:8080 ghcr.io/krunalsolanki/ofacmatch-api
pip install ofacmatch

from ofacmatch import Client

client = Client("http://localhost:8080")
result = client.screen("Aymen Zawahri", year_of_birth=1951)
for match in result["matches"]:
    print(match["score"], match["listedName"], match["explanation"])

# How two names score, part by part
print(client.compare("John Smith", "John Numbi"))

From .NET:

dotnet add package OfacMatch

There's also an MCP server, so AI assistants like Claude can screen names and explain the results.

Limits

  • It checks the SDN list only, not every US or international list.
  • A person must review every potential match. A score measures how alike two names are written, not whether two records are the same party.
  • It's a screening aid, not legal advice. Pick your threshold from your own risk assessment.

It's free and open source (Apache-2.0): github.com/krunalsolanki/ofac-match. I'd especially like to hear about name variations that score badly; open an issue with the pair and I'll look at it.

title: Implementing Large CSV/PDF Export Downloads with Object Storage (Presigned URL Retry)
description:
For a healthtech service, a large CSV or PDF export download can time out even after object storage reports a completed upload: a slow browser may outlive its presigned URL, while the signed clinical document still has to remain tenant-isolated and disappear on its retention deadline.

Short answer: generate each large CSV or PDF asynchronously into a tenant-scoped private object, validate its headers, and only then issue a presigned URL with enough lifetime for the slowest expected download; on retry, mint a fresh URL and let the client resume where its storage provider supports range requests.

This is an operating-cost decision, not a unit-price contest. The bill includes export compute, object storage, support contacts, retry traffic, and the engineering time required to integrate and observe the path. I've been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries; the same reflex applies here: make state transitions explicit and make every repeated action harmless.

For a team that wants one plain REST integration rather than another storage SDK, Infrai is worth trying for the private-object validation and link-issuance part of this workflow. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, so an integration can be driven from the actual contract. Infrai also uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this export path, that means the worker, deletion scheduler, and adjacent services share one credential model, leaving fewer keys to rotate and fewer invoices to reconcile in the runbook.

What the timeout is really telling you

"Download timed out" collapses several states into one browser message. The export may still be running. The upload may have completed with an unexpected size or content type. The signed URL may have expired while a slow client was reading it. Or the user may be retrying a link whose validity window has already closed. Treating all four as a storage-throughput problem sends the investigation in the wrong direction.

The invariant is simple: a link is publishable only after the private object passes validation. Keep an export record keyed by tenant and export ID, and move it through generating, uploaded, validated, available, and deleted states. The object key should carry the tenant boundary, for example tenants/acme-health/exports/exp_01J.../signed-records.pdf; authorization must check the tenant before the server requests any presigned URL. A hard-to-guess key is not authorization. Attach two different clocks to that record. The retention deadline controls object deletion, while URL expiry controls access through one link. A fresh link must never extend the object's retention deadline, and a deletion worker must be idempotent because schedules can deliver more than once. This separation matters in healthtech: a 30-minute link and a 30-day document are different promises. Before returning a link, inspect the object headers and compare the observed size and content type with the export record. Do not infer completion from queue acknowledgement alone. For a zero-byte or mismatched result, keep the export unavailable and retry the generation path under the same export ID; don't hand the browser a partial file and hope a later range request fixes it. If an old URL has expired, issue a new presigned URL only after repeating the tenant authorization and object check.

Keep it private.

Retry state is data.

How should a browser retry a slow large CSV/PDF export download?

The browser-facing API should return export status before it returns a location. While generation or upload is in progress, return a stable pending state. Once validation succeeds, return a short-lived application download endpoint or a newly minted presigned URL. For very large files, preserve the completed byte offset and request the remaining range when the provider supports it; if that support is not established for your chosen path, restart the transfer with a fresh link rather than claiming resumability.

There is a sharp edge here — URL lifetime has to cover transfer time, not just the delay before the first byte. Size the window from object size and the slow connection you intentionally support, then add room for browser and proxy delays. I'm not sure what that floor should be for your user population; production download telemetry and a deliberately throttled test resolve it. The rule is measurable even when the number is local.

Test the bad path too.

Do not send the Infrai bearer token to the returned presigned URL. The token authorizes the control-plane calls shown below; the signed URL carries its own limited authorization. Also treat HTTP 429 as backpressure. This Go program retries with Retry-After when present, otherwise uses exponential delay, checks the object first, and asks for a new link without inventing a storage response schema.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, path string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(nil))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: status %d: %s", method, path, resp.StatusCode, body)
            }
            return body, nil
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func objectPath(action, bucket, key string) string {
    parts := strings.Split(key, "/")
    for i := range parts {
        parts[i] = url.PathEscape(parts[i])
    }
    return "/storage/object/" + action + "/" + url.PathEscape(bucket) + "/" + strings.Join(parts, "/")
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 || os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: INFRAI_API_KEY=ifr_... go run main.go BUCKET OBJECT_KEY")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}

    head, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodGet, objectPath("head", os.Args[1], os.Args[2]))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("validated object: %s\n", head)

    presign, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, objectPath("presign", os.Args[1], os.Args[2]))
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("presign response: %s\n", presign)
}

The application must still compare the header response with its own expected size and content type before calling presign. That check is intentionally domain-specific: expected bytes come from the completed export record, not from a guessed constant in a sample. Likewise, the exact link lifetime belongs in the validated request schema exposed by discovery rather than in an undocumented field.

Choosing the storage boundary by tenant isolation and effective cost

Provider choice comes after the boundary is clear. The following table does not rank raw storage prices. It asks whether the provider can sit behind the same Infrai control-plane integration and what that means for this design.

Option Infrai vendor coverage Practical decision for this workflow
AWS S3 Included Consider it when the shared REST control plane and tenant-scoped private keys fit.
Cloudflare R2 Included Consider it under the same boundary; validate link lifetime and range behavior in your own throttled test.
Alibaba Cloud OSS Included A candidate when this vendor placement matches the deployment.
Tencent Cloud COS Included A candidate when this vendor placement matches the deployment.
Google Cloud Storage Not included Integrate directly or choose a specialist abstraction if GCS is mandatory.
Backblaze B2 Not included Integrate directly if B2's storage model is the deciding requirement.

Infrai's self-describing API is useful when integration labor and credential operations dominate the marginal storage calculation: discovery is public, and its broader surface spans 295 routes in 20 modules under one key. The catch is that abstraction does not erase provider behavior. Range recovery and expiration policy still need an end-to-end browser test, and downstream egress and retry traffic still belong in the workload model.

Model one normal month using your own export count, size distribution, retention days, failed-generation rate, redownload rate, and egress destination. Add worker compute, storage, requests, network transfer, retry amplification, and engineering ownership. Price can be evidence, but current provider pages should supply it at decision time; a copied unit-price leaderboard will age before the runbook does.

When this design is the wrong fit

This route is not suitable for permanent public links or static-site hosting because public/public-read ACL is unavailable. It also lacks object versioning and object lock, so a financial-grade WORM retention requirement needs an external compliance storage solution. Stick with a direct specialist such as Google Cloud Storage or Backblaze B2 when either provider is mandatory, because neither is in the covered vendor set.

There are more boundaries. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum, so an explicit deletion deadline measured in hours needs an application-controlled deletion worker. Strict concurrent writes need queue or database coordination because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. Browser direct-upload CORS cannot be self-configured through a dedicated route, and cross-region replication or cross-cloud bulk migration requires another tool. Metadata is not server-side searchable beyond prefix listing.

For the signed-document case, my decision rule is narrow: use the shared REST layer when tenant authorization remains in the application, objects are private, daily-or-longer lifecycle granularity is acceptable, and WORM is not required. Otherwise, pick the specialist that owns the missing guarantee. No amount of retry logic compensates for the wrong retention primitive.

The runbook should alert on exports stuck before validation, repeated link refreshes, deletion past deadline, and unusual retry bytes. On every retry, reuse the export identity, verify the tenant again, inspect the completed object again, and mint a new link. Boring is good.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage download and range-retry guide and confirm the live contract through discovery.

Sources

  • Infrai AI-readable capability index
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • Backblaze B2 pricing

title: Agents can now find Vercel CLI commands by describing the task
description:
Coding agents can now use vercel help search to find Vercel CLI commands by describing a task in plain language.

The search returns a list of matching commands. Add --with-help to include the help page for the first result in the same call. For example, vercel help search "roll back production" --with-help returns the options and examples for vercel rollback.

Search also supports:

  • API endpoints: When a Vercel API endpoint matches the task, search returns a vercel api command with the request path and placeholders for every required input. The agent can fill in the values without guessing the path.

  • JSON output: Use --json to return search results as JSON. Combine it with --with-help to include usage instructions, options, and examples for the first result.

Search recognizes common wording, such as “show” instead of “list,” and handles minor spelling mistakes.

The CLI also includes a skill that tells coding agents to start with vercel help search when looking for a command. Vercel doesn't log your search text.

Update to the latest Vercel CLI with vercel upgrade.

title: I Built a Claude Code Plugin Because I Was Becoming a Rubber-Stamp Reviewer
description:
My development team has two members: me and AI. And lately, I've been feeling like I'm becoming the less useful member of the team.

I've been using AI coding agents for years. Claude Code, and plenty of other tools. They're incredible at what they do, but somewhere along the way, my development process started looking like this:

Me: "Implement this feature."

AI: "Done! Changed 27 files, added 3,400 lines, refactored two modules. All tests passed."

Me: "LGTM."

Narrator: He did not, in fact, look.

The code gets written. Features get shipped. Productivity looks great. But here's what bothers me: Am I actually reviewing the code anymore, or am I just approving whatever the AI tells me?

And if I'm not making the technical decisions, what exactly is my role as a developer?

The problem isn't that AI writes code

I don't think developers need to manually write every line of code. That's not the point. The problem is that we're slowly outsourcing something much more important than typing: our judgment.

Think about how often this happens. The AI makes an architectural decision without asking you. It assumes a requirement that was never specified. It changes something outside the original scope. Then it confidently reports that all tests passed, and you trust the summary because reviewing everything yourself would take too long.

None of this necessarily means the AI is bad at coding. It means our development workflow hasn't caught up with how much code AI can produce.

I wanted a workflow where AI could do most of the implementation without quietly taking ownership of the decisions. I also didn't want to become an unpaid project manager, manually breaking everything into tiny tasks and supervising every step.

So I built human-rights.


GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

human-rights is an open-source Claude Code plugin built around a simple idea: Don't make humans review every line. Make sure they understand and approve the decisions that matter.

The requirements. The architecture. The risks. The acceptance criteria. And the evidence that the implementation actually works.

But there's an obvious problem with this approach. If every tiny change requires a design document, three approvals, and a meeting with yourself, nobody is going to use it.

So the workflow adapts to the task.

  1. Not every change deserves the same process

human-rights classifies development requests into four levels, from simple edits to high-risk changes.

Level

Example

Workflow

L0 — Direct

Center a login card

Make the change and check it

L1 — Focused

Add input validation hints

Short plan and targeted tests

L2 — Planned

Add Google authentication

Investigate, design, and review

L3 — Governed

Modify safety-critical control logic

Human approvals, integration tests, and final verification

The classification considers ambiguity, scope, architectural impact, risk, verification difficulty, and dependencies. A small UI change shouldn't require the same process as modifying authentication or controlling physical hardware.

For larger changes, the agent investigates the existing code, asks questions that could change the design, and creates a testable implementation plan. If the request is too large, it first breaks the work into smaller features that can be reviewed and verified independently.

The human decides what should happen. The AI figures out how to implement it.

  1. The AI cannot simply approve its own work

This was one of the most important design decisions. I didn't want to rely entirely on instructions like "Always ask the user for approval." An AI agent following a prompt is not the same thing as an enforced workflow.

So human-rights has two parts: a Claude Code skill that decides what process a task needs, and a deterministic Python runtime that enforces state transitions, approvals, test evidence, and failure handling.

Design approvals are tied to the approved plan, while final approvals are tied to the code being verified. If the plan changes, the previous design approval becomes invalid. If the code changes, the final approval becomes invalid too.

A test result is not accepted just because the agent says it passed. The runtime records the execution result and associates it with the relevant code version.

The goal is simple: stop trusting the AI's description of what happened and start requiring evidence of what actually happened.

  1. Then I realized something worse: humans can still blindly approve everything

Even with all those safeguards, there's a fundamental weakness in the system.

The human.

You can build the most carefully controlled approval system in the world, and I can still click "Approve" without reading anything.

So I added a feature called Red Pill Mode.

Here's how it works. When enabled, the system occasionally introduces a deliberately incorrect item into the review material. The developer is supposed to notice it before approving the work.

For example, suppose the original requirement says:

The system must support four simultaneous drone connections.

But the review table contains:

TEST-010: Verify that two simultaneous drone connections work correctly.

Would you notice the difference? Or would you just approve?

If you catch the incorrect item, the system records the catch and explains why it was wrong. If you blindly approve, the approval is blocked.

And yes, it makes fun of you:

You didn't really review this, did you, human? Keep approving like that and the AI really will take your job. lol.

It's intentionally a little ridiculous, but the underlying problem is serious. An approval button means nothing if the person clicking it isn't paying attention.

The planted mistakes never modify the actual implementation plan or executable code. They exist only in the review material, so they cannot accidentally become part of the software being built.

Red Pill Mode is optional and off by default. It also supports adaptive difficulty, so the review exercises can become harder as you successfully identify mistakes.

I find this particularly interesting because we're entering a world where developers may spend more time reviewing AI-generated work than writing code themselves. If that's where we're heading, shouldn't we be actively improving our review skills instead of letting them deteriorate?

  1. Bigger requests are split before implementation

Another issue I kept encountering was asking an agent to implement something too large. It would produce an enormous plan, and I'd be expected to approve the whole thing.

That's not meaningful review. That's just outsourcing a massive amount of work and hoping the result is correct.

So compound requests are split into independently verifiable features. The human approves the feature list before implementation starts, and each feature gets its own workflow, decisions, and verification.

After those features are implemented, the system checks that they work together. Independent tasks can also run in parallel using isolated Git worktrees, while conflicting tasks are kept sequential.

The idea isn't to slow down AI development. It's to gain the speed of AI agents without giving up control of the overall design.

  1. You can try it

The project is currently at v0.5.0 and is open source under the MIT license. It runs as a Claude Code plugin with a Python 3.8+ standard-library runtime.

Install it in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add kiduki77/human-rights

/plugin install hrs@human-rights

Initialize it in your project:

/hrs:init

Then start a task:

/hrs:new add Google authentication

Or, if you want to see whether you're actually paying attention during reviews, try:

/hrs:redpill on 5 adaptive

The repository includes an automated test suite, but this is still an early-stage project. Some integrations, including live GitHub adapter operation and real concurrent sub-agent execution, still need field validation.

GitHub: https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

Where this could go

Right now, human-rights focuses on individual development workflows, but I think the underlying problem could become much more important for engineering teams.

As AI generates more code, how do we know that code was meaningfully reviewed? How do we distinguish a real technical decision from a rubber-stamp approval? And how do we help developers improve at finding problems instead of gradually losing that skill?

Imagine an engineering team where AI generates most of the code. A developer approves a pull request without noticing that an important requirement was missed. Another developer catches the same issue immediately.

Today, we can track who approved a pull request, but that doesn't necessarily tell us how thoroughly it was reviewed. What if we could help developers identify the types of mistakes they tend to miss, practice reviewing realistic changes, and improve over time?

I think there's an opportunity to build something that doesn't just manage AI-generated code, but helps humans become better reviewers of it.

That's a longer-term idea, not something I'm claiming the current plugin already solves.

For now, I'm starting with the problem I experience every day: making sure I still understand and control the software I'm building.

I'd love to hear what other developers think

I'm especially curious whether other developers have noticed themselves reviewing AI-generated code less carefully over time. Would enforced approval gates help, or would they just become another form of bureaucracy? And would you actually enable something like Red Pill Mode in your own development workflow?

I don't have all the answers, and I'm sure there are things I've overlooked. That's why I'm releasing this as open source and looking for feedback from developers who are experiencing the same problems.

I built this because I don't want to stop using AI.

I just don't want to stop being a developer while using it.

human-rights — AI writes the code. Humans own the decisions.

https://github.com/kiduki77/human-rights

title: Underlining the spoken word without touching the book's HTML
description:
Hi, I'm Ishaan. I make Elsewhere, a reader that reads a book aloud and underlines each word as it is spoken. This post is about one decision the whole read-along rests on: the book's own markup is never changed to show where the voice is.

The obvious way, and why I dropped it

The obvious idea is to wrap each word in a span and swap a class on the current one. For a novel that is thousands of extra elements, and the book's own HTML is no longer the book's own HTML. A span can change line breaks, break a footnote link, or interfere with how the publisher styled a paragraph. And the word changes several times a second, so every change means touching the tree and hoping the layout holds still.

I wanted the text to stay exactly where the author's markup put it, so a line never jumps because a word got underlined.

Highlights that live outside the DOM

The CSS Custom Highlight API lets you register a Range and style it from CSS, with no element wrapped around it. You make a Highlight, put it in CSS.highlights under a name, and style that name with ::highlight().

The spoken word is one name, and the stylesheet gives it an underline:

::highlight(narration-word) {
text-decoration-line: underline;
text-decoration-thickness: 2px;
text-underline-offset: 0.22em;
}

I use an underline in the accent colour, so it still reads for someone who cannot tell the colours apart. And there is no transition. It moves with the voice instead of easing after it.

Painting is a few lines, trimmed here from what I run:

const highlight = new Highlight(range)
highlight.priority = WORD_PRIORITY
CSS.highlights.set('narration-word', highlight)

The same mechanism paints the sentence being read, the dimmer text around it, and the colours a reader picks when they mark a passage. None of them add a node to the page.

Finding the Range for a word

Each narrated passage comes with a start and end character for every word. A frame loop asks the audio element for its current time, looks up the word with a binary search, and turns that word's character offsets into a Range over the text nodes on screen.

Two details cost me an afternoon each.

One, the audible start of a word comes a little before the time stored for it. I measured about 40 ms on average, so the lookup adds 60 ms of lead and the underline lands on the word you are hearing.

Two, the Range is attached to text nodes, and the framework that renders the page will sometimes rewrite those nodes when the sentence highlight moves on. A Range can then collapse or slide onto other characters. So on each frame I compare the Range's text with the text it was painted over, and paint it again if they differ.

A priority bug I did not expect

The spoken word sits inside the sentence being narrated, and both are highlights. In Safari, the highest-priority highlight over a stretch of text decides its decoration outright. At the default priority the word's underline lost to the sentence's and never showed. Giving the word the top priority fixed it.

Pausing and tabs

The loop runs while audio plays and the tab is visible, and it cancels its frame on every way out. Paused, the word is painted once, and again after each seek, so it is never stale. Where a browser lacks the API, nothing is painted and the book still reads.

Try it

You can watch the underline move without making an account at https://listenelsewhere.com/try

Plainly, so nobody wastes an evening: Elsewhere opens DRM-free files, so Kindle store books will not open. The voice is a neural voice, not a human narrator. The tab has to stay open while narration is being made, and the app needs a connection (an exported audiobook plays offline).

I would like to hear from you. If you have used the Custom Highlight API, did you hit the priority quirk too, or find another way to keep a moving mark out of the DOM?

title: GLIDE: Scalable and Event-Aware Inductive Forecasting over Evolving Logistics Graphs
description:
arXiv:2611.23942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate forecasting of order volume at scale-effect hotspots (SEHs), spatially coherent groups of logistics flows that serve as distributed optimization units for real-time many-to-one dispatch, is a prerequisite for efficient order pooling in on-demand food delivery (OFD) platforms such as Meituan. However, real-world logistics networks present unique challenges that render standard spatiotemporal prediction model ineffective. (i) Dynamic Topology: Unlike static road networks, logistics graphs are ephemeral, with hotspot emerging and vanishing continuously; (ii) Scale--Volume Heterogeneity: Graph sizes vary from $10^2$ to $10^4$, while zero-inflated, long-tailed volumes create computational bottlenecks and bias predictions toward inactivity; and (iii) Event-Driven Disruption: Exogenous events (holidays, weather, academic calendars) induce systematic demand shifts that purely data-driven backbones cannot anticipate. In this paper, we present GLIDE, a production-ready framework that models evolving logistics graphs in a scalable latent space while adapting to heterogeneous demand regimes and event-driven shifts. GLIDE introduces a Graph-Guided Latent Aggregation mechanism, which dynamically projects varying physical subgraphs into a fixed-size, semantically stable latent space via a differentiable sparse assignment...

title: So sicherst du einen MCP-Server mit codex sandbox ab
description:
MCP-Server in der Codex-Sandbox ausführen: Berechtigungsprofile für stdio-MCP-Server

Um einen MCP-Server in der Codex-Sandbox auszuführen, definierst du ein Berechtigungsprofil in ~/.codex/config.toml und setzt dann das command des Servers auf codex sandbox --permission-profile <name> --, gefolgt vom ursprünglichen Befehl. Codex sandboxt stdio-MCP-Server standardmäßig nicht – ohne diesen Wrapper läuft ein npx-Server mit deinen vollen Benutzerberechtigungen.

Probiere Apidog heute aus

OpenAIs Engineering-Beitrag Inside the Codex sandbox vom 18. November 2026 bringt es auf den Punkt: Codex kann nicht zuverlässig erraten, welche Dateien oder Netzwerkdienste ein Server benötigt, deshalb lässt es den Startbefehl des Servers unangetastet. Jeder MCP-Server, den du mit npx -y hinzufügst, kann deinen Home-Ordner lesen, überall schreiben, wo du schreiben kannst, und jeden Host im Internet aufrufen.

Im Folgenden erstellst du ein Profil für den Apidog MCP Server, bindest es bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk an eine lokale OpenAPI-Datei, weist mit codex sandbox nach, dass das Profil funktioniert, und übergibst die Routinearbeit dann über die Apidog CLI an deinen Coding-Agenten.

Warum Codex stdio-MCP-Server ohne Sandbox lässt

Ein stdio-MCP-Server ist ein lokales Programm, das Codex startet und mit dem es über Standard-Ein- und -Ausgabe kommuniziert. Codex sandboxt die Shell-Befehle, die sein Modell ausführt, aber nicht den Befehl, der einen MCP-Server startet, weil es nicht erkennen kann, welche Dateien oder Hosts dieser Server benötigt. Der Server erbt deine vollen Benutzerberechtigungen.

Befehle, die das Modell ausführt, erhalten das eingebaute :workspace-Profil: Schreibzugriff nur innerhalb des Workspace, .git und .codex schreibgeschützt, umfangreiche Lesezugriffe, kein Netzwerk. Ein MCP-Server unter [mcp_servers] bekommt davon nichts.

Diese Lücke ist relevant, weil MCP-Server fremder Code sind, den du erst beim Start herunterlädst. Eine typische Konfiguration sieht so aus:

[mcp_servers.memory]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory@1.0.0"]

npx -y lädt das Paket herunter und führt es ohne Rückfrage aus. Ist dieses Paket kompromittiert, kann es deine .env-Dateien und SSH-Schlüssel lesen und an beliebige Orte senden. Unser Leitfaden zu MCP-Sicherheitsrichtlinien behandelt das übergeordnete Bedrohungsmodell; dieser Beitrag schließt das eine Loch in deinem Codex-Setup.

So funktioniert ein Codex-Berechtigungsprofil

Ein Berechtigungsprofil ist eine benannte Sammlung von Dateisystem- und Netzwerkregeln unter [permissions] in config.toml. OpenAIs Beitrag und die Codex-Dokumentation zu Berechtigungen beschreiben drei Dateisystemstufen:

Wert Auswirkung
read Nur Lesezugriff
write Lese- und Schreibzugriff
deny Überhaupt kein Zugriff

Drei Schlüssel erledigen den Großteil der Arbeit:

  1. ":root" = "read" gewährt umfangreiche Lesezugriffe, die Node.js und npm benötigen, um ihre eigenen Dateien zu laden.
  2. Ein Pfad wie "~/.npm" = "write" gewährt Schreibzugriff ausschließlich auf diesen Ordner.
  3. Eine ":workspace_roots"-Tabelle wendet Regeln relativ zu jedem Workspace-Root an. "**/*.env" = "deny" blockiert jede .env-Datei darunter.

Beim Netzwerk gibt es drei Modi: aus, über Codex' Proxy mit einer Domain-Allowlist geleitet oder voller Zugriff.

Die Open-Source-Codex-CLI setzt diese Regeln über das Betriebssystem durch: Seatbelt unter macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp unter Linux und auf kompatiblen Windows-Geräten Microsofts MXC. Kindprozesse erben die Limits, sodass alles, was der Server startet, in derselben Box bleibt.

Schritt 1: Den sichersten Modus für den Apidog MCP Server wählen

Der Apidog MCP Server (apidog-mcp-server auf npm, derzeit Version 0.0.18) läuft in zwei Modi:

  • Projektmodus: mit --project-id=<id> und einem APIDOG_ACCESS_TOKEN ruft er deine API-Dokumentation über das Netzwerk aus einem Apidog-Projekt ab.
  • OAS-Modus: mit --oas=<url-or-path> liest er eine Swagger- oder OpenAPI-Datei direkt.

Der OAS-Modus mit einer lokalen Datei braucht überhaupt kein Netzwerk. Das ist das strengste Profil, das du schreiben kannst, deshalb ist es hier das Hauptbeispiel. Die Apidog CLI hält die Spec von außerhalb der Sandbox aktuell (Schritt 5).

Wir haben das Paket in Version 0.0.18 analysiert, um herauszufinden, was der Server schreibt: Er legt Daten in ~/.apidog-mcp-server ab (oder im Ordner aus APIDOG_DATA_LOCATION) und ruft im Projektmodus https://api.apidog.com auf, sofern du nicht --apidog-api-base-url übergibst.

Schritt 2: Das Berechtigungsprofil definieren

Füge Folgendes zu ~/.codex/config.toml hinzu:

[permissions.apidog-mcp.filesystem]
# Broad reads so Node.js and npm can load their own files.
":root" = "read"
"~/.npm" = "write"
"~/.apidog-mcp-server" = "write"

[permissions.apidog-mcp.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
"**/*.env" = "deny"

[permissions.apidog-mcp.network]
enabled = false

Der Server kann die Spec lesen und in zwei Cache-Ordner schreiben. Er kann keine .env-Datei im Workspace öffnen und hat kein Netzwerk.

Schritt 3: Den Serverbefehl in codex sandbox einbetten

Ersetze nun den einfachen npx-Start durch codex sandbox. Das Flag -C legt das Arbeitsverzeichnis fest, das zugleich der Workspace-Root ist, auf den die .env-Regel angewendet wird:

[mcp_servers.pets-api-docs]
command = "codex"
args = [
  "sandbox",
  "--permission-profile", "apidog-mcp",
  "-C", "/Users/you/code/pets-api",
  "--",
  "npx", "--offline",
  "apidog-mcp-server@0.0.18",
  "--oas=/Users/you/code/pets-api/openapi.json"
]

Drei Details sind wichtig:

  • Version pinnen. @0.0.18 bedeutet, dass ein neues Release den Code nicht unter dir austauschen kann.
  • npx --offline verwenden. Bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk muss npx das Paket im Cache finden.
  • Absolute Pfade verwenden. Codex reicht args ohne Shell direkt durch, daher wird ~ nicht expandiert.

Die Apidog-README empfiehlt, den Server nach der API zu benennen, die er dokumentiert, etwa „Pets API Documentation“, damit das Modell weiß, wann es ihn einsetzen soll.

Schritt 4: Das Paket vorab cachen und nachweisen, dass das Profil funktioniert

Die Sandbox kann in den Cache-Ordner schreiben, ihn aber nicht anlegen, und sie kann nichts herunterladen. Führe Folgendes einmal außerhalb der Sandbox aus:

mkdir -p ~/.apidog-mcp-server
npx -y --package=apidog-mcp-server@0.0.18 -c true

Teste das Profil dann, bevor du ihm vertraust. codex sandbox führt jeden beliebigen Befehl unter einem Profil aus und ist damit ein schneller Testrahmen:

cd /Users/you/code/pets-api

# 1. A .env file in the workspace is unreadable
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- cat .env
# cat: .env: Operation not permitted

# 2. Writes outside the allowed folders fail
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- bash -c 'echo x > /tmp/probe.txt'
# bash: /tmp/probe.txt: Operation not permitted

# 3. The allowed cache folder is writable
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- touch ~/.apidog-mcp-server/probe
# (no output, exit 0)

# 4. No network
codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- curl -sS https://api.apidog.com/
# curl: (6) Could not resolve host: api.apidog.com

Das sind die Ergebnisse, die wir unter macOS erhalten haben. Prüfe anschließend, ob der Server noch funktioniert, indem du ihm einen MCP-Handshake sendest:

printf '%s\n' \
 '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-06-18","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"t","version":"1"}}}' \
 '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}' \
 '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list"}' \
| codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp -- \
  npx --offline apidog-mcp-server@0.0.18 --oas=$PWD/openapi.json

Bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk antwortete der Server mit drei Tools: eines, das die OpenAPI-Spec liest, eines, das von $ref referenzierte Dateien liest, und eines, das die Spec aktualisiert. Mehr braucht Codex nicht, um Code gegen deine API zu schreiben.

Unter macOS kannst du jedem codex sandbox-Aufruf --log-denials hinzufügen, um die Seatbelt-Verweigerungen nach dem Beenden des Befehls auszugeben. Das ist der schnellste Weg, einen Ordner zu finden, den der Server legitim benötigt.

Schritt 5: Die Spec mit der Apidog CLI aktuell halten

Ein Offline-Server liest eine Datei, also muss irgendetwas diese Datei aktualisieren. Übergib diese Aufgabe mit der Apidog CLI an deinen Coding-Agenten. Sie läuft außerhalb der MCP-Sandbox unter den normalen Befehlsregeln von Codex, und der MCP-Server benötigt nie einen Token.

Einrichtung (einmalig):

npm install -g apidog-cli
apidog auth login --with-token <your-access-token>

Wenn du die CLI noch nicht in Codex eingebunden hast, folge So verwendest du die Apidog CLI in Codex.

Prompt für deinen Agenten:

Export the OpenAPI 3.1 spec for Apidog project 1234567 to ./openapi.json,
then run test scenario 637132 in environment 358171 against it and give me
a CLI summary. Don't touch any .env file.

Befehle, die der Agent ausführt (Flags aus apidog export --help und apidog run --help, CLI 2.2.12):

apidog export --project 1234567 --format openapi --oas-version 3.1 --output ./openapi.json
apidog run -t 637132 -e 358171 -r cli,junit --out-dir ./apidog-reports

export überschreibt die Datei, die der gesandboxte Server liest, sodass der nächste MCP-Aufruf die neuen Endpunkte sieht. run führt dein Testszenario aus und schreibt einen JUnit-Bericht für CI. Füge --upload-report hinzu, wenn du den Lauf in der Apidog-App überprüfen möchtest. Der Free-Plan von Apidog deckt bis zu 4 Benutzer ab.

Wenn der Server Netzwerk braucht: die Domain-Allowlist

Der Projektmodus muss api.apidog.com erreichen. Codex' Antwort darauf ist der Netzwerk-Proxy: Setze enabled = true, liste die erlaubten Domains auf und aktiviere das Feature network_proxy. Das ist die dokumentierte Form aus OpenAIs Beitrag, angepasst an Apidog:

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.filesystem]
":root" = "read"
"~/.npm" = "write"
"~/.apidog-mcp-server" = "write"

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
"**/*.env" = "deny"

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.network]
enabled = true

[permissions.apidog-mcp-live.network.domains]
"api.apidog.com" = "allow"

[features]
network_proxy = true

Ein explizites deny hat Vorrang vor allow, und der Proxy löst einen Hostnamen erst auf, nachdem eine Regel ihn erlaubt hat – denn selbst eine DNS-Abfrage kann Daten preisgeben. OpenAI warnt, dass breite Wildcards weiterhin DNS-basierte Exfiltration erlauben können; liste deshalb exakte Hosts auf.

Eine Warnung aus unserem eigenen Test. Auf unserem Mac startete der Proxy und injizierte HTTP_PROXY und Co. in die Sandbox, antwortete aber bei jedem Host mit 403 und x-proxy-error: blocked-by-allowlist – auch bei den erlaubten. Unser Rechner leitet DNS über eine lokale Proxy-App, was der Grund dafür sein könnte. Führe codex sandbox --permission-profile apidog-mcp-live -- curl -sS https://api.apidog.com/ auf deinem eigenen Rechner aus, bevor du dich auf dieses Profil verlässt. Wenn der erlaubte Host fehlschlägt, falle auf den OAS-Modus aus Schritt 1 zurück.

Welches Profil solltest du verwenden?

Servertyp Netzwerk Schreibzugriffe im Dateisystem Beispiel
Liest nur lokale Dateien enabled = false npm-Cache + eigener Datenordner Apidog MCP Server mit --oas
Ruft eine bekannte API auf Proxy + exakte Domains npm-Cache + eigener Datenordner Apidog MCP Server mit --project-id
Braucht offenes Internet Vermeiden oder in einer VM isolieren So eng wie möglich Web-Browsing-Server

Wenn du Codex im Team einsetzt, können Administratoren mit allowed_permission_profiles in requirements.toml festlegen, welche Profile Benutzer auswählen dürfen. Und falls du versucht bist, die Sandbox stattdessen einfach abzuschalten: Lies nach, warum du beim Umgehen der Codex-Sandbox genau diesen Schutz aufgibst.

FAQ

Sandboxt Codex MCP-Server standardmäßig? Nein. OpenAI stellt klar, dass Codex den Befehl nicht sandboxt, der einen in config.toml konfigurierten stdio-MCP-Server startet. Du fügst die Sandbox selbst hinzu, indem du den Server über codex sandbox --permission-profile <name> -- startest.

Warum npx --offline statt npx -y verwenden? Bei network.enabled = false kann npx nichts herunterladen. --offline weist es an, die Kopie zu verwenden, die du mit npx -y --package=<pkg>@<version> -c true gecacht hast, und das Pinnen der Version verhindert, dass ein neues Release den Code ersetzt.

Schützt die Sandbox meine API-Schlüssel? Sie blockiert, was du verweigerst. Das :workspace-Profil erlaubt umfangreiche Lesezugriffe, also ergänze deny-Regeln für .env-Dateien und Secret-Ordner. Bei abgeschaltetem Netzwerk kann der Server außerdem nichts senden, was er liest.

Funktioniert das unter Linux und Windows? Ja. Dasselbe Profil gilt überall; Codex setzt es unter Linux mit bubblewrap und seccomp und auf kompatiblen Windows-Geräten mit einer MXC-basierten Sandbox durch. Teste jeden Rechner mit codex sandbox, da sich Pfade und DNS-Setups unterscheiden.

Kann ich andere MCP-Server auf dieselbe Weise sandboxen? Ja. Jeder stdio-Server funktioniert: Finde heraus, in welche Ordner er schreibt und welche Hosts er aufruft, gib ihm ein Profil, umhülle den Befehl, cache das Paket vorab und teste. OpenAIs eigenes Beispiel sandboxt @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory mit Schreibzugriffen nur auf ~/.npm und ~/mcp-data.

title: Sub-6ms In-Process AI Runtime in Rust: Eliminating HTTP Bottlenecks and Enforcing Zero-Wipe Invariants
description:
Deep Dive: Sub-6ms Sovereign Autonomous Code Runtime in Pure Rust

How Omni Engine Eliminates HTTP IPC Latency and Enforces Zero-Wipe Invariants (W = ∅)

By Ibrahim El Feqi (@ielfeqi)

1. The Core Problem with Local Coding Agents

Most local coding agents today are built on a fragile layer: they spin up an external HTTP daemon (such as Ollama, vLLM, or llama-server), and communicate with it over localhost:11434 via REST or Server-Sent Events (SSE).

When a multi-agent loop executes 20–50 consecutive tool-calling cycles:

  1. Serialization Bottleneck: Every prompt prefix, system prompt, AST diff, and token stream undergoes full JSON encoding/decoding and TCP/socket context-switching.
  2. Context Eviction & KV thrashing: Each turn invalidates or forces costly prefix re-evaluation in external server buffers. Latency balloons from milliseconds to tens of seconds per turn.
  3. Destructive Hallucinations (File Wiping): As attention degrades over long context windows, models emit truncated replacements (// ... rest of code unchanged ...) that silently wipe hundreds of lines of code.

To solve this, we architected Omni Engine: a sovereign, autonomous software engineering runtime in pure Rust that embeds llama.cpp directly in-process via C-FFI.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        Omni Engine (Rust)                         |
|                                                                   |
|   +-----------------------+              +--------------------+   |
|   |  Maestro Coordinator  |              |  AST Diff Enforcer |   |
|   |    (Rayon Runtime)    |              |  (Zero-Wipe W=∅)   |   |
|   +-----------+-----------+              +---------+----------+   |
|               |                                    |              |
|               v                                    v              |
|   +-----------------------+              +--------------------+   |
|   | In-Process C-FFI      |              | Bubblewrap Sandbox |   |
|   | (libllama in RAM)     |              | (Hermetic Cleanroom|   |
|   | <6ms KV-Cache Slicing |              | Net=None, PID/MNT) |   |
|   +-----------------------+              +--------------------+   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+

2. In-Process C-FFI vs. Localhost HTTP

Instead of spawning child processes or querying daemons, Omni Engine links directly against llama.cpp using Rust FFI bindings:

  • Zero IPC Overhead: Token generation pointers write directly into Rust memory arenas.
  • O(1) KV-Cache Arena Slicing: By maintaining pre-allocated contiguous memory slabs, switching context between subagents drops to sub-6ms on consumer silicon (Apple Silicon M-series, x86_64 AVX2, or NVIDIA RTX).
  • Zero Cloud Tokens: 100% of execution occurs air-gapped on device with zero telemetry.

3. Strict Zero-Wipe Invariant (W = ∅)

A critical guarantee of Omni Engine is mathematical verification before disk mutation:

If a model attempts to generate a destructive diff, partial snippet, or malformed AST, the transaction fails closed. Host files remain completely untouched until tests pass within an isolated sandbox.

4. Hermetic Bubblewrap Cleanrooms

Every tool invocation (compiling, running test suites, executing scripts) is contained within a Linux kernel namespace jail via bwrap:

  • unshare-net: Completely disables external network access.
  • Read-only mounts for system root libraries.
  • Ephemeral writable tmpfs workdirs that isolate mutations until verification completes.

5. The ATLR Concurrency Benchmark Results

To benchmark agent robustness under high load, we conducted a 50-thread concurrent refactoring stress test on a single Tesla T4 GPU:

Architecture Engine / Runtime Concurrency Success Rate Wall-Clock Time Destructive Wipes (W) Exit State
Omni Engine In-Process C-FFI (Rust) 50 Threads 50/50 (100%) 37m 58s 0 (W = ∅) Exit 0 (Clean)
Aider + Ollama Local HTTP Daemon 50 Threads 11/50 (22%) 5h 24m 14 partial wipes SIGKILL
Aider + Gemini 2.5 Flash Cloud REST API 50 Threads 38/50 (76%) 12m 41s 3 truncations Panic 101

6. Get Started & Links

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/omni-engine-ai/omni_engine
  • Official Documentation: https://omni-engine-ai.github.io/omni_engine/
  • 1-Line Install: 
curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/omni-engine-ai/omni_engine/main/install.sh | bash

title: Why SPF, DKIM & DMARC Matter for Email Security
description:
Email is an essential part of modern web applications and business communication. Websites use email for password resets, account verification, order confirmations, invoices, notifications, and many other purposes.

But email has a security weakness: attackers can make messages appear to come from a trusted domain without being authorized to send them.

This is known as email spoofing. It is commonly used in phishing attacks, business email compromise, and online scams.

Three important email authentication standards help protect domains against this problem:

  • SPF (Sender Policy Framework)
  • DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)
  • DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance)

Let's understand how they work and why every domain administrator should care about them.

1. What Is SPF?

SPF identifies which mail servers are authorized to send emails on behalf of a domain.

It works through a DNS TXT record. When an email is received, the receiving mail server checks whether the sending server is authorized by the sender's SPF policy.

Example SPF record:

v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.10 include:mailprovider.example -all

This example authorizes a specific IP address and an external email provider. Other sources are marked as unauthorized.

Why SPF matters:

  • Helps prevent unauthorized servers from sending email using your domain.
  • Reduces certain types of email spoofing.
  • Helps receiving servers evaluate email authenticity.
  • Supports better email security.

Common SPF mistakes include publishing multiple SPF records, forgetting third-party email providers, and exceeding the DNS lookup limit.

For DNS configuration, you can use an SPF Generator or check an existing record with an SPF Validator.

2. What Is DKIM?

DKIM uses cryptographic digital signatures to help verify that an email was authorized by a signing domain and that signed parts of the message have not been modified.

The sending mail server signs outgoing emails using a private key. The corresponding public key is published in DNS.

The receiving server retrieves the public key and verifies the email's signature.

Why DKIM matters:

  • Helps verify the authenticity of signed emails.
  • Detects changes to signed message content.
  • Makes it harder to forge valid signatures for your domain.
  • Provides an important authentication layer for DMARC.

Common DKIM problems include incorrect public keys, missing DNS records, and mismatched selectors.

You can prepare a DKIM DNS record using a DKIM Generator and check its configuration with a DKIM Validator.

3. What Is DMARC?

DMARC builds on SPF and DKIM.

It checks whether at least one authentication method passes with the required domain alignment to the address shown in the email's visible From field.

It also allows domain owners to publish instructions for receiving mail servers when messages fail DMARC authentication.

Example DMARC record:

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com

DMARC supports three main policies:

  • p=none – Monitor authentication without requesting quarantine or rejection.
  • p=quarantine – Ask receiving servers to treat failing messages as suspicious.
  • p=reject – Ask receiving servers to reject messages that fail DMARC.

Why DMARC matters:

  • Helps protect domains against email impersonation.
  • Provides visibility through aggregate reports.
  • Helps identify unauthorized email sources.
  • Allows domain owners to define authentication policies.
  • Connects SPF and DKIM results with the visible sender domain.

You can prepare a DMARC policy using a DMARC Generator or check an existing record with a DMARC Validator.

SPF vs DKIM vs DMARC: What's the Difference?

Although these standards work together, each has a different responsibility.

Standard Main purpose
SPF Checks whether a sending server is authorized.
DKIM Verifies an email's digital signature.
DMARC Checks authentication and domain alignment, and defines a policy.

In simple terms:

  • SPF: Is this server allowed to send email?
  • DKIM: Does this email have a valid digital signature?
  • DMARC: Does the message pass an aligned SPF or DKIM check, and what should happen if it does not?

Using all three provides a stronger email authentication framework.

Why Should Every Business Configure Them?

Whether you manage a personal domain, business website, SaaS platform, or online store, your domain is part of your online identity.

Proper email authentication helps you:

  1. Protect your domain reputation – Make unauthorized use of your domain more difficult.
  2. Reduce email spoofing – Help receiving servers identify suspicious messages.
  3. Support email deliverability – Provide authentication information expected by many email providers.
  4. Monitor email activity – Use DMARC reports to identify sending services and authentication failures.
  5. Build customer trust – Help protect customers from messages impersonating your organization.

Email authentication does not guarantee inbox delivery or prevent every phishing attack, but it is an important part of a reliable email security strategy.

How to Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC

If you manage a domain or mail server, follow these steps:

  1. Identify every service that sends emails using your domain.
  2. Create one SPF record containing all legitimate sending sources.
  3. Enable DKIM signing and publish the correct public key in DNS.
  4. Publish a DMARC record, initially using p=none.
  5. Review DMARC reports and fix authentication or alignment problems.
  6. Gradually move to quarantine or reject once legitimate email sources are properly configured.

Avoid enforcing a strict DMARC policy before identifying all legitimate email services. Otherwise, genuine business emails may be affected.

Final Thoughts

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are important building blocks of modern email security.

SPF identifies authorized sending servers, DKIM verifies digital signatures, and DMARC adds domain alignment, reporting, and policy enforcement.

For developers, website owners, and system administrators, understanding these standards is an important step toward protecting domain identity and reducing email spoofing risks.

If you work with DNS and website administration, having reliable tools for creating and validating records can make these tasks easier.

You can also explore DevUtilityKits, a collection of 150+ free online developer tools covering DNS, email security, JSON, SEO, coding, images, data conversion, and Cloud & DevOps.

Email security starts with knowing who is authorized to send messages using your domain.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is SPF enough to protect my email domain?

No. SPF checks authorized sending servers, while DKIM verifies digital signatures. DMARC connects these checks through domain alignment and policy enforcement.

Do I need SPF, DKIM, and DMARC together?

Yes. They provide complementary protection and are widely recommended for business and website email domains.

Which DMARC policy should I use first?

A monitoring policy (p=none) is often a good starting point. Review reports and fix authentication problems before moving to quarantine or reject.

Does DMARC stop all phishing emails?

No. It helps protect your domain against direct impersonation, but attackers can still use lookalike domains or compromised accounts.

Can SPF, DKIM, and DMARC improve email deliverability?

They help receiving providers authenticate your messages, but inbox placement also depends on sender reputation, content, recipient engagement, and other factors.

  • DKIM Generator
  • DKIM Validator
  • DMARC Generator
  • DMARC Validator
  • DNS & Website Tools

title: AI Rate Limiting for LLM Calls in TypeScript
description:
You fire 50 LLM calls at once. A batch job, a fan out over documents, a busy hour. The provider only lets 10 through at a time, so the rest come back as 429 Too Many Requests.

The usual fix is to retry 429s with backoff. That helps, but notice what it means: every retry is a request you sent after you already got rate limited. You are reacting to a limit you could have stayed under.

This post shows the difference with real numbers and how to rate limit LLM calls in TypeScript with VernLLM, before the provider says no.

Retrying 429s vs not causing them

I ran a 50 call burst against a scripted provider that accepts 10 requests in flight and rejects the rest with 429. Both runs used maxRetries: 2.

Retries only rateLimit: { maxConcurrent: 10 }
Calls answered 20 50
Calls failed 30 0
Provider 429s 110 0
Requests sent 130 50

Retries alone sent 130 requests, collected 110 rejections, and still lost 30 calls. With a local limit, every call waited its turn and went out once.

Rate limiting LLM calls with VernLLM 

npm i vern-llm openai

import OpenAI from 'openai';
import { VernLLM } from 'vern-llm';
import { fromOpenAI } from 'vern-llm/adapters';

const llm = new VernLLM({
  client: fromOpenAI(new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY })),
  model: 'gpt-6.2-sol',
  rateLimit: {
    requestsPerMinute: 500,
    tokensPerMinute: 200_000,
    maxConcurrent: 20,
  },
});

const results = await Promise.all(tickets.map((t) => llm.call({ userContent: t.text })));

rateLimit has three buckets, each optional:

  • requestsPerMinute caps how many requests leave per minute. It refills continuously, so it does not reset all at once every 60 seconds.
  • tokensPerMinute caps token throughput. It checks an estimate before the request goes out, then corrects it with the real usage the provider reports.
  • maxConcurrent caps requests in flight, and frees a slot the moment one finishes.

A call goes out only when every configured bucket has room. Otherwise it waits.

A fair queue

Calls that cannot go out yet wait in strict first in, first out order. A large call is never starved by smaller ones behind it.

You decide how long a call may wait and how deep the queue may get:

rateLimit: {
  requestsPerMinute: 60,
  maxQueueMs: 10_000, // default 30000
  maxQueueSize: 50,   // default unbounded
},

When a call gives up waiting, it fails with a rate_limited error and a code you can branch on (rate_limit_queue_timeout or rate_limit_queue_full). These never reached the provider, so VernLLM does not retry them. A call too big to ever fit under tokensPerMinute fails right away with rate_limit_capacity_exceeded instead of blocking the queue forever.

Retries count too

Capacity is taken per attempt, not per call. A retry is a real request against the same provider limit, so it waits in the same queue as everything else. That is what keeps retries from turning one 429 into a storm of them.

Adaptive limits: AIMD

You often do not know the provider's real limit, or it changes with your tier and their load. aimd lets the requests ceiling adjust itself: it grows a little on every success and shrinks on a real 429.

rateLimit: {
  requestsPerMinute: 500,
  aimd: { increaseBy: 10, decreaseFactor: 0.5, minCapacity: 50, maxCapacity: 1000 },
},

It shrinks at most once per 60 seconds, so a burst of 429s from calls already in flight counts as one overload. With proactiveFloor, adapters that can read rate limit headers shrink the ceiling when the provider reports low remaining capacity, before a 429 happens.

A 429 that still gets through keeps its own code, provider_rate_limited, so you can tell a real provider limit apart from VernLLM's own queue in your logs.

One limit per provider

With fallback, each target gets its own limiter. A burst against a struggling primary cannot use up the slots a healthy backup needs:

const llm = new VernLLM({
  client: fromOpenAI(openai),
  model: 'gpt-6.2-sol',
  rateLimit: { maxConcurrent: 50 },
  fallback: {
    client: fromGemini(gemini),
    model: 'gemini-4-neon',
    rateLimit: { maxConcurrent: 10 },
  },
});

Scaling past one process

The built in limiter lives in one process. If you run several instances, pass your own RateLimiterAdapter, backed by Redis or anything else, so every instance shares one budget against the provider.

Wrap up

Retrying 429s is damage control. A local limit keeps you under the provider's ceiling in the first place: queue in order, count every retry, adapt when the provider pushes back.

npm i vern-llm

Docs: Rate limiting

title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
description:
arXiv:2611.23456v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

title: Announcing the general availability of a new AWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia
description:
Today, AWS announces the general availability of a new Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia, bringing AWS infrastructure closer to end users for applications that require single-digit millisecond latency. You can use the Bogotá Local Zone for workloads such as real-time gaming, live video streaming, medical imaging, and financial transaction processing.

AWS Local Zones are infrastructure deployments that place compute, storage, networking, and other select AWS services closer to metropolitan areas, with the same APIs and tools as AWS Regions. You pay only for what you use, with no minimum commitment. Pricing options include On-Demand, Savings Plans, and Spot Instances. AWS Local Zones are available in more than 30 locations worldwide.

To get started, enable the AWS Local Zone in Bogotá (us-east-1-bog-1a) from the Regions and Zones tab in the AWS Global View or by using the ModifyAvailabilityZoneGroup API. For pricing information, visit the AWS Local Zones pricing page. To learn more, visit the AWS Local Zones overview page.
