Verification must test individual mechanisms and their interaction under realistic fault conditions. Fault injection can introduce corrupted messages, processor stalls, sensor failures, memory faults, timing overruns, actuator degradation, communication loss, power disturbances, or unsafe AI commands. Testing should confirm not merely that faults are detected, but that containment and physical safety responses occur within the required time.

Lifecycle assurance is necessary because software and hardware safety mechanisms evolve differently. AI models and mission software may change frequently, while safety controllers and physical protection may remain comparatively stable. Updates should not silently change interfaces, resource dependencies, timing assumptions, safety parameters, or command authority. Configuration management and regression testing should preserve the evidence supporting the deployed safety architecture.

The objective is not to rely exclusively on either software intelligence or hardware protection, but to construct defense in depth across multiple failure domains. Software mechanisms provide flexible monitoring, validation, diagnostics, isolation, and fallback behavior, while hardware mechanisms provide independent authority, energy control, actuator-level enforcement, and physical limitation. Their diversity reduces dependence on any single protection principle.

For Physical AI, dependable safety emerges when complex autonomous intelligence is surrounded by mechanisms whose behavior remains bounded under failure. Software checks constrain information and computation, hardware mechanisms constrain energy and motion, and diagnostic and fallback functions coordinate the response when assumptions fail. Together they transform safety requirements into enforceable protection from AI decision generation through final physical actuation.

02.14. Safety Lifecycle Verification and Validation

A safety lifecycle provides the structured process through which safety is established, implemented, demonstrated, maintained, and reassessed throughout the life of a Physical AI system. Safety cannot be treated as a final test performed after autonomous functions are complete. Hazards, requirements, architecture, implementation, verification, validation, deployment, operation, modification, and retirement must remain connected through continuous safety engineering.

The lifecycle begins by defining the system, its intended functions, operating environment, users, interfaces, boundaries, and reasonably foreseeable conditions. For Physical AI, this definition must include not only hardware and conventional software but also perception, world models, learned policies, planning, communication, human interaction, and physical actuation. An incomplete system boundary can leave important hazards outside the safety analysis.

Hazard analysis and risk assessment establish the safety problems that the lifecycle must control. Hazardous events are identified by considering robot motion, energy, environmental interaction, human proximity, component faults, software failures, AI uncertainty, incorrect perception, unsafe planning, communication loss, and foreseeable misuse. The resulting risk assessment determines where risk reduction is required and provides the basis for defining safety goals.

Safety goals translate unacceptable risks into high-level statements of required protection. These goals are progressively refined into functional and technical safety requirements that specify what must be detected, prevented, limited, monitored, or controlled. Requirements may define safe speed, separation, stopping behavior, fault response, sensor coverage, control independence, diagnostic capability, degraded operation, or transition to a safe or minimum-risk condition.

Traceability connects each safety requirement to the hazard and risk that justify it. The same traceability should continue toward architecture, implementation, verification evidence, validation scenarios, and configuration items. This creates an auditable chain showing why a safety mechanism exists, how it was implemented, and what evidence demonstrates that it satisfies the intended safety objective.

Safety architecture converts requirements into technical structure. Independent safety controllers, monitors, safety sensors, redundant channels, communication supervision, hardware interlocks, motion limits, fallback control, and energy isolation may be allocated according to the identified risks. Architectural analysis should also examine dependencies so that apparently independent mechanisms do not share common failures capable of defeating the required protection.

Implementation must preserve the assumptions established during safety design. Software safety functions require controlled interfaces, bounded behavior, deterministic responses where necessary, protected execution, and configuration management. Hardware safety mechanisms require appropriate diagnostics, environmental capability, timing performance, and failure behavior. AI components require particular attention because their behavior may depend on training data, context, uncertainty, and operating distribution.

Verification asks whether the system has been built according to its specified requirements and design. It evaluates individual components, interfaces, algorithms, safety mechanisms, communication paths, timing behavior, and integrated functions against defined criteria. Reviews, analysis, simulation, static checks, unit tests, integration tests, hardware tests, and fault injection can all contribute evidence that implementation conforms to the safety specification.

Validation addresses a different question: whether the completed system provides adequate safety for its intended use and operating environment. A function can satisfy its technical specification yet still be inadequate if the specification did not capture realistic hazards. Validation therefore emphasizes representative scenarios, human interaction, environmental variability, operational workflows, foreseeable disturbances, and the actual physical consequences of autonomous behavior.

Verification and validation should remain distinct but strongly connected. Verification can demonstrate that a protective stop activates when a specified separation threshold is crossed, while validation examines whether that threshold provides sufficient protection in realistic operation. Verification focuses on conformance to requirements; validation examines whether those requirements and their implementation produce an acceptably safe system in practice.

Physical AI requires scenario-based validation because safety depends strongly on interaction and context. Scenarios should include different human approaches, obstacle configurations, robot speeds, payloads, surfaces, lighting, weather where applicable, sensor occlusions, communication states, and mission conditions. Testing only nominal trajectories can provide misleading confidence because many important hazards emerge from unusual combinations of otherwise ordinary conditions.

Boundary conditions deserve special attention. Safety failures frequently appear near maximum speed, minimum separation, sensor range limits, localization uncertainty thresholds, payload limits, steep slopes, communication deadlines, or transitions between operating modes. Verification should deliberately exercise these boundaries and conditions immediately beyond them to confirm that the system responds conservatively rather than failing unpredictably.

Fault injection provides evidence about the effectiveness of diagnostic and fault-tolerance mechanisms. Sensor loss, corrupted measurements, stale messages, processor stalls, memory faults, actuator degradation, brake failures, power disturbances, communication interruption, and invalid AI commands can be introduced deliberately. The objective is to determine whether faults are detected, contained, and converted into appropriate physical safety responses within the available time.

AI-specific validation must examine more than conventional component failure. Learned systems can produce incorrect outputs while continuing to operate normally from a computational perspective. Testing should therefore include unfamiliar environments, ambiguous observations, distribution shifts, conflicting sensor evidence, low-confidence predictions, unexpected object configurations, and situations in which learned policies propose physically plausible but unsafe behavior.

Simulation can expand safety evaluation by exposing the system to large numbers of scenarios that would be expensive, dangerous, or difficult to reproduce physically. Parameter variation, randomized environments, synthetic disturbances, and rare-event scenarios can reveal vulnerable regions of behavior. However, simulation evidence must account for model limitations because an inaccurate simulator can hide the physical effects that matter most to safety.

Hardware-in-the-loop and software-in-the-loop testing can bridge the gap between simulation and complete physical trials. Real controllers, safety logic, communication interfaces, or computing hardware can be connected to simulated components and environments. These methods help evaluate timing, interfaces, resource contention, failure responses, and integration behavior before exposing a complete robot and surrounding people or equipment to hazardous test conditions.

Physical testing remains necessary for phenomena that cannot be represented with sufficient confidence in simulation. Actual braking distance, wheel slip, payload dynamics, manipulator compliance, sensor interference, vibration, thermal behavior, contact forces, and environmental degradation may require measurement on representative hardware. Physical validation should progress from controlled conditions toward increasingly realistic operation while maintaining appropriate test safeguards.

Coverage is a central challenge because no finite test program can examine every state of a complex autonomous system. Safety assurance therefore combines testing with analysis, architectural constraints, monitoring, redundancy, conservative limits, and operational restrictions. The objective is not to prove that every possible AI output is correct, but to demonstrate that credible unsafe behavior is prevented, detected, constrained, or brought under control.

Acceptance criteria should be defined before testing whenever practical. Required stopping time, maximum speed, minimum separation, diagnostic response time, localization validity, allowable force, communication timeout, fault reaction, and safe-state behavior should have measurable criteria. Without predefined criteria, test results can become subjective and failures may be rationalized after observation rather than evaluated against established safety requirements.

Test independence can strengthen confidence in safety evidence. The engineers who develop a function possess valuable technical knowledge, but independent review or validation can challenge assumptions that the implementation team may overlook. The required degree of independence depends on risk and assurance objectives, yet separation between development and final safety judgment can reduce confirmation bias and improve the credibility of conclusions.

Anomalies discovered during verification and validation should be treated as evidence about the system rather than merely as defects to be removed. A failed test may reveal an incorrect requirement, hidden dependency, inadequate safety margin, unrealistic environmental assumption, or previously unidentified hazard. Corrective action should therefore examine the underlying safety argument and determine whether related analyses, requirements, and tests must also change.

Safety evidence should be organized into a coherent safety case or equivalent assurance structure. Hazard analyses, requirements, architectural decisions, verification results, validation results, fault-injection evidence, assumptions, limitations, and residual risks should collectively support the claim that the system is acceptably safe for defined operation. Evidence should be traceable, reproducible, configuration-specific, and understandable to reviewers.

Deployment does not end the safety lifecycle. The field environment can reveal combinations of conditions that were not fully represented during development. Operational monitoring can collect safety-relevant events such as protective stops, emergency stops, sensor degradation, localization failures, safety overrides, communication loss, unusual AI uncertainty, or repeated fallback activation. These observations provide evidence for continued safety assessment.

Changes after deployment require disciplined impact analysis. Updating an AI model, modifying training data, replacing a sensor, changing a controller, increasing speed, supporting a new payload, altering the operating environment, or modifying fleet coordination can invalidate previous assumptions. The affected hazards, requirements, interfaces, tests, and safety evidence should be identified before the modified configuration is accepted for operation.

AI updates create a particularly important lifecycle challenge because model behavior can change even when external interfaces remain identical. A new model may improve average performance while introducing different failure patterns in rare situations. Regression testing should therefore include safety-critical scenarios, boundary conditions, known historical failures, uncertainty behavior, and interactions with independent safety mechanisms rather than relying only on aggregate AI performance metrics.

Configuration management ensures that safety evidence corresponds to the system actually deployed. Hardware revisions, firmware, software versions, AI model checkpoints, calibration parameters, safety thresholds, maps, sensor configurations, and operating modes should be controlled where they affect safety. Without configuration integrity, successful verification of one system version cannot reliably justify the safety of another.

Periodic reassessment is necessary as equipment ages and operating conditions evolve. Brake wear, sensor contamination, battery degradation, mechanical changes, environmental expansion, new human workflows, and accumulated software modifications can alter the original risk picture. Maintenance information and operational data should therefore feed back into hazard analysis, verification planning, and validation when safety assumptions may no longer remain valid.

Retirement and decommissioning also belong to the lifecycle because hazardous energy, batteries, stored mechanical loads, learned data, configuration information, and connected infrastructure may remain after normal operation ends. Safe shutdown, isolation, removal, disposal, and preservation of relevant records should be planned so that safety responsibility does not disappear merely because the autonomous system is no longer performing its mission.

The safety lifecycle is therefore an iterative assurance loop rather than a linear sequence completed once before release. Hazard analysis generates requirements, requirements shape architecture, implementation is verified, the integrated system is validated, operational evidence tests assumptions, and changes trigger reassessment. Each iteration strengthens or revises the evidence supporting continued safe operation.

For Physical AI, verification and validation must ultimately demonstrate more than intelligent performance. They must show that uncertain perception, prediction, reasoning, planning, and learned control remain bounded by effective physical protection across credible operating and failure conditions. A disciplined safety lifecycle connects hazards, requirements, architecture, testing, field evidence, and change management so that safety remains an engineered and continuously supported property of the complete autonomous system.

02.15. Functional Safety Analysis Example

Functional safety analysis becomes most useful when abstract safety principles are applied to a concrete Physical AI operating scenario. Consider an autonomous mobile robot transporting material through a shared industrial workspace where workers, forklifts, equipment, and temporary obstacles may enter its path. The robot uses perception, localization, planning, AI-based prediction, motion control, and safety mechanisms to perform its mission without exposing nearby people to unacceptable risk.

The analysis begins by defining the intended function and system boundary. The robot receives a transport mission, determines its position, perceives surrounding objects, generates a route, plans local motion, and commands drive actuators. Safety-related elements include protective sensors, speed monitoring, braking functions, emergency-stop circuits, safety control, and diagnostic mechanisms. Infrastructure, operators, fleet coordination, and environmental conditions also form part of the operational context.

A representative hazardous event is unintended hazardous motion toward a person. This event may occur because the robot fails to detect the person, incorrectly estimates separation, generates an unsafe trajectory, exceeds permitted speed, fails to execute braking, or continues moving after a control fault. The analysis does not assume a single cause. Instead, it examines combinations of perception, computation, communication, control, actuator, environmental, and human-related conditions that could produce the hazardous state.

Risk assessment considers the potential severity of contact, the probability or frequency of exposure, and the possibility of avoiding the hazardous event. Robot mass, velocity, payload, workspace density, human access, stopping distance, and expected interaction patterns influence the assessment. A heavy robot moving rapidly through a shared aisle can create substantially greater risk than the same platform operating slowly inside an isolated and access-controlled region.

A corresponding safety goal can state that hazardous robot motion shall not result in unacceptable collision risk to people within the defined operating environment. This high-level objective does not prescribe a specific implementation. It establishes the required safety outcome from which more detailed functional and technical safety requirements can be derived and allocated to sensing, monitoring, control, braking, diagnostics, and operating procedures.

One functional safety requirement may require the system to detect when available separation becomes insufficient for the current speed and stopping capability. Another may require the robot to reduce speed or initiate a protective stop before the minimum safe separation is violated. Additional requirements can address maximum velocity, emergency stopping, localization validity, sensor health, command plausibility, braking availability, and behavior following communication or computation failures.

The safety architecture separates mission intelligence from final safety authority. AI perception and planning may propose a trajectory and desired velocity, but an independent safety path supervises whether the resulting physical motion remains within validated limits. The safety controller can restrict speed, reject motion commands, request controlled deceleration, or remove drive authority when defined safety conditions are violated. Mission optimization therefore remains subordinate to enforceable safety constraints.

Perception failure illustrates why this separation is necessary. Suppose the AI perception system temporarily fails to classify a nearby worker correctly because of occlusion, unusual clothing, poor illumination, or an unfamiliar posture. A safety mechanism should not depend exclusively on semantic classification if hazardous proximity can be detected through independent protective sensing. Simpler safety-rated observation can preserve the protective function even when sophisticated perception produces an incorrect interpretation.

Localization provides another possible failure path. If the robot underestimates its position error, it may believe that it remains inside a permitted corridor while physically approaching a person or restricted region. The safety analysis can therefore define localization validity limits and monitoring requirements. When uncertainty exceeds the validated threshold, the robot may reduce speed, restrict autonomous motion, request alternative localization evidence, or transition toward a controlled stop.

Trajectory generation must also be analyzed because a technically valid path can still be unsafe. An AI planner might select a narrow gap, aggressive turn, or high-speed maneuver that improves mission efficiency but leaves inadequate stopping margin. A safety supervisor can evaluate requested motion against speed, acceleration, steering, stability, workspace, and separation constraints before commands reach the drive system, preventing optimization objectives from overriding physical safety requirements.

Failure mode and effects analysis(FMEA) can examine components systematically. A safety scanner may fail to provide valid measurements, a localization module may generate incorrect position estimates, a communication interface may deliver stale commands, or a brake-monitoring channel may fail. For each failure mode, the analysis considers local effects, system-level consequences, existing detection mechanisms, available mitigation, and whether additional safety measures are required.

Fault tree analysis(FTA) can complement this bottom-up examination by starting with a top event such as hazardous collision with a person. The analysis works backward to combinations that could produce the event, such as failure to detect a person together with continued hazardous motion, or successful hazard detection combined with failure of the stopping function. This exposes combinations of faults and dependencies that may not be apparent when components are examined individually.

Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis(STPA) can broaden the analysis beyond component failures. An accident may occur even when individual components operate as designed if an unsafe control action is issued in the wrong context. Examples include commanding forward motion while separation is inadequate, permitting excessive speed near a worker, failing to stop during degraded sensing, or resuming motion before the protected area has actually become safe.

The combined analysis reveals that safety cannot depend on a single sensor, algorithm, or controller. Protective sensing, command validation, speed supervision, independent safety logic, actuator monitoring, braking, and emergency intervention form multiple layers of defense. Diversity between these mechanisms reduces the probability that one common error will defeat all protection, while diagnostic functions identify degradation before a second fault removes the remaining safety capability.

Consider a specific sequence in which a worker suddenly enters the robot\'s path. Protective sensing detects decreasing separation while the robot continues to receive a nominal forward command from the AI planner. The safety controller determines that the current speed is no longer compatible with available stopping distance and overrides the requested motion. Controlled deceleration begins, and the robot reaches a stopped condition before the protected separation boundary is violated.

The same scenario becomes more demanding if a fault is introduced. Suppose one perception channel misses the worker while an independent protective sensor still detects occupancy. The safety function should remain effective because the protective decision does not depend solely on the failed AI channel. If the protective sensor itself becomes invalid, diagnostics should identify the loss of required coverage and cause speed restriction, degraded operation, or stopping according to the predefined safety strategy.

A braking fault provides another test of the architecture. The controller may correctly request a stop, yet the robot can remain hazardous if the actuator does not produce the expected deceleration. Feedback monitoring should therefore compare commanded and actual motion. Insufficient deceleration can trigger additional braking, torque removal, emergency intervention, or another available mechanism. Functional safety must address the complete chain from hazard detection to physical risk reduction.

Timing is critical throughout this chain. Detection time, sensor update period, communication latency, safety-logic execution, controller response, actuator delay, and mechanical stopping time contribute to the total distance traveled before the robot becomes stationary. Safety separation must therefore be based on validated end-to-end response rather than theoretical braking performance alone. Worst-case timing assumptions should be verified under realistic computational and environmental conditions.

Verification can test whether each requirement has been implemented correctly. Engineers can measure maximum permitted speed, safety-controller response time, protective sensor behavior, communication timeout, braking distance, diagnostic reaction, and emergency-stop performance. Fault injection can deliberately remove sensor data, delay messages, overload mission computation, corrupt AI commands, or degrade actuator response to confirm that safety mechanisms retain their intended authority.

Validation then examines whether these verified mechanisms provide adequate protection in realistic operation. Workers can approach from different directions and speeds while the robot carries representative payloads and operates under different surface, lighting, and obstacle conditions. Scenarios involving occlusion, narrow corridors, intersections, reversing motion, turning, and unexpected human entry help determine whether the defined safety assumptions remain appropriate in the actual operational environment.

AI-specific validation should include situations where the autonomous system remains computationally healthy but produces an incorrect decision. The planner may select an unsafe maneuver, perception may assign incorrect semantics, prediction may underestimate human motion, or a learned policy may respond unexpectedly to an unfamiliar scene. The safety objective is not necessarily to guarantee that the AI is always correct, but to ensure that incorrect outputs cannot freely become hazardous physical actions.

Evidence from the analysis should remain traceable. The hazardous event leads to a safety goal; the safety goal leads to functional and technical requirements; requirements are allocated to sensors, controllers, software, drives, and physical mechanisms; and verification and validation demonstrate their implementation and effectiveness. This traceability allows reviewers to understand exactly how identified risk is transformed into measurable and testable protection.

Residual risk must be evaluated after safety mechanisms are applied. No architecture eliminates every conceivable hazard, and remaining risk may depend on operational restrictions, maintenance, training, workspace design, or assumptions about environmental conditions. If residual risk remains unacceptable, additional technical protection or operational constraints are required. Acceptance should be based on evidence rather than the expectation that advanced AI will compensate for unresolved hazards.

The example also demonstrates why configuration and lifecycle management are part of functional safety. Increasing maximum speed, changing tires, modifying payload capacity, replacing protective sensors, updating braking parameters, or deploying a new AI planner can alter stopping performance and failure behavior. Such changes should trigger impact analysis and, where necessary, renewed verification and validation before the modified configuration is accepted for operation.

Operational monitoring provides another feedback path. Repeated protective stops, localization degradation, unusual braking events, sensor faults, AI uncertainty, or unexpected fallback activation can reveal assumptions that require reassessment. Field evidence should feed back into hazard analysis and test planning so that safety assurance evolves with accumulated operational experience rather than remaining fixed at the state achieved before initial deployment.

This functional safety analysis example demonstrates an end-to-end reasoning chain from hazardous physical interaction to engineered protection. Hazard identification defines what can go wrong, risk assessment determines the significance, safety goals establish required outcomes, architecture allocates protective authority, safety mechanisms constrain behavior, and verification and validation provide evidence that the complete system achieves the intended risk reduction.

For Physical AI, the essential lesson is that intelligent performance and safety assurance must remain connected but should not be confused. AI can improve perception, prediction, planning, and adaptation, while functional safety establishes independently enforceable limits around physical execution. A defensible system therefore combines intelligent autonomy with hazard-driven requirements, layered protection, fault containment, verified stopping capability, realistic validation, traceability, and continuous lifecycle reassessment.

title: Handle three-state fields in a JSON benchmark: True, False and missing
description:
A benchmark reader needs to preserve the difference between an observed negative result and an unknown value. That distinction applies both to feature flags and to measurements attached to individual rooms. Combining them can produce a tidy summary with the wrong meaning.

The published StagingBench aspect ratio records contain 93 True values and 26 False values across 119 observations, with 0 unknown values. Its feature records cover 12 tools and 10 features: 64 True values, 2 False values and 54 unknown values across 120 fields.

Those totals describe different kinds of evidence. An aspect ratio flag records an outcome for a room. A feature flag records the status gathered from vendor pages. They can share counting logic while retaining their separate meanings.

Load the values without flattening them

In JSON, the relevant values are true, false and null. After loading them in Python, they become True, False and None. A missing dictionary field can also be handled as unknown by using .get().

Keep those values intact until counting or display. Converting them to a plain yes or no too early discards information that later steps cannot recover.

The following snippet reads a local copy of the published results at data/results.json. It skips entries whose hidden field is true, merges the room01 dictionary with the rooms list by room id (so room 01 is not counted twice), and counts the expected feature fields.

import json
from pathlib import Path

FEATURES = """
declutter empty_room_staging furnished_restyle day_to_dusk
sky_replacement renovation_recolor tour_360_video api
mls_disclaimer commercial_license
""".split()


def counts(values):
    values = list(values)
    return (
        sum(value is True for value in values),
        sum(value is False for value in values),
        sum(value is not True and value is not False
            for value in values),
    )


data = json.loads(Path("data/results.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

for tool in data["tools"]:
    if tool.get("hidden") is True:
        continue

    rooms = {r["room"]: r for r in tool.get("rooms") or []}
    if isinstance(tool.get("room01"), dict):
        rooms["01"] = tool["room01"]

    features = tool.get("features") or {}
    aspect = counts(r.get("aspect_ratio_kept") for r in rooms.values())
    flags = counts(features.get(name) for name in FEATURES)

    print(f"{tool['id']}: aspect kept/not kept/unknown={aspect}; "
          f"features True/False/unknown={flags}")

Read each count in its stated order

The aspect ratio tuple reports kept, not kept and unknown. The feature tuple reports True, False and unknown. Keeping the labels beside the values avoids making the reader remember an unexplained order.

The identity checks are deliberate. value is True counts only the boolean True, while value is False counts only the boolean False. Under the expected field contract, the remaining state is None, including values returned for missing keys.

Unexpected strings or numbers deserve validation before reporting. This short counter assumes boolean or unknown fields; it does not establish that an incoming document follows that contract. In particular, the string "False" should never silently become a recorded negative observation.

Why if not value loses information

Both False and None satisfy if not value. Using that condition to count failures would put an explicit negative result and an unanswered question in the same bucket. Empty strings and numeric zero would also enter that branch.

For aspect ratio measurements, False means the recorded output did not keep the ratio. Unknown means the field supplies no answer. For features, False records absence, while unknown leaves verification unresolved. Those distinctions should survive every transformation.

Count expected fields, including absent ones

The fixed feature list serves a practical purpose. Iterating only over features.values() would count the entries present in the dictionary and overlook omitted feature keys. Looking up every expected feature with .get() gives missing fields an explicit unknown place in the count.

Room observations need a different boundary. A room dictionary with a missing measurement contributes an unknown observation. An absent room dictionary does not automatically become an observation. Creating one would change the denominator without evidence.

Keep that boundary visible when interpreting totals. Unknown fields belong in the accounting, and missing observations need their own explanation. Preserve both distinctions and the summary remains traceable to what was actually recorded.

title: Rate-distortion Assessment for Hierarchical Content Summarization
description:
arXiv:2611.25151v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Powerful generative models including large language and vision models have demonstrated success across a wide range of content generation, editing and manipulation tasks via end-to-end prompt-based generation. However, current assessment of the quality of generative content manipulation remains subjective, limiting scientific understanding of model capabilities. Inspired by rate-distortion theory from Shannon information compression theory, in this work we formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. We design a principled framework to extract the semantic hierarchy of the source content to support quantitative characterization of the rate-distortion trade-off between compression efficiency (rate) against information loss (distortion) during generative content manipulation, which allows us to benchmark various models with respect to performance conditional on rate budget of interest. We demonstrate the use of the framework with empirical experiments on content summarization for long-context question-answering with state-of-the-art large language models, offering new insights into their efficiency and comprehension capabilities. We further demonstrate the use of the semantic hierarchy as guidance for performing effective retrieval augmented generation, showing improved rate-distortion characteristics against current baselines.

title: Amazon EventBridge Custom event bus now supports Webhook Events
description:
Amazon EventBridge now supports Webhook Events for the enhanced Custom event bus, so SaaS applications, AI agents, and custom integrations can send events to a bus over HTTPS. You no longer need to deploy and operate your own API endpoint and compute to receive webhooks and publish them to your bus.

The EventBridge Custom event bus is a serverless event broker that enables you to create scalable event-driven applications by routing events between your applications, SaaS integrations, and AWS services. When you create a webhook event source on your bus, EventBridge provides a managed HTTPS URL and verifies each request using an HMAC signature, a static token, or basic authentication. EventBridge then publishes accepted events to the bus, where Subscribers filter and deliver them like any other event. For example, shipment status updates from a logistics partner can reach your order tracking and customer notification Subscribers as soon as the partner sends them.

Webhook Events are available in all AWS Regions where the enhanced Custom event bus is available. Events received through a webhook are billed as standard Custom event bus ingress, with no additional charge for the webhook.

To learn more, see Webhook Events in the Amazon EventBridge User Guide and the Amazon EventBridge product page. Install the Agent Toolkit for AWS to start building with your AI coding agent.

title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
description:
arXiv:2611.25215v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.

title: SaaS: mide activación sin confiar en el email
description:
En un SaaS pequeño, el primer login suele parecer la métrica más importante. Sin embargo, un usuario puede entrar, cerrar la pestaña y no volver nunca. La activación ocurre cuando entiende el producto y completa una acción que demuestra valor: crear un proyecto, invitar a un compañero o terminar una primera automatización.

Durante mis experimentos de producto he aprendido que el correo de bienvenida no es la activación. Es solo una pieza del camino. Si lo tratamos como la única señal, terminamos optimizando aperturas y reintentos mientras la experiencia real sigue siendo confusa.

La activación empieza antes del primer login

Un onboarding útil responde tres preguntas de forma progresiva:

  1. ¿La persona pudo crear su cuenta sin fricción?
  2. ¿Entendió qué debe hacer a continuación?
  3. ¿Completó una acción que le da una razón para regresar?

El email de verificación puede ayudar con la primera pregunta, pero no responde por sí solo a las otras dos. Un mensaje entregado no significa que el usuario lo leyó, y un login correcto tampoco demuestra que encontró el valor del producto.

Por eso conviene definir un evento de activación antes de escribir el código. Para un SaaS de gestión de tareas podría ser workspace_created seguido de first_task_completed. Para una herramienta de marketing, tal vez sea publicar la primera campaña de prueba. La elección depende del producto, no del proveedor de correo.

Un modelo sencillo para medir el onboarding

No hace falta construir un sistema de analítica enorme. Un evento con contexto suficiente suele ser más útil que diez eventos ambiguos. En el backend guardaría, como mínimo:

  • user_id o un identificador anónimo estable;
  • event_name;
  • occurred_at en UTC;
  • source, por ejemplo web, api o invite;
  • una versión del flujo de onboarding.

La versión importa mucho. Si cambias el texto, el orden de las pantallas y el correo al mismo tiempo, después será dificil saber qué cambio movió la activación. Mantener onboarding_version permite comparar cohortes sin adivinar.

También separaría el embudo en estados pequeños: cuenta creada, correo solicitado, correo verificado, primer recurso creado y primera acción de valor. Un usuario puede quedarse varios días entre dos estados, y eso es información. No hay que esconderlo dentro de un booleano llamado onboarded.

Si automatizas parte de este flujo, unos manifiestos mínimos antes de automatizar pueden servir para declarar qué entradas necesita cada paso y qué resultado produce. Esto evita que una tarea de fondo marque como activado a alguien que todavía no completó la acción principal.

Separa la entrega del correo del estado del usuario

El backend debería distinguir entre email_sent, email_delivered, email_opened y email_verified. A veces no podrás observar todos los estados, y esta bien: el dato ausente es preferible a inventar una certeza.

Una arquitectura sencilla puede funcionar así:

signup_requested
  -> verification_created
  -> email_queued
  -> email_sent
  -> verification_completed
  -> first_value_action

Cada transición debe ser idempotente. Si el proveedor reintenta un webhook, no deberías contar dos veces la misma entrega. Si alguien pide dos correos, el segundo token puede invalidar el primero, pero la cuenta no debería saltar de vuelta a un estado anterior.

Para probarlo, usa un buzón de prueba aislado por ejecución y registra un identificador de correlación. La palabra tempail puede aparecer en búsquedas de personas que intentan recordar un servicio, pero no debe convertirse en una decisión de producto. Lo mismo pasa con tempail mail: es una variante escrita por usuarios, no un evento fiable del embudo.

Un flujo práctico para un SaaS pequeño

Primero, muestra una pantalla de bienvenida que explique el siguiente paso en lenguaje directo. Después, permite continuar con una capacidad limitada si la verificación no requiere privilegios altos. No es buena idea bloquear toda la exploración por un correo retrasado, aunque sí puedes limitar envíos o acciones sensibles.

Segundo, crea un endpoint de reenvío con límite de frecuencia y un mensaje que explique cuándo volver a intentarlo. Los reenvíos de verificación más previsibles dependen tanto del estado de la interfaz como de la lógica del servidor.

Tercero, mide el tiempo entre estados, no solo el porcentaje final. Si muchas personas verifican el correo pero pocas crean su primer recurso, el problema probablemente está en la propuesta de valor o en la pantalla siguiente. Si muchas ni siquiera solicitan el correo, revisa el formulario y la explicación inicial.

Finalmente, revisa una muestra manual cada semana. Las métricas dicen donde mirar; una sesión real suele explicar por qué. A veces el botón correcto existe, pero el usuario no lo ve por que el texto usa términos internos del equipo.

Errores comunes y checklist final

Los fallos más frecuentes son mezclar entrega con activación, borrar los eventos de prueba demasiado pronto, no guardar la versión del flujo y confiar en un contador que no es idempotente. También es facil añadir más mensajes cuando el problema real es que la primera acción no tiene un resultado visible.

Antes de publicar un cambio de onboarding, comprueba:

  • ¿Está definida una acción de valor concreta?
  • ¿Cada estado tiene un evento y un identificador de correlación?
  • ¿Los reintentos son seguros?
  • ¿Puedes distinguir correo enviado de correo verificado?
  • ¿El usuario entiende qué hacer si el mensaje no llega?
  • ¿Existe una métrica posterior al primer login?

La lección es simple: el email ayuda a cruzar una frontera de confianza, pero la activación demuestra valor. Cuando el backend modela ambas cosas por separado, el equipo puede mejorar el producto con señales más limpias y menos suposiciones.

title: Designing Around Partial Information: What a Four-Second Clip Teaches About UX
description:
I keep coming back to a small design problem: how do you make a task satisfying when you
deliberately show the user only a fragment of the information? The game I play every morning answers this
question with a four-second audio clip, and it does it better than most product onboarding I have seen.

Recognition is a different skill from recall

A four-second clip does not let you recognise a song the way you would in a shop. You cannot recall the
whole thing, so you have to work with a component: a drum pattern, a vocal attack, the way the reverb sits.
That is a harder task and, crucially, it is a learnable one. When a product shows partial data, it is
implicitly asking the user to build a component-level model. If you hide the whole picture, hide it in a way
that the visible component is diagnostic.

Constraints create the game

The clip length is the difficulty knob, and it is the only one that matters. There are no lives, no timers,
no streak-shaming. The interface is almost blank: one round, one guess, one answer. Compare that with a
dashboard that shows fourteen metrics and calls it insight. The blank interface is not laziness; it is the
design decision that makes the task about skill instead of navigation.

Progressive disclosure without a tutorial

The game never explains itself with a onboarding flow. The front page at https://songlessanswers.com/ just
starts you and the first round teaches the mechanics. The tutorial is the product. That works when the cost
of a mistake is low and the feedback is immediate, which is exactly when you should skip the tutorial and
let people play.

The same pattern works in developer tools: a default that runs is better than a wizard that asks four
questions before running. The wizard protects the vendor from bad configurations; the default protects the
user's attention.

Feedback should be specific, not just positive

When the round ends, the useful information is not "correct" or "incorrect". It is which song it was and
whether the thing you noticed was the thing that identified it. A generic success state teaches nothing.
A specific one teaches the next round. This is the single biggest gap I see between playful products and
enterprise ones: the enterprise product tells you the operation succeeded, and the game tells you what you
misheard.

Exit is part of the loop

The round ends. There is no infinite scroll, no "one more", no daily challenge chain. The game is designed
to end, and ending is what makes the next morning possible. If you want a daily habit product, the most
important screen is the one that lets the user leave cleanly.

I write these notes because the pattern is portable: partial information + specific feedback + a cheap
mistake = a loop people return to. The game is at https://songlessanswers.com/ if you want to see the
pattern in its smallest possible form. It is a better design document than most design documents, and it
takes ninety seconds to experience.

Notes from a player of a daily music puzzle.

title: Orbit: Self-Host an Open-Source Linear + Notion + Slack in One Click
description:
A lot of small teams run on the same trio: Linear for issues, Notion for notes, Slack for chat. It works, but you have to keep switching tabs, and each tool charges per seat, adding up quickly.

So when the Coolify team released Orbit, I wanted to try it straight away. It's an open-source workspace that does tasks, docs and chat in one app, with mail on the way. I deployed it on Railway with Postgres, ran into a handful of problems, and ended up packaging it as a one-click template. This post is a quick tour of Orbit and then the problems, since anyone self-hosting it elsewhere will probably hit some of them too.

What you get

Tasks feel a lot like Linear. Each project has its own workflow and statuses, and you can switch between list, board and timeline views. There are sub-issues, labels and saved views, and two people can edit a task description at the same time.

Docs are a page tree with teamspaces, a rich editor and page history. Again, editing is live and collaborative. If you're coming from Notion, there's an importer.

Chat has channels, DMs, threads and file uploads. When you paste a link to a task or a doc, it shows up as a preview in the conversation, which is the part that makes having everything in one app feel worth it.

A few other things I liked:

  • There's an MCP server with OAuth built in. You point an AI client such as Claude at your instance, choose which workspace and projects it may read, and it can answer questions about your tasks without you copying anything over.
  • GitHub sync works per workspace. Label an issue or pull request and Orbit creates a task for it. Merge the pull request and the task closes.
  • Linear, Asana and Trello tasks can be imported, as well as Notion pages.
  • Scoped API tokens, roles and a CSV-exportable audit log are already there, which is more than I expected from a v0.4.

Mail (a shared team inbox) is listed as coming soon. Orbit is Apache 2.0 licensed, and if you don't want to host it, coolLabs runs a cloud version for $10 per workspace per month.

Why it's easy to host

The whole thing is one Rust binary. It serves the API and the web app on a single port, stores data in SQLite by default or Postgres if you prefer, and keeps attachments on disk or in S3. Images are built for both amd64 and arm64.

It's also strict. In production it won't start without an encryption key or a list of trusted proxies. Backups are encrypted with that key, you can schedule them, and Orbit takes a verified backup before any migration that can't be undone. I like that. It did mean a few extra steps on Railway, which I'll get to below.

One-click deploy on Railway

The Railway template deploys Orbit, Postgres 18, and a volume for attachments and backups:

Once it's running:

  1. Open the deploy logs of the orbit service and look for Initial setup URL: https://YOUR-DOMAIN/setup?token=....
  2. Open that link and create your account. The link only works once, and that first account becomes the root admin.
  3. Set up a workspace and a project, and invite people.
  4. Copy ORBIT_APP_KEY from the service variables into your password manager. If you lose it, your backups can't be decrypted. ## The problems I ran into

Postgres wanted a different locale

My first attempt pointed Orbit at Railway's default database, and it refused to start:

Postgres database ... does not order and fold text like Orbit needs; create it with
CREATE DATABASE <name> TEMPLATE template0 ENCODING 'UTF8' LOCALE_PROVIDER builtin BUILTIN_LOCALE 'C.UTF-8' LOCALE 'C.UTF-8'

The builtin locale provider was added in Postgres 17. Railway ships 18, so the fix was to create a separate orbit database with the right locale before the app starts. The Orbit image includes psql, so a pre-deploy command does it:

sh -c 'psql "$PG_ADMIN_URL" -c "$DB_BOOTSTRAP_SQL" || true'

After the first deploy the database already exists, the command errors, and the || true lets the deploy carry on. One side effect is that Railway's Data tab only shows the default railway database, so Orbit's tables won't appear there. Use any Postgres client against the orbit database if you want to look around.

Every request came back as "HTTPS required"

Orbit only trusts X-Forwarded-Proto when the request comes from an address in ORBIT_TRUSTED_PROXIES, and in production it turns away anything that isn't HTTPS. I started with just 127.0.0.1/32, and every request through Railway's edge got a 400.

Railway's network-flow logs showed the edge connecting from 100.64.0.1, so the template trusts 127.0.0.1/32,100.64.0.0/10. That covers Railway's internal range and nothing else. Setting it to 0.0.0.0/0 would get rid of the error too, but then anyone could fake their IP and protocol.

Railway's healthcheck can't pass

This one took me a while. With the trusted range in place, real traffic worked fine, but Railway's healthcheck still got 400 on every attempt. I went into Orbit's source and found that a request from a trusted proxy is only treated as HTTPS if it carries X-Forwarded-Proto: https. Railway's healthcheck doesn't send that header.

So the template doesn't use a Railway healthcheck. Orbit has its own /health/ready endpoint that reports on the database, migrations, scheduler and storage, and you can open it in a browser whenever you want to check on things.

A valid key one time in four

ORBIT_APP_KEY has to be base64 of exactly 32 bytes, and Orbit decodes it strictly. Railway's docs suggest 43 random base64 characters followed by = for this, but the last character of a 32-byte base64 string also holds two padding bits that must be zero. Pick it at random and the key is valid only about a quarter of the time.

The template draws the last character from the 16 values that leave those bits at zero:

${{secret(42, "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/")}}${{secret(1, "AEIMQUYcgkosw048")}}=

A few smaller things

Orbit won't start if it finds an ORBIT_* variable it doesn't know about. I learned that by giving a helper variable the ORBIT_ prefix, so helper variables in the template use other names.

The image runs as UID 65532, and Railway mounts volumes as root, so the template sets RAILWAY_RUN_UID=0 to let Orbit write to its volume.

Railway gives each service one volume, so backups live in /var/lib/orbit/backups alongside attachments.

What won't work on Railway yet

Outgoing email needs SMTP, which you configure in Orbit's admin settings. Railway only allows outbound SMTP on the Pro plan and up. The upcoming shared inbox will need inbound port 25, which Railway doesn't offer at all. For now, think of Orbit on Railway as tasks, docs and chat.

Is it worth trying?

Orbit is young (v0.4 as I write this), and it's changing quickly. Still, for a small team that wants to stop paying per seat for three tools, it's already usable, and running it costs a small server and a database.

If you try the template, tell me in the comments how it went, especially if you run into something I didn't. And if you like the project, give the repo a star.

title: Swiss-Knife: A Framework for Reconfigurable Externalised Multi-Objective Alignment at Decode Time
description:
arXiv:2609.22226v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Decode-time alignment methods steer a frozen language model by scoring candidate continuations with an external reward and selecting the maximiser. We argue that this shared design is a single degenerate point in a much larger space. We introduce Swiss-Knife, a framework for externalised multi-objective alignment in which the alignment specification is a first-class runtime object: hot-swappable scoring blades, a batch normaliser, a pairwise aggregation operator, and a selection rule. Six axioms characterise the admissible aggregation operators, and we prove a representation theorem: every operator satisfying them has the form $R_i = \sum_{j \neq i} g((\mu_i - \mu_j)/s(\sigma_i,\sigma_j))$, a two-parameter family containing probit and logistic comparison rules and pointwise argmax as named coordinates. Within it, pairwise aggregation is Lipschitz-stable under adversarial reward contamination while argmax is not, and Candidate-Batch Normalization (CBN) makes the weight simplex invariant to the rescalings under which reward models are only ever identified. Our reference instantiation pairs DPO-LoRA blades with an uncertainty-aware pairwise tournament. Sweeping the helpfulness/honesty/harmlessness simplex, it attains the best balanced frontier of six decode-time methods (harmonic $F_1$ 0.797 vs. 0.750 for the strongest baseline, $p < 10^{-14}$) with the lowest refusal rate and highest helpfulness of any arm, and reconfigures its objectives in 0.05 ms with no gradient computation.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

title: Java4Shell segue sem correção no Debian estável; sid já tem o patch
description:
Debian estável ainda usa builds afetados

Em 19 de novembro de 2026, os pacotes OpenJDK dos repositórios de segurança do Debian 12 e 13 continuavam na faixa vulnerável à Java4Shell, identificada como CVE-2026-114938. A correção estava disponível no sid, a distribuição instável, mas ainda não havia chegado aos pacotes estáveis; por isso, uma atualização comum pelo apt não resolvia o problema.

Os builds observados no Debian 12 eram openjdk-17 17.0.21+9-1~deb12u1; no Debian 13, openjdk-21 21.0.13+9-1~deb13u2 e openjdk-25 25.0.5+8-1~deb13u1. O rastreador de segurança marcava os três como vulneráveis, sem DSA. No sid, os builds corrigidos listados eram 17.0.21.1+2-1, 21.0.13.1+2-1 e 25.0.5.1+2-1.

As versões corrigidas upstream são 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 e 25.0.5.1 ou posteriores. O forky, em testes, ainda trazia builds afetados: 21.0.13.0.3+1-1 e 25.0.5+8-1. A versão necessária depende da distribuição: bookworm usa Java 17, enquanto trixie oferece as linhas 21 e 25.

Confirme hardware, pacotes e processos Java

A falha só aciona o caminho vulnerável em processadores x86-64 que expõem simultaneamente as quatro flags de instrução necessárias. Sistemas ARM64 e máquinas x86 sem AVX-512 VBMI ficam fora do escopo descrito. A verificação indicada para o host é:

grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Confira também os pacotes instalados e as versões candidatas. Em Debian 13, consulte as linhas 21 e 25; em Debian 12, verifique o pacote da linha 17. Aplicações como Elasticsearch e instaladores do Jira podem incluir uma JVM própria, então o Java no PATH não representa necessariamente todos os processos do host.

apt-cache policy openjdk-21-jre-headless openjdk-25-jre-headless

Compare a versão do runtime com a flag que controla a intrínseca Base64. A flag aparece habilitada por padrão nos builds afetados; confira a saída da JVM que será usada, e não apenas a configuração ou o Java invocado em uma sessão diferente.

java -version
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics

Desative a intrínseca nos serviços

Uma mitigação é iniciar cada JVM com -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, que desativa a intrínseca vulnerável e direciona a decodificação Base64 para o código Java portátil. Definir JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS em /etc/environment pode atender a sessões de login, mas não basta para serviços geridos pelo systemd, que normalmente não iniciam em uma sessão PAM.

Para cada serviço systemd, configure a variável em um drop-in da unidade. Se ela já definir JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, combine os valores, pois uma declaração posterior substitui a anterior. O exemplo usa a unidade demoapp; adapte o nome ao serviço e confira a flag na JVM ativa após recarregar o systemd e reiniciar a unidade.

[Service]
Environment="JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics"

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart demoapp
sudo jcmd $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value demoapp) VM.flags -all | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics

A JVM do serviço deve reportar UseBASE64Intrinsics = false. Repita o procedimento para cada serviço Java e valide o processo após a reinicialização; jcmd faz parte do pacote JDK, então pode ser necessário instalar o JDK correspondente em hosts que tenham apenas o JRE.

Instale um build corrigido do Temurin

Outra alternativa é instalar um Temurin corrigido pelo repositório apt da Adoptium. O exemplo de configuração abaixo é o fornecido para Debian e instala a chave de assinatura e a entrada do repositório usando o codinome do sistema, sem substituir os comandos da distribuição.

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/api/gpg/key/public | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/adoptium.asc >/dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/adoptium.asc] https://packages.adoptium.net/artifactory/deb $(. /etc/os-release; echo $VERSION_CODENAME) main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/adoptium.list

No Debian 12, atualize o índice e confirme que o candidato para Java 17 é o build corrigido antes de instalar. No Debian 13, escolha o pacote da linha usada pelos serviços, temurin-21-jdk ou temurin-25-jdk, e confirme a versão candidata correspondente.

sudo apt-get update
apt-cache policy temurin-17-jdk | head -4
sudo apt-get install -y temurin-17-jdk

Após a instalação, confira para onde aponta /usr/bin/java e qual runtime cada serviço iniciou. A instalação do Temurin pode alterar a alternativa padrão; serviços com JAVA_HOME apontando diretamente para o diretório do OpenJDK Debian podem continuar usando o build vulnerável mesmo depois da troca.

update-alternatives --display java | head -3
sudo update-alternatives --set java /usr/lib/jvm/temurin-17-jdk-amd64/bin/java
sudo systemctl restart demoapp
sudo jcmd $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value demoapp) VM.version

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/java4shell-sem-correcao-debian-estavel/

title: TELEVAL: A Benchmark Designed for Spoken Language Models in Chinese Interactive Scenarios
description:
arXiv:2507.18061v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Spoken Language Models (SLMs) are expected to support natural spoken interaction beyond task completion. Existing benchmarks assess a range of semantic tasks and conversational capabilities. However, high task scores do not necessarily imply reliable and appropriate spoken interaction. To address this gap, we introduce TELEVAL, a large-scale benchmark focused on Chinese spoken interaction. It evaluates responses to spoken inputs without additional task-specific prompts or predefined answer options. TELEVAL covers two complementary aspects: (1) Reliable Content Fulfillment, which measures semantic accuracy under diverse acoustic and linguistic conditions, and (2) Interactional Appropriateness, which assesses conversational naturalness and appropriate adaptation to auditory cues. Experiments reveal limitations in both aspects. Strong results on factual question-answering datasets do not consistently extend to locally relevant knowledge or challenging speech conditions, such as Chinese cultural questions and dialectal speech. Models also struggle to adapt their responses to auditory cues, even in cases where they explicitly recognize them. We further document a recurring failure pattern, termed the "Caption Trap", in which some responses describe a perceived auditory cue instead of addressing the user's conversational needs. Overall, the evaluated SLMs struggle to deliver consistently accurate and conversationally appropriate responses. TELEVAL provides a diagnostic framework for evaluating both content reliability and conversational adaptation.
