title: You Don't Need a Design System. You Need Ten Decisions Written Down.
description:
"We should build a design system" is one of the most expensive sentences a small team can say out loud.

It sounds responsible. Big companies have them. Every conference talk about consistency ends with one. But a design system as usually pictured — a documented component library with tokens, variants, a Storybook, a versioning policy and a team to maintain it — is infrastructure. Infrastructure has a cost, and for a three-person startup shipping its first product, that cost often arrives long before the benefit.

What the team actually wants is smaller: screens that look like they belong together, and fewer arguments about padding. You can get most of that with ten decisions written down on one page.

What a design system is really for

Strip the ceremony away and a design system does three things:

  1. It removes repeated decisions. Nobody re-picks the button radius every time they build a form.
  2. It makes inconsistency visible. If the rules are written down, a deviation is either a bug or a deliberate exception.
  3. It lets more people build without a designer in every thread.

The third one is the only one that truly needs scale. The first two work with a team of two. So the question isn't "should we have a design system?" It's "which decisions are we making over and over, and can we make them once?"

The ten decisions

Here is the list we'd write before building any component library. Each is a short answer, not a document.

1. Colors, with jobs. One ink color for text, one background, one surface for cards, one accent, and the status colors (success, warning, error). Name them by job — text, surface, accent — not by hue. "Blue-500" tells you nothing about when to use it.

2. Neutral scale. Four or five greys for borders, muted text, disabled states and dividers. Resist adding a sixth.

3. Type scale. A handful of sizes — say body, small, large, and two or three heading levels — with line heights attached. Pick one typeface, maybe two. Decide the weights you'll use and ignore the rest.

4. Spacing scale. A short list of values built on a base unit (4 or 8 pixels is common). The value isn't in the specific numbers; it's that everyone picks from the same list instead of typing 13px.

5. Radius. One or two values. Cards and buttons usually share one; pills and avatars get another.

6. Borders and shadows. Decide whether the interface separates things with lines, shadows, or background shifts, and then mostly stick to that one. Mixing all three is a common source of "something feels off."

7. Button hierarchy. Primary, secondary, and a quiet text-style button. Decide the rule: one primary per view. Write down the destructive variant too, because it will be needed at 11 p.m. before a release.

8. Form fields. Height, label position, error message placement, focus ring. Forms are where inconsistency is most visible to users and most painful to fix later.

9. States. Every interactive element has hover, focus, active, disabled, loading. Decide once what each looks like. Empty states and error states belong here too — they're the screens teams forget to design.

10. Motion. One easing curve and two or three durations. If you use animation at all, it should feel like one product moved it.

That's the whole list. If a team can answer all ten, it already has a design system in the sense that matters. It just lives in a page instead of a package.

Where to write it down

The best format is the one people will actually open. For most small teams that means one of:

  • CSS variables (or a theme file) in the codebase. The decisions become code, so they can't drift from what's shipped. This is the most durable option.
  • A single page in your design tool, showing the colors, type, spacing and the five or six core components.
  • A short README next to the code explaining the rules in words: "one primary button per view," "errors appear under the field, never in a toast."

Notice what's missing: a documentation site. That can come later, if ever.

The crucial part is that design tokens exist in the code, not just in the mockups. A mockup that says "16px" and a codebase with 14 different paddings is the usual gap. Close that gap first.

Components: build the boring ones, late

Once the ten decisions exist, you can build components. But build them from real screens, not from imagination.

A reliable sequence:

  • Build the product screens first, using the tokens.
  • When you copy the same thing a third time, extract it into a component. Two is a coincidence; three is a pattern.
  • Start with the boring components: button, input, card, modal, tag. These show up everywhere and have the clearest shape.
  • Leave the clever ones (data tables with every feature, multi-step wizards) until the product demands them.

Extracting too early is a real cost. You guess at the variants people will need, guess wrong, and then work around your own abstraction. A component with eleven props and three of them unused is a sign it was designed before it was needed.

What to skip at the start

  • Full documentation for every component. If the component is used in four places, the code is the documentation.
  • Dark mode, unless your users ask. If your tokens are named by job, you can add it later without a rewrite. If they're named by hue, you'll be sorry.
  • A separate "design system team." At small scale, whoever builds the screen owns the rules.
  • Pixel-perfect parity between tools. Matching your design file to your code to the last decimal is a time sink. Match the decisions, not the decimals.
  • Perfect naming. A decent name that everyone uses beats a perfect one that's argued about.

When it's time for the full version

A real component library starts to pay for itself when some of these become true:

  • More than one product or surface shares the same look (marketing site, app, admin, mobile).
  • More than a few people ship UI, and review comments are mostly about consistency.
  • You've started to see the same bug fixed in multiple places because the same pattern was copied.
  • New hires spend their first weeks asking "which button do we use?"
  • Accessibility has become a requirement you need to guarantee, not just hope for. A shared, tested component is the best place to get focus handling and keyboard behaviour right once.

If you recognize two or three of these, it's time to promote the page into a package. And because you wrote the ten decisions first, the migration is mostly mechanical.

A one-afternoon exercise

If your product already exists, here's a quick way to start:

  1. Open five of your main screens side by side.
  2. List every distinct text size, color and corner radius you can see.
  3. Circle the ones that look like accidents.
  4. Pick the survivors. Those are your scales.
  5. Replace the strays in code with the tokens, one screen at a time.

You'll probably discover that you have nine greys and five border radii, and that nobody chose any of them on purpose. That's normal. It's also the cheapest consistency win available.

The short version

  • A design system is a tool to cut repeated decisions, not a deliverable.
  • Ten written decisions — color, neutrals, type, spacing, radius, borders/shadows, buttons, forms, states, motion — cover most of the value.
  • Put them in code first, docs second.
  • Extract components when something repeats a third time.
  • Graduate to a full library when more people and more surfaces make consistency expensive.

Which of the ten does your team still decide from scratch every time?

We're nothink, a small team that designs and builds products for startups — more at nothink.site.

title: Our website is 786 phone screens tall, and 111 of those screens are the same footer 76 times
description:
Page width gets measured all the time. I had never measured Nakodo's pages the other way, so I took every URL in the sitemap, overrode the device metrics with CDP, and read document.documentElement.scrollHeight at a phone width and a laptop width.

await page.cdp("Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride", { width: 390, height: 844, deviceScaleFactor: 1, mobile: true });
await page.goto(url);
const r = await page.evaluate(() => ({
  scrollHeight: document.documentElement.scrollHeight,
  header: document.querySelector("header").getBoundingClientRect().height,
  footer: document.querySelector("footer").getBoundingClientRect().height,
  h1: document.querySelector("h1").getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY,
}));

76 pages, twice, no errors.

The totals

At 390x844 (a phone)
Total height of the site 663,300px
That in screens 786
Median page 9,104px, 10.8 screens
Tallest /how-it-works, 14,012px, 16.6 screens
Shortest /alternatives, 3,202px, 3.8 screens
At 1280x800 (a laptop)
Total height of the site 423,716px
Median page 5,771px, 7.2 screens
Tallest /how-it-works, 8,834px
Shortest /blog, 1,822px

The median page is 1.57 times taller on the phone than on the laptop. The extremes of that ratio are interesting: the two template-heavy guides are the least affected at 1.45, because a block of monospaced message text wraps the same way at both widths, and /youtubers is the most affected at exactly 2.0, because its card grid goes from three columns to one.

Per word, the median page spends 6.15px of height on every word at 390px and 3.91px at 1280px. That is a decent rule of thumb for anyone estimating how long a page will feel before building it: on a phone, a 1,500-word page is about ten screens.

The footer is a constant 

header height, all 76 pages, both widths:     65px
footer height, all 76 pages, at 390px:     1,233px
footer height, all 76 pages, at 1280px:      501px
elements inside the footer:                   515

One value. Not a range, not a median: every page on this site carries exactly the same 1,233px of footer on a phone, because the footer is one component with a landscape drawing in it, and nothing in it is conditional.

That makes the arithmetic easy and a bit uncomfortable. 1,233 x 76 = 93,708px of footer, which is 14.1% of the whole site's height, and 111 of those 786 phone screens. The median page spends 13.5% of its scroll on it.

The distribution is the problem rather than the number:

footer as a share of page height, at 390px
/alternatives     38.5%
/tiktokers        37.6%
/instagrammers    37.3%
/blog             37.2%
...
/glossary         10.9%
/guides/youtube-outreach-email-templates  10.9%
/how-it-works      8.8%

The four worst are all index pages, and index pages are exactly the pages where a reader has not yet decided to stay. /alternatives is 3,202px tall, of which 65px is header and 1,233px is footer, leaving 1,904px of actual page: the furniture is 68% the size of the content it frames. An earlier audit of this site found that the same index pages were the most duplicated by text as well, with two thirds of their words appearing elsewhere. Two different measurements, same six pages, same cause: those pages have almost nothing of their own on them.

Where the important things sit

Every one of the 76 H1s is above the fold on a phone. There are only three distinct starting positions on the whole site, 121px, 157px and 181px, which is the page-type template showing through: a breadcrumb or an eyebrow line is the only thing that varies.

The primary call to action is a different story:

pages with a "Start free" control:            74 of 76   (/privacy and /terms have none)
above the fold at 390x844:                     2         (/, and one blog post)
above the fold at 1280x800:                    4
median distance from the top of the page:  6,704px

On a phone the median reader meets our main button nearly eight screens down. This is not obviously wrong for a content site: the guides are there to answer a question, and a button in your face before the answer is the pattern everyone complains about. It is a choice though, and until today it was an unexamined one. The two pages where the button is above the fold are the two pages someone arrives at having already decided to look at the product.

Nothing is skipped 

$ grep -c "content-visibility\|contain-intrinsic" src/app/globals.css
0

On the tallest page, 471 of its 814 elements (58%) start below the fold, and 515 elements on every page belong to the footer, the vast majority of them the paths of one drawing. All of it is laid out and painted on first load. At these sizes that is survivable, and our first-paint numbers are fine, but content-visibility: auto plus a contain-intrinsic-size on the footer is a two-line change that would let the browser skip 1,233px of landscape on every page until it is scrolled into view.

The reason I have not done it already is that contain-intrinsic-size has to be close to the real size or scrollbars jump, and I did not know the real size. Now the real size is a constant, which is the easiest possible case: 1,233px at 390, 501px at 1280.

What I am changing

  1. content-visibility: auto with contain-intrinsic-size: 1233px on the footer, measured rather than guessed, and the same treatment for the last sections of the two 14,000px pages.
  2. The index pages get content. They are short, repetitive and mostly furniture, and this is the third separate measurement that has said so.
  3. A rule I will try rather than adopt: no page shorter than four screens on a phone. Below that, the page is a list of links to somewhere else, and a reader who scrolls past it sees more of our footer than of our site.
  4. The call-to-action position stays where it is on guides, and I will put the measurement in the repository so the next person who argues about it has 6,704px to argue with.

title: VLRS-Bench: A Vision-Language Reasoning Benchmark for Remote Sensing
description:
arXiv:2602.07045v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled complex reasoning. However, existing remote sensing (RS) benchmarks remain heavily biased toward perception tasks, such as object recognition and scene classification. This limitation hinders the development of MLLMs for cognitively demanding RS applications. To address this, we propose a Vision Language ReaSoning Benchmark (VLRS-Bench), which is the first benchmark exclusively dedicated to complex RS reasoning. Structured across the three core dimensions of Cognition, Decision, and Prediction, VLRS-Bench comprises 2,000 question-answer pairs with an average question length of 129.87 words, spanning 14 tasks and up to eight temporal phases. VLRS-Bench is constructed via a specialized pipeline that integrates RS-specific priors and expert knowledge to ensure geospatial realism and reasoning complexity. Experimental results reveal significant bottlenecks in existing state-of-the-art MLLMs, providing critical insights for advancing multimodal reasoning within the remote sensing community.

title: AWS Marketplace now supports agentic payments with AgentCore
description:
AWS Marketplace now supports agentic payments over the x402 protocol, so AI agents can discover and buy select products and pay per request in US dollars through AgentCore payments, part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Agents often need paid APIs, data, or content mid-task, but access usually requires a person to sign up, add a payment method, and create an API key. With agentic payments, customers skip that per-seller setup, and charges settle on their existing AWS bill with no crypto wallet required.

Customers enable the AWS Marketplace payment connector in AgentCore payments, then they or their agents find listings through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. For example, a research agent can buy a single web search, or a coding agent can call a paid guardrail service. Customers can set spending limits, approved sellers, and guardrails before agents transact, Private Marketplace policies still apply, and transactions appear in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer.

AWS Marketplace sellers can charge AI agents per request without building a sign-up flow or billing system. They register with AWS Marketplace, configure agentic payments for their listings, and integrate the AWS Marketplace x402 SDK. AWS Marketplace collects customer payments and pays sellers through their AWS Marketplace seller disbursements, like other AWS Marketplace transactions.

The capability is available in all AWS Regions where AgentCore payments is available. To learn more, see AWS Marketplace and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To list as a seller, see the AWS Marketplace Seller Guide.

title: Spatial CSS preview puts 3D models on transform and anchor positioning
description:
Put three 3D models on a page and you get three separate worlds. Each <model> has its own space and its own lighting. If you want one block to sit on a board, you work out the numbers yourself or you write JavaScript to do it.

In a post on the WebKit blog dated November 16, Brandel Zachernuk proposes giving that job to CSS. Safari on visionOS 27.3 includes a limited feature preview of the proposed spatial CSS API, starting with the <model> element. The post says spatial CSS "is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax." That's what makes it interesting to me. The new parts look a lot like CSS you already write.

To try it on Vision Pro or in the visionOS Simulator, turn on Settings > Apps > Safari > Advanced > Feature flags > CSS Portals.

One container, one shared space

Everything starts with spatial: portal. Per WebKit, any element that can contain other elements, such as a <figure> or a <div>, can act as a portal, and all of its children share one space. The preview focuses on models, but the post says the specification is written so the approach should work for all content.

Once models share a portal, transform moves, rotates and scales them. The post says it's the same DOMMatrix class that produces 2D and pseudo-3D transforms elsewhere, but inside a portal it becomes a true 3D transform. This is WebKit's starter scene, with a board and two blocks moved off to the sides:

<div class="world" style="spatial:portal;">
  <model id="board" src="board.usdz"></model>
  <model id="octagon" src="octagon.usdz"></model>
  <model id="star" src="star.usdz"></model>
</div>
<style>
  #octagon { transform: translateX(-50cm); }
  #star { transform: translateX(50cm); }
</style>

Each model moves on its own. A model's animation timeline can only play through one sequence, and WebKit says independent transforms give you the extra freedom you need for interaction or configuration.

Anchor positioning gets a third axis

This is the part I like most. <model> is a void element, so you can't nest one model inside another to attach it. WebKit borrows from anchor positioning instead. You name an anchor on one model, point another model at it, and add position-context: anchor so the alignment applies.

<style>
  #board { anchor-name: --board; }
  #octagon {
    position-anchor: --board#octagon-position;
    position-context: anchor;
  }
</style>

The #octagon-position part is the clever bit. In WebKit's example, the board file includes two reference positions, one per slot. 3D editors call these "null objects" or "empties". The CSS points straight at a marker inside the model. You don't copy coordinates out of the 3D editor or guess at a transform. Per the post, these anchor points can be animated as well.

If you've placed a tooltip with anchor-name and position-anchor, you already know how this works. It's the same idea with one more axis.

Lighting becomes an at-rule

An environment map is the lighting that reflects off an object. It started out as an HTML attribute on <model>. Now that more elements can share one, WebKit has moved it into an at-rule modelled on @keyframes. You define it once and refer to it by name.

@environment-map {
  name: "spooky";
  format: equirectangular;
  src: url("night.hdr");
}

.world.spooky {
  environment-map: "spooky";
}

The preview supports 360-degree HDR images. Because the lighting is attached with a class, changing it is a matter of changing the class, and the cascade does the rest.

Orbiting, and leaving the window

The preview has two more pieces. portal-action: orbit lets users rotate the scene in place. It mirrors the stagemode attribute on <model>, and WebKit says it's more flexible as CSS. The post mentions pan-x and pan-y as modes that could be useful later.

The only JavaScript API is requestVolumetricScene(). When a user action calls it, the content leaves its portal and appears in the user's space as what WebKit calls a Connected Volumetric Scene. The page stays connected to the scene, so you can still add, remove or move objects.

launchSpaceButton.addEventListener("click", event => {
  const world = document.querySelector(".world");
  world.requestVolumetricScene();
});

Why CSS and not a script

WebKit's reasoning holds up. When spatial settings live in declarative CSS, media queries for aspect ratio, color theme and reduced motion can adjust the scene too. That means less JavaScript and no complicated state to keep track of. The numbers can be animated and transitioned like any other value. The post also says spatial web standards shouldn't be headset-only, since 3D content now appears on phones, tablets and computers.

Where it actually stands

To be clear about status: this is a preview behind a flag, it runs only on visionOS, and the API is a proposal. The <model> element is the part that has shipped. Per the post, it's in Safari 27 on all platforms. Spatial CSS has not shipped. The WebKit post covers only WebKit and says nothing about other engines, so there's no cross-browser story to tell yet.

If you have the simulator, rebuild the board-and-blocks demo and see how position-anchor behaves in three dimensions. WebKit is asking authors to try the preview and report issues at bugs.webkit.org. Early feedback from people building real pages is how a proposal like this gets better before it settles.

title: CodeGraph: Pre-Indexed Code Knowledge Graphs for Agent Tool Calls
description:
Coding agents burn tokens on repeated file reads. Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex scan the same functions over and over because they lack persistent memory of codebase structure. CodeGraph solves this by maintaining a live semantic graph that agents query instead of scanning files.

The project sits at 78K+ GitHub stars and trending #11 in TypeScript. It runs 100% local with a Rust-powered kernel that watches file changes and incrementally updates the graph. The MCP server exposes this graph as a tool boundary for agents.

The Problem: Context Waste in Agent Tool Calls

Coding agents typically operate in two modes:

  1. Scan mode: Read entire files to understand structure, then discard context.
  2. Edit mode: Read files again to make changes.

This pattern wastes tokens and introduces latency. A 10,000-line monorepo might require 50+ file reads per agent session. Each read costs tokens and round-trip time.

CodeGraph pre-indexes the codebase into a queryable graph. Agents ask "show me all functions that call authenticate" instead of reading 20 files to find them. The graph persists across sessions, so repeated queries cost nothing.

Architecture: Rust Kernel + MCP Server

CodeGraph splits into two layers:

Rust kernel: Watches file system events, parses code into AST nodes, and updates the graph incrementally. When you edit a function, only that function's subgraph updates. Full re-indexing happens only on initial setup or major refactors.

MCP server: Exposes the graph as a tool boundary. Agents call structured queries like find_callers(function_name) or get_dependencies(module_path). The server translates these into graph traversals and returns results as JSON.

The kernel uses tree-sitter for parsing, which supports 40+ languages. Each language gets its own parser, but the graph schema is uniform: nodes represent symbols (functions, classes, variables), edges represent relationships (calls, imports, inheritance).

Storage Format

The graph lives in a local SQLite database. Schema looks like this:

  • Nodes table: id, type (function/class/variable), name, file_path, line_start, line_end, signature
  • Edges table: source_id, target_id, relationship (calls/imports/extends)

SQLite handles query speed well for graphs under 100K nodes. For larger monorepos, the kernel can export to a graph database like Neo4j, but most projects stay under the SQLite threshold.

Query Interface: Structured vs. Natural Language

The MCP server exposes two query modes:

Structured queries: Direct graph operations. Example:

{
  "tool": "codegraph.find_callers",
  "arguments": {
    "function_name": "authenticate",
    "max_depth": 2
  }
}

Returns a list of functions that call authenticate, plus functions that call those functions (up to depth 2).

Natural language queries: The server embeds a small LLM (Phi-3 or similar) that translates plain English into structured queries. Example: "What functions depend on the database connection?" becomes a graph traversal for all nodes with edges to the db_connection module.

Natural language queries add 50-200ms latency but reduce the need for agents to understand the graph schema.

Incremental Updates: How the Kernel Avoids Full Re-Indexing

File watching uses platform-native APIs (FSEvents on macOS, inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows). When a file changes:

  1. Kernel reads the diff (not the full file).
  2. Parser identifies changed AST nodes.
  3. Kernel updates only the affected nodes and edges in the graph.

Example: You rename a function from login to authenticate. The kernel:

  • Updates the node name in the nodes table.
  • Finds all edges where source_id or target_id matches the old node.
  • Updates edge metadata to reflect the new name.

This takes 10-50ms for typical changes. Full re-indexing (parsing every file) happens only when you add a new language or change the graph schema.

Polyglot Codebases: Cross-Language Dependencies

CodeGraph handles polyglot repos by treating imports as opaque edges. If a TypeScript file imports a Python module, the graph stores:

Node: TypeScript function `fetchData`
Edge: imports → Python module `data_loader`

The kernel doesn't parse Python's internal structure from TypeScript. It just records the dependency. When an agent queries "what depends on data_loader?", it sees fetchData in the results.

For deeper cross-language analysis, you run the kernel with multiple parsers enabled. The Python parser indexes data_loader, the TypeScript parser indexes fetchData, and the graph links them via the import edge.

Agent Integration: MCP Server as a Tool Boundary

CodeGraph ships with MCP server configs for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and others. The agent sees CodeGraph as a tool with these capabilities:

  • find_definition(symbol_name): Returns file path, line number, and signature.
  • find_callers(function_name): Returns all functions that call the target.
  • find_dependencies(module_path): Returns all modules imported by the target.
  • search_symbols(query): Full-text search across function and class names.

Agents call these tools instead of reading files. Example flow:

  1. Agent receives task: "Refactor the authentication flow."
  2. Agent calls find_definition("authenticate") to locate the function.
  3. Agent calls find_callers("authenticate") to see where it's used.
  4. Agent reads only the files returned by the query (3 files instead of 20).
  5. Agent makes changes and commits.

This reduces token usage by 60-80% for typical refactoring tasks.

Trade-Offs: When CodeGraph Helps and When It Doesn't

Scenario CodeGraph Benefit Limitation
Large monorepo (10K+ files) High. Avoids scanning thousands of files. Initial indexing takes 5-10 minutes.
Frequent refactors High. Agents query structure instead of reading. Graph updates lag by 50-200ms after file save.
Polyglot codebase Medium. Cross-language imports work, but deep analysis requires multiple parsers. Parser support varies. Obscure languages may not work.
Small project (<100 files) Low. File scanning is fast enough. Overhead of running the kernel isn't worth it.
Dynamic languages (Python, Ruby) Medium. Static analysis misses runtime behavior. Graph shows imports and calls, but not dynamic dispatch.

Failure Modes and Observability

Graph corruption: If the kernel crashes mid-update, the SQLite database can end up in an inconsistent state. CodeGraph includes a codegraph repair command that re-indexes from scratch.

Parser errors: If a file has syntax errors, the parser skips it and logs a warning. The graph remains incomplete until you fix the syntax. Agents see a partial view of the codebase.

Memory usage: The kernel holds the graph in memory for fast queries. A 100K-node graph uses ~500MB RAM. For larger repos, you can configure the kernel to use disk-backed storage, but queries slow down by 2-3x.

Observability: The MCP server logs every query with timing data. You can pipe logs to Prometheus or Datadog to track:

  • Query latency (p50, p99)
  • Cache hit rate (for repeated queries)
  • Kernel update lag (time between file save and graph update)

Deployment Shape

CodeGraph runs as a local daemon. Install via npm:

npm install -g @colbymchenry/codegraph
codegraph init /path/to/repo
codegraph serve

The kernel starts in the background and watches the repo. The MCP server listens on localhost:3000. Agents connect via HTTP or WebSocket.

For team deployments, you can run CodeGraph on a shared server and point multiple agents at the same MCP endpoint. This works if everyone on the team uses the same codebase. If developers work on different branches, each needs their own CodeGraph instance.

Security Boundaries

CodeGraph runs locally and never sends code to external servers. The MCP server has no authentication by default, so any process on the same machine can query the graph. For production deployments, you should:

  • Run the MCP server behind a reverse proxy with API key auth.
  • Restrict file system access so the kernel can only read the target repo.
  • Disable natural language queries if you don't want to run a local LLM.

The kernel has read-only access to the file system. It never writes to source files, only to the SQLite database.

Technical Verdict

Use CodeGraph when:

  • You work on a monorepo with 1K+ files and agents repeatedly scan the same code.
  • Your agents spend more than 30% of their token budget on file reads.
  • You need cross-file analysis (call graphs, dependency trees) and don't want to build it yourself.

Avoid CodeGraph when:

  • Your codebase is under 100 files. File scanning is fast enough.
  • You use a language that tree-sitter doesn't support well (COBOL, Fortran, obscure DSLs).
  • You need runtime behavior analysis. CodeGraph only sees static structure.

The project is stable but young. Expect rough edges in polyglot repos and large-scale deployments. The Rust kernel is solid, but the MCP server API may change as agent tooling evolves.

Source Links

  • CodeGraph GitHub Repository
  • CodeGraph Documentation

title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2611.25061v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/

title: WCAG 2.2 AA Accessibility Audit Checklist for Modern Web Apps & SaaS
description:
Key Takeaways

  • WCAG 2.2 AA adds nine new success criteria to 2.1, focusing on cognitive load, mobile interactions, and authentication.

  • SaaS accessibility requires testing dynamic states (modals, toasts, virtualized lists), not just static pages.

  • Automated tools catch ~30% of issues; manual keyboard and screen reader testing is non-negotiable for AA conformance.

  • Contrast ratios (4.5:1 text, 3:1 UI components) must be verified in all themes—light, dark, and high-contrast modes.

  • Document remediation in a living audit report tied to your issue tracker to prove ongoing compliance.

Why WCAG 2.2 AA Matters for Modern Web Apps

WCAG 2.2 (released October 2023) is the current benchmark for legal compliance (ADA, EAA, AODA) and procurement requirements (VPAT/ACR). For SaaS accessibility, the stakes are higher: single-page applications (SPAs), real-time collaboration, and complex dashboards introduce failure modes that static marketing sites never encounter.

The 2.2 update introduces nine new Success Criteria (SC). Six apply at Level AA. If your product targets enterprise or government buyers, a WCAG 2.2 AA checklist is now a sales enablement artifact, not just a compliance exercise.

The Six New AA Criteria You Must Test

| Criterion | Short Name | What It Breaks in SaaS |

| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| 2.4.11 | Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) | Sticky headers, chat widgets, or cookie banners hiding keyboard focus. |

| 2.4.12 | Focus Not Obscured (Enhanced) | Same as above, but no part of the focus indicator may be hidden. |

| 2.5.7 | Dragging Movements | Kanban boards, slider inputs, map pinching—must offer a single-pointer alternative. |

| 2.5.8 | Target Size (Minimum) | 24×24 px CSS hit area for icons, avatar menus, dense toolbar actions. |

| 3.2.6 | Consistent Help | Help link/chat icon must appear in the same relative order on every page/view. |

| 3.3.8 | Accessible Authentication (Minimum) | No cognitive function tests (puzzles, recall) for login/MFA unless an alternative exists. |

Note: 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance) is Level AAA in 2.2 but widely adopted as a de-facto AA standard. Treat it as required.

5-Step Practical Audit Checklist

1. Automated Baseline Scan

Run a web accessibility audit tool (axe-core, WAVE, or Lighthouse) against every unique route and major component state (open modal, error toast, loading skeleton).

  • Action: Export JSON results; deduplicate by component, not URL.

  • Gap: Automation misses focus order, drag alternatives, and authentication flows.

2. Keyboard-Only Navigation Sweep

Disable the mouse. Tab through every interactive element in this sequence:

  1. Global: Skip link → Header → Main → Footer.

  2. App Shell: Sidebar navigation, user menu, notification bell.

  3. Data Dense: Virtualized tables (ensure focus moves into rows), pagination, inline edit.

  4. Modals/Drawers: Focus trap, restore focus on close, Esc dismiss.

  • Verify: Focus Not Obscured (SC 2.4.11/12) against sticky headers (position: sticky) and fixed footers.

3. Visual & Contrast Validation

Use a contrast checker (e.g., Colour Contrast Analyser, Figma plugin, or browser DevTools) on computed styles.

  • Text: 4.5:1 (normal), 3:1 (large ≥18.5px bold / 24px regular).

  • UI Components & Graphics: 3:1 against adjacent colors (borders, icons, chart segments).

  • States: Hover, focus, active, disabled, error, and forced-colors/high-contrast mode.

  • Themes: Run the matrix for Light, Dark, and System-preference modes.

4. Cognitive & Interaction Barriers

  • Dragging (2.5.7): For every drag-and-drop UI, provide arrow-key reorder, "Move to…" menu, or input field alternative.

  • Target Size (2.5.8): Measure hit areas in DevTools (offsetWidth/Height). Pad small icons with transparent ::before pseudo-elements if visual design cannot change.

  • Authentication (3.3.8): Audit login, MFA, password reset, and account recovery. Allow password managers, WebAuthn/passkeys, magic links, or SMS/email codes without memorization or transcription puzzles.

5. Screen Reader & Live Region Testing

Test with NVDA (Windows) + Chrome and VoiceOver (macOS) + Safari.

  • Announcements: Toast notifications, form validation errors, loading state changes (aria-live="polite" vs "assertive").

  • Virtualized Lists: Ensure aria-setsize/aria-posinset update on scroll.

  • Landmarks: Unique aria-label on each <nav>, <aside>, <section role="region">.

  • Consistent Help (3.2.6): Verify help/chat link position is identical in DOM order across Dashboard, Settings, and Help Center views

Free Browser-Local Tool: Free WCAG 2.2 Audit Tool (zero signup, runs 100% in your browser)

Originally published at https://b2appsdev-del.github.io/blog/wcag-2-2-aa-accessibility-audit-checklist.html. Educational and planning guide only; not financial, tax, or legal advice.

title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research
description:
arXiv:2611.25219v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Missing data are common in biomedical research, particularly when biomarkers are costly or require invasive procedures to obtain, such as cerebrospinal fluid measures in Alzheimer's disease. Although a wide range of missing data methods exists, from traditional statistical approaches to modern machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, their comparative performance under different missingness mechanisms remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we provide an empirical evaluation of eight methods for handling missing covariates, including complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, ML-based techniques, and DL frameworks such as multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. We summarize their conceptual foundations, practical implementation considerations, strengths, and limitations. Through extensive simulations, we assess estimation bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage, and computational burden across different missingness mechanisms and proportions. An application to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project further illustrates the implications of different methods for regression analysis in a real-world biomedical setting. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for method selection and highlight remaining challenges that warrant future investigation.

title: PNG, JPG or WebP? A developer's rule of thumb for picking image formats
description:
Most image-format bugs I see in code review aren't exotic. A logo ships as a 900 KB JPG with fuzzy edges. A hero photo ships as a PNG that weighs more than the rest of the page combined. A product cut-out loses its transparency and shows up on a white box over a dark theme. All three come from the same gap: picking a format by habit instead of by what the pixels are.

Here's the rule of thumb I actually use.

First, know what you're compressing

A 1920×1080 image is 2,073,600 pixels. Stored raw with an alpha channel (4 bytes per pixel), that's 8,294,400 bytes — about 8.3 MB before any compression. Every format below is a different strategy for shrinking that number, and each one is good at a different kind of image.

  • PNG is lossless. It reproduces every pixel exactly and supports full alpha transparency. It compresses well when the image has large flat areas and repeated patterns — UI, text, diagrams, icons.
  • JPG is lossy. It throws away detail the eye is bad at noticing, which works beautifully on photos with gradients and noise. It has no alpha channel at all.
  • WebP can do both: a lossy mode for photos and a lossless mode for graphics, with alpha in either. For most web delivery it's the format to reach for first.

The decision, in three questions

1. Does it need transparency? If yes, JPG is out. Use PNG for a source asset you'll keep editing, WebP for what you actually serve.

2. Is it a photo or a graphic? Photos (people, landscapes, product shots on a background) → JPG or lossy WebP. Graphics (screenshots, logos, charts, anything with sharp text) → PNG or lossless WebP. JPG's compression smears hard edges, which is why a screenshot saved as JPG gets that halo of artifacts around every letter.

3. Where does it end up? If an upload form, email client or legacy CMS only accepts JPG, the decision is made for you — convert and move on.

What happens when you convert PNG to JPG

Two things change, and both are worth knowing before you script it.

First, the alpha channel has to go somewhere. JPG can't store it, so transparent pixels get flattened onto a solid background — usually white. A logo designed for a dark header will suddenly sit on a white rectangle. If that matters, don't convert to JPG; convert to WebP and keep the alpha.

Second, quality is a dial, not a switch. Around 85–90 is the usual sweet spot for photos: visibly identical, much smaller. Pushing below ~70 starts to show blocky artifacts in skies and skin tones. And every lossy re-save compounds the damage, so keep your lossless original and always export from it.

Common mistakes

  • Serving PNG photos because "PNG is higher quality." Lossless doesn't mean better-looking on a photo — just heavier.
  • Saving screenshots and UI as JPG and wondering why the text looks dirty.
  • Converting a transparent asset to JPG without noticing the new white background.
  • Re-compressing the same JPG over and over instead of exporting once from the source.

I wrote a longer walkthrough of the PNG-versus-JPG trade-off — when a conversion is worth it and when to leave the file alone — on the Toolonium blog. When you just need the conversion done, there's a free PNG to JPG converter that runs in your browser, so the image never leaves your machine.

title: Writing Help Text for a Tiny Game: What Three Hint Tiers Taught Me
description:
I spent a week reading the help text of a small daily word game and taking notes, which is a strange thing to do for fun. What came out of it is a short set of rules about hint copy that I think applies to every product with a "show me" button.

The game in question is a four-letter word ladder: change one letter at a time, get from one word to another, and the dictionary decides which steps are legal. It has three hint tiers. The first nudges a letter or points at a region, the second describes the shape of the route, and the third gives the answer. That structure is worth copying because it separates two different user problems that most help systems conflate.

Problem one is search. The user knows what kind of thing they need but cannot find it. The right help is narrow: name the letter, the filter, the file. Problem two is planning. The user has found things but cannot choose a route. The right help is broader: describe the shape, not the content.

A single answer button serves neither problem well. If the user was searching, the answer is too much help and it kills the task. If the user was planning, the answer is also too much, but for a different reason: it makes the decision instead of informing it. Two tiers at minimum, three if you can afford the copy.

The copy rule that follows from this is simple. Each tier should say one true thing at the size of the problem it solves. The first tier should fit in a sentence and be verifiable by trying the next step. The middle tier should describe a region without naming anything inside it. The top tier can name the answer, but it should be the only one that does.

The other thing I took away is about wording. "You're close" is not a hint. Closeness needs a scale: close in what, measured how? A hint that cannot be checked is just encouragement, and encouragement does not unstick anyone.

If you want to study a live example, this daily word ladder hooks the tiers into the graded hints and keeps the first one genuinely small. Take one on a puzzle you have already finished and read the hints from the top down. The difference between the tiers is easier to feel than to read about, and it is the part I would copy into any small game I ship.

title: Como localizar runtimes Java vulneráveis à Java4Shell no Windows
description:
Java4Shell exige verificar cada runtime

Um servidor Windows pode executar várias instalações de Java, e a correção da Java4Shell, identificada como CVE-2026-114938, precisa alcançar cada runtime vulnerável. Além do JDK associado ao PATH, serviços e aplicativos podem carregar cópias próprias que não aparecem em java -version e não recebem a atualização aplicada a outra instalação.

Os builds upstream corrigidos indicados no guia são 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 e 25.0.5.1 ou posteriores. A disponibilidade varia conforme o fornecedor: em 19 de novembro de 2026, os instaladores Windows do Eclipse Temurin ainda não tinham esses builds, enquanto outros fornecedores já ofereciam correções para algumas linhas.

Confira se a CPU pode executar o código afetado

O caminho vulnerável descrito depende da presença simultânea das instruções de CPU avx512f, avx512bw, avx512_vbmi e bmi2. Se faltar qualquer uma das quatro, o processador não executa esse trecho específico, embora a versão instalada ainda possa exigir atualização por segurança.

O guia usa uma consulta do próprio Java para identificar os recursos reconhecidos pela máquina. No teste descrito, um Windows Server 2025 em uma instância AWS m6i com processador Intel Ice Lake tinha as quatro instruções; máquinas com menos recursos ficavam fora daquele caminho específico de execução.

Builds corrigidos por fornecedor

A tabela resume a disponibilidade para Windows x64 informada em 19 de novembro de 2026. A versão e o canal de distribuição importam: alguns fornecedores já ofereciam builds corrigidos, enquanto outros mantinham instaladores vulneráveis ou ainda não listavam correções para determinadas linhas.

FornecedorBuilds ou situação informadaDistribuição e observaçõesMicrosoft Build of OpenJDK17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 e 25.0.5.1MSI ou ZIP da Microsoft; winget oferecia 17.0.21.102, 21.0.13.102 e 25.0.5.102.Eclipse TemurinSem builds Windows corrigidos; instaladores em 17.0.21+9, 21.0.13+9 e 25.0.5+8.Os builds corrigidos estavam disponíveis para Linux x64 e Macs Apple silicon; no Alpine, apenas para 17 e 21. O winget oferecia 21.0.13.9, ainda vulnerável.Amazon Corretto17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2 e 25.0.5.1.2.MSI da Amazon; Amazon.Corretto.21.JDK no winget oferecia 21.0.13.1.Azul Zulu17.0.21.1 (zulu17.70.201), 21.0.13.1 (zulu21.54.201) e 25.0.5.1 (zulu25.38.201).MSI da Azul; Azul.Zulu.21.JDK no winget oferecia 21.54.201. As builds JavaFX (fx) ainda estavam na linha vulnerável .0.3.BellSoft Liberica17.0.21.1+5, 21.0.13.1+5 e 25.0.5.1+5.MSI da BellSoft.Oracle JDK21.0.13.1 e as demais linhas .1.Página de downloads da Oracle; Oracle.JDK.25 no winget oferecia 25.0.5.1, enquanto Oracle.JDK.21 ainda oferecia 21.0.12.0.Red Hat build of OpenJDK17.0.21.1 e 21.0.13.1; a build Windows 25 ainda aparecia como afetada.Portal de clientes da Red Hat; avisos RHSA-2026:100566 e RHSA-2026:100570.

Localize cópias de Java no Windows

O script PowerShell somente leitura procura runtimes em processos que carregaram jvm.dll, serviços Java e serviços procrun, variáveis JAVA_HOME e PATH, programas instalados e arquivos java.exe em pastas bin nos discos fixos. A varredura completa também encontra cópias empacotadas em aplicativos que não estejam em execução.

No servidor usado como exemplo, a primeira varredura completa levou cerca de três minutos e meio; uma repetição com o cache aquecido levou 27 segundos. A opção -SkipDiskScan terminou em 1,5 segundo, mas pode deixar de encontrar uma JRE incluída em um aplicativo que não esteja rodando.

Salve o conteúdo a seguir como Find-JavaRuntimes.ps1. A fonte relata testes no Windows PowerShell 5.1 e não informa testes no PowerShell 7; execute em um prompt elevado e considere que a verificação integral do disco é a etapa mais demorada.

Find-JavaRuntimes.ps1: lista todos os runtimes Java em um host Windows e sinaliza exposição à Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938).

Somente leitura. Execute em um prompt elevado do PowerShell 5.1 ou 7. Use -SkipDiskScan para uma verificação rápida.

[CmdletBinding()]
param([switch]$SkipDiskScan)
$fixed = @{ 17 = [version]'17.0.21.1'; 21 = [version]'21.0.13.1'; 25 = [version]'25.0.5.1'; 27 = [version]'27.0.1.1' }
$homes = @{}
function Add-JavaHome([string]$Path, [string]$Source) {
if (-not $Path) { return }
$Path = $Path.Trim().Trim('\"')
$Path = $Path -replace '\bin\(server\jvm.dll|javaw?.exe)$', ''
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath (Join-Path $Path 'bin\java.exe'))) { return }
$key = (Resolve-Path -LiteralPath $Path).Path.TrimEnd('\')
if (-not $homes.ContainsKey($key)) { $homes[$key] = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[string] }
if (-not $homes[$key].Contains($Source)) { $homes[$key].Add($Source) }
}

1. Processos em execução que carregaram uma JVM, qualquer que seja o nome do .exe (tomcat10.exe, prunsrv, javaw)

$running = @()
foreach ($p in Get-Process) {
try { $jvm = $p.Modules | Where-Object ModuleName -eq 'jvm.dll' | Select-Object -First 1 } catch { continue }
if ($jvm) {
Add-JavaHome $jvm.FileName "process $($p.ProcessName) ($($p.Id))"
$running += [pscustomobject]@{ PID = $p.Id; Process = $p.ProcessName; Jvm = $jvm.FileName }
}
}

2. Serviços: java.exe no caminho da imagem ou serviço procrun (estilo Tomcat) apontando para jvm.dll

foreach ($s in Get-CimInstance Win32_Service) {
if ($s.PathName -match '"?([^\"]+\bin\javaw?.exe)') { Add-JavaHome $Matches[1] "service $($s.Name)" }
}
foreach ($root in 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Apache Software Foundation\Procrun 2.0', 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Apache Software Foundation\Procrun 2.0') {
Get-ChildItem $root -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object {
$jvm = (Get-ItemProperty "$($.PSPath)\Parameters\Java" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Jvm
Add-JavaHome $jvm "procrun service $($.PSChildName)"
}
}

3. JAVA_HOME e PATH, nos escopos de máquina e usuário

foreach ($scope in 'Machine', 'User') {
Add-JavaHome ([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('JAVA_HOME', $scope)) "JAVA_HOME ($scope)"
foreach ($dir in ([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path', $scope) -split ';')) {
if ($dir -and (Test-Path -LiteralPath (Join-Path $dir 'java.exe'))) { Add-JavaHome (Split-Path $dir) "PATH ($scope)" }
}
}

4. Programas instalados (instaladores MSI e EXE registram um local de instalação)

$uninstall = 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall*', 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall*'
Get-ItemProperty $uninstall -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $.DisplayName -match 'Java|JDK|JRE|OpenJDK|Temurin|Corretto|Zulu|Liberica|SapMachine|Semeru' -and $.InstallLocation } | ForEach-Object { Add-JavaHome $.InstallLocation "installed: $($.DisplayName)" }

5. Cada java.exe nos discos fixos, para encontrar JREs incluídas em aplicativos

if (-not $SkipDiskScan) {
foreach ($d in Get-CimInstance Win32_LogicalDisk -Filter 'DriveType=3') {
Get-ChildItem -Path "$($d.DeviceID)\" -Filter java.exe -Recurse -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object { $.DirectoryName -like '*\bin' } | ForEach-Object { Add-JavaHome $.FullName 'disk scan' }
}
}
function Get-JavaVersion([string]$JavaHome) {
$release = Join-Path $JavaHome 'release'
if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $release) {
$r = Get-Content -LiteralPath $release
$v = ($r | Select-String '^JAVA_VERSION="([^"]+)"').Matches.Groups[1].Value
$vendor = ($r | Select-String '^IMPLEMENTOR="([^"]+)"').Matches.Groups[1].Value
$build = ($r | Select-String '^JAVA_RUNTIME_VERSION="([^"]+)"').Matches.Groups[1].Value
}
if (-not $v) {
$out = & (Join-Path $JavaHome 'bin\java.exe') -version 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$" }
$v = ([regex]::Match(($out -join ' '), 'version "([^"]+)"')).Groups[1].Value
}
[pscustomobject]@{ Version = $v; Build = $build; Vendor = $vendor }
}
function Get-Verdict([string]$Version) {
if (-not $Version) { return 'UNKNOWN' }
$clean = ($Version -replace '^1.8.0', '8.0.') -replace '[^0-9.].*$', ''
$parts = $clean.Split('.')
$feature = [int]$parts[0]
$ver = version)[0..3] -join '.')
if ($feature -lt 17) { return 'not affected' }
if ($feature -eq 17 -and $ver -lt [version]'17.0.6') { return 'not affected' }
if ($fixed.ContainsKey($feature)) {
if ($ver -ge $fixed[$feature]) { return 'fixed' } else { return "VULNERABLE (fixed in $($fixed[$feature]))" }
}
if ($feature -lt 27) { return 'VULNERABLE (line has no fix, move to 21 or 25)' }
return 'check vendor'
}

CPU: consulta os recursos vistos pela JVM; o trecho vulnerável exige os quatro.

Java 8 não tem -Xlog, então testa cada runtime até encontrar um que responda.

$cpu = $null
foreach ($h in $homes.Keys) {
$cpu = & (Join-Path $h 'bin\java.exe') '-Xlog:os+cpu' -version 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$" } | Select-String 'CPU: total' | Select-Object -First 1
if ($cpu) { break }
}
if ($cpu) {
$need = 'avx512f', 'avx512bw', 'avx512_vbmi', 'bmi2'
$has = $need | Where-Object { $cpu -match "[ ,]$(,|$)" }
"CPU features for the Base64 stub: $($has -join ', ') ($($has.Count) of 4)"
if ($has.Count -eq 4) { 'This CPU can run the vulnerable code path.' } else { 'This CPU cannot run the vulnerable code path.' }
''
} elseif ($homes.Count) { 'CPU features could not be read (no runtime here supports -Xlog); treat this CPU as capable.' '' }
$homes.GetEnumerator() | Sort-Object Name | ForEach-Object {
$v = Get-JavaVersion $.Key
[pscustomobject]@{ JavaHome = $.Key; Version = $v.Version; Vendor = $v.Vendor; Verdict = Get-Verdict $v.Version; FoundBy = ($_.Value -join '; ') }
} | Format-List
if ($running) { 'Running JVMs:'; $running | Format-Table -AutoSize }

Execute o inventário e corrija as instalações

O guia orienta a salvar o arquivo como Find-JavaRuntimes.ps1 e executá-lo em um prompt elevado do PowerShell 5.1. O comando de exemplo, com desvio da política de execução somente para esse processo, é powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\lab\Find-JavaRuntimes.ps1.

O inventário informa versão, fornecedor, resultado da avaliação e onde cada runtime foi encontrado. No laboratório, foram localizados um Temurin usado por um serviço Tomcat, uma cópia Temurin na pasta de um aplicativo e um Microsoft OpenJDK associado ao JAVA_HOME; corrigir apenas o Java padrão não resolveria as instalações separadas.

Depois da varredura, compare cada versão e fornecedor com os builds corrigidos correspondentes e planeje a atualização de todas as cópias afetadas. A verificação deve abranger serviços e aplicativos, não só o terminal, porque eles podem carregar runtimes diferentes daquele associado ao PATH do administrador.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/guia-localiza-runtimes-java-vulneraveis-windows/

title: Game UI/UX Design Cost: Screens, HUD and Budget
description:
The short answer

UI and UX design for a hyper-casual game with 5 to 8 screens costs about $1,500 to $5,000. A casual or mid-core mobile game with 20 to 40 screens, a HUD, a shop and icons costs about $8,000 to $25,000. A complex RPG, strategy or live-service game with 60 or more screens costs $30,000 to $80,000 or more. The number of screens, and how late they change, decide the bill.

UX and UI are different jobs

  • UX design decides what the player needs to do, in what order and with how many taps. Its outputs are flows, wireframes and prototypes.
  • UI design decides how it looks: style, layout, colour, type, icons and motion.
  • UI implementation builds the screens in the engine so they scale to every device and respond to input.

Some people do all three. On larger games they are separate roles, and missing any one of them shows.

Budget bands

Game size Screens Typical cost
Hyper-casual 5 to 8 $1,500 to $5,000
Casual or mid-core mobile 20 to 40 $8,000 to $25,000
RPG, strategy or live service 60+ $30,000 to $80,000+

Implementation in the engine is sometimes quoted separately. Ask whether a price covers design files only or working screens.

What you are paying for

  1. Flow map. Every screen and how the player moves between them.
  2. Wireframes. Grey-box layouts that fix content and hierarchy before any art.
  3. Style exploration. Two or three directions for the look, applied to one key screen.
  4. Screen design. Final art for each screen, including empty, loading, error and locked states.
  5. HUD. The in-game display: health, score, controls, timers, minimap.
  6. Icons. Currencies, items, abilities, settings. Icon sets grow quickly in RPGs.
  7. Motion. Transitions, button feedback, reward animations.
  8. Implementation. Prefabs or widgets, anchoring, safe areas and input handling.
  9. Testing. Watching real players use it and fixing what confuses them.

What makes it expensive

  • Screen count. A shop, inventory, quests, settings, social, events and passes add up fast.
  • States. Each button and panel has normal, pressed, disabled and highlighted versions.
  • Aspect ratios. Phones, tablets, foldables and desktop monitors all need layouts that hold. See foldable game design.
  • Languages. German is long, Arabic is right to left, and Asian languages need different fonts. See Arabic game development and RTL and game localization cost.
  • Ornate styles. Fantasy frames and hand-painted panels cost more than flat, clean styles.
  • Late changes. Adding a feature after UI art is final means redesigning the screens around it.

The HUD deserves its own attention

The HUD is on screen for the entire game. It must be readable at a glance, stay out of the way and work under a thumb. On mobile, controls sit where hands rest, and important information should sit away from fingers and notches. In VR there is no screen edge, so information is attached to hands, objects or the world. Test the HUD in real play as early as possible.

Accessibility

Good interface design includes players with different needs: readable text sizes, colour choices that do not rely on red and green alone, subtitles, remappable controls and options to reduce motion. Building these in from the start costs little. Adding them later costs a lot. The European Accessibility Act has also made this a legal topic for some products.

Monetization screens

The shop, offers and pass screens directly affect revenue, so they get more iteration than most. Clear prices, honest value and fast purchase flows convert better than tricks, and stores have rules against misleading designs. See battle pass design and ads vs in-app purchases.

How to brief UI work

  • A list of features and screens, even if rough.
  • Three or four reference games for style, with what you like about each.
  • Target devices and orientations.
  • Languages at launch and later.
  • Whether you need implementation or design files only.

A game design document should contain most of this.

How to lower the cost

  1. Wireframe everything first. Changes at wireframe stage cost minutes. Changes after final art cost days.
  2. Build a component kit. Buttons, panels, tabs and popups designed once and reused.
  3. Choose a simple style that suits the game and scales to many screens.
  4. Reuse layouts. Inventory, shop and collection screens can share one grid design.
  5. Test with five players before polishing. Most problems appear in the first sessions.

Getting a quote

Send us a screen list and reference games. We quote UI and UX as a fixed price per milestone, and it is included in our full game packages on the offer page.

Sources: Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Designing for games · Game Accessibility Guidelines · Game UI Database. Checked November 11, 2026.

Related: 2D game development · Mobile game development · Get a quote

Originally published on A Plus Games Studio, a game, AR and VR development studio in Sacramento, CA.

title: Go 爬虫第三讲：做一个"有礼貌"的爬虫
description:
Go 爬虫第三讲：做一个"有礼貌"的爬虫

爬虫的行为规范，总结成一句话就是：别把人家网站打挂。礼貌 = 可持续，粗暴抓取迟早被封。

一、礼貌的三条做法

  1. 控制抓取频率：请求之间加延时，比如每次间隔一两秒；别像机关枪一样连发；
  2. 控制并发数：同时只开固定数量的抓取任务，别几百个连接一起压过去；
  3. 看时间段：能避开对方业务高峰就避开，深夜低峰跑批量任务是基本体贴。

二、三条线不碰

  • 需要登录才能看到的内容，不抓；
  • 反爬措施（验证码、IP 封禁后的绕行），不绕；
  • 网站的服务条款，遵守。

三、数据用途的底线

抓下来的数据自己用：不倒卖、不公开他人隐私。数据一旦流出，你就失去了对它的控制——这条线守不住，前面所有的合规动作都白做。

四、可运行示例：带延时和并发上限的抓取器

下面这段程序实现"有礼貌"的两个核心机制：请求间延时 + 信号量控制并发数。用本地测试服务器记录每次请求的时间和并发峰值，程序自己校验是否达标：

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "sync"
    "sync/atomic"
    "time"
)

// PoliteFetcher：有礼貌的抓取器
// sem 控制最大并发数；tokens 是令牌桶，ticker 每 delay 发放一个令牌，
// 全局限速——拿不到令牌的请求就等着，不会一拥而上。
type PoliteFetcher struct {
    sem    chan struct{}
    tokens chan struct{}
}

func NewPoliteFetcher(delay time.Duration, maxConcurrent int) *PoliteFetcher {
    p := &PoliteFetcher{
        sem:    make(chan struct{}, maxConcurrent),
        tokens: make(chan struct{}, 1),
    }
    // 令牌只由 ticker 发放：第一个请求也要等第一个 tick，
    // 之后每 delay 补一个。注意：令牌发放间隔是严格的，
    // 但请求实际发出的间隔还受本地调度抖动影响，约等于 delay。
    go func() {
        t := time.NewTicker(delay)
        defer t.Stop()
        for range t.C {
            select {
            case p.tokens <- struct{}{}:
            default: // 桶满就丢弃，避免令牌堆积造成突发
            }
        }
    }()
    return p
}

func (p *PoliteFetcher) Fetch(url string) ([]byte, error) {
    p.sem <- struct{}{}        // 占一个并发名额
    defer func() { <-p.sem }() // 释放名额
    <-p.tokens                 // 取令牌：全局限速，取不到就等

    resp, err := http.Get(url)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    return io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
}

func main() {
    var cur, peak int64
    var mu sync.Mutex
    var hits []time.Time

    // 本地测试服务器：记录每次请求到达的时间和并发数
    ts := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        n := atomic.AddInt64(&cur, 1)
        for {
            old := atomic.LoadInt64(&peak)
            if n <= old || atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64(&peak, old, n) {
                break
            }
        }
        mu.Lock()
        hits = append(hits, time.Now())
        mu.Unlock()
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond) // 模拟服务器处理耗时
        atomic.AddInt64(&cur, -1)
        fmt.Fprint(w, "ok")
    }))
    defer ts.Close()

    f := NewPoliteFetcher(200*time.Millisecond, 2)

    // 预热一次连接：把 TCP 建连成本排除在测量之外，只测限速机制本身。
    // 注意要读完并关闭 Body，否则连接无法复用，预热就白做了。
    if resp, err := http.Get(ts.URL); err != nil {
        fmt.Println("预热失败:", err)
        return
    } else {
        io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
    }
    base := len(hits) // 预热请求不计入测量

    // 阶段一：限速验证——单 goroutine 顺序抓 6 次
    // 同一个 worker 不存在调度竞速，测到的是纯粹的令牌间隔，结论稳定
    for i := 0; i < 6; i++ {
        if _, err := f.Fetch(ts.URL); err != nil {
            fmt.Println("抓取失败:", err)
            return
        }
    }
    rateOK := true
    minGap := time.Hour
    for i := base + 1; i < len(hits); i++ {
        if gap := hits[i].Sub(hits[i-1]); gap < minGap {
            minGap = gap
        }
    }
    span := hits[len(hits)-1].Sub(hits[base]) // 首尾跨度：5 个名义 200ms 间隔
    // 不断言每一跳精确 200ms：本地调度抖动会让单跳有 ±20ms 级浮动；
    // 机制保证的是"令牌每 200ms 发放一个"，所以断言总跨度与单跳底线。
    if span < 900*time.Millisecond || minGap < 150*time.Millisecond {
        rateOK = false
    }
    fmt.Printf("阶段一（限速）：6 次请求，总跨度 %dms，平均间隔 %dms，最小间隔 %dms -> %s\n",
        span.Milliseconds(), span.Milliseconds()/5, minGap.Milliseconds(),
        map[bool]string{true: "达标", false: "未达标"}[rateOK])

    // 阶段二：并发验证——6 个 goroutine 同时抓，信号量上限 2
    // 并发峰值是构造性保证（信号量满了就进不去），与调度抖动无关
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for i := 0; i < 6; i++ {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()
            if _, err := f.Fetch(ts.URL); err != nil {
                fmt.Println("抓取失败:", err)
            }
        }()
    }
    wg.Wait()
    peakOK := atomic.LoadInt64(&peak) <= 2
    fmt.Println("阶段二（并发）：并发峰值", atomic.LoadInt64(&peak), "->", map[bool]string{true: "达标", false: "未达标"}[peakOK])

    if rateOK && peakOK {
        fmt.Println("PASS：限速与并发上限双双达标")
    } else {
        fmt.Println("FAIL：礼貌机制没生效")
    }
}

运行输出：

阶段一（限速）：6 次请求，总跨度 1002ms，平均间隔 200ms，最小间隔 196ms -> 达标
阶段二（并发）：并发峰值 1 -> 达标
PASS：限速与并发上限双双达标

（具体毫秒数每次运行略有浮动，这是本地调度的正常抖动。）

关键点：sem 这个带缓冲的 channel 是"并发名额池"，tokens 令牌桶是"全局节流阀"——令牌由单个 ticker 每 200ms 补充一个，无论多少个 goroutine 同时想抓，请求之间都约间隔 200ms（实测 196–212ms，抖动来自本地调度）。两个机制都很便宜，但决定了你的爬虫是"客人"还是"攻击者"。

五、本讲小结

  • 礼貌三做法：控制频率、控制并发数、避开业务高峰；
  • 三条线不碰：登录墙不碰、反爬不绕、服务条款遵守；
  • 数据用途：自用，不倒卖、不公开他人隐私；
  • 核心思想：礼貌 = 可持续。

本文为学习笔记（编纂），用自己的话重写；知识点源自公开的网络爬虫行业惯例与 Go 并发编程常识。

Author: Guangyi Zhao (Ezra Zhao). Originally published on GitHub (go-study-notes); this page is a mirror archive against single-platform failure — the GitHub version prevails.
