How do I plot NMR or FTIR spectra with a reversed x-axis (ppm or wavenumber decreasing left to right)?

Set flippedCoordinates on the X axis. Zoom, pan, annotations and hit-testing all follow the reversed axis, so you do not need to transform the data.

How do I display diode array data (time × wavelength × absorbance) as a heatmap with contour lines?

Plot the matrix as a uniform heatmap with a color map, then overlay a contours series on the same data. Use the non-uniform heatmap when wavelength or time steps are uneven.

How do I let analysts drag integration limits or mark a peak region by hand?

Use editable annotations: vertical line or box annotations with isEditable set can be dragged on the chart at data coordinates. Read their X positions to define the integration window; the integration itself stays in your application code.

How do I keep zoom and cursors synchronized across stacked detector traces, such as UV, MS and pressure?

Link the charts so they share the X range and cursor. SciChart.js has a dedicated tutorial on linking multiple charts, and SciChart WPF supports the same pattern for stacked panels.

How do I stream detector data for hours without memory growth?

Use a data series in FIFO mode with a fixed capacity, so old points drop off as new ones arrive, and append in batches rather than point by point. Declaring that X is sorted and contains no NaN values lets SciChart skip those checks on every append.

How do I show a gap where acquisition paused or a detector dropped out?

Append a NaN value at the gap so the line breaks instead of joining across missing data.

How do I keep full precision for high-resolution m/z values or nanosecond timestamps?

SciChart is a 64-bit library: data series, axes and API functions use double-precision floating point, so values with many significant figures or large offsets are not rounded the way 32-bit GPU pipelines can round them.

How do I render a 96- or 384-well plate of qPCR amplification curves on one screen?

Use the SubCharts API, which places a grid of small charts on one surface sharing a single WebGL context. SciChart's worked example builds a 10×10 grid, and the same approach scales to plate layouts.

Can I reuse chart code between a WPF acquisition app and a SciChart.js review tool?

Not directly: one is C# and the other is TypeScript. The concepts (series, axes, modifiers, annotations, themes) mirror each other, so you can match behavior and styling across both, and SciChart.js charts can be serialized to JSON to save and restore chart state.

How do I qualify SciChart as SOUP under IEC 62304?

Pin a specific version, record it in your SOUP list, review the published changelog and known issues against your device's intended use, and monitor new releases for anomalies. SciChart's versioned releases and direct support make that evidence easier to gather; the qualification itself remains your responsibility.

Can SciChart be used in regulated diagnostic or medical software?

SciChart is used in rigorously assessed environments, including cancer diagnostics research with the Mayo Clinic. As a commercial component with versioned releases, documented limitations and direct support, it is easier to qualify than an unsupported library.

title: Stop Hardcoding CRM Field Mappings: Let Each Customer Map Their Own
description:
Your product syncs contacts into whatever CRM a customer connects. Your contact has firstName, jobTitle and a nested company.name.

Customer A wants those in Salesforce FirstName, Title and Company. Customer B keeps job titles in a custom field. Customer C wants Leads, not Contacts.

You can't hardcode that. Only the customer, looking at their own account, knows where your jobTitle belongs.

Building it yourself means a settings screen, field-listing endpoints per CRM, per-user storage and a hand-written transform. With ByteChef Embedded it's three pieces:

  1. A field_mapping input on the integration's workflow
  2. A Field Mapping step that applies the saved mapping
  3. A mapObjectFields config on the Connect dialog that loads options from the user's own account

This is part 14 of the ByteChef Embedded series. The full version, with every edge case and API call, is on the ByteChef blog. You need an @bytechef/embedded release newer than 0.4.0.

Two halves, one string

Design time: you declare a field_mapping input with "objectName": "Contacts" and add a Field Mapping step.

Runtime: the connected user opens the Connect dialog, picks an object type and pairs each of your fields with one of theirs.

The two halves meet on the object name. The workflow stores neither the option lists nor the mapping. Object types and fields come from the user's live connection through callbacks you write, and the Field Mapping step fetches the saved mapping by object name when it runs.

The running example

Your product emits a contact.created app event:

{
  "contactId": "c_123",
  "firstName": "Ada",
  "lastName": "Lovelace",
  "email": "ada@example.com",
  "jobTitle": "CTO",
  "company": {"name": "Analytical Engines"}
}

You want a Salesforce workflow, Sync new contacts to Salesforce, where each customer decides Lead or Contact, and which Salesforce field each of yours lands in.

Step 1: Declare the input

The Workflow Inputs panel only offers scalar types, so add this one in the Workflow Code Editor (the code icon in the integration workflow's right sidebar) and click Save:

{
  "inputs": [
    {
      "name": "contactMapping",
      "label": "Contact Mapping",
      "type": "field_mapping",
      "required": false,
      "objectName": "Contacts"
    }
  ]
}
  • type: field_mapping makes the Connect dialog render the mapping UI instead of a text box.
  • objectName joins the two halves. The match is exact: Contacts isn't contacts.
  • name is how you read the saved value: ${contactMapping}.
  • label is the heading above the mapping in the dialog.

The editor's validation list may say type must be a scalar type. Ignore it. Saving and publishing still work.

Step 2: Apply it with the Field Mapping component

Field Mapping lives under Helpers and has one action per direction:

Action Turns Into Use it
mapToIntegration your object (firstName, jobTitle) their shape (FirstName, Title) before writing into the user's app
mapToApplication their record (FirstName, Title) your shape (firstName, jobTitle) before handing a record back to yours

Both take objectName, inputType (OBJECT or ARRAY), data and includeUnmapped.

Notice what's missing: the mapping. You never wire the input into the action. At run time it finds the workflow's field_mapping input by object name and loads the connected user's saved value on its own.

Here's the complete workflow, ready to paste into the code editor:

{
  "label": "Sync new contacts to Salesforce",
  "description": "Creates a Salesforce record for every contact.created event, using the connected user's field mapping.",
  "inputs": [
    {
      "name": "contactMapping",
      "label": "Contact Mapping",
      "type": "field_mapping",
      "required": false,
      "objectName": "Contacts"
    }
  ],
  "triggers": [
    {
      "label": "Contact Created",
      "name": "trigger_1",
      "type": "appEvent/v1/newEvent",
      "parameters": {"appEventId": 1}
    }
  ],
  "tasks": [
    {
      "label": "Map to Salesforce fields",
      "name": "fieldMapping_1",
      "type": "fieldMapping/v1/mapToIntegration",
      "parameters": {
        "objectName": "Contacts",
        "inputType": "OBJECT",
        "data": "${trigger_1}",
        "includeUnmapped": false
      }
    },
    {
      "label": "Create Salesforce record",
      "name": "salesforce_1",
      "type": "salesforce/v1/createRecord",
      "parameters": {
        "object": "${contactMapping.objectType}",
        "fields": "${fieldMapping_1}"
      }
    }
  ]
}

Replace 1 with your own app event's id. For a user who mapped your fields to Lead fields, the mapping step outputs:

{
  "FirstName": "Ada",
  "LastName": "Lovelace",
  "Email": "ada@example.com",
  "Title": "CTO",
  "Company": "Analytical Engines"
}

The Salesforce object comes from the mapping too. ${contactMapping.objectType} is the object type the user picked. Rule of thumb: use the data pill when a step needs to read the mapping, and the Field Mapping actions when it needs to apply it.

The renaming rules decide what reaches the user's account, so know them:

  • Dotted paths work both ways. company.name is read out of a nested object, and mapping back builds it again.
  • Absent keys are skipped. A payload without jobTitle never blanks Title. A key present with null copies the null.
  • Unmapped keys are dropped by default. With includeUnmapped on they pass through under their original names, which a strict API like Salesforce rejects.
  • Arrays are mapped item by item, and every item must be an object.

Both actions work from a Script step too, through context.component:

function perform(input, context) {
  const contacts = context.component.fieldMapping.mapToApplication({
    objectName: "Contacts",
    inputType: "ARRAY",
    data: input.records
  });

  return contacts.filter((contact) => contact.email);
}

Step 3: Give the editor a test value

The editor's Test button runs without a connected user, so there's no saved mapping to read. Instead the actions look for a sampleMapping under the object name in the input's test value:

{
  "objectType": "Lead",
  "Contacts": {
    "sampleMapping": {
      "mappings": [
        {"applicationField": {"custom": false, "label": "First name", "value": "firstName"}, "integrationField": "FirstName"},
        {"applicationField": {"custom": false, "label": "Last name", "value": "lastName"}, "integrationField": "LastName"},
        {"applicationField": {"custom": false, "label": "Email", "value": "email"}, "integrationField": "Email"},
        {"applicationField": {"custom": false, "label": "Job title", "value": "jobTitle"}, "integrationField": "Title"},
        {"applicationField": {"custom": false, "label": "Company", "value": "company.name"}, "integrationField": "Company"}
      ],
      "objectType": "Lead"
    }
  }
}

Open Workflow Inputs, click the edit icon on contactMapping, paste it into Test Value and save. Leave the Type list alone.

sampleMapping has exactly the shape the Connect dialog saves, so you can paste a real one in later. The top-level objectType makes ${contactMapping.objectType} resolve to Lead in test runs, so the Create Salesforce record step runs from the editor too. Without a sample, the step fails with a message that tells you to add one.

Step 4: Publish and enable

  1. Publish the integration.
  2. Make sure its configuration is enabled, on the new version, with this workflow enabled in it.
  3. The user connects Salesforce in the Connect dialog and enables the workflow. The mapping shows up among that workflow's inputs.

Step 5: Wire the Connect dialog

Pass mapObjectFields to useConnectDialog, keyed by the same object name:

import {useConnectDialog, type MapObjectFieldsType, type OptionType} from '@bytechef/embedded';

interface SoqlResponseI {
    records?: Array<{Label: string; QualifiedApiName: string}>;
}

const SALESFORCE_OBJECT_TYPES: OptionType[] = [
    {label: 'Lead', value: 'Lead'},
    {label: 'Contact', value: 'Contact'},
];

const mapObjectFields: MapObjectFieldsType = {
    Contacts: {
        objectTypes: {
            get: async () => SALESFORCE_OBJECT_TYPES,
        },
        integrationFields: {
            get: async ({executeAction, objectType}) => {
                const response = (await executeAction('salesforce', 1, 'soqlQuery', {
                    q: `SELECT QualifiedApiName, Label FROM FieldDefinition WHERE EntityDefinition.QualifiedApiName = '${objectType}'`,
                })) as unknown as SoqlResponseI;

                return (response.records ?? [])
                    .map((record): OptionType => ({label: record.Label, value: record.QualifiedApiName}))
                    .sort((first, second) => first.label.localeCompare(second.label));
            },
        },
        applicationFields: {
            fields: [
                {label: 'First name', value: 'firstName'},
                {label: 'Last name', value: 'lastName'},
                {label: 'Email', value: 'email'},
                {label: 'Job title', value: 'jobTitle'},
                {label: 'Company', value: 'company.name'},
            ],
            userCanCreateFields: true,
            userCanRemoveMappings: true,
        },
    },
};

export function ConnectSalesforceButton({integrationId, jwtToken}: {integrationId: string; jwtToken: string}) {
    const {openDialog} = useConnectDialog({
        baseUrl: 'https://bytechef.example.com',
        environment: 'DEVELOPMENT',
        integrationId,
        jwtToken,
        mapObjectFields,
    });

    return <button onClick={openDialog}>Connect Salesforce</button>;
}

Each entry has three parts:

  • objectTypes.get fills the Object type select. It doesn't have to call the remote system. A fixed list guarantees the objectType the next callback receives is one you chose.
  • integrationFields.get runs each time the user picks an object type. Here it runs Salesforce's SOQL Query action on the user's own connection against FieldDefinition, so custom fields show up too.
  • applicationFields is your side of the table: fields (values can be dotted paths like company.name), optional defaultFields, plus userCanRemoveMappings and userCanCreateFields.

Using the Integration Marketplace instead of your own page? Pass the same object to its mapObjectFields prop.

What executeAction actually does

You never build it. The SDK creates it, bound to the current user and the integration instance being configured. Each call is one request to the same embedded actions endpoint the ComponentKit uses, with the user's JWT and an X-Instance-Id header. ByteChef checks that the JWT's user owns that instance and answers 403 if not, so a callback can't reach another user's account.

Two things that will bite you:

  • It resolves to whatever the action returns. It's typed as an array, but SOQL Query returns an object, hence the cast.
  • It never throws. A network error or error status is logged to the console as Failed to execute action and resolves to []. An unexpectedly empty select means: check the console.

What the user sees

The mapping sits with every other workflow input in the Connect dialog's managed view. Here's that view for a workflow with no inputs:

With the example workflow enabled, the INPUTS section holds a Contact Mapping heading, an Object type select, and one row per application field. Each row's select stays disabled until an object type is chosen, then lists what integrationFields.get returned.

There's no Save button. Every change saves on its own, 600 milliseconds after the user stops editing.

The mapping is stored as the input's value. Your app can read it back with GET /api/embedded/v1/integrations/{id} to show something like "Leads, 5 fields mapped" in your own UI. Your backend can pre-fill a sensible default with your environment's API secret key right after a user connects. Send all of the workflow's inputs when you do: whatever you leave out is removed.

Try it in the sample app

The embedded sample app ships a Field Mapping Playground at /field-mapping. It walks through preparing the workflow, describing your application's fields, mapping in the Connect dialog, reading the stored mapping back and previewing a sample record in both directions.

One warning: the sample's Integrations pages call listObjects and listObjectFields on the salesforce component as placeholders. Those actions don't exist, so the selects stay empty. Swap in the SOQL Query callback above.

Gotchas

  • Text box instead of a mapping editor? You're on @bytechef/embedded 0.4.0. Upgrade before you debug your callbacks.
  • No mapObjectFields entry for the object name means the dialog renders nothing for that input. No error, no placeholder.
  • Two field_mapping inputs with the same object name make the Field Mapping actions fail rather than guess.
  • Switching Lead to Contact keeps existing pairings, which may name fields the new object lacks. Have users review every row.
  • Rows come from your config every time. A custom field added earlier stays in the saved value but gets no row back, and the next change saves without it. If custom fields matter, list the common ones in fields.
  • required isn't enforced in the dialog. The user can close it with nothing mapped. The example uses required: false so the failure shows up as a readable Field Mapping error in Workflow Executions.
  • The mapping can't know the target's rules. Salesforce won't create a Lead without LastName and Company.
  • Build queries from values you trust. The SOQL string is only safe because objectTypes.get returns a fixed list. Validate the value if object types come from the remote system.

Before you ship

  • Run an @bytechef/embedded release newer than 0.4.0 in every frontend that shows the Connect dialog.
  • Replace placeholder callbacks with actions your integration really has. Try them in the ComponentKit first.
  • Pass environment explicitly. It defaults to PRODUCTION, and executeAction uses it too.
  • Write a sampleMapping for every field-mapping input.
  • Pre-fill defaults from your backend and point users at the mapping right after they connect.
  • Test the full loop per integration: connect, map, trigger an event, check the run and the record in the user's app.

Who owns what

You own: the field-mapping input and its object name, the workflow and its test value, which of your fields are mappable, the callbacks that decide which remote objects and fields are offered, and any defaults your backend writes.

ByteChef owns: the mapping UI, running your callbacks' actions on the user's credentials with ownership checks, storing every user's mapping, null-safe nested renaming in both directions, and the run-time lookup by object name.

One input, one step, one config object with two callbacks. Every customer gets a mapping screen for their own account.

Next in the series: Shared Connections, for when the account is yours instead of the user's, like the Slack workspace your alerts go to or the API key you pay for.

ByteChef is an open-source workflow automation and AI agent platform (Apache 2.0). Star it on GitHub and read the full guide on the ByteChef blog.

title: The Key Expires in 24 Hours. The Retry Arrives on Monday.
description:
itsvicmoreno left a comment on my last piece about the crash between the key insert and the charge, and it named the hole my run never tested. My rig crashed the receiver between writing the key and charging the card, in both orders, and measured what each shape lost. But every retry in that run arrived seconds later, while the provider still held the key. itsvicmoreno asked about the retry that arrives after the key is gone.

The provider's own docs say an idempotency key can be pruned once it is at least 24 hours old. A retry that waits past that, a dead-letter replay after a weekend outage or a row reclaimed the next day, is treated as a brand-new request. The shape as I ran it never tested a retry outside the window. So I built the weekend: same event, same $29 payment for order ORD-1042, a crash after the first charge lands, and then the retry arriving 25 hours later, after the key has expired. Two candidate fixes, and one of them survives. The other one refuses the retry and leaves the order stuck.

My claim before the numbers: the retry-age cap would be the fix, because refusing a stale retry is simpler than teaching the retry to look anything up. I was wrong about which one holds.

Problem 1: the expired key charges twice, exactly as the docs say

The control arm is the shape most systems actually have. First attempt: the charge lands at the provider, then the receiver dies before marking it done. Twenty-five hours later the dead-letter queue replays it. The provider's key is 90,000 seconds old. The lifetime is 86,400. The provider no longer holds it, so the retry looks like a new request, and the provider charges again.

Two provider charges. $58.00 for a $29.00 order. One local charge on the books, one charge the customer sees twice and nobody on our side can explain from the local record alone, because the local record says the order was charged once. The retry returned 200, status processed, and nothing in that response says anything went wrong. The double charge is invisible until the customer finds it, which is the same asymmetry as the last piece: a false "already charged" costs one charge nobody sees, and a false "not charged" costs a double charge somebody sees. This one is the second kind, and it still took a customer to notice, because our side of the record looked clean.

I ran the whole thing twice, and both runs gave the same numbers in every arm. The double is not a flake. It is what the shape does.

Problem 2: the order-id lookup makes the provider's clock irrelevant

The second arm changes one thing. Before retrying, the receiver searches the provider by our own order id, ORD-1042, instead of asking by the key. The key is still expired. The lookup does not care. The provider finds the first charge under that order id, answers "already charged", and the retry stops there.

One provider charge. $29.00. The retry returns 200, status duplicate, detail "provider already charged (order-id lookup)", and nothing is charged a second time. The order lands in "done" on the local record, which is the part the other fix never manages.

itsvicmoreno said it first in his follow-up: search the provider by your own order id before retrying, and the provider's clock stops mattering. He was right, and the run proves it in the shape that matters most: the retry that arrives after the key is dead is exactly the retry the lookup saves. The key is a convenience for the first 24 hours. The order id is the record that outlives it. If your retry path only knows the key, it has a 24-hour memory and a weekend-long blind spot.

Problem 3: the age cap refuses in time, and abandons the order

The third arm is the fix I believed in before the run. The retry path refuses any retry older than a 23-hour cap, set below the provider's 24-hour lifetime. The replay arrives at 25 hours. The receiver refuses it with a 422: retry older than cap, needs manual reconciliation.

One provider charge. $29.00. No double. The money is safe. But look at the local record: the order is still sitting in "processing". Zero local charges. The customer was charged once, the order was never marked done, and the only thing standing between that row and a human is a dead-letter entry that says "needs manual reconciliation". The cap protected the money and abandoned the job. Somebody has to go and finish it by hand, and if nobody does, the customer paid for an order the system still thinks is unfinished.

That is the honest shape of the cap. It is a backstop, not a fix. It stops the bleeding and leaves the wound open. On a quiet week, one manual reconciliation is nothing. On a weekend outage with a queue full of replays, it is a Monday morning of manual work, and every row in that queue is a customer who already paid.

Problem 4: the two fixes are not symmetric, and the order matters

So which one holds? The lookup, and it is not close. The lookup finishes the order: one charge, done on the record, no human needed. The cap refuses the retry: one charge, processing on the record, human needed. Both keep the money at $29. Only one finishes the work.

The right shape is both, in this order: lookup first, cap as the backstop. The lookup handles the replay that arrives after the key is gone, which is the common case after an outage. The cap handles the replay the lookup cannot settle — the provider that cannot be searched by order id, the lookup that fails, the answer that comes back "unknown". The cap is the fence at the edge. The lookup is the road.

The limit I have to state plainly: the provider here is a second table in the same process, modelling exactly one property — an idempotency-key lookup with a 24-hour lifetime. It has no network failures, no provider-side timeouts, no partial provider state. The 25-hour gap was simulated by ageing the stored key in place, not by waiting a day. What the run proves is the shape of the three arms against a key that is gone, not the behaviour of any real provider's prune. And the lookup only works if the provider lets you search by your own order id. If yours does not, the cap is all you have, and you should know what it leaves behind.

What do you do with retries older than the key lifetime: cap them, look them up, or let them through? I would like to hear which one your system does, and whether you found out from the design or from the second charge.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
description:
arXiv:2611.25000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model.
  At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps.
  Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

title: You Can Outsource the Work, Not the Ownership
description:
Lessons from years of turning vendor engagements into long-term wins

Recently, a colleague messaged me to say a project wasn't going well. We had brought in an outside consultant to build our disaster recovery failover plan, and the consultant didn't have the domain knowledge for our systems. The work was drifting.

My colleague's instinct was right. Instead of asking someone else to write our plans, we should have focused on learning the recovery service ourselves.

My reply was simple: never leave it to the vendor. My most successful engagements worked because I learned the platform as if I were going to run it myself, and someone on our side took full ownership. Without that, you get exactly what we were looking at.

That exchange is why I'm writing this post. Most vendor engagements don't fail because the vendor is bad. They fail because the organization hands over the problem and walks away.

Companies bring in vendors and contractors because they lack a skill. That part is reasonable. The trouble starts when the engagement is treated as insurance: if it goes wrong, it was the vendor's fault. That mindset is the root of most failures I have seen.

I'm a database and infrastructure engineer. Over the years I've led engagements with Oracle, Splunk, AppDynamics, AWS, and a managed database support provider. Every one of them paid off, some in seven-figure savings and some in ways most organizations never measure: faster incident resolution, reusable know-how, and teams that could stand on their own once the vendor left.

This post covers what made those engagements work, the stories behind them, and the mistakes I'd tell anyone to avoid.

Think like a homeowner hiring a contractor

If you hired a contractor to finish your basement, build a deck, or redo your kitchen, you wouldn't just sign and disappear. You'd learn what needs to be there, short of building it yourself.

That knowledge lets you challenge the contractor, ask questions they have to answer, and track real progress. It keeps you from overpaying, from getting cheaper parts than you paid for, and from paying for parts the project never needed.

I apply the same philosophy to every vendor engagement. I may be completely new to the technology on day one. But to make the project succeed, I have to learn it well enough to support it myself. The question I keep asking from start to finish is simple: how will my organization run this when the vendor is gone?

Story 1: Oracle GoldenGate — when the vendor becomes your teacher

I've run GoldenGate projects since my time at Verizon. One of the most valuable engagements of my career was working directly with Oracle to build bidirectional GoldenGate replication.

Bidirectional replication is unforgiving. Conflict handling, loop prevention, and trail management all have to be right, or data drifts quietly until someone notices. I didn't treat Oracle's engineers as people doing the work for me. I treated them as teachers, and I asked questions until I understood why every setting was there.

That knowledge became the real deliverable. It carried my career forward, and over the following years it saved the company seven figures, because we could design, run, and troubleshoot replication ourselves instead of paying for outside help each time.

Lesson: build learning into the engagement. The license or the statement of work ends; what your team learned keeps paying.

Story 2: Splunk — make the vendor prove your worst log

Vendor presentations are usually polished, and mostly accurate. But they show the clean cases. Every organization grows its own edge cases over the years, and a demo never covers those.

In Splunk, sourcetypes are where the parsing logic lives: how a raw log line is broken into fields you can search, alert on, and graph. During the proof of concept, I didn't ask Splunk to parse a clean, well-formatted log. I picked the worst log in the company, the one nobody wanted to touch, and asked them to prove the platform could handle it.

Their engineers wrote the sourcetype configuration to parse it during the POC. I studied how they built it, reverse-engineered the approach, and reused it to onboard logs for several other projects afterward.

That work could easily have turned into a paid professional services engagement. It didn't, because I learned how the code worked while the vendor's experts were in the room.

Lesson: design the POC around your hardest case, not the vendor's easiest one. Then learn from how they solve it.

Story 3: AppDynamics — let your internal customers certify the POC

With AppDynamics, I leaned on the vendor's know-how to write custom extensions that monitored what the product didn't cover out of the box. Getting close to their architects mattered here. That relationship is what makes or breaks an engagement like this.

But the bigger lesson was about adoption. The product teams were part of the decision and the POC from the start. They weren't handed a tool someone else had picked. They tested it on their own applications and APIs, and they liked what they saw.

So the rollout was fast. Teams adopted it without being pushed, and started thinking about how to use it in their own development cycles. The same approach worked for our Splunk rollout.

The payoff showed up during incidents. Problems that used to take hours of cross-team digging got resolved in a fraction of the time, often by Tier 1 support engineers who could now see API and database performance issues themselves.

Lesson: if one team certifies a POC and pushes the result onto everyone else, you won't get adoption. Make your internal customers partners in the evaluation.

Story 4: AWS — learn how the provider's experts think

A cloud provider is a different kind of vendor. You aren't buying a project; you're buying services, and the expertise behind them is easy to leave on the table if all you do is open support tickets.

When we worked with AWS on Database Migration Service (DMS) and AWS Backup, I treated their specialists as a source of knowledge, not just a help desk. I wanted to understand how they think about these services: where they fit, where they don't, and what trips up other customers at scale.

That understanding shaped how we designed migrations and backup strategy, instead of us discovering the limits the hard way in production.

Lesson: your cloud provider's architects have seen thousands of customers. Ask them what goes wrong, not just how to configure things.

Story 5: A managed DBA team — set the rules early, let them evolve

Sometimes you bring in a vendor because your internal bench is thin. We partnered with a managed database support provider whose DBA team covered work we didn't have the internal depth to handle alone.

At the start, I set up the procedures and rules of engagement: how work comes in, how it's escalated, who owns what, and what "done" means. It wasn't glamorous work.

But that foundation held. The support ran seamlessly for years. The rules evolved as both sides gained experience, but we never had to tear them down and start over.

Lesson: with a managed service, the first few weeks of process design decide how the next several years go.

The playbook: what to do

  1. Write requirements and expectations down up front. Vague goals give the vendor room to declare victory on their terms.
  2. Ask internal customers what success looks like to them. They become your partners in the result, not critics of it.
  3. Make the vendor prove it on your platform. A thorough POC on your complex scenarios is worth more than any slide deck.
  4. Get close to the vendor's architect. That relationship decides whether hard problems get solved or escalated forever.
  5. Learn what you'll be supporting. Even if the technology is new to you, learn it well enough to run it alone.
  6. Build learning into the engagement. Knowledge transfer is a deliverable, not a favor.
  7. Use AI for research. Before the engagement, research what success metrics other organizations use for the same kind of platform. It sharpens your requirements and your questions.

And remember: the vendor wants your project to succeed too. A failed engagement doesn't help their reference list.

What not to do

  • Don't trust the vendor to do the whole job. That's the most reliable recipe for failure I know. Work with them closely, every step.
  • Don't treat the engagement as cover. "We hired experts, so it's on them" protects no one when the system breaks after the vendor leaves.
  • Don't let one team certify the tool for everyone. Adoption you force rarely becomes adoption you keep.
  • Don't skip the hard cases in the POC. If the vendor never touched your messiest system, you haven't tested anything.
  • Don't buy what you can't support. If no one internally can run the product, you'll pay for it for years and get little back.
  • Don't let internal friction go unaddressed. Some engineers would rather build it themselves and see the vendor as a competitor. They focus on why the vendor is failing instead of sharing the context that would make the solution better.

A note for leaders

The engineer running a vendor engagement carries a lot. These projects are usually meant to solve a real problem or prepare the organization for the future, and that responsibility sits on their shoulders.

Three things help them succeed:

  • Give them time. Don't assume the vendor is doing the work and the internal owner needs only a few hours a week. If you want the project done right, budget real time for it.
  • Set expectations with the team. Make it clear why the vendor is there and what the internal owner is accountable for. Clear up concerns early, before they turn into resistance.
  • Give credit where it's earned. It's common for people to assume "the vendor did it" and overlook the internal engineer who made it work. Recognize the people who make these partnerships succeed.

How to measure success

Some wins show up on a budget line, like the seven-figure savings from owning GoldenGate in-house. Many don't, and organizations often have no KPI for them.

The measure I care most about is this: does the platform enable other people? When a Tier 1 support engineer can resolve an API or database performance issue in a fraction of the time it used to take, without escalating, the engagement worked. When teams adopt a tool into their development cycles on their own, it worked. When your team can run the platform after the vendor has gone, it worked.

Leaders should look for these outcomes and recognize the people who deliver them.

Closing thought

Vendor engagements aren't the most exciting work for strong engineers. There's process to design, requirements to chase, and a lot of time spent learning someone else's product.

But this is foundation work. Done well, it shapes how an organization operates for years. Bring the vendor in for their expertise, and keep the ownership for yourself.

If you've led vendor engagements of your own, I'd like to hear what worked and what didn't. Share your experience in the comments.

title: Website Design And Development Rfp
description:
Website Design and Development RFP: A Comprehensive Breakdown

In the realm of digital transformation, a well-crafted Website Design and Development RFP (Request for Proposal) is pivotal for businesses seeking to establish a robust online presence. However, the propensity to rely on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often leads to subpar outcomes, failing to meet the unique needs and objectives of the organization. This approach neglects the intricacies of bespoke design and development, which are crucial for capturing the brand's essence, enhancing user experience, and driving conversion rates.

The failure of generic templates and forms can be attributed to several factors:

  • Lack of Personalization: Off-the-shelf solutions are designed to cater to a broad audience, thereby lacking the personal touch that sets a brand apart from its competitors.
  • Inadequate Scalability: As a business grows, its digital platform must be capable of adapting to increased traffic, new features, and evolving user behaviors, which generic solutions often cannot accommodate efficiently.
  • Insufficient Integration: The inability to seamlessly integrate with existing systems, tools, and third-party services can lead to operational inefficiencies and a disjointed user experience.

From an engineering standpoint, there are several key takeaways to consider when crafting a Website Design and Development RFP:

  1. Customization and Flexibility: Prioritize solutions that offer a high degree of customization to align with the brand's identity and goals. This includes flexible architectures that can evolve with the business.
  2. User-Centered Design: Emphasize the importance of user experience (UX) and user interface (UI) design that is tailored to the target audience, enhancing engagement and conversion.
  3. Technical Scalability and Security: Ensure that the proposed solution is built on a scalable and secure technical foundation, capable of handling growth and protecting sensitive data.

In conclusion, the process of creating a Website Design and Development RFP requires a nuanced understanding of the pitfalls associated with generic solutions and the benefits of bespoke approaches. By focusing on customization, user-centered design, and technical scalability, businesses can ensure their digital presence is both effective and sustainable.

Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/website-design-and-development-rfp

title: Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS
description:
Uber redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while maintaining a cache hit rate above 99.9% and p99 disk-backed cache miss latency below 100 microseconds. The hybrid architecture combines in-memory keys and frequently accessed values with disk-backed storage, reducing garbage-collection overhead and memory consumption.

By Leela Kumili

title: Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?
description:
arXiv:2611.23938v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a  tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, with each document conditioned on a fact presented in the prompt. We evaluate how deeply the model believes the facts provided in the prompt using evaluations from prior work and a new Jacobian lens evaluation. We find that the belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts, making this a cheap, promising avenue for making models believe false facts, though preliminary experiments on applying it to alignment audits on the small model we studied showed negative results due to these small models often already acting as if they believed facts provided in regular honeypot system prompts. Using RL to reduce the rate at which models verbalize following a false fact in the prompt, on top of prompt-conditioned SDF, generalizes to held-out evals and almost matches SDF on some evaluations. But training against one of our metrics for belief depth makes it harder to trust those evaluations.

title: Web App Log Management for Node.js Express Rollouts (Choosing Replaceable Contracts)
description:
The hard constraint is not collecting another stream of text. A customer-support SaaS rolling out a new pricing rule behind a flag must be able to attribute the rule's cost, investigate a disputed ticket after a process restart, and replace its logging vendor without rewriting business code. Short answer: keep Node.js Express log events as a vendor-neutral application contract, send them to a hosted searchable service, and retain console output as a transport or development sink rather than the system of record. Infrai is worth trying when a small startup wants hosted logs, metrics, and the realtime channel carrying rollout updates through one REST contract, a single API key, and one consolidated bill; that breadth matters because a later migration stays concentrated in one adapter rather than spreading through request handlers and workers.

A local console file can survive a terminal closing. It does not automatically survive an ephemeral container, correlate work across an Express API process and a queue worker, or give support agents a shared search surface. Self-hosted OpenSearch or ELK can do much more, but its clusters, retention policy, access controls, and upgrades become another production system. For an ordinary web app feature owned by a junior team, that is usually the wrong first management burden.

Files stay local.

How should a startup choose web app log management?

Start with the decision you may need to reverse. For each evaluation of the pricing flag, emit an event with a stable event name, timestamp, deployment identifier, flag key, variant, pseudonymous account identifier, request or job correlation identifier, and a cost-attribution label such as pricing_preview or pricing_committed. Keep free-form messages for humans, but do not make them the only evidence. The structured event is the durable boundary.

Do not put raw ticket text, email addresses, or payment details into that boundary. This matters especially here because the hosted option has no per-user deletion route, no bulk export or subscription interface, and no exposed control for retention or cold storage. A compliance-heavy archive therefore needs a different store and a lifecycle that has been reviewed explicitly.

The flag itself also has a narrow boundary. The platform exposes flag operations, but the surface has no flag-change audit log, evaluation statistics, parent-child dependencies, deletion recovery, or client push; clients poll. Record the rollout decision in your own neutral event shape, and treat Martin Fowler's distinction between release toggles and long-lived configuration as an architectural warning, not taxonomy trivia. A pricing rule that outlives its rollout should graduate from a temporary flag.

Put the contract before the transport

The adapter should accept application events, not vendor SDK objects. Define the event schema in your repository, version it, and make the hosted sink replaceable. The same rule applies to queries: expose operations such as find_rollout_evidence(correlation_id) in your application boundary instead of allowing route handlers to assemble a provider's filter syntax.

This is not theoretical caution. The service provides search, yet the filter parameters for logs.search are not declared in discovery metadata. Pretending those filters are stable would turn an undocumented detail into application architecture. Keep search wiring inside the adapter and verify it against discovery during integration.

The following program demonstrates the cross-capability seam without inventing request fields. It loads schema-valid payloads from files, sends the metric result into a caller-selected field in the realtime payload, and uses one key and one base URL. The files are deliberate: discovery, not an article snippet, remains authoritative about each payload shape.

import json
import os
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path
from urllib import error, request

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def call(method, path, body=None, attempts=5):
    data = None if body is None else json.dumps(body).encode("utf-8")
    headers = {"Accept": "application/json", "Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"}
    if data is not None:
        headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        req = request.Request(f"{BASE}{path}", data=data, headers=headers, method=method)
        try:
            with request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except error.HTTPError as exc:
            reason = exc.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if exc.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path} failed: {exc.code} {reason}") from exc
            retry_after = exc.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("retry loop exhausted")


def load_json(path):
    return json.loads(Path(path).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))


metric_payload = load_json(sys.argv[1])
publish_payload = load_json(sys.argv[2])
handoff_field = os.environ["REALTIME_HANDOFF_FIELD"]
metric_result = call("POST", "/metrics/report", metric_payload)
publish_payload[handoff_field] = metric_result
print(json.dumps(call("POST", "/realtime/publish", publish_payload), indent=2))

Before running it, retrieve the two capability descriptions from the public discovery surface and construct both input files from their current request schemas. That public surface is self-describing and requires no key; across the platform it reports 295 routes in 20 modules, while documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages. The program uses only two production routes, checks errors, and backs off on 429. These calls report telemetry and publish an update, so retry behavior must follow the current discovery declarations rather than an invented idempotency promise.

This design has a cost. One key and one bill also mean one vendor to trust, one credential with a wider blast radius, and one outage surface across both steps. Separate the adapter, restrict where the credential is available, and decide what the application does if telemetry succeeds but realtime publication does not. Do not erase that partial failure with a cheerful except.

That is the trade-off.

Compare the operating boundaries, not the logos

The relevant alternatives are meaningfully different. No row wins every column.

Option Migration boundary Operational burden Better choice when Material limit for this rollout
Infrai Plain REST adapter spanning logs, metrics, flags, and realtime Hosted; one key across the combined path A small backend team values breadth under a consistent contract No alert routes, trace query or span tree, source-map decoding, session replay, synthetic checks, or heartbeat monitoring
Datadog Agent, APIs, and Datadog-specific query/monitor configuration Hosted, with a broad observability program to configure Logs must sit beside mature monitors, APM, and wider operational workflows The application boundary can absorb more vendor-specific concepts than a narrow log sink
Better Stack Logs Hosted logging integration and its query surface Hosted and log-focused The team wants a focused hosted log workflow rather than a broad backend API Cross-capability realtime delivery remains a separate integration decision
Grafana Loki Loki's push/query contracts, commonly paired with Grafana and an agent Managed or self-operated, depending on deployment Label-oriented logs and Grafana workflows are already organizational standards Self-operation restores control but also ownership of capacity, upgrades, and retention
Elastic Stack Elastic ingestion, index mappings, and query model Highest when self-hosted; managed service reduces cluster work Complex search, indexing control, or compliance architecture justifies the platform It is excessive machinery for a junior team shipping one normal SaaS rollout

A Datadog-plus-Pusher version of the metric-to-channel handoff would require two vendor signups, two credential sets, and glue that translates the metric result into a Pusher event while handling independent errors and billing contexts. The combined Infrai path removes that credential and integration split. It does not remove the need for an outbox or retry policy when business correctness requires eventual publication.

The limitation is decisive: Infrai is not a fit when alerting, distributed trace queries, compliance-heavy archival, or frontend crash diagnosis drives the purchase. Use Datadog when alerts and a broader APM program drive the purchase; choose Elastic when controlled indexing, export, and retention dominate; prefer Loki when the team already operates around Grafana and accepts its label model. Frontend crashes need a specialist because this surface does not include source-map deobfuscation, crash symbolication, Electron minidump parsing, or session replay. Silent workers need a heartbeat service such as Healthchecks because there is no synthetic or heartbeat monitor.

Roll out with an exit route

Ship the pricing rule in stages, but make the migration test concrete before exposure grows. First, freeze a versioned event fixture containing a flag evaluation, the attributed operation, and a worker completion. Second, send that fixture through the adapter and confirm that centralized search can recover the evidence after the application process is gone. Third, replay the same fixture through a second adapter in a test environment. If business code changes, the boundary is leaking.

During rollout, compare counts by variant and attribution label in your own reporting layer; do not claim that a flag system supplies evaluation analytics when it does not. Keep a rollback decision tied to application outcomes, and store the decision record outside ephemeral console files. Searchable logs help explain a result. They are not the result.

Finally, rehearse removal: rotate the credential, disable the sink, and verify that the pricing path continues with an explicit telemetry-degraded state. This compact drill reveals whether logging is truly an adapter or a hidden runtime dependency.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai capability sheet and generate payloads from discovery rather than copying stale request fields.

Sources

  • Martin Fowler: Feature Toggles
  • Datadog Logs documentation
  • Better Stack Logs documentation
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Elastic Stack documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Infrai capability sheet

title: Terraform: un contrato de email para CI
description:
CI puede terminar en verde y aun dejar una duda: ¿llegó el correo al buzón correcto y hay evidencia para investigar?

En equipos de infraestructura, ese problema suele aparecer como un fallo intermitente. Un job crea una cuenta, espera un mensaje y funciona. Otro reutiliza la dirección, recibe un mensaje viejo y también pasa. Días después, varias ejecuciones comparten el mismo buzón sin que nadie lo note.

La solución no es añadir más reintentos. Es definir un contrato pequeño para el email de prueba: identidad aislada, credenciales con vida corta, retención explícita y señales para explicar un fallo. Terraform convierte esa frontera en infraestructura revisable.

El síntoma: CI verde, evidencia perdida

Imaginemos un pipeline que prueba el alta de usuario. La aplicación envía un enlace, el test consulta el buzón y confirma el token. El caso básico es correcto, pero quedan varios riesgos:

  • Dos ejecuciones pueden leer el mismo mensaje.
  • Un mensaje anterior puede parecer una confirmación nueva.
  • El nombre del entorno puede acabar en una bandeja de producción.
  • Un secreto escrito en los logs puede sobrevivir mas de lo esperado.
  • Cuando falla la entrega, solo vemos un timeout y no la causa.

Por eso trato una dirección de correo falsa como un recurso de prueba con límites, no como una variable global conveniente. La dirección de correo desechable es parte del aislamiento del test, igual que un namespace separado o una base de datos efímera.

El contrato mínimo de Terraform

El módulo no tiene que conocer todos los detalles del proveedor de email. Puede declarar las decisiones importantes y dejar el acceso a un adaptador. Un ejemplo simplificado sería:

variable "environment" {
  type = string
}

variable "retention_minutes" {
  type    = number
  default = 30
}

resource "test_mailbox" "ci" {
  name              = "ci-${var.environment}-${substr(uuid(), 0, 8)}"
  retention_minutes = var.retention_minutes
  labels = {
    owner = "ci"
    scope = var.environment
  }
}

output "mailbox_id" {
  value     = test_mailbox.ci.id
  sensitive = true
}

El recurso es ilustrativo: el proveedor real puede exponer otra API o requerir un módulo interno. Lo importante es el contrato: cada ejecución obtiene una identidad distinguible, la retención no queda indefinida y la salida sensible no se imprime como texto normal.

En una implementación real evitaría uuid() si provoca cambios continuos durante cada plan. Prefiero que el pipeline entregue un identificador de ejecución como variable y que el módulo valide su formato.

Separar identidad, secretos y buzón

Hay tres datos que suelen mezclarse por comodidad: la dirección, el token para leerla y la etiqueta del entorno. Deben tener ciclos de vida distintos.

La identidad del buzón puede aparecer en logs de diagnóstico. El token no. El nombre debe incluir el entorno, pero nunca un secreto ni datos personales. El proveedor debe limitar la lectura al buzón de esa ejecución, y el job debe revocar el acceso al terminar, incluso si el test falla.

Para pruebas manuales o exploratorias puede ser práctico usar un buzón temporal, siempre que el equipo aplique la misma regla: nada de datos reales, ningún token en el repositorio y una eliminación clara al acabar.

Conviene marcar la cuenta con etiquetas como ci, pull-request y repository para limpiar recursos huérfanos. En incidentes reales he visto que la limpieza se rompe por que un paso depende del resultado del test; una tarea final independiente suele ser más seguro.

Medir antes de reintentar

Un timeout de email mezcla demasiadas posibilidades: el mensaje no se envió, el proveedor lo rechazó, el buzón no se consultó, el filtro ocultó el mensaje o el test buscó el asunto equivocado. Antes de reintentar, registraría un evento por etapa:

  1. mail_requested: la aplicación aceptó la solicitud.
  2. mail_accepted: el proveedor confirmó la entrega al buzón.
  3. mail_seen: el lector encontró el mensaje esperado.
  4. token_consumed: el test usó el enlace una sola vez.

Cada evento llevan run_id, identificador del buzón y marca de tiempo, nunca el cuerpo completo ni el token. Así se puede localizar la pérdida y reintentar solo la etapa que corresponde. El panel de CI deja de decir “esperando correo” y cuenta una historia útil.

El mismo criterio aplica a los jobs programados: estas alertas útiles para jobs programados deben distinguir una ausencia esperada de una ejecución que quedó sin limpiar.

Alertas que explican el fallo

No alertaría por cada mensaje retrasado. Usaría señales agregadas:

  • porcentaje de mail_requested sin mail_seen por entorno;
  • edad del buzón más antiguo que sigue activo;
  • número de tokens consumidos dos veces;
  • recursos CI sin evento de limpieza;
  • lecturas rechazadas por una política de acceso.

La notificación debe decir qué cambió, qué ejecución está afectada y dónde está la evidencia. Un enlace a correos de rollback con contexto operativo es más útil que mandar un mensaje genérico de “pipeline rojo”. En email de test, un asunto como CI FAIL run=1842 stage=mail_seen ayuda bastante mas durante una guardia.

Checklist de revisión

Antes de aprobar el módulo o el pipeline, revisaría:

  • ¿Cada ejecución tiene un buzón o namespace que no comparte con otra?
  • ¿El token de lectura es sensible, limitado y revocable?
  • ¿La retención está definida y tiene un límite máximo?
  • ¿El contenido de los mensajes queda fuera de los logs?
  • ¿La evidencia permite separar envío, entrega, lectura y consumo?
  • ¿La limpieza corre también cuando el test termina en error?
  • ¿Las alertas incluyen entorno, run_id y siguiente acción?
  • ¿Se puede borrar un recurso huérfano por sus etiquetas?

Si una respuesta es “depende de una variable manual”, todavía no existe un contrato operativo. El pipeline puede seguir pasando, pero la seguridad y la capacidad de diagnóstico quedan a merced de la memoria del siguiente compañero.

Preguntas rápidas

¿Hace falta un buzón nuevo para cada test?

No siempre. Para una suite pequeña puede bastar uno por ejecución de CI, con mensajes identificados por run_id. Compartirlo entre ejecuciones paralelas sí introduce carreras y hace más difícil atribuir la evidencia.

¿Los reintentos están mal?

No. Son útiles después de clasificar el fallo. Reintentar una consulta cuando el proveedor aún procesa el mensaje es razonable; repetir todo el alta sin una frontera idempotente solo añade ruido.

¿Qué hago con tempail mail en una búsqueda del equipo?

Trátalo como una variante escrita por usuarios o por documentación antigua, no como una palabra clave principal del diseño. Puede ayudar a encontrar casos históricos, pero el contrato debe usar nombres claros y consistentes.

La idea final es sencilla: Terraform define quién puede crear el recurso, CI define cuánto vive y la observabilidad explica qué ocurrió. Con esa separación, las pruebas de email dejan de ser una dependencia invisible y se convierten en una pieza revisable de la plataforma.

title: I built a job application tracker that works with AI agents
description:
Like many developers, I'm currently looking for a new job. I've applied to quite a few positions, and I quickly realized how difficult it is to keep track of everything.

There are several things to manage:

  • Finding relevant job openings.
  • Checking whether a position actually matches your experience and requirements.
  • Keeping track of the jobs you've applied to.
  • Remembering which company contacted you and when.
  • Following up on applications and keeping their status up to date.

At first, I thought about using a spreadsheet. But I wanted something a bit more useful, especially with all the possibilities AI agents offer today.

So, I decided to build my own tool: Job Applications Tracker.

GitHub: https://github.com/kapantzak/job-applications-tracker

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/job-applications-tracker

What does it do?

The idea is pretty simple: have one place to manage your job search, while letting AI agents handle some of the repetitive work.

1. Find relevant job openings

Instead of manually browsing job boards and company career pages, you can ask an AI agent to investigate the web and find opportunities that match your profile.

You provide your CV, experience, preferred roles, locations, and other requirements.

The agent uses this information to search for relevant openings and collect the results.

It's not just about finding jobs with matching keywords. The goal is to investigate opportunities and determine whether they're actually relevant to your profile.

2. Keep track of your applications

Once you find an interesting position, you can add it to your tracker.

You can keep all the important information about each opportunity in one place, including the company, position, job description, application date, and current status.

No more searching through browser history or trying to remember whether you already applied to a particular position!

3. Let AI track your application status through Gmail

This is probably one of my favorite parts.

Whenever you apply for a job, you usually receive some kind of confirmation email. Later, you might receive an invitation for an interview, a rejection, or another update.

All these emails contain useful information about your application progress.

The idea is to let an AI agent inspect your Gmail history and identify relevant updates for each application.

For example:

  • You receive an application confirmation.
  • The agent identifies the email and associates it with the corresponding application.
  • A few days later, you receive an interview invitation.
  • The agent detects the update and suggests changing the application's status.

You don't have to manually update everything. The agent does the investigation, while you stay in control of the changes.

Why local-first?

I wanted this tool to run locally rather than depend on another hosted service.

Your job search data can contain quite a lot of personal information: your CV, employment history, salary expectations, and email conversations.

I prefer keeping that information under my control.

That's why the application uses a local SQLite database and runs on your machine.

Of course, when you use an external AI model or connect to Gmail, those integrations have their own data-handling considerations. Local storage doesn't mean every external service interaction stays on your machine.

Built to work with AI agents

I didn't want to build another application that simply adds an AI chatbot to an existing interface.

Instead, I wanted AI agents to be part of the actual workflow.

The application is designed to work with different AI coding agents, including Claude Code and Codex, as well as custom agent commands.

This makes it possible to delegate different tasks to an agent while keeping the actual job application data organized in one place.

Give it a try

If you're currently looking for a job or simply want to experiment with AI agents, give it a try!

You can start it with:

npx job-applications-tracker

Requires Node.js 22 or newer.

  • GitHub repository
  • npm package

Feedback, ideas, and contributions are always welcome!

title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
description:
arXiv:2611.23702v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

title: File size is the wrong number for sizing a Java heap
description:
When a Java service runs out of memory, the first assumption is usually a leak. A leak has a recognisable shape on the heap graph: a sawtooth that never quite returns to baseline, a slow climb over days. Most of the incidents I’ve been asked to look at had a different shape. Memory sat flat for hours, went vertical on one request, and the service fell over. Somebody had sent a file, and on disk it was a few megabytes.

What a decoded image costs

Once decoded, an image costs width times height times bytes per pixel, whatever the file size was. A 6000 by 4000 photo is 96 MB in a BufferedImage at 4 bytes per pixel, from an 8 MB JPEG. An A4 PDF page rendered at 300 DPI is about 35 MB, from a file that might be 50 KB. Converting colour spaces, rotating or scaling usually allocates a second buffer while the first is still live, so one operation can briefly need double.

The default heap is a quarter of the container

With no -Xmx, the JVM caps the heap at 25% of the container’s memory limit. A 2 GB container gets about 512 MB, which fits two of those photos with working copies.

Older JDKs can’t read cgroup v2 limits, which most current Linux distributions use. Support arrived in JDK 15 and was backported to 11.0.16 and 8u372. Earlier builds size the heap from the host’s memory, so it can end up larger than the container. Java 17 and later are fine. Running java -XshowSettings:vm -version inside the container shows what the JVM actually picked.

Concurrency multiplies it

Worker pools sized by core count assume small tasks. Eight workers each holding a 96 MB image and a copy need about 1.5 GB at once. It passes every test because test fixtures are small. Bounding work by estimated memory, with a bounded queue or a semaphore, fixes more of these than heap tuning does.

Two ways to die

Heap exhaustion throws an OutOfMemoryError with a stack trace, and -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError adds a dump. Container exhaustion means the kernel sends SIGKILL and the process exits with 137, leaving nothing to debug. Setting -Xmx to the full container limit turns the first into the second, because code cache, direct buffers, GC bookkeeping, metaspace and thread stacks all live outside the heap. Direct memory alone defaults to the same limit as the heap. Start -XX:MaxRAMPercentage around 70 to 75 and measure.

Untrusted files

Image headers declare their own dimensions and decoders trust them. A single-color 20,000 by 20,000 PNG is about a megabyte on disk and over a gigabyte decoded. Read the dimensions from the header first (ImageIO’s ImageReader can do this without decoding pixels) and reject or subsample anything over a pixel limit. A limit in megabytes won’t catch this file.

What the fixes cost

Bigger heaps cost money per instance. Capped concurrency costs throughput. Strip or tile decoding helps most but depends on the API and the format, and ImageIO’s convenience methods return the whole image regardless. Subsampling costs detail, which matters if the output goes through OCR.

Before it ships

Know four numbers: how many inputs decode at once, the largest input in pixels or pages, the max heap the JVM picked in the real container, and what’s left outside the heap. Most teams find them after the first 137.

Disclosure: I work at a company that builds pure Java libraries for image and PDF processing. The arithmetic is the same whichever library you use.

title: One User-Agent string got a 403. curl, wget and Go went straight through.
description:
Where the block actually happens, measured with eight clients on the same URL.

I publish everything I build to a small private ops portal. It sits behind basic auth, and in front of that nginx there is a Cloudflare zone for the domain. Today I sent it a request from a Python client with the library's default User-Agent and got back a 403 whose body was 17 bytes long: error code: 1010. The two explanations that come first are the credential file and a forgotten firewall rule. Neither was true. The site answered normally to every other client I tried, and the only difference between the request that failed and the ones that worked was the string the client used to introduce itself.

Eight strings, one blocked

I sent the same GET to the same host, in the same minute, changing one header:

User-Agent Status
Python-urllib/3.14 403
Python-urllib/3.12 403
python-requests/2.32.3 401
curl/8.5.0 401
Wget/1.21.4 401
Go-http-client/2.0 401
my-app/1.0 401
Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) Chrome/126.0 401
(no User-Agent header at all) 401

Two strings failed and both were the same token with a different version number. Everything else reached nginx and got the 401 that basic auth is supposed to produce. That rules out the explanations that come to mind first. A rate limit would have cut the run short, not blocked two specific strings. A broken credential would have produced the same status for all of them. An outage would not care which version of Python the client claims to be. And the blocked clients are not the automated ones: wget and the Go standard library look nothing like a browser, and both were allowed through.

The block happens before your server sees anything

The 403 came with headers I had never looked at closely:

HTTP/2 403
content-type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
content-length: 17
cache-control: private, max-age=0, no-store
server: cloudflare
cf-ray: a5da0ee3dee9dd6b-DFW

No www-authenticate, no content-type: text/html, no nginx version. The body in hex is error code: 1010 plus a newline, 17 bytes, exactly what content-length announces. That is not a page my server generated.

Cloudflare's documentation for error 1010 describes it as access denied based on the browser's signature, and lists among the common causes "the default Python urllib user agent" as an example of what Browser Integrity Check treats as a non-browser client (developers.cloudflare.com/support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-1xxx-errors/error-1010/, read on 2026-11-20). The check is part of the zone configuration, not of my application, which explains why nothing in my nginx logs would ever show this request.

The origin answers in 34 milliseconds

To confirm the server was innocent I kept the hostname and TLS handshake and pointed only the connection at loopback:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}\n' \
  --resolve portal.example.com:443:127.0.0.1 \
  -A "Python-urllib/3.14" https://portal.example.com/

The answer was 401 0.034. Three repetitions gave 0.036, 0.034 and 0.034 seconds. The same request through the public hostname took about 130 to 160 milliseconds and returned 403. --resolve keeps the certificate validation and the virtual host match, so this is the same request as far as nginx is concerned, and nginx answered with the auth challenge, meaning it never considered the User-Agent at all. The shape matters more than the milliseconds: the origin is a local round trip, the edge adds a network round trip and a WAF decision.

That single command splits the two halves of the problem. If the origin fails too, your configuration is the suspect. If the origin is fine and the public name is not, the difference is in whatever sits between them, and no amount of reading the server config will show it.

A credential cannot fix a request the edge rejected

The part that cost me the most time: the 403 came back even with valid credentials attached.

source ~/.site_auth
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u "$SITE_AUTH" \
  -A "Python-urllib/3.14" https://portal.example.com/    # 403
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -u "$SITE_AUTH" \
  -A "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) Chrome/126.0" https://portal.example.com/    # 200

Same user, same password, same URL, one header different. The WAF evaluates the request before nginx gets a chance to read the Authorization header, so the credential was never examined. That is the practical rule I took from it: when a URL that normally answers 401 starts answering 403, the password was not looked at. Rereading the credential file, rehashing it, or trying another user is work in the wrong layer.

Removing the header is not the fix

The absence of a User-Agent also passed, with a 401. That makes "delete the header" look like a solution, and it is a bad one for two reasons. The rule matches a signature, so a client that stops signing itself is still an unnamed client, and the log entry it leaves is no more useful than before. And the monitor that only alarms on 403 would go green while the request still does not identify itself.

The documented fix is the simpler one: send a descriptive User-Agent. I tested two, my-app/1.0 and jonas-check/1.0, and both passed the edge with a 401. No browser impersonation needed.

That matters to me because of what my own scripts do. Several of them set a constant at the top of the file, and the constant is a full Chrome string:

UA = ("Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 "
      "(KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/126.0 Safari/537.36")

A scraper that calls itself Chrome is lying to every server it talks to, including servers I own, and it makes the access logs of those servers useless for telling a real browser from a script. my-app/1.0 is one line, passes the check that blocked the original request, and tells anyone reading the log what is happening.

Which layer my smoke test is allowed to judge

My deploy script runs a set of checks after each publish. Every one of them goes through this function:

check() {
  local url="$1" expect="$2" desc="$3"
  local code
  # --resolve aponta o hostname do cert para o loopback local, para nao
  # depender de DNS/Cloudflare no smoke test
  code="$(auth_curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
    --resolve "portal.example.com:443:127.0.0.1" "${BASE}${url}" || echo 000)"
  [[ "$code" == "$expect" ]] && echo "    OK   ${desc} (${code})" \
    || { echo "    FAIL ${desc} esperado=${expect} obtido=${code}" >&2; fail=1; }
}

check "/"                            "200" "index"
check "/health"                      "200" "health"
check "/css/style.css?v=${ASSET_SHA}" "200" "css"
check "/js/app.js"                   "200" "js"

The comment in the middle is the decision. The smoke test deliberately bypasses DNS and Cloudflare, because a deploy should not fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the files it just wrote. The price of that choice is the corollary: a green deploy proves nginx has the files, and proves nothing about a client reaching them through the edge.

Both checks are worth having, and they answer different questions. If I pointed this one at the public hostname, a 403 from the edge would turn every deploy red for a reason unrelated to the release, and a 401 would pass while proving nothing about the content. The arm that goes through the edge needs its own client with a known User-Agent, its own expected status, and its own message.

When one client fails and the others do not

The sequence that worked, in the order that saved the most time:

  • Reproduce with the exact client that failed. A browser standing in for a script hides the whole problem.
  • Change one header at a time and keep URL, method and credentials fixed.
  • Read the body and the server header before reading the status code. Seventeen bytes of plain text is not your application.
  • Test the origin with --resolve to separate edge from server in one command.
  • Treat 403 on a URL that normally answers 401 as "the application never saw this request".
  • Give every script a fixed, descriptive User-Agent, written in the code, not passed through the environment.

Quem mantém painel privado atrás de Cloudflare já levou um 403 desses e sabe o tempo que se perde procurando no lugar errado. Se aconteceu com você, conta nos comentários qual foi o cliente e o que apareceu no corpo da resposta.
