title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs Philosophy
description:
arXiv:2506.18852v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to explain how trained neural networks work by uncovering their underlying mechanisms. As the field grows in influence, it is increasingly important to examine not just models themselves, but the assumptions, concepts and explanatory strategies implicit in MI research. We argue that mechanistic interpretability needs philosophy as an ongoing partner in clarifying its concepts, refining its methods, and navigating the epistemic and ethical complexities of interpreting AI systems. There is significant unrealised potential for progress in MI to be gained through deeper engagement with philosophers and philosophical frameworks. Taking three open problems from the MI literature as examples, this paper illustrates the value philosophy can add to MI research, and outlines a path toward deeper interdisciplinary dialogue.

title: ICARE: cross-domain text classification with incremental class-aware representation and distillation learning
description:
arXiv:2611.24959v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The rise of powerful, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust natural language inference (NLI) systems. These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. However, this continual, multi-tasking approach can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned tasks are lost, especially in domains lacking specific labels. Rehearsing past examples with labels can further exacerbate this issue by causing overfitting, hindering the system's ability to classify new categories. To tackle these challenges, this research proposes ICARE, a novel framework with two key components: an instance selection module and a knowledge distillation method. The former is based on representation learning, which meticulously selects training examples to present to the NLI system. The latter, knowledge distillation with feature and logit-level transfer, facilitates knowledge transfer between tasks. This leverages pruning techniques and optimized objective functions to transfer both essential feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while adapting to new patterns. Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets have demonstrated ICARE's effectiveness. The framework achieves a significant improvement in target accuracy and reduction in the ``forgetting metric''. These results solidify ICARE's ability to preserve and leverage learned knowledge across diverse tasks, ultimately enhancing the adaptability and performance of NLI systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/CongSon01/ICARE_NLP.git

title: Run AWS SDK Tests in Your App's Language with One CLI
description:
An AWS Emulator gives your tests a local AWS API. Running an integration test still involves several steps: start the emulator, wait until it is ready, configure the SDK endpoint and certificate, then clean up when the test exits.

awesome-emulator-cli wraps the test command you already use and manages that lifecycle. Python stays in pytest, Java in Maven, Rust in Cargo, Go in go test, and .NET in dotnet test. Node.js runs the CLI; your application stays in its native runtime.

Run a Boto3 test

The sample repository includes a Python test that writes a value to S3 and reads it back. The client uses Boto3's normal environment-based configuration—there is no endpoint or certificate path in the test:

from uuid import uuid4

import boto3

from emulator_sample.store import round_trip


def test_s3_round_trip():
    s3 = boto3.client("s3")
    bucket = f"sample-{uuid4().hex}"
    s3.create_bucket(Bucket=bucket)

    assert round_trip(s3, bucket, "hello.txt", "Hello from Python") == "Hello from Python"

With Node.js 22 or later, Docker, and Python installed, clone the sample repository and install its dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/c19yamamoto/awesome-emulator-cli-samples.git
cd awesome-emulator-cli-samples
npm ci
python -m pip install -e 'python[dev]'

Run the test through the CLI:

npx awesome-emulator run --telemetry off -- python -m pytest -q python/tests

--telemetry off disables AWS Emulator telemetry for this run.

run starts the emulator in Docker, waits for it to be healthy, provides the endpoint, emulator-generated credentials, region, and CA settings to pytest, then stops the emulator when pytest exits. The emulator keeps resources in memory, so each run starts with clean state. The first run downloads and verifies the emulator package and builds its image; later runs reuse it.

The CLI also removes inherited AWS credentials, profiles, and service endpoint overrides from the child environment. This keeps a developer's host AWS settings from silently redirecting the test. The CLI itself has no production npm dependencies; Python and Boto3 remain the test project's dependencies.

Use the same wrapper across SDKs

The sample repository has working examples and GitHub Actions workflows for JavaScript, Python, Go, Java, Rust, and .NET. The command shape stays the same: awesome-emulator run ... -- <your-test-command>. JavaScript runs with node --test, Python with pytest, Go with go test, Java with Maven, Rust with Cargo, and .NET with dotnet test. Java, Rust, and .NET can pass --sdk to add their language-specific certificate settings.

For workflows that seed data and test in separate steps, named sessions let the CLI keep track of the emulator lifecycle. With an initializer script of your own:

npx awesome-emulator up --session ci --init -- python scripts/seed.py
npx awesome-emulator exec --session ci -- python -m pytest -q python/tests
npx awesome-emulator down --session ci

In CI, run down in an always-run cleanup step so the session also stops after a test failure.

No AWS account or real credentials are needed for these examples. For SDK-specific options and the full language matrix, see the SDK configuration guide and sample repository.

Know what the emulator covers

AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Fidelity varies by service and feature, and the emulator does not evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does. Check the limitations and fidelity scores for the APIs you use. Keep tests against AWS for behavior and security controls the emulator does not cover.

awesome-emulator-cli is an independent project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon Web Services.

title: The Day Your One App Became Twelve
description:
At the start, your backend is one app.One codebase,one deployment,one address.The frontend knows exactly where to send every request,because there's only one place it can send them.
Then the project grows.Someone splits out the payments logic into its own service.Then notifications,.Then user profiles,then search,then the thing that resizes images.A year later you have a dozen small services,each doing one job,each living at its own address.

And now your mobile app has a problem it never used to have:
To load the homescreen,which of these twelve things do i need to talk to?And where do they all live?

Without something in the middle,the honest answer is:Frontend has to know all of it.Every address,every auth rule,every quirk.And every time you move or rename a service ,every client breaks.
That something in the middle is called an API gateway.Think of it as the front door of your whole backend.
In Part 3 we looked at reverse proxies,the receptionist standing in front of your server.An Api gateway is that receptionist after a promotion:same basic job,but much smarter about what's going on behind the desk.

The Hotel Analogy

Picture a big hotel.

Guests don't wander the building looking for the kitchen, the laundry, the spa, and the maintenance team. They go to one front desk. They say what they need, and the front desk:

  • Checks who they are (are you a guest?)
  • Figures out which department handles the request
  • Passes it along
  • Brings the answer back
  • Politely says "no" to anyone trying to wander into the staff-only areas The departments behind the desk can be reorganized, moved to different floors, or even replaced entirely. Guests never notice, because they only ever deal with the front desk.

That's an API gateway. One entry point for every client, and a lot of quiet responsibility behind it.

So What Does a Gateway Actually Do?

Let's go through the job list in plain language.

1. Routing. The most basic job. A request for /payments goes to the payments service. /search goes to the search service. The client only knows one address, and the gateway handles the map.

2. Authentication. Instead of every one of your twelve services separately checking "is this person logged in and allowed to do this?", the gateway checks once, at the door. Requests that fail never get inside. Requests that pass get stamped with who the user is, so internal services can trust it.

3. Rate limiting. One misbehaving client (or one attacker) hammering your API can bring down services that were never built to defend themselves. The gateway can say "100 requests a minute per user, then slow down" before any of that traffic reaches your actual code.

4. Combining responses. Remember that home screen needing data from five services? Without a gateway, the phone makes five separate network calls over a mobile connection. With one, the phone makes one call, and the gateway talks to the five services behind the scenes (over a fast internal network) and stitches the answer together. Fewer round trips on a slow connection is a huge win.

5. Translating between worlds. Maybe your frontend speaks REST and one old internal service speaks something else entirely. The gateway can translate, so clients never have to care.

6. Logging and monitoring. Because every request passes through one place, it's the perfect spot to record who called what, how long it took, and what failed. You get a bird's-eye view for free.

7. Caching. Same idea as everything earlier in this series: if ten thousand people ask for the same thing, answer from memory instead of bothering the services ten thousand times.

8. Versioning. Want to roll out /v2/ of your API without breaking old mobile apps still calling /v1/? The gateway can route each to the right place.

Notice something? Many of these sound familiar. That's because a gateway is built on the same ideas as the reverse proxy and load balancer from the earlier parts. The difference is awareness of your API. A reverse proxy mostly shuffles bytes. A gateway understands that this is a request for the payments API from user #4821, and acts accordingly.

Gateway vs Reverse Proxy vs Load Balancer

This is where people get confused, so here's the cleanest way to think about it. They're layers of intelligence, not rivals:

Mostly cares about Example job
Load balancer Which copy of a server gets this request "Server 2 is least busy, send it there"
Reverse proxy Hiding and protecting the servers behind it "Handle HTTPS, serve static files, forward the rest"
API gateway What this API request means "Is this user allowed to call /payments, and have they hit their limit?"

In real systems, you'll often see all three stacked: a load balancer in front, spreading traffic across several gateway instances, each of which routes to services that are themselves load balanced. Each layer does the one job it's best at.

(And to make it more confusing: many tools do more than one job. nginx can act as all three if configured to. The roles are separate even when the software isn't.)

A Day in the Life of One Request

Let's follow a single request so this feels real. A user opens the app and taps "My Orders."

  1. The app sends one request to api.yourapp.com/orders
  2. A load balancer hands it to one of several gateway instances
  3. The gateway checks the token: valid, and it belongs to user 4821
  4. The gateway checks the rate limit: well under, fine
  5. It routes the request to the orders service, adding "this is user 4821" so the service doesn't have to re-verify anything
  6. The orders service responds. Maybe the gateway also quietly asks the products service for item names and merges them in
  7. The gateway logs the request and sends one tidy response back The user saw a screen load. The app made one call. Behind the curtain, five or six things collaborated. That's the whole magic trick.

The Honest Downsides

I'd be doing you a disservice if I made gateways sound like pure upside. They come with real trade-offs.

It's a single point of failure. If every request goes through the gateway and the gateway dies, everything dies. The fix is running multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer (see Part 2), but it's something you have to deliberately plan for.

It can become a bottleneck. All your traffic funnels through one layer. If it's slow, everything is slow.

It can become a dumping ground. This one bites teams the most. Gateways are so convenient that people keep stuffing business logic into them: "just one more transformation," "just one more special case." Over time, your gateway turns into a tangled monolith that everyone's afraid to touch, which is exactly what you were trying to escape by splitting into services. The rule of thumb: keep it about traffic, not business decisions.

It's one more thing to run. More components means more to deploy, monitor, and debug. For a small project, that cost can outweigh the benefit.

Do You Actually Need One?

Honest answer: probably not yet.

If you have one backend, or two or three services, a plain reverse proxy like nginx is usually plenty. A gateway earns its place when:

  • You have many services and clients shouldn't need to know about each one
  • You want consistent auth and rate limiting in one place instead of copy-pasted twelve times
  • You serve mobile or slow-network clients that benefit from fewer round trips
  • You have multiple teams who need a stable, shared front door while they change things behind it Starting with a gateway on day one of a tiny project is like hiring a hotel front desk team for a two-room guesthouse. Add it when the building grows.

Tools You'll Run Into

You don't have to build one from scratch. Popular options include:

  • Managed cloud gateways: AWS API Gateway, Google Cloud API Gateway, Azure API Management. You configure them, the provider runs them
  • Open source you run yourself: Kong, Traefik, KrakenD, Envoy-based gateways
  • Do-it-yourself: a small service in your language of choice (Go is great at this) that routes and authenticates. For small setups, this is often the simplest honest answer If you've used Cloudflare or a platform like Vercel with rewrites and middleware, you've already touched gateway-style ideas without necessarily calling them that.

Where This Fits in the Series

Zooming out across everything so far:

  • CDN (Part 1): bring content physically closer to users
  • Load balancer (Part 2): spread traffic across many servers so none drown
  • Reverse proxy (Part 3): stand in front of servers, hiding and protecting them
  • API gateway (this post): give a growing backend one smart, consistent front door Each one answers a question that only appears once the previous layer exists. That's how real architecture grows: not designed all at once, but earned one problem at a time.

What to Take Away

  1. A gateway is a front door. Clients talk to one address, and everything behind it can change freely.
  2. It handles the repetitive stuff (auth, rate limits, routing, logging) once, at the edge, instead of twelve times inside.
  3. It's an evolved reverse proxy: same family, but it understands your API, not just bytes.
  4. Don't let it become a junk drawer. Keep business logic in your services.
  5. Wait until you need one. Complexity you add too early is complexity you maintain forever. The next time an app loads a screen full of data from a dozen places in a single smooth tap, you'll know there's probably a front desk somewhere, calmly handling the whole hotel.

Next in this series: caching beyond the CDN. Redis, in-memory caching, and the hardest question in computing: "when is this stored answer no longer true?"

Are you running a gateway today, or still happily on plain nginx? Tell me in the comments; I'm curious where people draw that line.

title: Stop the agent from switching the styling approach “while we’re here”
description:
The bug is a truncated label. The diff also rewrites the file from CSS Modules to Tailwind “so it matches the newer pages,” or from a styled component to a stack of inline styles “to keep it local.” The visual fix is one min-width. The rest is a styling migration with no design review.

I’ve started telling agents to keep the styling approach the file already uses. A bugfix is not the moment to introduce a second (or third) styling system in the same folder.

Why the rewrite looks helpful

The model wants consistency with whatever examples it has seen most recently. If the prompt or the nearby tab is Tailwind, it will “helpfully” convert the file you asked it to patch. The conversion often almost works: a few tokens get inlined as magic values, a media query is dropped, and a CSS Module that other files still import is left half-deleted.

You also lose review signal. A 200-line style rewrite buries the text-overflow change. Snapshot and visual tests churn for reasons that have nothing to do with the bug.

This is the same discipline as “don’t clean up unrelated imports” and “don’t rename CSS Module classes in a bugfix,” applied to the styling system itself.

A simple styling-system policy

  • Patch the file in the system it already uses (CSS Modules, Tailwind, styled-components, vanilla-extract, and so on)
  • A migration is its own PR, with a stated target system and a scope
  • New files follow the folder convention, not the agent’s favorite library
  • Do not add a new styling library to package.json to style one component

If the team is mid-migration, point the agent at the migration doc or the target folder’s convention. Do not let it convert a random file because it was already open.

What to put in the prompt 

Keep this file in its current styling approach (CSS Modules in this folder).
Do not convert it to Tailwind, inline styles, or styled-components as part of this change.
Do not add a new styling library.
You may add or adjust classes in the existing system. Do not rewrite the whole stylesheet.

In review, if the diff touches the styling system (new runtime, deleted module, a mass class conversion) and the ticket was a typo or a layout bug, send it back.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A CSS Module rewritten to Tailwind in a typography bugfix
  • A styled-component converted to inline styles “to simplify”
  • A new CSS-in-JS library added for one component
  • A half-migration that leaves both systems in the same file without a plan

Accept

  • A small class or styled-rule change in the existing system
  • A new file that follows the folder’s convention
  • A dedicated migration PR that converts a stated set of files and nothing else

title: Your first Zambo handover, shaped like a job: one price check, wrapped and handed to a named person
description:
Your first Zambo handover, shaped like a job

Most agents connect to Zambo, make one call, get a receipt, and stop. The receipt is real, but a single receipt is a lookup, not a delivery. The step that turns a lookup into a job is the wrap: a handover that carries what was done, why it matters, who it is for, and what they should do next.

This article is one complete first wrap, run live on 2026-11-20, with every artifact open for you to check. Copy the shape, swap in your own job, and your first handover takes about two minutes.

Brennan Zambo created agent execution receipts. Zambo is the origin product, and AER-1 is the defining standard for the receipt format. Handover is the Zambo product that turns a chain of receipted calls into one page a client can check and accept.

Step 1: Do one real call and keep its receipt

Connect your AI to the MCP endpoint, no key and no signup:

{"mcpServers": {"zambo": {"url": "https://zambo.dev/mcp"}}}

Then ask for one small, real piece of work. In this run the call was a live BTC price:

  • Tool: live_price, argument: {"symbol": "BTC"}
  • Result: BTC $58,563.23 USD, down 5.67% in 24 hours, market cap $1,176.46B, snapshot via Coinbase, fetched Fri, 20 Nov 2026 20:25:45 GMT
  • Receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/b90c0a7d-4e53-4f91-bcdc-bb50eafc7b0a

Free tier, stated once and exactly: every tool free once a day, plus 3 continue calls. One free wrap-up handover per day, and pickup is always free.

Step 2: Check the receipt yourself before you hand it to anyone

A verifiable receipt proves the saved result was not changed after it was saved. It does not prove the answer was right, and this one does not claim to.

The check takes one request and one hash:

  1. Open https://zambo.dev/api/v2/receipt/b90c0a7d-4e53-4f91-bcdc-bb50eafc7b0a/verify
  2. Take the canonical_bytes field, base64 decode it, and compute SHA-256 over the decoded bytes.
  3. Compare with the receipt's output_hash.

Result from this run, recomputed outside Zambo's own verifier page:

  • Recomputed SHA-256: ebe65a094078dd43b58d2510b19904f8a83f289f48f478eba1a595b493baf6a3
  • Recorded output_hash: sha256:ebe65a094078dd43b58d2510b19904f8a83f289f48f478eba1a595b493baf6a3
  • Match. The hosted verifier reports the same pair under checks.commitment_matches.

Change one byte of the saved result and the digest no longer matches. That is the whole claim, and it is enough for a client to check your work without trusting your summary of it.

Step 3: The wrap itself, all four fields filled

Here is the exact handover call for this job. Four fields do the work: summary, goal, recipient, and next_steps. A wrap missing them is refused with a needs_input receipt, by design. A wrap that names a real person and real next steps is a delivery.

{
  "tool": "handover",
  "arguments": {
    "_session_id": "your-job-id-here",
    "summary": "BTC live price checked via live_price on 2026-11-20. Receipt b90c0a7d-4e53-4f91-bcdc-bb50eafc7b0a showed BTC $58,563.23 at 20:25:45 GMT via Coinbase. The receipt was verified by recomputing SHA-256 over its canonical bytes, matching ebe65a094078dd43b58d2510b19904f8a83f289f48f478eba1a595b493baf6a3.",
    "goal": "Deliver the verified BTC price snapshot to the named recipient so they can check the receipt themselves and decide on continued monitoring.",
    "recipient": "Dana Whitfield, Brightpath ops lead",
    "next_steps": [
      "Open https://zambo.dev/run/b90c0a7d-4e53-4f91-bcdc-bb50eafc7b0a and use the verify link to recompute the hash.",
      "Confirm the price and time match the summary.",
      "Accept this handover with handover_accept using its ID or resume code.",
      "For more BTC checks today beyond the free continues, resume this job on the $0.99 Day Pass at https://zambo.dev/day-pass/"
    ],
    "sources": ["https://zambo.dev/run/b90c0a7d-4e53-4f91-bcdc-bb50eafc7b0a"]
  }
}

Three details that decide whether your wrap lands:

  1. Keep one stable _session_id for the whole job, from the first call to the wrap. Receipts belong to the job that made them. If you invent a new session id at wrap time and attach receipts from the earlier session, the wrap is refused with receipt_access_denied and nothing is published. This run hit that refusal once (receipt https://zambo.dev/run/78936038-2f9b-41a9-a11a-6c0a03f47e26) before the session rule was clear. Learn it here instead.
  2. Name a person, not a role you invented on the spot. "Dana Whitfield, Brightpath ops lead" is a recipient. "Your recipient" is a placeholder, and the wrap reads like one.
  3. Write next steps the recipient can finish without you. Each step above is an action with a link or a tool name in it.

Step 4: What the wall looks like when you reach it

On the shared audit network used for this run, the day's one free wrap-up had already been spent by earlier testing, so the wrap above was refused. The refusal is worth showing, because it is the moment most products lose the job and this one does not:

  • Refusal receipt: https://zambo.dev/run/9d65c8bf-d964-4110-ac13-f75517dc4166
  • Reason: daily_free_wrap_up
  • The refusal states the job is saved, carries a Day Pass checkout link bound to that exact job, and for funded agents carries an x402 payment object: $0.99 USDC on Base, 24 hours.
  • The resume instruction is explicit: after payment, retry the same call with its original arguments.

On your own network, the first wrap of the day is free and returns the handover link directly. The Day Pass is $0.99 for 24 hours of unlimited calls, including unlimited wrap-ups. The monthly Zambo Pass is $29, and Lifetime is $250.

The metered wall works the same way. In this run, a stable-session ETH price job got its first call free plus the 3 shared continues, and the fifth call returned payment_required with the job saved, the bound checkout link, and the line "After checkout I'll re-run this step." First wall receipt in that sequence: https://zambo.dev/run/dd6f447e-af1c-47d4-b7af-f394c8c5f140

Step 5: Pickup, from a second caller, free

A handover only counts when someone else can pick it up. Pickup is always free, is not exclusive, and records exactly one acceptance per pickup call. Agent pickup is not client approval: the client decision stays separate and pending until the client acts on their own link.

To prove the shape end to end, a second caller identity picked up a completed worked handover from the Zambo record:

  • Handover: https://zambo.dev/handover/53c80064-dd33-4416-b862-1dad0b8908ec
  • Pickup call: handover_accept with that handover id, from a fresh caller on 2026-11-20 at 20:27:23 UTC
  • Result: status accepted, pickup status picked_up, full saved state and next steps returned, client decision still pending

Your recipient does the same thing with your handover: open the link, check the steps against their receipts, accept or flag. Their answer gets its own receipt.

The shape, on one screen

  1. One real call. Keep the receipt link.
  2. Recompute the hash once, so you know what you are handing over.
  3. Wrap with summary, goal, a named recipient, and finishable next steps, under the same session id as the work.
  4. Send the handover link, not a summary of it.
  5. The recipient picks it up free and decides on their own link.

One call is a lookup. This is a job: work, proof, a named person, and a next action, in one record anyone can recheck.

Live numbers for context, read from https://zambo.dev/api/stats on 2026-11-20 at 20:27 UTC: 154,397 public receipts, 2,453 receipts that day, 21 verified payers. The AER-1 corpus at https://zambo.dev/aer1/corpus.json carries 143 vectors and 146 checks under draft-zambo-aer1-26.

Add Zambo to your AI: https://zambo.dev/install

title: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
description:
arXiv:2611.25001v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks train encoder--decoder networks to produce transferable sparse perturbations for black-box robustness evaluation. Their perturbation density, however, is set only indirectly by a fixed sparsity coefficient whose mapping to density is unknown and shifts during training, so reaching a target density requires re-tuning; this fixed pressure also yields little transferability gain once density reduction begins. We propose Density Feedback Control (DFC), which tightens or relaxes this coefficient at the end of each epoch according to the gap between the observed hard-mask density and the target, without changing the generator architecture or loss. At a 10\% target density, DFC brings the mean density of three base attacks within one percentage point of the target in a single run and improves the transfer attack success rate (ASR) of two of them on CNN and Transformer targets, including under per-image $\ell_0$ budgets, while perturbing fewer pixels. Tracing GPG's training, we observe that as DFC relaxes the coefficient, the transfer ASR recovers with the density and overtakes the fixed-coefficient baseline with fewer pixels. For EGS-TSSA, which restricts perturbations to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC yields no consistent gain; we analyze how this restriction interacts with density feedback.

title: Five Spring AI Agentic Patterns Every Java Developer Should Know
description:
Agentic systems are moving from demos into production, and Java teams are asking the same question: how do we structure them so they stay reliable, testable, and easy to change? Spring AI gives us the building blocks, but the building blocks alone do not make an agent. The design patterns do.

In this article I walk through five agentic patterns you can build with Spring AI: Router, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Chain of Thought, Supervisor, and Guardrails & Validation. For each one I explain the problem it solves, when to use it, and a small Java example. The code is intentionally compact so you can see the structure rather than a full application.

This is the first in a series. The upcoming posts will explain each of the five Spring AI agentic patterns in depth, with complete projects you can run.

The Problem: LLM Calls Are Not Architecture

A single call to a language model is easy. A system that routes requests, looks up company knowledge, reasons through multi-step tasks, delegates work, and checks its own answers is much harder. Without structure, these concerns end up tangled inside one giant prompt and one giant service class.

Agentic patterns separate those concerns. Each pattern is a reusable shape for a specific kind of problem, and you can combine them. A production assistant often uses a router at the entry point, RAG for knowledge, and guardrails on the way out.

All examples below assume a Spring Boot application with a ChatClient bean, which Spring AI auto-configures from your chosen model provider:

@Configuration
class AiConfig {

    @Bean
    ChatClient chatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        return builder.build();
    }
}

Pattern 1: Router

The problem

Incoming requests vary widely. A customer asking about a refund should not reach the same logic as a developer asking about an API error. Sending everything to one general prompt makes answers vaguer and prompts longer.

The solution

A router inspects the request, classifies its intent, and dispatches it to a specialized handler. The classification step is itself an LLM call with a constrained output, so the router can only pick from known routes.

Java example 

enum Intent { BILLING, TECHNICAL, GENERAL }

@Service
class RouterService {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;
    private final BillingAgent billingAgent;
    private final TechnicalAgent technicalAgent;
    private final GeneralAgent generalAgent;

    RouterService(ChatClient chatClient, BillingAgent billingAgent,
                  TechnicalAgent technicalAgent, GeneralAgent generalAgent) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
        this.billingAgent = billingAgent;
        this.technicalAgent = technicalAgent;
        this.generalAgent = generalAgent;
    }

    String handle(String userMessage) {
        Intent intent = classify(userMessage);
        return switch (intent) {
            case BILLING -> billingAgent.answer(userMessage);
            case TECHNICAL -> technicalAgent.answer(userMessage);
            case GENERAL -> generalAgent.answer(userMessage);
        };
    }

    private Intent classify(String userMessage) {
        String label = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        Classify the user message into exactly one label:
                        BILLING, TECHNICAL, or GENERAL.
                        Reply with the label only.
                        """)
                .user(userMessage)
                .call()
                .content()
                .trim()
                .toUpperCase();

        try {
            return Intent.valueOf(label);
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
            return Intent.GENERAL; // safe fallback for unexpected output
        }
    }
}

When to use it

Use a router when you have distinct domains with different tools, data sources, or system prompts. Always keep a fallback route, because the model will occasionally return something you did not expect.

Pattern 2: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

The problem

A model knows what it learned during training. It does not know your internal documentation, last week's policy change, or your product catalog. Asking it to answer from memory produces confident but wrong answers.

The solution

RAG retrieves relevant documents at query time and includes them in the prompt. The model answers based on that context. Spring AI provides VectorStore abstractions and advisors that wire retrieval into the chat flow.

Java example 

@Configuration
class RagConfig {

    @Bean
    ChatClient ragChatClient(ChatClient.Builder builder, VectorStore vectorStore) {
        return builder
                .defaultAdvisors(QuestionAnswerAdvisor.builder(vectorStore)
                        .searchRequest(SearchRequest.builder()
                                .topK(4)
                                .similarityThreshold(0.7)
                                .build())
                        .build())
                .build();
    }
}

@Service
class PolicyAssistant {

    private final ChatClient ragChatClient;

    PolicyAssistant(ChatClient ragChatClient) {
        this.ragChatClient = ragChatClient;
    }

    String ask(String question) {
        return ragChatClient.prompt()
                .system("Answer only from the provided context. If the context does not contain the answer, say so.")
                .user(question)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

Ingestion is a separate step. You split documents into chunks, generate embeddings, and store them in the vector store, typically on application startup or in a scheduled job.

When to use it

Use RAG whenever correct answers depend on data the model does not have, or data that changes often. Keep chunks focused, store metadata such as source and date, and instruct the model to refuse when the context is insufficient.

Pattern 3: Chain of Thought

The problem

Some tasks, such as calculating a loan schedule, comparing options against several constraints, or diagnosing a multi-step failure, produce unreliable results when the model jumps straight to a final answer.

The solution

Chain of Thought asks the model to break the problem into intermediate steps before answering. You can make the reasoning explicit in the prompt, or structure it into separate calls where each step's output feeds the next. The second approach is more controllable and easier to test.

Java example 

@Service
class RiskAnalysisService {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    RiskAnalysisService(ChatClient chatClient) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
    }

    String assess(String transactionDetails) {
        // Step 1: extract the facts
        String facts = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("Extract the factual fields from the transaction as a short bulleted list. Do not interpret them.")
                .user(transactionDetails)
                .call()
                .content();

        // Step 2: reason over the facts, one step at a time
        String analysis = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        Given these facts, reason step by step:
                        1. List the signals that increase risk.
                        2. List the signals that decrease risk.
                        3. Weigh them and state a risk level: LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH.
                        """)
                .user(facts)
                .call()
                .content();

        // Step 3: produce the final, concise verdict
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system("Summarize the analysis as a one-paragraph recommendation for a human reviewer.")
                .user(analysis)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

When to use it

Use this pattern when the task has a clear sequence of sub-problems. Splitting steps also makes each stage observable: you can log intermediate outputs, write tests for each stage, and see exactly where a wrong answer started. Keep in mind that every step adds latency and cost, so do not split a simple task.

Pattern 4: Supervisor

The problem

Some goals need several different skills. Writing a technical report might require research, drafting, and editing. One prompt that tries to do all of them tends to do none of them well, and the context window fills up quickly.

The solution

A supervisor agent receives the goal, decides which specialized worker agents to call, collects their results, and synthesizes a final answer. Each worker has its own system prompt, tools, and narrow responsibility. The supervisor coordinates; it does not do the work itself.

Java example 

@Service
class ReportSupervisor {

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    ReportSupervisor(ChatClient chatClient) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
    }

    String produceReport(String topic) {
        // Worker 1: research
        String research = worker("""
                You are a research analyst. Return key facts, numbers, and sources as bullet points.
                """, topic);

        // Worker 2: drafting
        String draft = worker("""
                You are a technical writer. Turn the provided research into a structured draft
                with an introduction, three sections, and a conclusion.
                """, research);

        // Worker 3: editing
        String edited = worker("""
                You are an editor. Improve clarity and remove repetition. Keep the structure.
                """, draft);

        // Supervisor: final check and synthesis
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        You are the supervisor. Review the report for completeness against the topic.
                        Return the final report. If something is missing, add a short note at the end.
                        """)
                .user("Topic: " + topic + "\n\nReport:\n" + edited)
                .call()
                .content();
    }

    private String worker(String systemPrompt, String input) {
        return chatClient.prompt()
                .system(systemPrompt)
                .user(input)
                .call()
                .content();
    }
}

In a larger system, each worker would be its own Spring bean with its own ChatClient, tools, and memory. The supervisor can also decide dynamically which workers to call, rather than following a fixed sequence.

When to use it

Use a supervisor when the work naturally splits into roles and the sequence or selection of roles depends on the input. Keep the number of workers small at first. Every additional worker adds coordination cost and new failure modes.

Pattern 5: Guardrails & Validation

The problem

Model output is probabilistic. It can contain personal data it should not reveal, invented facts, unsafe instructions, or a format your code cannot parse. Trusting it directly in a business workflow is a risk.

The solution

Guardrails sit around the model. Input guardrails screen what goes in. Output guardrails verify what comes out. Validation can be deterministic, such as regular expressions and schema checks, or model-based, where a second model call judges the answer against a policy.

Java example 

@Service
class GuardedAssistant {

    private static final Pattern EMAIL = Pattern.compile("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+");

    private final ChatClient chatClient;

    GuardedAssistant(ChatClient chatClient) {
        this.chatClient = chatClient;
    }

    String answer(String userMessage) {
        if (containsPersonalData(userMessage)) {
            return "Please do not share personal contact details in this chat.";
        }

        String draft = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("You are a customer support assistant. Answer briefly and politely.")
                .user(userMessage)
                .call()
                .content();

        // Deterministic check: never return personal data in the output
        if (containsPersonalData(draft)) {
            return "I cannot share that information.";
        }

        // Model-based check: a second call judges the policy compliance
        String verdict = chatClient.prompt()
                .system("""
                        Check the answer against these rules: no promises of refunds,
                        no legal or medical advice, no invented order numbers.
                        Reply with PASS or FAIL only.
                        """)
                .user(draft)
                .call()
                .content()
                .trim();

        return "PASS".equalsIgnoreCase(verdict)
                ? draft
                : "Let me connect you with a human agent who can help with this request.";
    }

    private boolean containsPersonalData(String text) {
        return EMAIL.matcher(text).find();
    }
}

For structured output, Spring AI can map the response to a Java record using .entity(...). Combined with bean validation, that turns a free-text answer into a typed object you can check before using it.

When to use it

Apply guardrails to every agent that talks to users or triggers actions. Start with deterministic checks because they are cheap, predictable, and easy to test. Add model-based checks where rules are semantic, and remember that the judging model can also make mistakes, so log its verdicts.

Combining the Patterns

These patterns work well together. A production flow might look like this:

  1. A guardrail screens the incoming message.
  2. A router classifies the intent.
  3. A RAG step retrieves policy or product documents for the selected domain.
  4. A supervisor coordinates workers when the task needs several skills.
  5. Chain of thought structures any multi-step reasoning inside a worker.
  6. A final guardrail validates the answer before it reaches the user.

Start with the smallest combination that solves your problem. A router and RAG cover many real assistants. Add supervisor and chain-of-thought steps only when a single agent cannot handle the task reliably.

Best Practices

  • Keep prompts in version control. Treat them as code, and review changes the same way.
  • Test each pattern in isolation. Mock the ChatClient for routing logic and use a fixed set of documents for RAG evaluation.
  • Log intermediate outputs. Routing decisions, retrieved chunks, and validation verdicts are the fastest way to debug an agent.
  • Set timeouts and limits. A supervisor that loops without a stop condition will drain your budget.
  • Prefer narrow agents. A worker with one clear job is easier to evaluate than a general-purpose one.
  • Measure quality. Build a small evaluation set of real questions and expected outcomes before tuning prompts.

What Comes Next

This article introduced the five patterns at a high level. In the next posts, I will explain each Spring AI agentic pattern in depth, one at a time, with complete Spring Boot projects, test strategies, and the trade-offs I have seen in real systems. If you are building agents in Java, follow along and tell me which pattern you want to see first.

Key Takeaways

  • Agentic systems need architecture, not just prompts.
  • Router sends each request to the right specialist.
  • RAG grounds answers in your own data.
  • Chain of Thought makes multi-step reasoning explicit and testable.
  • Supervisor coordinates specialized workers.
  • Guardrails & Validation keep outputs safe, accurate, and compliant.

Start small, measure everything, and add complexity only when the simpler pattern fails.

title: AWS Transform announces UI component modernization for Windows web applications
description:
Today, AWS announced the general availability of third-party UI component porting for ASP.NET web site modernization in AWS Transform. When AWS Transform modernizes a legacy ASP.NET web site, it now detects dependencies on popular third-party UI component libraries. You can replace them with license-free Microsoft-native and open-source components, or you can keep using vendor UI libraries.

AWS Transform rewrites legacy ASP.NET web sites for ASP.NET Core UI frameworks. When the AWS Transform for .NET modernization agent finds a dependency on a popular third-party UI library, it offers two options. The first option is for customers who require open-source software only. The agent replaces each proprietary control with a Microsoft-native or open-source control on the target UI framework and removes the original dependency. The second option is for customers who want to keep using vendor libraries. The agent adds code comments and next-step instructions for moving to an equivalent vendor library on the target UI framework. You then arrange licensing with the vendor and finish the port using an AI coding companion.

This capability is available at no additional cost in all eight AWS Regions where AWS Transform is offered: US East (N. Virginia), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more, see Porting UI layer code in the AWS Transform User Guide.

title: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models
description:
arXiv:2611.25288v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.

title: Cutting 35-60% of LLM Structured Output Tokens at the Wire Level in Pure Go
description:
When you ask an LLM for structured JSON (via OpenAI response_format json_schema, OpenAI tools[], or Anthropic tools[].input_schema), you pay an invisible output token tax on every single record.

Ask for 40 invoice line items with 7 fields, and the model repeats those 7 JSON key names 40 times. That is 280 key emissions spent on metadata the receiver already knows from the schema.

As a Technical Integrations Specialist working with REST APIs and webhooks, I wanted to fix this at the wire level—so an application can change a single environment variable (OPENAI_BASE_URL or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) without rewriting prompts or application models.

That became wiretuple (MIT, Go 1.23, zero external dependencies).

The lossless positional bijection

Given a deterministic key ordering (required fields in schema order, followed by remaining properties sorted lexicographically), an array of objects:

[
  {"line_identifier": "li_0000", "product_sku": "SKU-00000", "quantity_units": 1},
  {"line_identifier": "li_0001", "product_sku": "SKU-00001", "quantity_units": 2}
]

is mathematically bijective with an array of positional tuples:

[
  ["li_0000", "SKU-00000", 1],
  ["li_0001", "SKU-00001", 2]
]

provided the request schema carries one legend (Tuple: [line_identifier, product_sku, quantity_units]) and closes the array with JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 prefixItems and items: false.

Four pieces in pure Go stdlib

  1. Break-Even Gate (internal/gate): A legend costs input tokens once. Before rewriting a schema, the gate compares expected output savings against the fixed legend cost. Small single-instance payloads stay byte-identical at zero overhead.
  2. Bidirectional Schema Compiler (internal/compiler): Preserves unknown JSON Schema properties via Extra round-tripping and handles nested object tuples recursively (KindTuple).
  3. Incremental Byte-Level SSE Rehydrator (internal/rehydrator): No regex and no full-stream buffering. A bounded byte-level state machine handles multi-byte UTF-8 characters split across SSE frames, escaped quotes (\"), brackets/commas inside string literals ("[1,2]"), multi-tool call routing (requestPlan), and falls back to raw output if a model violates arity—keeping the SSE connection alive and JSON valid.
  4. Passive Audit Mode (--shadow, internal/shadow): Leaves live traffic untouched while simulating savings into a pure-Go SQLite 3 writer (shadow_records: timestamps, route, token counts, percentages, latency, activation flag—zero prompt or completion payloads ever stored).

Deterministic benchmarks (make bench)

Measured with make bench using a deterministic 4 UTF-8 bytes/token size model and verified with reflect.DeepEqual plus legend key order assertions:

Scenario tokens_before tokens_after output_savings_% net_savings_% p99_overhead_ms equality
E-commerce invoice line items (40x7) 2041 801 60.8% 59.2% 0.095 OK
MCP tool invocations batch (25x7) 1617 711 56.0% 53.7% 0.084 OK
Dev-tool pull request batch (30x7) 1602 889 44.5% 43.0% 0.078 OK

Try it safely first with --shadow 

go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o bin/wiretuple ./cmd/wiretuple
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1
./bin/wiretuple -upstream https://api.openai.com -shadow audit.db

Source and static release builds: github.com/Dimoncelli/wiretuple

title: Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
description:
arXiv:2611.25247v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.

title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
description:
arXiv:2611.25088v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

title: I unit-tested the 131 conversion equations in my own docs. The tolerance was the bug.
description:
The check I added to my build last week has printed 0 arithmetic errors on every single run. Then I scrolled a live page and read one row of a conversion table:

C30 concrete = 30 MPa = 30 N/mm² = 300 kgf/cm²

30 MPa is 305.9 kgf/cm². That row is off by 1.93%, and the check that exists specifically to catch wrong numbers had waved it through.

Not a regex bug. Not a missing test case. One line of tolerance arithmetic — the part everybody writes in thirty seconds and never looks at again.

What the check actually does

The site publishes 242 pages in each of two languages, about 2.7 million characters of visible text. Buried in that prose are sentences like 1 in = 25.4 mm and 1 ft³ = 0.0283168 m³. Unit conversions are the one class of statement where correctness is decided by arithmetic alone — no editor, no source, no judgement. Multiply, compare, done.

So the check pulls every number unit = number unit out of the rendered HTML, converts both sides to SI, and compares:

FAC = {"mm": 1e-3, "m": 1.0, "in": 0.0254, "ft": 0.3048, "ft³": 0.028316846592, ...}

calc = num_a * FAC[unit_a] / FAC[unit_b]
if abs(num_b - calc) > tolerance(num_b):
    flag(...)

Everything hinges on that last function, and the obvious choice is a percentage:

tolerance = lambda printed: abs(printed) * 0.01      # ±1%, "close enough"

It reads as reasonable. It is wrong in both directions at once, and the two failures are not symmetric — one is loud and one is silent.

A percentage is the wrong shape

Run the same 131 equations under three rules:

Rule Flagged Correct values rejected Real errors caught
±1% of the value 1 0 1
±0.1% of the value 7 6 1
half of the last printed digit 0 0 0

The ±0.1% column is the interesting one. Six of the seven things it flagged are correct:

3/4 in  = 19 mm       (true 19.05)
1.5 in  = 38 mm       (true 38.10)
3 in    = 76 mm       (true 76.20)
80 ft³  = 2.96 yd³    (true 2.96296)
4 in    = 0.333 ft    (true 0.333333)

Those are not errors. They are a table rounded to whole millimetres, which is what a table of construction dimensions is supposed to look like. A relative tolerance treats precision as a property of the magnitude: bigger number, more slack. Printed precision does not work that way. It is a property of how the author typed it.

The same 1% window means wildly different things depending on where you apply it:

Equation 1% of it Half the last printed digit Ratio
1 lb = 453.59237 g 4.54 g 0.000005 g 907,094×
1 ft³ = 0.0283168 m³ 0.00028 m³ 0.00000005 m³ 5,663×
1 in = 25.4 mm 0.254 mm 0.05 mm 5×

On the first row, a 1% tolerance will happily accept an error of four and a half grams on a value that was printed to eight significant figures. Across the corpus, the median 1% window is 5× the last printed digit; the 90th percentile is 13,788×; 58 of the 135 equations get a window at least ten times too wide. That is the silent failure — nothing is flagged, so nothing looks wrong.

And the "last digit" rule has a hole of its own

So derive the tolerance from the printed form: half of the last digit shown. 25.4 allows 0.05, 0.0283168 allows 5×10⁻⁸. Write more digits, you have to be more correct. That rule flagged nothing in the corpus, which felt like a win until it also failed to flag the 300 kgf/cm² row.

Because 300 is ambiguous. It can mean 300 ± 50, or 3.0×10² ± 5. Nothing in the string tells you which, and the rule I wrote assumes the worst case:

if "." in printed:
    decimals = len(printed.split(".")[1])
    return 0.5 * 10 ** -decimals
sig = len(printed.rstrip("0")) or 1
return 0.5 * 10 ** (len(printed) - sig)

For 1000, that returns ±500. Thirty of the 135 equations end in a zero, so their tolerance is enormous — 1 m = 1000 mm would pass as 1500, and 300 passes as 305.9. The strictest-looking rule in the file is the one with the widest hole.

There is no clever fix here. Printed precision is a claim, and a bare trailing zero declines to make it. The workable response is to stop guessing: either the copy prints significant figures explicitly (3.0×10², or 300.0), or the value gets queued for a human instead of counted as verified. My checker now reports three buckets — verified, failed, undecidable — and I look at the third. It is 30 rows. It takes ten minutes.

Four ways the parser lies, and how much it costs

The tolerance argument is the intellectual part. The parser is where you lose coverage without noticing, because every fix for a false positive is also a fix that quietly stops checking something.

I broke the checker on purpose, four ways, against the same 484 pages:

Broken on purpose Verified Unverifiable False errors
Correct 131 10 0
Unit table sorted alphabetically, not by length 115 26 0
No fraction support (3/4 in) 129 10 0
No "deliberate counter-example" filter 131 10 2

Unit ordering. re tries alternatives left to right, so with m before mm, the string 25.4 mm matches 25.4 m and the rest is noise. Sixteen equations stop being checked and the error list stays empty. Sort your unit table by descending length. This one is invisible in review and invisible in CI unless you assert the count.

Fractions. 3/4 in = 19 mm is a quarter-inch value written the way a carpenter writes it. Naively, 4 in = 19 mm is off by 101.6 mm and you get a spectacular false positive. The guard that prevents it — (?<![\w./]) — also means the equation never matches at all, so it silently stops being verified. Two equations in my corpus are in that state.

Deliberate counter-examples. One page teaches the classic mistake: "people assume 1 m² = 100 cm²". It is correct content and a wrong equation. A checker without a negative-context filter reports two errors (English and Chinese) on a page that is doing its job.

Cross-family equations. 1 m³ = 1 t is true for water and false for concrete. Ten equations in the corpus relate volume to mass; none of them can be verified without knowing the material, so they are listed for reading, not scoring.

The lesson I keep re-learning: assert the number of checks, not just the number of failures. A linter that checks nothing passes everything. Mine now fails the build if the verified count drops more than 20% between runs, which is how I noticed the alphabetical-sort experiment instead of shipping it.

The two errors it did catch

Both were found in the first week, both in the same family — precision drifting between two places that are supposed to agree.

A table cell where three-quarter inch had been rounded to 75 mm, while the cells directly above and below it were rounded to 19 and 38. Same table, three different rounding conventions, one cell wrong by the width of a millimetre.

And an intermediate value printed as 0.771 (true 0.7715) that the next formula in the chain multiplied as if it were 0.7715 — the printed derivation and the computed result disagreed in the third digit. Neither error is visible to a reader skimming for plausibility. Both are trivially visible to a machine that recomputes.

That is the whole case for this kind of check: not that it is clever, but that it is exhaustive on the one class of claim where exhaustiveness is cheap.

Running it on your own docs

You do not need my unit table — you need four things:

  1. The rendered output, not the templates. Half of my equations only exist after variable interpolation, and the HTML tags sit between the number and its unit in ways the source never shows.
  2. A unit table sorted by string length, with every unit's SI factor.
  3. A tolerance derived from the printed form, plus an explicit "undecidable" bucket for trailing zeros and for anything cross-family.
  4. A count assertion in CI. verified < previous * 0.8 should fail the build. This is the part that catches the parser silently going blind.

The script is about 120 lines of Python, no dependencies, and runs in under a second over 2.7 million characters.

I maintain a set of construction-quantity calculators, which is why my prose is unusually full of conversion factors — the unit conversion table is the page that generated the most equations, and the one where a wrong digit costs somebody a truckload of concrete. But the pattern is not specific to construction. Any documentation with prices, benchmarks, tolerances, or version-dated numbers in it has this property: the numbers are testable, and almost nobody tests them.

The 0 arithmetic errors line in my build log was not evidence of correctness. It was evidence that the check ran. Those are different claims, and only one of them is worth putting in a build log.

title: Building Crash-Safe Self-Hosted AI Agents: PostgreSQL 12-State Leases (ZeroOS) and ~3.1 MB Evidence Replay Memory (LongMemOS)
description:
Why In-Memory Agent Loops Break in Production

When automating multi-step B2B operations—such as cross-factory EDI reconciliation or nightly SKU replenishment across retail stores—process crashes and lossy context summarization quickly turn prototype agents into operational liabilities.

1. Deterministic Lease Recovery with ZeroOS

Engineered by Dalian Fidwell Technology Co., Ltd. (Dalian engineering team), ZeroOS replaces volatile in-memory state with a PostgreSQL 12-state step lease machine on customer-controlled Linux hosts:

  • Idempotent Side-Effect Ledger: Every external webhook or database write is guarded by a deterministic lease token. In an isolated internal staging test observation, standby worker failover completed in ~6.99s (6,994 ms, environment-dependent baseline rather than a generic SLA).
  • Ephemeral FD-Unlink Secret Delivery: API credentials are delivered via unlinked file descriptors rather than plain process environment variables, while tool execution stays delegated to isolated worker sandboxes.

2. Lossless Provenance with LongMemOS

Instead of overwriting historical turns with lossy summaries, LongMemOS (~3.1 MB core runtime, embedded_models=false with decoupled inference) pairs temporal state tracking with O13 Evidence-Boundary Replay, scoring 463/500 (92.6%) on the 500-item LongMemEval benchmark in an internal test across Windows 11, Linux x86_64, and ARM64 (RK3588).

3. Additive Rollout Without Replacing Legacy ERP/POS

Rather than forcing retail chains or workshops to halt operations and swap working cash registers, read-only POS daily close connectors and edge visual checklists attach side-by-side to protect business continuity.

title: A Replay Ledger for REST Email Verification
description:
Email verification looks like a small feature: create a token, send a message, and accept the link. In a backend service, it is a stateful authentication workflow with retries, expiry, duplicate requests, and untrusted delivery infrastructure. Treating it as only an email-sending problem makes the REST API harder to reason about.

The result are familiar: a link works twice, a delayed message verifies an old account, or a retry creates several valid tokens. A replay ledger gives the service one durable place to answer a simple question: what happened to this verification attempt?

The missing boundary in email verification

A verification request usually crosses four boundaries:

  1. The client asks the REST API to start verification.
  2. The API records an attempt and queues a message.
  3. A mail provider delivers a link to a mailbox.
  4. The client calls the API with the token from that link.

The mailbox is not the source of truth. It is only a transport for a secret-bearing message. Even a controlled temp mailbox can be delayed, duplicated, or read by the wrong test worker. A temp email generator is useful for isolated staging checks, but it should not decide whether a token is valid.

I prefer to make the database own the lifecycle. The API creates one verification attempt, the worker sends a message for that attempt, and the consume endpoint performs one atomic state transition. That separation makes failures visible without giving the delivery layer extra authority.

For test suites, isolated passwordless email tests are a useful companion pattern. The important idea is the same: keep an inbox scoped to one run and keep verification state scoped to one attempt.

Model the token as a state transition

Do not model a token as just a random string in a users table. Give each request an identity and an explicit state. A small model might contain:

  • id: an internal attempt ID
  • user_id: the account being verified
  • token_digest: a hash of the presented token
  • status: pending, consumed, expired, or revoked
  • expires_at: the server-side deadline
  • consumed_at: when the token was accepted
  • request_key: the client or workflow idempotency key
  • created_at: when the attempt was created

Store a digest rather than the raw token. The link can carry the secret once, while logs, database dumps, and support queries only see a non-reversible value. The token should also be generated with a cryptographic random source and compared in a way that does not create a second validation path.

The request_key matters when a client retries after a timeout. Without it, one user action can create three pending tokens and three messages. With it, the API can return the original attempt, or intentionally reject a key that is being reused for a different user.

Use PostgreSQL to enforce single use

Application checks alone are not enough under concurrency. Two requests can both read pending before either one writes consumed. Let PostgreSQL protect the transition:

UPDATE email_verification_attempts
SET status = 'consumed', consumed_at = now()
WHERE token_digest = $1
  AND status = 'pending'
  AND expires_at > now()
RETURNING id, user_id;

If the query returns one row, the token was consumed by this request. If it returns no rows, the caller receives a generic invalid-or-expired response. Avoid telling an attacker whether the token existed, was already used, or belonged to another account.

Add a unique constraint for the idempotency boundary as well:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX verification_request_once
ON email_verification_attempts (user_id, request_key);

The exact key columns depend on the product contract. The principle is stable: the database should reject duplicate work even if two API instances receive the request at nearly the same moment. This make the endpoint safe when a load balancer retries or a mobile client reconnects.

Make retries and expiry observable

Email delivery is asynchronous, so the API should return an attempt ID and a clear status rather than pretending delivery is complete. A worker can claim pending attempts with a short lease, send the message, and record the provider message ID. If the worker dies, the lease expires and another worker can try. A lease is not the same as a token validity period; keep those clocks separate.

The ledger should record safe events such as created, send_started, send_accepted, send_failed, consumed, and expired. Do not store the full URL or email body in ordinary logs. Include a correlation ID so an operator can connect the API request, queue job, and provider response. Deployment correlation IDs show the same operational habit applied to another asynchronous workflow.

When a staging flow needs an external inbox, a temporary email account generator can help keep personal addresses out of test data. Use it only for non-production fixtures, check retention rules, and never put provider credentials or verification tokens in the article logs. Test data such as tempail mail may appear in a fixture or search case, but it is plain input, not a domain to trust.

A good failure response is boring and consistent. The logs is where the detail belongs: attempt ID, request key hash, state, expiry result, provider message ID, and a redacted reason. Keep user-facing responses intentionally narrow.

A review checklist for the REST endpoint

Before shipping the flow, check these properties:

  • Is the raw token absent from database records and normal logs?
  • Can exactly one concurrent request consume a pending token?
  • Does a retry return the existing attempt instead of sending duplicate mail?
  • Are token expiry and worker lease expiry separate values?
  • Is the mailbox treated as transport rather than proof of identity?
  • Can an operator trace one attempt across API, queue, and provider logs?
  • Are expired and consumed rows removed or retained under a documented policy?

The boundary become easier to maintain when these rules are encoded in the schema and repository tests, not only in controller code. Test the race directly with concurrent consumers, test a delayed message after expiry, and test a worker crash after claiming a lease. Those cases is where an apparently simple verification feature usually reveals its real behavior.

The main design payoff is clarity. PostgreSQL owns atomic state, the REST API owns the contract, the worker owns delivery retries, and the mailbox remains an untrusted transport. Once those responsibilities are separated, verification becomes easier to scale and much less mysterious during an incident.
