On a volatile altcoin, 3% is...","published":true,"published_at":"2026-11-01T01:01:48.511Z","slug":"adaptive-stop-loss-thresholds-instead-of-hardcoded-percentages-300a","path":"/mattleeee/adaptive-stop-loss-thresholds-instead-of-hardcoded-percentages-300a","url":"https://dev.to/mattleeee/adaptive-stop-loss-thresholds-instead-of-hardcoded-percentages-300a","comments_count":0,"public_reactions_count":0,"page_views_count":30,"published_timestamp":"2026-11-01T01:01:48Z","body_markdown":"A fixed -3% stop does not mean the same thing on every instrument. On a volatile altcoin, 3% is inside the normal noise band, so the stop fires on routine wiggles and the strategy never gets to express its edge. On a low-volatility index product, 3% is a wide move, so the stop sits far beyond where the strategy's own logic would have exited. The same number produces opposite behaviour depending on the thing it's attached to. The fix is not to tune the percentage per instrument by hand. It's to derive the safety floor from the strategy's own stop calculation, so the floor protects capital without overriding the strategy's exit logic. The formula used here:

python threshold = -max(3.0, abs(strategy_stop_pct) * 2.0)

Read it as two clauses. The abs(strategy_stop_pct) * 2.0 clause says: never force-close before the strategy's own stop has had a chance to work, and only intervene once the position has drifted to roughly twice the intended stop distance. The max(3.0, ...) clause says: there is always at least a 3% floor, so a strategy with a very tight stop (say 0.5%) doesn't get a 1% force-close that would fire on spread and slippage alone. ## What each clause is protecting The * 2.0 multiplier is the interesting part. A strategy that stops at 2% has a defined risk budget. If the price is at -2.5%, the strategy's stop should have already acted; if it hasn't, something is wrong (stale data, a gap, a broker reject). Waiting until -4% gives the strategy room to do its job and cuts the position only when the loss is clearly beyond what the strategy signed up for. That's the "respect the strategy" half. The max(3.0, ...) half is the "protect capital" floor. Without it, a strategy with a 0.5% stop yields a 1% force-close threshold, which is noise-level for most liquid instruments. The force-close would become the actual stop, and the strategy's own logic would be irrelevant. The 3% minimum guarantees the force-close is a genuine backstop, not a second, tighter stop. The result is a threshold that scales with the instrument's volatility as the strategy sees it, because strategy_stop_pct is itself volatility-derived. That's the whole point: the floor inherits the strategy's view of normal movement instead of imposing an external one. ## Computing strategy_stop_pct per instrument strategy_stop_pct must come from the strategy's own stop logic, not from a separate volatility estimate. If the strategy uses ATR-based stops, use that. If it uses a percentage of price derived from recent range, use that. The floor and the strategy must agree on what "the stop" means, or the * 2.0 multiplier is meaningless. A common pattern is an ATR stop with a multiplier:

python import pandas as pd def atr(df: pd.DataFrame, period: int = 14) -> pd.Series: high, low, close = df["high"], df["low"], df["close"] prev_close = close.shift(1) tr = pd.concat([ high - low, (high - prev_close).abs(), (low - prev_close).abs(), ], axis=1).max(axis=1) return tr.ewm(alpha=1 / period, adjust=False).mean() def strategy_stop_pct(df: pd.DataFrame, atr_mult: float = 2.0, atr_period: int = 14) -> pd.Series: """Stop distance as a fraction of current price.""" a = atr(df, atr_period) return (atr_mult * a) / df["close"]

Then the floor follows directly:

python def safety_floor_pct(stop_pct: pd.Series, min_floor: float = 3.0, mult: float = 2.0) -> pd.Series: """Returns positive magnitude; apply as -value when comparing PnL.""" return (stop_pct.abs() * mult).clip(lower=min_floor)

Two details matter here. First, stop_pct is a series, not a scalar. ATR changes, so the stop distance changes, so the floor changes. Recompute it on every bar or every position update. A floor computed once at entry will be wrong by the time the position has moved. Second, clip(lower=min_floor) implements the max() cleanly and keeps the output vectorised. For a strategy with a 2% stop, the floor is 4%. For a 0.8% stop, the floor is 3% (the minimum wins). For a 6% stop, the floor is 12%. One caveat on the ATR version: ATR is in price units, so dividing by close converts it to a fraction. For instruments with very different price scales (a $0.02 token vs. a $400 stock), the fraction is the only comparable quantity. Keep everything in fractional terms until the final PnL comparison. ## Applying it to open positions The check itself is a simple comparison against unrealised PnL as a fraction:

python def should_force_close(entry_price: float, current_price: float, stop_pct_now: float, min_floor: float = 3.0, mult: float = 2.0) -> bool: pnl_pct = (current_price - entry_price) / entry_price * 100.0 floor = max(min_floor, abs(stop_pct_now) * mult) return pnl_pct <= -floor

Call this on every tick or bar, passing the current stop_pct_now rather than the value at entry. If the instrument has calmed down since entry, the floor tightens; if volatility has expanded, the floor widens. That's the adaptive part, and it's what a hardcoded percentage can't do. For a batch of positions, vectorise it:

python def force_close_mask(entry: pd.Series, current: pd.Series, stop_pct_now: pd.Series, min_floor: float = 3.0, mult: float = 2.0) -> pd.Series: pnl_pct = (current - entry) / entry * 100.0 floor = (stop_pct_now.abs() * mult).clip(lower=min_floor) return pnl_pct <= -floor

## Backtesting the floor's effect on surviving trades The number that matters is not how many trades the floor cuts. It's how many trades the floor cuts that would have recovered, and how much tail risk it removes. A floor that never fires is doing nothing; a floor that fires on trades that would have hit their own stop anyway is redundant. The useful cases are the ones in between: trades that drifted past the strategy's intended stop without triggering it, and trades that recovered. Tag each trade with whether the floor fired and whether the trade would have been profitable without it:

python def evaluate_floor(trades: pd.DataFrame) -> dict: """ trades columns: pnl_pct (final, without floor), floor_pnl_pct (PnL at the moment the floor would have fired, NaN if it never fired), would_recover (bool: final pnl_pct > 0 without floor). """ fired = trades["floor_pnl_pct"].notna() cut = trades[fired] return { "n_trades": len(trades), "n_fired": int(fired.sum()), "fired_rate": fired.mean(), "avg_pnl_fired": cut["floor_pnl_pct"].mean(), "avg_pnl_if_held": cut["pnl_pct"].mean(), "recovered_after_cut": int(cut["would_recover"].sum()), "recovered_pnl_cost": cut.loc[cut["would_recover"], "pnl_pct"].sum(), "tail_saved": ( trades.loc[~fired, "pnl_pct"].nsmallest(20).mean() - cut["floor_pnl_pct"].mean() if fired.any() else float("nan") ), }

The two numbers to read together are recovered_pnl_cost and the change in the worst-case tail. If the floor cuts a handful of trades that would have recovered for a small total PnL cost, and it removes a fat left tail, it's earning its keep. If recovered_pnl_cost is large relative to the tail it removes, the multiplier is too tight: raise mult from 2.0 toward 2.5 or 3.0 and re-run. If the floor barely fires, the multiplier is too loose or the strategies' stops are already doing the work. Also break the results down by instrument. A floor that looks good in aggregate can be doing all its work on one volatile instrument and nothing elsewhere. If one instrument accounts for most of the fired trades, its strategy_stop_pct is probably mis-specified rather than the floor being wrong. Watch the sample size. Floor events are rare by construction, so a backtest with 200 trades may produce a dozen firings, which is not enough to conclude anything. Pool across instruments and across a long enough window that the volatility regime shifts at least once. If the floor's contribution only shows up in a single high-volatility month, you're measuring one event, not an edge. ## When a hard floor must override the adaptive value The adaptive threshold assumes strategy_stop_pct is meaningful. That assumption fails in specific, recognisable cases, and in those the hard floor must win outright. *Stale or missing volatility data.* If ATR is NaN, zero, or computed from a thin book, stop_pct collapses toward zero and the adaptive floor tightens to the 3% minimum. That's benign. But if stop_pct is stale — carried over from a prior regime — the floor can be far too wide. Detect it:

python def effective_floor(stop_pct_now: float, stop_pct_prev: float, min_floor: float = 3.0, mult: float = 2.0, max_floor: float = 15.0) -> float: if not (stop_pct_now > 0): return min_floor # bad data: fall back to hard floor adaptive = max(min_floor, abs(stop_pct_now) * mult) if abs(stop_pct_now - stop_pct_prev) / stop_pct_prev > 0.5: adaptive = max(adaptive, min_floor) # regime jump: don't trust the ratio return min(adaptive, max_floor) # hard ceiling regardless

*A hard ceiling.* The adaptive formula has no upper bound. A strategy with a 10% stop yields a 20% force-close threshold, which for most instruments is not risk management, it's capitulation. Cap it. The max_floor argument above enforces a ceiling that no adaptive value can exceed. The exact number depends on the instrument's typical drawdown distribution, but it should exist and it should be hardcoded, because its purpose is to override the adaptive logic when the adaptive logic produces something absurd. *Gap and liquidity events.* The floor is evaluated on observed prices. If an instrument gaps through the threshold overnight, the force-close executes at a worse price than the threshold. That's unavoidable, but it means the floor's effective loss can exceed its nominal value. In backtests, model the fill at the next available price, not at the threshold, or the floor will look more protective than it is. *Strategy stop wider than the ceiling.* If strategy_stop_pct * 2.0 exceeds max_floor, the ceiling wins and the strategy's stop is effectively overridden. That's the correct outcome: the strategy has asked for more risk than the account's policy allows, and the policy should win. Log these cases — they usually mean the strategy is mis-parameterised for that instrument, not that the floor is too tight. ## The design principle The floor exists to catch what the strategy's own stop missed: gaps, stale stops, broker rejects, logic errors. It should be the outer layer of defence, not the first line. Deriving it from strategy_stop_pct keeps it in the right place — wide enough that the strategy's exit logic runs first, tight enough that a runaway loss gets cut before it compounds. The hard floor and the hard ceiling bracket the adaptive value so that bad inputs can't push it into useless territory. Everything between those brackets is the strategy's own risk definition, scaled by a constant. Set it...","published":true,"published_at":"2026-10-31T01:01:47.169Z","slug":"partial-take-profit-bank-half-at-3-let-the-rest-run-3fi","path":"/mattleeee/partial-take-profit-bank-half-at-3-let-the-rest-run-3fi","url":"https://dev.to/mattleeee/partial-take-profit-bank-half-at-3-let-the-rest-run-3fi","comments_count":0,"public_reactions_count":0,"page_views_count":10,"published_timestamp":"2026-10-31T01:01:47Z","body_markdown":"## The Problem With a Single Take-Profit A fixed take-profit forces a binary choice. Set it tight and you cut winners that would have kept running. Set it wide and you watch a 5% open profit evaporate back to zero because the target was never hit. Both outcomes come from the same design flaw: the exit is a single point, and the market gets one vote on whether you keep everything. Partial take-profit splits that vote. The version I run in the paper trader: when unrealized profit on the open position reaches 3%, sell half the position and move the stop on the remainder to break-even. The remaining half targets the original 6%. The first leg banks a guaranteed gain; the second leg keeps upside exposure at zero risk (modulo fees, which we'll get to). The strategy logic is trivial. The bookkeeping is where implementations break, so most of this post is about state. ## Position State Every open position needs enough state to answer: how much is left, what did it cost, what's been realized, and has the partial already fired. A dataclass is the cleanest container:

python from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Position: entry_price: float qty: float stop_price: float target_price: float partial_level: float partial_fraction: float = 0.5 partial_done: bool = False realized_pnl: float = 0.0 fees_paid: float = 0.0 initial_qty: float = field(init=False) def __post_init__(self): self.initial_qty = self.qty

Two fields do the heavy lifting. partial_done is the latch that guarantees the 3% rule fires once, not on every candle that closes above the threshold. initial_qty preserves the original size so you can report percentage-of-position metrics after the exit. Note that entry_price never changes. After a partial exit, the remaining shares still carry the same cost basis — the average entry of the remaining position is unchanged. What changes is how much capital is at risk. If you recompute an "average entry" by blending realized and unrealized, you'll corrupt the R-multiple math later. Keep cost basis immutable; track realized PnL separately. ## The Candle Loop and Check Order The rule must be evaluated exactly once per candle, and the order of checks matters because a single candle can touch the stop, the partial level, and the target. Here's the loop I use:

python def process_candle(pos: Position, candle, fee_rate: float = 0.001): o, h, l, c = candle.open, candle.high, candle.low, candle.close # 1. Gap handling: if the open is already beyond a level, # fill at the open, not at the level. # 2. Stop check first (conservative: assume worst case within candle). stop_hit = l <= pos.stop_price target_hit = h >= pos.target_price partial_hit = (not pos.partial_done) and h >= pos.partial_level # Conservative ordering: stop before target when both touched. if stop_hit: fill = min(o, pos.stop_price) if o < pos.stop_price else pos.stop_price close_remainder(pos, fill, fee_rate) return "stopped" if partial_hit: take_partial(pos, max(o, pos.partial_level), fee_rate) # Re-evaluate target on the same candle with reduced size. if h >= pos.target_price: fill = max(o, pos.target_price) close_remainder(pos, fill, fee_rate) return "partial+target" return "partial" if target_hit: fill = max(o, pos.target_price) close_remainder(pos, fill, fee_rate) return "target" return "open"

The ordering decisions, spelled out: *Stop before partial.* If a candle's range covers both the stop and the 3% level, assume the stop got hit first. Without tick data you cannot know the intrabar sequence, and assuming the favorable fill first is how backtests develop a personality disorder. Conservative ordering costs you some hypothetical profit and keeps the equity curve honest. *Partial before target.* Once the 3% level triggers, the target check runs against the reduced position. If one candle runs from below 3% straight through 6%, you take the partial at 3% and the remainder at 6%. That's the intended behavior: the rule is a schedule, not an either/or. *Gap opens.* If the candle opens above the target, the fill is the open, not the target — you don't get to sell at a price the market skipped. The max(o, level) / min(o, level) expressions handle long positions; flip them for shorts. Gap opens beyond both the partial and the target (open at 7%) mean the partial fills at the open too, and the remainder also fills at the open. Bank it and move on. ### The Partial Fill Itself

python def take_partial(pos: Position, fill_price: float, fee_rate: float): qty = pos.qty * pos.partial_fraction proceeds = qty * fill_price fee = proceeds * fee_rate cost = qty * pos.entry_price pos.realized_pnl += proceeds - fee - cost pos.fees_paid += fee pos.qty -= qty pos.partial_done = True # Move stop to break-even, adjusted for fees already sunk. pos.stop_price = pos.entry_price

Two subtleties here. First, pos.qty -= qty uses the fractional quantity, so a 50% exit on an odd lot leaves a fractional remainder — fine for crypto, and for equities you'd round down and keep the residual. Second, the break-even stop is set to entry_price, not to entry_price + fees. That's the version most people write, and it's slightly wrong; see the fee section. ## Edge Cases That Bite *The "free ride" isn't free.* Moving the stop to break-even means the remainder exits flat before fees. If you paid 0.1% on entry and 0.1% on exit, a break-even stop on the remainder loses roughly 0.2% of the remaining notional. Over hundreds of trades this shows up. The fix is to set the stop at the fee-adjusted break-even:

python def breakeven_price(entry: float, entry_fee_rate: float, exit_fee_rate: float) -> float: # Price at which net PnL on the remainder is zero. return entry * (1 + entry_fee_rate) / (1 - exit_fee_rate)

With 0.1% each way, that's entry × 1.001 / 0.999 ≈ entry × 1.002. Two basis points above entry — small, but it converts "free ride" from a slogan into an arithmetic fact. Whether the fee-adjusted stop or the plain break-even stop performs better is an empirical question; test both. *Partial level below entry after slippage.* If your fill model includes slippage, the realized PnL on the partial can be negative even though the trigger price was 3% above entry. Guard the expectancy math against this by using actual fill prices everywhere, never the trigger levels. *Restart safety.* If the trader persists state between runs, partial_done must be serialized. Reconstructing a position from "current qty and entry" alone will re-fire the partial after a restart. Persist the full dataclass. *One partial per position.* The latch is not an optimization; it's the semantics. If you want multiple scale-out levels (3%, 5%, 7%), replace the boolean with a list of pending levels and pop them as they trigger. The bookkeeping pattern is identical. ## How Partial TP Changes Expectancy The standard expectancy formula for a single-target system is:

plaintext E = p_win * avg_win - p_loss * avg_loss

Partial exits break avg_win into two components and change the outcome distribution. With half out at 3% and half at 6% (ignoring fees and the break-even stop for a moment), a full winner returns 0.5 * 3% + 0.5 * 6% = 4.5% of position notional. A trade that reaches 3% but stalls returns 0.5 * 3% + 0 = 1.5% instead of riding back to zero. A trade stopped at break-even after the partial returns 1.5% instead of a full loss. The trade-off: you've capped the average winner at 4.5% instead of 6%, in exchange for converting some would-be losers into small winners and shrinking the loss tail. Whether that improves expectancy depends on the distribution of maximum favorable excursion (MFE) — specifically, how many trades reach 3% versus 6%. If most trades that hit 3% also hit 6%, the partial just costs you half a percent per winner. If a large fraction stall between 3% and 6%, the partial is where the edge lives. You can't reason your way to the answer; you measure it. Log MFE per trade and build the histogram:

python import numpy as np def mfe_histogram(trades, bins=(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10)): mfe = np.array([t.max_favorable_pct for t in trades]) hist, edges = np.histogram(mfe, bins=bins) for lo, hi, n in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:], hist): print(f"{lo:>4.0f}%-{hi:<4.0f}% {n:>5d} {'#' * int(50 * n / max(hist))}")

If the 3–6% bucket is fat, the partial earns its keep. If it's nearly empty, a single wider target is simpler and better. ### A Cleaner Expectancy Formula Once partials exist, per-trade expectancy is best computed from realized cash flows rather than win/loss averages:

python def expectancy(closed_trades): # Each trade: dict with 'pnl_pct' (net return on initial notional) pnl = np.array([t["pnl_pct"] for t in closed_trades]) return pnl.mean(), pnl.std() / np.sqrt(len(pnl))

Because every trade now has a continuum of outcomes (full stop, partial + break-even, partial + target, direct target), the win/loss split loses information. Mean net return per trade on initial notional, with a standard error, is the honest summary. Report it alongside the MFE histogram and the fraction of trades where the partial fired. ## What Actually Matters The partial take-profit is a small piece of logic wrapped in a lot of state discipline. Get these right and the rest follows: - Latch the partial with an explicit flag and persist it. - Evaluate stop → partial → target, once per candle, with gap-aware fills. - Keep entry price immutable; track realized PnL separately. - Use fee-adjusted break-even if you care about the "free" part being real. - Judge the rule by the MFE distribution and net expectancy, not by how it feels. Consecutive-loss breakers answer a different question: "is the process still behaving the way I validated it?" A strategy can be down 4% over a month through a slow bleed of small wins and losses — normal. Or it can lose five trades in a row in two days — also possible under a valid edge, but far less likely, and much more informative. The breaker treats the streak as a signal about regime change, broken data feeds, or an implementation bug, not as a verdict on your equity curve. The rule is deliberately blunt: three consecutive losing trades trips the strategy into cooldown. No auto-restart. A human reviews the trade history, checks whether the edge is still there, and re-arms the breaker explicitly. ## The State Machine Four states, three transitions, one manual gate:

plaintext ACTIVE ──(3 losses)──> TRIPPED ──(notify + persist)──> COOLDOWN ^ │ └──────────(manual review / resume)────────────────────┘

- ACTIVE: strategy trades normally, counter increments on each closed loss and resets on each closed win. - TRIPPED: transient state entered the moment the third loss closes. Its only job is to fire the notification and persist the trip record. Execution must already be blocked here. - COOLDOWN: strategy is paused. No orders, no sizing, no "just one small trade to test." - Resume: only via an explicit call after review. Never on a timer, never on a new day, never on "market looks better now." The important design decision is that TRIPPED blocks execution before the notification is sent. If the notification service is down, the strategy still doesn't trade. Failure to notify must never mean failure to stop. ## Where the Counter Lives An in-memory counter is worthless. Strategies get restarted by deploys, crashes, and Windows Task Scheduler reboots. If the counter resets on restart, a strategy that lost two trades before a restart gets a free pass on the third. Persist the counter and the state together, atomically, on every closed trade. SQLite is enough for a single-strategy setup and survives process death:

```python import sqlite3 from contextlib import contextmanager from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime, timezone from enum import Enum class State(str, Enum): ACTIVE = "active" TRIPPED = "tripped" COOLDOWN = "cooldown" @dataclass class BreakerRecord: strategy_id: str state: State consecutive_losses: int updated_at: str class BreakerStore: def __init(self, path: str = "breaker.db"): self.path = path with self._conn() as c: c.execute(""" CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS breaker ( strategy_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, state TEXT NOT NULL, consecutive_losses INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, updated_at TEXT NOT NULL ) """) @contextmanager def _conn(self): conn = sqlite3.connect(self.path, isolation_level=None) try: conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL") yield conn finally: conn.close() def load(self, strategy_id: str) -> BreakerRecord: with self._conn() as c: row = c.execute( "SELECT state, consecutive_losses, updated_at FROM breaker WHERE strategy_id=?", (strategy_id,), ).fetchone() if row is None: return BreakerRecord(strategy_id, State.ACTIVE, 0, _now()) return BreakerRecord(strategy_id, State(row[0]), row[1], row[2]) def save(self, rec: BreakerRecord) -> None: with self._conn() as c: c.execute(""" INSERT INTO breaker (strategy_id, state, consecutive_losses, updated_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?) ON CONFLICT(strategy_id) DO UPDATE SET state=excluded.state, consecutive_losses=excluded.consecutive_losses, updated_at=excluded.updated_at """, (rec.strategy_id, rec.state.value, rec.consecutive_losses, rec.updated_at)) def _now() -> str: return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()

Two things matter here beyond persistence. First, `isolation_level=None` with WAL gives you autocommit plus concurrent readers, which is fine for this write pattern. Second, the state and the counter are one row — they can never disagree after a crash. ## The Breaker Logic The transition function is small and should stay that way. Every closed trade goes through it; nothing else mutates the counter.

python from dataclasses import replace MAX_CONSECUTIVE_LOSSES = 3 class LossBreaker: def __init(self, store: BreakerStore, strategy_id: str, threshold: int = MAX_CONSECUTIVE_LOSSES): self.store = store self.strategy_id = strategy_id self.threshold = threshold def can_trade(self) -> bool: return self.store.load(self.strategy_id).state is State.ACTIVE def on_trade_closed(self, pnl: float, trade_meta: dict) -> BreakerRecord: rec = self.store.load(self.strategy_id) if rec.state is not State.ACTIVE: # Breaker is latched; closed PnL from any straggler orders # must not move the counter. return rec losses = rec.consecutive_losses + 1 if pnl < 0 else 0 new_state = State.TRIPPED if losses >= self.threshold else State.ACTIVE rec = replace(rec, state=new_state, consecutive_losses=losses, updated_at=_now()) self.store.save(rec) if new_state is State.TRIPPED: # Execution is already blocked by the persisted state. self._handle_trip(rec, trade_meta) return rec def _handle_trip(self, rec: BreakerRecord, trade_meta: dict) -> None: history = self._recent_trades() # Move to COOLDOWN before notifying so a crash mid-notification # still leaves the strategy paused. self.store.save(replace(rec, state=State.COOLDOWN, updated_at=_now())) notify_trip(self.strategy_id, history, trade_meta) def _recent_trades(self) -> list[dict]: # Pull the last N closed trades from your trade log. return load_recent_closed_trades(self.strategy_id, limit=10) def resume(self, reviewer: str, note: str) -> BreakerRecord: rec = self.store.load(self.strategy_id) if rec.state is not State.COOLDOWN: raise RuntimeError(f"cannot resume from state {rec.state}") log_review(self.strategy_id, reviewer, note, rec.consecutive_losses) rec = replace(rec, state=State.ACTIVE, consecutive_losses=0, updated_at=_now()) self.store.save(rec) return rec

Note the ordering in `_handle_trip`: persist `COOLDOWN` first, then notify. If `notify_trip` throws, the strategy is already stopped. The notification is a side effect, not part of the safety mechanism. Also note that `on_trade_closed` ignores PnL while the breaker is latched. This handles the real-world case where a stop order fills after the trip — you don't want that fill to silently reset a loss counter or, worse, re-trip an already-tripped breaker and re-fire notifications. ## Wiring It Into the Execution Loop The check has to sit in front of order submission, not inside the strategy logic. Strategy code is where you're most tempted to add exceptions.

python def run_bar(breaker: LossBreaker, strategy, market_data) -> None: if not breaker.can_trade(): return # paused: no signals, no orders, no sizing signal = strategy.evaluate(market_data) if signal is None: return fill = execute_order(signal) if fill is not None and fill.closed: breaker.on_trade_closed(fill.pnl, fill.meta)

If your strategy emits orders from multiple places, wrap `execute_order` itself with the `can_trade()` guard as a second line of defense. Belt and suspenders is cheap here. ## Notifications That Are Actually Useful A push that says "strategy tripped" wastes the meeting. The notification should carry the evidence: the losing trades, their entry/exit, size, PnL, and the timestamps. That's what makes the review a review instead of a shrug.

python import json import requests def notify_trip(strategy_id: str, history: list[dict], trigger: dict) -> None: lines = [f"Circuit breaker tripped: {strategy_id}", ""] for t in history: lines.append( f"{t['closed_at']} {t['side']:<4} size={t['size']:<8} " f"pnl={t['pnl']:+.2f} {t.get('exit_reason', '')}" ) lines.append("") lines.append(f"Triggering trade: {json.dumps(trigger, default=str)}") body = " ".join(lines) requests.post( "https://ntfy.sh/your-private-topic", data=body.encode("utf-8"), headers={"Title": f"BREAKER: {strategy_id}", "Priority": "high"}, timeout=10, ) ``

Keep the payload small and text-based. It should be readable on a phone lock screen. If you use a different channel — email, Telegram, a local webhook — the shape stays the same: strategy id, the streak, the trades. ## Consecutive Losses vs. Drawdown Limits These are not substitutes, and running only one is a common gap. | | Drawdown limit | Consecutive-loss breaker | |---|---|---| | Measures | Cumulative capital loss | Process deviation | | Typical trigger | Slow bleed over weeks | Fast streak over days | | Reset | New equity high | A single win | | Failure mode it catches | Sizing too large for the edge | Edge decay, feed corruption, bug | | Response | Reduce size / stop | Pause and review | A drawdown limit won't fire on three losses if the prior month was strong. A consecutive-loss breaker will. Conversely, a breaker won't catch a strategy that loses 55% of trades in a steady grind — you need the drawdown limit for that. Run both. They answer different questions and they fail in different directions. One more distinction worth stating: the breaker is per strategy, not per account. If you run five strategies and one trips, the other four should keep running. Coupling them turns a single-strategy problem into a portfolio-wide outage. ## The Psychology Part The breaker is not punishment. It's a forced meeting with your own statistics. Three losses in a row is not rare. For a strategy with a 45% win rate, the probability of any given three-trade window being all losses is about 16.6%. Over a few hundred trades you'll see it constantly. That's precisely why the rule is mechanical: if you decide case-by-case whether a streak is "just variance," you will decide it's variance every time, because that's the answer that lets you keep trading. The manual resume step is the actual feature. It forces you to write down what you saw — the trades, the market context, whether the fills looked normal — before the strategy goes live again. Sometimes the review takes two minutes and you're back. Sometimes it takes a week and the strategy gets retired. Both are correct outcomes. What's not correct is a timer that restarts everything at midnight and calls it risk management. Two practical habits make reviews fast: 1. **Log the review.** The log_review call in resume() writes who resumed, when, and why. After a few months you have a record of which strategies trip often and whether those trips preceded real problems. That's data about your breaker, not just your strategy. 2. **Tune the threshold per strategy, not globally.** Three is a reasonable default for strategies trading a few times a day. For a high-frequency strategy, three losses is noise; use a larger threshold or a percentage-based variant. For a low-frequency strategy, three losses might span months — there, a drawdown limit does more work. ## Adapting It The same structure generalizes cheaply: - **Percentage-based streak**: trip when cumulative loss over the current streak exceeds *x*% of equity, instead of a fixed count. - **Time-bounded streak**: only count losses within a rolling window, so a loss in January and a loss in June aren't "consecutive." - **Per-instrument breakers**: key the store on strategy_id + symbol` if your strategy trades several instruments with independent behavior. In all cases, keep the same invariants: persist state and counter together, block execution before notifying, and require an explicit, logged resume. Every filter must pass, so the output rate is the product of the individual pass rates. This is obvious arithmetic and almost nobody instruments for it. Instead, we tune filters one at a time, looking at each in isolation, and feel good about every one of them. "The trend filter is correct. The volume filter is correct. The momentum filter is correct." Seven correct filters, zero positions. That was the situation with our resonance scanner: a seven-layer entry gate that produced watchlist entries for weeks and never opened a position. The forensics were not subtle once we looked. The binding constraint was pullback confirmation, the last layer, and the reason it bound was structural, not statistical: the moves we were trying to catch do not, by their nature, offer a clean three-candle pullback. ### Anatomy of the Gate The pipeline looked like this, in order: 1. Trend — higher-timeframe EMA alignment. 2. Volume — relative volume above a rolling baseline. 3. Momentum — rate-of-change percentile. 4. Volatility — ATR band, to skip dead and berserk regimes. 5. Session — allowed trading hours. 6. Blacklist — symbol exclusion list. 7. Pullback confirmation — a defined retracement over N candles, then a resumption candle. Each filter is a pure function of a dataframe slice, which makes the whole thing easy to test and easy to instrument. The entry point was a single evaluate() that short-circuited on the first failure. That short-circuit was efficient and it was also why we were blind: a candidate rejected at layer 2 never touched layers 3 through 7, so we had no idea how many candidates each layer would have killed independently. ## Instrumenting the Filters The fix for blindness is cheap. Keep the short-circuit for live use, but add a shadow pass that evaluates every filter regardless of earlier failures and records the result. Two things matter in the record: the per-filter pass boolean, and the order of the first failure. The second is what tells you which filter is binding.

python from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class FilterTrace: symbol: str ts: int results: dict = field(default_factory=dict) # name -> bool @property def first_failure(self): for name, passed in self.results.items(): # insertion order = pipeline order if not passed: return name return None def shadow_evaluate(symbol, ts, ctx, filters): """Evaluate all filters without short-circuiting. Order preserved.""" trace = FilterTrace(symbol=symbol, ts=ts) for name, fn in filters: # list of (name, callable), in pipeline order try: trace.results[name] = bool(fn(ctx)) except Exception: trace.results[name] = False # fail closed, but record it return trace

Note the except clause. A filter that throws is a filter that rejected, and silently swallowing the exception is how you end up with a layer that never passes and nobody notices. Fail closed, but count it separately so exceptions do not masquerade as legitimate rejections. Live evaluation stays fast:

python def live_evaluate(ctx, filters): for name, fn in filters: if not fn(ctx): return False, name return True, None

Both paths share the same filter list, so they cannot drift apart. ### Aggregating the Traces With a few weeks of traces stored, the analysis is a groupby. For every filter we want the independent pass rate (how often it would pass if it were the only gate), and the conditional pass rate given that all earlier filters passed. The gap between those two numbers is where the interesting failures live.

python import pandas as pd def filter_report(traces: list[FilterTrace]) -> pd.DataFrame: rows = [] for t in traces: rows.append({"symbol": t.symbol, "ts": t.ts, "first_failure": t.first_failure, **t.results}) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) order = list(traces[0].results.keys()) out = [] for i, name in enumerate(order): independent = df[name].mean() if i == 0: conditional = independent reached = 1.0 else: prior = order[:i] reached_mask = df[prior].all(axis=1) reached = reached_mask.mean() conditional = df.loc[reached_mask, name].mean() if reached_mask.any() else float("nan") out.append({ "filter": name, "independent_pass": round(independent, 4), "reached_rate": round(reached, 4), "conditional_pass": round(conditional, 4), }) return pd.DataFrame(out)

reached_rate is the fraction of candidates that survived everything before this layer. conditional_pass is the pass rate among those that got there. A filter with a high independent pass rate and a low conditional pass rate is doing real work at the margin. A filter with a low independent pass rate is a candidate for removal regardless of where it sits. Then the binding constraint is simply the mode of first_failure:

python binding = df["first_failure"].value_counts(dropna=False) print(binding.head())

Our output looked roughly like this (numbers rounded, structure exact): | filter | independent_pass | reached_rate | conditional_pass | |---|---|---|---| | trend | 0.31 | 1.00 | 0.31 | | volume | 0.44 | 0.31 | 0.52 | | momentum | 0.38 | 0.16 | 0.61 | | volatility | 0.72 | 0.10 | 0.79 | | session | 0.83 | 0.08 | 0.88 | | blacklist | 0.97 | 0.07 | 0.98 | | pullback | 0.11 | 0.07 | 0.11 | Read the last row carefully. Seven percent of candidates reached the pullback layer, and only eleven percent of those passed it. The first six filters were, individually and collectively, behaving as designed: they cut a large universe down to a small, sensible set of live movers. The seventh filter then threw away 89% of that set. The mode of first_failure confirmed it: pullback was the last rejection for the overwhelming majority of candidates that got that far. ## The Structural Problem The naive conclusion is "loosen the pullback filter." That would have been wrong, and it took a while to articulate why. The scanner's thesis was resonance: trend, volume, and momentum aligned on a symbol that was being actively accumulated. In practice, the moves that satisfied the first six filters were fast, high-volume expansions, often on altcoins during a coordinated push. These moves have a characteristic shape: a steep impulse, a shallow consolidation or a single red candle, then continuation or exhaustion. What they almost never have is a textbook three-candle retracement followed by a clean resumption candle. The pullback filter was written for a different market behavior: orderly trends that breathe. By the time a clean three-candle pullback prints on a fast expansion, the expansion is over. The filter was not rejecting noise. It was rejecting the exact events the scanner existed to find. This is the general failure mode of stacked filters: each one is validated against the full population, but the conjunction selects a subpopulation with different conditional statistics. A pullback filter that works beautifully on a broad universe of trending names can have near-zero pass rate on the narrow slice that survives six upstream gates, because the upstream gates have already selected for the behavior the pullback filter excludes. Filters are not independent, and a pipeline is not a bag of good ideas. ## The Design Tradeoff The real decision was not "keep or drop pullback." It was where to sit on the spectrum between few but clean and so strict it never trades. The discipline argument for strictness is sound. Every filter you add is a degree of freedom, and every degree of freedom is an opportunity to fit the last regime. A seven-condition entry is nearly impossible to overfit by accident, because the search space of ways to be wrong is enormous and the sample of trades is tiny. If a strict system trades rarely, at least the trades it takes are well-supported. The counterargument is that a scanner which never trades is not conservative, it is broken. It provides no information, accumulates no live sample, and its filters are never validated against real outcomes. You cannot distinguish a disciplined system from a mis-specified one if the mis-specification happens to be the last gate in the chain. Strictness that produces zero fills is not a virtue; it is a measurement failure wearing a virtue's clothes. The resolution we landed on was to treat the pullback layer as a regime-conditional filter rather than a universal one, and to replace the hard three-candle rule with a graded score so the layer can be strict in one regime and permissive in another without being deleted outright.

python def pullback_score(df, lookback=3, min_retrace=0.25, max_retrace=0.75): """ Score 0..1 instead of boolean. Measures whether the recent action shows a controlled retracement rather than a vertical run. """ impulse = df["close"].iloc[-lookback-1] - df["close"].iloc[-lookback*2-1] if impulse <= 0: return 0.0 retrace = (df["close"].iloc[-lookback-1] - df["close"].iloc[-1]) / impulse if retrace < min_retrace: return 0.0 # no pullback at all: vertical run if retrace > max_retrace: return 0.0 # too deep: structure broken # peak score at mid-retrace, taper toward both edges mid = (min_retrace + max_retrace) / 2 width = (max_retrace - min_retrace) / 2 return max(0.0, 1.0 - abs(retrace - mid) / width) def pullback_gate(ctx, threshold=0.5): score = pullback_score(ctx.df) # Fast-expansion regime: accept a shallower structure. if ctx.regime == "expansion": return score >= threshold * 0.6 return score >= threshold

Two changes matter here. First, the layer now returns a continuous score, so you can see how close near-misses were instead of only pass/fail. Second, the threshold is regime-dependent, which encodes the actual finding: fast expansions legitimately do not pull back like orderly trends do, and pretending otherwise is a modeling error, not a discipline. Crucially, we did not just lower the threshold globally until trades appeared. That is the opposite failure: tuning a filter until it stops binding, then calling the result validated. The regime split came from the trace data (pullback pass rates differed sharply by regime upstream), and the new threshold was chosen on out-of-sample traces, not on the same window that produced the diagnosis. ### What to Keep The instrumented pipeline is worth keeping permanently, not just for this investigation. The FilterTrace records cost almost nothing, and the filter_report table is the single most useful diagnostic a multi-condition scanner can have. Run it monthly. If the binding constraint moves, you have learned something about the market. If it never moves, you have learned something about your filters: one of them is doing all the work, and the other six are decoration. The lesson generalizes past this scanner. A conjunction of filters is only as good as its weakest link, and you cannot find the weakest link by inspecting filters individually. You find it by counting first failures, computing conditional pass rates, and asking whether the surviving subpopulation is the one you actually meant to trade. The filter that rejects last is the filter that defines your system, whether or not you intended it to. The usual debate goes like this: the strict variant looks cleaner on the equity curve, the relaxed variant trades more, and someone argues the extra trades are "noise." That argument is almost never tested. It is asserted from the shape of the curve. The right question is narrower: what happens to the trades that exist only because of the relaxed rule? If that incremental set has positive expectancy, the strict filter is not cleaning up noise. It is deleting the strategy's core. In the case I worked through, the strict rule rejected 52 trades that the relaxed rule took. Those 52 trades had a 48.1% win rate, +0.131U expectancy per trade, and a profit factor of 1.50. The "worse" rule was rejecting the profitable part. This post is about the method, not the specific rule: run both variants over the same window, diff the trade lists, and evaluate the rejected set on its own statistics. ## Why the Headline Curve Can't Settle It Two variants produce two equity curves. Comparing them tells you which variant made more money over one sample. It does not tell you whether the filter is doing what you think it is doing, because the curves aggregate everything: shared trades, rejected trades, and the timing of both. A strict filter can improve a curve for three different reasons: 1. It removes genuinely bad trades (the intended effect). 2. It removes trades that were fine but happened to lose in this sample (overfitting to noise). 3. It changes position sizing or trade sequencing in a way that masks the removal of good trades. Only the first is a reason to keep it. The diff isolates the trades that differ, and their statistics tell you which of the three you are looking at. ### The diff is the unit of analysis Think of the two variants as generating two sets of trades over an identical window. The shared trades are irrelevant to the filter decision — both rules took them, so they contribute equally to both curves. The decision lives entirely in the symmetric difference: - Rejected-only: trades the strict rule skipped and the relaxed rule took. - Accepted-only: trades the relaxed rule skipped and the strict rule took (this happens when the rules are not strictly nested). If the rejected-only set has positive expectancy with a reasonable sample size, the filter is destroying value. If it has strongly negative expectancy, the filter is earning its keep. If the set is tiny, you have no evidence either way and should not pretend otherwise. ## Building the Two Trade Lists The prerequisite is that both variants log trades in the same schema, over the same data, with the same execution assumptions. Any difference in slippage model or fill logic between runs will contaminate the diff.

python from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime @dataclass(frozen=True) class Trade: symbol: str entry_time: datetime exit_time: datetime direction: str # "long" / "short" entry_price: float exit_price: float size: float # units pnl: float # realized, in account currency rule_variant: str # "strict" / "relaxed"

A trade key needs to identify the same opportunity across runs. Entry timestamp plus symbol plus direction is usually enough; if a strategy can re-enter the same symbol on the same bar, add an entry-sequence index.

python def trade_key(t: Trade) -> tuple: return (t.symbol, t.entry_time, t.direction)

Run both variants over the same window and the same instrument universe:

python strict_trades = run_backtest(strategy, data, params=STRICT_PARAMS) relaxed_trades = run_backtest(strategy, data, params=RELAXED_PARAMS) strict_by_key = {trade_key(t): t for t in strict_trades} relaxed_by_key = {trade_key(t): t for t in relaxed_trades} rejected_only = [t for k, t in relaxed_by_key.items() if k not in strict_by_key] accepted_only = [t for k, t in strict_by_key.items() if k not in relaxed_by_key] shared = [t for k, t in strict_by_key.items() if k in relaxed_by_key]

Sanity check before analyzing anything: len(shared) + len(rejected_only) should equal the relaxed run's trade count, and the PnL of the shared set should be identical in both runs. If it is not, the two runs are not comparable and the diff means nothing. ## Statistics for the Incremental Set The rejected-only set is just a list of trades. Evaluate it exactly as you would a standalone strategy, but report the full picture, not one number.

python import statistics as st def summarize(trades: list[Trade]) -> dict: n = len(trades) if n == 0: return {"n": 0} pnls = [t.pnl for t in trades] wins = [p for p in pnls if p > 0] losses = [p for p in pnls if p < 0] gross_win = sum(wins) gross_loss = -sum(losses) return { "n": n, "win_rate": len(wins) / n, "avg_win": st.mean(wins) if wins else 0.0, "avg_loss": st.mean(losses) if losses else 0.0, "expectancy": st.mean(pnls), "profit_factor": gross_win / gross_loss if gross_loss > 0 else float("inf"), "total_pnl": sum(pnls), }

For the 52 rejected trades this returns something like:

text n=52 win_rate=0.481 avg_win=+0.71U avg_loss=-0.41U expectancy=+0.131U profit_factor=1.50 total_pnl=+6.81U

Read it as a whole. A 48.1% win rate sounds unremarkable until you pair it with the payoff ratio: average win is roughly 1.7x average loss, so sub-50% accuracy still yields positive expectancy. Profit factor 1.50 over 52 trades is not spectacular, but it is clearly the wrong side of zero for a filter that is supposed to be removing bad trades. A filter that rejects a set with PF 1.50 is rejecting trades you would have wanted. ### Interpret the shape, not just the sign Three patterns are worth distinguishing when you look at the rejected-only set: - Negative expectancy with a normal win rate: the filter is removing losers. Keep it. - Near-zero expectancy with a large sample: the filter is removing noise. Keep it only if it materially reduces drawdown or costs; otherwise it is not earning its complexity. - Positive expectancy: the filter is removing profit. The strict variant needs a different justification, or it should go. The 52-trade case is the third pattern, and the win rate alone would have hidden it. This is why the diff has to be evaluated with expectancy and profit factor, not just hit rate. ## Guarding Against One Lucky Trade The most common way a diff analysis lies is concentration. Fifty-two trades with +0.131U expectancy can be twelve good trades and forty flat ones, or one trade that made the entire set. Before trusting the result, check: ### Per-trade contribution

python def concentration_report(trades: list[Trade], top_k: int = 5) -> dict: pnls = sorted((t.pnl for t in trades), reverse=True) total = sum(pnls) top = sum(pnls[:top_k]) return { "total_pnl": total, "top_k_pnl": top, "top_k_share": top / total if total != 0 else float("inf"), "expectancy_ex_top_k": (total - top) / (len(pnls) - top_k) if len(pnls) > top_k else None, }

If the top five trades account for most of the set's PnL and expectancy excluding them collapses toward zero, the incremental set is not evidence of a better rule. It is evidence of a handful of outcomes. ### Per-symbol breakdown The diff can also be dominated by one instrument. Group the rejected-only trades by symbol and compare each group's count and expectancy against its share of the full sample.

python from collections import defaultdict def by_symbol(trades: list[Trade]) -> dict[str, dict]: groups = defaultdict(list) for t in trades: groups[t.symbol].append(t) return {sym: summarize(ts) for sym, ts in groups.items()}

If one symbol supplies most of the rejected trades and all of the positive expectancy, the honest conclusion is "the relaxed rule helps on this symbol in this window," not "the relaxed rule is better." A filter decision made on a single-symbol diff is a single-symbol decision. ### Sample size and stability Fifty-two trades is enough to see a signal but not enough to be confident about its magnitude. Split the rejected-only set in half by time and check whether expectancy holds in both halves. If the first half carries everything and the second half is flat or negative, the incremental set is not a stable property of the rule.

python def split_half(trades: list[Trade]) -> tuple[list[Trade], list[Trade]]: ordered = sorted(trades, key=lambda t: t.entry_time) mid = len(ordered) // 2 return ordered[:mid], ordered[mid:]

## What the Method Actually Decides The diff analysis does not tell you which rule is "correct." It tells you what each rule is doing. In this case, the strict pullback filter was not removing noise — it was removing a set of trades with positive expectancy, a 1.50 profit factor, and a payoff profile that made a sub-50% win rate profitable. The relaxed rule was not sloppier; the strict rule was over-filtered. The general procedure generalizes beyond pullback filters. Any time you compare two entry conditions, two exit rules, or two position-sizing schemes, the shared trades cancel and the decision lives in the diff. Evaluate the incremental set with count, win rate, average win and loss, expectancy, and profit factor, then check whether that set is concentrated in a few trades or a single symbol. If it is, you have a hypothesis, not a result. The headline curve is a summary of everything at once. The diff is the only place the filter's actual effect is visible. Signal logic, position sizing, and exit rules are fixed. The only thing that changes between variants is the pullback confirmation that must be true before an entry fires. The strict filter requires all three of the following on the entry bar: 1. At least one down candle among the last three 15-minute candles. 2. Current price below the high of the last five candles. 3. The latest candle is not a large bullish candle (body above a threshold, e.g. 0.8 × ATR). The relaxed filter drops the three-candle window and the big-bullish veto, keeping only: at least one down candle within the last five candles. It still demands a pullback, just a looser one. Both variants run on the same 90-day window, 24 symbols, same fee model, same slippage assumption. That is the whole point of the experiment: a single boolean changes, everything else is held constant. ## Why the Comparison Is Easy to Get Wrong The tempting move is to compare the two versions by their win rates or average PnL per trade. That comparison is contaminated. The strict filter does not just change how trades are taken — it changes which trades exist. The strict set is a subset of the relaxed set, so you are comparing two different populations of trades, not the same trades under two treatments. To say anything honest about the filter, you need to look at the trades the strict filter rejects. Those rejected entries are where the answer lives. If the rejected trades have positive expectancy on their own, the filter is destroying edge. If they are negative, the filter is earning its keep. So the experiment has three outputs, not two: - Trades taken by both variants (the intersection). - Trades taken only by the relaxed variant (rejected by strict). - Expectancy of each group. The base strategy under the relaxed filter is the control population. The strict filter is a treatment applied to the signal stream. Treat it like an A/B test where the "B" arm is a subset of "A", and you want to know whether the excluded slice is better or worse than average. ## Counting the Incremental Trades The cleanest way to run this is to evaluate the signal stream once, tag every candidate entry with the filter booleans, and then slice. Here is a minimal harness that does exactly that.

python from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Callable @dataclass class Trade: symbol: str ts: int entry: float exit: float pnl: float # net of fees and slippage, in quote units def strict_pullback(candles, i: int, atr: float) -> bool: # candles: list of (ts, o, h, l, c) ascending, i = entry bar index last3 = candles[i-2:i+1] has_down = any(c[4] < c[1] for c in last3) five_high = max(c[2] for c in candles[i-4:i+1]) body = candles[i][4] - candles[i][1] not_big_bull = body < 0.8 * atr return has_down and candles[i][4] < five_high and not_big_bull def relaxed_pullback(candles, i: int, atr: float) -> bool: last5 = candles[i-4:i+1] return any(c[4] < c[1] for c in last5)

The backtest engine stays untouched. You generate candidate entries from the momentum signal, then record both filter verdicts alongside the realized PnL. Note that the entry price and exit price are identical for a given candidate regardless of which filter accepted it — the filter does not move the entry bar, it only decides whether the bar is tradeable at all. That assumption matters: if your strict filter also shifts entry timing (e.g. waiting for confirmation on the next bar), you have changed two variables and the comparison is dead.

python def run_backtest(candles_by_symbol, signal_fn, exit_fn): rows = [] for sym, candles in candles_by_symbol.items(): atr_series = compute_atr(candles, 14) for i in range(20, len(candles) - 1): if not signal_fn(candles, i): continue atr = atr_series[i] entry = candles[i][4] exit_price = exit_fn(candles, i) pnl = (exit_price - entry) - fee_and_slip(entry, exit_price) rows.append({ "symbol": sym, "ts": candles[i][0], "pnl": pnl, "strict": strict_pullback(candles, i, atr), "relaxed": relaxed_pullback(candles, i, atr), }) return rows

Now the analysis is just a groupby. No second backtest run, no risk of drift between the two code paths.

python def slice_expectancy(rows): both = [r["pnl"] for r in rows if r["strict"] and r["relaxed"]] strict_only = [r["pnl"] for r in rows if r["strict"] and not r["relaxed"]] relaxed_only = [r["pnl"] for r in rows if r["relaxed"] and not r["strict"]] # note: strict implies relaxed by construction only if the # relaxed rule is a strict superset — verify this before trusting it return { "both": (len(both), sum(both) / len(both) if both else 0), "strict_rejected": (len(relaxed_only), sum(relaxed_only) / len(relaxed_only) if relaxed_only else 0), "strict_only": (len(strict_only), sum(strict_only) / len(strict_only) if strict_only else 0), }

One check before you trust any of this: confirm the strict rule is actually a subset of the relaxed rule. If your relaxed rule is "any down candle in the last five" and your strict rule also requires "price below the five-candle high," then strict does not imply relaxed — a bar can satisfy strict's down-candle condition and high condition while failing nothing in relaxed, but the reverse can also happen if the down candle is outside the five-bar window in strict's three-bar check. Run the set-difference both ways and print the counts. If strict_only is non-empty, your two rules are not nested, and you should compare them as two separate populations rather than a control and a treatment. ## The Numbers On the 90-day, 24-symbol run: | Variant | Trades | Expectancy (U/trade) | |---|---|---| | Strict pullback | ~1,900 | -0.013 | | Relaxed pullback | ~2,600 | +0.011 | The strict filter rejects roughly 700 candidate entries. Those rejected trades carry positive expectancy — enough to flip the whole strategy from negative to positive. The filter did not remove noise; it removed the profitable tail. The win rate on the strict set was actually slightly higher. That is the trap. A filter that raises win rate while lowering expectancy is selecting for small, frequent wins and occasional large losses — exactly what a late, tired move produces. ## Why "Safer" Is Worse Here The strict filter's three conditions all bias toward the same failure mode: entering after the move has already extended and then rolled over. - Requiring a down candle in the last three bars means you enter on the first sign of weakness. In a momentum regime, that is often the start of a real reversal, not a healthy pullback. - Requiring price below the five-candle high means you are buying into a local dip — but only after the high was already set. The move is mature. - Vetoing a big bullish candle removes exactly the bars where momentum is re-accelerating. Those are the entries with the best follow-through. The relaxed filter keeps the pullback requirement but gives the move room to breathe. It accepts entries where the pullback happened four or five bars ago and price has since resumed. Those entries are earlier in the next leg, not later in the current one. Put differently: the strict filter is a proxy for "the setup looks clean right now." But clean-looking setups are, by construction, the ones where the crowd has already noticed. The relaxed filter accepts messier setups that the strategy's exit logic can still harvest. The filter was supposed to reduce drawdown. It reduced trade count and took the edge with it. ## Practical Rules for Filter A/B Tests A few habits that keep this kind of test honest: *Keep the exit fixed.* If you tune the exit for each filter variant, you are no longer measuring the filter. Any difference in expectancy is confounded by the exit change. *Always report the rejected slice.* A filter's value is the expectancy of what it excludes. If you do not compute that number, you do not know what the filter does. *Check nesting before slicing.* Confirm which candidate population each rule accepts, and whether one is a subset of the other. Non-nested rules need separate baselines. *Watch win rate and expectancy diverge.* When a filter raises win rate but lowers expectancy, you have found a filter that trades frequency for size. That trade is only good if the size reduction is larger than the frequency gain — usually it is not. *Run the test on out-of-sample data.* A 90-day window with 24 symbols is enough to see a sign flip, not enough to trust the magnitude. Re-run on a held-out period and check whether the rejected-slice expectancy keeps the same sign. ## Closing Filters that feel safe are often filters that select for late entries. Measure what they reject, not just what they keep. Optimize hard enough over enough combinations and something will look great by luck alone. The question is not "does this rule make money in the backtest?" but "does this rule make money for reasons that survive contact with slightly different assumptions?" The gate I use before any rule reaches the live scanner has three layers: a parameter sweep, a monthly consistency check, and a component ablation. Each layer answers a different question, and each has a hard pass/fail threshold. A rule has to clear all three. This post walks through the mechanics, then through a real rejection: a MACD divergence entry that passed layer 1 and died on layers 2 and 3. ## Layer 1: Parameter Sweep ### The question it answers Is the edge a plateau or a spike? If performance only exists at fast=12, slow=26, signal=9, you have found noise, not a rule. Neighboring parameter values should produce comparable results, and the chosen point should sit near the center of a profitable region, not on its edge. ### The metrics For each parameter combination in the grid, record: - Trade count — anything under ~50 is too thin to say much. - Profit factor (PF) — gross wins / gross losses. - Expectancy per trade — in R units (risk multiples), so results are comparable across parameter sets. - Max drawdown — in R, not percent, so it doesn't depend on position sizing. - Plateau score — the fraction of neighboring combinations (within one step in each dimension) that stay above the PF threshold. ### The thresholds - Median PF across the sweep ≥ 1.3 - At least 70% of combinations with ≥ 50 trades have PF > 1.0 - Plateau score at the chosen point ≥ 0.6 - Chosen point is not on the grid boundary ### The code

python import itertools import numpy as np import pandas as pd def sweep(params_grid, run_backtest, min_trades=50): rows = [] for combo in itertools.product(*params_grid.values()): params = dict(zip(params_grid.keys(), combo)) res = run_backtest(**params) if res["trades"] < min_trades: continue rows.append({**params, **res}) return pd.DataFrame(rows) def plateau_score(df, param_names, chosen, pf_col="pf", threshold=1.0): """Fraction of 1-step neighbors of `chosen` with PF above threshold.""" neighbors = [] for name in param_names: values = sorted(df[name].unique()) idx = values.index(chosen[name]) for offset in (-1, 1): j = idx + offset if 0 <= j < len(values): mask = pd.Series(True, index=df.index) for n in param_names: target = chosen[n] if n != name else values[j] mask &= df[n] == target if mask.any(): neighbors.append(df.loc[mask, pf_col].iloc[0]) if not neighbors: return 0.0 return float(np.mean(np.array(neighbors) > threshold)) grid = { "fast": [8, 10, 12, 14, 16], "slow": [20, 24, 26, 30, 34], "signal": [7, 9, 11], } results = sweep(grid, run_macd_divergence_backtest) chosen = {"fast": 12, "slow": 26, "signal": 9} score = plateau_score(results, list(grid.keys()), chosen) print(f"median PF: {results['pf'].median():.2f}") print(f"share PF>1: {(results['pf'] > 1.0).mean():.0%}") print(f"plateau score at chosen point: {score:.2f}")

A plateau score of 0.6 means most one-step neighbors still clear PF 1.0. That is a low bar, deliberately. If a rule can't survive a one-step nudge, it has no business being tested further. ## Layer 2: Monthly Consistency ### The question it answers Is the annual result distributed across time, or is it one monster month doing all the work? A strategy with one +40% month and eleven flat months is not a strategy. It's a lottery ticket that already paid out, and the next ticket is unlikely to pay again. ### The metrics Bucket trades by calendar month and compute: - Share of profitable months — count of months with positive PnL / total months. - Best-month contribution — best month's PnL / total PnL. - Top-3-month contribution — same, for the three best months. - Median monthly return and worst month in R. ### The thresholds - ≥ 55% of months positive - Best month ≤ 30% of total PnL - Top 3 months ≤ 55% of total PnL - Worst month no worse than −3R (scaled to your per-trade risk) The best-month cap is the important one. It is the metric that catches curve-fit strategies that happen to overlap a single volatility event. ### The code

python def monthly_consistency(trades: pd.DataFrame, risk_per_trade=1.0): """trades: columns ['exit_time', 'pnl_r']""" monthly = (trades .assign(month=trades["exit_time"].dt.to_period("M")) .groupby("month")["pnl_r"] .sum() .sort_index()) total = monthly.sum() if total <= 0: return {"pass": False, "reason": "non-positive total PnL"} best = monthly.max() top3 = monthly.nlargest(3).sum() stats = { "months": len(monthly), "positive_share": (monthly > 0).mean(), "best_share": best / total, "top3_share": top3 / total, "median_month": monthly.median(), "worst_month": monthly.min(), } stats["pass"] = ( stats["months"] >= 24 and stats["positive_share"] >= 0.55 and stats["best_share"] <= 0.30 and stats["top3_share"] <= 0.55 and stats["worst_month"] >= -3 * risk_per_trade ) return stats

The months >= 24 requirement matters. With twelve months, "positive share" is dominated by a handful of observations and the test is close to meaningless. ## Layer 3: Robustness Ablation ### The question it answers Does each component of the rule contribute, and does the rule degrade gracefully when a component is removed? A robust rule loses some edge when you strip a filter. A fragile rule collapses to zero, or worse, only works with every component present — a sign the components were fitted to each other. ### The metrics For each component, run the backtest with that component removed (or replaced by a neutral version) and record: - PF delta — component PF minus full-rule PF. - Expectancy delta in R. - Retention — component expectancy / full-rule expectancy. ### The thresholds - Removing any single component leaves expectancy ≥ 60% of the full rule (graceful degradation). - Removing the core component (the entry trigger itself, not a filter) drops expectancy below 50% and PF below 1.1 (the core actually matters). - No component removal improves expectancy by more than 15% (if it does, that component is hurting and should be cut). The third criterion is the one people skip. It catches filters that were added to patch a specific losing streak in the sample and do nothing out of sample. ### The code

python def ablation(full_result, variants: dict, core="divergence"): """variants: name -> backtest result dict with 'pf' and 'expectancy_r'""" base_pf = full_result["pf"] base_exp = full_result["expectancy_r"] rows = [] for name, res in variants.items(): rows.append({ "component": name, "pf": res["pf"], "expectancy_r": res["expectancy_r"], "retention": res["expectancy_r"] / base_exp if base_exp else 0.0, "pf_delta": res["pf"] - base_pf, }) df = pd.DataFrame(rows) checks = { "graceful": (df.loc[df["component"] != core, "retention"] >= 0.60).all(), "core_matters": df.loc[df["component"] == core, "retention"].lt(0.50).all(), "no_harmful": (df["retention"] <= 1.15).all(), } return df, checks

## The Case Study: A MACD Divergence Entry The rule: enter long when price makes a lower low but MACD histogram makes a higher low (bullish divergence), confirmed by a close above the signal line. Exit on a fixed 2R target or a time stop of 20 bars. Filters included a trend filter (price above the 200-EMA), a volume filter (volume above its 20-bar average), and a volatility floor (ATR above its 20-bar median). ### Layer 1: passed The sweep over fast ∈ [8,16], slow ∈ [20,34], signal ∈ [7,11] produced 75 combinations, 68 with enough trades. Median PF was 1.41, 78% of combinations had PF above 1.0, and the plateau score at (12, 26, 9) was 0.71. The chosen point sat comfortably inside the grid. Nothing suspicious yet. ### Layer 2: failed Over 31 months, only 48% of months were positive. Worse, the best month contributed 44% of total PnL, and the top three months contributed 71%. The best month coincided with a broad volatility expansion — the rule caught one regime and did nothing in the other thirty. Median monthly PnL was slightly negative. Verdict: fail on positive_share (0.48 < 0.55), best_share (0.44 > 0.30), and top3_share (0.71 > 0.55). This alone is enough to reject the rule. ### Layer 3: failed The ablation was run anyway, out of curiosity: | Removed | PF | Expectancy (R) | Retention | |---|---|---|---| | Trend filter | 1.38 | 0.11 | 0.73 | | Volume filter | 1.52 | 0.17 | 1.13 | | Volatility floor | 1.09 | 0.06 | 0.40 | | Divergence (core) | 0.94 | −0.01 | −0.07 | Two problems. The volatility floor is doing most of the work — removing it drops retention to 0.40, well below the 0.60 floor. That means the "divergence" rule is largely a low-volatility regime filter wearing a costume. And removing the volume filter improves expectancy by 13%, which is under the 15% harm threshold but close enough to be a warning sign: the filter was probably added to patch a specific stretch of the sample. The core divergence component does matter (removal sends expectancy negative), but that doesn't save the rule. A rule whose edge lives mostly in a regime filter, and whose only positive months come from one volatility event, is not a rule. It's a description of one period. ### The rejection Three-layer result: pass, fail, fail. The rule went into the rejected list with the metrics recorded, so future me doesn't re-test it in six months and get excited all over again. That bookkeeping is half the value of the process. ## Practical Notes - Run the layers in order. Layer 1 is cheap and filters out most junk. Layer 2 is cheaper than layer 3 and catches the most common failure mode. Don't run ablations on rules that can't pass a monthly check. - Log every metric, including failures. A rejection is only useful if it's documented. Keep the sweep DataFrame and the ablation table next to the rule definition. - Thresholds are conventions, not laws. The numbers above are tuned to my trade frequency and risk unit. If your rules trade twenty times a year, months >= 24 is too strict; if they trade daily, best_share <= 0.30 is probably too loose. Pick thresholds once, write them down, and don't move them after seeing a result you like. - The ablation is the most informative layer. It tells you why a rule works, not just whether it did. When a rule fails layer 3, you often learn something reusable about the market — in this case, that low-volatility regimes are where this class of divergence entry lives, which is a hypothesis worth testing on its own.
