title: supabase-schema-architect proves your RLS policies as two users before it hands back the migration
description:
In Supabase, your policies are the authorization layer

In a Supabase project the browser talks to Postgres directly. The Data API exposes every table, view and function in the exposed schemas (public by default) to anyone holding the project’s publishable key, and each request runs as the role anon when signed out or authenticated when signed in. There is no application server in the middle deciding what comes back.

That means your grants and Row Level Security policies are not a safety net on top of an authorization layer. They are the authorization layer. A table without a policy is a public endpoint, and a policy nobody ran is a guess.

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2122066551289368720-190'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2122066551289368720&theme=dark" }

This keeps happening at scale, and it keeps happening to teams who thought the schema was fine because the app looked fine.

Install it 

npx claude-code-templates@latest --agent database/supabase-schema-architect

That writes .claude/agents/supabase-schema-architect.md in the project. A project copy wins over one in ~/.claude/agents/, so a team can pin its own version.

Two things in its frontmatter are worth knowing before you run it. tools is set to Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep, and in a subagent tools is an allowlist that restricts: this agent cannot reach your MCP servers, which an agent that writes SQL and starts a database probably should not. model: inherit means it runs on whatever model the session is on, and since 2.1.251 that frontmatter value wins over CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL.

One correction to the catalog entry: its description opens with “MUST BE USED”, which is prompt text, not a documented trigger. The phrase Anthropic documents for proactive delegation is “use proactively”. Delegation still comes down to Claude reading that description and deciding, so ask for the agent by name the first few times.

// Detect dark theme var iframe = document.getElementById('tweet-2122937536565641711-36'); if (document.body.className.includes('dark-theme')) { iframe.src = "https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?id=2122937536565641711&theme=dark" }

It does not hand back SQL it has not run

This is what separates it from a prompt that knows Supabase trivia. Before it reports, it applies the migration and acts as real users.

With Docker it runs supabase start, supabase db reset, supabase test db for pgTAP tests, and supabase db advisors for Supabase’s own security and performance checks. Without Docker it starts a scratch Postgres with initdb, creates only the parts of Supabase the migration touches (the anon, authenticated and service_role roles, an auth schema, and auth.uid() and auth.jwt() shims that read request.jwt.claims), and grants nothing else, so the test also proves your explicit grants.

Then it becomes each user, inside a transaction it rolls back:

begin;
set local role authenticated;
select set_config('request.jwt.claims',
  json_build_object('sub', '<user uuid>', 'role', 'authenticated')::text, true);
select count(*) from public.tasks;
rollback;

It seeds two users in two organizations and shows, per table, that a member reads their own organization’s rows and none of the other’s, that inserting into the other organization fails, that updating a row to move it across tenants fails, that a member cannot change their own role, and that anon reads nothing it should not.

The line worth stealing even if you never install this agent: a superuser skips RLS, so a test that never switches role proves nothing. That is why most hand-written policy tests pass.

One caveat the post does not mention: that run is conditional. If there is no Docker and no Postgres it can start, the agent says so plainly and lists what is untested instead of pretending. Read that part of its report before you deploy.

The mistakes it is written against

Its instructions are a list of things that are easy to get wrong in exactly this stack:

  1. insert ... returning (supabase-js .insert().select()) checks the new row against the SELECT policy during the insert, before any after insert trigger runs. That is why “create an organization and become its owner” fails with new row violates row-level security policy. The fix is created_by uuid default auth.uid() plus a SELECT policy that matches it.
  2. A policy on memberships that queries memberships raises infinite recursion detected in policy. That lookup belongs in a security definer function in a private schema, with set search_path = '' and execute revoked from anon.
  3. Never authorize on user_metadata. Users can change it themselves with updateUser. Use app_metadata or a table.
  4. Views run as their owner and bypass RLS unless you create them with (security_invoker = true).
  5. On UPDATE, using says which rows may change and with check says what they may become. A with check looser than using lets a user move a row into another tenant. Column privileges stop the writes a row policy cannot express, like a member editing their own role.
  6. An unwrapped auth.uid() is evaluated once per row. (select auth.uid()) is evaluated once per query. Supabase’s own linter flags this as auth_rls_initplan.
  7. supabase db diff misses view security_invoker, column privileges, alter policy and alter publication. Those get written by hand.

It also hands off instead of guessing: large online migrations go to database-architect, query tuning to postgres-pro, Realtime load to supabase-realtime-optimizer.

Where the agents live

  • The agent’s page: supabase-schema-architect on aitmpl.com
  • The related skill: Supabase Postgres best practices
  • For non-Supabase Postgres and online migrations: database-architect
  • The rest of the catalog: aitmpl.com

title: 7,472 write bursts and 48,216 rows: what a prediction log can and cannot prove
description:
Every prediction platform eventually has to answer one question from a customer, a regulator, or its own postmortem: was this row produced by an analysis of this match, or was it replayed?

The model card describes intent, not execution. The only artifact describing execution is the row itself — its write time, its measured duration, its payload. So I treated our own production log as a forensic object.

The table is ai_predictions: 48,216 rows, 47,167 graded, 3,853 models, 17,235 matches, 116 distinct days from 2026-06-21 to 2026-11-20. Orientation: 26,806 hits over 47,167 graded rows, 56.83%.

Cluster the writes into bursts

A prediction is not an event, it is a member of a batch. To see batches you do not need a job table — you need the gap between consecutive writes. I used 120 seconds: any longer silence starts a new burst.

with t as (
  select id, created_at, model_id, match_id,
         created_at - lag(created_at) over (order by created_at, id) as gap
  from ai_predictions
), b as (
  select *, sum(case when gap is null or gap > interval '120 seconds' then 1 else 0 end)
           over (order by created_at, id) as burst_id
  from t
)
select count(distinct burst_id) as bursts, count(*) as rows,
       max(n) as largest_burst,
       percentile_disc(0.5) within group (order by n) as p50_size
from (select burst_id, count(*) n from b group by 1) s;

bursts | rows  | largest_burst | p50_size
7472   | 48215 | 645           | 2

7,472 bursts for 48,215 rows, mean 6.45, median 2. The distribution is bimodal: 2,951 bursts hold exactly one row, while 41 bursts hold more than 100 and together account for 7,540 rows — 15.6% of the log written in 41 windows.

The largest ran on 2026-10-10, 00:44:10 to 01:24:58: 645 rows, 214 matches, 160 distinct models, 2,448.4 seconds of wall clock. That is already a finding. 160 models produced 645 predictions across 214 matches in 41 minutes — a fan-out, not a per-match loop.

Does a model write the same match twice in one burst?

Yes: of 32,110 (burst, model) pairs, 8,070 contain more than one row; 1,008 contain five or more; the maximum is 50 rows from one model inside one contiguous burst. A model emitting 50 rows in one window is iterating a slate.

The arithmetic of concurrency

analysis_duration_ms over 29,991 non-null rows: p5 = 4,465 ms, p50 = 58,730 ms, p95 = 182,816 ms, max 1,569,409 ms. Median ~58.7 seconds per prediction.

Now compare with the burst above: 645 rows in 2,448 seconds, i.e. 3.8 seconds of wall clock per row. You cannot spend 58.7 seconds of compute per row and emit one row every 3.8 seconds unless rows are produced concurrently. The ratio per burst is the implied parallelism:

with t as (
  select id, created_at, analysis_duration_ms,
         created_at - lag(created_at) over (order by created_at, id) as gap
  from ai_predictions where analysis_duration_ms is not null
), b as (
  select *, sum(case when gap is null or gap > interval '120 seconds' then 1 else 0 end)
           over (order by created_at, id) as burst_id
  from t
), s as (
  select burst_id, sum(analysis_duration_ms)/1000.0 as compute_s,
         extract(epoch from max(created_at)-min(created_at)) as span_s
  from b group by 1 having count(*) >= 5
)
select count(*) as bursts,
       round(percentile_disc(0.5) within group (order by compute_s/nullif(span_s,0))::numeric, 2) as p50,
       round(percentile_disc(0.9) within group (order by compute_s/nullif(span_s,0))::numeric, 2) as p90
from s where span_s > 0;

bursts | p50  | p90
1477   | 3.77 | 10.54

Across 1,477 bursts of at least five instrumented rows, the median burst packs 3.77 seconds of measured compute into every second of wall clock; p90 is 10.54. For the 645-row burst, only 277 rows carry a duration and those 277 alone sum to 16,520.6 seconds inside a 2,448-second window — a lower bound of 6.7x. Extrapolating the measured mean of 59.6 s/row to all 645 gives ~38,400 seconds, about 15.7x.

First honest conclusion: the log proves concurrency. It cannot prove which worker produced which row, because there is no run_id and no worker_id. Two rows 400 ms apart from two processes are indistinguishable from two threads of one process, and both are indistinguishable from a replay that copies a stored analysis. Concurrency is measurable; provenance is not.

The missing 37.8%

18,225 rows (37.8%) have analysis_duration_ms IS NULL, and not at random:

month rows null duration share
2026-06 2,735 2,735 100.0%
2026-07 2,637 2,637 100.0%
2026-08 164 164 100.0%
2026-09 9,757 5,563 57.0%
2026-10 21,886 4,317 19.7%
2026-11 11,037 2,809 25.5%

Instrumentation arrived in September, stabilised in October, then drifted back to 25.5% in November. Any cost-per-prediction, latency SLO, or "how long does the model think" figure computed on non-null rows is a sample stratified by month, and months are not exchangeable: model composition, match volume and prompt length all moved. The correct denominator is 48,216 and the correct summary is "63.2% of rows have a measured duration".

Latency carries no quality signal

duration bucket rows graded hit rate
< 10 s 5,440 5,371 58.09%
10–60 s 9,666 9,391 57.56%
1–3 min 13,313 13,081 56.87%
> 3 min 1,572 1,562 57.17%
null 18,225 17,638 56.41%

Full spread 1.68 points across buckets differing by an order of magnitude in size, and the ordering is not monotonic. The 362 rows finishing under one second sit in the same band as rows taking four minutes.

I report this as a negative result because it constrains the fix. If longer analysis produced better predictions, the response to a 15.7x concurrency finding would be "add capacity". Since it does not, the response is "record what happened, then decide".

Identical payloads across different matches

Hashing full_analysis is the cheapest provenance check available without a schema change:

select count(*) as dup_hashes, sum(n) as rows_in_dup_groups,
       sum(case when dm > 1 then n else 0 end) as rows_spanning_multiple_matches,
       max(n) as largest_group, max(dm) as matches_in_largest_group
from (
  select md5(full_analysis) h, count(*) n, count(distinct match_id) dm
  from ai_predictions
  where full_analysis is not null and length(full_analysis) > 100
  group by 1 having count(*) > 1
) g;

dup_hashes | rows_in_dup_groups | rows_spanning_multiple_matches | largest_group | matches_in_largest_group
736        | 3780               | 3361                           | 123           | 77

736 payloads repeat, covering 3,780 rows, and 3,361 of those rows sit in groups spanning more than one match. The largest single text appears 123 times across 77 matches. It is not prose — it is a 240-character JSON stub beginning {"prediction": {"direction": "home", "confidence": 6, "score_prediction": "2-1"}, a fixed default stamped onto whatever match was in the loop when real analysis failed.

That is the finding a schema cannot catch alone, and why payload hashing belongs in the audit. 7,539 rows carry 100–500 characters; 40,510 carry more than 500. Length will not separate a stub from an analysis, but a hash will.

The column that exists and records nothing

cache_expires_at is declared on the table. Populated: 0 of 48,216. A column that is always null is worse than an absent column, because it invites analysis that silently returns zero: anyone auditing cache reuse against it concludes "no caching occurred" — true, or merely unrecorded. Same rule for prediction_source: free-text (match_center 30,062, system 11,458, scheduled 5,343, match_center+ahfill 986, then 16 one-off values). Free-text provenance is not provenance.

What the schema should have recorded

Five columns would have made every question above answerable without forensics:

alter table ai_predictions
  add column run_id             uuid    not null,  -- one value per batch invocation
  add column worker_id          text    not null,  -- process that wrote the row
  add column input_snapshot_id  text    not null,  -- hash of the frozen input bundle
  add column contract_version   text    not null,  -- prompt + training-word version
  add column duration_ms        integer not null;

create unique index ai_pred_run_model_match on ai_predictions (run_id, model_id, match_id);
create index ai_pred_input_snapshot on ai_predictions (input_snapshot_id);

"Did this row come from this match's data" then becomes a join instead of an argument: group by run_id, compare sum(duration_ms) to the run's wall clock, assert input_snapshot_id is unique per (run, match).

A verifier you can run before adding anything 

import psycopg2

DSN = "postgresql://user:pass@127.0.0.1:5433/soccerdream"

def main():
    cur = psycopg2.connect(DSN).cursor()
    cur.execute("""select count(*), count(*) filter (where analysis_duration_ms is null),
                          count(distinct md5(full_analysis)) from ai_predictions""")
    rows, nulls, distinct_payloads = cur.fetchone()
    print(f"rows={rows} null_duration={nulls} ({100.0*nulls/rows:.1f}%) "
          f"distinct_payloads={distinct_payloads}")

    cur.execute("""select count(*) from (
          select md5(full_analysis) h from ai_predictions
          where full_analysis is not null and length(full_analysis) > 100
          group by 1 having count(distinct match_id) > 1) g""")
    cross = cur.fetchone()[0]
    print(f"payloads_reused_across_matches={cross}")

    assert nulls < 0.05 * rows, "duration coverage regressed"
    assert cross == 0, "identical analysis text spans multiple matches"
    print("invariants ok")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run against today's table it fails both assertions — 37.8% nulls, 736 cross-match payloads. The failure is the baseline; the useful question is whether tomorrow's number is smaller.

The general lesson

A prediction log does not document what the model thought. It documents what the process did, and only to the depth the schema chose to record. Ours records time and duration — enough to establish fan-out batches, heavy concurrency, 50 rows from one model in one window, and 3,361 payloads shared across matches. It does not record run, worker, or input identity, which makes the difference between "analysed" and "replayed" unprovable for 100% of rows.

That is a schema gap, not a modelling failure. The cheapest audit this week is the burst reconstruction above: it needs nothing but created_at, and it tells you within an hour whether your pipeline is per-match or per-batch — and whether anyone could prove it either way.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

本内容仅供数据分析与研究参考，不构成任何决策建议。

title: Prowler title matches lead to scan-account and role inventory
description:
Prowler title matches lead to scan-account and role inventory

Prowler is a cloud security assessment tool with a local server and dashboard. A deployment can store findings, provider credentials, account ownership, scan configuration, and API keys. When a title query returns a small population, the useful work is to identify which matches are actual Prowler applications and which scan identities they can control.

Observation

At 07:51 on November 20, 2026 (UTC+8), a count-only ZoomEye SDK query used sub_type=all, page 1, and pagesize 1. app="Prowler" returned 0 matches. title="Prowler" returned 226 matches.

Prowler is also an ordinary English word, so the title count can include unrelated pages. The result is an inventory lead, not 226 confirmed installations. A verified match should be checked against the application's documented login and dashboard paths before being added to an ownership queue.

Separate users from cloud authority

The Prowler application documentation describes user roles and permissions, including API keys for programmatic access. The local-server guide says provider authentication settings are available to users who can manage the account. Those two layers should be reviewed together: a user with a management role may be able to add a cloud provider credential that extends the tool's reach.

Inventory the tenant, users, roles, API keys, provider connections, scan accounts, and finding visibility. Confirm whether a role can initiate scans, edit provider credentials, export findings, or invite users. For each cloud connection, record the external identity, permission set, resource scope, and rotation owner.

Test a read-only analyst, a scan operator, an account manager, and a revoked API key. Attempt to change provider configuration from each role and verify that the denial happens in the API rather than only in the interface.

Evidence and retention

Scan findings can disclose account identifiers, resource names, public endpoints, and configuration weaknesses. Review the database and object-store retention, backups, and export controls. The dashboard should not treat a public title match as an authorized target; ownership must come from cloud account records and DNS or network inventory.

Prowler's value is in mapping the scan configuration to the identities that can change it. ZoomEye supplies 226 title leads for that review. It cannot establish cloud account ownership or the permissions of a provider credential found in a self-hosted instance.

References

  • Prowler App RBAC tutorial
  • Prowler local server guide
  • ZoomEye title query for Prowler

title: GitHub Copilot cloud sandboxes start drawing from Actions compute on November 23
description:
Suppose a GitHub Team organization has already consumed USD 15.50 of its USD 18 compute allowance on CI. That leaves USD 2.50. At the assumed sizes below, 23 half-hour Copilot cloud sessions fit; the 24th crosses the allowance. CI and sandbox runtime draw from the same allowance, independently of model usage.

GitHub's November 19 changelog update gives November 23, 2026 as the billing start date without specifying a time or time zone. The following is a worked operating plan based on published rates, not a measured workload or bill.

01. Identify the environment and the account paying for it

Environment What is billed When to use it
Local No separate cloud sandbox runtime fee; model usage is separate Small changes and reviews that reproduce locally
Cloud GitHub-hosted isolated Linux; running CPU and memory, with retained snapshots metered separately Isolation or parallel work materially improves turnaround
Actions The rules for the selected Actions runner and repository A prescribed CI environment, Windows, specialized hardware, or a self-hosted runner is required

The sandbox owner pays, not necessarily the person who starts the session. For repository work, GitHub bills the account that owns the repositories, which must all share one owner in a given session. Without a repository, the selected organization or personal account pays; if none is selected, billing goes to the personal account. A developer can run an organization task and a personal experiment without drawing from the same allowance. Billing and ownership

02. Know which meters use included compute

Included compute is a monetary value, not a shared count of minutes. Eligible standard hosted runners for private and internal repositories share it with Cloud CPU and memory, with no priority between usage types. Eligible larger runners can also draw from it on Team and Enterprise Cloud. Standard hosted runners for public repositories and self-hosted runners are independently free under the Actions rules. That does not make public-repository Cloud sessions or public-repository larger runners free.

The included usage table lists USD 12 for both personal and organization Free, USD 18 for personal Pro and Team, and USD 300 for Enterprise Cloud. The allowance resets at the start of the billing cycle. These are GitHub account plans, not Copilot subscription levels.

Meter Measured as Rate (USD) Included compute
CPU Running seconds × allocated vCPU 0.000024 per vCPU-second Yes
Memory Running seconds × allocated GiB 0.000003 per GiB-second Yes
Snapshots Actual GiB-month kept after stop, until deletion 0.005 per GiB-month Separate
Model usage The applicable Copilot plan and usage meter Excluded here Separate

03. Find the boundary: 23 sessions versus 24

Running cost = running seconds × (allocated vCPU × 0.000024 + allocated memory GiB × 0.000003). For a 30-minute 2-vCPU, 4-GiB session, CPU costs USD 0.0864 and memory USD 0.0216, for USD 0.108. Low utilization does not reduce this allocated-resource meter. Count every session's running time rather than peak concurrency. Six 30-minute sessions total 180 session-minutes, or USD 0.648, whether they run in parallel or in sequence; turnaround can differ.

Assumed use in one billing cycle Sandbox runtime Including CI Above USD 18
20 sessions × 30 min USD 2.16 USD 17.66 USD 0
40 sessions × 30 min USD 4.32 USD 19.82 USD 1.82
20 sessions × 60 min USD 4.32 USD 19.82 USD 1.82

Worked Team example: $15.50 in eligible CI leaves $2.50 of the $18 allowance. Running overage and snapshot storage are calculated separately.

With CI fixed at USD 15.50, floor(2.50 ÷ 0.108) = 23. The 24th brings runtime to USD 2.592, exceeding the remaining allowance by USD 0.092. This assumes identical configurations, no other increase in eligible usage, a valid payment method, and no blocking budget. These estimates exclude taxes, model usage and snapshots.

04. Account for the cost after a session stops

Stopping ends CPU and RAM metering. A snapshot can be retained for resuming and is metered separately until deletion. Twenty actual 5-GiB snapshots held for one full month would be 100 GiB-month × USD 0.005 = USD 0.50. The 5 GiB refers to stored data, not the 4 GiB of RAM in the running example. Preserve any needed changes before deleting sessions you won't resume. GitHub's storage meter

05. Verify it in your team's billing account

  1. Before running: Find the billing owner, cycle and remaining entitlement. Reserve enough headroom for the CI you need before month-end. If headroom is tight, default small work to Local and use Cloud where warranted.
  2. Set the correct limit: Use a sandbox product budget or an applicable SKU budget. A Bundled AI credits budget cannot cap sandbox infrastructure spend. Hard limits block additional use when reached, not necessarily every active session immediately. Check for overlapping limits: capacity in one does not override a blocking limit in another. GitHub budget configuration
  3. After rollout: For each sampled session, record owner, UTC start/stop, allocated vCPU and GiB, and actual snapshot size and deletion status. Match estimates to the three Billing meters separately; if they disagree, check the time window, owner and running intervals before changing the budget. UULab has no measured account result to report here.

Decision: Compare the real turnaround improvement against runtime plus storage, not just model tokens. On a team with essential CI, treat the unspent allowance as shared headroom rather than a sandbox-only budget.

Official sources

  • GitHub Changelog: cloud experience rollout and November 19 billing-date update
  • GitHub Docs: cloud and local sandbox billing
  • GitHub Docs: cloud sandbox execution modes

title: Make-It-Poseable: Feed-forward Latent Posing Model for 3D Characters
description:
arXiv:2512.16767v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Posing 3D characters is a fundamental task in computer graphics. However, existing paradigms, ranging from traditional auto-rigging to recent pose-conditioned generative models, frequently struggle with inaccurate skinning weights, fixed mesh topologies, and poor pose conformance. These challenges have become particularly pronounced with the recent explosion of AI-generated 3D assets, which often exhibit flawed structures and fused geometry. To address these issues, we introduce \textbf{Make-It-Poseable}, a novel feed-forward framework that reformulates character posing as a skinning-free latent-space transformation problem. By decoupling shape deformation from the constraints of fixed mesh connectivity, our method directly operates on compact latent representations to reconstruct characters in target poses. To achieve this, our framework integrates a latent posing transformer for shape manipulation, a dense pose representation for fine-grained control, and an adaptive completion module optimized via a bipartite-matched latent loss to robustly handle topological changes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines in posing quality. Furthermore, our design shows promising generalization to diverse morphologies such as quadrupeds in our qualitative tests, and supports various 3D authoring applications such as part replacement and refinement.

title: Virtual Try-On in 2026: A Map of the Landscape, and 5 Design Decisions Behind Every Product
description:
Disclosure: we build Pastely, one of the products mentioned below. We have tried to describe every tool, including ours, by what it is built for.

Virtual try-on has had a busy year. Doji raised $14M in 2025 to make avatar try-ons fun, Google shut down its standalone Doppl app in April 2026 and moved try-on into Search, and ASOS launched virtual try-on in February 2026 on around 10,000 products in its iOS app.

If you are building anything in this space, or are just curious how these products differ, here is the map we use.

Three product shapes

1. Shopper apps. The user tries clothes on themselves before buying or getting dressed.

  • Avatar or likeness apps: Doji (iPhone, iOS 18+) builds an AI likeness from a few photos and adds a style feed and a browser extension.
  • Closet apps: Alta (iPhone, Android, web) and Whering start from the clothes you already own.
  • Outfit editors: Pastely (web) lets you combine pieces into one outfit and preview it on your photo.

2. Creator tools. The goal is an image to post, not a purchase decision. Magic Hour swaps one garment onto a person photo; Dreamina turns an outfit idea into a styled visual.

3. Commerce tools and APIs. Sellers need model shots or try-on at scale: FASHN AI (with an API) and Photoroom's virtual model, plus try-on built into retail surfaces like Google Shopping listings and ASOS.

Five design decisions that shape the product

These are the choices we had to make, and every product in the list above made them differently.

Platform: native app or web. A native iPhone app can feel more polished, but it excludes Android and laptop users. We went web-first so the same editor works on any device without an install.

Unit of try-on: one garment or a whole outfit. Trying on a single product is the simplest flow and fits a product page. But the question people actually ask is "does this jacket work with these trousers and these shoes?", so we made the outfit the unit.

Identity input: likeness, single photo, or sample model. A likeness built from several photos gives consistent results but adds setup friction. A single photo is faster. A sample model lets people start without uploading anything, which matters for privacy-conscious users. ASOS chose a hybrid: shoppers either upload a photo or pick an AI model that resembles them.

Context: one image or several settings. The same outfit reads differently in a studio, on a street and in a park. Showing several settings helps people judge the look, not just the garment.

Honesty about fit. A preview shows how a look reads: colour, proportion, style. It does not tell you how a garment fits. Every try-on product should say so clearly, and point to the size chart.

What a good input photo looks like

Whatever the model behind a try-on, it has to infer body shape, pose and lighting from one image. Results get much better with:

  • a full-body photo, facing the camera
  • even, natural light
  • fitted clothes, so the body outline is visible
  • a plain background

If your product takes user photos, putting these four tips right next to the upload button is the cheapest quality improvement you can make.

Try it, and tell us what breaks

You can try Pastely in the browser: open the editor, pick a top, bottoms and shoes, and preview the outfit on your photo or a sample model. There are free daily previews and no account is needed to start.

We are launching on Product Hunt on November 24, and honest feedback, especially from developers, is very welcome in the comments here.

Sources: TechCrunch on Doji, Doji on the App Store, Google Labs (Doppl), ASOS, Alta, Magic Hour, Dreamina, WearView. Facts checked in November 2026.

title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
description:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

title: Why your CSS gradients look muddy in the middle (and the one-word fix)
description:
Blend blue into yellow with linear-gradient(90deg, blue, yellow) and the middle turns a dull grey. That isn't your colours' fault: by default browsers mix gradient colours in sRGB, where the straight line between two colours often passes through a desaturated zone.

The fix: interpolate in OKLab or OKLCH 

.muddy  { background: linear-gradient(90deg, blue, yellow); }
.clean  { background: linear-gradient(in oklab 90deg, blue, yellow); }
.vivid  { background: linear-gradient(in oklch 90deg, blue, yellow); }
  • oklab is perceptually even, so the midpoint looks like a real halfway colour.
  • oklch travels around the hue wheel, giving brighter, rainbow-like transitions (use shorter hue / longer hue to choose the direction).

Keep a fallback

Colour-space interpolation is supported in current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari, but declare the plain version first so older browsers still get a gradient:

.card {
  background: linear-gradient(90deg, blue, yellow);
  background: linear-gradient(in oklab 90deg, blue, yellow);
}

Two more tips

  • Add a middle stop instead of fighting the blend: linear-gradient(90deg, blue, #6aa 50%, yellow).
  • conic-gradient() works great for pie charts and colour wheels: conic-gradient(red 0 25%, gold 0 60%, teal 0).

Try it

Disclosure: I run GoToolsOnline. Its free CSS gradient generator does linear, radial and conic gradients with draggable stops and an OKLab/OKLCH option, and writes the fallback line for you: https://gotoolsonline.com/tools/css-gradient

title: Single-second static deployments now support more assets
description:
Instant deployments let you deploy eligible static sites to Vercel in about a second, without a build step. They now support CSS, images, fonts, and other assets alongside HTML and Markdown.

Deploy a landing page with its stylesheet and images, or a report created by your coding agent, through the Vercel CLI or REST API. With the CLI, run:

Newly supported file types include:

  • Styles and data: CSS, JSON, XML, plain text, and web manifests

  • Images: SVG, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, and ICO

  • Fonts: WOFF, WOFF2, TTF, OTF, and EOT

  • Documents and media: PDF, MP4, WebM, MP3, WAV, and OGG

Instant deployments support up to 100 files totaling 25 MB or less. Vercel detects eligible deployments automatically, with no configuration required.

Deployments that exceed these limits, include JavaScript or other unsupported files, or are triggered by Git still build as before. The same applies to projects with a framework preset, custom build settings, a root-level package.json or Vercel configuration file such as vercel.json, or a public/ directory.

This update is rolling out across all plans. Learn more in the deployment documentation.

title: Tailwind CSS v4 Resmi Rilis: Mesin Rust Oxide dan Paradigma CSS-First
description:
Tailwind Labs resmi merilis Tailwind CSS v4.0 pada Januari 2025 setelah melewati fase uji coba alpha dan beta sejak 2024. Rilis ini menandai perombakan arsitektur terbesar framework tersebut. Inti pemrosesan meninggalkan pipeline PostCSS berbasis JavaScript dan beralih ke engine native berbasis Rust bernama Oxide dengan konfigurasi CSS-first.

Arsitektur Baru: Engine Oxide Berbasis Rust

Pondasi Tailwind CSS v4 mengandalkan engine Oxide yang ditulis sepenuhnya dalam bahasa Rust. Transisi ini memangkas ketergantungan runtime Node.js yang membebani kompilasi proyek berskala besar.

Kompilasi Cepat dan Penghapusan Pipeline PostCSS Lama

Melalui Oxide, Tailwind Labs mengklaim kompilasi hingga 10 kali lebih cepat dibanding versi terdahulu berdasarkan pengujian internal vendor. Peningkatan performa bertumpu pada berkurangnya overhead parsing AST (Abstract Syntax Tree). PostCSS bukan lagi dependensi bawaan dan digantikan kompilator mandiri yang memproses utilitas secara paralel ke format biner.

Paradigma CSS-First Menggantikan tailwind.config.js

Perubahan mendasar bagi frontend developer terletak pada penghapusan berkas tailwind.config.js. Konfigurasi tema, varian, dan aturan utilitas kini beralih langsung ke berkas CSS utama.

Konfigurasi Desain Menggunakan Direktif @theme

Konfigurasi desain memanfaatkan direktif native @theme. Sistem ini memetakan token desain langsung ke CSS Custom Properties (CSS variables) standar peramban:

  • Variabel warna, tipografi, dan spasi terpasang langsung pada root dokumen.
  • Ekstensi palet warna tidak membutuhkan sintaks objek JavaScript kompleks.
  • Struktur konfigurasi menyatu dengan aturan CSS reguler.

Deteksi Otomatis Template Tanpa Deklarasi Content

Pada Tailwind v3, pengembang wajib mendaftarkan glob path template di opsi content. Di Tailwind CSS v4, Oxide memindai berkas proyek secara otomatis untuk menemukan kelas utilitas, meminimalkan kelas hilang akibat kesalahan penulisan glob.

Dukungan Fitur CSS Modern Secara Bawaan

Tailwind CSS v4 memanfaatkan kapabilitas CSS modern peramban tanpa dependensi pihak ketiga. Fitur bawaan mencakup native @property untuk transisi variabel, native cascade layers (@layer), serta container queries. Standarisasi ini mempermudah efisiensi styling pada arsitektur komponen React 19.

Tantangan Migrasi dari Tailwind CSS v3 ke v4

Adopsi Tailwind v4 menghadirkan sejumlah penyesuaian teknis bagi basis kode lama.

Kompatibilitas Plugin Pihak Ketiga

Mayoritas ekosistem plugin komunitas bergantung pada JavaScript Config API v3. Pustaka komponen pihak ketiga yang membutuhkan runtime JS memerlukan pembaruan arsitektur agar sesuai dengan skema @theme baru.

Kesiapan Dependensi Binary di Pipeline CI/CD

Pemanfaatan binary native Rust mewajibkan pipeline CI/CD mengenali arsitektur mesin target. Server monorepo enterprise dan sistem kompilasi lintas platform harus memastikan binary platform-specific terunduh dengan izin eksekusi yang sesuai. Modernisasi tooling ini melengkapi pergeseran infrastruktur frontend, termasuk evaluasi beban kerja komputasi pada arsitektur server-side rendering.

Cara Memulai Tailwind CSS v4 dengan Vite

Integrasi proyek diarahkan lewat plugin bundler resmi seperti @tailwindcss/vite. Alur kerja yang ringkas ini mempercepat setup tooling modern, melengkapi bantuan alat otomatisasi seperti AI Copilot dan generator kode dalam alur kerja developer. Konfigurasi membutuhkan beberapa langkah ringkas:

  • Pasang dependensi tailwindcss dan @tailwindcss/vite.
  • Daftarkan plugin Tailwind di dalam vite.config.ts.
  • Tambahkan baris @import "tailwindcss"; pada berkas CSS utama.

Analisis dan Kesimpulan

Tailwind CSS v4 mencerminkan tren tooling web modern: menggeser abstraksi JavaScript tebal ke performa kompilasi biner native dan spesifikasi CSS standar. Proyek baru memperoleh alur kerja bersih tanpa boilerplate konfigurasi. Untuk sistem enterprise lama, migrasi bertahap disarankan guna mengantisipasi kesiapan plugin pihak ketiga.

title: Feeding By Sectors
description:
A recount of a big table goes out the way food goes out in a zoo: by sectors, along the paths, one cart per sector - not one walker carrying everything through the night.

👋 Hi, I'm Anton - a software engineer. These days I work on a platform: contracts, generated code, data paths and the tooling around them. Running notes live on my GitHub: github.com/brilliant-almazov.

The backfill routine is built into the shared library as one of its thirteen generic routines; a few services use that runtime. The example of twenty windows below is an example cut, not a measurement of any real recount.

This is part 5 of the series on what a shared platform does for every service, told as a zoo. Maybe you already do it better, maybe you'd do it another way - this is how it is going, and where it stops.

In real life

Feeding time. Nora brings all the food for the whole zoo in one go and, to save time, tips it into the nearest pen. The nearest pen happens to be Ember's. Ember, a dragon, looks at the mountain and says the only thing a dragon can say: "Mine now. All of it." The rest of the zoo is hungry.

The next idea is the night walker. Biscuit takes a wheelbarrow and walks the whole zoo, pen by pen, all night: "Pen one... pen two... pen nine thousand..." It works, slowly, alone, and nobody can see how far he got or help him when he gets tired.

Then Pip does what keepers in real zoos do. Look at the first pen and the last pen. Cut the zoo into sectors. Write one note per sector, put the notes on the paths, and let whoever is free take a note: Biscuit takes pens one to a hundred, Pickle takes a hundred to two hundred. Nobody carries everything, everybody can see which notes are still waiting, and a dropped note is just picked up again.

A goroutine that walks the table

Every service eventually needs to recount something: fill a new column for old rows, rebuild a derived value, re-publish what changed. The tempting shape is a background goroutine that starts with the service, scans the table from top to bottom, and does the work as it goes.

That shape has all of Biscuit's problems. It is one walker per replica, or one walker with a lock. Nobody sees how far it got. If the process restarts, the walk restarts or needs its own bookkeeping. And it runs outside the one thing the platform already has for "work that happens later": the bus. In our platform that is not a style preference. Any asynchronous processing - a backfill, a recount, a re-publish - goes through the bus, producer to consumer; a goroutine that scans a table on its own is not an option at all.

One query, then windows on the bus

The backfill routine of the library does it in two halves.

The producer asks the table one question: the smallest and the largest key. It cuts that range into windows [from, to) and publishes each window as a message. The consumer takes a window and does the work for the rows in it, in one transaction. As a form - names illustrative:

producer:  SELECT min(id), max(id) FROM <table>;      -- one query
           publish { from: 1,      to: 100001 }
           publish { from: 100001, to: 200001 }
           publish ...                                -- one window per message
consumer:  BEGIN; <work on rows where from <= id < to>; COMMIT;

Everything the night walker could not do now comes from the bus. Progress is the number of window messages still waiting. A failed window is redelivered alone, without redoing the windows before it. More consumers means more sectors fed at once. And the producer does not scan anything: it reads two numbers.

Question Night walker Windows on the bus
how far did it get? inside one process's memory messages done vs waiting
what if a step fails? the walker decides, or stops that window is redelivered
can two help? only with extra locking any free consumer takes a window
what does planning cost? a scan of the whole table one query for min and max

What a window asks of the work

Moving a recount onto the bus changes one thing about the work itself: a window can arrive more than once. The bus delivers at least once, and a window whose consumer died after the commit but before the acknowledgement will come back. So the work for a window has to be safe to repeat.

For most recounts that comes for free, because they set a value rather than add to it: "fill the new column from the old ones" gives the same row the second time. For the few that add or send, the previous part of this series applies unchanged - the once-per-message routine punches the window's message id in the same transaction as the work.

There is also a question of size. A window is one transaction, and a transaction holds its locks until it commits. Wide windows mean fewer messages and longer locks; narrow windows mean more messages and shorter locks. How wide a window should be is a choice per table, and I do not claim a right number.

Window width Messages on the bus Locks held per transaction
wide few long
narrow many short

What twenty windows look like

To show the idea, an example: a key range cut into twenty windows, some done, some in flight, some still on the bus. The numbers are an example cut, not a run.

What went wrong

The thing this routine closes is a habit: the background goroutine that scans a table is the first thing anyone writes for a recount, because it is the shortest code. It is also the one shape that hides its progress, fights its own replicas and lives outside the bus. The rule that asynchronous work goes through the bus came first; the routine is what makes following that rule shorter than breaking it.

One more honest note: windows over a key range assume the keys are spread evenly enough that windows of equal width carry similar work. A range with a dense patch makes some windows heavy. The routine cuts by key, not by row count.

What I do not claim

  • Not a measured recount. The twenty windows are an example.
  • Not that windows of equal width carry equal work. They are cut by key.
  • Not that every recount in every service uses the routine. A few services use the runtime.
  • Not the exact message shape. The form above shows the idea.
  • Not a right window width. It is a choice per table.
  • Not that the work in a window is safe to repeat by itself. That is the work's job, or the once-per-message routine's.

What of this is method

  • Plan with one query, work through the bus. Min and max, then windows as messages.
  • One window, one transaction. A failure costs one window, not the whole walk.
  • Make the right path the short one. The rule says "through the bus"; the routine makes it less code than a goroutine.

Zoo keeping, built in - Part 5. Next: Thirteen Routines, One Keeper.

If you recount big tables, does the work run as a walker or as messages? If you cut by key range, what do you do with the dense patch? If a backfill failed halfway, how did you know where to restart? Who walks your zoo at night?

title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
description:
arXiv:2611.23476v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

title: PSA: check auto_stop_mins on your SQL warehouses if you deploy with bundles
description:
If you create SQL warehouses through Declarative Automation Bundles and leave out auto_stop_mins, the default isn’t what you get in the UI. Bundles default to 10 minutes for Serverless and 120 for Pro/Classic. The UI defaults to 10 for Serverless and 45 for Pro/Classic.

Apparently someone deployed a Serverless warehouse with a bundle, didn’t set the field, and got 120 minutes instead of the 10 the docs list. That hurts if you have a bunch of short scheduled alerts, because each one wakes the warehouse up and then it just sits there until auto-stop kicks in.

A few other things from the same writeup:

The Serverless UI won’t go below 5 min auto-stop, but the API, CLI and bundles accept 1 (databricks warehouses edit --auto-stop-mins 1). Pro and Classic bottom out at 10.

A single slow or spilling query points to warehouse size. Queries waiting at capacity point to max clusters. Peak queued queries above zero doesn’t tell you which one on its own.

Power BI DirectQuery can send a query on every dashboard interaction. If the business only needs fresh data every few minutes, Import or Hybrid mode cuts a lot of that.

DBU rate alone is misleading. In one AWS US East example, Serverless is about $0.70/DBU, Pro $0.55 and Classic $0.22, but Pro and Classic bill infrastructure on top.

Is anyone running a 1-minute auto-stop on serverless for scheduled jobs? Do the cold starts bother you?

Full article : https://select.dev/blog/serverless-sql-warehouse-cost-optimization

title: Cutting out a background colour with a canvas pixel loop: what I learned building Color to Transparent
description:
A few months ago I needed one boring thing: a logo on a white background that had to sit on a transparent one. Every online tool I found wanted an account, a watermark, or an upload of a file I would rather not send anywhere. So I wrote the loop myself, and it turned into Color to Transparent, a free browser tool that removes one chosen colour from an image and makes it transparent.

The core is shorter than you think

Every pixel is four numbers in a Uint8ClampedArray. Once you have the background colour you want gone, the rest is a distance check:

function keyOut(ctx, width, height, target, tolerance) {
  const img = ctx.getImageData(0, 0, width, height);
  const d = img.data;
  const [tr, tg, tb] = target;
  const limit = tolerance * tolerance * 3;

  for (let i = 0; i < d.length; i += 4) {
    const dr = d[i] - tr, dg = d[i + 1] - tg, db = d[i + 2] - tb;
    if (dr * dr + dg * dg + db * db <= limit) d[i + 3] = 0;
  }
  ctx.putImageData(img, 0, 0);
}

That is the whole idea. Everything else in the tool exists because the naive version looks bad.

Four details that decide whether it looks finished

Picking the colour from the edge. Asking people to type a HEX value is friction. A click on the image is faster, so the tool reads the pixel under the pointer and uses it as the target — and it can sample from the border by default, because the background is usually what touches the frame.

Tolerance needs to be a small number and a big one. A pure white background is not uniform once a JPEG has touched it: compression leaves bands and ringing. Too little tolerance leaves a soft grey halo; too much eats into the subject. A 0–100 slider that maps to a squared RGB distance is easy to reason about for both the user and the code.

Halo cleanup is separate from keying. Pixels blended between subject and background keep a hint of the old colour. Removing the old colour from them is a blending problem, not a threshold problem, and it is worth doing as a second pass.

The connected-area option saves a lot of retries. If a logo also happens to contain the background colour — white letters on a white page, for instance — a global key destroys them. Restricting the removal to the region connected to the click keeps the interior intact.

Per-pixel work belongs on the main thread only briefly

A 6,000 px image is 36 million pixels. For loops over typed arrays on that scale are fast enough in practice, but they are still long enough to drop frames. What helped most was keeping the preview at screen resolution and applying the same settings to the full-size image only when exporting, so nothing feels laggy while you drag a slider.

That is also why the files never leave the device: the browser reads the image, runs the loop, and hands back a PNG or WebP with an alpha channel via canvas.toBlob(). No queue, no storage, nothing to clean up.

What I would tell anyone building the same thing

  • Put the tolerance slider and the colour picker side by side; people adjust them together.
  • Offer an undo brush early. One bad tolerance value is usually all it takes.
  • Export PNG by default. There is no point in a transparent background you cannot keep.
  • Test with a JPEG, not a PNG. Real-world white is almost never white.

The tool itself is free, needs no sign-up and has no watermark, so if you want to see the finished version of this loop you can try it at colorremoverfromimage.com. If you are writing your own keying code, the two things I would invest in first are tolerance control and a connected-area mode — they are what turn a ten-line demo into something people can actually use.

title: I built code search from scratch in Rust: half Zoekt’s index, 60x faster at p95
description:
The Benchmark

The following benchmark has been run against Linux 6.12: 86,501 files, 1,011 MiB of source, and I was comparing my solution (built for Gitmoap) with the standard Zoekt:

Gitmoap Zoekt
Index size 1,405 MiB (1.39× source) 2,760 MiB (2.73×)
p50, all queries 2.35 ms 1.75 ms
p95 58 ms 3,586 ms
p99 276 ms 6,003 ms
Building the Linux index 12.8 s 117.6 s

1. How trigram code search works

First off, a trigram is any 3 consecutive bytes. Hence, for the following word:

config

There will be four trigrams:

config
con
 onf
  nfi
   fig

The idea

At index time, we keep, for each trigram, a so-called posting list. This is nothing but a list of all the files that contain that specific trigram.

Now, at query time, what's done is the following:

  • Split the query into its trigrams;
  • Intersect their posting lists and take those files as candidates;
  • Open and search these files to find actual matches.

Toy example

Now, let me briefly expand a little bit more on the second step. Let's consider that we want to search for the config word above, hence our set of trigrams is: ["con", "onf", "nfi", "fig"]. Now, suppose our index is a hashmap like:

{
 "gdf": ["file1", "file23", "file43"],
 "con": ["file2", "file53"],
 "ker": ["file2"],
 "onf": ["file53", "file423", "file9345"],
 "reg": ["file21"],
 "nfi": ["file2", "file53", "file21"],
 "rwe": ["file1", "file7"],
 "fig": ["file2", "file32", "file53"],
 ...
}

Of course we will then access the posting lists of only the trigrams of our word:

{
 "con": ["file2", "file53"],
 "onf": ["file53", "file423", "file9345"],
 "nfi": ["file2", "file53", "file21"],
 "fig": ["file2", "file32", "file53"]
}

At this point, we just intersect these lists, namely, we find the files that are common to ALL of these lists. In this case that would be just one file: ["file53"].

The third step, then, opens that file and does a search for the config word.

2. Where the time goes

Steps 1 and 2 are of course incredibly quick, while the slow part of the algorithm is opening the candidate files and doing the actual search.

Some specific examples on the Linux codebase:

Query Every trigram (plain index) Opened by Gitmoap Actually match p50 (ms)
cfvei_transmit 1 5 1 0.08
omap2xxx_dss_dispc_hwmod 3 37 3 0.16
drm_bridge 286 529 220 1.91
unwrap() 30 262 15 0.24
ramp_delay 1,878 1,331 79 1.81
become 5,752 2,357 2,252 2.77
/fn\s+\w+_test/ 11,209 7,797 3 2.03
/\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/ (scan) 86,078 86,078 351 59.65

3. Why three bytes?

Three seems like a sweet spot for this problem... how come?

  • Two bytes: There are only 65,536 possible pairs, hence, in source code the common ones would appear in almost every file, meaning that the filter would basically amount to nothing.
  • Four bytes: The lists filter better; however, there are many more distinct keys in the index. Moreover, three-letter queries cannot use the index, hence they would need a full scan.
  • Three bytes: Sweet spot that was used by Google Code Search, as described by Russ Cox in 2012.

4. Speeding up the algorithm

If we were just saving the trigrams with the posting lists containing only the files where the trigram occurs, the search would be slower, as we would need to open all those files and search through them.

Hence, in the postings we are also saving some more data that can allow us to discard files that for sure do not contain the word we are searching for.

I am going to explore two different kinds of data that we can save in the postings, as they have different trade-offs: positions or masks.

Positional (what Zoekt does): Each entry contains every offset where the trigram occurs in each file. How does this help? For our config you will need nfi to be at some position p and fig to be at p+1, which can then easily be checked from these lists without opening the file. The cost is bytes for each occurrence of the trigram in each file.
--> For the Linux codebase, when I built my engine this way, the postings came to 1,924 MiB.

Masks (from GitHub's Project Blackbird): This idea was developed at GitHub for their code search, and Cursor's post on fast regex search explains it really well. Each entry stores the file plus two single-byte summaries:

  • Position mask: bit p mod 8 is set for every position p where the trigram occurs (OR-ed together);
  • Next-byte mask: bit (next byte lowercased) mod 8 is set for each byte that follows each occurrence.

--> For the Linux codebase, the postings came to 361 MiB.

Let's see with a concrete example how these masks work.

Suppose we want to find the word become in the following content:

because the economy is common at home
^^^         ^^^         ^^^       ^^^
bec         eco         com       ome   <- all four present, no "become"

On Linux, for example, a plain index would make the algorithm open 5,752 files while Gitmoap only opens 2,357.

Now, in that example what would be the values of those bytes?

bec  at offset 0    0 0 0 0 0 0 0 1
rotate left by 1    0 0 0 0 0 0 1 0
eco  at offset 12   0 0 0 1 0 0 0 0
AND                 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0  -> zero, skip the file

If the result is zero, it means that the file, with certainty, does not contain the word become, meaning that it will never get opened. Conversely, if the result is not zero, it means that the file might contain become.

Of course, with this method we are losing some information to have a kind of heuristic that would at least allow us to remove some files from the possible candidates.

We are trading a smaller index size for a few false positives.

Currently, this is the trade-off that I've decided for Gitmoap: since all these indexes need to be stored in memory, postings more than 5 times smaller (and a whole index half the size) for about a millisecond of slowness in the p50 is a very acceptable trade (this delay is not really perceivable by humans anyway, and the network is what actually bounds a code search request's full round trip).

5. Should we compress the content?

LZ4 in 64 KiB blocks would halve the size of the index; however, in my testing, the p50 over all queries got a massive overhead, with a staggering 10-20x increase in time.

Conclusions

With the masks indexing implementation of Gitmoap compared to the positional one of Zoekt, the latter is faster at the median (p50), while Gitmoap is 20 to 60 times faster at p95 and p99. However, the Rust implementation, when indexing using the positional way, gave results that were a bit faster than Zoekt at the median too.

At the end of the day, that was a well-thought-out and accepted trade-off.

The correctness of the Gitmoap algorithm was tested against brute force, giving perfect results on a test suite of 10,000 cases.

Test your assumptions against the dumbest implementation you can write.

In Gitmoap, the code search feature is enabled on every tier (even the free plan), with a cap (limit) on how many bytes we are indexing... But still a very nice feature to have, that some other providers include only in their paid tiers.

Let me know if you would be interested in having a crate published with this implementation! I am probably going to do that soon enough, though it would be interesting for me to gauge the interest!

I hope you found this post interesting!

Till next time,
Kevin
