title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
description:
arXiv:2611.23445v2 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

title: Node.js Browser Storage: 5 Presigned URL Upload Choices for SaaS
description:
Tenant isolation matters more than the storage logo. Short answer: issue short-lived presigned PUT and GET URLs from your Node.js backend, derive every object key on the server, and keep the bucket private. For generated property reports, start with the option whose CORS controls, authorization model, and cleanup behavior you can verify before the first upload.

Option Best reason to shortlist it Question to settle first
AWS S3 Direct control of the established S3 upload and multipart workflow How much bucket policy and CORS configuration will the team own?
Cloudflare R2 An S3-compatible candidate for an existing S3-shaped client Does its region and access model match the report workflow?
Supabase Storage A candidate when storage belongs beside an existing Supabase application Can its authorization model express the application's tenant boundary?
UploadThing A candidate when a higher-level upload flow is more useful than raw object storage Does the abstraction preserve the required key and access controls?
Self-describing REST storage Discovery with request schemas and runnable TypeScript examples Can the required browser origin be configured, and are private links sufficient?

My recommendation is conditional, not fashionable. Use AWS S3 when the team wants direct ownership of storage configuration. Evaluate R2 when S3 compatibility is strategically useful. Put Supabase Storage or UploadThing first when either already defines the application's upload layer. The last option fits a team that values discovering and wiring a capability from one REST surface, but only when CORS is already compatible and permanent public URLs are unnecessary.

1. Should a browser upload direct to storage with a presigned URL?

A UUID makes a key difficult to guess. It does not prove that customer A may write or read customer B's report. The backend must obtain the authenticated tenant identifier, validate the report identifier against that tenant, and then construct the storage key itself. Never accept a complete object key from the browser.

Keys aren't authorization.

A useful shape is tenants/{tenantId}/reports/{reportId}/{fileId}.pdf. The exact punctuation is boring. Good. The security property is that tenantId comes from the authenticated server session, not a form field, while fileId prevents an accidental overwrite. Store the key with the report record and authorize each later download against that record.

Presigned URLs are bearer credentials. Keep their lifetime short, constrain the operation to PUT or GET, and return them only after authorization. Do not log the query string. A private GET URL should be minted after every download check; it should not become a permanent link copied into invoices or emails.

This is the first benchmark I care about: count the places where a browser-supplied tenant or key can cross the trust boundary. The target is zero. Latency numbers can wait. My first instinct with upload tooling is usually to compare time-to-first-call. Here that is incomplete. A five-minute setup that trusts a client-provided tenant key has failed the important test, while a slightly longer integration that derives the key after authorization has the better developer experience because its security rule is visible in one place.

2. Make CORS a release gate, not a dashboard chore

Browser direct upload crosses two enforcement systems. The signed URL authorizes storage. CORS decides whether browser JavaScript may make that cross-origin request. A valid signature does not repair a missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin response.

Test the exact production origin, method, and request headers. PUT plus Content-Type usually causes a preflight request, so the storage service must answer that OPTIONS exchange correctly. Avoid * when the workflow uses credentials or exposes more origins than intended. MDN's CORS guide is the useful baseline here.

This criterion changes the shortlist. S3 exposes a documented bucket configuration surface. R2, Supabase Storage, and UploadThing should each be checked against the team's actual origin and framework rather than accepted on the strength of a compatibility label. The self-describing REST option's storage model contains CORS rules, but self-service CORS configuration is not available through the API for this workflow. If the property portal's origin is not already allowed, browser direct upload can stop there.

Sharp edge. Test preflight before implementing progress bars.

3. Keep the Node.js upload contract tiny

The browser needs an application endpoint that returns a short-lived upload URL. It does not need a storage credential, a bucket name chosen by the user, or permission to list objects. The following TypeScript calls the verified presign route from a trusted Node.js process. Its base URL, key, bucket, and server-derived object key come from the environment; the response is preserved as JSON because the supplied contract does not establish a narrower response type.

const baseUrl = requireEnv("INFRAI_BASE_URL").replace(/\/$/, "");
const apiKey = requireEnv("INFRAI_API_KEY");
const bucket = requireEnv("STORAGE_BUCKET");
const objectKey = requireEnv("OBJECT_KEY");

function requireEnv(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Missing ${name}`);
  return value;
}

async function presign(attempt = 0): Promise<unknown> {
  const route = "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}";
  const path = route
    .replace("{bucket}", encodeURIComponent(bucket))
    .replace("{key}", objectKey.split("/").map(encodeURIComponent).join("/"));
  const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}${path}`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
  });

  if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 4) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1_000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return presign(attempt + 1);
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Presign failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
  }
  return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
}

presign().then((result) => console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)));

The object key passed to that process should have the server-derived tenants/{tenantId}/reports/... shape. The capability's discovery document supplies its full request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so use those schemas to consume the returned grant rather than guessing fields. Then measure time-to-first-byte and completed-upload rate with realistic report sizes. Also verify that the signed constraints and the browser's Content-Type agree byte for byte. That mismatch is a much more useful test than another abstraction layer.

For a self-describing API, discovery shortens the adapter work: one capability response provides the full request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples. Infrai covers 295 routes across 20 modules with a single API key and a single bill, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. For a property platform that also calls other backend services, one key avoids adding another credential format; one bill removes a separate reconciliation path. Those gains matter after the upload works, not before. They do not remove the need to test CORS or tenant authorization.

4. Treat large reports and retries as separate failure domains

Use single-request PUT for ordinary generated PDFs until measurements show it is inadequate. Multipart upload adds state: an upload ID, numbered parts, completion, and abort. AWS documents that uploaded parts continue consuming storage until the upload is completed or aborted. The same cleanup discipline matters for any provider that exposes multipart state.

With this storage capability, orphaned multipart parts are not cleaned automatically. Record the upload ID in a job table. On success, complete it explicitly; on cancellation or timeout, abort it. A periodic reconciler can find application jobs left in an uploading state, but prefix listing cannot query arbitrary metadata, so the database remains the source of cleanup intent.

Retries need narrower rules than “try again.” A failed presign request can be retried with backoff. A 429 response should honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use exponential backoff. A completed write should not be blindly repeated; use a stable client-supplied identifier or an idempotency key where the API supports it. There is no If-Match conditional write here, so strict concurrent replacement of the same report key needs a database transaction or queue.

No magic retry loop.

5. Know when the runner-up is the better design

Choose direct AWS S3 when detailed bucket CORS control and the documented multipart lifecycle are requirements your team is prepared to operate. Choose R2 when your architecture explicitly benefits from an S3-compatible target and its verified behavior meets the same preflight and private-download tests. I first thought compatibility would settle most of the decision. It doesn't. Compatibility reduces client changes; it does not prove identical policy semantics, tenant authorization, or a passing browser preflight from the production origin.

Supabase Storage is the more coherent runner-up for a product already centered on Supabase, provided its authorization rules pass cross-tenant tests. UploadThing deserves the same treatment in an application that wants an upload-focused integration rather than a general object API. In both cases, benchmark time-to-first-successful upload, configuration count, and the number of authorization decisions duplicated outside the application database. I would reject any option that makes those decisions hard to locate, even if its happy-path demo is shorter.

These limitations are decisive. The capability compared here is not suitable for static hosting, an image host, or any design that requires a permanent public object URL: public and public-read ACLs are unavailable, and public_url remains null. It also does not support object versioning or object lock, so it cannot recover an overwritten key or provide WORM guarantees by itself. Cross-region automatic replication and bulk cross-cloud migration are outside its scope. Lifecycle expiry starts at one day, not hours. The trade-off is clear: choose AWS S3 instead when those native controls are requirements, and choose a product-specific upload layer when reducing application integration matters more than a general storage API.

Those are architecture boundaries. For authenticated property reports, private presigned GETs are often the right behavior anyway. For public assets, regulated immutable records, active-active regional copies, or metadata-heavy search, pick a storage system designed around that requirement and prove it with an integration test before migrating data.

Sources

  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
  • AWS S3: Multipart upload overview
  • AWS S3: Configuring CORS
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Supabase Storage documentation
  • UploadThing documentation

title: Understanding S3 Prefixes When Using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
description:
Introduction

While working with Amazon S3 as a data source for an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base, I came across a concept that seems simple but is important to understand correctly:

S3 folders do not work like folders on a traditional file system.

When you open an S3 bucket in the AWS Management Console, you can create folders, upload files into them, and navigate through a familiar folder structure.

However, Amazon S3 uses a flat object storage model. What looks like a folder is generally a prefix within an object's key.

This distinction becomes particularly important when connecting an S3 bucket to an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base.

The prefixes configured in the Bedrock data source determine which objects are included when the Knowledge Base ingests documents.

In this article, I'll explain how S3 prefixes work, how they relate to Bedrock Knowledge Base ingestion, and how I organized documents for the Daara Media AI Creative Content Assistant.

1. The misconception: S3 folders don't really exist

When people first work with Amazon S3, they often assume that its folder structure works like the directory structure on a Linux server or Windows computer.

For example, consider this structure:

daara-media-content/
│
├── brand-guidelines/
│   └── DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf
│
├── past-scripts/
│   └── DAARA-Media-Script-Bank.pdf
│
├── captions/
│   └── DAARA-Media-Caption-Bank.pdf
│
└── proposals/
    └── DAARA-Media-Client-Proposal-Template.pdf

In the S3 console, this looks like a bucket containing four folders, each holding a document.

But S3 does not store objects inside nested directories in the same way a traditional file system does.

Instead, each object has a key.

For example:

brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

The entire string is the object's key.

The forward slash is simply part of that key. S3 uses the characters before it as a prefix that applications and the console can interpret as a folder-like hierarchy.

What S3 actually stores

Conceptually, the bucket contains objects like these:

Bucket: daara-media-content

Object 1:
Key = brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

Object 2:
Key = past-scripts/DAARA-Media-Script-Bank.pdf

Object 3:
Key = captions/DAARA-Media-Caption-Bank.pdf

Object 4:
Key = proposals/DAARA-Media-Client-Proposal-Template.pdf

There is no requirement for S3 to create a physical directory called brand-guidelines before storing an object with that key.

The key itself contains the prefix.

This is why the more accurate way to describe S3 organization is through object keys and prefixes, rather than traditional folders and subdirectories.

2. Understanding an S3 object key and prefix

Let's break down one of the Daara Media object keys:

brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

It contains two useful parts:

brand-guidelines/
        |
        v
      Prefix

DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf
        |
        v
    Object filename

The complete key is:

brand-guidelines/DAARA-Media-Brand-Guidelines.pdf

The prefix is:

brand-guidelines/

A prefix is simply the beginning portion of an object's key.

This means multiple objects can share the same prefix:

brand-guidelines/
│
├── brand-guidelines/brand-identity.pdf
├── brand-guidelines/logo-usage.pdf
└── brand-guidelines/brand-voice.pdf

All three objects have keys beginning with brand-guidelines/.

This is how S3 allows applications to organize and retrieve related objects without requiring a traditional directory structure.

3. Why prefixes matter when using Bedrock Knowledge Bases

Understanding prefixes becomes especially important when connecting an S3 bucket to an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base.

A Knowledge Base needs to know which documents it should ingest.

An S3 bucket might contain hundreds or thousands of objects, but not every object necessarily belongs in a particular Knowledge Base.

For example, a company might use one bucket to store:

  • Brand guidelines.
  • Marketing documents.
  • Customer support policies.
  • Financial reports.
  • Internal administrative files.
  • Archived documents.

If the Knowledge Base is intended to answer marketing questions, ingesting every object in the bucket may not be appropriate.

This is where inclusion prefixes become useful.

An inclusion prefix tells the Bedrock S3 data source which object keys should be included during ingestion.

Instead of treating the entire bucket as the document collection, you can restrict ingestion to selected key prefixes.

Example: Daara Media document organization

For the Daara Media AI assistant, I organized the source documents using four prefixes:


daara-media-content/
│
├── brand-guidelines/
│
├── past-scripts/
│
├── captions/
│
└── proposals/

Each prefix represented a category of company knowledge that the assistant could retrieve.

The data source needed to include these four categories rather than unrelated objects elsewhere in the bucket.

The intended ingestion scope was:

                 Amazon S3
                     |
                     v
          daara-media-content
                     |
          +----------+----------+
          |          |          |
          v          v          v
   brand-guidelines/ past-scripts/ captions/
          |
          v
      proposals/
          |
          v
    Bedrock Data Source
          |
          v
     Document Ingestion

The important part was not simply creating these folder-like paths in S3.

It was configuring the Bedrock data source to use the corresponding prefixes.

4. Configuring inclusion prefixes

When creating an S3 data source for a Bedrock Knowledge Base, you can specify the bucket and the prefixes that should be included.

A simplified example of the S3 data source configuration looks like this:

{
  "s3Configuration": {
    "bucketArn": "arn:aws:s3:::daara-media-content",
    "inclusionPrefixes": [
      "brand-guidelines/",
      "past-scripts/",
      "captions/",
      "proposals/"
    ]
  },
  "type": "S3"
}

The important part is:

"inclusionPrefixes": [
  "brand-guidelines/",
  "past-scripts/",
  "captions/",
  "proposals/"
]

Each entry identifies an S3 key prefix that the data source should include.

During ingestion, Bedrock uses these filters to determine which objects are within the configured scope.

Visualizing the selection

Imagine the bucket contains these objects:

daara-media-content/
│
├── brand-guidelines/
│   └── brand-identity.pdf
│
├── past-scripts/
│   └── campaign-script.pdf
│
├── captions/
│   └── caption-examples.pdf
│
├── proposals/
│   └── proposal-template.pdf
│
└── financial-reports/
    └── annual-report.pdf

If the inclusion prefixes are:

[
  "brand-guidelines/",
  "past-scripts/",
  "captions/",
  "proposals/"
]

The ingestion scope becomes:

                  S3 Bucket
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |                       |
          v                       v
    Included Prefixes       Not Included
          |                       |
          v                       v
  brand-guidelines/          financial-reports/
  past-scripts/                    |
  captions/                        v
  proposals/                  Not ingested
          |
          v
   Bedrock Ingestion

The financial report is still stored in S3. It simply does not match any of the configured inclusion prefixes.

This is an important distinction: an object can exist in the bucket without being part of the Knowledge Base's ingestion scope.

5. Why the trailing slash matters

Consider these two prefixes:

brand

and:

brand-guidelines/

S3 prefix matching is based on the beginning of an object's key. It does not interpret the prefix as a directory name with special folder-boundary semantics.

For example, the prefix:

brand

could match keys such as:

brand-guidelines/brand-identity.pdf
brand-assets/logo.png
brand-archive/old-guidelines.pdf

All these keys begin with brand.

But if the intention is to include objects under the brand-guidelines/ path, specifying the trailing slash makes the intended scope clearer:

brand-guidelines/

It matches keys beginning with that exact prefix, such as:

brand-guidelines/brand-identity.pdf
brand-guidelines/logo-usage.pdf

It does not match:

brand-assets/logo.png
brand-archive/old-guidelines.pdf

This is why I recommend using the full folder-like prefix, including the trailing slash, when the intention is to target a specific category.

It makes the configuration easier to understand and reduces accidental matches.

6. What happens when the prefixes are incorrect?

This is where the concept becomes practical.

Imagine uploading documents into:

brand-guidelines/
past-scripts/
captions/
proposals/

But configuring the Bedrock data source with:

{
  "s3Configuration": {
    "bucketArn": "arn:aws:s3:::daara-media-content",
    "inclusionPrefixes": [
      "documents/"
    ]
  },
  "type": "S3"
}

The problem is that the configured prefix does not match the object keys.

The documents exist in S3, but their keys do not begin with documents/.

As a result, the data source will not include those objects through that inclusion filter.

This can create a confusing situation:

  • The S3 bucket contains the expected PDFs.
  • The folder-like paths are visible in the console.
  • The Knowledge Base exists.
  • The ingestion job may run.
  • But the expected documents are not ingested.

The problem may not be the PDF files, the embedding model, or the Knowledge Base itself.

It may simply be an incorrect inclusion prefix.

A useful troubleshooting checklist

When documents are not appearing in a Knowledge Base, check:

  1. Is the correct S3 bucket configured?
  2. Are the object keys spelled exactly as expected?
  3. Do the inclusion prefixes match the beginning of those keys?
  4. Are there accidental differences in capitalization?
  5. Are the required S3 permissions configured for the Knowledge Base execution role?
  6. Has the data source actually been synchronized after the documents were uploaded?

S3 keys are case-sensitive, so these two prefixes are different:

brand-guidelines/
Brand-Guidelines/

A small difference in capitalization can prevent an expected match.

7. How to inspect S3 object keys using the AWS CLI

The AWS Management Console provides a convenient visual representation of S3 objects, but the AWS CLI is useful when troubleshooting prefix problems.

To list all objects in a bucket:

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket daara-media-content \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'Contents[*].Key' \
  --output table

This displays the actual object keys rather than relying on the folder-like presentation in the console.

To inspect objects under a specific prefix:

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket daara-media-content \
  --prefix brand-guidelines/ \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'Contents[*].Key' \
  --output table

This limits the listing to keys beginning with brand-guidelines/.

You can repeat the command for the other prefixes:

aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket daara-media-content \
  --prefix past-scripts/ \
  --region us-east-1 \
  --query 'Contents[*].Key' \
  --output table

The objective is to confirm that the actual object keys match the prefixes configured in the Bedrock data source.

For large buckets, remember that list-objects-v2 returns a limited page of results unless pagination is used. The AWS CLI normally handles pagination automatically, but options such as --no-paginate can change that behaviour.

8. Prefixes and Knowledge Base synchronization

Uploading a document to S3 does not automatically mean that it has been indexed by the Knowledge Base.

There is an important distinction between storing a document and ingesting it.

The process looks like this:

          Upload Document
                 |
                 v
             Amazon S3
                 |
                 v
          Object Stored
                 |
                 v
        Bedrock Data Source
                 |
                 v
         Start Ingestion Job
                 |
                 v
         Check Object Scope
                 |
                 v
          Process Documents
                 |
                 v
       Update Knowledge Base

The first synchronization processes the eligible content in the configured data source.

Subsequent synchronization jobs can detect added, updated, and deleted content and update the Knowledge Base accordingly.

This means that if a document is uploaded into an included prefix after the initial ingestion, you still need to synchronize the data source for the change to be reflected in the Knowledge Base.

For example:

Initial Ingestion
       |
       v
brand-guidelines/
       |
       v
brand-identity.pdf indexed
       |
       v
New document uploaded
       |
       v
logo-usage.pdf
       |
       v
Start another ingestion job
       |
       v
Knowledge Base updated

The prefix defines the scope of eligible objects. Synchronization is the process that discovers and processes changes within that scope.

9. Prefixes are not the same as access control

There is another important distinction worth understanding.

An inclusion prefix controls which S3 objects a particular Bedrock data source considers for ingestion.

It is not, by itself, an IAM security boundary.

For example, configuring:

"inclusionPrefixes": [
  "brand-guidelines/"
]

does not automatically prevent other AWS principals from reading objects under:

financial-reports/

Access to S3 objects is controlled separately through IAM identity policies, bucket policies, and other applicable access controls.

Similarly, once documents have been ingested, access to retrieved Knowledge Base content must be considered separately.

AWS warns that synchronized content can become available to principals with the relevant bedrock:Retrieve permissions, so ingestion scope should be designed with data access in mind.

The distinction is:

Mechanism Responsibility
S3 object prefix Identifies a portion of an object's key
Bedrock inclusion prefix Defines which matching objects are included in ingestion
IAM policy Controls permissions to perform AWS actions
S3 bucket policy Controls access granted through the bucket resource policy
Bedrock retrieval permissions Controls who can retrieve Knowledge Base content

This matters when a bucket contains documents with different sensitivity levels.

A well-organized S3 bucket does not automatically provide document-level authorization.

10. The architecture in the Daara Media project

The S3 document structure was part of the wider RAG architecture.

The original company documents were stored in S3. The Bedrock Knowledge Base used the configured data source to ingest eligible documents, process them, and make their content available for retrieval.

The overall flow was:

                 Company Documents
                         |
                         v
                    Amazon S3
                         |
             +-----------+-----------+
             |           |           |
             v           v           v
       Brand Guides   Past Scripts  Captions
             |           |           |
             +-----------+-----------+
                         |
                         v
                  Proposals
                         |
                         v
              S3 Inclusion Prefixes
                         |
                         v
             Bedrock Knowledge Base
                         |
                         v
                    Ingestion
                         |
                         v
                Searchable Knowledge
                         |
                         v
                 Application Retrieval
                         |
                         v
                  Claude Sonnet 4.5
                         |
                         v
                  Draft Response

The important point is that S3 and the Knowledge Base have different responsibilities.

Amazon S3 stores the original documents.

The Knowledge Base ingests eligible objects and prepares them for retrieval.

The application retrieves relevant information from the Knowledge Base and passes that context to the foundation model.

The prefix configuration connects the document organization in S3 to the ingestion scope of the Knowledge Base.

Conclusion

Understanding S3 prefixes is a small but important part of building a reliable RAG application with Amazon Bedrock.

What appears to be a folder in the S3 console is generally a prefix within an object's key. That prefix becomes important when configuring a Bedrock S3 data source because inclusion prefixes determine which objects are considered during ingestion.

In the Daara Media project, I used separate prefixes for brand guidelines, past scripts, captions, and proposals. This gave the Knowledge Base a clear document scope and made the source content easier to organize and maintain.

The biggest lesson is that storing documents in S3 and making them available to a Knowledge Base are two separate operations.

The objects must have the expected keys, the data source must include the correct prefixes, the Knowledge Base must have permission to access the objects, and the data source must be synchronized.

Once this distinction is understood, troubleshooting missing documents becomes much easier.

S3 stores objects using keys. Prefixes organize those keys. Bedrock uses the configured prefixes to determine which objects to ingest.

title: Why I Built a Sub-Millisecond Settlement Engine in Rust From Scratch
description:
If you have ever operated a tech consultancy, software export agency, or remote engineering team in an emerging market (like Bangladesh, Pakistan, Vietnam, or Nigeria), you are painfully familiar with international settlement friction.

A client sends $10,000 via wire from New York or Frankfurt. What follows is a multi-day waiting game:

  1. The funds bounce across 2 to 4 intermediary correspondent banks.
  2. 3 to 5 business days elapse.
  3. By the time the funds arrive in your domestic bank account, $300 to $700 has been deducted in intermediary fees, correspondent charges, and opaque foreign exchange spreads.

In regions where global aggregators like Stripe do not offer local merchant accounts, this friction directly drains economic output.

Most people blame local banking inefficiency. But looking into the technical plumbing, the bottleneck is architectural. Legacy interbank networks were designed in the 1970s for batch messaging, not atomic settlement.

Over the past few months, I set out to build a clean, sovereign core engine from first principles in Rust: PaySwitch.

Here is a breakdown of the core architectural decisions.

1. Zero Float Loss: The Integer Constraint

In conventional web development, developers frequently store monetary amounts as f64 or float. In high-throughput financial switching, floating-point arithmetic is a disaster due to IEEE 754 non-associative rounding errors:

0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3

In PaySwitch, floating-point types are strictly banned across all calculation paths. Every currency balance, fee, and foreign exchange conversion is represented in 128-bit unsigned atomic integer units (cents, pence, poisha):

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Amount(pub u128);

For foreign exchange conversions, exchange rates are computed using integer ratios rather than decimal multipliers:

// Atomic conversion: Net = (Source * RateNumerator) / RateDenominator
let target_amount = (net_source * self.rate_numerator) / self.rate_denominator;

This guarantees mathematical precision down to the single atomic unit, with zero rounding drift over millions of transactions.

2. Invariant Conservation in Double-Entry Accounting

Financial ledgers must uphold one fundamental law: money cannot appear or disappear. Every transfer must balance debit and credit legs identically:

$$\sum \Delta \text{Debits} \equiv \sum \Delta \text{Credits}$$

In PaySwitch, transfers are atomic memory operations that execute only after strict precondition checks:

pub fn execute_transfer(
    &self,
    debit_account_id: Uuid,
    credit_account_id: Uuid,
    amount: Amount,
    currency: Currency,
) -> Result<Transfer, PaySwitchError> {
    if debit_account_id == credit_account_id {
        return Err(PaySwitchError::IdenticalAccounts(debit_account_id));
    }

    let mut accounts = self.accounts.write();

    // 1. Verify debit account balance and currency
    let debit_account = accounts.get(&debit_account_id)
        .ok_or(PaySwitchError::AccountNotFound(debit_account_id))?;

    if debit_account.currency != currency {
        return Err(PaySwitchError::CurrencyMismatch(
            debit_account.currency.to_string(), currency.to_string()
        ));
    }
    if debit_account.available_balance().0 < amount.0 {
        return Err(PaySwitchError::InsufficientFunds(
            debit_account_id, amount.0, debit_account.available_balance().0
        ));
    }

    // 2. Verify credit account
    let credit_account = accounts.get(&credit_account_id)
        .ok_or(PaySwitchError::AccountNotFound(credit_account_id))?;

    if credit_account.currency != currency {
        return Err(PaySwitchError::CurrencyMismatch(
            credit_account.currency.to_string(), currency.to_string()
        ));
    }

    // 3. Atomically apply mutation
    accounts.get_mut(&debit_account_id).unwrap().settled_balance.0 -= amount.0;
    accounts.get_mut(&credit_account_id).unwrap().settled_balance.0 += amount.0;

    Ok(...)
}

3. Tamper-Evident SHA-256 Merkle Chaining

In conventional databases, an insider with root access can modify a balance row in a database table without leaving a cryptographic trace.

To prevent this, PaySwitch chains every transfer cryptographically:

let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
hasher.update(&prev_hash);
hasher.update(transfer_id.as_bytes());
hasher.update(debit_account_id.as_bytes());
hasher.update(credit_account_id.as_bytes());
hasher.update(&amount.0.to_be_bytes());
hasher.update(&(currency as u8).to_be_bytes());

let entry_hash: [u8; 32] = hasher.finalize().into();

Any modification to a past transfer invalidates every subsequent hash in the chain, providing instant mathematical proof of tampering.

4. Durability via Write-Ahead Log (WAL)

Holding state purely in memory provides sub-millisecond throughput, but memory is volatile. Putting PostgreSQL or MySQL in front of every transfer creates network and disk lock contention.

PaySwitch uses an append-only binary Write-Ahead Log:

  1. Before any balance mutation is applied in memory, a framed binary record is appended to disk.
  2. The record includes a 32-bit CRC checksum.
  3. On startup, the engine reads the WAL, validates checksums, and replays state. 
+----------------+-------------------+--------------------+------------------------+
| Magic (4B)     | Payload Len (4B)  | CRC32 Checksum(4B) | Serialized Payload     |
| "PSWL"         | uint32_be         | uint32_be          | JSON/Binary Record     |
+----------------+-------------------+--------------------+------------------------+

5. Bridging Global to Regional Rails

A settlement switch is only useful if it talks to the outside world. PaySwitch natively includes:

  • ISO 20022: Structural support for pacs.008 (Credit Transfer) and pacs.002 (Status Report) messaging.
  • Regional Payout Rails: Payload validation for domestic clearing networks (Bangladesh Bank NPSB, BEFTN, RTGS, and instant wallet formatting for bKash and Nagad).

Open Source and Next Steps

PaySwitch is dual-licensed under GNU AGPLv3 for open-source reference and commercial terms for private banking infrastructure.

The project is live on GitHub and published on crates.io:

  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Exploidus/payswitch
  • Crates.io: https://crates.io/crates/payswitch

If you are working on sovereign payment systems, distributed consensus, or financial accounting engines, I welcome your feedback, PRs, and architectural reviews.

title: Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents
description:
arXiv:2605.19149v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Agents operating with computer and Web use inevitably encounter errors: inaccessible webpages, missing files, local and remote misconfigurations, etc. These errors do not thwart agents based on state-of-the-art models. They helpfully continue to look for ways to complete their tasks.
  We introduce, characterize, and measure a new type of agent failure we call accidental meltdown: unsafe or harmful behavior in response to a benign environmental error, in the absence of any adversarial inputs. Because meltdowns are not captured by the existing reliability or safety benchmarks, we develop a taxonomy of meltdown behaviors. We then implement an agent-agnostic infrastructure for injecting simulated local and remote errors into the rollout environment and use it to systematically evaluate agents powered by GPT, Grok, Gemini, and Claude.
  Our evaluation demonstrates that meltdowns (e.g., conducting unauthorized reconnaissance or subverting access control) of varying severity and success occur in 64.9% of agent rollouts that encounter simulated errors, spanning all combinations of agent system, backing model, and error type. In half of all observed meltdowns, unsafe behaviors are not reported to the user. Comparing behaviors of the same agents with and without errors, we find that exploration in response to errors is correlated with unsafe and harmful behavior.

title: My MCP Scanner Scored 0 of 2 on a Real CVE. Here Is What Found It Instead
description:
sooperset/mcp-atlassian is an MCP server for Jira and Confluence with 6,139 stars on GitHub. Version 0.16.0 has two published CVEs, one of them critical. I maintain mcpscan, a static scanner for MCP servers, and back in September I extended its path traversal rule to cover file writes after reading about the critical one. This week I ran the scanner against the vulnerable release itself, and it found neither CVE.

TL;DR

  • mcpscan 0.21.0 reported 7 findings on mcp-atlassian v0.16.0. None was a real bug. It missed CVE-2026-27825 (file write, CVSS 9.1) and CVE-2026-27826 (SSRF).
  • The patched v0.17.0 got the same 7 findings, line for line.
  • Reading the code by hand, following each path parameter to the place it gets written, found the 4 sites upstream fixed in 0.17.0.
  • mcpscan 0.22.0, released today, flags the two vulnerable write sinks as HIGH and has no MCP007 finding on the patched release. It still does not see the SSRF, and it loses track of a path that passes through several functions.

The two CVEs

CVE Severity What Fixed in
CVE-2026-27825 Critical, CVSS 9.1 Arbitrary file write leading to code execution, through the unconstrained download path in confluence_download_attachment 0.17.0
CVE-2026-27826 High SSRF through the X-Atlassian-Jira-Url and X-Atlassian-Confluence-Url headers 0.17.0

The advisory range for the file write is <0.17.0. The fix calls validate_safe_path(...) before every download is written.

What mcpscan 0.21.0 reported

I scanned src/ of the v0.16.0 tag: 94 files, about 6 seconds, 30 rules, 7 findings.

Going through them one by one:

  • Two MCP005 "hardcoded secret" hits in utils/oauth.py:30 and :39. They are CLOUD_TOKEN_URL and DC_TOKEN_PATH, an OAuth endpoint URL and a path. The maintainers had already marked both # noqa: S105, the same complaint from their own linter.
  • Two MCP007 "path traversal" hits in utils/oauth_setup.py:141 and :149. Both are JavaScript window.open( calls inside an HTML page that Python builds as a string. My regex saw open( and fired.
  • Three MCP010 "TLS verification disabled" hits in utils/ssl.py:42, :43 and :69. That code only runs when the operator sets ssl_verify=false, so it is there by design.

Then I scanned v0.17.0, the release that fixes both CVEs. Same 7 findings, same files, same lines. Whatever the report was measuring, it was not the security of the download path.

What found it: a manual trace

The question I asked by hand was narrow. For every function that writes a file, where does the path come from, and does anything check that it stays inside a base directory before the write?

In src/mcp_atlassian/confluence/attachments.py on v0.16.0 the answer takes a few lines to find:

def download_attachment(self, url: str, target_path: str) -> bool:
    ...
    # Convert to absolute path if relative
    if not os.path.isabs(target_path):
        target_path = os.path.abspath(target_path)

    # Create the directory if it doesn't exist
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(target_path), exist_ok=True)

    # Use the Confluence session to download the file
    response = self.confluence._session.get(url, stream=True)
    response.raise_for_status()

    # Write the file to disk
    with open(target_path, "wb") as f:

target_path is a parameter. os.path.abspath makes it absolute and does nothing to limit where it points. os.makedirs creates whatever directory is missing. Line 198 writes the downloaded bytes there. jira/attachments.py has the same shape, with the write at line 50.

Following the callers turned up two more functions, download_content_attachments and download_issue_attachments, which take a target directory and write through those two. That makes 4 sites, and they are the same 4 that upstream patched in 0.17.0.

In download_attachment the upstream fix is one call after abspath:

    # Guard against path traversal (resolves symlinks)
    validate_safe_path(target_path)

validate_safe_path resolves the path, symlinks included, and raises ValueError unless the result is_relative_to the base directory, which defaults to the working directory.

Why MCP007 missed it

The September change added write sinks to MCP007, but the rule still only fired when the path was interpolated on the same line as the sink. It catches open(f"{base}/{name}", "w"). The vulnerable line here is with open(target_path, "wb") as f:. There is nothing on that line for a regex to object to. The danger is that target_path came in from the caller at the top of the function and nothing checked it in between, and a line-based rule has no view of that.

The fix in mcpscan 0.22.0

mcpscan 0.22.0 adds a small ast pass for each Python function, next to the existing line regex:

  1. Start from the function's parameters. Names assigned from a parameter p, from Path(p) or from os.path.abspath(p) count as the same value.
  2. Look for a write sink that receives one of those names: open with a w, a, x or + mode, write_text, write_bytes, shutil.copy, copy2, copyfile and move, and os.rename and os.replace.
  3. If the function has no boundary check, report it as HIGH. A boundary check is realpath or resolve followed by startswith, is_relative_to or commonpath, or a call to anything named like *safe_path* or *validate_path*.

It also stopped matching window.open(.

On v0.16.0, MCP007 now reports confluence/attachments.py:198 and jira/attachments.py:50 as HIGH. On v0.17.0 it reports nothing, and the total drops to 5: the unchanged MCP005 and MCP010 findings. The release has 8 new tests, the full suite passes 266 of 266, and mcpscan's scan of its own code is clean.

Getting that self-scan clean needed one suppression. drift.py writes mcpscan's own baseline file to a path that arrives as a parameter, which is exactly the shape the new check looks for:

with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:  # mcpscan: ignore[MCP007] baseline path is ours, not tool input

That is the noise the check will add elsewhere. In an MCP server, a path parameter often comes from a tool call, and an unchecked write to it is the bug. In a generic utility or a CLI that writes where its own user told it to, the same pattern is fine, and you will be suppressing it.

What it still cannot do

  • A path that passes through several functions before the write is not tracked. The pass looks at one function at a time. It flags the two functions that do the writing in mcp-atlassian, while the two download-all functions that pass a directory down to them get no finding of their own.
  • A check that lives in the caller is not recognised. If the caller validates the path and the writing function does not, 0.22.0 still reports the writing function.
  • The SSRF is still missed. 0.22.0 changed MCP007 and nothing else, so on this release it gets 1 of the 2 CVEs, the file write.
  • The "14 of 14, zero false positives" benchmark I published earlier measured synthetic fixtures I wrote myself. It says nothing about detection on real code, and this run shows the difference.

Where the scanner fits in a review

Automated MCP scanners are sold for about $0.25 per server on Apify. That price is fine for what a scanner does. In this case the review was the human trace: take every input a tool call controls, follow it to the file system, the network or a shell, and look for what stops it. The scanner is the second pass, useful for the code you did not get to and for catching the same mistake when it comes back.

mcpscan 0.22.0 is on PyPI as mcpscan-cli:

pip install -U mcpscan-cli
mcpscan ./path-to-an-mcp-server

If you run an MCP server and want that trace done before a release, I offer a free preflight.

title: From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger
description:
arXiv:2611.25197v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

title: Backup restore in the admin panel: short-lived signed links for private object storage
description:
Decision rule first: keep every backup object private, and let an admin-only route mint a short-lived signed download URL at the moment a human clicks restore. Use your own app server as the download path only when you have to read or rewrite the bytes on their way out — decryption, redaction, per-row filtering. Everything else belongs in a presigned GET.

That's the whole recommendation. The rest of this is why the second shape costs less than it looks, and what retention and deletion do to both of them.

The system I have in mind is a B2B SaaS reporting product. A nightly job generates a report archive per tenant, writes it to object storage, and support engineers use an internal admin panel to re-deliver or restore one of those archives for an authenticated customer. A few hundred MB per file, a contractual retention window, and a deletion promise we have to be able to keep. The panel is Node.js. The backup service behind it is Go.

Two shapes for a restore path, and the invariant each one holds

Shape one is the proxy: the browser hits your API, your server authenticates the admin, opens the object, and streams it through. The invariant is that every byte crosses your authorization layer, which means revocation is instant — kill the session and the download dies mid-transfer. You pay for that with your app server sitting in the data path. Long-lived connections, memory pressure on a 400 MB archive, egress billed twice, and a request that outlives your load balancer's idle timeout.

Shape two is the one I run: the object stays private, and an admin-only route issues a signed URL that the browser fetches directly from storage. The invariant here is different and worth saying out loud — the link is the capability. Anyone holding that string can download the archive until it expires, with no further check against your session or your database.

Both are defensible. They fail in different places, and the place they fail decides which one you want.

The Node-to-Go split is a small argument for shape two, since a signed URL is just a string that crosses a service boundary without dragging a storage client along with it. I run that route against Infrai's storage capability, and the reason is architectural rather than featural: the bucket sits behind one vendor-agnostic contract, so moving it from S3 to R2 later is a configuration change instead of a rewrite of the restore flow. The other half of that is plain HTTP — Infrai needs no SDK in the Go binary, one Bearer key, and the same request shape whether the caller is the Node panel or a worker.

How does an admin panel get a signed download URL out of a private storage API?

Two calls, in this order.

First GET /v1/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key}, which confirms the archive exists and gives you its size without pulling 400 MB through your process. Show that size in the panel. An engineer who sees a 12 KB file where last night's run should have produced 380 MB has caught a bad backup before restoring it over good data, which is the single most useful thing a restore UI does.

Then POST /v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key} with op: "get" and a short expires_seconds, and hand the returned URL to the browser.

One rule that people get wrong on the first try: do not attach your API Authorization header to the returned presigned URL. It already carries its own signature. Adding a second credential does nothing except put your platform key into a browser request.

package backups

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const apiBase = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type envelope struct {
    OK    bool            `json:"ok"`
    Data  json.RawMessage `json:"data"`
    Error json.RawMessage `json:"error"`
}

type grant struct {
    URL       string `json:"url"`
    Method    string `json:"method"`
    ExpiresAt string `json:"expires_at"`
}

// call performs one authenticated request and backs off on 429.
func call(method, path string, body any, idemKey string) (json.RawMessage, error) {
    var payload []byte
    if body != nil {
        payload, _ = json.Marshal(body)
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(method, apiBase+path, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        if payload != nil {
            req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        }
        if idemKey != "" {
            // Same key on every retry, so a retried restore is deduplicated.
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idemKey)
        }
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        raw, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if s, convErr := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); convErr == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(s) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }

        var env envelope
        if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &env); err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: HTTP %d, unreadable body", method, path, res.StatusCode)
        }
        if res.StatusCode >= 400 || !env.OK {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: HTTP %d %s", method, path, res.StatusCode, env.Error)
        }
        return env.Data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %s: still rate limited after 4 attempts", method, path)
}

// DownloadLink confirms the archive is there, then mints a 120-second GET link.
func DownloadLink(bucket, key, actor string) (grant, error) {
    head, err := call(http.MethodGet, "/storage/object/head/"+bucket+"/"+key, nil, "")
    if err != nil {
        return grant{}, err
    }
    var meta struct {
        SizeBytes int64 `json:"size_bytes"`
    }
    if err := json.Unmarshal(head, &meta); err != nil {
        return grant{}, err
    }
    if meta.SizeBytes < 1<<20 {
        return grant{}, fmt.Errorf("archive %s is only %d bytes, refusing to offer a restore", key, meta.SizeBytes)
    }

    raw, err := call(http.MethodPost, "/storage/object/presign/"+bucket+"/"+key,
        map[string]any{"op": "get", "expires_seconds": 120},
        "restore:"+actor+":"+key)
    if err != nil {
        return grant{}, err
    }
    var g grant
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &g); err != nil {
        return grant{}, err
    }
    // Give g.URL to the browser as-is. No platform credentials travel with it.
    return g, nil
}

Log the grant, not the URL: actor, bucket, key, expiry. When someone asks in three months who pulled tenant 4471's March archive, that record is the answer, and a signed URL in a log line is a credential sitting in your log store.

Retention and deletion are where this choice actually bites

Here's the part that decides the architecture for a reporting product with a contractual purge window.

A signed URL is a bearer capability with a clock on it. You cannot recall one mid-flight; the only lever you have is the expiry you chose when you minted it, so the TTL is your revocation window whether you think of it that way or not. Ours is 120 seconds, because a support engineer clicks within a few seconds of asking. I'm not sure there's a universally correct number — if your admins open a link and walk away, yours will be longer, and the honest way to write that down is as a documented risk rather than a default someone copied.

Deletion has to happen at the storage layer, and it has to be the thing your retention job actually does.

Two boundaries worth checking before you commit to shape two. Lifecycle expiry works in whole days — one day is the floor, and submitting a rule set replaces the whole list rather than merging into it — so a promise like "purged within an hour of cancellation" needs a scheduled delete you own, not a bucket policy. And object versioning is a capability Infrai lacks, which means an overwrite of the same key is not something you get back. That one changed how we restore: a restore never writes over the source key. It copies to a staging key, the app verifies the copy, and only then does the tenant-visible pointer move.

The same reasoning applies to concurrency. Conditional writes with If-Match are not part of the contract, so two admins triggering a restore for the same tenant have to be serialized somewhere you control — a row lock, a queue with a per-tenant key, whatever you already run. This is the failure that pages you at 03:00: two overlapping restores, last writer wins, and no version history to reconstruct what the earlier one wrote.

Backend comparison: the two columns that actually decide it

Option Download path Retention controls Immutability (WORM) Integration cost
Amazon S3 presigned GET lifecycle rules, day granularity Object Lock, compliance mode SDK per language, IAM policy work
Cloudflare R2 presigned GET (S3 API) lifecycle rules not offered S3-compatible SDK, no egress fees
Backblaze B2 signed download token lifecycle rules Object Lock S3-compatible SDK
MinIO (self-hosted) presigned GET lifecycle rules Object Lock you operate the cluster
Infrai storage presigned GET, ACL private or signed-only lifecycle rules, one-day floor lacks object lock, pair with S3 when audited one REST call, no SDK

It comes down to the last two columns. If an auditor is going to ask for immutable retention, that requirement outranks everything else in the table and you should be talking to S3 Object Lock or a B2 bucket with lock enabled. If nobody is asking, the integration column is where the ongoing cost actually lives, because a storage integration is the sort of code that gets rewritten every time procurement changes clouds.

What I would ship, and when I would pick something else

Ship shape two: private objects, HEAD before you offer the restore, a presigned GET with a TTL you can defend, a copy-to-staging restore, and an audit row per grant. It's a small amount of code and it keeps your app server out of a 400 MB transfer path.

If you're a small team serving generated reports to authenticated customers and you don't want to maintain a storage integration per cloud, Infrai is worth trying for exactly this slice of the flow — the presign call and the HEAD check — because the vendor behind the bucket can change later without the restore code changing with it. If that boundary fits your system, the storage reference is the page to read first; the ACL enum and the presign contract are the two things to check before you build against it.

Stick with S3 or MinIO directly when you need Object Lock, cross-region replication, or versioned buckets, and when your compliance story depends on those, don't approximate them. Stick with the proxy shape when the bytes must be transformed per request, or when your threat model says no capability may ever leave your perimeter as a URL. Those are real reasons, and they beat the convenience argument every time.

References

  • RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Amazon S3: sharing objects with presigned URLs — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock.html
  • Cloudflare R2: presigned URLs — https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/
  • MinIO Go client API reference — https://min.io/docs/minio/linux/developers/go/API.html

title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
description:
arXiv:2611.23639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

title: Cisco Expressway é invadido após PoC da falha CVE-2026-76466
description:
Invasores comprometeram dispositivos Expressway

Um grupo não identificado invadiu dispositivos Cisco Expressway em cluster de uma organização na Rússia e preparou ferramentas para se mover lateralmente pela rede, segundo a empresa de segurança F6. A ação ocorreu logo depois que um código de exploração proof-of-concept (PoC) para a falha CVE-2026-76466 se tornou público.

Os gateways Expressway dão a funcionários remotos, parceiros e usuários terceirizados acesso a serviços de colaboração, como chamadas de vídeo, voz e mensagens instantâneas. A vulnerabilidade, com pontuação CVSS 9,8, dispensa autenticação e permite que um atacante com alcance de rede execute comandos como root.

Falha em cookies persistentes permite comandos

O problema afeta as versões appliance e virtual do Expressway Core e do Expressway Edge, mas somente em configurações de cluster. A Cisco tornou a falha pública em 21 de outubro e a localiza no serviço de banco de dados do Expressway, com origem em cookies persistentes.

Quem obtém esses cookies pode alcançar o serviço de banco de dados e disparar comandos de chamada de procedimento remoto (RPC), abrindo caminho para executar comandos com privilégios de root no sistema operacional. A Cisco corrige a vulnerabilidade na versão X15.5.20, não oferece workaround e orienta clientes em X14 ou anteriores a migrar para uma versão corrigida.

O comunicado da Cisco não havia sido atualizado desde a publicação e ainda dizia que a empresa desconhecia anúncios públicos ou uso malicioso da falha. A PoC já circulava no GitHub, enquanto a F6 relatou uma invasão investigada após sua divulgação.

Invasores avançaram do cluster para a rede

De acordo com a F6, os atacantes comprometeram primeiro dois equipamentos Expressway X15.5.3 expostos à internet. A partir de um deles, avançaram para outros dois nós do cluster na rede interna da organização e usaram privilégios de root para preparar ferramentas de movimentação lateral.

Os invasores criaram scripts Python para varrer a rede, localizar recursos SMB, interagir com SQL Server e WinRM e procurar repositórios GitLab. A F6 descreveu essas ferramentas como voltadas a exfiltrar credenciais e outros dados sensíveis, sem afirmar que a coleta tenha sido concluída.

A F6 observou que os invasores ajustaram os scripts durante a operação. Comentários no código e descrições de correções levaram a empresa a apontar o possível uso de um assistente de IA; a vítima não foi identificada e a F6 não vinculou o ataque a um grupo de ameaça conhecido.

Detecção e contenção

Para procurar sinais da exploração, a F6 recomenda examinar o log de sistema Erlang dos dispositivos Expressway. A empresa também divulgou endereços IP e caminhos de arquivos associados ao ataque em um comunicado em russo.

Para organizações sem condições de aplicar o patch imediatamente, a F6 sugere bloquear no firewall conexões às portas TCP 4371–4372, mantendo exceções apenas para os endereços IP dos nós confiáveis do cluster. Essa é uma recomendação da empresa de segurança, não um workaround oferecido pela Cisco.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/cisco-expressway-invadido-divulgacao-codigo-exploracao/

title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
description:
arXiv:2611.24999v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.

title: This Week in Open Source for November 20, 2026
description:
by Daryl Ducharme, Open Source Programs Office

A look around the world of open source

Automated tools are flooding open source repositories with bug reports and pull requests faster than human maintainers can review patches, coordinate security embargoes, or fund the work behind critical infrastructure. Across this edition, we trace how builders are responding—replacing brute-force diff skimming with codified invariants, protecting newcomer on-ramps and neutral foundation governance instead of reactionary gatekeeping, and designing open social protocols that keep control with people rather than closed platforms.

Upcoming events

🗓️ December 2026

  • Yocto Project Virtual Summit 2026.12 (December 1–3, 2026) – Virtual. Community summit for embedded Linux engineers and maintainers building custom, reproducible Linux distributions across edge and Internet of Things (IoT) hardware.
  • Open Source Summit Japan 2026 (December 7–9, 2026) – Tokyo, Japan. The Linux Foundation's premier Asia-Pacific conference connecting open source developers, kernel maintainers, and enterprise leaders across cloud, embedded Linux, and open source AI—featuring a keynote by Google's Kaz Sato on building agents on open standards alongside sessions from Googlers Tanya Sharma and Tarun Sahu.
  • Open Compliance Summit 2026 (December 10–11, 2026) – Tokyo, Japan. Specialized gathering uniting legal, security, and Open Source Programs Office (OSPO) practitioners around OpenChain, Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX), software bills of materials (SBOMs), and global open source supply-chain compliance.
