title: Send Medusa order SMS from your own Android phone (Medusa v2 notification provider)
description:
Medusa's Notification Module can send texts, but the sms channel needs a provider. Here's one that hands each text to your own Android phone: the phone sends it from its own SIM, from your own number, so customers see a number they know and can simply reply to. There's no SMS provider account and no sender registration, and SMSTunnel doesn't charge per text. The same works from Payload CMS hooks and jobs, and there are Strapi and Directus versions at the end.

What you need

  • Medusa 2 (tested with 2.22.2) and Node.js 20 or newer.
  • An Android phone with a SIM card and the free SMSTunnel app, signed in to your SMSTunnel account. It sends the texts.
  • An SMSTunnel account. The free plan has 25 texts a day.

1. Get an API key

  1. Install the SMSTunnel app from Google Play on your Android phone and sign in.
  2. In the SMSTunnel dashboard, open Apps → Add an app, pick Node.js, name it (for example "My Medusa store") and click Create the key.
  3. Copy the key right away: it's shown only once. You can stop or delete the app there anytime, and the key stops working.

Put it in your Medusa environment (.env, or your host's secret settings), never in your code:

SMSTUNNEL_API_KEY=sk_live_...

2. Install the provider 

npm install @narcisbodea/smstunnel-medusa

It has no other dependencies.

3. Register it in medusa-config.ts 

module.exports = defineConfig({
  // ...
  modules: [
    {
      resolve: "@medusajs/medusa/notification",
      options: {
        providers: [
          {
            resolve: "@narcisbodea/smstunnel-medusa",
            id: "smstunnel",
            options: {
              channels: ["sms"],
              apiKey: process.env.SMSTUNNEL_API_KEY,
              // Optional:
              defaultCountryCode: "+1", // for numbers written without + or 00
              templates: {
                "order-placed": "Thanks {{ first_name }}! Your order #{{ display_id }} is confirmed.",
              },
            },
          },
        ],
      },
    },
  ],
})

Medusa takes one provider per channel: if another provider already handles sms, swap it for this one. Medusa won't start without an apiKey, so a missing variable shows up right away.

templates holds texts by template name, with {{ placeholders }} filled from the notification's data (dots reach inside objects: {{ customer.first_name }}). defaultCountryCode completes numbers written without + or 00, and deviceId picks the phone that sends when your account has several.

4. Text the customer when an order is placed

Add a subscriber, src/subscribers/order-placed.ts:

import type { SubscriberArgs, SubscriberConfig } from "@medusajs/framework"
import { ContainerRegistrationKeys, Modules } from "@medusajs/framework/utils"

// Texts the customer when an order is placed, from your own phone, through SMSTunnel.
export default async function orderPlacedText({ event: { data }, container }: SubscriberArgs<{ id: string }>) {
  const query = container.resolve(ContainerRegistrationKeys.QUERY)
  const notifications = container.resolve(Modules.NOTIFICATION)

  const {
    data: [order],
  } = await query.graph({
    entity: "order",
    fields: ["id", "display_id", "shipping_address.first_name", "shipping_address.phone", "billing_address.phone"],
    filters: { id: data.id },
  })
  const phone = order?.shipping_address?.phone || order?.billing_address?.phone
  if (!phone) return // the customer left no number: nothing to send

  await notifications.createNotifications({
    to: phone,
    channel: "sms",
    template: "order-placed",
    data: { first_name: order.shipping_address?.first_name ?? "", display_id: order.display_id },
    // Medusa sends a notification only once per key, and SMSTunnel won't send the same text twice either.
    idempotency_key: `order-placed-${order.id}`,
  })
}

export const config: SubscriberConfig = { event: "order.placed" }

With the order-placed template above, the customer gets: Thanks Ana! Your order #1042 is confirmed. The same pattern works for order.fulfillment_created, order.canceled, delivery.created and the other Medusa events.

Customers type phone numbers in many ways. Ask for the international format at checkout (+14155550123), or set defaultCountryCode for your country.

From a workflow step, an API route or a scheduled job, it's the same createNotifications call. Pass the words in content.text and they're sent as they are, without a template. One notification goes to one number: to text several people, create one notification each.

When a text doesn't go out

createNotifications throws, and Medusa stores the notification with status failure and SMSTunnel's reason:

  • 401: the key is wrong, deactivated or deleted.
  • 403: the key lacks a permission, or your plan doesn't include what was asked.
  • 429: more than 30 sends a minute for this key (Retry-After says how long to wait), or today's allowance is used up.
  • 5xx, or no answer: the text may or may not have gone out. Check the Messages page in your dashboard, or send it again with the same idempotency_key.

The provider never resends a text by itself. In a subscriber, a failure is logged by Medusa and doesn't affect the order. If the phone is offline, the text isn't lost: it waits on your account and goes out as soon as the phone is back online (for up to 3 days). Each stored notification keeps SMSTunnel's message id in external_id.

Payload CMS: a text from a collection hook

The Payload plugin gives you server-side helpers for hooks, endpoints and jobs. It works with Payload 3 (tested with 3.92.1).

npm install @narcisbodea/smstunnel-payload

Add it to payload.config.ts:

import { buildConfig } from 'payload'
import { smsTunnelPlugin } from '@narcisbodea/smstunnel-payload'

export default buildConfig({
  // ...
  plugins: [smsTunnelPlugin()],
})

It reads the key from process.env.SMSTUNNEL_API_KEY. It adds no collections, fields or endpoints, keeps its settings in config.custom (which Payload never sends to the admin panel) and warns at start-up when there is no key.

Then text the customer once, when an order is created. src/collections/Orders.ts:

import type { CollectionConfig } from 'payload'
import { sendText } from '@narcisbodea/smstunnel-payload'

export const Orders: CollectionConfig = {
  slug: 'orders',
  fields: [
    { name: 'customerName', type: 'text' },
    { name: 'phone', type: 'text' },
  ],
  hooks: {
    afterChange: [
      async ({ doc, operation, req }) => {
        // Text the customer once, when the order is created, from your own phone.
        if (operation !== 'create' || !doc.phone) return doc
        try {
          await sendText(req.payload, {
            to: doc.phone,
            message: `Thanks ${doc.customerName ?? ''}! We got your order #${doc.id}.`,
            // The id and the creation time keep the key unique, so a retry can't send a second text.
            idempotencyKey: `order-${doc.id}-${doc.createdAt}`,
          })
        } catch (error) {
          // A text that can't go out must not fail the save: log it.
          req.payload.logger.error(`SMSTunnel: ${(error as Error).message}`)
        }
        return doc
      },
    ],
  },
}

Keep the phone field a text field: a number field loses the + and leading zeros.

The hook waits for SMSTunnel's answer, usually well under a second. To keep saves from waiting at all, queue the text with Payload's Jobs Queue. The README has a ready textCustomer task that reuses its key on retries. Then, from a hook or an endpoint:

await req.payload.jobs.queue({ task: 'textCustomer', input: { to: doc.phone, message: '…' } })

sendText returns { messageId, queued, replayed }. sendCode sends sign-in codes. getSmsTunnel(payload) gives you a client with getStatus, listPhones and getUsage. On failure the helpers throw an SmsTunnelError with status, retryAfter and mayHaveSent, so you know whether a retry is safe.

Strapi and Directus, briefly

Strapi 5 gets a service for your lifecycles, controllers and cron jobs, plus a settings page in the admin panel. There you can paste the key: it's checked first, then stored encrypted. The page also shows your phones and sends a test text.

npm install @narcisbodea/smstunnel-strapi
npm run build   # rebuilds the admin panel with the plugin's settings page

const sent = await strapi.plugin('smstunnel').service('sms').send({
  to: '+14155550123',
  message: 'Your table for 4 is ready.',
});
// sent: { messageId: '6ae9952f7f9ac207c547af90', queued: false, replayed: false }

Directus 11 and 12 get a Send a text with SMSTunnel operation for Flows. Install it from Settings → Marketplace, where it runs in the extension sandbox. Then, for example, add an Event Hook flow on items.create for a leads collection, with:

  • To: {{ $trigger.payload.phone }}
  • Message: Thanks {{ $trigger.payload.name }}, we got your request and will call you back today.
  • Idempotency key: lead-{{ $trigger.key }}

The key stays in the environment (SMSTUNNEL_API_KEY, allowed with FLOWS_ENV_ALLOW_LIST), and Directus redacts it in the flow logs.

Good to know

  • One text goes to one number. For several people, send one each.
  • 30 send requests a minute per key; over that, a 429 with Retry-After.
  • The phone sends at Android's own pace (about 30 SMS parts a minute), and a long text counts as several parts.
  • Texts can be up to 1600 characters, and sign-in codes up to 320.
  • Phone offline? The text waits on your account and goes out when the phone is back online, for up to 3 days.
  • An idempotency key makes a retry within 24 hours return the first answer instead of sending a second text.
  • Send only texts people expect: order updates, pickup notices, reminders, sign-in codes. Unsolicited texts from a personal SIM break most carriers' terms.

Full guides, with every option and an AI prompt for each:

  • Medusa: https://smstunnel.io/integrations/medusa/
  • Payload: https://smstunnel.io/integrations/payload/
  • Strapi: https://smstunnel.io/integrations/strapi/
  • Directus: https://smstunnel.io/integrations/directus/

Disclosure: I build SMSTunnel. This post was written with AI from the official setup guides linked above.

title: We replayed 1,201 releases of popular Java libraries: 1 in 9 contains a breaking change
description:
Semantic versioning promises that minor and patch releases are safe to install. We wanted to know how often that holds today, so we replayed every minor and patch release published since January 2024 by 44 of the most-used Java libraries on Maven Central: 1,201 releases in total.

About 1 in 9 of them (141 of 1,201, 11.7%) contains at least one breaking change in its public classes.

The full report, with the per-library table, the data and every caveat, is here: How often does a "compatible" release break its users? This post is the short version.

How we counted

  • The sample was not ours to pick. We used the list of most-used Maven Central libraries that the authors of the Roseau paper published in 2025. Of its artifacts, 44 contain code and had minor or patch releases since 2024.
  • Each release was compared with the previous version, jar against jar, bytecode against bytecode. Pre-releases were left out. A change in the second version number is a minor release; anything after that is a patch.
  • Two tools had to agree. Every pair was checked by two independent checkers, japicmp (0.27.0) and the Bumpwise engine (1.0.6). A release counts only when both flag it.
  • Internal code does not count. Packages named internal, impl or shaded, repackaged third-party code, packages a library's module-info does not export, and code marked @Beta or @API(status = INTERNAL / EXPERIMENTAL) were excluded.
  • "Breaking" means binary or source incompatible: code compiled against the old version fails to link with the new one, or code written for the old version no longer compiles. Counting binary breaks only, the figure is 8.8%.

The numbers

Releases With a breaking change
Minor releases 163 58 (35.6%)
Patch releases 1,038 83 (8.0%)
All minor and patch 1,201 141 (11.7%)

28 of the 44 libraries shipped at least one such release in under three years. The median library is at 6.7%.

Minor releases carry most of the breaks. In these libraries the last number of the version means something: a patch release is about four times less likely to break than a minor one.

It used to be worse

We ran the same replay back to 2019 (3,096 releases):

Year Releases With a breaking change
2019 327 20.5%
2020 422 17.3%
2021 357 14.0%
2022 351 19.7%
2023 438 18.5%
2024 475 12.2%
2025 378 11.4%
2026 (to 8 Nov) 348 11.5%

From about 1 in 6 before 2024 to about 1 in 9 since. Better, not gone.

What breaks

Out of the 141 releases (one release can have several kinds):

Kind of change Releases
Method removed 62
Abstract method added (to a type users implement) 45
Method parameters changed 38
Class removed 30
Field removed 18
Generic types changed 16
Return type changed 15

Nothing exotic. These are removals and changed signatures: changes that compile and pass the library's own tests, and only fail in someone else's build or at runtime. If some of them surprise you, the first two posts in this series walk through the Java and Kotlin cases one by one.

Small libraries: more than 1 in 4

The 44 libraries above are maintained by foundations, companies and experienced teams. We also took a random sample of small libraries published under io.github.* (the namespace Maven Central gives to a GitHub account): 162 libraries with releases of version 1.0 or later.

Most-used libraries Small libraries
Minor releases with a break 35.6% 29.5%
Patch releases with a break 8.0% 28.2%
All minor and patch 11.7% 28.5%

The interesting line is the patch row. In the small libraries, a patch release breaks as often as a minor one: the version number goes up, but it no longer says what kind of change is inside.

Read this second set with more care: we did not check which of these projects promise semantic versioning, a break in a small library reaches fewer people, and ten libraries account for 206 of the 506 flagged releases (21.0% without them).

What these numbers do not say

  • Not "violates semver". A tool sees what is public in the bytecode, not what a project promises. We leave out @Beta, @API(status = INTERNAL) and packages not exported by module-info, but some projects document what is stable in other ways (a FAQ, their own annotations), and we did not read each project's policy. Three libraries account for 53 of the 141 (8.7% without them).
  • Not "broke its users". We did not measure how many clients actually call the changed code. The largest earlier study of Maven Central (Ochoa et al., 2022) found that only 7.9% of clients were affected by the breaking changes it found.
  • Not "Maven Central". This is 44 popular artifacts from about 25 projects, plus one family of small namespaces.
  • Two tools agreeing is not proof. We looked by hand at every case where they disagreed (one of those turned out to be a real break that one tool missed, which is the next post in this series), but we did not build a failing client for every flagged release.

Why it matters anyway

Most of these breaks never hurt anyone. But a modern application pulls in hundreds of libraries, and "it's only a minor update" is the assumption behind every automated dependency bump. When the version number is wrong, the cost lands on the user of the library, who did nothing but upgrade.

Tomasz Nowak and Predrag Gruevski, authors of the best-known study of this (for Rust, 2023), put the conclusion better than we can: "The maintainers are not to blame, and improved tooling is our best way forward." Every change on the list above is detectable before the release, by japicmp, Revapi or Kotlin's binary-compatibility validator in CI, or in the editor.

Disclosure: we make Bumpwise, an IntelliJ plugin that flags these changes while you type, and its engine was one of the two tools in this replay. The method, data and per-library results are public on the report page. If you maintain one of these libraries and think we got your numbers wrong, tell us and we will correct the report.

title: geojson-editor: عارض ومحرّر ومدقّق GeoJSON في المتصفح بنيته لأتعلّم RFC 7946
description:
يبدو GeoJSON بسيطًا: هو JSON فيه إحداثيات. ثم يرفض ملفٌ أن يُفتح في مكان ما، فتكتشف كم من القواعد الصغيرة تختبئ خلف هذه البساطة. حلقة مضلّع (ring) غير مغلقة. خط العرض وخط الطول بترتيب معكوس. حلقة ملفوفة في الاتجاه الخاطئ. عنصر crs لم تعد المواصفة الحالية تسمح به.

لأتعلّم هذه القواعد كما يجب، بنيت الأداة التي أريدها عندما يتصرف ملف بشكل غريب. geojson-editor عارض ومحرّر ومدقّق (validator) صغير لـ GeoJSON يعمل في المتصفح، مبني بـ MapLibre GL JS و terra-draw. كل شيء يعمل داخل المتصفح، ولا يُرفع أي شيء إلى أي خادم.

هذا مشروع تعليمي. والجزء المهم فيه ليس الخريطة، بل المنطق الصرف تحتها، والقرارات حول من يملك البيانات.

ماذا يقدّم

التحميل من أي مصدر. اختر ملفًا، أو اسحبه وأفلته على الخريطة، أو أعطِه رابطًا (URL، بشرط أن يسمح الخادم بـ CORS)، أو الصق النص مباشرة. إذا كان المحتوى Geometry مجردة أو Feature واحدة، تُغلَّف داخل FeatureCollection، فتعمل دائمًا على الشكل نفسه من المستند.

الرسم والتعديل. يمكنك رسم نقاط وخطوط ومضلعات ومستطيلات. ويمكنك سحب الرؤوس (vertices)، وإدراج نقاط وسطية، وتحريك عنصر كامل، والحذف بمفتاح Delete.

لوحة الخصائص (properties). أضِف المفاتيح وأعِد تسميتها وعدّلها واحذفها. نوع القيمة يُستنتج مما تكتبه: 42 يصبح عددًا، و true قيمة منطقية، و "42" نصًّا، و [1,2] مصفوفة. ترتيب المفاتيح محفوظ، فلا يعود الملف المُصدَّر مبعثرًا.

التدقيق وفق RFC 7946. الأخطاء تشمل إغلاق الحلقة، وطول الحلقة، وشكل الموضع (position)، وانعكاس lat/lon، والعناصر الخاطئة في الـ Feature. والتحذيرات تشمل اتجاه اللف (winding order)، ووجود crs، والمواضع بأكثر من ثلاثة أبعاد، وحالات GeometryCollection الغريبة. النقر على مشكلة يحدّد العنصر المعني، وزر "Fix winding" يطبّق قاعدة اليد اليمنى بنقرة واحدة.

التصدير. نزّل النتيجة أو انسخها، مع خيار تقريب الإحداثيات (precision) وخيار الإخراج المضغوط (compact).

الحفظ التلقائي. المستند الحالي يُحفظ في localStorage. وإذا كان التخزين محظورًا، يبقى المحرّر يعمل.

طريقة الاستعمال

لا شيء يحتاج تثبيتًا. النسخة التجريبية موقع ثابت على GitHub Pages، وملفاتك تبقى في المتصفح: https://abdeldjalilchougui.github.io/geojson-editor/

لتشغيله محليًّا أو استضافة نسختك الخاصة:

git clone https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geojson-editor.git
cd geojson-editor
pnpm install
pnpm dev          # http://localhost:5173/geojson-editor/, then Paste or Open file (try public/sample.geojson)
pnpm test         # vitest, pure logic only
pnpm build        # type-check + production build into dist/

بناء الإنتاج يستعمل مسار Vite الأساسي /geojson-editor/ (انظر vite.config.ts). غيّره إذا كنت تقدّم الموقع من مسار آخر.

طريقة سريعة لتجربة المدقّق: الصق مضلعًا حلقته غير مغلقة، أو مضلعًا كُتب فيه خط العرض أولًا. تظهر المشكلة في القائمة، والنقر عليها يحدّد العنصر على الخريطة.

ما بنيته من الصفر

الكود مقسوم إلى قسمين عن قصد. كل ما في src/lib/ منطق صرف، لا يلمس الـ DOM، ومغطّى باختبارات الوحدة (unit tests). أما src/main.ts فهو مجرد ربط: خريطة MapLibre، وأوضاع terra-draw، واللوحات.

src/lib/        pure, DOM-free, unit tested
  parse.ts      text -> JSON -> FeatureCollection (friendly errors, never throws)
  validate.ts   structural RFC 7946 validator, issues with JSONPath-like paths
  properties.ts value inference + immutable add/rename/set/delete
  winding.ts    signed area, orientation, rewind (exterior CCW, holes CW)
  bbox.ts       bounding boxes for fit-to-data
  export.ts     precision rounding (coordinates only) + serialisation
  storage.ts    injected key/value store with every access guarded
  model.ts      document items with stable uids, which geometries are editable
src/main.ts     glue: MapLibre map, terra-draw modes, panels

بعض هذه الملفات يحمل الدروس الحقيقية:

  • parse.ts لا يرمي استثناءً أبدًا. النص الخاطئ يعطي رسالة خطأ واضحة بدل استثناء يوقف الصفحة.
  • validate.ts يُرفق بكل مشكلة مسارًا شبيهًا بـ JSONPath، وهذا ما يجعل "انقر على المشكلة لتحديد العنصر" ممكنًا.
  • winding.ts يحسب المساحة الموقَّعة (signed area) للحلقة ليعرف اتجاهها، ثم يعيد لفّها لتكون الحلقات الخارجية عكس عقارب الساعة والثقوب مع عقارب الساعة.
  • export.ts يقرّب الإحداثيات فقط. قيم الخصائص لا يمسّها إعداد الدقة أبدًا.
  • storage.ts يستقبل مخزن مفتاح/قيمة يُحقن من الخارج ويحمي كل وصول إليه، ولهذا لا يتعطل المحرّر عندما يكون localStorage محظورًا.

ما تعلّمته

احتفظ بمستندك الخاص كمصدر للحقيقة. كان هذا قرار التصميم الأساسي. المحرّر يحتفظ بقائمة عناصر من الشكل {uid, feature}. العناصر التي يستطيع terra-draw تعديلها (Point و LineString و Polygon بحلقة واحدة) تُنسخ إلى terra-draw بنفس الـ uid. وخصائص المستخدم تبقى في المستند، فلا تصل الخاصية mode المحجوزة لـ terra-draw إلى الملف المُصدَّر أبدًا.

لو كانت مكتبة الرسم هي التي تملك البيانات، لتسرّبت حقولها الداخلية إلى المخرجات، ولضاع كل ما لا تستطيع تمثيله. عندما يكون المستند عندي، تصبح مكتبة الرسم مجرد عرض مع مقابض للتحريك.

ليست كل الأشكال قابلة للتعديل، ولا بأس بذلك. الأشكال التي لا يستطيع terra-draw تعديلها (أنواع Multi*، و GeometryCollection، والمضلعات ذات الثقوب، وكل ما يرفضه تدقيقه الداخلي) تُرسم للقراءة فقط بطبقة MapLibre عادية. تبقى في المستند، فيمكن تعديل خصائصها، وتُصدَّر كما هي دون تغيير. أسوأ ما يمكن أن يحدث في أداة كهذه هو أن يضيع عنصر بصمت لأن المحرّر لم يستطع التعامل معه.

RFC 7946 أكثر صرامة من أغلب الملفات. كتابة المدقّق تعني قراءة المواصفة سطرًا سطرًا. ومن هنا جاء الفصل بين الأخطاء والتحذيرات: حلقة غير مغلقة خطأ، أما حلقة خارجية مع عقارب الساعة فأمر تطلب المواصفة تجنّبه لكنها توصي القارئ بتقبّله. وانعكاس lat/lon من الأخطاء التي يسهل الوقوع فيها ويستطيع المدقّق أن يلتقطها عنك.

المنطق الصرف هو الجزء الذي يستحق الاختبار. الأمر pnpm test يشغّل vitest على وحدات src/lib/ فقط. ولأن أيًّا منها لا يلمس الـ DOM، لا تحتاج الاختبارات إلى متصفح. ويبقى كود الربط مع الخريطة رقيقًا، فلا يكاد يوجد فيه ما يمكن أن يخطئ.

أشياء يجب معرفتها

  • الأشكال المتعددة (Multi)، و GeometryCollection، والمضلعات ذات الثقوب للقراءة فقط على الخريطة.
  • لا يوجد تراجع/إعادة (undo/redo) بعد.
  • التدقيق بنيوي فقط. لا يكتشف التقاطعات الذاتية ولا الثقوب الواقعة خارج الحلقة الخارجية.
  • بلاطات الخريطة الأساسية تأتي من tile.openstreetmap.org، وهذا مقبول للاستعمال الشخصي الخفيف حسب سياسة استعمال بلاطات OSM. غيّر الـ style في src/main.ts لأي استعمال أثقل.
  • حزمة الإنتاج نحو 1.2 MB (MapLibre مع terra-draw) وليست مقسّمة (code-split).
  • التحميل من رابط لا يعمل إلا إذا سمح الخادم البعيد بـ CORS.
  • ملف العيّنة يحتوي أشكالًا تقريبية مرسومة يدويًّا، وليست بيانات حقيقية.

لماذا بنيته

مشاكل GeoJSON في العادة صغيرة ومزعجة: حلقة واحدة غير مغلقة أو زوج إحداثيات معكوس في ملف فيه مئات العناصر. ولرؤية المشكلة تحتاج ثلاثة أشياء معًا: الشكل على الخريطة، والخصائص، وقائمة بما يخالف المواصفة. وعندما يكون الملف غير قابل للمشاركة، تريد أداة تُبقيه داخل المتصفح.

بناء هذه الأداة كان أيضًا طريقًا مباشرًا لتعلّم RFC 7946 والتدرّب على فصل نظيف بين المنطق الصرف وكود الواجهة. هذا هو الدافع كله: محرّر صغير يشرح لماذا الملف خاطئ، مكتوب بطريقة أستطيع اختبارها.

احصل على الكود

الكود المصدري والاختبارات وملف العيّنة على GitHub: https://github.com/AbdeldjalilChougui/geojson-editor. الكود برخصة MIT. بيانات الخريطة © مساهمو OpenStreetMap (ODbL). الملاحظات (issues) وطلبات الدمج (pull requests) مرحّب بها.

نُشر في الأصل على abdeldjalilchougui.biz.

title: From transcription to semantic corpus analysis: unsupervised learning of sentence representations for ancient languages
description:
arXiv:2607.24542v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Automatic Text Recognition (ATR) now supplies digital humanities with large volumes of unstruc- tured, heterogeneous, and often noisy text in ancient languages. Downstream semantic analyses- text reuse identification, alignment, and semantic search-rely on sentence embeddings, yet ex- isting methods transfer poorly to ancient languages: generic multilingual encoders underperform, specialized language models yield anisotropic representation spaces, and labeled similarity data is scarce. We study two fully unsupervised strategies-TSDAE and unsupervised SimCSE (hence- forth CSE)-that adapt a specialized token-level language model into a corpus-specific sentence encoder using only raw sentences. We validate them on biblical reuse in patristic literature in Latin and Ancient Greek: 2,936 sentences carrying expert-verified reuses in works of Augustine, Jerome, and Athanasius, matched against the Vulgate, the Septuagint, and the Nestle--Aland New Testament. We decompose reuse identification into binary detection and correspondence retrieval, evaluate both tasks separately, and benchmark the adapted encoders against multilingual, specialized, distilled, and supervised fine-tuned baselines, on clean text and on text perturbed by simulated HTR errors and scribal abbreviations. On these test sets, the adapted encoders lead all baselines on both tasks, with complementary profiles: TSDAE leads detection given a large in-domain corpus, while CSE leads retrieval, reaches its optimum with as few as 4--8k raw in-domain sentences-a few tens of sec- onds of training on a laptop GPU-and transfers across works and authors. Under simulated noise, retraining CSE on the perturbed text itself outperforms a clean-trained encoder. Measurements of alignment, uniformity, and anisotropy relate the geometric effect of each strategy to the measured gains. The full pipeline-segmentation, fine-tuning, cross-corpus semantic search-is available to non-specialists through the online tool Paraphrasis.

title: ScaleDiag: Diagnosing the Limits of Test-Time Scaling in GUI Grounding
description:
arXiv:2611.25297v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1--11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement. Together, these results show that test-time scaling is constrained by distinct operating regimes rather than benefiting monotonically from more visual focus, richer instructions, or additional samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/YenanLiu/ScaleDiag.

title: Vercel completes ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification
description:
Vercel has completed its ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification, meeting the international standard for AI management systems.

This certification gives our customers confidence to ship fast with agents on Vercel, demonstrating how Vercel designs, builds, operates, and governs our AI products.

Our AI management system covers Vercel’s underlying infrastructure and core AI products, including AI Gateway, Vercel Agent, v0, AI-based open source software and frameworks, as well as the people and processes behind them.

Vercel’s certificate is available here, and additional audit documentation is available through our Trust Center.

What is ISO 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international standard for AI management systems and applies to any organization that develops, provides, or uses AI.

An AI management system is the set of policies, roles, processes, and controls through which an organization consistently governs AI activities. The standard includes requirements for leadership accountability, AI risk assessment, lifecycle management, data governance, transparency, and continual improvement.

The requirement that makes ISO 42001 distinct from security standards is the AI system impact assessment. Security frameworks cover how an organization protects information, but ISO 42001 covers how it builds and uses AI, including the assessment of how an AI system impacts the people it touches, and the benefits and harms that would result when that system materially changes.

To obtain the certification, we underwent a two-stage audit performed by an independent, accredited certification body, which evaluated whether our AI management system is designed correctly and operates effectively. The certificate is valid for three years, with annual surveillance audits in between.

“Enterprises want agents in production, but no one should have to choose between moving fast with AI and governing it well,” said Talha Tariq, CTO for Security. “We built our AI governance to run as continuously as we ship, and ISO 42001 is the independent check that it works.”

What this means for customers

AI moved into the critical path of how software gets built faster than the governance around it did. Teams are shipping agents, assistants, and model-backed features on Vercel every day, and the questions that follow are no longer hypothetical:

  • Who is accountable when a model behaves unexpectedly?

  • What data reached a model?

  • How is the system monitored once it’s live?

  • Who decided the system was ready?

We pursued ISO 42001 because we are committed to providing enterprise-grade AI products. This certification attests that we run deliberate, auditable AI systems.

How we govern AI at Vercel

There are three primary ways AI is governed at Vercel.

Impact assessments

Vercel conducts AI system impact assessments which cover foreseeable benefits, harms, failures, and misuse. We reassess these risks and benefits when the system materially changes.

Evaluations before release

We maintain evals for our AI systems covering performance, safety, and security, with human review for material changes.

Clear data commitments

Where it is not the default option based on pricing plan, we provide customers the ability to set their data handling preferences ranging from zero data retention (ZDR) to training opt-out. Our AI policy is available at v0.app/policy.

Ship fast, with confidence

We are committed to helping teams ship fast with confidence in the way AI is built and governed at Vercel. ISO 42001 is proof of that commitment, giving our customers:

  • Confidence in agentic infrastructure: Vercel’s AI systems have been audited, which means customers using our AI products start from a reviewed foundation instead of an unexamined one.

  • Governance can ship at the speed of the product: Agents now drive the development and deployment of applications. Governance and oversight that occurs quarterly can’t govern software that changes hourly, so we built a system that reviews AI as continuously as we ship it.

  • Simplified and accelerated assurance: Customers and partners can rely on this certification, alongside our other compliance attestations, to meet AI governance diligence requirements for faster third-party vendor onboarding.

  • Clear lines of responsibility: ISO 42001 requires that responsibilities be allocated across the AI supply chain. Our documentation outlines what Vercel is accountable for and what remains yours, the same shared-responsibility model we use for security.

  • Discipline that holds over time: Annual surveillance audits mean this isn’t a one-time claim. As our AI products change, the system that governs them stays under independent review.

AI is changing what people build on Vercel, and we intend for the governance around it to keep pace. We’ll continue to expand the scope of our certifications as our products grow.

title: I built a lightweight Coolify-style PaaS: one Go binary, ~200 MB idle, no Postgres to babysit
description:
I built a lightweight Coolify-style PaaS: one Go binary, ~200 MB idle, no Postgres to babysit

The moment that started this was a small one. I had a 2 GB VPS running a deploy platform and one side project, and the platform used more memory than the project. I was paying for the tool that deploys my app more than for the app.

That is not a knock on any tool. A web app with its own database, cache and proxy is a normal way to build a PaaS. I wanted to see what it looked like with fewer parts. I built Levelrail, an open source (Apache 2.0) deploy platform for your own servers: one Go binary with SQLite inside. This post is what I chose, what it costs, what I measured, and where Coolify is still the better choice.

TL;DR

Question Short answer
What is it One control plane binary, SQLite in WAL mode, embedded Caddy ingress and dashboard
Idle footprint About 200 MB resident on a 2 vCPU, 8 GB test box, no apps under load (docs/benchmarks.md)
How it reaches other servers A small agent dials out to the control plane over mutual TLS, no inbound port on the node
Where Coolify wins Maturity, the size of its community, a wide one-click service catalog, nothing to install on managed servers
Where I am honest Single node is the best tested path, and I have not measured Coolify's idle memory

What "no Postgres to babysit" means

Coolify's installer sets up a main application container, a PostgreSQL container named coolify-db and a Redis container named coolify-redis. <!-- source: https://coolify.io/docs/get-started/installation --> That design makes sense. It also gives your platform its own database to back up, upgrade and watch.

Levelrail keeps desired state, settings, deploy history, audit rows and encrypted secrets in a SQLite file in its data directory, with separate SQLite files for telemetry and alerting to keep their writes away from the main one. Container state is not copied anywhere. Docker is the source of truth for what is running.

The trade is real. SQLite is one writer and many readers, so the control plane is a single process on a single host. For a solo developer or a small team that is fine. For a platform team that wants an external HA database, it is the wrong shape.

The footprint, with the box named

The README says about 200 MB idle. Here is where that comes from. The benchmarks page records a live instance on a 2 vCPU, 8 GB test box with all features at defaults and no apps under load: idle RSS 200 MB, peak 253 MB, 273 goroutines, 1.5 percent CPU. A separate run inside a Linux container on Docker Desktop recorded 212 MB resident at zero apps and 216 MB at five stopped apps.

I also ran the current build for this article on my own Apple M4 Max laptop, started with levelrail-cli dev. Resident memory sat near 200 MB shortly after boot and dropped to about 90 MB eight minutes later, after the runtime returned boot-time garbage to the OS. That machine was busy with other work and I took two readings, so read it as a rough range, not a benchmark.

Two caveats from the performance page matter. The runs use dev builds, and the docs show no bare-metal or cloud VM run yet. Real running apps add probe and metrics load that the idle numbers do not include. I did not measure Coolify's memory use at all. Its docs list 2 cores, 2 GB RAM and 10 GB of disk for the server, and say smaller servers work but are not recommended. <!-- source: https://coolify.io/docs/get-started/installation --> That figure covers the whole server, so it says nothing about the platform's own share, and I will not pretend it does.

An agent that dials out, instead of SSH

Coolify manages each server over SSH from the control plane. <!-- source: https://coolify.io/docs/get-started/introduction --> The upside is real: it works with any server you can log into, with nothing extra installed beyond Docker.

Levelrail runs a node agent instead. It dials out to the control plane over gRPC with mutual TLS and talks to the Docker Engine API directly, so nothing shells out to the docker CLI and managed servers need no inbound port. A new server joins with a single-use token that expires after 15 minutes by default.

The cost is a second binary to run on every extra node. Multi-server is also the less proven path: the docs say single node is where most of the testing happened, and I know of checks for the add-a-node flow only against a real local Docker daemon, not across real cloud providers.

One deploy that fails safely

A lightweight platform still has to do the boring part right. Here is a throwaway test I ran on a local instance. I pushed a Dockerfile app, then pushed a second version that reports unhealthy on /healthz.

levelrail-cli apps health set my-app --probe readiness --path /healthz --interval 5s
# push the commit, then watch deploy history
levelrail-cli apps deploys list my-app

The second version built, started and never became ready. The deploy was recorded as failed with the reason ReadinessFailed and the message readiness probe: never became ready (context deadline exceeded), last attempt: GET /healthz returned 500, expected 200-299. Meanwhile I requested the app every 3 seconds for the whole window and got 200 from the old version each time.

Getting back to an older release is one command:

levelrail-cli apps deploys rollback-to my-app <DEPLOY_ID>

I ran it against the first good deploy and the app went back to serving the old version. Levelrail pins previous images so cleanup cannot remove a rollback target. This ran on my laptop against a local Docker daemon, so there was no DNS, no public TLS and no real network between the pieces.

Side by side

This is architecture, not a ranking. Coolify is the older and larger project.

Coolify Levelrail
Server management SSH from the control plane Agent dials out over mTLS, Docker Engine API
Platform state A PostgreSQL container plus Redis SQLite files in one data directory
Runs as A web application with its own database One control plane binary, one agent binary per extra node
Ingress Traefik, Caddy also offered Caddy embedded in the control plane
Maturity and community Established, large catalog Smaller community and catalog, active development
Third-party servers Any server you can reach over SSH Needs the agent installed

Where Coolify is the better pick

If Coolify already does what you need and your team knows it, stay. It has been around longer, more people have hit its edge cases, and its one-click catalog of maintained Compose templates is large. <!-- source: https://coolify.io/docs/get-started/introduction --> Levelrail ships a catalog too, but the end-to-end suite deploys a sample, not every entry, and I would not claim parity.

Coolify also wins when you want to manage servers you cannot or will not install anything on. SSH only is a genuinely simpler story.

If you are thinking of switching, the importer reads a Coolify instance through its API and changes nothing there. Databases and volumes come across empty, so you copy the data yourself. Start with a dry run:

levelrail-cli import platform coolify --url "$COOLIFY_URL" --dry-run

I did not run the importer for this article, because I have no Coolify instance to point it at. That line comes from the Levelrail docs.

FAQ

Is Levelrail a drop-in replacement for Coolify?

No. The job is the same, deploying apps and databases to your own servers, but the design differs. The importer helps with the move, and the migration guide lists what maps and what does not.

Do I need more than one server?

No. One server is the best tested path. Extra servers join with a one-time token and a small agent.

How do I deploy by pushing code?

Connect GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Gitea and pushes to the branch build and deploy through webhooks. A native git push remote on your own server also exists, but it is off by default and you switch it on in Settings.

Is it free?

Yes. It is Apache 2.0, one edition, with no license key.

What I would watch

The number I care about is not the idle footprint. It is how the same figure looks on a plain 2 GB Linux VPS with ten real apps running, because that is the box this was built for. I have the method to measure it and not yet a published result. If you try it on a small server, I would like to hear what your numbers say.

If this saved you time, a star on the repo helps others find it.

glincker / levelrail

Self-hosted alternative to Vercel and Coolify. Git push, HTTPS, logs, rollback. No Kubernetes.

Levelrail

Your own Vercel, on your own servers.
Push to deploy with HTTPS, logs, metrics and one-step rollback. One Go binary, no Kubernetes. Apache 2.0.

Website · Docs · Install · Compare · FAQ · Roadmap · Discussions

English · 简体中文 · Español · Português (BR) · Deutsch · Français · 日本語


Turn any Linux server into a private cloud: Git deploys, HTTPS, databases with verified backups, metrics, logs and alerts, without Kubernetes and without a monitoring stack to bolt on. Pre-1.0: single-server is production ready, multi-node is beta (Feature status).










200 MB

idle RAM, 1.5% of one CPU
measured, method included

1 binary

Go control plane, Docker runtime
no Kubernetes

360

one-click service templates
smoke-tested

240+

MCP tools for coding agents
scoped, read-only by default

Install

curl -fsSL https://levelrail.com/install.sh | sudo sh

Needs Linux (amd64 or arm64) with systemd and root; the installer adds Docker. Open ports…


View on GitHub


Sources checked

  • https://coolify.io/docs/get-started/introduction (SSH management, deploy sources, ready-made Compose templates)
  • https://coolify.io/docs/get-started/installation (server requirements, coolify-db PostgreSQL and coolify-redis containers)
  • Levelrail repo, release/v1.0.1: docs/performance.md, docs/benchmarks.md, docs/comparison.md, docs/coolify-alternative.md, docs/architecture.md, docs/deploying-apps.md, docs/git-integrations.md, README.md

title: Your Go MJML and Liquid libraries fail on hostile templates. I tested them all.
description:
While auditing the security of Notifuse, a self-hosted email platform I maintain in Go, I asked AI to generate hostile templates and ran them against every MJML library and every Liquid library I could find for the language.

Notifuse users write their own email templates, in MJML for the layout and Liquid for the personalization, and my server compiles whatever they paste in. Anyone with an account can paste in something written to hurt the server.

What broke

One MJML library crashes the whole process when two emails render at the same time. Another turns an escaped " back into a raw quote, so data that was escaped correctly still adds an onclick attribute to the HTML. With 1 MB of inline styles, the libraries that accept the template take between one and five minutes to render it.

For Liquid I used four templates: a loop of a billion iterations, a string doubled 40 times, a billion bytes of output, and 100,000 nested blocks. The Go library whose output is closest to Shopify's has no limits at all, so each of the four runs it out of time or memory. The best of the others stopped three.

The Go MJML libraries didn't match MJML's output well either. The best produced the same HTML as MJML on 82.4% of my test documents, and Outlook punishes anything that drifts from it.

So I wrote two engines

I want both to be the best implementations in the world, in any language: safe-mjml for MJML and liquidgo for Liquid. That is a big claim, and the rest of this post is how I measure it.

safe-mjml is an MJML compiler in pure Go. It started from gomjml, Preslav Rachev's Go port, which gave me a big head start. Version 1.1 follows MJML 5.4.1 and writes identical HTML on 99.3% of 8,093 test documents. Most of the remaining differences are on purpose, such as MJML writing NaN as a width.

For hostile templates, a panic comes back as an error. Nesting depth is limited, the HTML output is capped at 16 MB, and attribute values are always escaped.

liquidgo is a port of Shopify's Ruby gem, done file by file so that each Shopify release can be carried over. It stops all four hostile templates, as Shopify's own gem does, and a template never reads your Go values by reflection. Its output is identical to Shopify Liquid's on 94.2% of 963 templates, and the rest are differences I chose and wrote down. A newsletter template that loops over 50 products renders in 53 µs, against 368 µs for Shopify Liquid on Ruby 3.3 with YJIT.

Try them 

go get github.com/Notifuse/safe-mjml/mjml
go get github.com/Notifuse/liquidgo/v5

Both are MIT licensed and pure Go.

Where this runs: Notifuse 44

Both engines render every email in Notifuse 44, which came out on November 19. It is the largest release so far, with 194 changelog entries. I rebuilt almost every screen of the console on a new design system, and the editor now writes MJML 5. The release post has the screenshots.

There is a live demo, and the code is on GitHub. If one of your templates makes safe-mjml or liquidgo disagree with the reference implementation, open an issue with it and I'll fix it.

title: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard to compare models on quality, speed, and cost
description:
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart now offers a model leaderboard in Amazon SageMaker Studio. You can use it to compare foundation models side by side on throughput, latency, and cost, and then deploy or customize the model that fits your workload.

Comparing models has usually meant reading model cards one at a time and relying on benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. The JumpStart leaderboard puts consistent measurements in one view. AWS evaluates every model on three reasoning benchmarks, BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro, using the same evaluation setup for each model. AWS also measures time to first token, throughput, and instance cost on SageMaker for each JumpStart deployment configuration. You can use all of the filters already available for JumpStart models, such as model provider, license, and input and output modality, to narrow the list. You can also choose a use case profile and an optimization goal (balanced, cost, latency, or throughput) to see the metrics for the configuration you plan to deploy. At launch, the leaderboard covers more than 70 LLMs from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee.

The JumpStart model leaderboard is available at no additional charge in all AWS commercial Regions where Amazon SageMaker Studio is available. title: Calibrating 1σ Error Bars for Mountain Snow Forecasts (6 NWP Models + USDA SNOTEL)
description:
As everyone in AI jokes right now, open = close. By symmetry, close = open.

After enough ski friends nudged me, I built CloseSnow (close-snow.clifan.com), a 100% free, zero-paywall 15-day mountain snow forecaster covering all 120 Ikon and Epic Pass resorts.

Why single-number snow bars lie

Most snow apps show a single crisp integer on every day of a 10- or 15-day chart. To a skier planning PTO, 8" on Wednesday and 8" next Thursday look identical. Physically, they aren't even the same species of number:

  1. Snow-to-liquid ratio (SLR) swings 4× across storms. Half an inch of liquid water (0.50" SWE) falling through a saturated -15°C dendritic growth zone in Little Cottonwood Canyon stacks up to 9" of cold smoke (18:1 SLR). That same 0.50" SWE in a 31°F atmospheric river at Palisades Tahoe settles into 4" of sierra cement (8:1), or turns to rain at base lodge elevation.
  2. Ensemble spread explodes with lead time and marginal temperatures. At Day 2, high-resolution convection-allowing models like NOAA HRRR (3 km) and NBM v4.2 often agree within an inch. By Day 9, or whenever wet-bulb temperature sits within 1.5°C of freezing, global models routinely span 0" to 14". Hiding that variance behind a single mean tricks people into chasing phantom storms.

What CloseSnow computes instead

CloseSnow pulls live pressure-level profiles (850, 700, 600, 500 hPa) across six NWP models—NOAA HRRR 3km, NBM v4.2, ECMWF IFS 9km, ECMWF AI AIFS, DWD ICON, and GFS 16-day—at Base, Mid-Mountain, and Summit elevations for 120 resorts:

  • 3D Cobb/Alcott microphysics: Weights vertical motion through the -12°C to -18°C dendritic growth zone, penalizes 50+ mph ridge-top wind riming, and applies resort-specific 700 hPa canyon alignment multipliers.
  • Color-matched ±1σ I-beam error bars: Every bar displays a calibrated ±1σ range (5 ± 1", 7 ± 3", 6 ± 4"). Uncertainty grows monotonically with lead time and 0°C wet-bulb phase risk while staying physically non-negative.
  • Live USDA SNOTEL ground truth: 41 US mountain resorts pair directly with hourly USDA NRCS SNOTEL ultrasonic snow-pillow telemetry so you can check what actually fell over the past 15 days.

Out-of-sample SNOTEL & HRRR backtest

Before sharing it publicly, I evaluated the model out-of-sample (live Accuracy Lab):

  • Atmospheric sounding test (N = 7,863 held-out HRRR 3km soundings, 2,829 mountain events ≥1,500m, trained strictly on 31,178 ERA5 soundings): CloseSnow reached 3.23 SLR MAE on mountain snow events, compared to 3.91 for Kuchera, 5.12 for OpenSnow's temperature heuristic, and 5.43 for fixed 10:1.
  • Real 48-hour mountain storms (N = 221 held-out USDA SNOTEL storm cycles from Jan 16 – Apr 15, 2025 across 20 Ikon/Epic resorts):
    • CloseSnow ($0): 2.37" MAE (52.9% within ±2", 72.4% empirical ±1σ storm coverage)
    • Bergfex / MeteoBlue Pro ($25/yr): 3.21" MAE
    • OpenSnow ($49.99–$99.99/yr): 4.01" MAE
    • pow.fyi / Fixed 10:1 ($0): 4.14" MAE

Honest scope limits

Extended Days 11–15 reflect synoptic storm-window probabilities across ECMWF IFS, AI AIFS, and GFS rather than exact inch counts—which is why their ±1σ whiskers stretch wide. Also, SNOTEL snow pillows cover 41 US mountain resorts and sit in sheltered clearings; non-US resorts use Open-Meteo reanalysis for past-15-day history.

It is a solo, zero-ad, zero-login public-good build. Expect rough edges and bugs—if you spot a resort with weird canyon physics or mobile layout quirks, send feedback my way. Fixes ship between laps.

  • Live App: https://close-snow.clifan.com/
  • Overview & Architecture: https://clifan.com/close-snow/
  • Live Accuracy Lab: https://close-snow.clifan.com/?view=methodology

title: Apache Tomcat security flaw allows unauthorized access between servers
description:
CVE-2026-133325 affects Apache Tomcat cluster communication: with TLS 1.3 and a pre-shared key, a remote unauthenticated party could join a trusted cluster.

The affected releases are 11.0.28–11.0.29, 10.1.62 and 9.0.124.

Fixes are forthcoming; the stated workaround is TLS 1.2 for server-to-server communication.

How the problem works

In many cases, multiple servers work together to exchange data and manage user connections. To keep this exchange secure, the servers use special digital keys.

The issue occurs when servers are configured to communicate with each other using a specific version of the TLS 1.3 protocol, which relies on pre-shared keys. In this case, the system doesn't properly verify the identity of the other server. So, someone who shouldn't have access can pose as a trusted partner and infiltrate the group.

Which versions are affected?

The issue was discovered by researcher Mike Read and affects the following versions of the software:

  • 11.0.28 and 11.0.29
  • 10.1.62
  • 9.0.124

It is important to clarify that the problem only affects communication between the team's servers and not simple visitor connections via HTTPS.

What administrators need to know

There are no reports of the vulnerability being used in actual attacks so far, and it is also not confirmed whether accessing the server cluster would allow an attacker to execute code on the system.

title: When and How Much to Imagine: Adaptive Test-Time Scaling with World Models for Visual Spatial Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2602.08236v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Despite rapid progress in MLLMs, visual spatial reasoning remains unreliable when correct answers depend on how a scene would appear under unseen or alternative viewpoints. Recent work addresses this by augmenting reasoning with world models for visual imagination, but questions such as when imagination is actually necessary, how much of it is beneficial, and when it becomes harmful, remain poorly understood. In practice, indiscriminate imagination can increase computation and even degrade performance by introducing misleading evidence. In this work, we present an in-depth analysis of test-time visual imagination as a controllable resource for spatial reasoning. We first study when static visual evidence is sufficient, when imagination improves reasoning, and how excessive or unnecessary imagination affects accuracy and efficiency. To support this analysis, we then introduce AVIC, an adaptive test-time framework with world models that explicitly reasons about the sufficiency of current visual evidence before selectively invoking and scaling visual imagination. Finally, to further learn this gating and planning behavior without any annotation of when and how much to imagine, we introduce AVIC-R, which trains the policy via GRPO from QA-correctness rewards and penalties by imagination cost. Across spatial reasoning benchmarks (SAT, MMSI) and an embodied navigation benchmark (R2R), our results reveal clear scenarios where imagination is critical, marginal, or detrimental, and show that selective control can match or outperform fixed imagination strategies with substantially fewer world-model calls and language tokens. Our AVIC-R surpasses strong proprietary baselines including GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 while invoking the world model less often. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of analyzing and controlling test-time imagination for efficient and reliable spatial reasoning.

title: 8 Proptech Software Development Companies, Compared on Data Normalization
description:
Every proptech demo looks the same: a clean property card, a map, a filter panel. The engineering is in what the demo skips, normalizing property data pulled from an MLS feed, a county assessor export, and a legacy internal system that disagree on field names, units, and sometimes basic facts like whether a den counts as a bedroom. Bad data here doesn't throw an error. It shows up six months later as a wrong valuation, a duplicate listing, or a compliance report that doesn't reconcile, and by then nobody remembers which source fed it.

The six signals behind the shortlist

The source article scores vendors on a PropTech Depth Test, with an inclusion bar of 5 of 6 signals. Weights are in brackets:

  1. Named client or product (20%): a real, checkable deployment, not a service page.
  2. Problem-type match (20%): MLS integration, property management, and valuation modeling are different builds.
  3. Operational-change quote (15%): a before-and-after number, not "improved efficiency."
  4. Published, readable proof (15%): a case study or client reference you can verify.
  5. Post-launch continuity (15%): does the team stay after deployment?
  6. Data and integration depth (15%): has the vendor normalized data across several source systems, or only built against one clean feed? Signal 6 is the one worth testing in a technical interview, because it's invisible in a demo built on curated sample data. Brocoders wrote the source and left itself out of the scoring, so it appears below as an unranked disclosure, followed by the seven scored vendors.

What data normalization has to do

The pattern that holds up is one schema adapter per source, each mapping that source's quirks into a canonical property schema, with validation before anything reaches the database:

const sourceAdapters = {
  mls_reso: (raw) => ({
    address: raw.UnparsedAddress,
    bedrooms: raw.BedroomsTotal,
    sqft: raw.LivingArea,
    sourceId: raw.ListingId,
  }),
  county_assessor: (raw) => ({
    address: normalizeAddress(raw.property_address),
    bedrooms: raw.bedroom_count ?? null,      // often missing entirely
    sqft: convertToSqft(raw.building_area, raw.area_unit),
    sourceId: raw.parcel_number,
  }),
};

function ingest(source, rawRecord) {
  const adapter = sourceAdapters[source];
  if (!adapter) return reject(rawRecord, "unregistered_source");
  const normalized = adapter(rawRecord);
  const errors = validateCanonicalSchema(normalized);
  if (errors.length) return quarantine(normalized, errors); // don't silently insert bad data
  return canonicalStore.upsert(normalized, { idempotencyKey: `${source}:${normalized.sourceId}` });
}

The quarantine step matters as much as the adapter. A record that fails validation should stop and get flagged, not land with nulls that look like real data three queries later. RESO's Data Dictionary is the closest thing this space has to a shared standard, and a vendor who builds against it directly has already solved a chunk of the problem.

All eight at a glance

Company Founded Clutch Hourly Min. project Best for
Brocoders (unranked) 2014 5.0 (40) Not stated Not stated Multi-tenant platforms scaling past a pilot
MEV 2006 Not yet rated $45 to $85 $10,000+ RESO-certified MLS modernization
Django Stars 2008 4.9 (60) $50 to $99 $50,000+ Compliance-heavy valuation engines
Taazaa 2007 4.9 (28) $50 to $99 $10,000+ US legacy property management modernization
Clockwise Software 2014 4.9 (23) $50 to $99 $50,000+ Property management and deal-tracking platforms
Ascendix Technologies 1996 4.9 (15) $50 to $99 Not published CRE brokerages on Salesforce
Goji Labs 2014 4.8 (84) $100 to $149 $50,000+ Early-stage marketplace validation
Inoxoft 2014 5.0 (74) $25 to $49 $10,000+ Tenant and amenity apps

Compiled as of Q3 2026. Rates, headcounts, and delivery metrics are vendor-reported and not independently verified, so confirm current figures directly.

Eight vendors, evaluated on data depth and delivery record

1. Brocoders (unranked)

Stack: Node.js, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, AWS
Best for: proptech platforms where data has to scale from a pilot dataset to tens of thousands of properties without a rebuild

Brocoders treats multi-tenant architecture as a default and runs full-stack delivery with its own DevOps, no outsourced infra. Tallinn, 2014, 87 engineers, Clutch 5.0 across 40 reviews. Internal tooling at bcboilerplates.com covers auth and tenancy scaffolding so engineering time goes into the normalization layer.

Technical note: Lake, a vacation rental marketplace, had its WordPress monolith rebuilt in three months, and connected properties grew from about 500 to 40,000. That 80x only holds if ingestion was designed for the scale before it arrived. Also CondoGenie (550+ associations, 80,000+ registered users), a C.I.A. Services PWA on a third-party property management API, and AreaButler's location data work, including AI-generated descriptions.

2. MEV

Stack: RESO- and OData-compliant Web API, RETS legacy migration, IDX integration
Best for: MLS-integrated platforms where standards compliance isn't optional

San Diego, 2006, $45 to $85/hr, no Clutch reviews yet.

Technical note: the Hawaii Information Service platform holds 600,000+ properties across 300+ data fields, on a rebuilt search engine and a RESO/OData Web API that earned RESO Data Dictionary 2.0 certification. The source reports a zero-downtime, no-data-loss cutover with the legacy system live throughout, though no timeline is given. Two cautions: with no reviews, nothing is independently checkable, and the published quote comes from a hotel revenue software firm, not the MLS client.

3. Django Stars

Stack: Python, with GDPR and PCI-DSS compliance work
Best for: platforms proving a data-heavy product survives growth

Wilmington DE with engineering in Europe, 2008, 60 Clutch reviews at 4.9.

Technical note: Scoperty, a German valuation and search platform backed by ING Ventures, lists 35M+ properties, and the team grew from 1 engineer in 2018 to 14 in 2022. Also MoneyPark, a Swiss mortgage platform later acquired by Helvetia Group for CHF 107M. The portfolio leans fintech-adjacent.

4. Taazaa

Stack: .NET 2 to .NET 8, data warehouses, two-week sprints
Best for: platforms where bad data is costing operational time today

US-based, 2007, 28 Clutch reviews at 4.9.

Technical note: Tropicana Properties inherited a failed .NET 2 codebase managing 40 apartment complexes, and Taazaa migrated it to .NET 8. Monthly tenant account corrections fell from 60 to 15 to 20, roughly a 70% reduction and a direct measure of how much bad data used to get through. The source says this was done without downtime. Innago saw 150% business growth after a data warehouse and no-code support portal, with no timeline given.

5. Clockwise Software

Stack: not stated
Best for: property management and deal-tracking platforms that pull data in by API

Edinburgh, 2014, about 80 people, 23 Clutch reviews at 4.9, $50,000+ minimum.

Technical note: StoneBay, a US land-parcel deal management and analytics platform, automates data gathering through API connections and ships as white-label SaaS. That's the multi-source ingestion problem in miniature, though no figures are published. Propa, a UK landlord platform, went from iOS-only to web and Android, adding e-signed tenancy agreements, open-banking rent collection, and a tenant portal. Clockwise's own metrics (under 10% cost and timeline variance, 99.89% acceptance) are unverified, and a $50,000 starting budget plus limited capacity for several large parallel teams are the stated limits.

6. Ascendix Technologies

Stack: Salesforce, plus its own AscendixRE, Composer, and Marketspace products
Best for: commercial real estate on Salesforce

Dallas, 1996, 15 Clutch reviews at 4.9, $50 to $99/hr.

Technical note: 30 years in CRE means the data models already handle commercial lease structures that residential-first platforms bolt on later. Long-term Salesforce partner to JLL and builder of a product platform for Colliers International, with no figures for either. CRE-only focus and 15 reviews limit verification.

7. Goji Labs

Stack: not stated
Best for: teams that need product discovery before committing to a data architecture

Los Angeles, 2014, roughly 70 people, 84 Clutch reviews at 4.8, $100 to $149/hr, $50,000+ minimum.

Technical note: built Gitcha, a three-sided marketplace for buyers, sellers, and agents, and the source reports faster closings with no figures. Discovery-first matters here because a canonical schema chosen too early is expensive to unwind once several source adapters depend on it. The testimonial is attributed to the Gitcha team, not a named person.

8. Inoxoft

Stack: not stated, ISO 27001 certified, Microsoft Gold Partner
Best for: proptech builds touching regulated or sensitive user data

Philadelphia US office, 2014, 230 people, 74 Clutch reviews at 5.0, $25 to $49/hr, $10,000+ minimum.

Technical note: an amenity booking system for a luxury operator with 70+ buildings replaced manual calls and spreadsheets for thousands of residents, plus a buy, sell, and rent platform with a client portal for a US firm. Neither client is named and neither case carries an executive quote, which is the one signal the source says Inoxoft misses. The 100,000+ users claim is unverified.

What proptech development costs

Scope Range Includes
MVP, one user type $40K to $90K Core workflows, design, QA, launch
Standard platform, 2 to 3 user types $90K to $200K Full flows, integrations, payments, admin panel
Complex multi-tenant SaaS $200K+ Multi-tenant architecture, compliance, APIs, mobile

US and Western European agencies run $80 to $150/hr, and Eastern Europe and the Baltics $35 to $80/hr. A European team gives 4 to 6 hours of overlap with US time zones instead of a full day.

Engineering checklist before you sign

  • Source adapter pattern: is each source mapped through its own adapter into a canonical schema, or hardcoded per integration?
  • Validation before insert: is bad data quarantined and flagged, or written with nulls?
  • RESO or equivalent standard: does the vendor build against an industry standard, or a one-off schema?
  • Idempotent ingestion: can the same source record be re-ingested without duplicates?
  • Data lineage: can you trace a record back to its source and sync run?
  • Live cutover evidence: has the vendor moved a running system, with downtime stated?
  • Multi-tenant isolation: if the platform serves several owners or agencies, is their data separated? If you're evaluating proptech vendors and want a second technical opinion on whether their data pipeline is built for multi-source reality, brocoders.com is a reasonable place to start that conversation.

title: Migrate legacy code to Rust incrementally - rust-anything
description:
TL;DR: rust-anything sits alongside your existing codebase in TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby, or Java to facilitate a gradual migration to Rust. It operates by capturing inputs, return values, and thrown errors from the original implementation during automated test runs.
Best for: Developers migrating performance-critical legacy code or whole apps to Rust without breaking existing behavior.
Repository snapshot: ⭐ 5 212 stars · 🍴 417 forks · Rust · MIT
Daily picks: Follow GitHub Open Source on Telegram

What it is

rust-anything is an open-source development tool designed to facilitate the gradual migration of legacy codebases written in languages like TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby, or Java into pure Rust. Instead of a risky, all-at-once rewrite, it enables developers to port applications component by component while guaranteeing identical behavior.

How it works

The tool operates by capturing inputs, return values, and thrown errors from your original implementation during automated test runs. This creates a rigorous behavioral baseline. Developers or AI coding agents then write the Rust equivalent. Using differential replaying, thousands of recorded test cases are executed against the new Rust port to verify identical outputs before lifting the component into a standalone binary.

Key features

  • Record original application behavior on edge cases to establish a reliable baseline
  • Bridge generated Rust crates with wrappers so callers retain the original API structure
  • Replay thousands of recorded test cases against the Rust port to verify identical outputs
  • Profile codebases to identify hot paths and loops worth moving out of interpreted runtimes
  • Lift fully verified components and dependencies into a standalone pure Rust application

Getting started

Clone the repository from GitHub to begin your migration journey. Ensure you have Rust and your source language's runtime installed. Follow the documentation in the repository to start capturing test baselines for your specific project.

When not to use it

Do not use this tool if you are looking for an automated code translator; you still have to write the Rust code yourself. It is also unnecessary for greenfield projects or very small scripts where a total rewrite from scratch is faster and simpler.

Discuss

Which hot path in your current stack would you rewrite in Rust first?

title: Improving On-board Shape Models Using Sun Sensors and Implicit Representations
description:
arXiv:2611.24976v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We propose an original, end-to-end approach to generate and refine the onboard 3D shape model of irregular small bodies, such as asteroids, using only low-cost Sun sensor eclipse data and coarse a priori knowledge, tailored for resource-constrained missions like CubeSats. Leveraging EclipseNets, a differentiable neural model of eclipse boundaries, our pipeline first refines 2D silhouettes by learning from real-time entry and exit events during spacecraft orbits, avoiding the limitations of traditional imaging or lidar in bandwidth-starved environments. These silhouettes then supervise a compact neural signed-distance field with periodic activations, enabling incremental updates to a high-fidelity implicit geometry representation capable of capturing fine-scale features and concavities. In simulations of the body Eros under realistic orbital dynamics, the method increases silhouette IoU from 0.70 to 0.87 and produces coherent 3D reconstructions, suggesting our approach could find a place in future autonomous architectures for small-body exploration.

title: {\phi}TD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions
description:
arXiv:2611.25208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.

title: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance
description:
arXiv:2611.23572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.

title: Connect MCP servers in one click, and keep working when a sign-in expires
description:
Connecting a tool to your agent should take one click, not a hunt for an API key. In Atlarix 15.19 it does.

One click, with a name you recognise

When an MCP server supports sign-in, pressing Connect opens its consent screen in your browser. The screen names Atlarix and shows its logo, so you know what you're approving. Approve it, and the server's tools are ready in the chat. This works in the desktop app, the CLI, VS Code, Zed and JetBrains.

Some servers accept either a sign-in or an API key. Atlarix now offers the sign-in first, and keeps "Use an API key instead" one click away for when you need it.

A sign-in that expires mid-task no longer ends the task

Sign-ins expire. Before, a refused token ended the task with the server's error, and you started again. Now Atlarix pauses and asks you to reconnect:

  • in the app, a card in the chat: Reconnect, Save key, Open settings, or Go on without it;
  • in the CLI and the editors, a Reconnect prompt.

Reconnect, and the task carries on from where it stopped. A server that simply drops its connection reconnects on its own, without asking.

Try it

Update Atlarix, open Integrations → MCP servers (or type /mcp in the CLI), and connect a server marked Verified.

title: Java4Shell: What OpenJDK Teams Need to Know About CVE-2026-114938
description:
A malformed Base64 value can do more than make a Java decoder reject input. On some x86-64 systems, it can trigger a memory write beyond the intended array. That is the core of CVE-2026-114938, the OpenJDK flaw being called Java4Shell.

Red Hat reports pre-authentication RCE demonstrations against some widely deployed applications, while Calif.io explains that reliable exploitation depends on an application-specific chain. This is serious, but not one exploit that works against every Java service.

What is vulnerable?

The flaw sits in an optimized Base64 decoding path in HotSpot, OpenJDK's virtual machine. Base64 turns binary data into text and is often used to carry credentials and certificate data through text-based systems.

In certain supported configurations, HotSpot replaces part of the Java decoder with a faster native routine. This routine can use AVX-512 VBMI instructions available on some x86-64 processors. Calif.io's technical analysis describes a length calculation error when the decoder handles a short final input fragment with invalid padding. The calculated output size can become negative. The native routine then builds a write mask from that value without checking that it is valid, allowing the write to pass the end of the destination array.

That is a memory-safety bug inside the runtime, not simply a bad input-validation rule in one application. An application may catch the decoder's exception and still have memory corrupted before the exception is raised.

The exposure is conditional

A vulnerable Java version alone does not tell you whether a specific service can trigger the flaw. Calif.io's analysis identifies several conditions that matter:

  • The service uses an affected Java runtime.
  • It runs on x86-64 hardware with AVX-512 VBMI support and enters the vulnerable decoder path.
  • Attacker-controlled data reaches the relevant Base64 decoder without being rejected or transformed first.

Review endpoints that pass untrusted data to java.util.Base64.Decoder; confirm the exact runtime build and CPU support.

Affected-version lists differ because notices cover different vendors. OpenJDK names the 17/21 and 25/27 lines; Red Hat says its OpenJDK 8/11 lines lack the path, while Oracle's CVE-specific entry has separate scope. Check the exact vendor advisory for your runtime.

Why the severity numbers differ

The CVE record lists 8.1 under CVSS 3.1. Calif.io reports 9.2 under CVSS 4.0. These scores use different scoring systems and are not directly comparable. Neither score replaces checking the JDK and CPU capabilities, then confirming whether attacker-controlled input reaches the decoder.

Oracle's quarterly patch covers many products; a version appearing in that broad list does not mean every CVE affects it. Check the vendor's exact CVE entry.

What Java teams should do

First, find the runtime each production process actually uses. Check application containers, vendor appliances, build agents, application servers, and Java runtimes bundled with products. The java command on an administrator's shell may not be the runtime used by a running service.

Check the JVM and CPU inside the container

Run these checks inside the same container that runs the Java service. If the image has more than one JDK, use the runtime binary that the service starts.

java -version 2>&1
grep -o avx512vbmi /proc/cpuinfo | head -1
jcmd <PID> VM.flags

The first command prints the runtime vendor and full build. The second scans the CPU flags visible to the container for AVX-512 VBMI. If it prints avx512vbmi, the hardware requirement is present. If it prints nothing, no CPU visible to the container reports that feature and the hardware prerequisite is absent. Seeing avx512f, avx512bw, or bmi2 without avx512vbmi does not meet the stated VBMI condition.

If jcmd is available in the image and can attach to the process, substitute the Java process ID for <PID>; this reports flags for the running JVM. Otherwise, inspect that process's startup arguments. A separate java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version invocation reports flags for a new JVM, not necessarily the service process. UseAVX=3 and UseBASE64Intrinsics=true do not prove that the CPU exposes AVX-512 VBMI.

Treat the runtime as potentially exposed only when all four conditions hold: the exact vendor build is affected and unpatched; the JVM runs on x86-64 and avx512vbmi is visible; its active UseAVX setting is not 2 or lower; and attacker-controlled Base64 reaches java.util.Base64.Decoder. Red Hat documents these conditions and the CPU check in its CVE-2026-114938 bulletin.

For Kubernetes, check each Java container and every node pool where its pod may be scheduled. A pod can move to a node with a different CPU feature set. This is a Java runtime vulnerability, not a Kubernetes control-plane flaw.

Apply the fix

Use the full runtime version and vendor to choose the fix. Amazon's Corretto 21 changelog lists version 21.0.13.1.2, released November 17, 2026, as addressing CVE-2026-114938. Corretto 21.0.13.0.11 predates that release. For Amazon Linux 2023, AWS lists package build 21.0.13.1.2 in advisory ALAS2023-2026-3479 and gives this update command:

dnf update java-21-amazon-corretto --releasever 2023.12.20261117

For a container, apply the package update in the image build. Other base images and JDK vendors may use different package versions, so verify the exact CVE advisory before changing the image.

Rebuild the image and roll out new pods. Restarting a process does not replace an old runtime inside an unchanged image. After deployment, run the same checks again and confirm the new build is active in every replica.

If a fixed build is not yet available, Red Hat recommends the temporary JVM option -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. It disables the affected accelerated Base64 path. On x86-64 only, -XX:UseAVX=2 is another option, but it also disables AVX-512 for other JVM work and can reduce performance. Do not use UseAVX=2 on ARM64. Apply a workaround at JVM startup, restart the process, and remove it after installing a fixed runtime.

The useful lesson in Java4Shell

Inventory the runtime build, CPU features, and untrusted Base64 paths. Patch and verify every deployed replica, but do not assume all Java services are equally exposed.

Sources

  • Datadog Security Labs: Java4Shell analysis
  • OpenJDK Vulnerability Group: November 17, 2026 advisory
  • Red Hat: Java4Shell security bulletin and affected conditions
  • Calif.io: Java4Shell technical analysis
  • Amazon Corretto 21 changelog
  • Amazon Linux 2023 advisory ALAS2023-2026-3479
  • Oracle JDK 21 jcmd reference
  • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: Oracle Java alert
  • CVE Program record for CVE-2026-114938
  • New Zealand NCSC: CVE-2026-114938 alert
  • UC Berkeley: Java security update notice
  • Oracle: November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update
