title: VisAlloc: Allocating Visual Supervision for On-Policy Self-Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.25069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising approach to improving visual reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, not all samples benefit equally from privileged visual guidance, and uniform token supervision can dilute visually grounded signals. We propose VisAlloc, a dual-level framework combining sample-level visual filtering with token-level counterfactual reweighting. A fixed paired-teacher filter retains samples answered correctly from an evidence-centered positive crop but incorrectly from a spatially displaced negative crop. At the token level, both EMA teachers score the same student-generated response, and their absolute log-probability differences measure view sensitivity. Additional supervision targets tokens admitted by sensitivity or teacher-distribution disagreement, with shared frozen-prior, template-bigram, and student--teacher divergence gates. Inverse-frequency redistribution preserves the total additional weight within each micro-batch, while the positive teacher remains the sole distillation target. Inference requires only the full-image student. Across eight benchmarks, our 4B and 9B models achieve macro-averages of 81.44 and 84.92, outperforming Vision-OPD reproductions by 0.97 and 0.52 points, respectively. Code on GitHub: https://github.com/Kaelyn01/VisAlloc

title: Traditional Data Warehouse vs Modern Data Platform: What’s the Difference?
description:
Traditional data warehouses have supported business reporting for decades. However, growing data volumes, changing reporting requirements and the rapid adoption of AI are exposing the limitations of older architectures.


A Modern Data Platform provides a more flexible way to bring together structured, semi-structured and unstructured data across databases, business applications, cloud services and other systems. The result is a scalable, governed foundation for reporting, analytics and AI.


The infographic below compares the infrastructure, processing and operational requirements of a traditional data warehouse with a Modern Data Platform.



Traditional data warehouses remain effective, but can be costly to operate


A traditional data warehouse generally collects structured data from selected source systems, transforms it through ETL processes and loads it into a central database for reporting. This model remains suitable for stable, structured reporting requirements. However, it can become harder and more expensive to maintain as data volumes, sources and business needs grow.


Common challenges include:


Database, operating system and ETL licensing costs
Separate compute, storage and backup infrastructure
Significant database and infrastructure support requirements
High data engineering effort when sources or reports change
Duplication of data across different systems
Limited support for unstructured data
Additional platforms and processing required for AI

These dependencies can increase operational overhead and make it harder for organisations to respond quickly to new reporting, analytics and AI requirements.


How a Modern Data Platform changes the model


A Modern Data Platform separates storage, processing and consumption into flexible components that can scale according to demand. Raw data from databases, SaaS applications, files, APIs, sensors and cloud environments can be brought into a central data lake. Automated pipelines then clean, organise and prepare the data for reporting, analytics or AI applications.


This approach can provide:


Support for structured and unstructured data
Scalable cloud-based storage and processing
Reusable, automated data pipelines
Reduced dependency on database and infrastructure specialists
Centralised data governance and platform management
More efficient integration of new data sources
A trusted data foundation for analytics and AI
Greater visibility and control over data platform costs

The exact benefits depend on the platform architecture, workloads, governance model and existing technology environment.


Traditional Data Warehouse vs Modern Data Platform

Does a Modern Data Platform replace your data warehouse?


Not necessarily and here's why - a Modern Data Platform does not require an organisation to discard every existing database or reporting system. In many cases, the best approach is to retain valuable systems while gradually modernising the way data is collected, governed, processed and used.


The right architecture may combine:


Existing operational databases
A cloud-based data lake or lakehouse
Automated ingestion and transformation pipelines
A data warehouse for structured reporting
Business intelligence and visualisation tools
Governance, security and data quality controls
Private AI or machine-learning capabilities

Modernisation can therefore be delivered progressively, based on business priorities, platform risks and the value of each use case.


When should you consider modernising?


It may be time to review your data architecture if:


Reports take too long to produce
Teams rely on manual spreadsheet consolidation
Different departments report conflicting figures
Data is trapped across disconnected systems
Licensing and infrastructure costs continue to rise
Platform changes require significant engineering work
The organisation lacks confidence in data quality
Existing data cannot be used safely or effectively for AI

Build a trusted foundation for reporting, analytics and AI


Blue Crystal Solutions helps Australian organisations assess, design, implement and manage Modern Data Platforms across cloud and hybrid environments.


We bring together experience across databases, cloud infrastructure, data engineering, managed services and Private AI to help you modernise without losing control of your critical systems or information.


Whether you need to replace a costly legacy data warehouse, improve reporting or prepare trusted data for AI, we can help you determine the most practical path forward.


Talk to a Modern Data Platform specialist


Join our webinar on 30 September at 1:00 PM ACST


to dive deeper into the topic and gain practical insights.


.....................


Frequently asked questions


What is a Modern Data Platform?
A Modern Data Platform is an integrated architecture for collecting, storing, processing, governing and analysing data from multiple sources. It can support business intelligence, advanced analytics, automation and AI across cloud or hybrid environments.

What is the difference between a data warehouse and a Modern Data Platform?


A data warehouse is primarily designed to store structured, processed data for reporting. A Modern Data Platform supports a broader range of data types and workloads, potentially incorporating data lakes, lakehouses, warehouses, automated pipelines, governance, analytics and AI services.

Is a Modern Data Platform cheaper than a traditional data warehouse?


It can reduce database licensing, fixed infrastructure and operational support costs, but savings depend on platform design and usage. Cloud consumption, data movement, storage growth and poorly governed workloads can still create unnecessary costs.

Can a Modern Data Platform use our existing databases?


Yes. Existing Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL and other databases can remain operational data sources. Information from these systems can be integrated into a Modern Data Platform without requiring an immediate full replacement.

How does a Modern Data Platform support AI?


It brings data together, applies quality and governance controls, and makes trusted datasets available for AI applications. This helps reduce the risk of AI producing answers from incomplete, inconsistent or unauthorised information.

title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior
description:
arXiv:2611.25109v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.

title: Z-Erase: Enabling Concept Erasure in Single-Stream Diffusion Transformers
description:
arXiv:2603.25074v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Concept erasure serves as a vital safety mechanism for removing unwanted concepts from text-to-image (T2I) models. While extensively studied in U-Net and dual-stream architectures (e.g., Flux), this task remains under-explored in the recent emerging paradigm of single-stream diffusion transformers (e.g., Z-Image). In this new paradigm, text and image tokens are processed as a single unified sequence via shared parameters. Consequently, directly applying prior erasure methods typically leads to generation collapse. To bridge this gap, we introduce Z-Erase, the first concept erasure method tailored for single-stream T2I models. To guarantee stable image generation, Z-Erase first proposes a Stream Disentangled Concept Erasure Framework that decouples updates and enables existing methods on single-stream models. Subsequently, within this framework, we introduce Lagrangian-Guided Adaptive Erasure Modulation, a constrained algorithm that further balances the sensitive erasure-preservation trade-off. Moreover, we provide a rigorous convergence analysis proving that Z-Erase can converge to a Pareto stationary point. Experiments demonstrate that Z-Erase successfully overcomes the generation collapse issue, achieving state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of tasks.

title: Node.js App Logging Explained: Error Tracking and Metrics for Recovery
description:
For a nightly property-management import, use app logging to reconstruct retries, error tracking to group failures, and metrics to follow production trends; preserve the logical job identity before adding another dashboard.

TL;DR: Use application logging to reconstruct what happened, error tracking to group exceptions, and metrics to follow rates and latency. A beginner Node.js SaaS needs those distinct responsibilities, plus a separate heartbeat check for a job that never starts. For cost attribution, connect each attempt to the property portfolio and logical import before trying to explain which recovery activity consumed resources.

An exception count cannot tell an operator which portfolio needs a replay. A searchable log cannot establish that a silent scheduler is healthy. Those are different questions, even if one interface displays their answers together.

Decision: keep recovery evidence attached to the import

Consider an illustrative nightly pipeline that imports property records, with a stable run identifier and a fresh attempt identifier whenever work is retried. The operational question is specific: which structured records explain the failed attempt, and which additional work belongs to recovery rather than the original import? That question drives the design more usefully than a contest over dashboard appearance.

Keep the boundaries explicit.

The import owns its business idempotency: repeating the same logical operation must not apply the same property update twice. The logging layer records evidence of those attempts. Error tracking groups exceptions so an operator can distinguish recurring failures from isolated ones, while metrics expose changes in completion rates and latency over time. None of those signals, by itself, proves that the destination data is durable or that every update committed; make the destination's commit boundary an explicit part of the pipeline design.

For a small property-management SaaS that wants logs, error capture, and metrics behind one service contract, try Infrai for that instrumentation layer: its 295 routes across 20 modules share one key, so adding another backend capability can reuse the same integration contract. Its consistent per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata provides a second reason to evaluate it here, because those records can support attribution when the application joins them to a portfolio and run.

That join is your responsibility. Per-call metadata does not automatically become a complete portfolio cost ledger, and the cost of emitting a log record is a different accounting item from the cost of the import operation described by that record.

How should a beginner use app logging, error tracking, and metrics during recovery?

Use three identities in the application event design: a portfolio identifier, a logical run identifier, and an attempt identifier. Give each emitted event its own stable identifier as well. These are proposed application fields, not a claim about any vendor's ingestion schema. Keep resident names, addresses, and lease contents out of this recovery example; opaque identifiers are enough to demonstrate the correlation.

Here is the trap: deduplicating by logical run alone erases the distinction between an original attempt and its replay, while treating every received copy as a new event can make duplicate delivery look like additional work. Preserve both levels of identity. An event ID handles repeated delivery of the same evidence; an attempt ID identifies a separate execution that may consume resources even when the destination write is idempotent.

Count attempts separately. Don't count duplicate delivery as another attempt.

A useful recovery record names the stage that failed and the last acknowledged business boundary, but an acknowledgment must mean something defined by the application. Do not label an event “committed” merely because a request was sent. If a worker stops between a destination commit and emitting its completion record, absence of the log leaves the result uncertain; recovery must consult the destination or its own durable checkpoint before replaying the write. A logging success is not a transaction guarantee.

Rate limits create another boundary: a remote telemetry sender should honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, back off between retries, and use supported idempotency controls for repeated writes. Keep those delivery retries separate from import retries in the event model. Otherwise, an operator searching for repeated work cannot tell whether the data pipeline ran again or its evidence was merely sent twice.

For a nightly job that never starts, there may be no exception and no event to search. Assign that detection to a Healthchecks-style heartbeat service, and assign threshold notifications to an alerting system. Carry trace and span identifiers as correlation fields if useful, but use a tracing system when the investigation needs a span tree. Rich crash analysis, source-map de-minification, symbolication, and session replay belong in the specialist evaluation too.

Compare the systems at the failure boundary

The options below address different parts of the same workflow. Evaluate them against a replay investigation, not against the number of features on a landing page; a beginner team still has to decide who receives an alert and what evidence authorizes recovery.

Option Reason to evaluate it Boundary and trade-off for nightly imports
Infrai Logs, error capture, and metrics under one API contract, with consistent per-call attribution metadata Fits teams reducing integration glue; pair the evidence layer with dedicated alert delivery and heartbeat monitoring, and validate data-lifecycle requirements before adopting it as a record of account.
Sentry A specialist option for exception investigation Evaluate it when crash analysis drives the decision; retain structured job events for portfolio-level recovery and accounting context.
Grafana Cloud An option for a workflow centered on logs and metrics Evaluate it when signal exploration drives operations; define application run identity before expecting dashboards to explain a replay.
Datadog An option for broader production monitoring Evaluate it when the team needs a wider monitoring workflow; keep business idempotency and allocation rules in the application design.
Healthchecks A focused option for detecting a missing scheduled-job heartbeat Complements the other choices; a missed check does not reconstruct which property records committed.

The specialist choices deserve a real trial if their boundary is the one causing operational pain. An integrated API is attractive when maintaining separate client contracts is the burden; it is weaker as a selection argument when the required investigation depends on specialist crash tooling or a particular alert workflow. Before choosing a long-term log store, require evidence for retention, export, and deletion obligations as well. Searchability alone does not establish archival durability or data-governance suitability.

Critical path: retrieve the evidence before authorizing recovery

This Python 3 example retrieves log-search evidence for an operator investigating a Node.js pipeline. It uses only the standard library, reads the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, and prints the response without assuming an undocumented result schema. The request deliberately sends no filter parameters. Correlate returned evidence with application-owned portfolio, run, attempt, and event identities before deciding what to replay; don't treat an unscoped response as proof that a particular run completed.

import json
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def retry_delay(header, attempt):
    delay = 2 ** attempt
    if header:
        try:
            requested = float(header)
        except ValueError:
            retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(header)
            requested = (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
        delay = max(delay, requested)
    return delay


def fetch_logs():
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(4):
        request = Request(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/logs/search",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {key}"},
            method="GET",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
                if not 200 <= response.status < 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected HTTP status {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code == 429 and attempt < 3:
                time.sleep(retry_delay(error.headers.get("Retry-After"), attempt))
                continue
            raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(fetch_logs(), indent=2))

Save it as a Python file, set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment, and run it with Python 3. The four-attempt budget bounds retries; HTTP 429 waits at least the exponential delay or the server's Retry-After value, whichever is longer. Other HTTP errors surface their status and response body. This read does not mutate the import, so retrying it cannot reapply a property update.

Retrieval is only evidence.

For an illustrative attribution check, suppose attempt a1 records 9 work units and a recovery attempt a2 records 3. Receiving a duplicate copy of an a1 event must not increase its total, but the separate a2 execution still counts. Those are synthetic application counters, not measured vendor costs. Stable event identities make the distinction possible; a search result alone doesn't enforce it.

In a production design, bound the event search and persist any deduplication state needed across restarts. Compare actual call metadata with the corresponding attempt before allocating costs, and record an explicit allocation policy for shared operations. A shared call serving two portfolios cannot be charged in full to both merely because both appear in its context.

Rejected option: make logs responsible for every signal

For this pipeline, reject a logs-only monitoring design. It combines event reconstruction, exception grouping, trend analysis, and missing-job detection into one stream, then leaves the operator to infer the missing pieces precisely when recovery needs a clear answer. Keep log queries focused on evidence; use error tracking for grouped failures, metrics for rates and latency, and heartbeat monitoring for absence.

Logs alone still have a valid narrow use case: investigating a known event trail when paging, trend monitoring, and scheduled-job checks already live elsewhere. The decision changes with the responsibility, not with enthusiasm for an integrated platform.

References

  • Sentry documentation
  • Grafana Cloud documentation
  • Datadog documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Logback manual, appenders

If the shared-contract boundary fits your pipeline, start with the Infrai documentation and validate the telemetry contract against one recoverable import before extending it.

title: How Do You Build a Fast, SEO-Friendly Landing Page with Next.js?
description:
To build a fast, SEO-friendly landing page with Next.js, render it as a Server Component, set metadata with the Metadata API, optimize images with next/image, add JSON-LD structured data, and keep client-side JavaScript to a minimum. Below is a practical setup using the App Router.

Why does Next.js suit landing pages?

Landing pages are mostly static content. The App Router renders Server Components to HTML on the server (or at build time), so crawlers and users get full content immediately, with little JavaScript to download.

How do you set metadata and a canonical URL?

Export a metadata object from app/page.tsx:

import type { Metadata } from "next";

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "Acme Scheduler: Book meetings without back-and-forth",
  description: "A short, specific description of what the product does and who it is for.",
  alternates: { canonical: "https://example.com/" },
  openGraph: {
    title: "Acme Scheduler",
    description: "Book meetings without back-and-forth.",
    url: "https://example.com/",
    images: ["/og.png"],
  },
};

Give every page its own self-referencing canonical. A canonical pointing every subpage to the homepage can stop those pages from being indexed.

How do you keep images from hurting performance?

Use next/image with explicit dimensions and priority only for the above-the-fold hero image, and always write meaningful alt text:

import Image from "next/image";

<Image src="/hero.png" alt="Dashboard showing a weekly meeting calendar" width={1200} height={700} priority />

Explicit dimensions prevent layout shift (CLS).

How do you add structured data?

JSON-LD helps search engines and AI answer engines understand the page:

const jsonLd = {
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "SoftwareApplication",
  name: "Acme Scheduler",
  applicationCategory: "BusinessApplication",
};

export default function Page() {
  return (
    <>
      <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(jsonLd) }} />
      {/* page content */}
    </>
  );
}

If you add an FAQ section, mark it up with FAQPage only when the questions are visible on the page.

How do you limit client-side JavaScript?

Keep components as Server Components by default. Add "use client" only to small interactive pieces such as a form or menu. Load third-party scripts with next/script and strategy="lazyOnload".

How do you add a sitemap and robots file? 

// app/sitemap.ts
import type { MetadataRoute } from "next";

export default function sitemap(): MetadataRoute.Sitemap {
  return [{ url: "https://example.com/", lastModified: new Date() }];
}

Then verify with Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights and measure real results rather than assuming them.

FAQ

Do I need SSR for SEO? No. Static generation or server rendering both deliver crawlable HTML; what matters is that content is in the initial HTML.

Pages Router or App Router? The App Router's Metadata API and Server Components make this simpler for new projects.

How do I check it works? View the page source for your content, test with PageSpeed Insights, and inspect the URL in Google Search Console.

I'm Muhammad Afzal, a Python developer building web projects at INDUS Web Agency.

title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
description:
arXiv:2611.23611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
description:
arXiv:2611.25257v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions. Because the repair lives in the weights, it combines with budget forcing where held-out questions favor it: on the best available weights, Keel has the best average accuracy on both models, significantly above every training-free baseline we compare on the larger one.

title: 60 FPS in Canvas: State Loops and Vector Hitboxes in Sky Isles: Flight SIM 3D
description:
60 FPS in Canvas: State Loops and Vector Hitboxes in Sky Isles: Flight SIM 3D

Browser-based gaming has come a long way from CPU-throttling flash animations. Today, modern HTML5 and Canvas/WebGL engines enable developers to build crisp, responsive games that boot instantly in any browser.

In this technical breakdown, we analyze Sky Isles: Flight SIM 3D, an agile action release playable directly via play Sky Isles: Flight SIM 3D with zero installation required.

1. Core Mechanics & State Design

Sky Isles Flight Simulator is a 3D airplane game set over a chain of tropical islands. Players begin each flight on the ground, starting the engine, taxiing to the…

To achieve snappy gameplay without micro-stutters, the game decouples the logical tick loop from the presentation layer:

// High-precision fixed delta-time loop example
let lastTime = performance.now();
const MS_PER_UPDATE = 1000 / 60;

function gameLoop(currentTime) {
    let elapsed = currentTime - lastTime;
    lastTime = currentTime;

    while (elapsed >= MS_PER_UPDATE) {
        updateGameState(MS_PER_UPDATE);
        elapsed -= MS_PER_UPDATE;
    }
    renderScene();
    requestAnimationFrame(gameLoop);
}

2. Dynamic Viewport Scaling & HiDPI Support

To ensure razor-sharp graphics on 4K monitors and Retina mobile screens alike, Sky Isles: Flight SIM 3D adjusts canvas pixel density using window.devicePixelRatio:

  • Canvas dimensions are scaled up to match hardware screen resolution.
  • CSS display size is locked via flexbox containers with touch-action: none to eliminate mobile scroll latency.
  • Touch event listeners are registered as { passive: false } for instantaneous finger-tracking response.

3. Memory & Garbage Collection Optimization

Garbage collection (GC) pauses are the primary cause of frame drops in JavaScript web games. Sky Isles: Flight SIM 3D avoids GC thrashing through:

  1. Object Pooling: Reusing particle and trajectory instances rather than allocating fresh objects every frame.
  2. Typed Arrays: Using Float32Array for coordinate and physics calculations.
  3. Web Audio Buffers: Pre-decoding audio assets into reusable sound buffers at boot time.

Test out the live implementation firsthand on the experience the official web version of Sky Isles: Flight SIM 3D and inspect the performance profiling in Chrome DevTools!

title: 2026 Node.js Monitor: Sending Domain Health on Schedule, Records and Mail Metrics (and Limits)
description:
Short answer: treat sending-domain health as a reconciliation record, not a single status check. A marketplace should read the mail service's view and the published SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records on a daily schedule, emit both observations as metrics, and alert only when an active domain's two views disagree.

That decision matters because a record edited by hand last month can leave the mail provider reporting “ready” while DNS publishes something else. A missing domain is different: it may be a retired seller or a completed offboarding job. The alert boundary is disagreement, not absence.

This is a small governance loop. It gives the team an audit trail for intent versus publication, while leaving provider-specific delivery analytics to the system that actually owns those analytics. The example uses Python because the API contract is plain HTTP; the same request sequence fits a Node.js scheduler without an SDK.

Infrai fits this early part of the workflow when the worker needs one REST surface for domain records, mail status, and metrics. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and requires no key, while one key spans 295 routes across 20 modules. That combination removes credential and schema-hunting friction; it does not decide what a marketplace considers an active tenant.

The alert is the product.

How should I monitor sending domain health on a schedule with records?

There are two useful facts for each active marketplace domain: the mail-side status and the published records. Compare canonical observations, then report both observations and the disagreement result through the metrics capability. Keep the route details in the runnable example, where they can be tested rather than mistaken for a complete catalog.

Do not compare raw JSON blindly in production. Response ordering, an incidental timestamp, or an unrelated metadata field can create noise. During implementation, save representative responses as fixtures and define a projection containing only the SPF, DKIM, and DMARC values that matter to the sending decision. Version that projection. A change from projection version 1 to version 2 should be visible in the audit record, otherwise a new parser can look like a DNS incident.

The rule is intentionally asymmetric: an active domain with different projections is actionable; a retired domain that is absent is expected. An API error is neither agreement nor disagreement. It is a failed check that should remain visible to the scheduler.

Can a daily reconciliation job be made reproducible?

Yes, if the experiment comes before the cron entry. Keep four fixtures: an active domain whose views match, an active domain with one changed record, a retired domain absent from the inventory, and an API error. For each fixture, store the two normalized observations, the projection version, the emitted metric values, and the expected alert decision.

Keep it boring.

The following implementation shows the request mechanics and a deliberately small metric envelope. Before deployment, use the public discovery response to confirm the account's request schema for metrics; discovery is the right place to learn fields rather than guessing them. The request path, bearer authentication, explicit methods, status handling, and rate-limit behavior remain the same.

import hashlib
import json
import os
import time
from urllib.parse import quote

import requests


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
DOMAIN = os.environ["SENDING_DOMAIN"]


def request_json(method, path, body=None):
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}
    for attempt in range(5):
        request_url = path if path.startswith("https://") else BASE_URL + path
        response = requests.request(
            method=method,
            url=request_url,
            headers=headers,
            json=body,
            timeout=20,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(min(delay, 60))
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"{method} {path} failed with {response.status_code}: "
                f"{response.text}"
            )
        return response.json()
    raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path} was rate-limited five times")


def digest(value):
    serialized = json.dumps(value, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256(serialized.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


mail_status = request_json(
    "GET",
    f"https://api.infrai.cc/v1/email/domain/get/{quote(DOMAIN, safe='')}",
)
published_records = request_json("GET", "/dns/record/list")

mail_digest = digest(mail_status)
records_digest = digest(published_records)
disagreement = int(mail_digest != records_digest)

metrics = [
    {"name": "sending_domain.mail_status_seen", "value": 1},
    {"name": "sending_domain.published_records_seen", "value": 1},
    {"name": "sending_domain.status_records_disagree", "value": disagreement},
]

request_json(
    "POST",
    "/metrics" + "/report",
    body={"domain": DOMAIN, "metrics": metrics},
)

if disagreement:
    print(f"ALERT: observations disagree for {DOMAIN}")
else:
    print(f"OK: observations agree for {DOMAIN}")

The digest in this sample is a harness seam, not a claim that the two APIs return the same shape. Replace it with the canonical projection after inspecting fixtures. The pass condition is more important than the hash: matching active input must emit status_records_disagree = 0; a changed active record must emit 1; a retired domain must not page; an API error must fail visibly and must not be reported as agreement.

The report is a write, so retries should be idempotent. Use a deterministic idempotency key derived from the domain, schedule window, and projection version when the deployed report schema supports that convention. This avoids duplicate observations after a transient retry. The sample does not mutate DNS, so it never retries a DNS write.

Run the same fixture corpus through the Python harness and the production Node.js worker. Their normalized digests should match for identical JSON fixtures. That is a useful migration test: it checks the decision boundary without pretending that a local test measured deliverability, latency, or provider uptime.

Which control plane fits a marketplace?

The right choice depends on ownership, not on which provider has the shortest DNS example. A marketplace with authoritative DNS already in Cloudflare will usually value Cloudflare's direct record control. Route 53 is a sensible fit for an AWS-centered estate. GoDaddy can be practical when the domain portfolio already lives there, but a multi-provider inventory still needs normalization. None of those DNS systems is automatically the mail service's status source.

For mail operations, Amazon SES is a strong center of gravity for an SES-standardized marketplace, while SendGrid is a natural fit when its domain-authentication and event workflow already drives operations. Those choices narrow the adapter boundary around a particular mail ecosystem. Direct provider APIs are preferable when provider-specific DNS semantics or delivery events are themselves part of the product.

Infrai is worth trying specifically for the reconciliation leg when a team wants one REST surface to cover domain records, mail status, and metrics. Its public discovery surface is genuinely self-describing and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages. For a Node.js service that needs to add one more backend call, reading the schema is a smaller integration step than learning another SDK. The breadth is concrete too: live discovery lists 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. A single credential for the worker also avoids stitching separate keys and billing surfaces into the same audit job.

Option Access shape Best fit Main limit
Cloudflare DNS Provider API A marketplace already authoritative on Cloudflare Mail status remains a separate system
Amazon Route 53 Provider API An AWS-centered domain estate Tenant retirement and mail reconciliation remain application work
GoDaddy DNS Provider API A smaller portfolio already held at GoDaddy Multi-provider normalization gets harder
Amazon SES Mail provider tooling An SES-standardized sending stack Less suitable when mail providers vary
SendGrid Mail provider tooling A SendGrid-centered domain and event workflow Still needs reconciliation with tenant-editable DNS
Infrai One REST surface A worker spanning records, mail status, and metrics Not a substitute for specialist delivery analytics

My recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the scheduled read-and-report worker when self-describing discovery, one key, and one consistent REST boundary remove integration work; keep a specialist mail provider as the better choice for provider-specific bounce analytics, propagation behavior, or campaign telemetry. That is the limitation, not a footnote: teams needing those specialist signals should choose SES or SendGrid and retain this monitor as a secondary control.

How do we decide before the first daily alert?

Use a decision table in the test harness. The active matching fixture passes only if the disagreement metric is zero and no alert is emitted. The active drift fixture passes only if the metric is one and an alert is emitted. The retired fixture passes if absence is recorded without a page. The error fixture passes if the run is marked failed and no agreement metric is emitted.

Ship the daily schedule only when all four outcomes are stable across two implementations and the raw inputs can be reconstructed from the audit record. A daily run is enough for configuration that should never change on its own. Metrics still reveal slow drift between runs, which is the reason to keep the observations instead of storing only the final alert bit.

Before enabling it, label each metric with the domain and projection version, retain enough raw response data to explain a disagreement, and make the retired-domain inventory an explicit input. If a fixture fails, fix the projection or ownership policy first. More polling cannot resolve an ambiguous comparison.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the public discovery documentation and verify the live schemas before wiring the adapter.

Sources

  • RFC 7489: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • Amazon SES documentation
  • SendGrid Domain Authentication documentation

title: 13 popular Python projects moved to 3.11 and still can't close their soupsieve alerts
description:
Last week I wrote about a small trap: raising requires-python to 3.11 does not close the soupsieve alerts, because every fixed soupsieve release needs Python 3.11.5. I wanted to know how common this is, so I measured it.

What I checked

I took the 300 most-starred Python repos on GitHub that had a push this month. 94 of them use uv (they have a uv.lock), and I could analyze 92.

For each one I read the lock file, listed the vulnerable packages, and then asked PyPI a simple question: does any fixed release still install on the oldest Python this project supports? If the answer is no, no upgrade can close that alert. Someone has to decide to drop a Python version first.

Everything was read-only. I didn't run a resolver or change anything in anyone's project.

What I found

  • 70 of the 92 projects had open alerts.
  • 40 of those 70 (57%) have at least one vulnerable package that no fixed release reaches on their oldest supported Python.
  • Counting packages, it's 100 of 831 vulnerable packages (12%).

The packages behind it: soupsieve, filelock, pillow, dnspython, tornado, plus a few more. For the fixes, pillow, filelock, dnspython and tornado all need Python 3.11, and soupsieve needs 3.11.5.

The 3.11.5 trap

30 projects have a vulnerable soupsieve that they can't fix on their oldest Python. The part that surprised me: 13 of them already require Python 3.11, and they're still blocked, because 3.11.0 to 3.11.4 are still allowed.

Those 13 are manim, prefect, skyvern, airflow, graphrag, mlflow, serena, pydantic, python-telegram-bot, spotify-downloader, hindsight, wagtail and private-gpt.

For them, requires-python = ">=3.11" isn't enough. It has to be ">=3.11.5".

What this is not

This is not a criticism of any project. Supporting older Pythons is a fair choice, and some projects keep it on purpose. The point is that Dependabot or any other tool can't close these alerts by itself: someone has to decide.

Some limits, so you can judge the numbers:

  • The alerts come from pip-audit, not from Dependabot. They mostly agree, but not 100%.
  • "Blocked" comes from PyPI metadata, not from running a resolver. A project can still close an alert with an environment marker.
  • Counting alerts makes pillow look bigger (it has many advisories), so the per-package numbers are the fair ones.
  • It's one snapshot, from November 20, 2026.

Check it yourself

The scripts, the method and the data for every package are here: https://github.com/samuelrojas-dev/depquiet/tree/main/research/2026-11-python-floor

I measured this with depquiet, the tool I'm building. If you have alerts stuck like this, depquiet --fix-plan --raise-python-floor finds the exact floor (3.11.5, not 3.11) and checks it with uv or Poetry before you change anything.

title: Variance-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bounds for Multi-Armed Bandits with Kaplan--Meier Survival Estimation
description:
arXiv:2611.24988v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem in which the reward associated with each arm is the survival probability at a pre-specified time horizon, and the observed outcome is a right-censored time-to-event variable. Standard bandit algorithms face delayed and partial observations in this setting. Prior adaptations for the Kaplan--Meier (KM) estimator rely on Hoeffding-type bounds that ignore the inherent heteroscedasticity of continuous survival processes. To bridge this gap, we propose KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive policy that unites continuous-time survival analysis with discrete sequential decision-making. By leveraging martingale theory and continuous influence functions, we derive a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound parameterized by Greenwood's variance formula. For realtime allocation, we retain the Greenwood index and use a survival bound from completed records to review the recommended arm. Under catch-up reporting, the policy has logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term in the exploration bound. We evaluate the original policy in a dual-layer delayed simulation and a retrospective replay of breast cancer trial data, and evaluate the correction in a separate paired simulation.

title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
description:
arXiv:2611.25073v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows.
  In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.

title: AWS Transform announces support for .NET 11 and expanded project types
description:
Today, AWS announced the general availability of .NET 11 support in AWS Transform for .NET. Support for VB.NET, desktop projects, and mobile projects, previously in preview, is also now generally available. You can modernize a broad range of Windows .NET workloads to the latest version of .NET and lower costs by running them on Linux. Modernized workloads gain the performance improvements, new C# language features, and improved diagnostics in .NET 11.

AWS Transform modernizes both legacy .NET Framework applications (version 3.5 and later) and modern .NET applications (versions 5 through 10) to .NET 11. It transforms code written in C# and VB.NET. Supported project types include class libraries, console applications, ASP.NET web projects (MVC, Web API, and Web Forms), web services (ASMX and WCF), desktop applications (WinForms and WPF), mobile applications (Xamarin), unit test projects (MSTest, NUnit, and xUnit), and Windows services. You can run all transformed applications except desktop and mobile projects on Linux, which can reduce operating costs by up to 40%.

This capability is available at no additional cost in all eight AWS Regions where AWS Transform is offered: US East (N. Virginia), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London).

To learn more, see Modernizing .NET with AWS Transform in the AWS Transform User Guide.

title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
description:
arXiv:2611.24206v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.

title: Modeling Multi-Country Customs VAT, Duties & IATA Volumetric Weight in Python (GCC, EU & Australasia Landed Costs)
description:
If you are building a cross-border checkout calculator, e-commerce ERP, or procurement assistant for buyers ordering from US retailers (RockAuto, Amazon US, Sweetwater, Summit Racing, B&H Photo), hardcoding a single courier flat rate will break your landed-cost estimates immediately.

In production international air cargo, three compounding variables determine the real landed cost:

  1. IATA Volumetric (Dimensional) Weight: max(actual_kg, (L_cm * W_cm * H_cm) / 5000)
  2. Consolidation & Void-Space Repacking: Removing retail outer cartons and consolidating multi-store orders over a free 30-day window regularly reduces billable volumetric weight by 45%–70% and unlocks lower commercial per-kg brackets (>= 8.0 kg).
  3. Destination VAT & Customs Duty Thresholds: Every GCC, EU, UK, and Australasian customs authority applies different VAT rates, de minimis rules, and brokerage triggers.

Below is a clean, deterministic Python landed-cost model mirroring the live commercial corridors shipped from our LAX export hub (309 E Arbor Vitae St, Inglewood, CA 90301).

1. Python Landed-Cost Engine Across 15 Customs Regimes 

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CorridorRule:
    country: str
    consolidated_usd_per_kg: float  # >= 8.0 kg billable
    express_usd_per_kg: float       # < 8.0 kg billable
    vat_rate: float                 # decimal (e.g., 0.15 = 15%)
    duty_rate: float                # standard general tariff
    duty_threshold_usd: float       # approximate CIF de minimis
    customs_system: str

RULES: dict[str, CorridorRule] = {
    "saudi-arabia": CorridorRule("Saudi Arabia", 8.50, 15.50, 0.15, 0.05, 266.0, "ZATCA FASAH"),
    "united-arab-emirates": CorridorRule("UAE", 8.50, 15.50, 0.05, 0.05, 81.0, "Dubai Trade / Mirsal 2"),
    "bahrain": CorridorRule("Bahrain", 8.50, 15.50, 0.10, 0.05, 0.0, "Bahrain NBR / OFOQ"),
    "kuwait": CorridorRule("Kuwait", 8.50, 15.50, 0.00, 0.05, 0.0, "Kuwait General Customs"),
    "oman": CorridorRule("Oman", 8.50, 15.50, 0.05, 0.05, 0.0, "Royal Oman Police Bayan"),
    "qatar": CorridorRule("Qatar", 8.50, 15.50, 0.00, 0.05, 0.0, "Qatar Al-Nadeeb"),
    "united-kingdom": CorridorRule("United Kingdom", 8.50, 15.50, 0.20, 0.025, 170.0, "HMRC CDS"),
    "germany": CorridorRule("Germany", 9.00, 15.50, 0.19, 0.03, 165.0, "ATLAS / EUSt"),
    "france": CorridorRule("France", 9.00, 15.50, 0.20, 0.03, 165.0, "DELTA / TVA"),
    "spain": CorridorRule("Spain", 9.00, 15.50, 0.21, 0.03, 165.0, "AEAT / IVA"),
    "netherlands": CorridorRule("Netherlands", 9.00, 15.50, 0.21, 0.03, 165.0, "Douane / BTW"),
    "sweden": CorridorRule("Sweden", 9.00, 15.50, 0.25, 0.03, 165.0, "Tullverket / Moms"),
    "portugal": CorridorRule("Portugal", 9.00, 15.50, 0.23, 0.03, 165.0, "AT Alfândega / IVA"),
    "australia": CorridorRule("Australia", 11.00, 15.50, 0.10, 0.05, 650.0, "ABF ICS / GST"),
    "new-zealand": CorridorRule("New Zealand", 11.00, 15.50, 0.15, 0.05, 600.0, "NZCS / GST"),
}

def estimate_landed_cost(
    corridor_slug: str,
    goods_value_usd: float,
    actual_kg: float,
    dims_cm: tuple[float, float, float],
    repack_factor: float = 0.45,
) -> dict:
    rule = RULES[corridor_slug]
    l, w, h = dims_cm
    raw_vol_kg = round((l * w * h) / 5000.0, 2)
    repacked_kg = max(0.5, actual_kg, round(raw_vol_kg * repack_factor, 2))

    rate = rule.consolidated_usd_per_kg if repacked_kg >= 8.0 else rule.express_usd_per_kg
    freight_usd = round(repacked_kg * rate, 2)
    cif_usd = goods_value_usd + freight_usd

    duty_usd = round(cif_usd * rule.duty_rate, 2) if cif_usd > rule.duty_threshold_usd else 0.0
    vat_usd = round((cif_usd + duty_usd) * rule.vat_rate, 2)

    return {
        "country": rule.country,
        "customs_system": rule.customs_system,
        "raw_volumetric_kg": raw_vol_kg,
        "repacked_billable_kg": repacked_kg,
        "rate_usd_per_kg": rate,
        "freight_usd": freight_usd,
        "est_duty_usd": duty_usd,
        "est_vat_usd": vat_usd,
        "total_landed_usd": round(cif_usd + duty_usd + vat_usd, 2),
    }

2. Example: 11 kg Auto Parts Consolidation (USA to Bahrain & Portugal)

Suppose a workshop orders brake rotors, control arms, and gaskets across 3 US warehouses totaling 11.0 kg actual weight, packed in oversized retail cartons measuring 60 × 50 × 45 cm (27.0 kg raw volumetric weight):

  • Unconsolidated courier billing (27.0 kg): You pay for 16.0 kg of empty cardboard air!
  • Consolidated LAX repacking (12.15 kg billable): Unlocks commercial tier (>= 8.0 kg):
    • USA → Bahrain ($8.50/kg): $103.28 air freight (2–4 business days) + 10% Bahrain VAT.
    • USA → Portugal ($9.00/kg): $109.35 air freight (2–4 business days) + 23% IVA via AT Alfândega.

3. Live Regional Corridor Guides & Open Tools

Every corridor rule above maps to live air freight calculators, customs breakdowns, and MCP agent endpoints:

  • Interactive Landed-Cost & Volumetric Calculator: AQX Live Shipping Calculator
  • GCC Corridor Guides: USA to Saudi Arabia | USA to UAE / Dubai | USA to Bahrain | USA to Kuwait | USA to Oman | USA to Qatar
  • Europe & Australasia Corridor Guides: USA to Portugal | USA to UK | USA to Germany | USA to Australia | USA to New Zealand
  • Official API & MCP Docs (Read the Docs): aqx-shipping-rates-mcp.readthedocs.io
  • Open-Source Python MCP Server (MIT): AQXLOGISTICS/aqx-shipping-rates-mcp (also inspectable live on Glama MCP Registry)

Feel free to reuse or extend the CorridorRule dataclass above for your own cross-border checkout or ERP quoting scripts!

title: Introducing Amazon EC2 T9g instances based on Graviton5
description:
AWS is announcing the general availability of new low-cost burstable Amazon EC2 T9g instances, which offer the best price performance among general-purpose EC2 instances. These instances are powered by AWS Graviton5 processors and built on the latest sixth generation AWS Nitro cards. T9g instances deliver up to 45% better price performance compared to previous generation T4g instances, and offer four sizes: nano, micro, small, and medium. These instances are designed for workloads requiring low to moderate CPU utilization, including data processing, login gateways, small databases, microservices, low-traffic websites, freemium services, staging and development, and short-duration compute tasks such as batch processing, event-driven functions, and CI/CD pipelines.

T9g instances deliver up to 2.3x the compute performance, 1.5x higher network bandwidth, and 2.8x higher EBS bandwidth compared to T4g instances. They are built on the sixth-generation AWS Nitro System and feature the Nitro Isolation Engine, harnessing formal verification to provide mathematical assurance that customer workloads are isolated from each other and AWS operators, pioneering a new standard for mathematically proven cloud security. 

T9g instances use the same CPU credit system as T4g with Standard and Unlimited modes, so existing T customers can upgrade to T9g and immediately benefit from better price performance, enabling them to lower their TCO. For customers new to AWS or migrating from on-premises, T9g instances provide one of the most cost-effective entry points to run a variety of lightweight workloads.

T9g.micro and T9g.small are available under the AWS Free Tier. T9g instances are available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (N. California, Oregon), Canada (Central), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt, Spain), and Asia Pacific (Malaysia, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo) regions. T9g instances are available to purchase via Savings Plans, On-Demand instances, and Spot instances. To learn more, visit the Amazon EC2 T9g instances page.

title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
description:
arXiv:2611.23520v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

title: Adobe ArtCraft: Is This Pure Rust, Open-Source Photoshop Suite the Real Deal?
description:
If you work in digital media, you’ve probably spent the last couple of years looking for an exit door from the Adobe Creative Cloud ecosystem.

Between the $60/month subscription tax, background update daemons that eat 8GB of RAM while idling, and terms of service updates that sparked privacy panics over creative work, everyone wants an alternative. But the usual suggestions always had friction: GIMP’s interface feels permanently frozen in 2004, and while Affinity is solid, it remains closed-source and was recently acquired by Canva.

That’s why ArtCraft caught my attention.

Instead of wrapping a web app in Electron or slapping a fresh skin on vintage C++ codebases, the developers behind the project (storytold on GitHub) are doing something genuinely ambitious: rewriting the entire creative suite from scratch in pure Rust.

I took a deep dive into the ArtCraft suite—from PhotoCraft to their AI workflows—to see how good it actually is, how it compares to Photoshop, and how to get it running on your machine.

1. What Is the ArtCraft Suite?

At its core, ArtCraft open source is split into two distinct layers:

A. The Native Craft Apps (Desktop & Offline)

These are standalone, native desktop executables written in Rust with zero Electron runtime overhead. They are direct, clean-room alternatives to traditional creative software:

  • PhotoCraft: Layer-based raster editing and photo manipulation (Photoshop alternative).
  • VectorCraft: Bézier paths, vector illustration, and typography (Illustrator alternative).
  • FilmCraft: Non-linear video editing and multi-track audio (Premiere Pro alternative).
  • LightCraft: Non-destructive RAW processing and batch asset management (Lightroom alternative).
  • EffectCraft: Timeline-based motion graphics and VFX (After Effects alternative).
  • DesignCraft: Multi-page layout and desktop publishing (InDesign alternative).

Because they are compiled native binaries, they launch instantly, run 100% offline, and don't require an account just to crop an image.

B. ArtCraft Studio (The AI Workspace)

Alongside the desktop tools sits ArtCraft Studio—their cloud workspace for generative assets (generating cinematic video clips, 3D meshes, and sound design).

Unlike pure prompt-to-image generators that treat you like a spectator, ArtCraft approaches generative tools as a compositor: you block out the scene, layout 3D cameras and reference moodboards, and use the AI models as asset layers that feed back into the editing timeline.

2. PhotoCraft vs. Photoshop: How Good Is It in Practice?

When people talk about finding an open-source alternative to Photoshop, the baseline requirements are pretty brutal. It can't just be an image viewer with a paintbrush tool; it has to handle real production habits:

What Works Surprisingly Well

  • Raw Speed & Startup: PhotoCraft boots in milliseconds. On a system where Photoshop spends 20 seconds initializing font caches and cloud sync plugins, opening a file in PhotoCraft feels like opening a native text editor.
  • Native PSD Support: It parses .psd files out of the box, preserving layer structures, blend modes, and clipping masks without mangling the hierarchy.
  • Modern Memory Footprint: Because it’s written in memory-safe Rust with contiguous memory buffers, RAM usage stays remarkably tight even when stacking high-resolution uncompressed layers.

Where You’ll Still Feel the Difference

It is an active open-source project, not a 35-year-old corporate legacy. If your daily workflow relies on obscure legacy third-party .8bf plugins, proprietary Pantone spot-color libraries, or automated CMYK pre-press prep for high-volume commercial offset printers, Adobe still holds the institutional monopoly.

For 95% of digital creators, game designers, and UI artists who need reliable masking, non-destructive layer adjustments, and fast export pipelines, PhotoCraft already does the heavy lifting without the bloat.

3. How to Download and Install ArtCraft

You have three clean options to install the suite depending on how hands-on you want to be:

Option A: The ArtCraft Launcher (Recommended)

The simplest way to manage the suite is downloading the ArtCraft Launcher from the official site:

  1. Head to getartcraft.com/apps.
  2. Download the launcher for your OS (Windows, macOS, or Linux).
  3. The launcher lets you pick and choose which apps you want (e.g., just installing PhotoCraft without downloading the video editor) and keeps them updated automatically.

Option B: Standalone GitHub Binaries

If you don't want a launcher running on your system, you can grab standalone release builds directly from the GitHub repositories:

  • Go to the project’s GitHub organization (github.com/storytold).
  • Open the repository you want (e.g., storytold/photocraft).
  • Click on Releases on the right side and download the pre-compiled binary:
    • Windows: .exe installer or portable archive.
    • macOS: .dmg drag-and-drop bundle.
    • Linux: AppImage, .deb, .rpm, or Flatpak package.

Option C: Compiling From Source via Cargo

If you have the Rust toolchain installed and want to build the absolute latest commit locally:

# Clone the photo editor repository
git clone https://github.com/storytold/photocraft.git
cd photocraft

# Build and run with optimizations
cargo run --release -p photocraft -- my_image.psd

The Verdict: A Genuinely Exciting Alternative

For years, escaping the Adobe ecosystem meant making significant compromises: either paying another private vendor or enduring sluggish legacy open-source tools with confusing interfaces.

Seeing a dedicated team build an entire creative suite in pure Rust—with offline-first native performance, transparent open-source code on GitHub, and an AI integration model that respects the human artist's layout—is easily one of the most promising software developments in the creative space right now.

If you’re tired of background sync daemons and subscription fees, download PhotoCraft from getartcraft.com/apps or clone it from GitHub and take it for a spin.
