title: IndexedDB in React: Offline-First Apps with WatermelonDB
description:
Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.

IndexedDB is the browser's built-in database. It is the right place to keep the data a React app needs to keep working when the network drops. You can use it directly through a small wrapper like idb for simple caching. If you need relations, reactive queries and two-way sync with a server, put WatermelonDB on top of it. This tutorial walks through both approaches, with code you can adapt.

I used WatermelonDB on browser storage to build the offline-first data layer of Oscar, a restaurant and retail POS. A POS can't stop taking orders just because the Wi-Fi went down. The patterns below are the ones I'd reach for again. If you want the product-level story first, read lessons from building an offline-first POS in React. This post is the hands-on developer version.

What is IndexedDB, and why not just use localStorage?

IndexedDB is an asynchronous, transactional object store that ships with every modern browser. You don't define tables with fixed columns. Instead you create object stores that hold JavaScript objects identified by a key. You add indexes on the fields you want to search by, and you read or write inside transactions. Anything the structured clone algorithm can copy, including Blobs and files, can be stored. It also works inside Web Workers, so heavy database work can stay off the main thread.

localStorage feels easier, but it has two problems for offline apps:

localStorage IndexedDB
API style Synchronous, blocks the main thread Asynchronous, event or promise based
Data Strings only Structured objects, Blobs, files
Querying Read by key only Indexes, key ranges, cursors
Size 5 MiB per origin A share of total disk (see below)
Transactions None Read-only and readwrite transactions

The 5 MiB figure comes from MDN's storage quota guide. A product catalogue, a few days of orders and some images will pass that quickly. IndexedDB quotas are far larger. Chromium browsers allow an origin up to 60% of total disk. Recent Safari versions (macOS 14 and iOS 17 onward) allow about 60% for browser apps. Firefox gives best-effort storage the smaller of 10% of the disk or 10 GiB.

How do you use IndexedDB in React without the boilerplate?

The raw API is built on request objects and onsuccess callbacks, which is awkward in modern code. The idb library by Jake Archibald wraps it in promises and adds TypeScript types. It is tiny, and version 8.0.4 was the latest on npm when I checked in November 2026.

npm install idb

Here is a small, typed data module for a list of orders:

// db.ts
import { openDB, type DBSchema } from "idb";

interface ShopDB extends DBSchema {
  orders: {
    key: string;
    value: {
      id: string;
      status: "pending" | "paid";
      total: number;
      updatedAt: number;
    };
    indexes: { by_status: string };
  };
}

export const dbPromise = openDB<ShopDB>("shop", 1, {
  upgrade(db) {
    const store = db.createObjectStore("orders", { keyPath: "id" });
    store.createIndex("by_status", "status");
  },
});

export async function saveOrder(order: ShopDB["orders"]["value"]) {
  const db = await dbPromise;
  await db.put("orders", { ...order, updatedAt: Date.now() });
}

export async function pendingOrders() {
  const db = await dbPromise;
  return db.getAllFromIndex("orders", "by_status", "pending");
}

A few things are worth knowing:

  • The schema only changes in upgrade. When you add a store or index, bump the version number and handle oldVersion inside upgrade. Never delete a store your users already have data in without migrating it.

  • Generate IDs on the device. crypto.randomUUID() lets you create records offline without asking the server for an ID. It also makes duplicate detection easy later.

  • Keep transactions short. A transaction closes once you stop giving it work, so don't await a network call in the middle of one.

In a component, read the data inside an effect and store it in state:

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { pendingOrders } from "./db";

export function PendingOrders() {
  const [orders, setOrders] = useState<Awaited<ReturnType<typeof pendingOrders>>>([]);

  useEffect(() => {
    pendingOrders().then(setOrders);
  }, []);

  return <p>{orders.length} orders waiting to sync</p>;
}

This works well for caching and small offline features. It breaks down once your data has relations (an order with items, modifiers and payments) and many screens that must update the moment something changes. Then you are writing your own query layer, change tracking and sync protocol. That is what WatermelonDB already does.


Photo: imgix on Unsplash

Setting up WatermelonDB on top of IndexedDB

WatermelonDB is a reactive database for React and React Native. On the web it runs through its LokiJS adapter, which can save data incrementally to IndexedDB. The current npm release is 0.28.0.

npm install @nozbe/watermelondb

It uses decorators for models, so your bundler needs the Babel decorators and class-properties plugins. The installation guide lists them. Start with a schema:

// model/schema.ts
import { appSchema, tableSchema } from "@nozbe/watermelondb";

export const schema = appSchema({
  version: 1,
  tables: [
    tableSchema({
      name: "orders",
      columns: [
        { name: "status", type: "string", isIndexed: true },
        { name: "total", type: "number" },
        { name: "created_at", type: "number" },
      ],
    }),
    tableSchema({
      name: "order_items",
      columns: [
        { name: "order_id", type: "string", isIndexed: true },
        { name: "name", type: "string" },
        { name: "qty", type: "number" },
      ],
    }),
  ],
});

Then create the adapter and the database. The adapter options are where most of the production problems get solved, so don't skip them:

// database.ts
import { Database } from "@nozbe/watermelondb";
import LokiJSAdapter from "@nozbe/watermelondb/adapters/lokijs";
import { schema } from "./model/schema";
import { migrations } from "./model/migrations";
import { Order, OrderItem } from "./model";

const adapter = new LokiJSAdapter({
  schema,
  migrations,
  dbName: "shop",
  useWebWorker: false,
  useIncrementalIndexedDB: true,
  onQuotaExceededError: () => showStorageFullBanner(),
  onSetUpError: () => offerReloadOrLogout(),
  extraIncrementalIDBOptions: {
    // Another tab overwrote this tab's data: sync now, warn if offline
    onDidOverwrite: () => syncNow(),
    // The database was deleted in another tab (e.g. logout)
    onversionchange: () => window.location.reload(),
  },
});

export const database = new Database({
  adapter,
  modelClasses: [Order, OrderItem],
});

The multi-tab handlers matter more than they look. Staff often have the same app open in two tabs. If you ignore those callbacks, one tab can quietly overwrite what the other wrote.

Reading and writing records

Every write goes through database.write, which keeps changes consistent:

import { Q } from "@nozbe/watermelondb";

export async function createOrder(items: { name: string; qty: number }[]) {
  await database.write(async () => {
    const order = await database.get<Order>("orders").create((o) => {
      o.status = "pending";
      o.total = 0;
    });
    for (const item of items) {
      await database.get<OrderItem>("order_items").create((i) => {
        i.order.set(order);
        i.name = item.name;
        i.qty = item.qty;
      });
    }
  });
}

export const pendingQuery = () =>
  database.get<Order>("orders").query(Q.where("status", "pending"));

The real benefit is that queries are observable. Call pendingQuery().observe() (or use the withObservables helper) and any component reading it re-renders when a matching record changes, whether a cashier made the change or a sync did. You stop passing refresh callbacks around.

For synced apps, delete with markAsDeleted() so the deletion reaches the server. Use destroyPermanently() only for data that never leaves the device.

How does sync work between IndexedDB and your backend?

WatermelonDB's synchronize() function needs two things from you:

  1. pullChanges({ lastPulledAt }) calls your API and returns { changes, timestamp }. changes holds everything created, updated or deleted on the server since the last pull.
  2. pushChanges({ changes }) sends local changes to your API. It must reject if the server fails to apply them. 
import { synchronize } from "@nozbe/watermelondb/sync";

export async function syncNow() {
  await synchronize({
    database,
    migrationsEnabledAtVersion: 1,
    pullChanges: async ({ lastPulledAt, schemaVersion }) => {
      const res = await fetch(
        `/api/sync?since=${lastPulledAt ?? 0}&schema=${schemaVersion}`,
      );
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Pull failed");
      return res.json(); // { changes, timestamp }
    },
    pushChanges: async ({ changes, lastPulledAt }) => {
      const res = await fetch(`/api/sync?last_pulled_at=${lastPulledAt}`, {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify(changes),
      });
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Push failed");
    },
  });
}

The changes payload is grouped by table, with created, updated and deleted lists. Deleted records are sent as IDs only, and fields use the raw column names from your schema. Your backend has to keep its side of the deal:

  • Track changes on the server. Add a last_modified column to every table and set it on every write. Pull returns rows where it is newer than lastPulledAt. Ignore any value the client sends for it.

  • Track deletions. Use a soft-delete flag or a table of deleted IDs. Otherwise devices never learn that a record is gone.

  • Make push all-or-nothing. Apply the whole batch in one database transaction. If anything fails, roll back and return an error. A half-applied order is worse than one that retries.

  • Reject stale pushes. If a record changed on the server after the client's lastPulledAt, fail the push. The client then pulls, resolves the conflict and pushes again. That's why the docs suggest retrying a failed sync once.

  • Never run two syncs at once. Guard syncNow() with a flag. Call it when the app starts, on the browser's online event and on a timer.

Production checklist for an offline-first React app

The tutorial code works on your laptop. These are the things that decide whether it survives real users:

  • Ask for persistent storage. By default, browser storage is "best effort" and can be evicted when the device is low on space. Call navigator.storage.persist() after the user has used the app for a while. Firefox shows a prompt. Chrome and Safari decide on their own based on how the user engages with the site.

  • Watch your usage. navigator.storage.estimate() gives a rough figure for usage and quota. Use it to prune old records before you hit QuotaExceededError.

  • Handle quota and setup errors in the UI, not just in the console.

  • Plan for Safari's 7-day rule. With tracking prevention on, Safari deletes script-written storage for an origin the user hasn't interacted with in the last 7 days of browser use. Treat the local database as a cache of the server, never as the only copy.

  • Remember that eviction is all-or-nothing. When an origin is evicted, its IndexedDB, Cache API and other storage go together. Sync often so there is little unsynced data at risk.

  • Write migrations from day one and never delete old ones. Users may open an app version that is months old.

  • Test the bad days. Turn off the network mid-order, open two tabs, fill the disk, log out in one tab. Those are the bugs real users will find.

Don't store secrets in IndexedDB: Anything in IndexedDB can be read by any script running on your origin, including a malicious third-party script. Keep auth tokens short-lived and never cache data the current user isn't allowed to see.

What this means if you own the app

Offline-first is a product decision before it is a technical one. If your users work in kitchens, warehouses, shops, field sites or anywhere with patchy signal, a "you're offline" screen costs you sales and trust. Building it properly means designing the data model and sync rules first, then the screens. Adding it to an existing app later is possible, but usually means reworking how every feature reads and writes data.

A rough guide:

  • Caching a few screens or drafts: IndexedDB with idb is enough.

  • The whole app must keep working offline, with relational data and multiple devices: use WatermelonDB (or a similar sync engine) and budget real time for the backend sync endpoints.

  • Not sure: start by listing what your users must be able to do with no connection. That list decides the architecture.

If you're planning an app that has to work offline, or your current one loses data when the connection drops, see how I approach offline-first app development. For point of sale systems specifically, there is also POS development.

Sources

  • MDN: IndexedDB API

  • MDN: Storage quotas and eviction criteria

  • idb on GitHub and npm

  • WatermelonDB: Installation

  • WatermelonDB: Setup (web adapter)

  • WatermelonDB: Create, Read, Update, Delete

  • WatermelonDB: Sync frontend

  • WatermelonDB: Sync backend

  • WatermelonDB on npm

  • Cover photo: Mohammad Rahmani on Unsplash

I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

title: LoC-Path: Learning to Compress for Pathology Multimodal Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2512.05391v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Whole Slide Image (WSI) multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are difficult to build and deploy because gigapixel slides induce thousands of highly redundant visual tokens that must be learned from sparse slide-level language supervision. Existing slide-level pathology MLLMs typically combine heavy slide-level encoders with long visual prefixes, making development and deployment expensive under limited computational resources. We revisit this regime and show that WSI tile features are highly redundant at both global and local scales, while task-relevant evidence is sparse and query-dependent. We therefore introduce LoC-Path, a resource-efficient slide-level MLLM that compresses before fusion. LoC-Path uses a sparse token merger and a masked-autoencoder (MAE)-pretrained resampler to replace expensive slide-level encoding with a compact latent interface. A token importance scorer selects the most relevant latents and cross-attention routing adapters fuse them into a few LLM decoder layers. This design lowers both multimodal tuning cost and inference-time latency/memory by avoiding heavy slide-level encoding and long visual prefixes. Extensive experiments show that the inference TFLOPs of LoC-Path are 97% lower and inference memory is also 39% lower. LoC-Path enables efficient end-to-end development and deployment under limited computational resources while remaining competitive with prior slide-level MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/WinstonHuTiger/loc_path.

arXiv:2609.16023v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Medical evaluation is shifting from static option-based questioning to realistic clinical scenarios with open-ended output modes. Grading these at scale naively, however, is expensive, and rubric-based evaluation has become the dominant scalable alternative. We ask what happens when the rubrics themselves are not airtight, and whether such flaws can be detected and corrected. We apply RIFT, a global rubric failure taxonomy, to three clinical benchmarks (HealthBench Professional, LiveMedBench, and MentalHealthBench), and find failure modes are meaningful: on HealthBench Professional an LLM judge flags 29.6% of criteria as non-atomic and 65.4% as misaligned/rigid, although these rates vary severalfold across five detection judges. Then, we show that these flaws are meaningful and not simply cosmetic. As an example, rewriting bundled criteria of the form "at least one of / all of the following" as equally weighted children and regrading identical responses shifts scores by up to 15.9 percentage points on affected conversations, with disjunctive bundles inflating scores and conjunctive bundles deflating them. Across six answering models and two common graders, these shifts leave the model ranking unchanged, and their net direction depends on how many bundled criteria are penalties. We also find that RIFT can under-detect bundling on clinical rubrics, by an amount that depends on the detection judge: on the same LiveMedBench criteria, judges flag 3.8-15.9% as non-atomic against an estimated 7-19% that are genuinely bundled.

title: Amazon MSK now supports in-place upgrade from Standard brokers to Express brokers
description:
You can now upgrade existing Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters from Standard brokers to Express brokers in place, with fully managed data migration and no application changes. Express brokers are designed to deliver up to 3x more throughput per broker, scale up to 20x faster, and recover up to 90% faster compared to Standard brokers. With in-place upgrade, you can get the performance and operational benefits of Express brokers in hours, without needing to create a new cluster or having to migrate your data and applications to it. The upgrade keeps cluster endpoints unchanged, eliminating application cutovers, and preserves consumer offsets, so stateful applications such as Apache Flink and Kafka Streams continue without reprocessing or duplicates.

Express brokers make Apache Kafka simpler to manage and more cost-effective to run at scale, with pay-as-you-go storage that scales automatically and built-in best practice defaults for higher resilience. Previously, upgrading to Express brokers meant creating a new cluster and migrating workloads to it, which required careful planning and cross-team coordination. With this launch, you can upgrade your existing Standard brokers to Express brokers in-place, without interrupting your applications, while maintaining complete control over the upgrade process. The upgrade adds Express brokers to your cluster and moves your topics to them, either automatically or in batches you control. Your Standard brokers stay in the cluster until you choose to decommission them to complete the upgrade, so you can validate your applications and roll back if needed.

In-place upgrade is available for MSK Provisioned clusters running Standard brokers on Apache Kafka version 3.9 with KRaft, in all AWS Regions where Express brokers are available. You can upgrade to Express brokers on M7g or M8g instances. Express brokers on M8g deliver up to 30% cost savings compared to Express brokers on M7g. There's no additional charge for the upgrade itself. You pay for both Standard and Express brokers while the upgrade is in progress. To get started, visit the Amazon MSK Developer Guide and the Migration to Express brokers product page.

title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
description:
arXiv:2611.25071v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
description:
arXiv:2611.25226v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10^{-6} FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.

title: AI Agent Deployment Gates: How to Scale Productivity Without Losing Control
description:
AI agents can already complete parts of multi-hour tasks, but their performance remains uneven. Businesses need deployment gates that combine measurable outcomes, restricted access, and human escalation.

AI adoption in business is entering a new phase. The question is no longer simply whether employees use chatbots. Increasingly, organizations are working with agents that can analyze information, write code, monitor processes, and complete tasks that previously required several hours of human effort.

Yet the latest research material points to an important conclusion: AI progress is uneven. An agent may perform strongly in one part of a workflow while still requiring close human supervision in another. A mature deployment model should therefore be built around controlled gates rather than unrestricted automation.

Agent capabilities are uneven

OpenAI’s research acceleration report shows that agent performance varies significantly by task. Agents now complete nearly half of tasks estimated to require two to four hours of human work, but the results depend heavily on the nature of the task.

For example, the reported success rate was 79 percent for monitoring training runs, 35 percent for launching them, and 25 percent for writing code for inference and serving systems. A single measure of “AI automation” can therefore be misleading. Organizations need to evaluate specific actions, not just the technology label.

The practical lesson is straightforward: break a workflow into individual tasks and assign each one its own level of trust.

Three deployment gates for business

1. The outcome gate

The first gate defines what the agent is expected to achieve and how quality will be assessed. This should not be an abstract promise of productivity. It might be a shorter analysis cycle, less manual coding, or faster preparation of a management proposal.

The Sumitomo Life case shows why usage volume alone is not enough. The company tracks how employees use ChatGPT, which parts of their work it supports, and how usage relates to reported time savings. The company reports an overall estimated ROI of 203 percent and an estimated 524 percent ROI among employees using the tool at least 101 times per month. These figures are based on employee-reported time savings and should not be treated as a universal promise, but they illustrate why organizations should measure practical impact.

2. The access gate

The second gate defines what the agent can see and change. The Codex sandbox approach relies on restricting access to the filesystem and network. This allows an agent to perform useful work while limiting the potential impact of mistakes or unwanted data transfers.

In a business environment, this means an agent does not automatically need administrator privileges. It may be allowed to read selected documents, work inside a project area, or prepare changes for review while leaving the final action to a person.

3. The escalation gate

The third gate defines when the agent must stop and hand the task back to a human. This is especially important in finance, legal work, customer service, and software development.

The frontier AI risk framework emphasizes defense in depth. During research and training, organizations use sandboxes, virtual machines, network restrictions, and monitoring. During internal and external deployment, behavioral testing, monitoring, and safeguards against misuse become increasingly important.

For a business, the principle can be stated simply: the greater the agent’s access and potential impact, the more independent layers of control are required.

Leadership matters more than one-time training

Technology adoption does not happen simply because employees receive accounts. The Sumitomo Life case suggests that executives and managers helped move the organization from a pilot to broader adoption by using the technology themselves and encouraging employees to try it.

Leadership, however, should not mean pressuring teams to use AI everywhere. A stronger signal is to explain where the tool creates value, what data must not be shared, and when human review is mandatory.

What does a mature first project look like?

A good initial project has limited scope, a defined outcome, and measurable risk. For example, a planning team can use an agent to review public sources and prepare an initial proposal structure. Experts can then verify the findings and add firsthand context.

Another example is using AI to draft statistical analysis code. Analysts can accelerate the preparatory work while checking the assumptions, data, and calculation logic before using the result. The agent speeds up the workflow without taking responsibility for the final decision.

Control is not the opposite of productivity

AI discussions often move between two extremes: giving agents maximum autonomy or avoiding them because of potential risk. The research material suggests a more practical path. Agent capabilities are already sufficient for some tasks, but performance remains uneven and risk depends on access and context.

Business advantage will therefore belong not necessarily to the organization that automates everything first, but to the one that best connects three elements: a measurable outcome, limited access, and continuous evaluation. This allows AI use to expand gradually while preserving the ability to understand, verify, and stop an agent’s actions when necessary.

Conclusion: AI agent deployment should be managed as an architecture of access and trust. Each new level of autonomy should be supported by measured results, safe boundaries, and a clear escalation rule. This reduces risk and helps turn productivity gains into a sustainable operating model.

Originally published at insights.aisys.lt/di-agentu-diegimo-vartai-kaip-auginti-produktyvuma-neprarandant-kontroles.

title: A Unified Plug-and-Play Algorithm with Projected Landweber Operator for Split Convex Feasibility Problems
description:
arXiv:2408.12100v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In recent years Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods have achieved state-of-the-art performance in inverse imaging problems by replacing proximal operators with denoisers. Based on the proximal gradient method, some theoretical results of PnP have appeared, where appropriate step size is crucial for convergence analysis. However, in practical applications, applying PnP methods with theoretically guaranteed step sizes is difficult, and these algorithms are limited to Gaussian noise. In this paper,from a perspective of split convex feasibility problems (SCFP), an adaptive PnP algorithm with Projected Landweber Operator (PnP-PLO) is proposed to address these issues. Numerical experiments on image deblurring, super-resolution, and compressed sensing MRI experiments illustrate that PnP-PLO with theoretical guarantees outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as RED and RED-PRO.

title: How PERT Estimation Assists in Better Project Planning
description:
Project planning is a crucial component for the successful execution of any project, be it a website, a product development or a management task. Sufficient planning would involve breaking down all the tasks to be handled and estimating the time you would take in completing each of them. But this isn't necessarily an easy task to do!

That's where PERT comes in. PERT - which is short for Program Evaluation and Review Technique - is a project management technique that involves predicting task durations based on three separate duration estimates as opposed to a single estimate or guess. https://projecttimecalculator.com/pert-calculator/

What is PERT Estimation?

PERT calculation considers three different values for the tasks: Optimistic; Pessimistic; and Most Likely.

The longest realistic time the job should take.

The specified time that a task will probably take when performed normally.

Pessimistic estimate (P): The upper time limit within which the task will be completed when faced with unforeseen difficulties.

With these three estimates, project managers will be able to plan a schedule more realistically and help plan for delay.

How to Calculate Expected Project Time

The PERT formula is simple and gives more weight to the most likely estimate.

Expected Time = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6

A website development project can be estimated with three values: an optimistic estimate of 5 days, a most likely estimate of 8 days, and a pessimistic estimate of 17 days.

Using the formula:

Expected Time = (5 + 4 × 8 + 17) ÷ 6

Expected Time = 54 ÷ 6 = 9 days.

This is an estimate of the length of time it will take for team members to complete a specific task.

Why Is PERT Important for Project Managers?

Project managers are regularly faced with uncertain time frames for completing projects, evolving expectations for project deliverables and unexpected difficulties during the life cycle of a project. PERT (Program Evaluation Review Technique) provides a method of reducing the uncertainty associated with developing a schedule for a project through the development of numerous estimates.

This software helps teams determine which tasks require additional time, allocate resources more efficiently, and make better decisions regarding project deadlines. It is especially beneficial for projects that include multiple sequential tasks.

A PERT (program evaluation and review technique) calculator can help you calculate the expected time for a project to be completed, its variability, the standard deviation of its completion time, and how likely it is that you will finish the project before your deadline.

Estimation Techniques that Improve Projects Schedules

In developing timelines for projects, realistic estimates should always be considered. There is no need to make estimates under the assumption of idealistic situations. It's important to think about the possible problems, availability of necessary resources, and complexity of tasks to be accomplished.
The splitting up of a large task into manageable small parts can assist with the estimate as well. After all of the manageable small parts have been estimated for the amount of time required to accomplish them, then the total will give you the estimate of completing the large task.

Conclusion

PERT (Program Evaluation & Review Technique) may be a great tool for project managers in developing better schedules and dealing with uncertainty of project deadlines. After making an evaluation of the best, the most probable, and the worst case scenarios, the project manager can get a better schedule and be closer to meeting project deadlines.

There would be much more organization and effectiveness in project management if there were proper estimation techniques and identifying of potential unknowns.

title: Agent as Policy for Robotic Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2609.12541v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We demonstrate that a general-purpose coding agent can directly drive a physical robot throughout task execution without any task-specific or environment-specific training. We introduce Agent as Policy (AGP), which places task planning and execution under the agent's control. Given a task and a robot interface, the agent interprets visual evidence, writes executable programs, issues motion commands, and revises its actions in response to physical outcomes. This brings the agent's reasoning and programming capabilities into continuous interaction with the physical world. We study AGP across multiple real-world manipulation tasks spanning precision manipulation, dynamic motions, and deformable objects. These include assembly from human videos, block construction from goal images, dice flipping, targeted throwing, and bimanual towel folding. AGP achieves success rates of at least 80% in seven of eight task configurations and significantly outperforms previous agentic robot systems. We further study efficiency through task experience accumulation and find that reusing saved procedures and programs shortens execution time across repeated trials. These findings support a path for general-purpose agents to act as robot policies, extending their autonomy to physical manipulation through runtime reasoning, programming, and interaction.

title: Why I Chose a Node.js Queue for Browser Image Uploads to Object Storage (and Webhooks)
description:
Short answer: upload the original image from the browser straight to private object storage, finalize it in the backend, and put a small job on a Node.js queue for thumbnail generation. Use a storage notification or webhook only as a delivery signal. The backend database remains the authority for tenant access and processing state.

That split keeps large bytes away from the application process. It also gives every retry a clear boundary. The browser moves bytes. The API grants a narrowly scoped upload. A worker reads a finalized original and writes deterministic thumbnail keys. A notification wakes the worker; it does not grant permission.

I choose this shape for a gaming media pipeline where players upload large screenshots or clips and the UI needs a quick preview. I've learned to draw the trust boundary before choosing a queue library. Otherwise a perfectly good resize function ends up deciding who may read an image.

What should a browser upload prove before a Node.js worker generates thumbnails?

The upload starts with an authenticated request for an upload intent. The backend derives a key from the account and asset IDs, records the expected content type and size, and returns a short-lived signed upload operation. The browser sends the original image directly to object storage. XMLHttpRequest can expose upload progress events for the progress bar; the application server never has to proxy the image bytes (see the MDN reference below).

The browser then calls a finalize operation. Finalize is important because an object appearing in storage is not the same thing as an authorized, complete asset. In one database transaction, the backend checks the tenant, expected metadata, and an idempotency token, then marks the asset ready for processing. A notification that arrives before that commit is simply deferred or ignored by the worker.

Here is the part I keep copyable. The queue interface is deliberately generic, so the access checks stay visible instead of hiding inside a vendor SDK.

type ThumbnailJob = {
  tenantId: string;
  assetId: string;
  originalKey: string;
  widths: number[];
};

async function processThumbnailJob(job: ThumbnailJob) {
  const asset = await db.assets.find(job.assetId);
  if (!asset || asset.tenantId !== job.tenantId || asset.status !== "ready") {
    return; // Duplicate or early delivery is a no-op.
  }

  const original = await objects.get(job.originalKey);
  for (const width of job.widths) {
    const thumbnail = await resizeToWidth(original, width);
    const key = `tenants/${job.tenantId}/assets/${job.assetId}/thumb-${width}.webp`;
    await objects.put(key, thumbnail, { contentType: "image/webp" });
  }

  await db.assets.markThumbnailsReady(job.assetId, job.widths);
}

Notice what the job does not contain: a bearer token, a public URL, or an arbitrary bucket path. The object key is only a routing hint. The database check decides access. I log the tenant ID, asset ID, event ID, and attempt number; I don't log signed URLs or image bytes.

Small boundary. Big payoff.

How do object-storage webhooks, notifications, and a Node.js queue fit together?

A webhook is an HTTP delivery attempt to your receiver. A native storage notification may deliver to a queue directly. Either way, delivery is a signal that must be persisted and deduplicated. RFC 9110 is useful here: a successful HTTP response reports handling of the request, not completion of downstream thumbnail work.

The receiver should verify the message signature when one is provided, insert the event ID into an inbox table, acknowledge quickly, and enqueue only new events. The queue then supplies backpressure when a game launch produces a burst of uploads.

type StorageEvent = {
  id: string;
  tenantId: string;
  assetId: string;
  originalKey: string;
};

async function acceptStorageEvent(event: StorageEvent) {
  const inserted = await db.inbox.insertIfNew(event.id, event);
  if (!inserted) return;

  await thumbnailQueue.add("generate", {
    tenantId: event.tenantId,
    assetId: event.assetId,
    originalKey: event.originalKey,
    widths: [320, 640, 1280],
  }, { jobId: event.id });
}

The queue must tolerate duplicates and retries. A deterministic thumbnail key makes a retry idempotent. If the storage system supports conditional writes, use them when replacing an existing derivative would be dangerous. Mark the asset ready only after every required width exists; a partial set should be observable as partial, not reported as success.

This is where metrics help. Track upload-finalize latency, notification-to-worker latency, retry count, abandoned uploads, and the age of the oldest queued job. Alert on a growing queue and on a high ratio of finalized originals with no completed thumbnail set. Those signals tell you whether the problem is delivery, authorization, or image processing.

The access-control trade-off is bigger than the transfer speed

Keep originals private. A signed upload operation delegates one transfer; it does not replace the application authorization check. On download, authenticate the player, verify ownership of the asset row, and mint a short-lived signed read operation. Never let a client submit an arbitrary prefix and treat that as an export. Prefixes are naming conventions, not policy.

The before-and-after mental model is simple:

Before After
API receives every image byte Browser sends bytes directly to object storage
Upload completion implies processing Finalize transaction creates an explicit ready state
Notification triggers trusted work Notification is deduplicated input to a tenant-checked job
Thumbnail names vary per retry Keys are deterministic and safe to replay

There is a real cost. The service now owns an upload-intent record, an inbox, queue retries, dead-letter review, and cleanup for abandoned originals. I'm not sure every small internal tool needs those moving parts. If files are tiny, traffic is low, and one trusted operator owns the catalog, a synchronous multipart endpoint can be easier to test and operate. Stick with the simpler path when your recovery drill cannot exercise the queue and cleanup states.

What should I test before calling the image pipeline finished?

Test the gaps, not only the happy path. Upload an original, delay finalize, then deliver the same storage event twice. Revoke the user session before the worker runs. Submit an event whose tenant ID does not match the asset row. Kill a worker after writing one thumbnail and replay the job. In a useful replay script, I give each event a fixed ID, advance a fake clock between upload and finalize, and record the database row after every worker attempt. I then inspect the object keys, not just the queue result: there should be no key outside the tenant prefix, no second derivative with a random suffix, and no success state while one requested width is missing. Finally, I run the same sequence with a stale signed upload operation and with a duplicate finalize request. The expected result is one authorized derivative set, no cross-tenant reads, and a visible retry or partial state when work is interrupted.

The browser should also handle a rejected or expired signed operation without exposing credentials. A fresh upload intent can be requested after the user is still authorized. Keep retry delays bounded, and record the reason for each retry so a temporary delivery pause is distinguishable from a bad object key.

The catch is delivery simplicity versus access control. Direct browser uploads reduce proxy bandwidth and make progress reporting pleasant, but they add state that must be cleaned up. A worker queue absorbs bursts, but it cannot make an unsafe object key safe. Choose this architecture when the original files are large and thumbnail work is asynchronous; choose a smaller synchronous design when those conditions do not hold.

That decision is easy to revisit. Keep the upload intent, finalize record, event inbox, and thumbnail status as separate records, and you can change the queue or resize implementation without changing the browser contract. If the team cannot name who owns each record during an outage, the design is still too implicit.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XMLHttpRequest_API/Using_XMLHttpRequest

title: Quita tus 3 mejores trades: la prueba de 5 minutos que desarma un backtest
description:
En corto: antes de creerle a un backtest, borra sus 3 mejores operaciones y vuelve a calcular. Si el resultado cambia de signo, lo más probable es que no tengas una estrategia, sino tres golpes de suerte (hay una excepción, la explico más abajo). Abajo está el código en pandas, un ejemplo que se puede reproducir y los casos en que esta prueba engaña.

El problema: el promedio esconde de dónde viene la ganancia

Un backtest te devuelve un número: ganancia total, profit factor, Sharpe. Lo que no te dice es cómo se reparte esa ganancia entre las operaciones.

Dos estrategias pueden terminar con el mismo resultado total:

  • una gana un poco en muchas operaciones;
  • otra pierde un poco en casi todas y se salva con dos o tres operaciones enormes (un pump, una noticia, un hueco de precio).

La primera tiene algo que se puede repetir. La segunda depende de que vuelvan a pasar exactamente esos eventos, y en el mismo lado.

Un ejemplo que puedes correr

Datos sintéticos (inventados a propósito, no son resultados reales de nadie): 200 operaciones normales con resultado medio levemente negativo, más 3 operaciones excepcionales.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# 200 trades "normales": resultado medio levemente negativo (costos incluidos)
normales = rng.normal(loc=-0.05, scale=1.0, size=200)
# 3 trades excepcionales (un pump, una noticia, un hueco de precio)
excepcionales = np.array([9.0, 7.5, 6.0])

trades = pd.DataFrame({"pnl": np.concatenate([normales, excepcionales])})
trades = trades.sample(frac=1, random_state=7).reset_index(drop=True)

def resumen(pnl: pd.Series) -> dict:
    ganancias = pnl[pnl > 0].sum()
    perdidas = -pnl[pnl < 0].sum()
    return {
        "trades": len(pnl),
        "pnl_total": round(float(pnl.sum()), 2),
        "profit_factor": round(float(ganancias / perdidas), 2),
        "win_rate": round(float((pnl > 0).mean()), 3),
    }

def sin_top_k(pnl: pd.Series, k: int) -> pd.Series:
    return pnl.sort_values(ascending=False).iloc[k:]

print("Con todo:  ", resumen(trades["pnl"]))
print("Sin top-3: ", resumen(sin_top_k(trades["pnl"], 3)))

Salida:

Con todo:   {'trades': 203, 'pnl_total': 6.41, 'profit_factor': 1.08, 'win_rate': 0.478}
Sin top-3:  {'trades': 200, 'pnl_total': -16.09, 'profit_factor': 0.8, 'win_rate': 0.47}

Con todo, la estrategia "gana": profit factor 1.08. Sin las 3 mejores, pierde: profit factor 0.80. El win rate casi no cambia (47.8% → 47.0%), por eso mirar solo el win rate no te avisa de nada.

La curva de fragilidad

Quitar exactamente 3 es una convención. Es más informativo ver qué pasa al quitar 0, 1, 2… hasta 10:

for k in range(0, 11):
    print(f"sin top-{k:<2} pnl_total = {sin_top_k(trades['pnl'], k).sum():7.2f}")

sin top-0  pnl_total =    6.41
sin top-1  pnl_total =   -2.59
sin top-2  pnl_total =  -10.09
sin top-3  pnl_total =  -16.09
sin top-4  pnl_total =  -18.95
sin top-5  pnl_total =  -21.05
sin top-6  pnl_total =  -23.12
sin top-7  pnl_total =  -25.07
sin top-8  pnl_total =  -26.79
sin top-9  pnl_total =  -28.46
sin top-10 pnl_total =  -30.06

Aquí basta con quitar una sola operación para que el resultado cambie de signo.

Y una métrica que lo resume:

total = trades["pnl"].sum()
top3 = trades["pnl"].nlargest(3).sum()
print(f"Los 3 mejores trades explican el {top3 / total:.0%} del resultado total")

Los 3 mejores trades explican el 351% del resultado total

Si el total es positivo, más de 100% significa que el resto de las operaciones, juntas, pierden.

Contraste: cómo se ve una estrategia que aguanta la prueba

Para que quede claro que la prueba no descarta todo: una estrategia con una ventaja pequeña pero repartida (datos sintéticos de nuevo).

sana = pd.Series(rng.normal(loc=0.15, scale=1.0, size=203))
print("Sana con todo: ", resumen(sana))
print("Sana sin top-3: ", resumen(sin_top_k(sana, 3)))

Sana con todo:  {'trades': 203, 'pnl_total': 35.3, 'profit_factor': 1.54, 'win_rate': 0.581}
Sana sin top-3:  {'trades': 200, 'pnl_total': 27.1, 'profit_factor': 1.42, 'win_rate': 0.575}

Baja, como es lógico, pero no cambia de signo ni se desarma.

Cuándo esta prueba engaña

1. Estrategias que viven de los extremos. Algunas estrategias, como las de seguimiento de tendencia, están diseñadas para perder poco muchas veces y ganar mucho pocas veces. A esas, quitarles el top-3 siempre les hace daño. Ahí la pregunta útil es otra: ¿cuántos de esos extremos hay en tu muestra y con qué frecuencia aparecen? Con 3 extremos en 5 años, no sabes casi nada. Con 40, empiezas a saber algo.

2. Pocas operaciones. Con 30 trades, quitar 3 es quitar el 10% de la muestra. Mira la curva completa, no un solo número.

3. Compáralo contra el azar. Una prueba más fuerte: genera entradas aleatorias con la misma cantidad de operaciones y el mismo tiempo en el mercado, aplica la misma curva de fragilidad y compara. Si tu estrategia se desarma igual que el azar, la ventaja no está en tus reglas.

Decídelo antes de mirar

La trampa más común no es olvidarse de esta prueba. Es correrla, ver que falla y empezar a buscar razones para que "esos 3 trades sí cuenten".

Por eso conviene escribir la regla antes de ver el resultado. Por ejemplo: "si sin el top-3 el resultado cambia de signo, la estrategia se archiva". Si tu estrategia vive de los extremos, ajusta la regla a eso antes de mirar (por ejemplo, exigir un mínimo de extremos en la muestra), no después. Sobre eso escribí aquí: Escribí las reglas antes de ver los resultados.

Esta prueba es una de las 7 de una guía gratuita que preparé: 7 sesgos que inflan tu backtest (PDF en español, con código en pandas y una checklist de una página).

Material educativo de metodología. No contiene señales, recomendaciones de inversión ni proyecciones de rentabilidad. Todos los números de este artículo salen de datos sintéticos.

title: EgoPass-Bench: Identifying Objects That May Affect the Wearer's Passage in Egocentric Video
description:
arXiv:2611.24995v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
description:
Vercel Blob can now delete blobs automatically. Pass ttlDays when you write a blob and it is deleted that many days after upload, from 1 to 730 days. The TTL counts from the blob's upload date.

Use TTLs for blobs you would otherwise delete yourself, such as session transcripts, exports, and temporary uploads.

ttlDays works on put(), copy(), putImage(), multipart uploads, and presigned upload URLs. Every write result and head() response now includes expiresAt, so you know when a blob is due for deletion.

setTtl() changes or removes the TTL of blobs you already have, one URL or up to 1,000 at a time, without re-uploading them.

In Vercel CLI 65.16.0 and later, pass --ttl-days to vercel blob put, put-image, copy or presign, and use vercel blob set-ttl on existing blobs.

Setting a TTL costs one Advanced Operation per started 60 days, on top of the write. A 7-day TTL costs one, and the 730-day maximum costs 13. Clearing a TTL and the deletions themselves are free. You can track TTL operations in the Blob section of the Observability tab.

npm install @vercel/blob@2.9.0

Learn more in the Vercel Blob documentation.
