title: Beyond the Prompt: Why Your AI Chose a Spinner Instead of a Skeleton
description:
The real work of an AI agent doesn’t necessarily begin when you press Enter.

"Create a loading component."

That's it.

One sentence.

No extra context.

No design guidelines.

No UX requirements.

No product description.

Yet an AI coding agent somehow returns a complete component.

Maybe it's a spinner.

Maybe it's a skeleton screen.

Maybe it's a progress bar.

Maybe it doesn't render anything at all.

At first glance, it feels like magic.

But the interesting part isn't the component that was generated.

The interesting part is everything the AI decided before writing the first line of code.

That's what this series is about.

Welcome to Beyond the Prompt.

The Prompt Is Only the Beginning

When people talk about AI-assisted development, they usually focus on prompts.

"Prompt engineering is the future."

"Just write better prompts."

But prompts are only inputs.

The real engineering happens after the model receives them.

An autonomous coding agent doesn't simply autocomplete code.

It starts making decisions.

Lots of them.

Some are obvious.

Most are invisible.

For something as simple as a loading component, the agent has to answer questions that the user never asked.

  • Is this page loading once or continuously?
  • Is there existing UI that should remain visible?
  • Is the loading duration expected to be milliseconds or several seconds?
  • Does the application already have a design system?
  • Is accessibility required?
  • Is the component reusable?
  • Is this mobile?
  • Desktop?
  • Dashboard?
  • Form?
  • Table?
  • Search results?

None of these questions were in the prompt.

Yet every answer changes the implementation.

The First Decision: What Kind of Loading Is This?

One of the earliest choices an AI agent makes is identifying what is actually loading.

Not every loading state represents the same user experience, which means not every situation deserves the same loading component.

Fetching an Entire Page

A Skeleton is usually the best choice.

The user is waiting for content that hasn't been rendered yet, so showing the page structure helps reduce uncertainty and makes the application feel faster.

Waiting for a Button Action

A Spinner inside the button is often enough.

The rest of the interface is already available. The user only needs confirmation that their action is being processed.

Uploading a File

A Progress Bar is the better option.

Unlike a spinner, it tells users how much work remains, which becomes increasingly important as the operation takes longer.

Streaming an AI Response

In many cases, the best loading state is no traditional loader at all.

Displaying the content as it's generated creates a more natural experience than making users wait for the complete response.

Refreshing Data in the Background

Sometimes the best loading component is none.

If users can continue interacting with the application, a subtle indicator - or no indicator at all - often creates a smoother experience than interrupting the interface with a visible loader.

Notice something.

The loading component isn't chosen because it looks better.

It's chosen because it communicates a different kind of progress.

A spinner says:

Something is happening.

A skeleton says:

The content is coming, and this is roughly where it will appear.

A progress bar says:

We know how much work is left.

These aren't just different UI components.

They're different ways of communicating with the user.

Why Skeletons Often Feel Faster

One of the biggest UX discoveries over the last decade is that perceived performance matters almost as much as actual performance.

Imagine waiting three seconds.

Version A

Version B

Still three seconds.

Yet users consistently report the second experience as faster.

Nothing changed technically.

Everything changed psychologically.

Skeleton screens reduce uncertainty.

They tell users:

"The page already exists. We're just filling it in."

Why an Agent Might Ignore Skeletons

Now here's something interesting.

Many developers assume that skeletons are always better.

They're not.

Imagine clicking a button that triggers a network request lasting 400 milliseconds.

Rendering a complex skeleton for less than half a second creates unnecessary visual noise.

An AI agent evaluating this scenario might decide:

  • Spinner
  • No animation
  • Optimistic update
  • Keep previous content visible

instead of replacing the UI with placeholders.

Again, the decision isn't aesthetic.

It's contextual.

Context Changes Everything

Suppose the prompt is still exactly the same.

Create a loading component.

Now imagine four different applications.

Banking App

Trust matters.

Aggressive animations can make financial operations feel unreliable.

A subtle progress indicator is usually preferable.

Social Media Feed

Content is consumed continuously.

Skeleton cards preserve layout stability.

File Upload

Users care about completion.

A progress percentage is far more valuable than an infinite spinner.

AI Chat

The response is generated token by token.

The best loading state may be…

No loading state at all.

Streaming content often feels more natural than waiting for completion.

Same prompt.

Four different answers.

Invisible Constraints

Modern coding agents rarely work in an empty project.

They're usually analyzing an existing codebase.

That changes everything.

Before writing a loading component, an agent may inspect:

  • Existing design system
  • UI library
  • Component naming conventions
  • Theme tokens
  • Accessibility helpers
  • Animation utilities
  • Existing Loader component
  • Storybook documentation
  • ESLint rules
  • TypeScript configuration

If the project already contains:

<LoadingSpinner size="md" />

creating another spinner component would actually be a bad decision.

The best code is often the code that isn't written.

The Accessibility Decision

Loading indicators aren't only visual.

Screen readers also need to understand what's happening.

An experienced engineer immediately thinks about:

aria-busy="true"

or

role="status"

or announcing completion once loading finishes.

An AI agent trained on production-quality patterns may include these automatically.

Not because the prompt requested accessibility.

Because accessibility is part of good engineering.

Performance Is Also a Design Decision

Performance Is Also a Design Decision

Suppose your skeleton consists of twenty animated placeholders.

Each uses gradients.

Each animates indefinitely.

Looks beautiful.

Now place fifty of them inside a virtualized table.

Suddenly your loading animation becomes one of the most expensive parts of the page.

Good loading components should disappear quickly.

That doesn't mean they should be expensive while they're alive.

Design Systems Change the Question

In mature engineering organizations, developers rarely ask:

"Should we use a spinner or a skeleton?"

That decision has often already been made.

A well-designed Design System defines when each feedback pattern should be used, creating consistency across the entire product.

For example, the guidelines might look something like this:

Component When to use
Spinner When the duration of an operation is unknown.
Skeleton When replacing content that hasn't loaded yet.
Progress Bar When the application can measure how much work remains.
Linear Progress For background operations that shouldn't interrupt the user.
Toast To communicate that an operation has completed successfully.

These aren't hard rules.

They're conventions that help every team build a consistent user experience.

An AI agent working inside an established codebase isn't inventing a loading pattern from scratch.

Instead, it's looking for the product's existing language.

If the Design System already defines that lists always use skeletons, generating a spinner would actually be the wrong decision - even if it technically works.

This is one of the biggest differences between writing code and building products.

The correct answer isn't always the one that solves the problem.

It's the one that solves the problem the same way the rest of the product does.

Understanding those conventions often matters more than understanding React itself.

What Actually Happened Inside the Agent?

From the outside, it looks like this:

Prompt
  ↓
Code

Reality is much closer to this:

Prompt
  ↓
Understand intent
  ↓
Identify user experience
  ↓
Inspect project conventions
  ↓
Find reusable components
  ↓
Evaluate accessibility
  ↓
Evaluate performance
  ↓
Choose loading strategy
  ↓
Generate implementation

The code is almost the final step.

The interesting work happened long before.

How to Apply This Today

The next time you ask an AI agent to build something, don't stop at the generated code.

Instead, ask questions like:

  • Why did you choose a spinner?
  • Why not a skeleton?
  • What alternatives did you consider?
  • What assumptions did you make?
  • What information was missing from my prompt?
  • How would this change for a mobile app?
  • Would your decision be different if this were a design system component?

These follow-up questions expose the reasoning behind the implementation.

And that's often more valuable than the code itself.

The goal isn't to make the AI justify every line.

It's to understand the trade-offs that led to the solution.

That's how you move from using AI as an autocomplete tool to collaborating with it as an engineering partner.

Final Thoughts

A loading component seems trivial.

It's one of the first things most frontend developers learn to build.

But it's also a perfect example of something larger.

The prompt may contain only seven words:

"Create a loading component."

Yet those seven words trigger dozens of engineering decisions.

Some relate to UX.

Others to accessibility.

Some to performance.

Others to consistency with an existing design system.

The component you see is only the visible result of those decisions.

The real work happened long before the first return ( appeared in the editor.

That's what Beyond the Prompt is really about.

Not the prompts we write.

But the engineering decisions that happen after them.

Because once you start seeing those invisible decisions, you'll realize something important:

Great AI-assisted development isn't about getting code faster. It's about understanding why that code was the right choice in the first place.

title: Uber reduz em mais de 90% a memória inicial do cache de traduções em Go
description:
Cache híbrido reduz uso de memória

A Uber redesenhou seu cache de traduções em Go para reduzir em mais de 90% o consumo inicial de memória sem perder eficiência. A arquitetura híbrida mantém chaves e valores acessados com frequência na memória e armazena os demais valores em disco. O sistema atende milhões de traduções por segundo, com taxa de acerto superior a 99,9%.

Alocações pressionavam a coleta de lixo

O perfilamento de serviços da empresa mostrou que a coleta de lixo consumia mais de 20% da CPU em alguns casos, enquanto as traduções respondiam por cerca de 70% dos objetos alocados. Como primeira otimização, a equipe substituiu sync.Map por um map[string]string protegido por RWMutex, adequado ao padrão de muitas leituras e poucas atualizações do serviço.

Uma primeira mudança não bastou

A troca reduziu objetos e ponteiros criados para cada tradução e levou a uma melhora superior a 30% na utilização de CPU no serviço afetado. Ainda assim, conjuntos com dois a três milhões de chaves mantinham um custo elevado, embora cada serviço normalmente acessasse apenas uma pequena parte delas. Atualizações do cache também podiam manter duas cópias na memória ao mesmo tempo.

Valores pouco usados vão para disco

Para evitar esse pico durante atualizações, a Uber adotou o armazenamento híbrido mantendo a mesma API Get() e Put(). Todas as chaves continuam disponíveis na memória para buscas rápidas, enquanto os valores das traduções ficam em arquivos respaldados por disco. A empresa considerou cache externo e subconjuntos específicos por serviço, mas essas opções trariam custos adicionais de operação ou manutenção.

Divisão em fragmentos e gestão de acesso

A implementação distribui os dados por 256 fragmentos, cada um com seu próprio bloqueio de leitura e escrita, entradas em memória e arquivo em disco. Chaves baseadas em hashes de seis bytes reduzem o custo de metadados, com retorno ao formato original para lidar com colisões. Uma política global de LRU baseada no tempo mantém os itens usados com maior frequência.

Atualizações preservam dados recentes

Antes de trocar o cache, o serviço usa o histórico de acessos para carregar previamente as traduções consultadas nos 15 minutos anteriores, evitando que a nova versão comece sem dados frequentes. Em um exemplo, um conjunto que antes ocupava cerca de 800 MB passou a exigir aproximadamente 40 MB de metadados; com limite de 50 mil itens em memória, o uso real ficou entre 80 MB e 120 MB.

Métricas orientam a escolha da arquitetura

Em outra carga relatada pela Uber, cerca de 30 mil de mais de quatro milhões de entradas ficaram na memória, com taxa de acerto acima de 99,9%. A latência p99 para falhas de cache atendidas pelo disco permaneceu abaixo de 100 microssegundos. Em outro resultado divulgado, o uso de memória caiu de aproximadamente 2,7 GB para 750 MB. A experiência reforça a recomendação de reduzir referências de objetos e medir a frequência de acesso antes de manter grandes conjuntos inteiros em memória.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/uber-reduz-memoria-inicial-de-cache-de-traducoes-em-go/

title: React Hook useEffect Has a Missing Dependency: Every Fix
description:
The warning looks like this, and if you work in React or Next.js you have seen it many times:

React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency: 'userId'. Either include it or remove the dependency array
  react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

It comes from the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ESLint rule. Next.js ships it in eslint-config-next, and Vite's React template enables it too. The rule compares the values an effect reads with the values in its dependency array. When one is missing, React keeps running the effect with an old copy of that value. That is a bug, even when the page looks fine today.

The rule tells you what is missing. It doesn't tell you which of the usual fixes is right, and some of the quick fixes cause an infinite loop. To get this post's examples and messages right, I ran the rule (eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1, React 19.3.1) against ten small components. Every warning quoted below is copied from that run.

What the rule flags and what it ignores

The rule only asks for values that can change between renders. Some values are known to be stable, so it never asks for them. This is what came back for each case:


eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 against ten components, 19 Nov 2026.

The two dispatch results are worth noticing. A dispatch from useReducer is not flagged, because React guarantees it never changes. A dispatch from Redux's useDispatch() is flagged. It comes from a custom hook, and the rule can't see inside one. navigate from React Router is flagged for the same reason. If you search "missing dependency dispatch" or "missing dependency navigate", that is why.

Fix 1: add the dependency (most of the time this is the answer)

This is the most common case: a prop or state value is used inside the effect but missing from the array.

function Profile({ userId }) {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
  }, []); // warning: missing dependency 'userId'

  return <p>{name}</p>;
}

The empty array means "run once". So when userId changes, the profile keeps showing the first user's name. Adding userId fixes the bug. Once the effect can run more than once, also add a cleanup flag, so a slow response for the old user can't overwrite the new one:

useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetchUser(userId).then((u) => {
    if (!ignore) setName(u.name);
  });
  return () => {
    ignore = true; // a slower, older request can't overwrite the newer one
  };
}, [userId]);

If adding the dependency makes the effect run too often, don't remove it. The effect is reading something it shouldn't depend on, and the fixes below deal with that.

Fix 2: move the function inside the effect

The second most common message names a function, not a value. Adding the function just swaps one warning for another:

function load() {
  fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
}

useEffect(() => {
  load();
}, []); // missing dependency: 'load'

useEffect(() => {
  load();
}, [load]); // The 'load' function makes the dependencies of useEffect Hook
            // change on every render.

A function declared in the component is a new object on every render. Listing it makes the effect run on every render. If that function sets state, the effect never stops re-running. That is the infinite loop people get after "fixing" the warning. If only the effect uses the function, move it inside. The real dependency, userId, then shows up in the array:

useEffect(() => {
  function load() {
    fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
  }
  load();
}, [userId]);

Fix 3: useCallback or useMemo when the value is shared

If the function is also used elsewhere, for example by a "Refresh" button, wrap it in useCallback. It then only changes when its own inputs change, and the rule is satisfied:

const load = useCallback(() => {
  fetchUser(userId).then((u) => setName(u.name));
}, [userId]);

useEffect(() => {
  load();
}, [load]); // no warning: load only changes when userId does

An object or array built during render has the same problem, and the warning says so:

const options = { id, limit: 10 };
useEffect(() => {
  search(options);
}, [options]);
// The 'options' object makes the dependencies of useEffect Hook change on every render.

// Fix: depend on the primitives, build the object inside
useEffect(() => {
  search({ id, limit: 10 });
}, [id]);

Depending on the primitive values (id) is usually cleaner than wrapping the object in useMemo. Keep useMemo for a value that is expensive to compute or used in several places. That is the practical answer to "useCallback vs useMemo": useCallback keeps a function's identity, useMemo keeps a computed value's.

Fix 4: useEffectEvent for values you read but don't react to

Sometimes an effect needs the latest value of something, but that value changing is not a reason to re-run it. A timer that logs the current count, or a chat connection that reports the current theme, are typical examples. Listing the value would restart the timer or reconnect on every change.

React 19.2 added useEffectEvent for exactly this. Put the code that reads those values in an Effect Event and call it from the effect. It always sees the latest values, and the rule doesn't ask you to list it:

import { useEffect, useEffectEvent } from "react";

function Ticker({ roomId, count }) {
  // reads the latest roomId and count, but is not a reason to restart the timer
  const onTick = useEffectEvent(() => {
    log(roomId, count);
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setInterval(onTick, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(t);
  }, []); // no warning

  // ...
}

Listing it anyway is a mistake the rule catches, with its own message:

}, [onTick]);
// Functions returned from `useEffectEvent` must not be included in the dependency array.
// Remove `onTick` from the list

Effect Events are only for code called from inside effects. Don't use them to hide a value the effect really depends on. In the example above, if a new roomId should start a new connection, roomId belongs in the array.

Fix 5: dispatch and navigate: just list them

For the two custom-hook values in the table, the fix is simply to add them:

const dispatch = useDispatch();          // Redux: flagged
const [state, localDispatch] = useReducer(reducer, init);  // not flagged

useEffect(() => {
  dispatch({ type: "init" });
  localDispatch({ type: "init" });
}, [dispatch]); // add dispatch; localDispatch never needs listing

Redux documents that dispatch stays the same as long as the store does, so listing it never causes an extra run. Listing navigate is also correct. If its identity ever changes, the effect runs again, which is harmless for a redirect guard like "send logged-out users to /login". Disabling the rule to avoid typing one word leaves a warning comment in your code for no benefit.

Why eslint-disable is the wrong fix (and stopped working)

The old shortcut was a comment that switches off the rule for one line. With the plugin's current recommended preset, that comment hides one warning and leaves the bigger problem in place. In my test, an effect that only set state from a prop had its exhaustive-deps warning disabled, and the build still reported this error:

useEffect(() => {
  setN(userId.length);
}, []); // eslint-disable-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps

// still reported with the recommended preset:
// error  Error: Calling setState synchronously within an effect can trigger cascading renders
//   react-hooks/set-state-in-effect

That rule is pointing at the real fix. A value calculated from props during render doesn't belong in an effect at all:

// no effect, no dependency array, no warning
const n = userId.length;

React's own guide on this, You Might Not Need an Effect, covers the other cases: data you can calculate, state that resets when a prop changes, and work that belongs in an event handler. Most "missing dependency" warnings in real projects disappear once the effect is gone.

What I found in this site's own code

It seemed fair to check my own projects too. This site runs on Next.js 16, whose ESLint config ships the same plugin version I tested. Its source has five eslint-disable comments for exhaustive-deps and three for set-state-in-effect, all in admin screens and data hooks.

  • Four sit on useCallback loaders that read a whole props object but list only three of its fields. That is the "missing dependency: 'props'" case. The fix is to destructure the fields and list them.
  • One is a rich-text editor effect that leaves the editor instance out on purpose, so typing doesn't reset the cursor. That is the job useEffectEvent was made for.
  • Of the three set-state-in-effect ones, one sets state after an await, which isn't the synchronous cascade the rule guards against. The other two read something that only exists in the browser after mount: headings in injected article HTML, and navigator.platform. Each comment says why.

None of them is a live bug today, but each one is a place where the next change could quietly read a stale value. They are on the list. When a React build behaves differently in production than locally, it is often a different problem: stale cached HTML pointing at old chunks, covered in ChunkLoadError after a Next.js deploy, or a page served from the cache, covered in Next.js page not updating.

Quick decision list

  1. The missing value should re-run the effect (a prop, an id, a query): add it, and add a cleanup if the effect fetches.
  2. The missing value is a function only the effect uses: move the function inside the effect.
  3. The function or object is shared: useCallback for functions; depend on primitives, or useMemo, for objects.
  4. The effect needs the latest value but shouldn't re-run when it changes: useEffectEvent (React 19.2+).
  5. dispatch or navigate: list them.
  6. The effect only calculates state from props: delete the effect and calculate during render.

FAQ

What does 'React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency' mean?

The react-hooks/exhaustive-deps ESLint rule found a value the effect reads, such as a prop, state, or a function declared in the component, that isn't in its dependency array. The effect then keeps the value from the render it was created in and doesn't re-run when it changes, which causes stale-data bugs.

Is it OK to ignore the missing dependency warning?

Rarely. Leaving a value out means the effect can read an old copy of it. If the effect really shouldn't re-run when that value changes, use useEffectEvent (React 19.2 and later) for the code that reads it. Disabling the rule hides the warning, and with the plugin's recommended preset other rules such as set-state-in-effect still report the underlying problem.

Why does adding the dependency cause an infinite loop?

Usually the dependency is a function or object created during render, so it is new on every render. The effect runs, sets state, the component re-renders, the value is new again, and the effect runs again. Move the function or object inside the effect, depend on primitive values, or wrap it in useCallback or useMemo.

Do I need to add dispatch to the useEffect dependency array?

For dispatch from useReducer, no: React guarantees it is stable and the rule doesn't flag it. For dispatch from Redux's useDispatch, the rule does flag it because it comes from a custom hook. Add it; Redux keeps it stable while the store is the same, so it causes no extra runs.

Should navigate be in the useEffect dependency array?

Yes. navigate from React Router comes from a custom hook, so the rule asks for it, and listing it is correct. If its identity changes, the effect runs again, which is harmless for a redirect such as sending logged-out users to the login page.

What is useEffectEvent?

useEffectEvent is a React hook, stable since React 19.2, that wraps code an effect calls but whose values shouldn't trigger a re-run. The wrapped function always sees the latest props and state. It must not be listed in the dependency array; the exhaustive-deps rule reports an error-style warning if it is.

useCallback vs useMemo: which fixes the warning?

useCallback keeps a function's identity between renders, so use it when an effect depends on a function that is also used elsewhere. useMemo keeps a computed value, such as an object or array. For objects, depending on the primitive values inside the effect is often simpler than either.

title: Identity World Model: Recognizing People in an Imagined Latent World
description:
arXiv:2611.25204v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Whole-body human recognition has advanced rapidly with large vision models. However, existing methods remain fragile under real-world variations, as they tie identity to transient cues such as clothing, texture, pose, or viewpoint. We argue that a robust recognizer should not merely learn to ignore these cues, but imagine how a person would be represented if they changed. To this end, we propose IDWorld, an identity world model: just as a latent world model predicts the features of a scene after an action, IDWorld predicts how a person would be represented under a changed condition. In a single forward pass, IDWorld imagines these counterfactual features under shared canonical conditions, such as the same outfit, a fixed view, or a bare silhouette, without rendering any pixels. Compared with explicit imagination in pixels, this latent imagination keeps nearly the same accuracy while being over 11x faster, at 5.9 ms per frame. Since each imagined condition has its own strengths, IDWorld then fuses them adaptively, weighting each condition for every probe-gallery pair. Extensive experiments show that IDWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on CCPG and CCGR-MINI, outperforms the compared methods on MEVID, and generalizes best to CASIA-B* and SUSTech1K, with the best mAP on CCVID. These results suggest identity world models offer a simple yet effective path to robust recognition. Code will be released.

title: How I Built a 100% Client-Side PDF Powerhouse with WebAssembly and React (Zero Cloud Uploads)
description:
Why Does Every Online PDF Tool Want Your Credit Card and Your Tax Returns?

Earlier this month, I had to upload a signed certificate to a government application portal. The portal had one strict requirement:

"Uploaded PDF must be strictly below 100 KB."

I did what everyone does: searched "compress PDF under 100kb" on Google.

Every single top result was a multi-million-dollar SaaS product that:

  1. Forced me to upload a sensitive personal document to an undisclosed remote server.
  2. Compressed it to 125 KB (still rejected by the portal!).
  3. Locked the "Extreme Compression" slider behind a $12/month subscription.
  4. Or hit me with: "You have reached your free daily quota of 2 files. Enter your credit card."

I got frustrated enough that I decided to see how far we could push modern web browser primitives—WebAssembly, HTML5 Canvas, Web Workers, and pdf-lib—to build a completely private, zero-server alternative.

That experiment became PDFCraft (Source on GitHub).

Here is the technical breakdown of how we achieved 100% client-side PDF manipulation with zero cloud leaks.

1. The Core Architecture: Zero-Cloud Processing

Traditional PDF websites use server-side Python/C++ pipelines (e.g., Poppler, Ghostscript, or LibreOffice in Docker containers). That architecture has major drawbacks:

  • Massive Server Costs: Running headless PDF engines across millions of files costs thousands in server bills.
  • Privacy Risks: Uploading legal contracts, tax documents, and medical scans creates massive GDPR and compliance liabilities.

Instead, PDFCraft operates entirely on the client device:

User Device (Local Memory)
├── File Input (Drag & Drop)
│    └── ArrayBuffer / Blob in Local Memory
├── Local Processing Engines
│    ├── pdf-lib (Vector streams, page tree manipulation, e-signatures)
│    ├── HTML5 Canvas (Quantization, resolution scaling, image crunching)
│    └── Web Workers (Off-main-thread compute without freezing the UI)
└── Instant Download
     └── Direct Blob URL (0 bytes transmitted to any backend)

2. The Target Size Squeezer: Hitting Exact 100KB/200KB Ceilings

Standard compressors just say "Low, Medium, High". But portal upload bots don't care about "High"—they care about ≤ 95 KB or ≤ 195 KB.

To guarantee that a PDF always comes in under the portal limit:

  1. Binary Stream Extraction: We extract embedded page streams and rasterize page canvases at high DPI.
  2. Dynamic Binary Search Quantization: Instead of guessing a single JPEG quality factor, our algorithm runs an in-memory binary search across resolution scale and quantization factors:
    • It tests quality brackets (e.g. 0.85 -> 0.65 -> 0.45) in milliseconds.
    • If the generated PDF stream exceeds the target ceiling (say, 95 KB), it immediately downscales background image coordinates while preserving vector text edge sharpness.
  3. Iterative Verification: The final byte buffer is measured before download. If it's 94.2 KB, it is delivered immediately.

3. Zero-Account E-Signing (ESIGN Compliant)

Instead of forcing users to sign up for DocuSign or Adobe Sign just to put an initials stamp on a 2-page lease, we implemented an in-browser vector signature pad:

  • Signatures are captured via HTML5 Canvas with cubic Bézier curve smoothing for natural pen strokes.
  • The vector paths are converted directly into clean PNG byte streams and embedded into the PDF page tree using pdf-lib's drawImage and drawText.
  • The entire signing session happens offline—even with airplane mode turned on!

4. 60-Second ATS Resume Studio

Most online resume builders let you design your resume for 30 minutes, only to hit you with a paywall modal at the download step.

PDFCraft includes a built-in ATS Resume Studio that:

  • Formats single-page vector PDF resumes compatible with applicant tracking systems (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever).
  • Includes a local keyword scanner that compares your resume against any job description in real-time.
  • Exports directly as clean, uncompressed vector text that machine parsers can read with 100% accuracy.

5. What We Learned

Modern browser engines (V8, WebAssembly, Web Workers) are powerful enough to replace 90% of cloud utilities. You don't need a heavy backend server to compress a PDF, sign an agreement, or extract spreadsheet tables.

  • 🌐 Live Web App: https://pdf-craft-vert.vercel.app/
  • 📦 Open Source Repository: https://github.com/Vishnu-cod/pdf-craft

I'd love to hear feedback from the developer community! What utilities would you like to see built into the client-side suite next?

title: HapBO: Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
description:
arXiv:2611.25100v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($\pi: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $\alpha$-$\pi$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

title: How Flutter's Rendering Engine Works
description:
The big idea

Most UI frameworks hand your buttons and text to the operating system's built-in widgets. Flutter doesn't. It draws every pixel itself, the way a game engine does. The OS gives Flutter a blank canvas, and Flutter paints everything on it: buttons, text, shadows, scrolling lists.

That's why a Flutter app looks the same on every platform, and why Flutter needs its own rendering pipeline.

1. The three layers of Flutter

Think of Flutter as a three-storey building. Your code lives on the top floor, and each floor only talks to the one below it.

flowchart TD
    A["Your app code (Dart)"] --> B
    subgraph B["Framework (Dart)"]
        B1["Material / Cupertino"]
        B2["Widgets"]
        B3["Rendering: layout and paint"]
        B4["Animation, Gestures, Painting"]
    end
    B --> C
    subgraph C["Engine (C++)"]
        C1["Dart runtime"]
        C2["Impeller / Skia graphics"]
        C3["Text layout"]
    end
    C --> D
    subgraph D["Embedder (platform code)"]
        D1["Window / surface"]
        D2["Input and vsync"]
        D3["Plugins"]
    end
    D --> E["OS and GPU"]
Layer Written in What it does
Framework Dart Widgets, Material/Cupertino, animation, gestures, layout and paint logic
Engine C++ Runs Dart, rasterizes graphics (Impeller or Skia), lays out text, talks to the GPU
Embedder Kotlin/Java, Swift/ObjC, C++ Creates the window, passes in touches and vsync, hosts plugins

2. The three trees

This is the most important idea in Flutter rendering. When you write widgets, Flutter actually maintains three parallel trees.

Analogy: building a house

  • Widget = the blueprint. A cheap paper description: "a wall, 3 metres, painted blue". You throw it away and draw a new one whenever something changes.
  • Element = the site manager. They hold the blueprint, remember what's already built, and compare each new blueprint with the old one to decide what actually needs changing.
  • RenderObject = the actual building. The real, expensive structure that has a size, a position and knows how to paint itself. 
flowchart LR
    subgraph W["Widget tree (blueprints)"]
        W1["Container"] --> W2["Padding"] --> W3["Text"]
    end
    subgraph E["Element tree (managers)"]
        E1["Element"] --> E2["Element"] --> E3["Element"]
    end
    subgraph R["RenderObject tree (buildings)"]
        R2["RenderPadding"] --> R3["RenderParagraph"]
    end
    W1 -.-> E1
    W2 -.-> E2
    W3 -.-> E3
    E2 -.-> R2
    E3 -.-> R3

Not every widget has a render object. Container is just a composition of other widgets, so only the widgets that actually lay out or paint (like Padding and Text) create one.

Tree Lifetime Job
Widget Very short; rebuilt often Immutable configuration. Just data.
Element Long-lived The link. Knows its place in the tree, holds State, decides whether to update or replace. Your BuildContext is the Element.
RenderObject Long-lived The heavy work: layout, painting, hit-testing.

Why three trees?

Because widgets are cheap and render objects are expensive. When you call setState, Flutter rebuilds the widgets, then each element compares the new widget with the old one:

flowchart TD
    A["setState called"] --> B["Widget rebuilt (new cheap object)"]
    B --> C{"Same type and same key as before?"}
    C -- yes --> D["Keep the Element and RenderObject. Just update their properties."]
    C -- no --> E["Throw away that subtree. Create new Elements and RenderObjects."]
    D --> F["Fast: e.g. only the color changes"]
    E --> G["Slower: full rebuild of that part"]
Text('Hello', style: TextStyle(color: isRed ? Colors.red : Colors.blue))

When isRed changes, a new Text widget is created, but the same RenderParagraph just gets a new color and repaints. Flutter rebuilds blueprints, not buildings.

Keys: without keys, elements are matched by position. When you reorder a list, the wrong State can attach to the wrong item. A Key says "match me by identity, not by position".

3. The rendering pipeline: one frame

Every frame goes through the same stages, triggered by the screen's vsync signal.

flowchart TD
    V["Vsync signal (an event on the event loop)"] --> A
    subgraph UI["UI thread (your Dart code)"]
        A["1. Animate: tickers update values"] --> B["2. Build: only dirty widgets rebuild"]
        B --> C["3. Layout: measure and position"]
        C --> D["4. Paint: record drawing commands into layers"]
        D --> E["5. Composite: send the layer tree to the engine"]
    end
    E --> F
    subgraph RT["Raster thread (C++)"]
        F["6. Rasterize: Impeller / Skia turns layers into GPU pixels"]
    end
    F --> G["Frame appears on screen"]
  • Step 0: setState, an animation or a scroll calls scheduleFrame(). Nothing happens immediately; Flutter waits for the next vsync.
  • Animate: AnimationControllers update their values for this frame.
  • Build: only widgets marked dirty rebuild, not the whole app.
  • Layout: sizes and positions are calculated (next section).
  • Paint: render objects record commands ("draw a rounded rect here"). No pixels yet.
  • Composite: the layer tree goes to the engine, and the UI thread is free again.
  • Rasterize: the raster thread turns commands into real pixels on the GPU.

4. Layout: the golden rule

Constraints go down. Sizes go up. Parent sets position.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Parent
    participant C as Child
    P->>C: Constraints: width 0 to 400, height 0 to 800
    Note over C: Child picks its own size within the limits
    C-->>P: My size: 300 x 50
    Note over P: Parent decides where to place the child
    P->>P: Position child at (50, 100)

Analogy: a manager tells an employee, "Your desk can be at most 2 metres wide." The employee picks a 1.5 m desk. The manager decides where in the office it goes. The employee never chooses their own position.

This explains classic Flutter puzzles:

  • Why Container(width: 100) sometimes fills the whole screen: its parent gave it tight constraints, so it had no choice.
  • Why you get "unbounded height" errors: a ListView inside a Column receives infinite height constraints and can't pick a size.

Layout is a single pass through the tree, which is why it's fast. Relayout boundaries stop a change from spreading upward when a child's size can't affect its parent.

5. Paint and layers

Painting doesn't create pixels. It records commands into pictures, which are grouped into a layer tree.

flowchart TD
    R["Root layer"] --> A["AppBar layer"]
    R --> B["Body layer"]
    B --> C["List item layers (RepaintBoundary)"]
    B --> D["Spinner layer (RepaintBoundary)"]
    D -.-> E["Spinner changes every frame: ONLY this layer repaints"]

RepaintBoundary gives a part of the UI its own layer. When something inside it changes, only that layer repaints, not the whole screen. Flutter adds these automatically in some places, such as list items and routes.

6. The threads involved

Thread Job
Platform OS main thread: receives touches, runs plugins and platform views
UI Runs your Dart code: event loop, build, layout, paint
Raster Turns the layer tree into GPU pixels
IO Decodes images and loads assets

Flutter pipelines frames: while the raster thread draws frame 1, the UI thread is already building frame 2.

sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as UI thread
    participant RT as Raster thread
    participant S as Screen
    UI->>UI: Build, layout, paint frame 1
    UI->>RT: Layer tree for frame 1
    par Work in parallel
        RT->>RT: Rasterize frame 1
    and
        UI->>UI: Build, layout, paint frame 2
    end
    RT->>S: Show frame 1
    UI->>RT: Layer tree for frame 2
    RT->>RT: Rasterize frame 2
    RT->>S: Show frame 2

That gives you two places where jank can come from:

Jank source Cause Fix
UI thread Slow Dart code, big rebuilds, heavy layout const widgets, smaller widgets, isolates
Raster thread Expensive scene: saveLayer, Opacity, clipping, blurs, shadows Simplify effects, use RepaintBoundary wisely

Flutter DevTools' performance view shows both threads as separate bars, so you can see which one is slow.

7. Impeller vs Skia

The engine needs a graphics library to turn drawing commands into pixels.

Skia (original) Impeller (new default on iOS and modern Android)
Built for General 2D graphics (also used by Chrome) Flutter specifically
Shaders Compiled at runtime, the first time an effect appears Precompiled at build time
Result Possible stutter on first animations ("shader compilation jank") Smooth from the first frame
GPU APIs OpenGL, Metal, Vulkan Metal (iOS), Vulkan (Android)

As an app developer you rarely touch either directly. You just get smoother first frames with Impeller.

8. A tap, end to end 

sequenceDiagram
    participant OS as OS / Platform thread
    participant UI as UI thread (Dart)
    participant RT as Raster thread
    participant GPU as GPU / Screen
    OS->>UI: Touch event posted to event loop
    UI->>UI: Hit-test render tree, find the button
    UI->>UI: onTap runs, setState marks element dirty
    UI->>OS: scheduleFrame (wait for vsync)
    OS->>UI: Vsync event
    UI->>UI: Animate, Build (dirty part only), Layout, Paint
    UI->>RT: Layer tree
    RT->>GPU: Rasterize and display
    Note over OS,GPU: All within ~16 ms at 60 Hz
  1. Your finger touches the screen, and the platform thread receives it.
  2. The engine posts it to the UI thread as an event.
  3. Flutter hit-tests the render tree ("which render object is under this point?").
  4. onTap runs and calls setState. The element is marked dirty and a frame is scheduled.
  5. Vsync arrives: animate, then build, layout, paint and composite.
  6. The raster thread draws it on the GPU, and the updated UI appears.

9. What this means for your everyday code

Practice Why it helps internally
const widgets The same instance is reused, so Flutter skips rebuilding that subtree
Small, split-up widgets setState marks a smaller subtree dirty
ListView.builder Only builds and lays out the visible items
Keys on reorderable lists Elements and State match the right items
RepaintBoundary around frequently changing UI Only that layer repaints
FadeTransition / AnimatedOpacity instead of animating Opacity Avoids expensive saveLayer work on the raster thread
Heavy computation in isolates Keeps the UI thread inside the frame budget

Quick summary

  • Flutter draws every pixel itself with its own engine.
  • Three trees: Widget (blueprint), Element (manager), RenderObject (real building).
  • Each frame: vsync, animate, build, layout, paint, composite, then rasterize.
  • Layout rule: constraints go down, sizes go up, the parent sets the position.
  • Paint records commands; the raster thread turns them into pixels.
  • Jank comes from either the UI thread (your Dart code) or the raster thread (expensive drawing).

title: Gaming Renewal Recovery: Node.js Queue Scheduling for 30-Day User Data Retention
description:
Short answer: For a gaming service that must delay a renewal reminder and then clean up user data after 30 days, keep the deadline in a durable ledger, let a cron trigger find due work, and use a retry queue only to carry an idempotent operation ID.

That separation is the operational recovery decision. A missed scheduler tick, a repeated webhook, or a worker that dies after deleting a row must leave the system able to discover what is still due and explain what happened. A delayed message is useful for a short retry; it is a poor legal clock. The retention deadline belongs in storage.

This is an architecture decision record for a Node.js service, with the critical path shown in Go because the transaction boundaries are easier to inspect in a compact interface. The language adapter is incidental. The invariants are not.

What should a Node.js webhook, cron trigger, and delayed retry queue guarantee?

Start with three records: a renewal-reminder intent, a retention operation, and an audit transition. The webhook should persist a stable operation ID, the subject reference, the policy version, and eligible_at; it should acknowledge the event only after that write commits. If the webhook arrives twice, both deliveries resolve to the same operation. The system must not create two erasure obligations merely because transport is at-least-once.

The worker may not delete before eligible_at, even if a queue message arrives early. A completed operation stays completed when its message is delivered again. Every terminal transition records the operation ID, attempt result, policy, and completion time without copying the personal payload into the audit trail. Legal holds and jurisdiction-specific rules belong in the policy decision, not in an arbitrary retry delay.

The deadline is data.

No shortcut.

The 30-day gaming example has two clocks: the reminder deadline and the retention deadline. They should be related by policy, but they should not be the same queue message. A player may renew after the reminder is scheduled, a subscription may be cancelled, or a legal hold may arrive. At execution time, re-read current state and make the destructive transition only if the policy still permits it. My test case is deliberately boring: deliver op-2048 twice, kill the worker after the datastore commit, and require one audit transition, not two deletions.

How can a Node.js service recover after a missed cron trigger or retry?

The cron handler should claim a bounded page of due intents and enqueue identifiers; it should not scan the whole retention population or perform deletion inline. A scheduled HTTP invocation has a 900-second execution limit, and a queue message has a 256 KB limit, so the useful payload is an operation ID or a small cursor, never a serialized user profile. Queue retention is at most 30 days, which is another reason the queue cannot be the authoritative record for a deadline that may need later explanation.

Cron timing has seconds-level jitter, and a paused schedule does not replay missed triggers. Compare eligible_at with the current time on every scan. Recovery then becomes an ordinary query: find due operations that are not terminal, including records whose prior claim expired. I’m not sure any scheduler can make a wall-clock tick an audit proof; the ledger can.

The publication boundary needs an explicit state model. Consider a renewal reminder for account acct-77: the scanner claims op-2048, publishes its identifier, and then loses its request context before it knows whether the queue accepted the message. If the claim is left permanent, one transient transport ambiguity becomes a silent retention miss; if every scan creates a fresh operation, a duplicate delivery can become a second destructive command. Store a claim token and a bounded claim expiry, and record the publication attempt separately from the terminal deletion state. A later scan may re-offer op-2048 after that expiry, while the consumer reads the operation's current state, verifies the account's current eligibility, and makes the only permitted transition. If the first message did arrive, the second delivery sees the same operation ID and the completed state. If it did not, the re-offer restores progress without inventing new policy. If publication fails, leave the intent recoverable; if consumption fails for a retryable reason, use a bounded retry policy or dead-letter path. A retry is another attempt on the same operation ID, not a new cleanup command.

package retention

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "time"
)

type Intent struct {
    OperationID string
    SubjectID   string
    EligibleAt  time.Time
}

type Ledger interface {
    RecordIntent(context.Context, Intent) error
    ClaimDue(context.Context, time.Time, int) ([]Intent, error)
    DeleteOnceAndAudit(context.Context, string, time.Time) error
}

type Queue interface {
    Publish(context.Context, string) error
}

type Service struct {
    ledger Ledger
    queue  Queue
    now    func() time.Time
}

func (s Service) AcceptWebhook(ctx context.Context, operationID, subjectID string) error {
    if operationID == "" || subjectID == "" {
        return errors.New("operation and subject IDs are required")
    }
    return s.ledger.RecordIntent(ctx, Intent{
        OperationID: operationID,
        SubjectID:   subjectID,
        EligibleAt:  s.now().UTC().Add(30 * 24 * time.Hour),
    })
}

func (s Service) EnqueueDue(ctx context.Context) error {
    intents, err := s.ledger.ClaimDue(ctx, s.now().UTC(), 100)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for _, intent := range intents {
        if err := s.queue.Publish(ctx, intent.OperationID); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

func (s Service) Apply(ctx context.Context, operationID string) error {
    return s.ledger.DeleteOnceAndAudit(ctx, operationID, s.now().UTC())
}

The datastore implementation must make RecordIntent idempotent on the operation ID. ClaimDue needs an atomic claim or a lease, and DeleteOnceAndAudit needs a state transition that remains correct after redelivery. Exactly-once delivery is not a promise to infer from queue behavior; it is the effect enforced by the application and datastore together. That distinction matters more than the scheduler brand.

Which scheduling options fit this recovery boundary?

Compare the options against recovery work, not timer vocabulary. A platform cron can launch the scan, a queue can absorb bounded fan-out, and a workflow engine can coordinate multiple dependent steps. None of those automatically supplies the retention ledger, legal-hold check, idempotency key, or audit evidence.

Option Appropriate use Boundary to verify
Platform cron plus a queue A periodic scan with independent workers The application still owns durable intent, leases, retries, and audit state.
Event-driven workflow engine Multi-step reminders, approvals, and coordinated recovery Execution history and retention settings must satisfy the deletion policy.
Database-backed scheduler A small deployment where due rows and workers share one datastore Locking, failover, and backlog recovery need explicit operational tests.
One delayed message per account A genuinely short reminder or retry It is unsuitable as the authoritative 30-day retention clock.

For the gaming renewal flow, the first option is usually the smallest defensible boundary: webhook writes intent, cron claims due rows, queue workers perform bounded cleanup, and reconciliation reads the ledger. The recommendation is conditional. The catch is that a platform cron plus queue is not suitable when the job needs native dependency graphs, fan-out/fan-in joins, or cross-system backfills; use a workflow engine when those capabilities are the actual problem. Stick with a workflow engine for that case, even though it adds operational machinery. The same option is unsuitable for a private-only deployment if the scheduler requires a public HTTPS target. Select a pull-based topology or an ingress boundary that respects the network model.

The operational dashboard should expose due count, oldest eligible_at, claim age, publish outcome, retry count, dead-letter count, and audit lag. Alerting on queue depth alone misses the most important case: a healthy queue with no scanner activity. Reconciliation should compare open ledger operations with source-of-truth account state and report mismatches without recreating deleted personal data.

Why reject one delayed message for the 30-day cleanup?

The design is attractive because it has one webhook and one future delivery. It fails the recovery requirement when the delay ceiling is seven days, and chaining several delayed messages turns a legal deadline into a fragile sequence of timer handoffs. A scheduler pause, an account change, or an operator review becomes difficult to reconstruct.

Use a short delayed message for a reminder retry that fits within its supported interval and can be safely regenerated from durable state. Do not use it as the sole evidence that a user-data retention obligation was met. The cleanup worker should re-check eligibility, commit the idempotent deletion and audit transition, and acknowledge only after the outcome is durable.

Compliance also has limits that code cannot settle: policy owners must define legal holds, jurisdictional schedules, evidence retention, and the scope of replicas or exports. A queue can deliver an operation. It cannot decide what the organization is permitted to erase.

References

  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cron-triggers/
  • https://www.inngest.com/docs

title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
description:
arXiv:2611.24032v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings. In this paper, we study test-time symmetrization, which uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group $G$ of rewritings. We prove that no amount of sampling and repeated decoding from a single representation can replace rewriting, while only $O(\log |G|)$ random rewritings suffice to recover the information provided by all $|G|$ rewritings. The same set of $O(\log |G|)$ rewritings provides simultaneous approximation across models, decoding rules, and sampled reasoning traces, and the logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. We validate the theory with experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B, with chain-of-thought reasoning, on graph reasoning, logical deduction, and multiple-choice question answering. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings of the input is substantially more accurate than spending them on repeated sampling from the original prompt whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written, and the number of rewritings needed grows only logarithmically with the number of possible rewritings, as the theory predicts. Our results provide a principled way to enforce symmetries at inference time when they cannot be built into the model, which we call model-agnostic symmetrization.

title: Why HTTP Status Codes Are Not Enough for Microservice Errors
description:
Why HTTP Status Codes Are Not Enough for Microservice Errors

HTTP status codes are essential to REST API design.

They tell us whether a request succeeded, failed because of a client problem, or encountered a server-side failure.

But when applications evolve into distributed systems, HTTP status codes become only part of the story.

Consider these questions:

  • What exactly caused the failure?
  • Which service owns the error?
  • Can the caller safely retry?
  • How should an unknown downstream error be handled?
  • How can operators trace the failure across services?

A 409 Conflict or 503 Service Unavailable cannot answer all of them.

While building NERV Exception, an open-source exception-handling library for Java and Spring Boot, I explored how a consistent error contract can address these limitations without tightly coupling independently deployed microservices.

Let's examine the problem from an API consumer's perspective.

1. The Same HTTP Status Can Mean Different Things

Imagine an e-commerce application with three services:

API Gateway
    |
    +-- Order Service
    |
    +-- Payment Service
    |
    +-- Inventory Service

Each service encounters a different failure.

Order Service

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

The order has already been processed.

Payment Service

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

The payment has already been captured.

Inventory Service

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict

Inventory is reserved by another transaction.

All three return 409 Conflict.

But should clients handle them identically?

Probably not.

An already-processed order may require no further action.

An already-captured payment may require reconciliation.

An inventory reservation conflict may require refreshing availability.

If the response contains only:

{
  "status": 409,
  "message": "Conflict"
}

the consumer cannot reliably distinguish these conditions.

Add stable application error codes

Instead, return:

{
  "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "The order has already been processed",
  "status": 409
}

For the payment failure:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_ALREADY_CAPTURED",
  "message": "The payment has already been captured",
  "status": 409
}

And for inventory:

{
  "code": "INVENTORY_RESERVATION_CONFLICT",
  "message": "Inventory is reserved by another transaction",
  "status": 409
}

Now clients can identify each failure without parsing message text.

HTTP status codes classify failures. Application error codes identify them.

Both are useful, but they solve different problems.

2. Why Exception Messages Are Poor API Contracts

A common mistake is to use exception messages as machine-readable identifiers.

For example:

if ("Order has already been processed".equals(errorMessage)) {
    // Handle already-processed order
}

This is fragile.

Suppose someone changes the message:

Old:
Order has already been processed

New:
This order has already been completed

The underlying business condition hasn't changed.

But the consumer may stop recognizing it.

Messages can change because of localization, improved wording, security requirements, or ordinary refactoring.

A stable error code avoids that problem:

if ("ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED".equals(errorCode)) {
    // Handle already-processed order
}

The message remains useful for humans.

The code remains stable for software.

This introduces an important API design principle:

Application error codes should be treated as published contracts.

Renaming a code can break consumers even when the HTTP status and JSON structure remain unchanged.

3. Designing a More Expressive Error Response

A useful error contract should communicate more than an HTTP status and message.

For example:

{
  "code": "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "The order has already been processed",
  "status": 409,
  "retryable": false,
  "category": "BUSINESS",
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "spanId": "def456",
  "path": "/api/orders/123/process",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-20T08:30:00Z",
  "origin": {
    "service": "order-service",
    "instance": "order-service-1",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "environment": "production"
  },
  "details": {}
}

This illustrates the response structure supported by NERV Exception's NervErrorResponse.

The business code, category, and example values are illustrative. Diagnostic fields depend on the application's configuration and available context.

Each field serves a purpose.

Field Purpose
code Stable application error identifier
message Human-readable explanation
status HTTP status
category General failure classification
retryable Recovery guidance
traceId Distributed tracing correlation
spanId Span correlation
path Request path
timestamp Response timestamp
origin Service-origin information
details Structured error-specific information

The goal isn't to expose as much information as possible.

It's to provide enough information for consumers to handle failures predictably while keeping sensitive internal details protected.

4. Modeling Application Errors in Spring Boot

Let's build a simplified example.

First, define an error response:

public record ApiError(
        String code,
        String message,
        int status,
        String category,
        boolean retryable
) {}

This is an educational example, not the full NERV Exception API.

Next, define an application exception:

public class OrderAlreadyProcessedException
        extends RuntimeException {

    public OrderAlreadyProcessedException() {
        super("The order has already been processed");
    }
}

Then handle it using Spring MVC:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(OrderAlreadyProcessedException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ApiError> handle(
            OrderAlreadyProcessedException exception
    ) {
        ApiError error = new ApiError(
                "ORDER_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
                "The order has already been processed",
                409,
                "BUSINESS",
                false
        );

        return ResponseEntity
                .status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
                .body(error);
    }
}

This produces a consistent response for that particular exception.

But there's an architectural problem.

What happens when you have 20 Spring Boot services?

If each application independently implements its own response DTO, exception handler, and error classification, inconsistencies eventually emerge.

One service includes an error code.

Another returns only a message.

Another exposes internal exception causes.

Another uses a different validation response structure.

This is where reusable exception-handling infrastructure becomes valuable.

A shared library can standardize the response contract and conversion mechanism while allowing applications to own their business errors.

5. HTTP Status, Category, and Retryability Are Different Concerns

A common shortcut is to derive retryability directly from HTTP status.

For example:

boolean retryable = status >= 500;

That is not a reliable rule.

A 500 response doesn't guarantee that repeating an operation is safe.

Likewise, a 409 may represent a permanent business conflict or a concurrency condition that could be resolved through a controlled retry.

Consider these illustrative examples:

Failure HTTP status Retryable
Invalid request 400 No
Resource not found 404 No
Already-processed order 409 No
Rate limit exceeded 429 Policy-dependent
Dependency unavailable 503 Potentially

The key distinction is that retryability describes a possible recovery strategy, not a guarantee of safe execution.

Applications still need to consider idempotency, unknown outcomes, retry limits, and backoff.

NERV Exception represents categories as strings, allowing applications to define classifications appropriate to their domains.

However, teams should establish conventions so that categories remain meaningful across services.

6. What Happens When One Microservice Returns an Unknown Error?

Consider a typical service-to-service interaction:

API Gateway
     |
     v
Order Service
     |
     v
Payment Service

Payment Service returns:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_ALREADY_PROCESSED",
  "message": "Payment has already been processed",
  "status": 409,
  "category": "BUSINESS",
  "retryable": false
}

But Order Service doesn't recognize PAYMENT_ALREADY_PROCESSED.

What should happen?

There are three common approaches.

Option A: Replace the error

Order Service converts the response into a generic integration failure.

{
  "code": "DOWNSTREAM_SERVICE_ERROR",
  "message": "Unable to process order",
  "status": 500
}

This may be appropriate when the downstream failure should be hidden behind Order Service's public API.

But it can discard useful information.

Option B: Share every error code

Every microservice imports a common library containing all business error definitions.

This makes errors recognizable but introduces coupling.

When Payment Service adds a new code, other services may need dependency updates despite having no direct ownership of that business rule.

Option C: Preserve unknown codes

Services agree on the error response structure without requiring every application to register every downstream business code.

This allows independently deployed services to evolve more freely.

NERV Exception's Feign integration supports this approach using RemoteNervErrorCode.

For unknown downstream codes, it can preserve the remote code, message, response-body status, category, and retryability.

For codes registered locally, the local definition determines status, category, and retryability.

That distinction matters.

Registering a downstream error code locally can change how the receiving service interprets it.

A shared error contract improves interoperability, but it does not eliminate decisions about semantic ownership.

7. Error Propagation Is Not Always Transparent

Suppose Payment Service generates an error while handling:

POST /payments

Order Service receives that failure while handling:

POST /orders

Which request path should appear in the final error response?

The original downstream path?

Or the current request path?

Both describe useful but different contexts.

The same question applies to timestamps and tracing information.

In the reviewed NERV Exception implementation, the downstream exception retains supported remote information such as the message, origin, and details.

It does not retain the original downstream traceId, spanId, path, or timestamp for direct reuse.

When the receiving application generates a new HTTP response, those fields are populated from its current context.

This is why consistent error contracts and distributed tracing solve different problems.

An error contract identifies and classifies failures.

Distributed tracing helps reconstruct how those failures moved through the system.

Neither replaces the other.

8. Why HTTP 503 Doesn't Automatically Mean Retry

Consider a payment operation.

Order Service submits a payment request.

The payment provider processes it successfully.

But the response is lost because of a network interruption.

Order Service
     |
     | Submit payment
     v
Payment Service
     |
     | Payment succeeds
     v
Payment Provider
     |
     X Response lost

Order Service experiences a timeout.

Did the payment fail?

Or did it succeed without confirmation reaching the caller?

The caller doesn't know.

Retrying without idempotency protection could produce a duplicate payment.

Now consider this response:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE",
  "message": "Payment provider is temporarily unavailable",
  "status": 503,
  "category": "DEPENDENCY",
  "retryable": true
}

The response communicates that retrying may be appropriate.

But the application must still decide whether the operation is safe to repeat.

NERV Exception's Feign decoder can wrap a retryable downstream failure in Feign's RetryableException.

However, the library does not automatically configure a retry policy.

Actual retry behavior depends on the application's Feign configuration.

There is another important consideration: after retry exhaustion, a generic exception handler may map the wrapper to an internal server error unless the application handles it explicitly.

Therefore:

Retry classification, retry execution, and final error presentation are separate responsibilities.

9. Error Contracts Are Also Compatibility Contracts

Consider an application that returns:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_TIMEOUT",
  "retryable": false
}

Later, the service changes its response to:

{
  "code": "PAYMENT_TIMEOUT",
  "retryable": true
}

The JSON schema hasn't changed.

The error code hasn't changed.

But the semantics have.

Consumers may begin retrying operations they previously treated as final.

Similarly, changing an error code from CUSTOMER_DISABLED to CUSTOMER_INACTIVE can break consumers that rely on the original identifier.

This is why error contract compatibility should consider:

  • Error code stability
  • HTTP status mappings
  • Category semantics
  • Retryability changes
  • Unknown-code behavior
  • Diagnostic information exposure

A structurally compatible response is not necessarily behaviorally compatible.

10. What Should API Consumers Depend On?

Different fields serve different purposes.

A consumer should use the appropriate information for the decision it needs to make.

Consumer decision Relevant information
Determine the HTTP outcome HTTP status
Identify a specific business failure Application error code
Display an explanation Safe message
Classify the failure Category
Evaluate potential recovery Retryability and operation semantics
Investigate an incident Tracing and origin information
Handle validation failures Structured details

The goal is not to replace HTTP status codes.

It's to supplement them with application-level meaning.

11. Where NERV Exception Fits

NERV Exception provides reusable infrastructure for consistent error handling in Java and Spring Boot applications.

Its modules include:

Module Responsibility
nerv-exception-api Shared error contracts
nerv-exception-core Core exception and error-code behavior
nerv-exception-spring-web Spring Web exception handling
nerv-exception-spring-feign OpenFeign error decoding
nerv-exception-spring-boot-starter Spring Boot integration
nerv-exception-jpa Persistence-related support
nerv-exception-event Event-related support
nerv-exception-spring-kafka Kafka-related support

The library doesn't eliminate application-specific responsibilities.

Each service still needs to own its business errors, define appropriate recovery policies, and determine what information is safe to expose.

The objective is to standardize common infrastructure without centralizing every business decision.

Final Thoughts

HTTP status codes remain essential to REST API design.

They provide a standardized way to communicate the outcome of an HTTP interaction.

But microservice architectures require more information.

Consumers need to distinguish business failures, interpret downstream errors, evaluate potential recovery, and correlate failures across service boundaries.

Stable application error codes, meaningful classifications, retryability guidance, and diagnostic context help address these requirements.

HTTP status codes tell us how a request ended. A well-designed error contract tells us what the failure means.

Explore NERV Exception

NERV Exception is part of the open-source NERV ecosystem of reusable Java and Spring Boot libraries.

Explore the projects on GitHub:

https://github.com/czetsuyatech

For the canonical article and the rest of the NERV Exception series, visit:

https://www.czetsuyatech.com

title: Why? Why do you need MongoDB?
description:
In applications, you can store data using a relational database.

The relational database already gives you the power to create complex relationships between data. Instead, you use a non-relational database.

Why? Why do you need MongoDB?

And if your argument is that MongoDB is a simple-to-use NoSQL database, so I prefer MongoDB, then actually, you don't understand the actual use case of MongoDB.

So, the use case starts when you build a social media application, a quick-commerce application, or an application where the attributes of a field are not fixed.

In this type of application, each product has different attributes, and for that, in a relational database, you need to create many optional fields so the table supports different types of product data.

This approach works, but after a certain level, it requires a heavily normalized design that supports all the products at a higher scale. This becomes more complex for querying and planning the database.

Whereas MongoDB has superpowers.

Because it uses documents to store data instead of records.

But what is a document?

Unlike relational databases, where all the details of a specific person or product are stored in a record, MongoDB stores information in documents in the form of a field-value structure. This gives you the ability to add any number of fields or unique fields to a document.

And the group of these documents is called a collection. A collection has different documents with different fields.

The problem that we face in relational databases is solved by this collection and document approach provided by MongoDB.

Now, this is one ability of MongoDB, and it has many other abilities.

Tell me in the comment section.

title: React Hook Form for Beginners: Forms That Don't Re-Render on Every Keystroke
description:
Forms are where React apps quietly get slow. The classic approach stores every keystroke in state, which re-renders the whole form on every character typed. React Hook Form takes a different path: it reads values from uncontrolled inputs, so your component barely re-renders at all.

Getting started takes minutes:

import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';

function SignupForm() {
  const { register, handleSubmit, formState: { errors } } = useForm();

  const onSubmit = (data) => console.log(data);

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onSubmit)}>
      <input {...register('email', { required: 'Email is required' })} />
      {errors.email && <p>{errors.email.message}</p>}

      <input
        type="password"
        {...register('password', { required: true, minLength: 8 })}
      />
      {errors.password && <p>Password must be at least 8 characters.</p>}

      <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
    </form>
  );
}

The register function connects each input to the form. Validation rules like required and minLength live right next to the field, and errors appear in formState.errors without any extra code.

This approach has two big wins. First, performance: typing in one field does not re-render the others, which matters a lot in long forms. Second, less code: no value and onChange handler for every single input.

React Hook Form also plays well with validation libraries like Zod and Yup, so you can define one schema and use it on the client and the server. It works with UI libraries too — there are wrappers for controlled components like date pickers and rich text editors.

React Hook Form is for anyone building signup forms, checkout forms, settings pages, or admin panels in React. If your forms have more than three fields, it will save you real code and real re-renders.

title: SWR for Beginners: Data Fetching in React Without the Boilerplate
description:
Fetching data in React used to mean writing the same useEffect + useState + loading flag in every component. SWR, built by the Vercel team, replaces all of that with one hook — and adds caching, revalidation, and error handling for free.

The name comes from "stale-while-revalidate": SWR shows you the cached data immediately, then quietly fetches fresh data in the background and updates the UI. Your app feels instant even on a slow network.

Here is the whole idea in a few lines:

import useSWR from 'swr';

const fetcher = (url) => fetch(url).then((res) => res.json());

function UserProfile({ id }) {
  const { data, error, isLoading } = useSWR(`/api/users/${id}`, fetcher);

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading...</p>;
  if (error) return <p>Something went wrong.</p>;
  return <h1>{data.name}</h1>;
}

That is it. No manual loading state, no effect cleanup, no duplicate requests. If two components ask for the same URL, SWR makes one request and shares the result. When you switch tabs and come back, it revalidates automatically. When the network drops and returns, it retries.

SWR also gives you mutate for optimistic updates. After a user edits their profile, you can update the cached data immediately instead of waiting for a refetch:

mutate(`/api/users/${id}`, { ...data, name: 'New Name' }, false);

SWR is for React developers who fetch data from APIs and are tired of writing the same loading and error logic everywhere. It is small, focused, and works beautifully with REST APIs and tools like Next.js. If your app mostly reads data and shows it, SWR is one of the simplest upgrades you can make.

title: Learning to Verify: Signature-Guided Training for Adaptive Adversarial Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.25271v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adversarial example detectors often fail when attackers explicitly attempt to bypass them. We propose a dual-model approach that keeps the original classifier fixed and trains a separate verifier to assess its predictions. During training, we identify patterns of internal neural network activations that distinguish genuine examples of each class from adversarial examples targeting that class. These patterns, called activation signatures, guide the generation of challenging adversarial examples that mislead the classifier, challenge the verifier, and internally resemble the target class. The verifier learns to recognize these examples while preserving its performance on clean inputs through knowledge distillation. At inference, the verifier evaluates the classifier's prediction without requiring activation signatures. We evaluate the approach on publicly available datasets against several adaptive attacks, including attacks unseen during training. The proposed verifier substantially outperforms directly attacked confidence-based and feature-based detectors under the evaluated L-infinity attacks. Ablation studies show that adaptive verifier training is the main source of this improvement, while signature guidance primarily benefits clean accuracy. Additional L2 evaluations reveal limitations in robustness across perturbation types.
