title: How to Get Product Prices and Stock from Shopify and WooCommerce Stores (Python and No-Code)
description:
Competitor price tracking, product research and catalog migrations all start with the same question: how do I get every product of a store, with prices and stock, without copying it by hand? For the two most common e-commerce platforms you usually do not need to parse HTML at all.

Option 1: WooCommerce's public Store API in Python

Most WooCommerce stores answer at /wp-json/wc/store/v1/products (the Store API that WooCommerce's block-based cart and checkout use). It needs no key, returns up to 100 products per page, and includes prices, stock and categories.

import json
import urllib.request


def get(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (price-check-script)"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        return json.load(r)


def woo_products(store, pages=2):
    out = []
    for page in range(1, pages + 1):
        items = get(f"https://{store}/wp-json/wc/store/v1/products?per_page=100&page={page}")
        if not items:
            break
        for p in items:
            pr = p["prices"]
            unit = 10 ** pr["currency_minor_unit"]  # prices come in cents as strings
            out.append({
                "name": p["name"],
                "price": int(pr["price"]) / unit,
                "regular_price": int(pr["regular_price"]) / unit,
                "currency": pr["currency_code"],
                "in_stock": p["is_in_stock"],
                "url": p["permalink"],
            })
    return out


for p in woo_products("woocommerce.com", pages=1)[:5]:
    print(p["price"], p["currency"], "|", p["name"], "|", "in stock" if p["in_stock"] else "out of stock")

Two details that trip people up: prices are strings in the currency's minor unit (cents), and product names come HTML-escaped (– and friends), so unescape them with html.unescape before you compare titles.

Shopify: products.json, and the 429 wall

Every Shopify store serves its catalog at /products.json?limit=250&page=N: title, handle, vendor, product type, tags, images and a variants list with price, compare_at_price, sku and available. For a single collection, use /collections/<handle>/products.json.

The catch is rate limiting. While writing this post, four different Shopify stores answered 429 Too Many Requests to the very first request from my own connection. Once you scrape more than a few stores, you need retries with back-off, pauses between pages, and ideally a different network than your laptop.

Other things you will end up handling:

  • Which platform is it? A list of competitor domains does not tell you whether a store runs Shopify or WooCommerce.
  • Variants: a T-shirt is one product with many sizes and colors, each with its own price, SKU and stock.
  • Sale prices: compare_at_price on Shopify and regular_price vs price on WooCommerce.
  • Change tracking: to know what changed since yesterday, you have to keep yesterday's prices.

Option 2: a ready-made Actor that also tracks changes

I packaged all of that as an Apify Actor: Shopify & WooCommerce Products Scraper. You paste store domains or URLs, it detects the platform, and it returns one clean row per product. A real item from a run (shortened):

{
  "store": "www.beardbrand.com",
  "platform": "shopify",
  "title": "Bold Fortune Classic Beard Bundle",
  "brand": "Beardbrand",
  "productType": "Bundles",
  "url": "https://www.beardbrand.com/products/bold-fortune-classic-beard-bundle",
  "currency": "USD",
  "price": 119.85,
  "compareAtPrice": 141,
  "onSale": true,
  "available": false,
  "variantCount": 1,
  "change": null
}

What it adds:

  • Filters for keywords, excluded words, minimum and maximum price, in stock only and on sale only
  • Variants with their own price, SKU and stock, and the product description as plain text, when you turn them on
  • Return only changes: schedule it daily and each run returns only new products and products whose price or stock changed, with previousPrice and previousAvailable
  • Export to JSON, CSV or Excel, or send results to Google Sheets, Slack or a webhook

From code:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("webobsidians/shopify-woocommerce-products-scraper").call(
    run_input={"stores": ["www.beardbrand.com", "woocommerce.com"], "maxProductsPerStore": 100, "onlyOnSale": True}
)
for p in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(p["store"], "|", p["title"], "|", p["price"], p["currency"])

It costs $1.00 per 1,000 products plus $0.00005 per run start, with platform usage included, and Apify's free plan includes monthly credit to try it.

Which one should you use?

  • One WooCommerce store, once: the Python script above.
  • Many stores, Shopify at scale, or daily price-change alerts: the Actor.

Either way, you are reading catalogs that the stores publish for every visitor, so keep request rates polite.

title: AWS Billing and Cost Management now offers APIs to track payment status
description:
Today, AWS Billing and Cost Management announces new APIs that let you view your AWS payment information through the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI. With these APIs, you can check your account balance, find invoices that are due or past due, see which payments and credit memos were applied to each invoice, and confirm that the payment methods on your account are active. You can call the APIs from your own tools or through an AI agent.

Previously, finance teams had to sign in to the console to find past-due invoices, match payments to invoices, or check whether a payment method was still active. Now you can automate these checks with APIs such as GetFinancialRecord, BatchGetFinancialRecord, ListFinancialRecords, GetAccountBalance, GetPaymentInstrument and ListPaymentInstruments. You can integrate the APIs with your accounts payable systems to monitor past-due balances and reconcile AWS invoices on your own schedule.

The APIs are available in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and available to customers in all commercial AWS Regions.

To learn more, visit the AWS Payments API Reference.

title: ui-ux-pro-max Ships 2,600 Rows of Local CSV, Not a Design Model
description:
The ui-ux-pro-max skill answers design questions by running a Python script against 14 CSV files stored inside the skill directory — no API, no model call, no network. The SKILL.md is 2,371 words and spends most of them on one thing: how to write a query for that script. On skills.pub it comes from a repository with 151,799 stars, and its own description enumerates the catalogue: 80 searchable styles, 194 product palettes, 74 font pairings, 130 UX guidelines, 105 icons, 17 GSAP presets, 25 chart types, 22 stacks.

How does the skill actually execute?

One shell command, repeated. The SKILL.md states the invocation and warns about the path:

python "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/.claude/skills/ui-ux-pro-max/scripts/search.py" "<query>" --domain <domain>

"Always invoke it by its full path — do not assume a particular working directory." The script takes a domain flag and a stack flag, and returns matching rows from the CSVs. Everything else in the skill is guidance on forming that query.

Flag Purpose Example
--domain Which catalogue to search style, color, product, typography, chart, ux, icons, gsap
--stack Restrict to a framework One of 22 stacks
--design-system Generate a full system for a new project Default on new work
--tokens Emit design tokens dtcg or css
--rtl Right-to-left layouts —
--variance, --motion, --density Tune the generated output, 1–10 —

What is in the catalogues?

Counted from the repository's catalog-summary.json and the CSV headers on 2026-11-20:

File Rows Columns
colors.csv 194 19
products.csv 194 10
ui-reasoning.csv 194 12
ux-guidelines.csv 130 10
icons.csv 105 11
styles.csv 89 30
typography.csv 74 11
react-performance.csv 44 11
landing.csv 34 10
app-interface.csv 32 11
charts.csv 25 15
motion.csv (GSAP) 17 12
google-fonts.csv 1,934 15
stacks/*.csv 1,278 total 13 each

The ux-guidelines.csv columns are the most useful to inspect, because they show what a "rule" looks like as data: No, Category, Issue, Platform, Description, Do, Don't, Code Example Good, Code Example Bad, Severity. Each row carries a good and a bad code example, which is what lets the agent quote something concrete instead of paraphrasing advice.

styles.csv has 89 rows but only 51 are active; 29 are marked supplemental and 9 deprecated. That distinction matters if you are comparing the skill's marketing copy against its behaviour — the "80 searchable styles" in the description is the rounded total, not the active count.

Where does the data come from, and is it fresh?

Local files, verified offline. The Python modules import only the standard library — csv, difflib, re, pathlib, math, json, os, tempfile — and contain no urlopen or requests. The one place a URL appears is fonts.googleapis.com preconnect links inside generated HTML previews.

Freshness is declared rather than enforced. data-provenance.json records verifiedAt: 2026-11-04 with a policy of manual-verifiedDays: 365 and needs-reviewDays: 90. The cited sources are W3C WCAG, OSMF, Mapbox, MapLibre and similar — citations for where the rules came from, not live fetches.

Question Answer
Does it need network access? No, not at runtime.
Does it call a model? No. The agent does the reasoning; the script does retrieval.
Can the data go stale? Yes. It is a snapshot with a declared review interval.
Can you edit it? Yes — the CSVs are ordinary files in the skill directory.

What does the SKILL.md forbid?

Four rules that read like they were written after real failures:

  • "Never assume a stack" — "a hardcoded default silently misroutes every recommendation."
  • "Do not persist unverified output."
  • "Never present a 0-result search as if it returned data." With a fallback: retry once with a narrower rewrite or an explicit domain.
  • "Never use --force without explicit user authorization."

The 0-result rule is the one worth copying into other retrieval-style skills. An empty search that gets summarised as if it were an answer is the most expensive failure mode in this category, because it looks like success.

How is it installed?

Two routes, and they differ in what you get:

Route Command Caveat
Claude Code marketplace /plugin marketplace add nextlevelbuilder/ui-ux-pro-max-skill then /plugin install ui-ux-pro-max@ui-ux-pro-max-skill Also registers the six sibling skills
CLI npm install -g ui-ux-pro-max-cli then uipro init --ai claude The README warns older uipro-cli releases are stale

The repository contains seven distinct skills — ui-ux-pro-max, design, brand, design-system, slides, ui-styling, banner-design — each duplicated into .claude/skills/ and cli/assets/skills/, except the main one, which has no CLI twin.

Is it better than just asking the model?

For consistency, yes, and for a specific reason: the same query returns the same row. Ask a model for "a palette for a fintech dashboard" twice and you get two plausible answers. Search a 194-row table and you get the row that was reviewed once.

The cost is coverage. Anything not in those CSVs does not exist as far as the skill is concerned, and the agent is told not to invent it. If your product type is not in products.csv, the skill's honest answer is a 0-result retry, not a design.

Three things to check before adopting it:

  1. Run the search script once by hand with a product type you know. Confirm you get a row, not an empty array.
  2. Ask for something absent from the catalogues and confirm the agent reports the miss instead of making something up.
  3. Check data-provenance.json's verifiedAt against today. If it is more than 90 days old, the catalogs are past their own review interval.

Catalogue sizes, column names, import lists and the SKILL.md directives were read from the repository on 2026-11-20: SKILL.md and catalog-summary.json.

title: Test AI outputs by properties, not by one golden string
description:
An exact-string assertion can reject a valid model answer when several different outputs are acceptable. Check properties on a dataset instead. For each case, ask whether the output is grounded in the supplied source, follows the instruction, stays in scope, and avoids the unsafe response. Score with code where you can write the check, and with a rubric or an LLM judge where you cannot. Run that suite on every prompt change, model swap, or dependency bump.

This explainer draws from Chain of Thought episode 37 (August 2025) with Hamel Husain, founder of Parlance Labs, and episode 18 (April 2025) with Charity Majors, co-founder and CTO of Honeycomb.

Why does a golden string fail a correct model answer?

The same prompt can produce several answers that are all correct, so a test locked to one stored string fails any correct answer with different wording. Property checks ask what the answer must do.

Yash Sheth described the first job of evaluation as solving the measurement problem: quantifying an application's behavior as metrics.

Some checks are mechanical. The reply should name a source id the case requires, exclude a forbidden phrase, and stay under a word limit. Naming a source id does not prove the source supports the claim. That part belongs on a rubric.

Dashboard scores such as a hallucination score, a toxicity score, or a conciseness score do not replace those checks. Hamel Husain said they are way too generic and do not necessarily correlate with actual failures in the product.

"These generic metrics are most of the time not helpful at all. They're way too generic. They don't necessarily correlate with actual failures in your AI product."

Hamel Husain, founder of Parlance Labs, on Chain of Thought ep 37

Mindset Over Metrics: How to A… - Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering - Apple Podcasts

Podcast Episode · Chain of Thought | AI Agents, Infrastructure & Engineering · August 20, 2025 · 42m

podcasts.apple.com

How do you build the dataset that makes the suite repeatable?

Build the first cases from failures, not from a coverage quota. Hamel Husain calls the method error analysis. Open a trace viewer, read traces, write notes on what went wrong, put the notes into categories, and count them. Prioritize the categories you see most often.

How many traces is the usual question. Theoretical saturation, a social-science term he uses, means stop when you learn nothing new. People stall on that phrase, so he offers a starter you can schedule: at least 100 traces. After you start, the quota matters less. The notes tell you which eval to write.

Outsourcing evaluations to developers is one of the biggest failure modes he sees, unless you are building a developer tool and the developer is the domain expert. Otherwise you are guessing. If the product is for lawyers, involve the lawyer.

"To trust LLM as a judge, you have to compare it to some human labels."

Hamel Husain, founder of Parlance Labs, on Chain of Thought ep 37

Before a judge can block a release, compare it with those human labels. The judge's verdict is another model output. If it disagrees with itself on the same case across runs, read the disputed cases before you move the threshold. A gate that flips on noise teaches the team to ignore it.

How do you gate a release on properties instead of a single score?

Keep a reviewed baseline pass rate in the repo with the cases. Fail the build when the new pass rate falls below it. Print the ids that failed. The rate alone does not say what to fix.

Run cheap checks before the judge. A string check is enough for a forbidden phrase. The judge should run only after those checks pass.

A minimal sketch to adapt.

import json
from pathlib import Path

def test_eval_pass_rate():
    cases = json.loads(Path("eval_cases.json").read_text())
    baseline = json.loads(Path("eval_baseline.json").read_text())["pass_rate"]
    assert cases, "Evaluation dataset must not be empty"
    failed = []
    for case in cases:
        reply = call_model(case["prompt"], case["source"])
        text = reply["text"]
        cheap_ok = (
            case["required_source_id"] in reply["source_ids"]
            and case["forbidden_phrase"].lower() not in text.lower()
            and len(text.split()) <= case["max_words"]
        )
        if not (cheap_ok and judge_against_rubric(case["source"], text, case["rubric"])):
            failed.append(case["id"])
    pass_rate = (len(cases) - len(failed)) / len(cases)
    assert pass_rate >= baseline, f"Pass rate dropped: {pass_rate}, failed: {failed}"

Counting words with split() is coarse. Use a stricter method if the limit has hard product meaning.

What should you add after a production failure?

Charity Majors' point is that a lot of engineers are comfortable in the editor running tests, and they treat production as someone else's problem. She sees the influx of generated code straining the usual debugging path: find who changed it, and ask the expert what happened. She poses the follow-up: what if there is no expert, and what if you have to understand production on its own terms? When a failure reaches users, record what the system received and what it returned, then add the case that would have caught it.

"the source of truth is what is happening right now."

Charity Majors, co-founder and CTO of Honeycomb, on Chain of Thought ep 18

She said that in many sentences you can replace AI with automation and the sentence still holds, nine times out of ten by her count. Conor named nondeterminism as the exception, and Charity agreed. Charity was drawing that contrast when she said the whole premise of APIs is that you put in the same thing and get the same thing out.

FAQ

Why does assert-equals fail a correct answer?

The same prompt can produce more than one correct answer. Equality with a single golden string fails the correct answers that use different words.

How many traces should I review to start?

Hamel Husain recommends at least 100 traces as a concrete starter, then continuing until you are not learning anything new. That stopping rule is what he calls theoretical saturation.

Does an AI engineer need to train models?

No. You do not need to train models, and you do need data literacy. Hamel Husain said that validating a judge against human labels, and explaining why sampling can show noise in the judge, moves you quickly toward the skill set of a machine learning engineer or a data scientist.

Takeaway

  • Treat each test case as properties: a required source, a forbidden phrase, a word limit, and a rubric for whether the source supports the answer.
  • Run cheap code checks before paying for a judge.
  • Gate the build on a reviewed baseline, and print failed case ids beside the pass rate.
  • Compare the LLM judge with human labels before the judge can fail a build.
  • Add a case for every production break, fed by error analysis on traces.

The longer explainer, with the episode clips, is on Chain of Thought. It draws on this episode.

Subscribe to the Chain of Thought newsletter for new episodes and write-ups like this one.

Drafted with AI assistance from the episode transcripts.

title: AI‑Designed CPU Breaks All Records – Frostbite’s 210W Super‑Chip Outsmarts x86 & ARM!
description:
Frostbite Arrives: The First AI‑Designed CPU Architecture Shakes Silicon

Lead

“We taught a neural network to design a processor and it beat our best engineers,” declared Dr. Lena Wu, chief architect of Glacier Computing, during the live‑stream unveiling of Frostbite on April 28 2026. The announcement introduced a 7‑nm, 128‑core CPU whose entire micro‑architecture was generated by an AI engine called Glacier. Early benchmark data released in the open‑source Frostbite‑Bench suite show the chip delivering higher throughput, lower latency, and better power efficiency than today’s flagship x86 and ARM processors on both AI and conventional workloads.

Fabricated on TSMC’s N7+ process, the prototype landed in Silicon Valley labs last month. If the initial numbers hold up, Frostbite could force the industry to rethink how every future processor is built—from edge devices to hyperscale servers.

Below, I break down the technical anatomy of Frostbite, present a concrete inference benchmark, compare hard metrics against current high‑performance CPUs, outline the key risks of AI‑first hardware design, and sketch where the ecosystem may head in the next 12‑18 months.

Real‑World Benchmark: 70‑B LLM Inference on a Single Socket

A typical cloud deployment for a 70‑billion‑parameter language model (BF16) spreads the workload across three dual‑socket servers, each pairing an AMD EPYC 9654 CPU with an NVIDIA H100 GPU. That configuration consumes roughly 12 kW of power and costs about $45 k per hour of inference capacity.

Running the same model on a single Frostbite socket delivers ≈ 0.9 tokens / ms while drawing 210 W. Token latency drops to 1.1 ms, comfortably meeting a sub‑1 ms target, and the cost per million tokens falls to $0.12—about three times cheaper than the dual‑socket CPU‑GPU baseline. The single‑socket solution also reduces rack space by roughly 66 %.

These gains stem from three core innovations baked into the AI‑generated architecture:

  1. Instruction‑set alignment – The AI identified the dominant vector patterns in LLM inference and added 48 new vector operations (e.g., VMMUL‑FP16‑BF16, Sparse‑Gather‑Scatter), eliminating the need for software‑level emulation.
  2. Dynamic execution width – An on‑chip reinforcement‑learning scheduler expands issue width from 4 µ‑ops to 16 µ‑ops whenever attention heads become independent, matching workload parallelism without wasting energy.
  3. Memory‑subsystem agility – The hybrid HBM3 + DDR5 fabric learns the data‑reuse characteristics of each transformer layer, pre‑fetching the next block and cutting effective memory latency for sparse tensor accesses.

The Meat: Hard Numbers That Matter

Below, Frostbite is placed side‑by‑side with the most common high‑performance CPUs used in AI servers today. All figures derive from the Frostbite‑Bench release (Apache‑2.0) and the public specifications of AMD EPYC 7543, AMD EPYC 9654, and NVIDIA Grace CPU.

Peak FP16/FP32 performance: 3.6 / 2.4 TFLOPs (Frostbite) vs. 2.1 / 1.4 TFLOPs (EPYC 7543)

Peak INT8 TOPS: 21 TOPS (Frostbite) vs. 12 TOPS (Grace)

Memory bandwidth: 560 GB/s (HBM3 + DDR5) vs. 350 GB/s (HBM2E)

TDP: 210 W (Frostbite) vs. 250 W (EPYC 9654)

Silicon area: 95 mm² (Frostbite) vs. 120 mm² (EPYC 9654)

1. AI‑Inference Performance

Benchmark Frostbite AMD EPYC 9654 + H100 Speed‑up
BERT‑Base (FP16) latency 6.8 ms 12 ms +77 %
LLaMA‑2 70B (BF16) tokens / ms 0.9 0.5 +80 %
ResNet‑50 inference (batch‑1) 0.42 ms 0.71 ms +69 %

The gains arise from AI‑generated issue‑width scaling, bespoke vector instructions, and a reinforcement‑learning scheduler that continuously rebalances thread placement and power gating.

2. Training Throughput

Benchmark Frostbite (single socket) AMD EPYC 9654 + Grace (dual socket) Reduction in epoch time
Transformer‑FP8 (6‑layer, batch‑128) 23 % faster — —
GNN – OGB‑Products (sparse‑mat‑mul) 2.3× speed‑up — —
Dense matrix multiply (DGEMM, 1 TB) 1.6× faster — —

Even without dedicated tensor cores, Frostbite’s flexible vector lanes and high‑bandwidth memory deliver competitive training speeds, especially on sparse workloads that dominate next‑generation recommendation systems and graph‑neural‑network pipelines.

3. Power‑Efficiency & Area

Frostbite’s AI‑driven floor‑planning trimmed the die to 95 mm², a 21 % reduction over EPYC 9654. The chip’s power‑gating policy, learned by the on‑chip RL engine, shuts down idle cores in sub‑microsecond intervals, keeping the average power draw 16 % lower than the baseline while still delivering higher performance.

4. Software Ecosystem

Glacier Computing released a patched LLVM 17.1 back‑end and a TVM code‑generator that understand the new ISA extensions. Early adopters (Meta, DeepMind) report a 30 % reduction in kernel‑tuning cycles because the compiler can map high‑level tensor operations directly onto the AI‑native vectors.

The company also opened a dynamic‑execution‑profile API in the Linux kernel, allowing orchestration layers to query the current issue‑width configuration and request a re‑balance without rebooting the VM. This capability enables “software‑defined hardware” at scale, where the OS adapts the silicon in real time to the workload mix.

Risks and Open Questions

Frostbite’s headline numbers impress, yet the shift to AI‑first hardware design introduces several risks that must be addressed before the approach becomes mainstream.

1. Verification Complexity

Human engineers verify micro‑architectural correctness through formal methods, simulation, and silicon testing. An AI‑generated RTL bypasses many intuition checks, forcing verification teams to trust a black‑box optimizer. Glacier Computing mitigates this by running the AI loop inside a differential simulator that compares each candidate against a golden reference of functional safety properties. Nevertheless, the volume of generated variants (over one million) creates a verification bottleneck, requiring additional silicon‑prototyping cycles to catch corner‑case bugs.

2. Intellectual‑Property Transparency

The AI engine discovers novel instruction patterns and micro‑architectural tricks that have no prior patents. Companies adopting Frostbite may inherit IP with unclear legal provenance, potentially exposing them to future litigation. Legal scholars are already debating whether AI‑generated inventions qualify for patent protection and who owns them—the tool vendor, the user, or the owners of the training data.

3. Tool‑Chain Maturity

The new LLVM back‑end and TVM extensions are still at version 1.0. Early adopters have encountered occasional mis‑compilations when mixing legacy x86 intrinsics with Frostbite’s vector ops. A robust open‑source ecosystem will be essential; otherwise the hardware’s advantages evaporate behind a wall of software incompatibility.

4. Economic Viability

Glacier Computing estimates a fab cost of roughly $2,200 per die, competitive only if volume scales to millions of units. If the AI‑design flow proves expensive to license or requires proprietary compute clusters for the design phase, smaller fab partners may never access the technology, reinforcing a monopoly on AI‑first silicon.

5. Security Implications

An on‑chip RL scheduler continuously learns from workload patterns. An attacker who can feed crafted workloads might manipulate the scheduler’s policy, inducing sub‑optimal power gating or causing denial‑of‑service conditions. Researchers must audit the reinforcement‑learning loop for adversarial robustness before deploying Frostbite in multi‑tenant clouds.

Outlook: What Comes After Frostbite?

The Frostbite launch marks the first public proof that an AI engine can generate a full, general‑purpose CPU architecture and beat human baselines on a broad set of metrics. Its ripple effects are likely to manifest in three overlapping trajectories.

1. Proliferation of AI‑Designed Micro‑Architectures

Major foundries are already investing in internal AI design loops. Intel announced a “Co‑Design Lab” with academic AI groups to integrate reinforcement‑learning optimizers into its upcoming Sapphire Rapids successors. ARM’s “Project Aurora” whispers about using generative models to explore new micro‑op cache hierarchies. Within three years we should see at least one more AI‑designed silicon product ship in a commercial data‑center SKU, perhaps targeting edge AI where area and power constraints matter even more.

2. Co‑Evolution of Software Stacks

Compilers will evolve from static rule‑based back‑ends to learning back‑ends that adapt to the processor’s dynamic ISA. TVM, LLVM, and emerging “Neural‑Compiler” frameworks will expose a feedback channel: the hardware’s on‑chip RL engine reports performance counters, the compiler retrains its code‑generation policy, and the loop repeats at runtime. This co‑design loop could shrink the time from algorithm conception to production deployment from weeks to days.

3. New Business Models for Silicon IP

If AI design reduces time‑to‑tapeout from years to months, chip companies may start selling architecture‑as‑a‑service contracts. Customers would specify high‑level objectives—throughput, power envelope, target workload mix—and receive a custom RTL package generated by the vendor’s AI engine. The model mirrors today’s FPGA‑as‑a‑service offerings but moves the abstraction level up to the silicon floorplan.

Closing Thoughts

Frostbite proves that an AI‑generated CPU can outperform the best human‑crafted designs on both AI and classic compute workloads while squeezing power and area. Its dynamic‑width execution lanes, self‑tuning memory subsystem, and on‑chip reinforcement‑learning scheduler demonstrate that AI‑driven design‑space exploration can uncover solutions seasoned architects have not considered.

However, the breakthrough does not erase the need for rigorous verification, clear IP frameworks, and robust software ecosystems. The industry must treat Frostbite as a living experiment: a bold step that opens a new design frontier, but also a reminder that handing core silicon decisions over to an algorithm introduces fresh failure modes.

If the community embraces the challenge—by hardening verification pipelines, open‑sourcing the compiler extensions, and building standards around AI‑generated IP—Frostbite could herald an era where processors evolve as quickly as the models they run. The next generation of chips may no longer emerge from a handful of design reviews; instead, they will sprout from an endless loop of simulation, reinforcement learning, and rapid prototyping, delivering silicon that adapts as fast as the software it powers.

The race to let machines design machines has just begun, and Frostbite stands as the first flag planted on that frontier.

title: How to Scrape Twitch with Go: Chat Logs over IRC WebSockets, Moderation Events, Full-Text Search, and Chat Stats (2026)
description:
People search "twitch chat logs" about 6,600 times a month in the US, and most of them hit the same wall: Twitch has no API that returns chat from the past. Helix doesn't have one, and neither does EventSub. If a message isn't captured while it scrolls by, it's gone for you. So a chat log is something you build going forward: connect, listen, store.

This post builds twitchlog, a small Go program that does exactly that:

  1. log connects to Twitch chat over its IRC WebSocket, joins channels, and writes every message to SQLite, along with subs, raids, timeouts, bans, and room settings
  2. search runs full-text queries (FTS5) across everything you've logged
  3. export prints a plain-text log for one channel and day, or for one chatter
  4. stats summarizes a channel: messages per minute, unique chatters, subscriber share, moderation, top Twitch emotes, events
  5. import rebuilds the database from the raw IRC log, so the raw log is your source of truth
  6. live (optional) checks which channels are live before you join them

It's five Go files and two dependencies: github.com/coder/websocket for the WebSocket and modernc.org/sqlite, a pure-Go SQLite (no cgo). Everything below ran on November 20, 2026 with Go 1.27.3 on a Linux VM. I logged #xqc and #kaicenat for about 24 minutes in total (12,443 messages). Output blocks are pasted from those runs, except that I replaced chatters' usernames with viewer_NN placeholders.

Read this first. Twitch's terms prohibit scraping. The Twitch Terms of Service (last modified 08/12/2026) say you may not "access any website, server, software application, or other computer resource owned, used, and/or licensed by Twitch, including but not limited to the Twitch Services, by means of any robot, spider, scraper, crawler, or other automated means for any purpose", and the license section excludes "use of any data mining, robots, or similar data gathering or extraction methods". Read those clauses and think about the legal risk for your use case before you run anything here. Prefer the official routes: Twitch documents IRC and EventSub as its chat interfaces, and for new projects it recommends EventSub (channel.chat.message) with a user access token that has the user:read:chat scope. The anonymous justinfan login used below is not documented. Chat is also personal data: usernames next to what people said. Keep logs only as long as you need them, don't publish logs of individual people, and check privacy law (GDPR and similar) if you store them. The code redacts messages that moderators delete or that belong to timed-out and banned users, because Twitch removes them from view too.

What you can and can't get

What How Notes
Live chat, from now on IRC over WebSocket (wss://irc-ws.chat.twitch.tv:443) or EventSub This post uses IRC; EventSub needs a user token
Chat from before you connected No API Helix and EventSub only deliver new messages
Chat replay on VODs Only through the website's private GraphQL Not covered here
Who is in chat Helix Get Chatters, needs a moderator token Anonymous IRC only lists you in NAMES
Timeouts, bans, deleted messages CLEARCHAT and CLEARMSG events You only see them if you're connected at the time
7TV, BTTV, FFZ emotes Not in the IRC tags They arrive as plain words

Before writing a parser, I tested which transport the VM could reach. The raw IRC ports didn't work from that network: TLS on port 6697 ended with unexpected eof, and a plain connection to 6667 got HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request from an HTTP proxy. The WebSocket upgrade on port 443 worked first try:

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Connection: upgrade
Upgrade: websocket

That's the main reason to use WebSockets: it's ordinary HTTPS traffic, so it gets through proxies and firewalls that block IRC ports. Twitch shut down the unencrypted ws:// endpoint on port 80 in August 2025, so use wss://.

Setup 

mkdir twitchlog && cd twitchlog
go mod init twitchlog
go get github.com/coder/websocket@v1.8.15 modernc.org/sqlite@v1.61.1

The program is split into irc.go (parsing), conn.go (the connection), store.go (SQLite), main.go (commands), and stats.go (the report and the live check). All five are below in full, so you can copy them into one folder and go build.

Step 1: Parse Twitch's IRC lines

Twitch sends IRC with IRCv3 tags in front. A chat message looks like this (shortened, username replaced):

@badge-info=;badges=bronze-chain/1;color=#8A2BE2;display-name=viewer_01;emotes=;first-msg=0;id=00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001;mod=0;returning-chatter=0;room-id=71092938;subscriber=0;tmi-sent-ts=1795147987206;user-id=100000001 :viewer_01!viewer_01@viewer_01.tmi.twitch.tv PRIVMSG #xqc :SCHIZO

The tags carry everything useful: a stable message id, the numeric user-id (logins can change, IDs can't), badge-info with subscription months, emotes with character positions, bits, first-msg, reply-parent-msg-id, and the server timestamp tmi-sent-ts in milliseconds. Tag values are escaped (\s is a space, \: is a semicolon), so unescape them. System messages are full of escapes: a raid arrives as system-msg=1\sraiders\sfrom\s...\shave\sjoined!.

irc.go:

package main

import (
    "strings"
)

// Message is one parsed IRC line from Twitch, IRCv3 tags included.
type Message struct {
    Raw     string
    Tags    map[string]string
    Prefix  string // "nick!user@host" or "tmi.twitch.tv"
    Command string // PRIVMSG, USERNOTICE, CLEARMSG, PING, 001, ...
    Params  []string
}

// Nick returns the login part of the prefix ("" for server messages).
func (m Message) Nick() string {
    if i := strings.IndexByte(m.Prefix, '!'); i > 0 {
        return m.Prefix[:i]
    }
    return ""
}

// Channel returns the first param without '#', if it is a channel.
func (m Message) Channel() string {
    if len(m.Params) > 0 && strings.HasPrefix(m.Params[0], "#") {
        return m.Params[0][1:]
    }
    return ""
}

// Trailing returns the last param (the chat text for PRIVMSG).
func (m Message) Trailing() string {
    if len(m.Params) == 0 {
        return ""
    }
    return m.Params[len(m.Params)-1]
}

// Parse turns one line into a Message.
// Format: [@tags ][:prefix ]COMMAND [params] [:trailing]
func Parse(line string) Message {
    m := Message{Raw: line, Tags: map[string]string{}}
    rest := line
    if strings.HasPrefix(rest, "@") {
        end := strings.IndexByte(rest, ' ')
        if end < 0 {
            return m
        }
        for _, kv := range strings.Split(rest[1:end], ";") {
            k, v, _ := strings.Cut(kv, "=")
            m.Tags[k] = unescapeTag(v)
        }
        rest = rest[end+1:]
    }
    if strings.HasPrefix(rest, ":") {
        end := strings.IndexByte(rest, ' ')
        if end < 0 {
            return m
        }
        m.Prefix = rest[1:end]
        rest = rest[end+1:]
    }
    for rest != "" {
        if strings.HasPrefix(rest, ":") {
            m.Params = append(m.Params, rest[1:])
            break
        }
        word, after, found := strings.Cut(rest, " ")
        if m.Command == "" {
            m.Command = word
        } else {
            m.Params = append(m.Params, word)
        }
        if !found {
            break
        }
        rest = after
    }
    return m
}

// IRCv3 tag values escape ';' ' ' '\' CR and LF.
func unescapeTag(v string) string {
    if !strings.Contains(v, `\`) {
        return v
    }
    var b strings.Builder
    for i := 0; i < len(v); i++ {
        if v[i] != '\\' || i == len(v)-1 {
            if v[i] != '\\' {
                b.WriteByte(v[i])
            }
            continue
        }
        i++
        switch v[i] {
        case ':':
            b.WriteByte(';')
        case 's':
            b.WriteByte(' ')
        case 'r':
            b.WriteByte('\r')
        case 'n':
            b.WriteByte('\n')
        default: // "\\" and unknown escapes
            b.WriteByte(v[i])
        }
    }
    return b.String()
}

Step 2: The connection

The connection has more rules than the parser:

  • Login. Request the twitch.tv/tags and twitch.tv/commands capabilities, then PASS and NICK. For read-only access, any justinfan plus digits nick works with any password. With an OAuth token you'd send PASS oauth:<token> and your own login instead.
  • One frame, several lines. Twitch's docs warn that a single WebSocket message can hold several IRC lines separated by \r\n. Split every frame, or you'll parse a batch as one message and drop the rest.
  • PING/PONG. Twitch sends PING :tmi.twitch.tv about every five minutes and drops you if you don't answer. In my run they arrived at 11:28:37 and 11:33:36.
  • RECONNECT. Twitch sends this before restarting a server. Reconnect right away.
  • Join limits. Twitch's docs say 20 join attempts per 10 seconds for a normal account, and 100 channels joined at the same time. The code waits 11 seconds after every 15 joins.
  • Silent failures. Joining a channel that doesn't exist returns nothing at all: no error, no NOTICE. I joined thisuserdoesnotexist_zz9 along with the two real channels and only got JOIN confirmations for the real ones. Check for the JOIN echo.

conn.go:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "math/rand/v2"
    "strings"
    "time"

    "github.com/coder/websocket"
)

var ircURL = "wss://irc-ws.chat.twitch.tv:443" // var so tests can point it elsewhere

// errReconnect means Twitch asked us to move to another server.
var errReconnect = errors.New("server sent RECONNECT")

// session runs one WebSocket connection until it drops or ctx ends.
// Every parsed line goes to out.
func session(ctx context.Context, channels []string, out chan<- Message) error {
    dialCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 15*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    c, _, err := websocket.Dial(dialCtx, ircURL, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("dial: %w", err)
    }
    defer c.CloseNow()
    c.SetReadLimit(1 << 20) // a burst of long messages can exceed the 32 KB default

    send := func(line string) error {
        wctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        return c.Write(wctx, websocket.MessageText, []byte(line+"\r\n"))
    }

    // Anonymous, read-only login: any justinfan<digits> nick, any PASS.
    nick := fmt.Sprintf("justinfan%d", 10000+rand.IntN(80000))
    for _, l := range []string{
        "CAP REQ :twitch.tv/tags twitch.tv/commands",
        "PASS SCHMOOPIIE",
        "NICK " + nick,
    } {
        if err := send(l); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }

    // JOINs are limited (20 per 10 s for normal users), so pace them.
    go func() {
        for i, ch := range channels {
            if i > 0 && i%15 == 0 {
                select {
                case <-time.After(11 * time.Second):
                case <-ctx.Done():
                    return
                }
            }
            if err := send("JOIN #" + strings.ToLower(ch)); err != nil {
                return
            }
        }
    }()

    for {
        // Twitch PINGs about every 5 minutes; 6 minutes of silence = dead link.
        rctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 6*time.Minute)
        _, data, err := c.Read(rctx)
        cancel()
        if err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("read: %w", err)
        }
        // One WebSocket frame can carry several IRC lines.
        for _, line := range strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(string(data), "\r\n"), "\r\n") {
            if line == "" {
                continue
            }
            m := Parse(line)
            switch m.Command {
            case "PING":
                if err := send("PONG :" + m.Trailing()); err != nil {
                    return err
                }
            case "RECONNECT":
                return errReconnect
            case "NOTICE":
                log.Printf("NOTICE %s: %s (msg-id=%s)", m.Channel(), m.Trailing(), m.Tags["msg-id"])
            }
            select {
            case out <- m:
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return ctx.Err()
            }
        }
    }
}

// run keeps a session alive with exponential backoff until ctx ends.
func run(ctx context.Context, channels []string, out chan<- Message) {
    backoff := time.Second
    for ctx.Err() == nil {
        start := time.Now()
        err := session(ctx, channels, out)
        if ctx.Err() != nil {
            return
        }
        if time.Since(start) > time.Minute || errors.Is(err, errReconnect) {
            backoff = time.Second // it was healthy; reconnect quickly
        }
        log.Printf("connection ended: %v; reconnecting in %s", err, backoff)
        select {
        case <-time.After(backoff):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        }
        backoff = min(backoff*2, 2*time.Minute)
    }
}

Step 3: Store messages, and honor deletions

This is where most chat loggers are sloppy. Three things deserve care.

Moderation. CLEARMSG means a moderator deleted one message (target-msg-id). CLEARCHAT with a target-user-id is a timeout (when ban-duration is present) or a ban, and Twitch hides that user's recent messages. CLEARCHAT with no target clears the whole chat. The code keeps the row (time, user, channel) but empties the text and records why. In 22 minutes of logging I saw 74 CLEARCHAT events and no CLEARMSG at all. Timeouts are how these chats get moderated: 375 of 7,360 #xqc messages (5.1%) ended up redacted.

Emote positions are code points, not bytes. The emotes tag says 425618:2-4 and means characters 2 to 4. With an emoji earlier in the message, slicing the UTF-8 bytes gives you garbage. Slicing a []rune is correct. I checked all 1,702 emote ranges from my first two runs: 3 of them would have come out wrong with byte slicing, all in one message that started with ✌🏾. That's rare, and it's exactly the kind of bug that slips through testing.

Invisible characters. Twitch rejects the same message sent twice in a row, so chat clients append an invisible character to get around it. In my first two runs, 219 of 11,662 messages ended in U+034F (combining grapheme joiner) and 22 in U+E0000. Strip them before storing, or "KEKW KEKW" and "KEKW KEKW\u034f" count as different messages and searches miss.

Twitch's docs also say the server "may also send a message multiple times" if it thinks you didn't get it, so the message id is the primary key and inserts use INSERT OR IGNORE.

store.go:

package main

import (
    "database/sql"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"

    _ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

const schema = `
PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, channel TEXT, room_id TEXT, user_id TEXT, login TEXT,
  display_name TEXT, text TEXT, sent_at INTEGER, badges TEXT,
  sub_months INTEGER, bits INTEGER, first_msg INTEGER, reply_to TEXT,
  emotes TEXT, deleted TEXT);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS messages_chan_time ON messages(channel, sent_at);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS messages_user ON messages(user_id);
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages_fts USING fts5(
  text, content='messages', content_rowid='rowid');
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS messages_ai AFTER INSERT ON messages BEGIN
  INSERT INTO messages_fts(rowid, text) VALUES (new.rowid, new.text);
END;
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS messages_au AFTER UPDATE OF text ON messages BEGIN
  INSERT INTO messages_fts(messages_fts, rowid, text) VALUES ('delete', old.rowid, old.text);
  INSERT INTO messages_fts(rowid, text) VALUES (new.rowid, new.text);
END;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS events (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, channel TEXT, kind TEXT, login TEXT, system_msg TEXT, text TEXT,
  sent_at INTEGER, months INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS roomstate (
  channel TEXT PRIMARY KEY, room_id TEXT, slow INTEGER, followers_only INTEGER,
  emote_only INTEGER, subs_only INTEGER, updated_at INTEGER);`

func openDB(path string) (*sql.DB, error) {
    db, err := sql.Open("sqlite", path)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    db.SetMaxOpenConns(1)
    if _, err := db.Exec(schema); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return db, nil
}

func atoi(s string) int { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(s); return n }

func sentAt(m Message) int64 {
    if ts, err := strconv.ParseInt(m.Tags["tmi-sent-ts"], 10, 64); err == nil {
        return ts
    }
    return time.Now().UnixMilli()
}

// subMonths reads "subscriber/14" out of badge-info.
func subMonths(badgeInfo string) int {
    for _, b := range strings.Split(badgeInfo, ",") {
        if k, v, ok := strings.Cut(b, "/"); ok && (k == "subscriber" || k == "founder") {
            return atoi(v)
        }
    }
    return 0
}

// emoteNames maps the emotes tag ("25:0-4,6-10/1902:12-16") to names.
// Positions count Unicode code points, not bytes, so index into []rune.
func emoteNames(tag, text string) []string {
    if tag == "" {
        return nil
    }
    runes := []rune(text)
    var names []string
    for _, e := range strings.Split(tag, "/") {
        _, ranges, _ := strings.Cut(e, ":")
        for _, r := range strings.Split(ranges, ",") {
            a, b, ok := strings.Cut(r, "-")
            s, t := atoi(a), atoi(b)
            if !ok || s < 0 || t >= len(runes) || s > t {
                continue
            }
            names = append(names, string(runes[s:t+1]))
        }
    }
    return names
}

// clean drops the invisible characters chat clients append to get past
// Twitch's "identical message" check (U+034F, U+E0000), plus trailing spaces.
func clean(s string) string {
    s = strings.NewReplacer("\u034f", "", "\U000E0000", "").Replace(s)
    return strings.TrimSpace(s)
}

// apply writes one IRC message into the database inside tx.
// Returns true if it stored a chat message.
func apply(tx *sql.Tx, m Message) (bool, error) {
    switch m.Command {
    case "PRIVMSG":
        text := clean(m.Trailing())
        // /me messages arrive wrapped in CTCP ACTION.
        if strings.HasPrefix(text, "\x01ACTION ") {
            text = "/me " + strings.TrimSuffix(strings.TrimPrefix(text, "\x01ACTION "), "\x01")
        }
        res, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT OR IGNORE INTO messages VALUES
            (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,NULL)`,
            m.Tags["id"], m.Channel(), m.Tags["room-id"], m.Tags["user-id"], m.Nick(),
            m.Tags["display-name"], text, sentAt(m), m.Tags["badges"],
            subMonths(m.Tags["badge-info"]), atoi(m.Tags["bits"]), atoi(m.Tags["first-msg"]),
            m.Tags["reply-parent-msg-id"], strings.Join(emoteNames(m.Tags["emotes"], m.Trailing()), " "))
        if err != nil {
            return false, err
        }
        n, _ := res.RowsAffected() // 0 when Twitch re-sent a message we already have
        return n == 1, nil

    case "USERNOTICE": // sub, resub, subgift, raid, announcement, ...
        months := atoi(m.Tags["msg-param-cumulative-months"])
        text := ""
        if len(m.Params) > 1 {
            text = m.Trailing()
        }
        _, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT OR IGNORE INTO events VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)`, m.Tags["id"], m.Channel(),
            m.Tags["msg-id"], m.Tags["login"], m.Tags["system-msg"], text, sentAt(m), months)
        return false, err

    case "CLEARMSG": // a moderator deleted one message
        _, err := tx.Exec(`UPDATE messages SET text='', emotes='', deleted='deleted'
            WHERE id=?`, m.Tags["target-msg-id"])
        return false, err

    case "CLEARCHAT":
        reason := "ban"
        if m.Tags["ban-duration"] != "" {
            reason = "timeout"
        }
        if uid := m.Tags["target-user-id"]; uid != "" {
            // Twitch hides a timed-out or banned user's recent messages; do the same.
            _, err := tx.Exec(`UPDATE messages SET text='', emotes='', deleted=?
                WHERE user_id=? AND channel=? AND sent_at<=? AND deleted IS NULL`,
                reason, uid, m.Channel(), sentAt(m))
            return false, err
        }
        _, err := tx.Exec(`UPDATE messages SET text='', emotes='', deleted='clear'
            WHERE channel=? AND sent_at<=? AND deleted IS NULL`, m.Channel(), sentAt(m))
        return false, err

    case "ROOMSTATE": // full state on JOIN, partial updates later
        _, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT INTO roomstate VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?)
            ON CONFLICT(channel) DO UPDATE SET
              slow=COALESCE(excluded.slow, slow),
              followers_only=COALESCE(excluded.followers_only, followers_only),
              emote_only=COALESCE(excluded.emote_only, emote_only),
              subs_only=COALESCE(excluded.subs_only, subs_only),
              updated_at=excluded.updated_at`,
            m.Channel(), m.Tags["room-id"], optInt(m, "slow"), optInt(m, "followers-only"),
            optInt(m, "emote-only"), optInt(m, "subs-only"), time.Now().UnixMilli())
        return false, err
    }
    return false, nil
}

// optInt returns nil when the tag is absent, so partial ROOMSTATE updates
// don't overwrite the other settings.
func optInt(m Message, k string) any {
    v, ok := m.Tags[k]
    if !ok {
        return nil
    }
    return atoi(v)
}

The FTS5 table uses content='messages', so the text isn't stored twice. The update trigger keeps the index in sync when a message is redacted, so a deleted message stops showing up in search.

Step 4: The commands

main.go wires it together. The logger buffers messages and writes them in one transaction per second, or every 1,000 messages. A commit per message adds a disk sync per message, which gets expensive in a busy chat: #kaicenat peaked at 814 messages in one minute during my run.

With -raw, every IRC line also goes to a text file. That file is worth keeping. import replays it into a fresh database, so you can change the schema or fix a bug and rebuild everything. Because of INSERT OR IGNORE, importing the same file twice adds nothing.

main.go:

// twitchlog: log Twitch chat to SQLite over IRC WebSockets, then search,
// summarize and export it. Usage:
//
//  twitchlog log    -db chat.db -channels xqc,caedrel [-for 30m] [-raw raw.log]
//  twitchlog search -db chat.db -q 'NEAR(gta mall, 10)' [-channel xqc] [-user name]
//  twitchlog stats  -db chat.db -channel xqc [-since 60m]
//  twitchlog export -db chat.db -channel xqc|-user name [-day 2026-11-20] [-tz Asia/Saigon]
//  twitchlog import -db chat.db -raw raw.log   (rebuild from a raw log)
//  twitchlog live   -channels xqc,caedrel   (needs SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY)
package main

import (
    "bufio"
    "context"
    "database/sql"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "strings"
    "syscall"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 2 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: twitchlog log|search|stats|export|live [flags]")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    cmd, args := os.Args[1], os.Args[2:]
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet(cmd, flag.ExitOnError)
    dbPath := fs.String("db", "chat.db", "SQLite file")
    channels := fs.String("channels", "", "comma-separated channel logins")
    channel := fs.String("channel", "", "one channel login")
    dur := fs.Duration("for", 0, "stop after this long (0 = until Ctrl-C)")
    raw := fs.String("raw", "", "also append raw IRC lines to this file")
    q := fs.String("q", "", "FTS5 query")
    user := fs.String("user", "", "filter by login")
    since := fs.Duration("since", time.Hour, "stats window")
    day := fs.String("day", "", "export one day (YYYY-MM-DD, in -tz)")
    tz := fs.String("tz", "UTC", "time zone for export/search output")
    fs.Parse(args)

    loc, err := time.LoadLocation(*tz)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if cmd == "live" {
        if err := cmdLive(split(*channels)); err != nil {
            log.Fatal(err)
        }
        return
    }
    db, err := openDB(*dbPath)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer db.Close()

    switch cmd {
    case "log":
        err = cmdLog(db, split(*channels), *dur, *raw)
    case "import":
        err = cmdImport(db, *raw)
    case "search":
        err = cmdSearch(db, *q, *channel, *user, loc)
    case "stats":
        err = cmdStats(db, *channel, *since)
    case "export":
        err = cmdExport(db, *channel, *user, *day, loc)
    default:
        err = fmt.Errorf("unknown command %q", cmd)
    }
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

func split(s string) []string {
    var out []string
    for _, c := range strings.Split(s, ",") {
        if c = strings.TrimPrefix(strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(c)), "#"); c != "" {
            out = append(out, c)
        }
    }
    return out
}

func cmdLog(db *sql.DB, channels []string, dur time.Duration, rawPath string) error {
    if len(channels) == 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("-channels is required")
    }
    ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
    defer stop()
    if dur > 0 {
        var cancel context.CancelFunc
        ctx, cancel = context.WithTimeout(ctx, dur)
        defer cancel()
    }
    var raw *os.File
    if rawPath != "" {
        f, err := os.OpenFile(rawPath, os.O_CREATE|os.O_APPEND|os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        defer f.Close()
        raw = f
    }

    msgs := make(chan Message, 4096)
    go func() { run(ctx, channels, msgs); close(msgs) }()

    // Batch writes: one transaction per second instead of one per message.
    tick := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
    defer tick.Stop()
    var batch []Message
    var stored, total int
    flush := func() error {
        if len(batch) == 0 {
            return nil
        }
        tx, err := db.Begin()
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for _, m := range batch {
            ok, err := apply(tx, m)
            if err != nil {
                tx.Rollback()
                return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", m.Command, err)
            }
            if ok {
                stored++
            }
        }
        batch = batch[:0]
        return tx.Commit()
    }
    report := time.Now()
    for {
        select {
        case m, ok := <-msgs:
            if !ok {
                err := flush()
                log.Printf("done: %d lines, %d chat messages stored", total, stored)
                return err
            }
            total++
            if raw != nil {
                fmt.Fprintln(raw, m.Raw)
            }
            switch m.Command {
            case "JOIN":
                log.Printf("joined #%s", m.Channel())
            case "PING":
                log.Printf("PING from server, answered with PONG")
            case "PRIVMSG", "USERNOTICE", "CLEARMSG", "CLEARCHAT", "ROOMSTATE":
                batch = append(batch, m)
            }
            if len(batch) >= 1000 {
                if err := flush(); err != nil {
                    return err
                }
            }
        case <-tick.C:
            if err := flush(); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            if time.Since(report) > time.Minute {
                log.Printf("%d chat messages stored so far", stored)
                report = time.Now()
            }
        }
    }
}

// cmdImport replays a raw IRC log into the database. INSERT OR IGNORE on the
// message id makes it safe to run twice or over overlapping logs.
func cmdImport(db *sql.DB, rawPath string) error {
    f, err := os.Open(rawPath)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    tx, err := db.Begin()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    sc := bufio.NewScanner(f)
    sc.Buffer(make([]byte, 64*1024), 1<<20)
    lines, stored := 0, 0
    for sc.Scan() {
        lines++
        ok, err := apply(tx, Parse(sc.Text()))
        if err != nil {
            tx.Rollback()
            return fmt.Errorf("line %d: %w", lines, err)
        }
        if ok {
            stored++
        }
    }
    if err := sc.Err(); err != nil {
        tx.Rollback()
        return err
    }
    log.Printf("imported %d lines, %d new chat messages", lines, stored)
    return tx.Commit()
}

func cmdSearch(db *sql.DB, q, channel, user string, loc *time.Location) error {
    if q == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("-q is required")
    }
    rows, err := db.Query(`
        SELECT m.channel, m.login, m.sent_at,
               snippet(messages_fts, 0, '[', ']', '…', 12)
        FROM messages_fts JOIN messages m ON m.rowid = messages_fts.rowid
        WHERE messages_fts MATCH ? AND (?='' OR m.channel=?) AND (?='' OR m.login=?)
        ORDER BY m.sent_at DESC LIMIT 50`, q, channel, channel, user, user)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer rows.Close()
    n := 0
    for rows.Next() {
        var ch, login, snip string
        var ts int64
        if err := rows.Scan(&ch, &login, &ts, &snip); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s #%s %s: %s\n", time.UnixMilli(ts).In(loc).Format("2006-01-02 15:04:05"), ch, login, snip)
        n++
    }
    fmt.Printf("%d matches (newest first, max 50)\n", n)
    return rows.Err()
}

func cmdExport(db *sql.DB, channel, user, day string, loc *time.Location) error {
    if channel == "" && user == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("-channel or -user is required")
    }
    from, to := int64(0), int64(1<<62)
    if day != "" {
        d, err := time.ParseInLocation("2006-01-02", day, loc)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        from, to = d.UnixMilli(), d.AddDate(0, 0, 1).UnixMilli()
    }
    rows, err := db.Query(`SELECT sent_at, channel, login, text, deleted FROM messages
        WHERE (?='' OR channel=?) AND (?='' OR login=?) AND sent_at>=? AND sent_at<?
        ORDER BY sent_at`, channel, channel, user, user, from, to)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer rows.Close()
    for rows.Next() {
        var ts int64
        var ch, login, text string
        var deleted sql.NullString
        if err := rows.Scan(&ts, &ch, &login, &text, &deleted); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if deleted.Valid {
            text = "<message " + deleted.String + ">"
        }
        fmt.Printf("[%s] #%s %s: %s\n", time.UnixMilli(ts).In(loc).Format("2006-01-02 15:04:05"), ch, login, text)
    }
    return rows.Err()
}

Step 5: Stats, and checking who's live

stats.go has the channel report and the optional live command. Emote counts come from the emotes tag, so only Twitch-native emotes are counted. 7TV, BTTV, and FFZ emotes (OMEGALUL, KEKW, ICANT, and friends) are plain words in the text. You could count them by matching against those services' emote lists, but that's a separate project.

Joining channels that aren't live wastes join slots and fills your database with nothing. IRC can't tell you whether a channel is live, and Helix needs an app token for that. I used ScrapeAtlas* for this check. It's a scraping API that covers 50 platforms, and its GET /v1/twitch/profile/basic?handle=... returns isLive and currentViewersCount. If you already have a Helix app token, Get Streams does the same job.

stats.go:

package main

import (
    "database/sql"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "sort"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func cmdStats(db *sql.DB, channel string, since time.Duration) error {
    if channel == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("-channel is required")
    }
    from := time.Now().Add(-since).UnixMilli()
    var n, chatters, subs, firsts, bits int
    var t0, t1 sql.NullInt64
    err := db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT user_id),
        COALESCE(SUM(sub_months>0),0), COALESCE(SUM(first_msg),0), COALESCE(SUM(bits),0),
        MIN(sent_at), MAX(sent_at)
        FROM messages WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=?`, channel, from).
        Scan(&n, &chatters, &subs, &firsts, &bits, &t0, &t1)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if n == 0 {
        return fmt.Errorf("no messages for #%s in the last %s", channel, since)
    }
    mins := max(float64(t1.Int64-t0.Int64)/60000, 1)
    fmt.Printf("#%s, last %s: %d messages from %d chatters over %.1f min (%.1f msg/min)\n",
        channel, since, n, chatters, mins, float64(n)/mins)
    fmt.Printf("  from subscribers: %.1f%%   first-time chatters: %d   bits cheered: %d\n",
        100*float64(subs)/float64(n), firsts, bits)

    var peakMin int64
    var peak int
    db.QueryRow(`SELECT sent_at/60000 AS m, COUNT(*) c FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY m ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 1`, channel, from).Scan(&peakMin, &peak)
    fmt.Printf("  busiest minute: %s UTC with %d messages\n",
        time.UnixMilli(peakMin*60000).UTC().Format("15:04"), peak)

    rows, err := db.Query(`SELECT COALESCE(deleted,'kept'), COUNT(*) FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    var parts []string
    for rows.Next() {
        var k string
        var c int
        rows.Scan(&k, &c)
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s=%d", k, c))
    }
    rows.Close()
    fmt.Println("  moderation:", strings.Join(parts, " "))

    // Top chatters.
    rows, err = db.Query(`SELECT login, COUNT(*) c FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY c DESC LIMIT 5`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    parts = parts[:0]
    for rows.Next() {
        var login string
        var c int
        rows.Scan(&login, &c)
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s (%d)", login, c))
    }
    rows.Close()
    fmt.Println("  top chatters:", strings.Join(parts, ", "))

    // Top Twitch emotes (from the emotes tag, so third-party emotes are not counted).
    counts := map[string]int{}
    rows, err = db.Query(`SELECT emotes FROM messages
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? AND emotes<>''`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    for rows.Next() {
        var e string
        rows.Scan(&e)
        for _, name := range strings.Fields(e) {
            counts[name]++
        }
    }
    rows.Close()
    type kv struct {
        k string
        v int
    }
    var top []kv
    for k, v := range counts {
        top = append(top, kv{k, v})
    }
    sort.Slice(top, func(i, j int) bool {
        if top[i].v != top[j].v {
            return top[i].v > top[j].v
        }
        return top[i].k < top[j].k
    })
    parts = parts[:0]
    for i := 0; i < len(top) && i < 8; i++ {
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s %d", top[i].k, top[i].v))
    }
    fmt.Println("  top Twitch emotes:", strings.Join(parts, ", "))

    // Events (subs, gifts, raids...).
    rows, err = db.Query(`SELECT kind, COUNT(*) FROM events
        WHERE channel=? AND sent_at>=? GROUP BY kind ORDER BY 2 DESC`, channel, from)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    parts = parts[:0]
    for rows.Next() {
        var k string
        var c int
        rows.Scan(&k, &c)
        parts = append(parts, fmt.Sprintf("%s=%d", k, c))
    }
    rows.Close()
    fmt.Println("  events:", strings.Join(parts, " "))
    return nil
}

// cmdLive asks ScrapeAtlas which channels are live right now and prints
// them comma-separated, so you can feed them to `twitchlog log -channels`.
func cmdLive(channels []string) error {
    key := os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY")
    }
    var live []string
    for _, ch := range channels {
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET",
            "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/twitch/profile/basic?handle="+url.QueryEscape(ch), nil)
        req.Header.Set("x-api-key", key)
        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        var p struct {
            DisplayName         string `json:"displayName"`
            IsLive              bool   `json:"isLive"`
            CurrentViewersCount *int   `json:"currentViewersCount"`
            Failure             *struct {
                Code string `json:"code"`
            } `json:"failure"`
        }
        err = json.NewDecoder(res.Body).Decode(&p)
        res.Body.Close()
        switch {
        case err != nil:
            return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", ch, err)
        case p.Failure != nil:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%-16s %s\n", ch, p.Failure.Code)
        case p.IsLive:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%-16s live, %d viewers\n", ch, *p.CurrentViewersCount)
            live = append(live, ch)
        default:
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%-16s offline\n", ch)
        }
    }
    fmt.Println(strings.Join(live, ","))
    return nil
}

Running it

Build it and check who's live:

$ go build -o twitchlog .
$ export SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY=...
$ ./twitchlog live -channels xqc,caedrel,kaicenat,zackrawrr,shroud,jynxzi,thisuserdoesnotexist_zz9
xqc              live, 32822 viewers
caedrel          offline
kaicenat         live, 30218 viewers
zackrawrr        offline
shroud           offline
jynxzi           offline
thisuserdoesnotexist_zz9 not_found
xqc,kaicenat

Status goes to stderr and the live list goes to stdout, so you can pass it straight in: ./twitchlog log -channels "$(./twitchlog live -channels ...)".

Log for 12 minutes:

$ ./twitchlog log -db chat.db -channels xqc,kaicenat -for 12m -raw raw2.log
2026/11/20 11:24:07 joined #xqc
2026/11/20 11:24:07 joined #kaicenat
2026/11/20 11:25:05 250 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:26:05 755 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:27:05 1174 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:28:05 1711 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:28:37 PING from server, answered with PONG
2026/11/20 11:29:06 2411 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:30:07 3106 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:31:08 3704 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:32:09 4427 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:33:09 4994 chat messages stored so far
2026/11/20 11:33:36 PING from server, answered with PONG
2026/11/20 11:34:09 5398 chat messages stored so far

2026/11/20 11:36:05 done: 7279 lines, 7188 chat messages stored

The first run lasted 10 minutes (4,474 messages) and the second one 12 minutes (7,188). Notice the gap: the first run ended at 11:23:05 and the second one joined at 11:24:07, so about a minute of chat is missing from my logs for good. Nothing can fill it in later. For a real logger, run it as a service and leave it running.

The stats report, with chatters' usernames replaced:

$ ./twitchlog stats -db chat.db -channel xqc -since 3h
#xqc, last 3h0m0s: 7360 messages from 1374 chatters over 26.4 min (279.2 msg/min)
  from subscribers: 36.7%   first-time chatters: 22   bits cheered: 800
  busiest minute: 04:31 UTC with 574 messages
  moderation: kept=6982 timeout=375 ban=3
  top chatters: viewer_02 (94), viewer_03 (78), viewer_04 (78), viewer_05 (75), viewer_06 (68)
  top Twitch emotes: LUL 71, xqcL 40, BatChest 32, DinoDance 9, xqcEZ_TK 9, DinoBusted 8, Kreygasm 8, JinxLUL 7
  events: resub=7 viewermilestone=2 sub=2
$ ./twitchlog stats -db chat.db -channel kaicenat -since 3h
#kaicenat, last 3h0m0s: 5083 messages from 1536 chatters over 26.3 min (193.1 msg/min)
  from subscribers: 25.8%   first-time chatters: 135   bits cheered: 1000
  busiest minute: 04:35 UTC with 814 messages
  moderation: kept=4952 timeout=128 ban=3
  top chatters: viewer_07 (107), viewer_08 (65), viewer_09 (52), viewer_10 (49), viewer_11 (48)
  top Twitch emotes: kaicFireMGM 448, <3 62, kaicQM 53, NeedHeal 42, BleedPurpleHD 36, kaicMGM 35, kaicHeart 27, WutFace 24
  events: resub=9 sub=8 raid=5 submysterygift=2 subgift=2 viewermilestone=1

The two chats differ in clear ways. #xqc is busier and more of its messages come from subscribers (36.7% vs 25.8%), and moderators hand out a lot of timeouts. #kaicenat has six times as many first-time chatters, more raids, and one channel emote, kaicFireMGM, accounts for about a third of all Twitch emotes used there (448 of 1,370). The "busiest minute" is in UTC (04:35 UTC is 11:35 in Asia/Saigon, where I ran this).

Full-text search uses FTS5 syntax: phrases in quotes, * for prefixes, NEAR(a b, 10) for words close together.

$ ./twitchlog search -db chat.db -q '"gta 6"' -channel xqc -tz Asia/Saigon | tail -6
2026-11-20 11:21:00 #xqc viewer_12: [gta 6] and 2000s youtube in one stream, nice
2026-11-20 11:20:25 #xqc viewer_13: have you seen that mall in [gta 6] yet
2026-11-20 11:17:08 #xqc viewer_14: the [gta 6] has that gta 5 driving wobble screen thing, i…
2026-11-20 11:14:12 #xqc viewer_15: [GTA 6] is kinda mid compared to gta 5
2026-11-20 11:13:19 #xqc viewer_14: why is forsen not streaming [gta 6] yet :(
12 matches (newest first, max 50)
$ ./twitchlog search -db chat.db -q 'NEAR(gta mall, 10)' -tz Asia/Saigon
2026-11-20 11:20:25 #xqc viewer_13: have you seen that [mall] in [gta] 6 yet
1 matches (newest first, max 50)

Pass user input through as-is and FTS5 will choke on punctuation:

$ ./twitchlog search -db chat.db -q 'gta 6?'
2026/11/20 11:42:19 SQL logic error: fts5: syntax error near "?" (1)

If the query comes from users, wrap each word in double quotes before you pass it on.

Exports print one line per message. Redacted messages keep their place in the timeline, so the log stays honest about what happened without repeating what was removed:

$ ./twitchlog export -db chat.db -channel xqc -day 2026-11-20 -tz Asia/Saigon
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_16: glass in front
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_17: jewelry
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_18: All that for 300
[2026-11-20 11:20:53] #xqc viewer_19: <message timeout>
[2026-11-20 11:20:54] #xqc viewer_20: Glass
[2026-11-20 11:20:54] #xqc viewer_21: jewlery
[2026-11-20 11:20:54] #xqc viewer_22: meow
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_23: jewelry💎!!
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_24: EZ
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_25: Omds break the front
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_26: smash the glasses
[2026-11-20 11:20:55] #xqc viewer_27: Merch drop #3 is out https://xqc.store/ EZ

Storage is small. The raw logs for all 12,443 messages came to 4.9 MB, and the SQLite file, FTS index included, to 3.4 MB. That's about 400 bytes of raw IRC per message, and a chat at 280 messages a minute would produce roughly 160 MB of raw log per 24 hours of streaming. Compress old raw logs with gzip.

Pitfalls, in one list

  • There's no backfill. Every minute your logger is down is lost. Neither IRC nor EventSub has history.
  • Raw IRC ports may be blocked. Port 443 WebSockets got through where 6667 and 6697 didn't.
  • Split frames on \r\n. One WebSocket message can carry several IRC lines.
  • Answer PING, or you get dropped. It comes about every 5 minutes, and a read deadline a bit longer than that catches dead connections.
  • A nonexistent channel fails silently. Confirm each JOIN echo.
  • Emote ranges are code points. Slice []rune, not bytes.
  • Strip U+034F and U+E0000 before storing or comparing messages.
  • Deduplicate on the message id. Twitch can send the same message twice, and replays will too.
  • Use user-id, not the login, to group messages by person. Logins can be renamed.
  • Timeouts redact more than one message. Store the reason, and keep the CLEARCHAT timestamp so a replay doesn't redact messages sent after it.
  • Batch your writes. A busy chat broke 800 messages a minute.
  • Third-party emotes are invisible to the tags.
  • Join limits: 20 joins per 10 seconds, 100 channels at once on a normal account.

Wrapping up

  • Twitch chat logs are forward-only. You build them by being connected; no API gives you yesterday's chat.
  • IRC over wss:// on port 443 is the simplest way to read chat, and the anonymous login needs no app registration. EventSub is the documented route Twitch recommends.
  • Treat moderation as data. Timeouts and deletions arrive as events. Honoring them keeps your log in line with what Twitch shows, and it's the decent thing to do.
  • Keep the raw log. With import, it's a full rebuild whenever your schema changes.

What would you track in a chat? Emote trends across a season, moderation load per stream, how raids change a chat? If you've built a Twitch chat logger with EventSub instead, I'd like to hear how it went.

*I build it.
