title: Build an avatar creator with layered SVG and Stimulus
description:
A while back I built a custom emoji composer using <canvas>. Fun project. But the canvas did all the work. It was responsible for the drawing surface, the drag logic and the export.

When I rebuilt the same idea as an avatar creator, I went for SVG instead. You pick a head, add some eyes, try a hat, then save the result as an image.

That cute face above is what I want to build today. 😊 A plain <svg>, a Stimulus controller and a folder of parts. No JS libraries except Stimulus.

As always, the code can be found on GitHub.

The HTML

Two elements: a <svg> for the preview and an empty <div> for the controls.

<div data-controller="avatar image-exporter" class="grid grid-cols-[300px_1fr] gap-8 max-w-5xl">
  <div>
    <svg data-avatar-target="preview" viewBox="0 0 300 300" width="300" height="300" class="bg-white border border-gray-200 rounded-lg"></svg>

    <div class="grid grid-cols-2 mt-2 gap-x-3 *:w-full *:bg-gray-300 *:rounded-md">
      <button data-action="click->avatar#reset">Reset</button>

      <button data-action="click->image-exporter#download">Save as image</button>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div data-avatar-target="controls" class="grid gap-4"></div>
</div>

The empty controls div is what the controller adds (more on why in a bit).

Why SVG instead of canvas?

The emoji composer drew glyphs onto a bitmap. Tracking where each one sat, converted mouse coordinates and cleared the surface before every redraw.

With this SVG version every part is real markup, so the browser handles layout and scaling. I keep the avatar as an object and turn it into an SVG string. When the object changes, rebuild a new string and drop it into the <svg>.

One win with this version: the avatar stays crisp at any size (because SVG!). With the emojis version this was not really possible.

Parts are data

Each part has its own file in app/javascript/avatar/parts/. Every option has a label and a render function that returns SVG:

const eyeball = (position) =>
  `<circle cx="${position}" cy="152" r="8" fill="#fff" stroke="#2b2b2b" stroke-width="2"/>` +
  `<circle cx="${position}" cy="153" r="4" fill="#2b2b2b"/>`

export const eyes = {
  round: { label: "Round", render: () => bothEyes(eyeball) },
  happy: { label: "Happy", render: () => bothEyes(happyEye) },
  wide: { label: "Wide", render: () => bothEyes(wideEye) },
  sleepy: { label: "Sleepy", render: () => bothEyes(sleepyEye) }
}

To add a new pair of eyes, add an entry. The rest of the component finds it on its own.

Skin and hair color work the same: just carrying a hex value instead of a render function:

export const skin = {
  light: { label: "Light", color: "#ffe0c2" },
  fair: { label: "Fair", color: "#f1c9a5" },
  tan: { label: "Tan", color: "#d99b6c" },
  brown: { label: "Brown", color: "#a96b3f" },
  dark: { label: "Dark", color: "#6b4226" }
}

The layer order

[AD] Spinal CMS: Git-based CMS for static site generators

An avatar is a stack of parts. The order decides what sits on top. Ears go behind the head. The nose goes over the face. The hat goes over the hair.

Hair is a fun one, because it has two layers. The front fringe covers the forehead. Long hair also has a back mass that falls behind the head. So the renderer asks hair for both:

export function renderAvatar(avatar) {
  const context = {
    ...avatar,
    skin: skin[avatar.skin].color,
    hairColor: hairColor[avatar.hairColor].color
  }

  const hairstyle = hair[avatar.hairStyle]

  return [
    hairstyle.back(context),
    ears[avatar.ears].render(context),
    head[avatar.head].render(context),
    hairstyle.front(context),
    eyes[avatar.eyes].render(context),
    nose[avatar.nose].render(context),
    mouth[avatar.mouth].render(context),
    hat[avatar.hat].render(context)
  ].join("")
}

Read it top to bottom and you can picture the face. The context carries the colors, so each part receives #f1c9a5 instead of the string "fair".

One object, full redraw

The controller adds the avatar as an object. Changing a part means copying that object with one new value, then re-rendering:

import { Controller } from "@hotwired/stimulus"
import { renderAvatar } from "avatar/renderer"
import { sections } from "avatar/sections"
import { defaultAvatar } from "avatar/defaults"

export default class extends Controller {
  static targets = ["preview", "controls"]

  #avatar = { ...defaultAvatar }

  connect() {
    this.#renderControls()

    this.#render()
  }

  setOption(event) {
    const { property, value } = event.currentTarget.dataset
    this.#avatar = { ...this.#avatar, [property]: value }

    this.#render()
  }

  reset() {
    this.#avatar = { ...defaultAvatar }

    this.#render()
  }
}

Controls that build themselves

One file adds every control on the page:

export const sections = [
  {
    label: "Hair",
    controls: [
      { property: "hairStyle", options: hair },
      { property: "hairColor", options: hairColor, type: "color" }
    ]
  },
  // head, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, hat, etc.
]

The controller goes over that list and creates a button for each option. A type: "color" control becomes a swatch. Everything else is a labeled button:

if (control.type === "color") {
  button.className = "size-8 rounded-full border border-gray-300"
  button.style.background = option.color
} else {
  button.className = "px-2 py-1 bg-white border border-gray-200 rounded-md text-sm hover:border-gray-400"
  button.textContent = option.label
}

Each button has a data-property and data-value.

Save as image

You cannot call toDataURL on an <svg> element. So I serialize the SVG to a string, load it into an Image, then draw that image onto a canvas:

const svg = this.element.querySelector("svg")
const source = new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(svg)
const image = new Image()

image.onload = () => {
  const size = 600
  const canvas = document.createElement("canvas")

  canvas.width = size
  canvas.height = size
  canvas.getContext("2d").drawImage(image, 0, 0, size, size)

  this.#trigger(this.#downloadLink(canvas.toDataURL("image/png")))
}

image.src = "data:image/svg+xml;charset=utf-8," + encodeURIComponent(source)

The canvas draws at 600×600, so the exported PNG comes out sharper than the on-screen preview. One thing to watch: any CSS the SVG relies on has to be inline. The serialized copy carries no external styles.

title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
description:
arXiv:2611.24994v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
description:
arXiv:2611.23678v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

title: Designing APIs Around Customer Workflows Instead of Resources
description:
I've been working on identifying gaps and improving our API. Initially, I discovered numerous endpoints that were missing, and I initially thought we needed to add them because having more endpoints is better, right? However, as I began researching further, I realized that adding too many endpoints could pose a security risk by exposing more information than necessary. This led me to consider how I could determine which API endpoints are essential and should be added to our product roadmap. This train of thought inspired me to create a scenario to help clarify my approach.

Imagine you're building an API for a food delivery app. Your main entities include restaurants, customers, menus, orders, payments, and delivery drivers. Naturally, you might start designing endpoints around these resources:

  • GET /restaurants
  • GET /menu-items
  • POST /orders
  • GET /orders/{id}
  • POST /payments

At first glance, everything looks good. You have endpoints to create, retrieve, and manage the various objects in your system. However, here’s an important question: Can someone actually order dinner using your API?

This question might seem obvious, but it highlights a crucial distinction in API design. A customer doesn’t wake up thinking, “I need to make a POST request to the orders endpoint.” Instead, they think, “I’m hungry, I want a burger, and I want it delivered before my next meeting.”

Customers think in workflows, while developers build integrations around those workflows. Therefore, APIs need to bridge the gap between these two perspectives.

The Problem with Designing APIs Around Resources

Let’s go back to our food delivery app. Imagine a developer is integrating your API into a restaurant's own ordering system. Their goal is to allow customers to browse the menu, customize a meal, place an order, pay, and track delivery all without ever visiting your app.

You've provided endpoints for restaurants, menu items, orders, and payments. However, when the developer begins building the integration, they encounter several problems:

  • They can retrieve a menu but cannot determine which items are currently unavailable.
  • They can create an order but cannot customize a burger with extra toppings.
  • They can submit a payment but cannot verify whether the payment was successful.
  • They can retrieve an order but cannot tell when the driver picks it up.
  • They can view an order but cannot cancel it after submission.

While you technically have an API that exposes all the major resources, the developer still cannot deliver the experience that their customers expect. This situation arises when we focus too much on the data our system stores and not enough on what people need to do with that data.

Start with the Customer's Journey, Not the Data Model

Instead of starting with resources like restaurants, menu items, and orders, let's start with the customer. What does the process of ordering dinner actually look like?

The Food Delivery Journey

A fictional customer ordering a burger

  1. Find a restaurant: Browse nearby restaurants and check whether they are accepting orders.
  2. Build a meal: Choose a burger, add toppings, select a side, and customize the order.
  3. Place an order: Submit the order and receive confirmation.
  4. Pay for dinner: Submit payment and receive confirmation that the transaction succeeded.
  5. Track the delivery: See when the restaurant accepts the order, when the food is ready, and when the driver is on the way.
  6. Resolve a problem: Cancel an eligible order, report a missing item, or request help.

Now we have a useful overview of the customer workflow. We can use each step to identify what functionalities the API needs to support.

Map the Workflow to API Capabilities

Once we understand the journey, we can translate each customer action into an API requirement:

Customer Action API Capability
Find a restaurant Search and filter restaurants
Browse the menu Retrieve menu items and availability
Customize a burger Submit item options and modifiers
Place an order Create an order
Pay for dinner Process and verify payment
Track delivery Retrieve order and delivery status
Receive updates Subscribe to order status webhooks
Cancel an order Cancel eligible orders
Report a missing item Submit a support request

Notice that we’re no longer just thinking about whether we have an endpoint for orders or restaurants. We're considering whether the API supports every action required to complete the entire experience. This perspective is where product opportunities begin to emerge. For example, if customers can create an order but cannot retrieve real-time delivery updates, we could introduce a polling endpoint, but would that actually provide the best experience? Perhaps webhooks would be a better solution. Instead of repeatedly asking the API whether the order has changed, the system could notify the integration when the order status changes from preparing to out for delivery, for example.

The right solution comes from understanding the workflow first.

Not Every Missing Endpoint Deserves to Be Built

This is where product management plays a vital role. Suppose customers are complaining that they can't modify an order after submitting it. Your first instinct might be to create an endpoint like:

  • PATCH /orders/{id}

While this might seem like a simple solution, it's important to consider a few critical questions before building it:

  • Can customers modify an order after the restaurant has started preparing it?
  • Should they be allowed to change their delivery address?
  • What other restrictions should be in place?

By approaching API design with a focus on customer workflows, you can create a more intuitive and efficient experience that meets the needs of both users and developers.

title: Amazon EventBridge Custom event bus now supports Amazon MSK as a target
description:
Amazon EventBridge now supports Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) as a target for the enhanced Custom event bus, so you can deliver events to Kafka topics without running your own producer.

The EventBridge Custom event bus is a serverless event broker that enables you to create scalable event-driven applications by routing events between your applications, SaaS integrations, and AWS services. To deliver events to MSK, you create a Subscriber that specifies the cluster ARN and topic. You can also configure Kafka producer settings such as partition key, acknowledgment level, and record headers. EventBridge supports both public and private, serverless and provisioned clusters. When you create a Subscriber for a private cluster, EventBridge automatically sets up a private connection to the cluster. For example, teams that publish to a shared Custom event bus can now deliver purchase-order events to the MSK topics their payments team already consumes from.

Amazon MSK targets are available in all AWS Regions where the enhanced Custom event bus is available. Delivery to MSK is billed as standard Custom event bus egress. EventBridge also supports compression before delivery, which is billed as an Event Evaluation.

To learn more, see Amazon MSK cluster target in the Amazon EventBridge User Guide and the Amazon EventBridge product page. Install the Agent Toolkit for AWS to start building with your AI coding agent.

title: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring
description:
arXiv:2611.25273v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Graph coloring, which entails assigning colors to nodes such that no adjacent nodes have the same color, is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem. In general, however, finding a node coloring with no monochromatic edges given a fixed palette is NP-hard. This motivates learning-based methods that can learn to exploit recurring structure across instances to efficiently produce high-quality colorings. Crucially, the validity of a coloring is invariant to permutations of the colors, and we show that exploiting this symmetry reduces the size of the effective state space over which the model has to learn its policy. At the same time, the coloring algorithm must be able to break some symmetries, for example to assign different colors to two adjacent nodes belonging to the same automorphism orbit. In this paper, we introduce Scone, a model that uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct colorings sequentially, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate and break node symmetries. Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including on sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and showcases generalization to graph families not encountered during training.

title: Google’s Gemini 4 Neon Is Here. How Should Developers Test It?
description:
A coding model can finish a pull request in two minutes. If an engineer spends twenty minutes finding the missing test and undoing an unnecessary refactor, how fast was the model?

That’s a useful question to ask about Gemini 4 Neon, which Google introduced on November 18. Google positions it between Hydrogen for everyday tasks and Carbon for deeper, longer-running work. Neon has a one-million-token context window, four thinking levels, and is rolling out through the paid Gemini API and Google Antigravity on eligible plans. Google’s launch announcement · Antigravity release details

Start with a pull request your team already fixed

Pick a recently resolved bug that required changes across a few files. Give Neon and your current coding model the same issue description, repository snapshot from before the fix, and acceptance criteria. Keep the merged patch out of the materials they can see. Use it afterward as a reference, while allowing for other valid solutions.

A good test case might be a settings change where existing users must keep their preferences and new users should receive a different default. The task is easy to describe, but a patch can look correct while quietly changing behavior for existing users.

Give both outputs the same review you’d give a teammate’s pull request.

Check What to record
Correctness Did the patch fix the issue and preserve existing behavior?
Scope Did it limit changes to the files and behavior the task required?
Review effort How many minutes did a developer spend checking and correcting it?
Cost What did the full attempt cost, including retries?

Try a change of direction midway

Real requirements change. Once each model proposes a fix, add a constraint: the old configuration format must remain readable for one more release.

See whether the model updates its plan, revises the relevant tests, and preserves the work that still applies. This tells you something a clean first attempt can’t: how much rework the model creates when you steer it halfway through a task.

You can also run the same issue at two thinking levels. A deeper setting earns its place if it catches a missed compatibility case or cuts review time enough to justify the extra latency. For simpler changes, the faster setting may already meet your acceptance criteria.

Decide where Neon fits

Try this with a small mix of tasks: one bug fix, one refactor, and one change that crosses module boundaries. Compare the total time from issue to review-ready patch. If Neon helps most on cross-module changes, that’s a good place to start using it. You can keep measuring as new tasks come in.

What would make you switch coding models first: less review time, fewer regressions, or lower cost per completed task?

title: Node.js SaaS Shipment Updates: Background Queue vs Cron for File, Email, Webhook Sync
description:
Short answer: for a Node.js SaaS that must fan out a shipment update, put each file processing, email sending, and webhook sync attempt behind a background job queue. Use cron to discover periodic work, such as a retry sweep. A clock can find work; it cannot remember which subscriber was delivered, which one timed out, or which side effect may have happened just before a crash.

Here is the small choice matrix I would start with:

Work Default Delivery reason
Process a file after an upload Queue job The job has one owner, attempt history, and a retry deadline
Send an email for a shipment update Queue job One slow recipient stays isolated from the fan-out
Sync a webhook subscriber Queue job Each endpoint needs its own backoff and idempotency key
Find work due at 02:00 Cron, then enqueue The schedule discovers records; a worker performs the effects
Remove expired temporary files Cron A later run can safely discover the same cleanup again

The easiest setup is usually a durable jobs table, one worker, and one scheduler. You do not need to start with a large messaging system to get the important guarantee. You do need durable state.

How should a beginner use a background job queue for file processing in a Node.js SaaS?

Start by naming the guarantee in plain English. For the shipment event shp_4821, the SaaS might need to attempt an email for subscriber sub_19, process a label PDF, and synchronize a webhook endpoint. Those are three jobs, even if one button created them. Each has a different destination, timeout, payload, and definition of success. Treating the fan-out as one function call hides the exact information an operator needs when a customer says, “the email arrived, but the partner system did not update.”

The useful promise is usually at-least-once processing with idempotent effects. Exactly-once delivery sounds tidy, but an external email or webhook can accept a request immediately before the worker loses power. The worker then cannot know whether repeating the request is safe. I would rather document that boundary than hide it behind a green status badge.

Keep these values with the job:

  • kind, payload, and the shipment event ID
  • attempts, nextAttemptAt, and a retry deadline
  • status, leaseUntil, and the last error category
  • a stable idempotency key for the logical side effect

The key should identify the effect, not merely the worker run. For example, shipment:shp_4821:subscriber:sub_19:webhook:v3 is more useful than a random UUID generated during a retry. A database uniqueness constraint can stop two workers from creating the same logical delivery record. The receiver still needs to honor a request key, or your system must accept that a crash can produce a duplicate.

Three words matter here: claim, effect, record. Claim a job for a limited lease. Perform one bounded effect. Record success only after the effect returns. If the process exits between the last two steps, the lease expires and the job becomes available again. That is the failure path your design has to explain.

RabbitMQ's consumer acknowledgement documentation describes the same handoff concern: an acknowledgement tells the broker that a consumer has handled a delivery, while an unacknowledged delivery can be made available again. The acknowledgement is useful state. It is not proof that an unrelated third-party side effect happened exactly once.

What delivery data belongs in the seven-day ledger?

Cron answers “when should I look?” It does not naturally answer “which of 18,000 subscribers is on attempt four, and which one is due in six hours?” A queue or durable job table can make that per-delivery state explicit.

This distinction matters for delayed messages up to 7 days. A retry due next week should have a stored deadline and a stored idempotency key. It should not depend on a Node.js process staying alive or on a cron script remembering local variables from last Tuesday.

Backoff should be bounded. A practical policy can use exponential delay with jitter, cap the delay at seven days, and move a permanently rejected job to a dead state. Classify errors before applying that policy. A timeout or transient network failure may be retryable. A malformed payload, invalid recipient, or authorization failure usually needs repair instead of twelve identical requests.

My test case includes a 409 from a deduplication constraint. I treat that as “the logical effect already exists,” not as a reason to send the email again. I'm not sure every provider uses that exact status or meaning, so the mapping belongs in the adapter for that provider, not in a generic worker.

The long delay also changes operations. Retain enough metadata to investigate a missed delivery without retaining secrets forever. Store a file reference instead of copying a large file into every job. Redact webhook credentials and email addresses in logs. A seven-day retry policy without a way to inspect or expire its payload is just a seven-day data-retention problem.

Can a cron workflow discover email and webhook work without owning it?

Make the scheduler a producer. It finds due work in bounded batches, inserts jobs with a uniqueness rule, and exits. Make the worker the owner of delivery. This division keeps a missed scheduled run recoverable and keeps a long webhook retry from turning into one enormous cron invocation.

The following TypeScript is deliberately an interface boundary. The database and queue implementations can change without changing the delivery rules.

type JobKind = "file.process" | "email.send" | "webhook.sync";

type DeliveryJob = {
  id: string;
  kind: JobKind;
  shipmentEventId: string;
  idempotencyKey: string;
  attempts: number;
  nextAttemptAt: number;
  expiresAt: number;
};

type JobStore = {
  claim(now: number, leaseMs: number): Promise<DeliveryJob | null>;
  markDone(id: string): Promise<void>;
  scheduleRetry(id: string, at: number, reason: string): Promise<void>;
  markDead(id: string, reason: string): Promise<void>;
};

type DeliveryEffect = {
  run(job: DeliveryJob): Promise<"done" | "retryable" | "permanent">;
};

async function processOne(store: JobStore, effect: DeliveryEffect): Promise<void> {
  const job = await store.claim(Date.now(), 60_000);
  if (!job) return;

  try {
    const result = await effect.run(job);
    if (result === "done") {
      await store.markDone(job.id);
      return;
    }

    if (result === "permanent" || Date.now() >= job.expiresAt) {
      await store.markDead(job.id, "delivery deadline reached");
      return;
    }

    const exponentialMs = Math.min(24 * 60 * 60 * 1000, 2 ** job.attempts * 1_000);
    const jitterMs = Math.floor(Math.random() * 1_000);
    await store.scheduleRetry(job.id, Date.now() + exponentialMs + jitterMs, "transient failure");
  } catch (error) {
    await store.scheduleRetry(job.id, Date.now() + 60_000, String(error));
  }
}

The adapter behind effect.run checks the idempotency key at the effect boundary. That matters because a lease can expire while a file processor is still finishing, allowing another worker to see the same logical job. A check only in the scheduler is too late.

Run the scheduler like this: select rows whose nextAttemptAt is due, insert a bounded batch, and let the uniqueness rule reject duplicates. GitHub Actions documents scheduled workflow triggers as a time-based mechanism; the same principle applies to any cron host. The scheduled process should not carry the delivery state in memory, and it should not report success until the discovered work is durable.

How can I benchmark the handoff before adding a broker?

Cron is a good fit for periodic, bounded work where lateness is acceptable and the next run can repair an omission. Expiring temporary files, reconciling a small table, and finding retryable rows are reasonable examples. A five-minute sweep can enqueue due delivery jobs without pretending that every subscriber is one five-minute task.

Measure it.

The catch is that cron alone is not suitable when subscribers have independent deadlines, rate limits, attempt histories, or dead-letter handling. It also becomes awkward when file processing takes longer than the schedule interval or when one failed email blocks later recipients in the same loop. Use a queue for that execution layer.

A queue can be the wrong first move, too. If the team cannot operate a broker and the workload is modest, a database-backed queue with polling may be easier to reason about. If the task has no meaningful recovery path and a missed run is harmless, adding durable per-item delivery state is configuration bloat. Keep the least complex mechanism that records the guarantee you actually need.

Do not choose by monthly price alone. Measure time to first call, queue age, p95 delivery latency, retry rate, dead-job count, and operator steps during a replay. I care about those numbers because a cheap queue that needs a custom script for every failure is not cheap in engineering time. There is a large difference between a job that is late for 30 seconds and one that is still pending after its subscriber's seven-day window; both can look like “the worker is running” in a shallow dashboard, while only the latter is a delivery incident. Your mileage may vary with traffic and latency targets.

What does the queue-versus-cron comparison say about low-stakes cleanup?

The failure drill belongs in this benchmark, not in a launch checklist nobody runs. Start two workers against the same job. Kill one after the outbound request returns but before markDone. Pause one webhook endpoint. Feed the file processor a large input. Advance the clock beyond the seven-day deadline.

The expected result is not “nothing runs twice.” The expected result is that repeated logical work is harmless or visible, the job can be traced by its idempotency key, and a permanent failure stops retrying. A green email response does not prove that the database update happened afterward.

Log the job ID, shipment event ID, attempt number, and outcome category. Do not log credentials or full webhook payloads by default. Alert on old pending jobs and an unusual retry rate, not only on a dead worker process. Those signals tell you whether delivery is drifting before a customer reports a missing update.

The decision rule is short: cron discovers time-based work; a background job queue owns independent delivery attempts. For a Node.js SaaS sending shipment updates to many subscribers, that boundary makes retries, idempotency, and delayed messages explicit without promising a guarantee the outside system cannot provide.

References

  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • GitHub Actions scheduled workflow triggers: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: Cron Backups of App Data to an S3-Compatible Bucket (Presigned Restore Included)
description:
Use a private bucket per tenant, date-based key prefixes, and a short-lived presigned URL for every restore. That one rule covers the boring 95% of app data backups on S3-compatible object storage: a cron job uploads the nightly database dump plus a zip of that tenant's media, nothing is ever publicly linkable, and a restore is an ordinary HTTPS download that expires on its own.

The upload is the easy half.

What gets you paged is the other half. I run the cron and queue tier for an edtech platform, and the two incidents that keep coming back are a job that silently didn't run and a job that ran twice — one leaves you with no backup, the other leaves you with two objects and no idea which one is complete. Neither shows up in a dashboard that only counts successful API calls. Both show up at 8am when a school asks for last term's gradebook.

So the design below is written backwards from those failure modes, rather than from a feature list. The worked example calls Infrai, which is a plain REST API over HTTP with no SDK to install, so the same request works from a Go worker and from the Node.js cron script it replaced.

The failure modes that decide the whole design

Four things go wrong, in roughly this order of frequency.

The job doesn't fire at all — the container was being redeployed during the cron window, and nothing anywhere records the non-event. The job fires but the dump is truncated, so you store a 40-byte gzip that unpacks into nothing. The job fires twice after a retry, and now two objects exist under near-identical keys. And the one that hurts most in a multi-tenant product: a restore writes tenant A's data into tenant B's prefix, because the key was assembled from a variable that was empty.

Every one of those is an idempotency and naming problem before it's a storage problem. Derive the key from data you already have — tenant id and UTC date — so the same run always produces the same object path. A retry then overwrites its own object rather than creating a sibling. Write the checksum next to the object, or the size at minimum, so "did this actually work" is answerable without downloading the file.

Tenant isolation is the axis I'd optimise for first. A bucket per tenant gives you a hard boundary and per-tenant usage numbers; a shared bucket with backups/{tenant}/{date}/ prefixes is cheaper to operate but puts the entire boundary inside a string you build at runtime. I've used both. The shared-bucket version is fine right up until someone writes a restore script with a default tenant argument.

What does the upload code look like for a nightly database dump to an S3-compatible bucket?

Sign a PUT, then send the bytes straight from the worker to the bucket. Your app process never touches the payload, which matters more than it sounds when the nightly archive is a few gigabytes of course video rather than a small SQL file.

Here's the shape of it in Go. It asks the storage API for a signed upload URL, then streams the file to that URL with no platform credentials attached:

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    apiBase     = "https://api.infrai.cc"
    presignPath = "/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
)

// One key per tenant per UTC day. A retried run recomputes the same key, so the
// second attempt replaces its own object instead of leaving a twin behind.
func backupKey(tenant string, day time.Time) string {
    return fmt.Sprintf("backups/%s/%s/dump.sql.gz", tenant, day.UTC().Format("2006/01/02"))
}

type presignRequest struct {
    Op             string `json:"op"`
    ExpiresSeconds int    `json:"expires_seconds"`
    ContentType    string `json:"content_type"`
    IdempotencyKey string `json:"idempotency_key"`
}

type presignResponse struct {
    URL string `json:"url"`
}

func presign(client *http.Client, bucket, key, op string) (string, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(presignRequest{
        Op:             op, // "put" to upload the dump, "get" to restore it
        ExpiresSeconds: 900,
        ContentType:    "application/gzip",
        IdempotencyKey: op + ":" + bucket + ":" + key,
    })
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    endpoint := apiBase + strings.NewReplacer("{bucket}", bucket, "{key}", key).Replace(presignPath)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", endpoint, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return "", err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return "", err
        }
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if after := res.Header.Get("Retry-After"); after != "" {
                if secs, convErr := strconv.Atoi(after); convErr == nil {
                    wait = time.Duration(secs) * time.Second
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return "", fmt.Errorf("presign %s: status %d: %s", op, res.StatusCode, body)
        }

        var out presignResponse
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &out); err != nil {
            return "", err
        }
        return out.URL, nil
    }
    return "", fmt.Errorf("presign %s: rate limited after 5 attempts", op)
}

// Send the archive to the signed URL. No Authorization header here: the
// signature is the credential, and the dump never passes through the app.
func uploadDump(client *http.Client, signedURL, path string) error {
    f, err := os.Open(path)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer f.Close()

    stat, err := f.Stat()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req, err := http.NewRequest("PUT", signedURL, f)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.ContentLength = stat.Size()
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/gzip")

    res, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        return fmt.Errorf("upload %s: status %d: %s", path, res.StatusCode, body)
    }
    return nil
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Minute}
    bucket, tenant := "edu-backups-prod", "tenant-4471"
    key := backupKey(tenant, time.Now())

    signedURL, err := presign(client, bucket, key, "put")
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    if err := uploadDump(client, signedURL, "/var/backups/dump.sql.gz"); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("uploaded", key)
}

Three details in there are worth copying regardless of which provider you pick. Derive the object key, never randomise it. The 429 branch honours Retry-After instead of spinning. And the signed URL gets no Authorization header — sending platform credentials to a pre-signed link is a habit worth breaking early.

The idempotency key in that request body is the platform's own convention rather than something I bolted on, and it's specified the same way across the whole surface — which is exactly what you want from a job that retries at 3am. If you need object versioning or a browser that uploads straight to the bucket, that's a different conversation, and it's the next section.

Retention, prefixes, and the part you can't undo

Lifecycle rules do the deleting. Point one at the backups/ prefix with a 7-day or 30-day expiration and stop writing cleanup cron jobs — with one constraint to plan around: the minimum expiration window is one day, so you can't express "keep these for six hours" as a lifecycle rule. For anything shorter, delete explicitly from your own job.

The harder constraint is what happens after a bad write.

Object versioning and object lock are not available on this platform, so an overwritten or deleted backup is gone in the ordinary sense — there's no previous version hiding behind it. That's a real boundary and it changes the design: you need the retention discipline outside the bucket. In practice that means a weekly copy to a second provider, and write access that's scoped to the backup worker's own credential rather than shared with the app. If you're under a regulatory regime that demands write-once storage — say student records under a records-retention rule — then stick with S3 and Object Lock in compliance mode, because nothing else here is a good fit for that requirement.

Same story for browser-direct uploads. Self-service CORS configuration isn't offered, so the pattern of handing a signed PUT to a browser tab doesn't apply cleanly; server-side workers and server-generated download links do. For a backup pipeline that's irrelevant, since the uploader is a worker. The catch is a media pipeline where the student's browser uploads a 2 GB lecture recording directly — for that, pick a bucket whose CORS rules you can set yourself.

Where the options actually differ

Nobody picks object storage on features any more; they pick it on operational shape. Roughly:

Option Fits when The catch
AWS S3 You need versioning, Object Lock, cross-region replication, or an existing IAM model Egress costs and IAM complexity; more surface than a backup job needs
Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility plus browser-facing uploads you configure yourself Fewer compliance primitives than S3; separate account and key
Backblaze B2 Cheap cold archive with an S3-compatible API Fewer regions; slower restores than you'd assume
MinIO (self-hosted) Data must stay on hardware you control You now operate the storage layer, including its own backups
Infrai You want the upload, the signed restore and the rest of your backend behind one key and one REST contract No object versioning or object lock; no self-service CORS

Two of those rows are about the storage; three are about what else you have to run. If you already have an IAM story and a compliance requirement, S3 wins and it isn't close. If your backup job is the only reason you'd create yet another cloud account, a platform with one key across storage and the rest of your backend removes an integration you'd otherwise maintain forever.

Test the restore before you need it

An untested backup is a belief, not a backup. The drill is short enough to run weekly from the same cron tier that writes the dumps:

pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" | gzip -9 > /var/backups/dump.sql.gz
sha256sum /var/backups/dump.sql.gz | tee /var/backups/dump.sql.gz.sha256

curl -fsS -o /tmp/dump.sql.gz "$SIGNED_GET_URL"
sha256sum /tmp/dump.sql.gz | awk '{print $1}' > /tmp/restored.sha256
awk '{print $1}' /var/backups/dump.sql.gz.sha256 | diff - /tmp/restored.sha256 || echo "checksum drift"
gunzip -c /tmp/dump.sql.gz | psql "$SCRATCH_DATABASE_URL"

Three signals are worth alerting on, and only three: the object for today's date prefix doesn't exist by 09:00 UTC, its size is below a floor you set per tenant, or the weekly drill didn't finish. The first one catches the missed run that no error log will ever mention, because a job that never started produces no error. I'd rather get that page than a clean dashboard.

Rollback is deliberately dull. Keep the previous day's key untouched, restore into a scratch database first, and only then swap. Since there's no versioning underneath you, the object you're restoring from must never be the object you're about to overwrite — restore from yesterday's prefix, write today's dump to today's prefix, and let lifecycle expire the old ones on its own schedule.

If your backup job is the only reason you'd open yet another cloud account, Infrai is worth a look for this one slice of the workflow, because one key covers the bucket, the signed restore and whatever else the app already calls — and the nightly-backup walkthrough covers schedule, upload, expiry and restore end to end. I'd still keep a second copy somewhere else. A backup you can lose in a single accident was never really a backup.

References

  • AWS S3: Managing the lifecycle of objects
  • AWS S3: Using S3 Object Lock
  • AWS S3: Using presigned URLs
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API
  • MinIO object storage documentation
  • PostgreSQL: pg_dump
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

title: Do Deep Stereo Models Learn Shape Priors?
description:
arXiv:2611.25113v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Localizing object boundaries is important for embodied visual systems, since small boundary errors can change the inferred geometry of physical surfaces. We study whether deep stereo models produce boundaries consistent with simple shape priors when local image and disparity cues are weak. We create a synthetic stereo dataset consisting of objects drawn from a highly constrained family of shapes, with randomized depth, slant, color and texture. Despite the simplicity of this shape space, we find that several state-of-the-art stereo models retain systematic boundary errors, even when finetuned or trained from scratch on the dataset. We then introduce a simple generative stereo model that jointly predicts disparity and a distance field representing object boundaries. The model improves boundary localization and produces contours that adhere more closely to the underlying shape space. These results expose limitations in the boundary predictions of current stereo architectures when local evidence is weak, and motivate further study of whether generative models can better combine regional grouping evidence with global geometric structure.

title: Daemons can now send traces to Vercel Tracing
description:
Vercel Daemons can now send OpenTelemetry traces to Vercel Tracing, allowing you and your agents to inspect background worker operations alongside the rest of your project's traces.

Vercel provides each daemon with a Unix socket for receiving OTLP/HTTP traces and sets the socket's path in VERCEL_OTEL_SOCKET_PATH.

Upgrading @vercel/otel to version 2.3.0 or later enables automatic trace export for Node.js daemons using the default configuration. The SDK detects this socket and sends the spans your worker records to Vercel.

These spans are available through the Vercel CLI, which can search by service name within a project and return JSON for your agents.

Learn more in the daemon tracing documentation.

title: LocalSend: Like AirDrop, but for Every Device, Free and Open Source
description:
LocalSend is a free open source app that sends files, photos, and messages between any of your devices over your local network. It works like AirDrop, but it covers Android, iPhone, Windows, Mac, and Linux, and it never touches the internet.

What LocalSend Is: AirDrop Without the Walled Garden

LocalSend is a free, open source app for sharing files and messages with nearby devices over your local network, and it needs no internet connection to do it. It is the cross-platform answer to AirDrop: send a photo from an Android phone to an iPhone, a document from a Windows laptop to a Mac, or a video from a Linux desktop to a tablet, all without a cable, an account, or a cloud service in the middle. It has 98,900 stars on GitHub, it is licensed under Apache 2.0, and it runs on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux, and Fire OS. The pitch is simple. Every phone already knows how to share with its own kind, and almost none of them know how to share with the other kind. LocalSend fills that gap with one app on every device, and it does it without asking you to trust a server you have never heard of, because there is no server at all.

How It Works: Your Wi-Fi Is the Only Infrastructure

LocalSend devices find each other on the same local network and talk directly, using a REST API over HTTPS. Every device generates its own TLS certificate on the fly, so the transfer is encrypted end to end even though nothing ever leaves your network. There are no third-party servers, no upload step, and no account to create. The app listens on port 53317 for TCP and UDP traffic, which is the one detail worth knowing before you use it: if a device does not show up, your firewall is the usual suspect. On Linux, allow the port with your firewall tool, for example sudo ufw allow 53317, and check that AP isolation is off on your router, since some routers, especially on guest networks, block devices from seeing each other. A VPN can also hide local devices, so allow local traffic or pause it while you send. If discovery still fails, LocalSend lets you send to a device by its exact address instead, and the command line client can target an IP Check result directly. When devices on the same network cannot see each other at all, a DNS Lookup can help confirm whether the network itself is resolving names the way it should.

What You Can Send: Files, Folders, and Messages

LocalSend moves more than files. You can send photos, videos, documents, and whole folders, and directories are collected recursively with their folder names and nested paths preserved on the receiving side. You can also send a short text message, a link, or a snippet of text, which is handy when you want to move a URL or a code from your phone to your computer without emailing it to yourself. Text longer than 64 KB is sent as a .txt file instead, and you can read text from standard input on the command line. Sharing works from other apps too: use the system share sheet on your phone to send a photo or a file straight into LocalSend, and it appears on the destination device as a normal download. There is no file size limit in the app itself, so the only real constraint is your Wi-Fi. The README is upfront about one speed quirk on Android and recommends 5 GHz Wi-Fi, with encryption off on both devices if a transfer feels slow.

Every Platform, Every Store

LocalSend is on every major platform, and it is in the stores and package managers people already use. Windows users can install it from Winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, or the Microsoft Store, or grab the EXE installer or a portable ZIP from the releases page. On macOS it is in the App Store and Homebrew, with a DMG installer as well. Linux users get Flathub, Snap, Nixpkgs, the AUR, DEB packages, AppImages, and TAR archives. Android has the Play Store, F-Droid, and a direct APK, and iOS has the App Store. There is even a Fire OS build for Amazon tablets. The README recommends installing from a store or a package manager rather than a manual download, because the app has no auto-update. Minimum versions are reasonable: Android 7, iOS 15, macOS 12 Monterey, and Windows 10, with older releases still available for older systems. That breadth is the point. AirDrop works because Apple controls both ends, and LocalSend works because it refuses to care which ends you have.

The Command Line Client: LocalSend in a Terminal

There is also a terminal client, localsend-cli, built on LocalSend Protocol v2. On macOS and Linux you install it with Homebrew, then send files with a single command: localsend-cli send report.pdf photo.jpg ./project-backup. The command opens the discovered-device list so you can pick a destination interactively, or you can skip the list and target a device by its exact alias or IP address, for example localsend-cli send --to "Cute Tomato" report.pdf. To send text instead of a file, add --text, and pass a dash to read the text from standard input. That makes the CLI useful in scripts: pipe a command's output into a file on another machine, or move a build artifact to a phone without touching a GUI. The same 64 KB text rule applies, and standard input must be UTF-8 and no larger than 16 MB. The CLI is a separate small install from the app, and it speaks the same protocol, so a terminal on one machine and the app on another work together without any extra setup.

Portable Mode, Hidden Starts, and Staying Out of the Way

LocalSend has a few quiet features for people who run it all day. Portable mode, added in version 1.13.0, stores settings next to the executable instead of in the system settings folder: create an empty file called settings.json beside the app and it keeps everything there, which makes it easy to carry on a USB stick. You can also start the app hidden, so it sits in the system tray without opening a window, using the --hidden flag, and an autostart option does the same at login. Windows binaries are signed, and the signing policy is published in the repo, which is a small detail that matters for an app that opens a network port on your machine. The project is actively maintained, with CI, translations through Weblate, and a Discord community, and it is also mirrored on Codeberg for anyone who prefers it. None of this changes the core idea, which is that moving a file between your own devices should not require the internet, an account, or a subscription.

Getting Started in Two Minutes

Install LocalSend on the two devices you want to move files between, then open it on both. Each device shows its own name and the devices it can see on the network. Pick the destination, choose the files, and the transfer starts over HTTPS with a progress bar on both ends. If a device does not appear, check the three usual causes in order: the firewall on port 53317, AP isolation on the router, and an active VPN blocking local traffic. The receiver can save files to a chosen folder or let LocalSend pick the default download location. That is the whole setup. There is no account to make, no QR code to scan, no cable to find, and nothing to upload first. For anyone who regularly moves files between an Android phone and a Windows PC, or an iPhone and a Linux desktop, LocalSend removes a daily friction that most people have quietly accepted as normal.

FAQs

What is LocalSend?

LocalSend is a free open source app that shares files, photos, folders, and messages between nearby devices over a local network. It works across Android, iPhone, Windows, Mac, Linux, and Fire OS, like AirDrop but for every device, and it needs no internet connection, no account, and no outside servers.

Is LocalSend free?

Yes. LocalSend is free and open source under the Apache 2.0 license. There is no paid tier, no account, and no subscription. It is available in the Play Store, App Store, Flathub, Homebrew, Winget, and other package managers at no cost.

Does LocalSend need an internet connection?

No. LocalSend works entirely over your local network. Devices discover each other on the same Wi-Fi and transfer files directly over HTTPS, with a TLS certificate generated on the fly on each device. Nothing is uploaded to the internet and no outside server is involved.

Is LocalSend secure?

Transfers are encrypted with HTTPS, and each device generates its own TLS certificate on the fly, so traffic is encrypted even though no central server exists. Your files never pass through a third-party server. The app listens on port 53317, so if a device does not show up, check your firewall, router AP isolation, and VPN settings.

Which devices does LocalSend work on?

Android 7 and newer, iOS 15 and newer, macOS 12 Monterey and newer, Windows 10 and newer, Linux, and Fire OS. It is available from the Play Store, App Store, F-Droid, Flathub, Snap, Homebrew, Winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, and direct downloads from the releases page.

Can I use LocalSend from the command line?

Yes. The localsend-cli terminal client is available through Homebrew on macOS and Linux. Run localsend-cli send followed by files or folders, pick a device from the list or target one by alias or IP address, and use --text to send a message instead of a file.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/localsend. Repo: localsend/localsend.
