title: De recomendaciones de Azure Advisor a acciones en tu dashboard
description:
Un dashboard de infraestructura no aporta mucho si se limita a replicar métricas. El salto de valor llega cuando convierte una señal de Azure en una decisión concreta: qué recurso está afectado, cuál es el impacto, quién puede actuar y dónde está la documentación para resolverlo.

Ese es precisamente el caso de uso que encaja en Goliat Dashboard: reunir señales de costes, seguridad, rendimiento y disponibilidad para que un equipo pueda priorizarlas sin saltar continuamente entre herramientas. En este post desarrollo una implementación de referencia para llevar las recomendaciones de Azure Advisor a una aplicación con Node.js y React.

El resultado sigue un principio sencillo: el navegador sólo habla con nuestra API; la API valida el acceso del usuario, consulta Azure Resource Manager y devuelve un DTO pequeño, paginado y preparado para la interfaz. Ni los secretos ni los tokens de Azure salen del servidor.

Qué devuelve Azure Advisor

Azure Advisor analiza la configuración y la telemetría de los recursos y agrupa sus recomendaciones en las categorías Cost, Security, Performance, HighAvailability y OperationalExcellence. Para cada recomendación podemos aprovechar, entre otros, la categoría, el impacto (High, Medium o Low), el recurso afectado, la descripción corta, el beneficio potencial y el enlace de ayuda.

La operación Recommendations - List de la API REST devuelve recomendaciones cacheadas y puede incluir un nextLink. Esto cambia el diseño: no debemos asumir que una sola respuesta contiene toda la suscripción ni que cada visita al panel recalcula Advisor.

Arquitectura mínima y segura

El flujo recomendado es el siguiente:

  1. React solicita GET /api/advisor/recommendations a nuestro backend con la sesión normal de la aplicación.
  2. El backend comprueba que el usuario puede consultar la suscripción solicitada. El subscriptionId enviado por el navegador nunca basta como autorización.
  3. Un servicio de servidor obtiene un token para Azure Resource Manager mediante una identidad administrada en producción.
  4. El servicio sigue todos los nextLink, normaliza la respuesta de Advisor y guarda una instantánea breve en caché.
  5. La interfaz recibe sólo los campos que necesita y los presenta con filtros, prioridad y paginación.

Para leer las recomendaciones, una identidad necesita permisos de lectura en el alcance adecuado y acceso a los recursos asociados. Reader permite consultarlas; si se define un rol personalizado, la acción mínima es Microsoft.Advisor/recommendations/read. Consulta los permisos oficiales de Azure Advisor antes de asignar permisos más amplios.

Dependencias e identidad

Instala la librería de identidad en el servicio Node.js:

npm install @azure/identity

En producción, asigna una Managed Identity a la aplicación y concede únicamente los permisos necesarios. En desarrollo, DefaultAzureCredential permite autenticarse con Azure CLI, Visual Studio Code u otras credenciales locales. La elección explícita de ManagedIdentityCredential en producción evita depender de secretos de cliente dentro del despliegue.

El código de este artículo es una implementación de referencia para el patrón de Goliat Dashboard; no expone credenciales ni debe ejecutarse desde React.

Servicio Node.js: consultar, paginar y normalizar

El siguiente servicio usa la API REST actual de Azure Resource Manager. Elegir REST aquí nos deja controlar de forma explícita la versión de API y el nextLink; también podrías usar el cliente oficial @azure/arm-advisor, que expone un iterador paginado.

import {
  DefaultAzureCredential,
  ManagedIdentityCredential,
  type TokenCredential,
} from '@azure/identity';

const ARM_SCOPE = 'https://management.azure.com/.default';
const ADVISOR_API_VERSION = '2025-01-01';

type AdvisorProperties = {
  category?: string;
  impact?: 'High' | 'Medium' | 'Low';
  impactedValue?: string;
  label?: string;
  potentialBenefits?: string;
  lastUpdated?: string;
  learnMoreLink?: string;
  shortDescription?: { problem?: string; solution?: string };
  resourceMetadata?: { resourceId?: string };
};

type AdvisorResource = {
  id?: string;
  name?: string;
  properties?: AdvisorProperties;
};

type AdvisorPage = {
  value: AdvisorResource[];
  nextLink?: string;
};

export type AdvisorRecommendation = {
  id: string;
  category: string;
  impact: 'High' | 'Medium' | 'Low' | 'Unknown';
  label: string;
  resourceId: string | null;
  problem: string;
  solution: string;
  potentialBenefits: string | null;
  lastUpdated: string | null;
  learnMoreLink: string | null;
};

function createCredential(): TokenCredential {
  return process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'
    ? new ManagedIdentityCredential()
    : new DefaultAzureCredential();
}

function toRecommendation(item: AdvisorResource): AdvisorRecommendation {
  const properties = item.properties ?? {};

  return {
    id: item.name ?? item.id ?? 'unknown',
    category: properties.category ?? 'Unknown',
    impact: properties.impact ?? 'Unknown',
    label: properties.label ?? properties.shortDescription?.problem ?? 'Recomendación de Azure',
    resourceId: properties.resourceMetadata?.resourceId ?? properties.impactedValue ?? null,
    problem: properties.shortDescription?.problem ?? '',
    solution: properties.shortDescription?.solution ?? '',
    potentialBenefits: properties.potentialBenefits ?? null,
    lastUpdated: properties.lastUpdated ?? null,
    learnMoreLink: properties.learnMoreLink ?? null,
  };
}

export async function listAdvisorRecommendations(subscriptionId: string) {
  const token = await createCredential().getToken(ARM_SCOPE);

  if (!token) {
    throw new Error('No se pudo obtener un token para Azure Resource Manager');
  }

  const firstPage = new URL(
    `https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/${encodeURIComponent(subscriptionId)}/providers/Microsoft.Advisor/recommendations`,
  );
  firstPage.searchParams.set('api-version', ADVISOR_API_VERSION);
  firstPage.searchParams.set('$top', '100');

  let nextUrl: string | undefined = firstPage.toString();
  const recommendations: AdvisorRecommendation[] = [];

  while (nextUrl) {
    const response = await fetch(nextUrl, {
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${token.token}`,
        Accept: 'application/json',
      },
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Azure Advisor respondió con HTTP ${response.status}`);
    }

    const page = (await response.json()) as AdvisorPage;
    recommendations.push(...page.value.map(toRecommendation));
    nextUrl = page.nextLink;
  }

  const impactOrder = { High: 0, Medium: 1, Low: 2, Unknown: 3 };
  return recommendations.sort((a, b) => impactOrder[a.impact] - impactOrder[b.impact]);
}

El DTO anterior es deliberadamente pequeño. Evita entregar al navegador el objeto ARM completo, que puede cambiar con el tiempo y contiene más metadatos de los que la UI necesita. Conserva el identificador completo del recurso sólo si va a utilizarse para enlazarlo con inventario, etiquetas o permisos propios.

Endpoint: autorización antes de consultar Azure

Aquí está el patrón del controlador. requireSession, acl y cache representan los servicios de autenticación, control de acceso y caché de tu aplicación; adapta sus nombres a tu stack.

app.get('/api/advisor/recommendations', requireSession, async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    const subscriptionId =
      typeof req.query.subscriptionId === 'string' ? req.query.subscriptionId : null;

    if (!subscriptionId) {
      return res.status(400).json({ error: 'subscriptionId es obligatorio' });
    }

    // Nunca conviertas el subscriptionId de la URL en un permiso implícito.
    const canRead = await acl.canReadSubscription(req.user.id, subscriptionId);
    if (!canRead) {
      return res.status(403).json({ error: 'No tienes acceso a esta suscripción' });
    }

    const snapshot = await cache.remember(
      `advisor:v1:${subscriptionId}`,
      5 * 60,
      () => listAdvisorRecommendations(subscriptionId),
    );

    const category = typeof req.query.category === 'string' ? req.query.category : null;
    const filtered = category
      ? snapshot.filter((item) => item.category === category)
      : snapshot;

    const page = Math.max(1, Number(req.query.page) || 1);
    const pageSize = Math.min(50, Math.max(1, Number(req.query.pageSize) || 10));
    const start = (page - 1) * pageSize;

    return res.json({
      items: filtered.slice(start, start + pageSize),
      total: filtered.length,
      page,
      pageSize,
      cachedAt: new Date().toISOString(),
    });
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
});

Una caché de pocos minutos reduce latencia y evita peticiones redundantes. En una plataforma multiusuario, incluye en la clave de caché el ámbito que pueda modificar la visibilidad de los datos. Además, registra de forma auditable quién consultó cada suscripción, sin escribir tokens ni secretos en los logs.

React: una vista accionable, no una lista interminable

Este componente consume el endpoint propio, reinicia la página al cambiar el filtro y cancela una petición anterior cuando cambian las dependencias. El diseño deja espacio para añadir acciones internas —por ejemplo, crear una incidencia o enlazar un runbook— sin otorgar permisos de escritura sobre Azure al navegador.

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

type Item = {
  id: string;
  category: string;
  impact: 'High' | 'Medium' | 'Low' | 'Unknown';
  label: string;
  resourceId: string | null;
  problem: string;
  solution: string;
  potentialBenefits: string | null;
  learnMoreLink: string | null;
};

type Response = {
  items: Item[];
  total: number;
  page: number;
  pageSize: number;
};

export function AdvisorRecommendations({ subscriptionId }: { subscriptionId: string }) {
  const [data, setData] = useState<Response | null>(null);
  const [category, setCategory] = useState('');
  const [page, setPage] = useState(1);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    const query = new URLSearchParams({
      subscriptionId,
      page: String(page),
      pageSize: '10',
    });

    if (category) query.set('category', category);

    setError(null);
    fetch(`/api/advisor/recommendations?${query}`, { signal: controller.signal })
      .then(async (response) => {
        if (!response.ok) throw new Error('No se pudieron cargar las recomendaciones');
        return (await response.json()) as Response;
      })
      .then(setData)
      .catch((reason: unknown) => {
        if ((reason as Error).name !== 'AbortError') setError('No se pudieron cargar las recomendaciones');
      });

    return () => controller.abort();
  }, [subscriptionId, category, page]);

  if (error) return <p role="alert">{error}</p>;
  if (!data) return <p>Cargando recomendaciones…</p>;

  const totalPages = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(data.total / data.pageSize));

  return (
    <section aria-label="Recomendaciones de Azure Advisor">
      <label>
        Categoría
        <select
          value={category}
          onChange={(event) => {
            setCategory(event.target.value);
            setPage(1);
          }}
        >
          <option value="">Todas</option>
          <option value="Cost">Coste</option>
          <option value="Security">Seguridad</option>
          <option value="Performance">Rendimiento</option>
          <option value="HighAvailability">Alta disponibilidad</option>
          <option value="OperationalExcellence">Excelencia operativa</option>
        </select>
      </label>

      <p>{data.total} recomendaciones</p>

      <ul>
        {data.items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <strong>{item.impact} · {item.label}</strong>
            <p>{item.problem}</p>
            <p>{item.solution}</p>
            {item.resourceId && <code>{item.resourceId}</code>}
            {item.learnMoreLink && (
              <a href={item.learnMoreLink} target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">
                Ver documentación de Azure
              </a>
            )}
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <button disabled={page === 1} onClick={() => setPage((value) => value - 1)}>
        Anterior
      </button>
      <span> Página {page} de {totalPages} </span>
      <button disabled={page >= totalPages} onClick={() => setPage((value) => value + 1)}>
        Siguiente
      </button>
    </section>
  );
}

En una UI de producción, representaría el impacto con color y texto —nunca sólo con color—, mostraría el momento de la última sincronización y enlazaría cada resultado con el recurso y el runbook correspondiente. La recomendación no debe aplicar cambios automáticamente: es una señal para que el equipo revise, apruebe y ejecute la acción mediante un flujo controlado.

Refrescar recomendaciones sin bloquear la interfaz

La ruta GET de Advisor lee datos cacheados. Si necesitas pedir una nueva generación, programa un trabajo de servidor que llame a generateRecommendations; es una operación asíncrona que responde 202, entrega un Location y debe consultarse respetando Retry-After antes de volver a listar. No la ejecutes cuando un usuario abre el panel ni la expongas directamente como botón del navegador.

Para iniciar ese proceso se necesita el permiso adicional Microsoft.Advisor/generateRecommendations/action. Incluso después de implementar una mejora, Advisor puede tardar en reflejarla; por ello es útil mostrar la hora de actualización y evitar prometer que el estado cambiará al instante. Los detalles del ciclo están documentados en Generate recommendations y Get generate status.

Checklist antes de llevarlo a producción

  • Usa Managed Identity en producción y limita RBAC al alcance necesario.
  • Mantén la llamada a Azure Resource Manager y los tokens exclusivamente en el backend.
  • Autoriza cada suscripción contra la identidad de usuario antes de leerla.
  • Sigue nextLink, devuelve un DTO estable y pagina el resultado para la UI.
  • Añade caché, límites de tasa y trazabilidad; registra metadatos operativos, no secretos.
  • Trata la generación como un trabajo asíncrono y conserva aprobación humana para cualquier cambio.

Con este patrón, Azure Advisor deja de ser una pestaña más del portal y se convierte en una fuente de trabajo priorizada dentro del flujo de DevOps y FinOps. La integración es pequeña, pero permite conectar cada recomendación con contexto, responsables y una acción verificable.

title: Introducing eve 1.0
description:
Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week.

Lindy's agent framework roundup names eve “Best for durable backend agents”.

Collaborate in multiplayer agent sessions

Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team.

In the native Slack channel, each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack.

Ambient mode lets an agent listen in channels you choose, even without being mentioned. Guided by goals you set per channel, it decides when to speak up, help, or take on a task, and when to stay quiet. To limit model costs, a small decision model screens every message first, and only the ones that might be for the agent start a turn.

Slack is one of several native channels, alongside Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat, and iMessage. The Chat SDK channel adds support for any Chat SDK platform adapter, including WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat, and email. Each channel is one file, and the same agent can work across all of them. See the integrations directory for the full list.

Build agent UIs with Next.js and other frameworks

eve 1.0 expands our native integrations for Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start, and Vite. The framework integrations build your agent alongside your app and set up its routes. On Vercel, you can deploy the agent and your site as one project, or host them separately.

The client libraries let you work with tool calls, approval requests, and questions in a consistent way across frameworks. Use that session data to build custom UIs: stream replies into agent chats, embed an agent in a page, or show the agent's tool calls in your own components.

Use eve add channel/web to scaffold a chat app with AI Elements components, or add eve's React, Vue, or Svelte bindings to an existing UI.

Build multi-tenant agents

One support-agent deployment can connect to each customer's ticketing system with their own credentials and apply that customer's approval rules.

Your application authenticates the user and identifies which tenant they belong to. You can then set memory, connection credentials, and approval policy for that tenant and user.

Before each model call in the main agent loop, dynamic definitions load the agent's capabilities from the session and external data. In 1.0, they cover models, connections, and subagents as well as tools, skills, and instructions.

Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in fileMemory keeps data in memory in eve dev and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

We rebuilt eve’s tracing around OpenTelemetry, so you can follow an agent’s work in the tracing tools you already use. eve dev records traces locally by default. If you host eve yourself, you can export them to an OpenTelemetry backend, including one you run yourself.

Tracing integrations include Raindrop, with more options in the integrations directory. Add one with eve add instrumentation/<name>, or use the instrumentation APIs to build your own integration.

Traces now show when an agent is waiting for a person, including tool approvals, questions, budget prompts, and sign-ins. They record model selections and approval decisions alongside model usage and cost, and follow calls into MCP servers and remote agents.

You choose what eve collects for tracing. Content you exclude from collection stays out of every destination. You can filter out spans or redact inputs and outputs per destination. Private conversations in production send only metadata by default, without prompts or tool results. The OpenTelemetry guide explains these controls.

On Vercel, Agent Runs uses the same traces to show sessions, model calls, tool execution, subagent activity, and approval decisions in the dashboard. When eve deploy creates a new Vercel project, it sets up trace sampling automatically. See the Agent Runs guide for setup and configuration.

Lower agent turn latency

At the start of September, our hosted stress test on Vercel Workflows took a median of 3.036s per turn. In 1.0, the same 100-turn workload took 414ms. The test sends messages one at a time, with one immediate mock-model response and no tool calls per turn. We measure from sending a message until the turn finishes, capturing eve and Workflow overhead without the time a model takes to generate a response.

Hosted stress run

Median turn latency

p95

September 1, beta baseline

3.036s

3.692s

November 15, 1.0.0

414ms

633ms

We worked with the Workflow team on spec 9, which gives each run a single orchestrator so background steps no longer replay the workflow. The team also moved event and stream writes to WebSockets and cut redundant history reads. eve agents get these improvements through Workflow SDK.

eve also caches the information it needs to route messages to each session and can move idle sessions to a newer deployment between turns. Web UIs can prewarm a session before the first message arrives, so the first reply starts sooner.

Lower workflow costs for long agent sessions

For a 50-turn Evo Docs session, the estimated Vercel Workflows cost drops from 5.4¢ to 1.3¢, about 76% lower. That assumes roughly two model steps per turn and 30-day retention. eve now uses Workflow SDK 5.5 and saves only the conversation data that changed between turns. We've also cut repeated work in workflow steps, checkpoints, and sandbox setup:

  • Workflow steps save changes and refer back to data already stored, instead of repeatedly copying a growing conversation into each step. Steps that don't need history no longer receive it.

  • Checkpoints store references to image files returned by tools, so they don't have to copy the image bytes each time.

  • Sandboxes from prepared snapshots skip repeated setup. Stop a sandbox and keep its files for reuse. Cleanup starts when the session ends.

The storage changes are part of the open-source Workflow SDK, so agents you host yourself on other Workflow backends also store less duplicate session data. The cost estimate above uses Vercel Workflows pricing.

On Vercel, workflow steps run on Fluid compute. They need extra storage writes for inputs above the payload size limit, so sending less session data helps keep turn times consistent as sessions grow. Images and files can still require those writes.

For model calls, tool and skill listings can stay out of the initial prompt until they're needed. Connection tools run through eve__search and eve__tool, so each search no longer has to expand the model's tool list. We also changed how eve marks parts of a prompt for provider caching, so more content can be reused between calls.

During an earlier migration to eve, an engineer at Evisions reported:

Share agent capabilities with extensions

Since the preview, we've added extensions so teams can share tools, skills, instructions, connections, channels, schedules, hooks, and subagents without copying files between agents. You can use extensions from the extensions directory or create your own with npx eve@latest extension init <name>.

For example, agent-browser adds browser automation, Mux Video adds tools for video assets and clips, and Link adds wallet and purchase tools.

eve builds workspace extensions from source and reloads changes during development. You can update shared capabilities in one package and try the changes in your agents as you work.

Build coding agents with eve’s shared tools

The 1.0 code extension builds on eve’s default file tools, adding coding instructions and skills that follow your repository’s AGENTS.md. It's included in the eve package, so there's nothing extra to install. Give it a repository in its sandbox and your agent can investigate code, edit files, and run the project's checks. It uses the same harness and extension system as your other agents, so you can replace or disable tools, override skills, and add your own instructions.

See the benchmark results for comparisons with other coding harnesses using the same tasks and model.

Add the coding extension to your agent:

The companion eve/extensions/git adds GitHub and pull request workflows, using credentials and authorization you configure. On Vercel, the optional remote self-modification extension lets your agent propose changes to its own source in a draft pull request. You review the changes, merge them, and deploy.

Build with the same public APIs eve uses

We built eve's subagents, sleep, and question tools on the same workflow system you can use through defineWorkflowTool. Your tools can return a result, start a background task, or keep accepting messages as a resumable task. They can wait for a person, webhook, or timer without keeping compute running, and their runs survive restarts. You don't need a separate background-job system to coordinate that work.

Once you've defined a reviewer subagent, this tool returns a receipt immediately. The task body waits for the reviewer's result, which is delivered to the model in a later message:

Upgrade to eve 1.0

If you already have an eve agent, the 1.0 upgrade guide walks through the changes to extension builds, agent APIs, session events, clients, and saved history. Follow it before deploying your upgrade.

eve follows semantic versioning, so breaking changes to stable APIs only happen in major releases. Experimental and internal APIs, including experimental fields, can change between major releases.

To work through the upgrade with your coding agent, copy this prompt:

Create your first eve agent

Start in the terminal to build locally, use the browser builder to create and deploy an agent, or choose a template for your use case.

Start in the terminal

Create a new agent from the CLI with Node.js 24 or newer:

In an interactive terminal, this installs dependencies and opens the eve terminal UI. If your selected team has AI Gateway access, you can start chatting without creating a Vercel project or copying an API key. eve can use your existing Vercel CLI credentials to call models through AI Gateway locally. Use /login to sign in to other connections.

In eve dev, you can ask the agent to add a tool, change its instructions, or write a skill. With self-modification, it edits its own source and reloads the change for the next turn.

Start in the browser

From the Vercel dashboard, the agent builder scaffolds an agent, creates its Git repo, and deploys it. Go to Add New → Agent, pick a model, and add web chat or Slack along the way.

Start from a template

Choose an eve template for your use case:

title: Your agent doesn't need a shell. It needs an allowlist that can't become a launcher.
description:
Last week I deleted the JavaScript implementation of agent-runner and rewrote it in Go. The agent loop ported cleanly. The interesting part was the tool layer, because that is where an agent stops being a demo.

In the JS version, run_command called exec() and let the shell sort it out. That is fine when the only thing running it is you, on your own machine, watching the output. It is not fine the moment the loop runs unattended against a repo you care about. A model that can reach a shell can do anything your user can do, and it will get there by accident long before it gets there on purpose.

So the Go port puts the whole safety story in three boring places.

1. There is no shell to reach

The command string is split into argv by hand. When the tokenizer meets a character a shell would interpret, it refuses instead of quoting it:

const shellChars = ";&|<>$`*?()[]{}~!\\"

// inside tokenize()
case strings.ContainsRune(shellChars, ch):
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("shell syntax is not supported: %c", ch)

A pipe is not a filename, and pretending otherwise is how a "safe" runner ends up executing the second half of a command someone else wrote. Refusing is the honest answer. There is no globbing either, so *.go is just a string that no allowlisted command will accept.

2. An allowlist entry has to promise flags, not just a binary

The first version of the allowlist was a set of names: ls, cat, wc, git. That is not a safety boundary. Plenty of ordinary binaries are launchers if you are allowed to pass the right argument:

  • node -e "..."
  • python3 -c "..."
  • git -c core.pager='...' log

None of those need a shell. All of them run arbitrary code. So every entry in the policy declares exactly which flags it accepts, and for a multiplexer like git, which subcommands and which flags under each:

var Commands = map[string]Command{
    "ls":  {Flags: []string{"-1", "-a", "-A", "-l", "-h", "-la", "-al", "-lah"}},
    "cat": {},
    "wc":  {Flags: []string{"-l", "-w", "-c", "-m"}},
    "git": {Subcommands: map[string][]string{
        "status": {"--short", "--porcelain", "-s"},
        "log":    {"--oneline", "--stat", "--decorate", "-n", "--max-count"},
        "diff":   {"--stat", "--name-only", "--cached"},
        "show":   {"--stat", "--oneline"},
    }},
}
```



The check is exact, including `--flag=value` forms where the value gets its own validation. When it fails, the error names the binary and the argument. That matters: the model reads the refusal as the observation for that step and re-plans. A vague "denied" makes it retry the same thing with a different spelling. `git: argument not allowed: -c` makes it stop.

`cat` with no flags is deliberate. `cat` on `/dev/urandom` was never reachable anyway, since absolute paths are refused, and `read_file` covers the useful case with a 2 MiB cap.

## 3. Paths go through their deepest existing ancestor

Rejecting `..` and absolute paths is the easy half. The half that bites is symlinks: `link/secret` looks like a relative path and resolves somewhere else. So a path is resolved by walking up to the deepest component that exists, calling `EvalSymlinks` on that, and rejoining the rest before checking that the result is the root or below it. If nothing resolves, the path is refused rather than guessed at.

Same rule for the git operands, with one exception: `rev:path` forms name objects inside the repository, not files on disk, so they skip the filesystem check.

## What this costs

You lose pipes and redirects. There is no `grep -r`, no `go test ./... | tail`. In practice the loop does fine: `git log --oneline -n 20`, `wc -l`, then `read_file` on what looks interesting. If a task genuinely needs more, you add an entry to the map on purpose, which is the point. The allowlist is a maintenance burden and I would rather carry it than carry a shell.

Eleven tests in `internal/tools` are named after the attacks, not the functions: `TestRefusesShellChaining`, `TestRefusesLauncherFlags`, `TestRefusesSymlinkEscape`. CI runs `gofmt -l`, `go vet`, and `go test -race ./...`. The default entry point runs against a deterministic mock planner, so a run is reproducible without an API key.

Runtime is about 1,300 lines of Go now. Repo: [marcus-beauregard/agent-runner](https://github.com/marcus-beauregard/agent-runner).

title: CAG-VLM: Fine-Tuning of a Large-Scale Model to Recognize Angiographic Images for Next-Generation Diagnostic Systems
description:
arXiv:2505.04964v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Coronary angiography (CAG) is the gold-standard imaging modality for evaluating coronary artery disease, but its interpretation and subsequent treatment planning rely heavily on expert cardiologists. To enable AI-based decision support, we introduce a two-stage, physician-curated pipeline and a bilingual (Japanese/English) CAG image-report dataset. First, we sample 14,686 frames from 539 exams and annotate them for key-frame detection and left/right laterality; a ConvNeXt-Base CNN trained on this data achieves 0.96 F1 on laterality classification, even on low-contrast frames. Second, we apply the CNN to 243 independent exams, extract 1,114 key frames, and pair each with its pre-procedure report and expert-validated diagnostic and treatment summary, yielding a parallel corpus. We then fine-tune three open-source VLMs (PaliGemma2, Gemma3, and ConceptCLIP-enhanced Gemma3) via LoRA and evaluate them using VLScore and cardiologist review. Although PaliGemma2 w/LoRA attains the highest VLScore, Gemma3 w/LoRA achieves the top clinician rating (mean 7.20/10); we designate this best-performing model as CAG-VLM. These results demonstrate that specialized, fine-tuned VLMs can effectively assist cardiologists in generating clinical reports and treatment recommendations from CAG images.

title: System.Threading.Channels
description:
Many background queue implementations still rely on BlockingCollection<T>. While simple, it relies on synchronous OS monitor primitives that block worker threads when empty or full.

System.Threading.Channels provides an asynchronous, lock-free alternative designed for high-throughput producer/consumer pipelines.

Before: BlockingCollection 

var queue = new BlockingCollection<WorkItem>(boundedCapacity: 1000);

// Blocks thread pool thread if full
queue.Add(item);

// Synchronously blocks thread if empty
var work = queue.Take();

After: Bounded Async Channel 

var options = new BoundedChannelOptions(1000)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,
    SingleReader = true,
    SingleWriter = false
};
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<WorkItem>(options);

// Asynchronously yields without blocking thread pool
await channel.Writer.WriteAsync(item, ct);

await foreach (var work in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct))
{
    await ProcessAsync(work, ct);
}

Why It Matters

  • No Thread Starvation: Awaiting ReadAsync or ReadAllAsync suspends the state machine instead of holding an active thread pool thread captive.
  • Optimized Concurrency: Setting SingleReader = true or SingleWriter = true enables lock-free single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer paths.
  • Zero-Allocation Reads: Returns ValueTask<T>, eliminating heap allocations when items are immediately ready.

Watch out: You must explicitly invoke channel.Writer.Complete() or channel.Writer.TryComplete(ex) on shutdown; otherwise ReadAllAsync() never terminates.

Have you transitioned your BackgroundService queues to Channels yet?

title: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
description:
arXiv:2611.23817v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.25228v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP.pdf and GDP.xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.

title: adqproxy: a Rust reverse proxy built on Cloudflare Pingora
description:
How Cloudflare uses Pingora, how it differs from NGINX, and how adqproxy adds site configuration, routing, and systemd installation to a Rust proxy.

adqproxy is my Rust reverse proxy built on Cloudflare Pingora. Its command-line tool is adqp. I wanted to combine programmable request handling with a familiar server workflow: site configuration, configuration checks, and a systemd service.

When I returned to the project, I found a problem at the boundary between those parts. The package installed and its configuration check passed, but the process exited before serving its first HTTP request. While fixing installation and routing, I tested the path from installing the package to running the service.

To explain adqproxy's design, I'll start with its foundation: what Pingora is, where Cloudflare uses it, and why people compare it with NGINX.

What a reverse proxy does, and where Pingora fits

A reverse proxy accepts a client request and contacts an application on the client's behalf. The application can run on another port, another server, or in a container. The proxy selects a destination and returns the application's response to the client.

Client → reverse proxy → application or backend group

For example, one domain can route /api/ to an API service and other requests to a frontend. This layer can also terminate TLS and distribute requests across application instances.

Pingora is an asynchronous, multithreaded Rust framework for building network services, including HTTP proxies. Cloudflare open-sourced it in February 2024. Developers use its libraries to build applications with their own traffic-handling logic. Pingora open-source announcement

The project supports HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, TLS, connection reuse, load balancing, and backend health checks. The application built on the framework determines which features it exposes and how operators configure them. Pingora repository

How Cloudflare uses Pingora

In the architecture Cloudflare described, Pingora handles requests from Cloudflare's network to origin servers: the servers hosting a customer's site or application.

In its 2022 engineering article, Cloudflare explained a limitation of its previous NGINX-based system. Connection pools belonged to individual worker processes, so a request could not always reuse a connection opened by another process. Pingora's architecture allowed connections to be shared across threads, reducing the need for TCP/TLS handshakes. How Cloudflare built Pingora

Why Pingora is compared with NGINX

Their responsibilities overlap in reverse proxying: accepting an HTTP request, selecting a backend, establishing a connection, and returning a response. An application built on Pingora can compete with NGINX on that part of the request path.

NGINX provides a ready-to-run web server with configuration, modules, static file serving, proxying, and load balancing. Pingora provides a foundation for developing a network service. A useful comparison therefore considers the features and operation of specific applications. NGINX capabilities · Pingora's purpose

Question NGINX Pingora and an application built on it
How do you get started? Run and configure an existing server Develop or choose an application built on the framework
Where is behavior defined? Configuration, modules, and extensions Rust code and the application's configuration interface
Who defines the site configuration format? NGINX The application author
What needs checking before adoption? Configuration and required modules Application features, configuration, installation, and upgrades

The ability to express custom logic in Rust is one reason Pingora interests me. If a proxy needs application data to make routing decisions or must integrate with internal services, explicit extension points are useful.

For straightforward proxying of a few sites, NGINX remains a practical choice. In my project, I evaluate Pingora primarily as a foundation for a programmable proxy. This work did not include an adqproxy-versus-NGINX benchmark under an identical workload.

How Pingora processes a request

The ProxyHttp interface exposes stages of request processing:

  1. request_filter: validate the request or produce a response before contacting a backend.
  2. upstream_peer: select a server and its connection parameters.
  3. upstream_request_filter: modify the request before forwarding it.
  4. response_filter and logging: process the response and record the result.

This is useful when backend selection requires more than a fixed path-to-address mapping. For example, the decision might depend on request context. The stages and retry behavior are described in the request lifecycle guide.

How adqproxy is put together

In adqproxy, I add site configuration and its management workflow on top of Pingora: sites-available, sites-enabled, configuration validation, and a systemd service. This is the interface a server administrator works with.

For this update, I upgraded Pingora from 0.6.0 to 0.9.1, adapted the cache and metrics integrations, and committed Cargo.lock. I then tested specific adqproxy behavior: startup without upstreams, backend selection, TLS, and upgrades over edited configuration files. Pingora 0.9.1 release

Why the default install failed

The installer enabled a default site with a simple return 200 "OK\n"; rule for /health. The proxy can serve that response directly. During startup, however, the binary always tried to take the first load balancer from its list of upstreams. The default site had none. The two pieces only failed when I ran them together.

The proxy can now start with zero upstreams. On a fresh Linux install with systemd, the installer enables the default site and the service responds at http://127.0.0.1:8080/health. Upgrades preserve proxy.yaml, site files, and their symlinks. If an administrator disables the default site, it stays disabled after the upgrade. Installer changes

The parts I kept from the NGINX workflow

Site files live in /etc/adq-pingora/sites-available/. Running adq-ensite creates a symlink in sites-enabled/. For example, /etc/adq-pingora/sites-available/demo can map a path to a named backend group.

server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name demo.example;

    location /api/ {
        proxy_pass demo_api;
    }
}

upstream demo_api {
    server 127.0.0.1:3000;
}

A request to /api/ with Host: demo.example goes to demo_api. Before the fix, two routes with different proxy_pass targets could end up at the same backend. I ran two local HTTP servers and checked the response bodies to see which one actually handled each request. For HTTPS, listen … ssl now creates a TLS listener on the configured port and loads the certificate specified in the site file.

Running the config check as the service user also checks that the process can read its configuration and TLS keys. Applying a change currently requires a systemd restart, so there can be an interruption.

sudo adq-ensite demo
sudo -u adq-pingora adqp -t && sudo systemctl restart adq-pingora

I used a similar approach to configuration and runtime checks when checking and updating NGINX after six CVEs: I verified the configuration and installed package, then checked request handling after the update.

NGINX verification on vm-voly in Kaku: package version, a successful nginx -t, an active service and an HTTP/2 200 response.

What CI checks before release

CI builds the binary from the locked dependency set, installs it on Ubuntu, starts the installed systemd service, and checks that the default /health route returns OK. Separate tests cover an upgrade over an edited configuration, malformed syntax, a missing upstream, routing to two distinct backends, HTTPS, and the request counter at /metrics. That exercises the installation a user gets as well as the proxy itself. GitHub Actions run

A successful adqproxy CI run: build, unit tests, smoke tests and startup of the installed systemd service.

An excerpt from the same CI log: proxying, metrics, installation, configuration preservation and HTTPS checks. Tests run in GitHub Actions; Kaku displays their log.

The source and build instructions are already on the main branch. Publication of the adqproxy npm package is still pending. Project repository

title: The best cold-email opener for an AI automation agency is in your prospect's reviews
description:
TL;DR: The cold email that gets a reply opens with a fact about the prospect's business that they can check in ten seconds. The best place I've found for that fact is their own Google reviews. Below: what to read, how a real booking page differs from a request form, a sample first line, how Helix checks this across many leads, and what it won't claim.

I'm Ramsis, founder of Helix, a lead research tool for agencies and builders who sell to local businesses. I'm also a GenAI engineer.

Why does "you need an AI chatbot" get deleted?

Owners have heard it ten times this week. It's a sentence about the seller, and it fits any business in town, so it says nothing true about this one. A reason gets a reply when it's about their business and they can check it in ten seconds.

That reason is rarely on their website. It's in their reviews, written by their own customers: someone called twice and nobody called back, or emails sat for days. That's the exact problem an AI receptionist or an automated reply fixes, described in the customer's words instead of yours.

Read the last twenty reviews, not the star rating

Open the full Google listing and read the last twenty reviews, or every review if there are fewer. The star rating hides the detail. A solid average can still contain three reviews that say nobody called back.

I'm looking for a repeated complaint about calls or messages going unanswered. Three rules I use:

  • One old complaint is not a pattern. Two or more recent ones are worth an email.
  • Note the month. Use the latest date. Skip anything older than a year, because an old complaint makes you look like you're reading last year's news.
  • Paraphrase, don't name. Write "a review from August says calls weren't returned." Never the reviewer's name, and never a quote you can't check word for word.

Request form or real booking?

This is where most cold emails go wrong. The owner sees "you don't have online booking", knows they do, and stops reading. You lose the reply, and maybe the chance to be taken seriously later.

Two pages can look alike from a distance. They aren't the same:

  • Real online booking. The visitor picks a slot and gets a confirmation straight away.
  • Request form. The visitor sends "request an appointment", and someone calls back later.

A request form is a real gap, because the booking waits for a human. But it's a different sentence from "no booking at all". Here's what I'd say for each:

What the page shows What you can honestly say
Live slot picker, confirmed now "Your site already lets people book online." Pitch the follow-up instead: reminders, no-shows, questions after hours.
Request form, call back later "Appointments come in by request form, and I couldn't see a time to pick."

Quote form answered later, or instant quote?

The same split applies to "Get a quote". Some sites show a price or an estimate on the page. Others take your details and say someone will be in touch. The second kind is where an automated reply earns its place: the prospect is waiting, and a fast first response matters.

I can't tell you how fast any given business replies. I haven't measured response times, and Helix doesn't either. What a page shows is narrower and checkable: the form is answered later.

A first line built on a dated fact

Here's the kind of opener I'd send after one of these checks. It's an illustrative example, not a real business:

Subject: Calls on your Google reviews

Hi there, two Google reviews since August say calls to your office weren't returned. I don't know how often that happens, but a call-answering assistant can take the first message and book the callback. Want a two-minute recording of how it would work for your team?

It opens on something the owner can verify in ten seconds, gives a month, makes no claim about their revenue, and asks one small question. The path from review to line looks like this:

How Helix checks this across many leads

Reading twenty reviews for one business is fine. Doing it for forty is where I'd start making mistakes, so Helix runs these checks inside the hunt. For each lead:

  • It reads the stored Google reviews and flags the ones saying calls or messages went unanswered, with the count and the latest date.
  • It opens the quote and booking pages and sorts them: instant quote or form answered later, live booking or request form.
  • Every row carries the date it was checked.

When Helix isn't sure, the row says Not checked, and that row never reaches an email. No reviews, an unreadable page or a low-confidence call all end up there. I'd rather a lead stay silent than say something wrong, because a wrong "you don't have X" costs the reply.

The campaign's Channel gaps panel counts how many leads have each gap. Email N drafts a message to every lead in that group, opening on the gap. Leads you've already emailed, and leads without an address, are left out. You approve every draft. The checks run inside the hunt, cost no Strands, and only run for campaigns that use this lens.

The small-sample numbers

I measured these before shipping. They're small samples, so treat them as a first signal, not a benchmark:

  • Review complaints: when Helix flagged a review, it was right 8 times out of 9. It found every clear complaint in the test set. The misses were reviews whose stored text was cut short.
  • Quote pages: "form answered later" was right on 17 of 18 pages.
  • Booking pages: wrong "no online booking" calls fell from 8 of 15 to 1 of 6 on hand-labelled pages. That's the mistake that costs the reply.
  • Industries: in this sample, real estate and law firms showed the most "can't reach them" complaints, then home services. That came from 5 to 10 sites per industry, so it's a hint about where to look.

What this won't do

  • It never calls, emails or fills in forms to test a business, and it doesn't measure response times. "Slow to reply" means customers wrote it, not that Helix timed it.
  • Live chat appears on the lead card only, never in an email. Many sites load chat through Google Tag Manager, which a plain page read can't see.
  • It needs reviews. A business with none shows Not checked.
  • Insurance agencies, car dealerships and banks look like a natural fit, but I haven't measured those industries yet.
  • Helix doesn't reply, call or text for you. It finds, reads and drafts. You approve, and the email goes out from your own mailbox.

Try it on one trade and one city

Pick one trade, one city and one offer. Run one hunt, then read five of the leads yourself before you trust the checks. Compare what Helix says with what you find. That comparison will teach you more than any number above.

title: When someone leaves, their API keys stay: how to offboard the access people create
description:
Most offboarding checklists stop at the same point: disable the login, collect the laptop, remove the person from the group chat. That handles the person. It doesn't handle what the person built.

Over a year or two, an engineer, analyst or ops lead creates access that isn't tied to their own sign-in. A service account for a nightly job. An API key pasted into a reporting script. An OAuth grant that lets a SaaS tool read the shared drive. And now, an AI agent connected to their mailbox or the ticketing system. Some of this breaks loudly when they leave. Most of it keeps running with nobody watching.

The quiet part is the risk. Verizon's 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report says credential abuse is still the most common way attackers get in, and that the median time to remediate leaked secrets found in a GitHub repository was 94 days. A key with no owner is a key nobody rotates.

This is the order I'd work in.

1. Start the list during the notice period

In the first week of notice, ask the person leaving for a written list: every service account, API key, token, webhook, scheduled job and AI tool they set up or connected. They know more than any scan will find. Make it a handover task with a due date, not a favour.

2. Check their list against what your systems show

Memory misses things, so verify. Look in:

  • Your identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra, Google Workspace): app grants and OAuth consents made by that user.
  • Cloud consoles (AWS, Azure, GCP): access keys, roles and service principals they created or last used.
  • Code repositories and CI/CD: secrets stored under their name, deploy keys, personal access tokens used by pipelines.
  • SaaS admin panels: integrations they installed, especially anything with "read all files" or "send as user" permissions.
  • AI tools: any agent or assistant connected through their account to mail, files, CRM or chat.

Anything the systems show that isn't on their list goes to the top of the review.

3. Give every item a named owner

A person, not a team. "The data team" owns nothing at 2 a.m. when a job fails. The new owner should know what the item does and be able to say whether it still needs to exist.

4. Decide: keep, move or retire

  • Keep it if it's needed and already runs on its own identity with narrow permissions. Change the owner and move on.
  • Move it if it runs on the departing person's own credentials. Create a dedicated service identity, give it only the permissions the job actually uses, switch the job over and confirm the next run succeeds.
  • Retire it if nobody can explain what it's for. Disable it rather than delete it, and wait two weeks to see if anything complains.

5. Rotate the secrets they could see

They probably had access to more secrets than they created: shared vault folders, .env files, config for tools they administered. Rotate those too. It isn't about trust. Former employees' laptops and password managers get compromised like anyone else's.

6. Disable the login on time, delete the account last

Cut interactive access on the last day as normal. Hold off deleting the account until steps 3 to 5 are done, because in some platforms deleting a user also removes or breaks what they owned. Then watch the logs for a week for failed authentications tied to the old account. Each one is something you missed.

7. Give AI agents their own line

Agents are where this gets harder each month. An agent connected "as me" inherits everything that person could do, and it may keep its own saved connections outside your identity provider. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 found that 13% of organisations reported breaches of AI models or applications, and 97% of those said they lacked proper AI access controls. For each agent the person connected, revoke its tokens in the source app (not only inside the agent), and if the work still matters, rebuild it under a dedicated identity with an owner.

8. Make sure the list exists next time

The real win is never having to rebuild this from memory again. Three habits cover most of it:

  • Every new service account, key or agent gets an owner and an expiry date when it's created.
  • Quarterly access reviews include non-human identities, not only people.
  • The offboarding checklist has a "things you created" section that both the manager and IT sign off.

You can do all of this with admin consoles and a spreadsheet. It's slower, and it depends on someone remembering every time, so it's worth automating the discovery step once you've done it by hand a couple of times. Whatever you use, the steps above are what matter: an owner, a decision and a rotation for everything a departing person leaves behind.

title: DNS Cutover Monitoring in Go: Check Records Against Resolution and Mail Outcomes
description:
Monitor hostname resolution and mail acceptance before switching a developer tools hostname, keep the previous target available for rollback, and use DNS record inspection to explain an alert rather than to declare the cutover successful.

Short answer: a record that looks correct is configuration evidence; a hostname resolving to the intended target or a test message being accepted is outcome evidence. Collect both. Make the propagation delay versus cutover speed decision against an explicit SLO, and decide which processors may receive the evidence before building the integration.

Consider a developer tools platform moving its API hostname while its domain also supports notification mail. The operational temptation is to read back the changed record and close the migration. That skips the failure mode that matters: a caching resolver or a provider check can still disagree with the configuration. A green record check cannot establish that clients have reached the new target, and a domain verification result cannot establish that a message was accepted.

Keep those distinctions visible in the dashboard. Otherwise the platform team will inherit a reassuring chart and an unexplained support ticket.

Should DNS monitoring check configuration records or resolution and mail outcomes?

The primary signal is resolution to the intended target from the observation point that matters to the service. Record contents explain why that signal might fail. For mail, separately observe the acceptance outcome; domain checks are diagnostic evidence, and acceptance should not be relabeled as delivery or inbox placement. The outcome being promised must match the outcome being measured.

Use an illustrative release gate of 99.9% successful resolution checks over a chosen observation window, with the window and probe placement agreed before the change. This is a proposed SLO, not a provider guarantee or a measured result. A team that needs an immediate switch should explicitly accept the uncertainty of a shorter observation period; a team that prioritizes confidence should budget time for disagreement between observations and keep rollback capacity available throughout it.

Capacity planning starts here. Budget concurrent checks, diagnostic reads after failures, and overlap between the old and new targets. A design that checks frequently but cannot absorb the diagnostic burst when many hostnames disagree has moved the bottleneck into incident response. No throughput measurement is available here, so load-test that budget before assigning a production fleet to it.

Don't retire early.

For teams building a small cutover controller, Infrai is worth trying for record inspection and reporting the resulting monitoring signals: its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so adding a capability starts with reading its contract rather than learning another SDK. One API key covers the backend services, which reduces credential integration work for the controller; that convenience also makes the controller's credential a trust boundary worth reviewing. Hostname resolution probes and actual mail acceptance evidence remain separate responsibilities.

Infrai provides one REST API with one key and one bill. No SDK required.

Choose the evidence boundary before choosing the API

The sensitive object is not necessarily a message body. A hostname can identify a customer, and a monitoring label can carry the same identifier into a second system. An API that is convenient to call does not, by that fact alone, establish an acceptable region, retention period, deletion process, or processor chain.

Start with an explicit proposed policy: keep detailed cutover evidence for 24 hours, retain aggregate success counts for 30 days, and omit mail bodies and recipient addresses from monitoring payloads. These durations are example requirements for this runbook, not documented retention behavior of any provider. Before adoption, require evidence that the chosen services can meet them, including what happens to backups and downstream copies after deletion. A deletion operation for a DNS resource should never be treated as proof that monitoring evidence has also disappeared.

The buy-versus-build decision should compare responsibility as well as interface effort:

Option Where to evaluate it for this cutover Boundary and operating trade-off
Cloudflare DNS A direct specialist candidate when that is the platform's DNS control plane Assess its direct controls and contractual terms; the team still needs outcome probes and a retention policy for their evidence.
Amazon Route 53 A direct specialist candidate for a platform already evaluating AWS services Assess the AWS account and processor boundary against the cutover requirements; do not infer mail acceptance from a DNS control-plane response.
BIND 9, self-hosted A build option when operating the DNS service is an explicit platform responsibility The team accepts capacity planning and on-call ownership, and must also operate the evidence collection and deletion process.
Infrai A shared API option for the controller's diagnostic and metrics integration Discovery reduces contract-reading effort; region, retention, deletion, and downstream processing terms still need verification for the intended data.

These are selection criteria, not a feature certification matrix. There is no evidence here establishing equivalent residency or deletion guarantees across the four options. If a specialist's direct contract and controls are required to satisfy the platform's data policy, choose that specialist for the relevant processing, even if a shared API would take fewer integration steps.

Contract review comes first.

The useful boundary for Infrai is narrow and concrete: inspect records and report monitoring evidence through the verified capabilities. Keep authority over the cutover decision in the controller, and keep responsibility for actual mail acceptance with the sending workflow and its specialist provider. No AI runtime is needed for this runbook, and introducing one would not establish residency or contractual guarantees for unrelated data.

Implement a probe whose result has a precise meaning

First retrieve the capability manifest before wiring diagnostic reads or metric reporting. This standalone Go program makes that discovery call, validates the JSON response, and prints only a completion signal. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment to use the authenticated form below; discovery itself is public and also supports access without a key. The program performs a read, so it needs no write-idempotency key. It retries rate limits with exponential backoff and honors Retry-After, while surfacing unsuccessful response bodies rather than treating them as valid manifests.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func discover() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY")
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            header := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if requested := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(header); err == nil {
                if requested := time.Until(deadline); requested > delay {
                    delay = requested
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery returned invalid JSON")
        }
        fmt.Println("discovery_manifest_received=1")
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := discover(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This completion signal proves only that discovery returned valid JSON, not that DNS or mail is healthy. Inspect the manifest locally, select the relevant capability, and use its declared schema and runnable example for the controller integration; do not guess request fields. Keep API error bodies in restricted diagnostic output rather than forwarding them automatically to shared telemetry.

Start the outcome check before changing configuration. Record its observation point, the intended target, and the previous target in the change record; inspect DNS records when the probe disagrees. Emit separate metrics for the configuration check and the resolution outcome so that gradual divergence is visible before a ticket arrives. Keep identifiers out of metric labels unless the evidence policy permits them.

This minimal Go program performs one address-resolution observation. Run it as a fresh process at each selected probe location, supplying a hostname and one expected address as positional arguments. It prints no hostname or resolved addresses, which keeps this particular output small enough to review as a monitoring payload.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net"
    "net/netip"
    "os"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) != 3 {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "usage: probe hostname expected-ip")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    expected, err := netip.ParseAddr(os.Args[2])
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "invalid expected IP address")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    addresses, err := net.DefaultResolver.LookupNetIP(ctx, "ip", os.Args[1])
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "resolution_success=0")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    matched := false
    for _, address := range addresses {
        if address.Unmap() == expected.Unmap() {
            matched = true
        }
    }
    if !matched {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "expected_target_present=0")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println("expected_target_present=1")
}

The five-second timeout bounds this probe's wait; it is not a propagation estimate. Success means that this resolver returned the expected address among its answers. It does not mean every returned address is approved, that every resolver agrees, or that the application behind the address is healthy. If the release gate requires an exact address set, extend the comparison to the entire approved set before using it as that gate. Presence alone is too weak for that requirement.

This deliberately small probe is useful because its limitation is inspectable. For mail, use a separate controlled test whose recorded outcome is acceptance by the sending workflow's provider, and keep that result separate from domain verification. DMARC supplies authentication-policy context; it is not a substitute for observing acceptance.

Verify the change and preserve the rollback budget

Before the switch, establish the previous target's observed resolution and the mail test's baseline outcome. During the switch, compare the new target's resolution results with the agreed SLO and retain configuration evidence for any disagreement. Afterward, continue the same observations through the agreed window; changing the definition of success midway makes the before-and-after comparison useless.

Set the rollback trigger before execution. For example, the change can require rollback when the selected resolution observations miss their release gate, while a mail acceptance regression triggers investigation against the separately recorded mail baseline. The thresholds belong to the service owner. They are not universal DNS constants.

Rollback is another cutover. Restoring the previous configuration does not prove that the outcome has recovered: the same caching-resolver disagreement that complicated the forward change can complicate the return. Keep the previous target provisioned, repeat the outcome checks, and close the change only when the agreed recovery evidence exists. This is the reason to budget overlap capacity rather than treating rollback as a free operation.

Finally, execute the evidence policy. Delete detailed observations on the approved schedule, verify the relevant deletion behavior with each processor, and preserve only the aggregates permitted by the policy. Fast propagation is a release objective; accountable handling of the evidence is an operating requirement that continues after the release is over.

References

  • RFC 7489, DMARC
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 documentation
  • BIND 9 documentation
  • Go net package reference

If this controller boundary fits your system, start with the schemas and runnable examples in the Infrai documentation.
