title: 3D GameDev Arena: Benchmarking Coding Agents That Plan, Build, and Playtest extreme Long-Horizon Browser Games
description:
arXiv:2611.24073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents now resolve repository issues and generate compact playable games, but whether they can build a large 3D game from scratch remains open. Such games tightly couple mechanics, scenes, assets, and interaction logic, and their quality rests on player enjoyment, which existing benchmarks rarely assess. Thus, we introduce 3D GameDev Arena, a first extreme long-horizon benchmark of 108 from-scratch game-development tasks across 14 genres. Given only a text specification and UI/UX reference images, a fully automated plan--implement--test--repair pipeline builds each task into a self-contained browser game. Runs average $\sim$1,000 LLM calls ; the longest uses 14,407 calls, 2.13B tokens, and 608 assets. Evaluation spans (1) objective code-level functional acceptance against the game specification, (2) agent-based QA and playtesting of 3D presentation and playability, and (3) blind pairwise Bradley-Terry human preference in a public arena. The preliminary findings indicate that long-horizon 3D game development remains far from solved, and code-level correctness alone does not dictate player preference. The public arena is hosted online.

title: Storybrand Website Framework
description:
Storybrand Website Framework: A Comprehensive Architectural Breakdown

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous websites that fail to effectively engage their audience and drive conversions. One primary reason for this failure is the reliance on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms. These templates often lack a clear understanding of the target audience's needs, desires, and pain points, resulting in a generic and unremarkable user experience.

Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms fail for several reasons:

  • They do not provide a clear and concise message that resonates with the target audience
  • They lack a well-defined narrative that guides the user through the website
  • They do not prioritize a clear call-to-action (CTA) that encourages users to take action

In contrast, the Storybrand website framework offers a structured approach to building websites that prioritize clarity, simplicity, and conversions. This framework is based on the principles of storytelling and provides a clear narrative that guides the user through the website.

Here are three concrete engineering takeaways from the Storybrand website framework:

  1. Clearly define the customer's problem: The Storybrand framework emphasizes the importance of clearly defining the customer's problem and presenting a solution that resonates with their needs and desires. This requires a deep understanding of the target audience and their pain points.
  2. Use a clear and concise message: The framework prioritizes a clear and concise message that communicates the value proposition and unique selling points of the product or service. This message should be consistent throughout the website and guide the user through the narrative.
  3. Prioritize a clear call-to-action (CTA): The Storybrand framework emphasizes the importance of prioritizing a clear CTA that encourages users to take action. This CTA should be prominent, visible, and consistent throughout the website, guiding the user towards the desired outcome.

By applying the Storybrand website framework, businesses can create websites that effectively engage their audience, communicate their value proposition, and drive conversions. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis:
https://vareli.info/blog/storybrand-website-framework

title: A/B testing script security after the Optimizely attack
description:
On November 16, an attacker used a flaw in Optimizely's Experimentation signup flow to write malicious code into the custom JavaScript field of customer projects. Visitors to sites like the BBC, CNN and IKEA got the code from a CDN their browsers already trusted. Security teams are now arguing about allowlists and hashes.

This piece is for the people who own the experimentation tool: CRO leads, product designers and growth managers. Your A/B testing platform is a code editor with a marketing login, and the fix is mostly about who can edit it, where it runs and how you notice change.

What the Optimizely attack actually did

Optimizely lets customers add a "Project JavaScript" field to their experimentation snippet. It is meant for custom variation logic. According to Socket's write-up, the attacker put a loader in that field, and Optimizely confirmed the entry point was a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow.

The affected sites did nothing wrong in the usual sense. They were not breached. Their pages loaded a script from the same Optimizely infrastructure they had loaded for years, and that script now carried extra code. Researcher Scott Helme found 188 infected snippets tied to 178 organizations, and he says the real number is probably higher.

The payloads were practical. A wallet clipper swapped cryptocurrency addresses in copied text, and later variants reportedly skimmed card data. ITPro's summary adds that the attacker revised the malware several times over a few hours on Monday, and that Optimizely has more than 9,000 customers.

Optimizely says the hole is fixed and the injected code is removed. Treat that as a statement about their side only. Whether your project was touched, and what your team does differently now, is your side.

Why allowlists and domain trust did not help

The standard answer to third-party script risk is a Content Security Policy. The numbers from this incident are not kind to it. Vendor cside's analysis counts 256 affected sites and says only 24 had a CSP that blocked the payload. Sixty-eight had no CSP at all.

The reason is structural. A script-src allowlist approves hosts, not code. Because the CDN host was already on the list, the loader ran. The address swap also happens entirely in the DOM, with no network request, so rules that restrict where data can be sent do not stop it. cside sells client-side monitoring, so weigh its framing accordingly, but the CSP mechanics are standard.

The same logic breaks vendor review. You approved Optimizely once, at onboarding. The domain, the script URL and the tag never changed. Only the contents of your project did, and the contents are edited by people and API tokens, which is a security question dressed as a marketing one.

I think this is the lesson most teams will miss. They will tighten the CSP, which is worth doing, and leave the actual door open: a long list of accounts that can publish code to every page of the store.

The experimentation tool is a production deploy path

Ask who can ship code to your checkout. Engineering will name the repository, the review rules and the CI pipeline. Then ask who can publish an experiment with custom JavaScript. The list is usually longer, with fewer controls: designers, agency contractors, a growth hire from two years ago, and API tokens nobody remembers creating.

Experiment code skips most of the safeguards, and it does so by design. The point of a visual editor is that a non-engineer can change a page in an afternoon. That speed is why teams buy the tool, and it is also why one stolen login can reach every page the snippet loads on.

Treat the platform as a deploy target. Enforce SSO and two-factor authentication. Remove collaborators who no longer need access. List API tokens and delete the ones without an owner. Then decide who is allowed to write custom JavaScript at all, as opposed to using the visual editor's built-in changes. For most stores that group should be two or three named people.

Review the change history for the days around November 16 and 17, and look for collaborators or tokens you do not recognize. This takes an hour. It is probably the most useful hour you will spend on this problem.

Keep experiments off the pages that handle money

Most conversion tests do not need to run on payment, account or login pages. Socket's advice to site owners makes the same point: ask whether experimentation and personalization scripts need to run on sensitive pages at all, because a script with page access can read whatever the page shows.

Platforms differ here. On Shopify, scripts can no longer be dropped into checkout freely. Shopify's pixel documentation says pixels run in a sandbox, and that sandboxes cannot render interface elements such as buttons, forms, banners or modals. That limit is annoying for testers and good for security. A tool that cannot touch the DOM cannot clip a wallet address from it.

If you run your own stack, you can copy the principle. Scope the experimentation snippet to catalog and cart pages by default. Put checkout tests through the same review as any other code change. The test you lose is usually a small one, since the large gains in a checkout come from fewer fields and clearer errors, not from a variant injected at runtime.

There is a compliance angle if you take cards on your own pages. Adyen's PCI DSS guidance describes requirement 6.4.3, which asks for a method to confirm each payment page script is authorized, a way to assure its integrity, and a written inventory with a justification for each script. Requirement 11.6.1 asks for tamper detection on payment page scripts as the browser receives them. Adyen notes that merchants eligible for SAQ A are outside this scope, so check which form you file.

Watch what scripts do, not where they load from

Hash pinning sounds like the obvious fix, and for most experimentation tools it does not work. cside points out that hashes break whenever an experiment changes, which for an active program is several times a week. A control that fails every Tuesday gets switched off.

The workable middle is cheaper. Record a hash of each third-party script as served and alert when it changes, rather than blocking. Run your CSP in report-only mode first and read the reports before you enforce anything. Watch for new outbound hosts, reads from payment fields and unexpected DOM rewrites on the pages that matter. None of this stops a determined attacker, and I would not claim otherwise, but it turns a silent change into an alert.

Add a pre-flight step to your own release habits too. If your team already freezes risky changes before peak season, as in the Black Friday code freeze checklist, put the experimentation platform inside the freeze. An experiment launched on the Wednesday before Black Friday is a production change like any other.

A checklist you can run this week

Start with access. Pull the list of everyone with edit rights in your experimentation tool and cut it to the people who ran an experiment in the last 90 days. Turn on SSO and two-factor authentication if either is missing. Revoke API tokens that have no named owner.

Next, inspect the code. Open every custom JavaScript field in every project and read it. Look for base64 strings, URLs on domains you do not recognize, and code that touches clipboard events or form fields. Compare the change history against November 16 and 17.

Then reduce exposure. List the pages the snippet loads on and remove it from checkout, login and account pages unless a live test truly requires it. Write the names of the two or three people allowed to publish custom code, and tell the agency that their logins no longer do.

Finally, add detection. Switch on CSP report-only mode, log script hash changes for every third-party script on cart and checkout, and decide who gets the alert. If a payment team exists, tell them what the snippet can reach.

Do the same for tag managers, personalization tools and chat widgets. They share the property that made this attack work: a trusted host, a marketing login, and no code review.

title: Payment timed out. Should we release the stock?
description:
Someone buys the last pair of headphones in our shop. We reserve them and ask the payment provider to authorize the purchase. Five seconds pass without a reply. Should we put the headphones back on sale?

I ran into a similar problem while working on an event-driven saga. I’ll use checkout as the example here because the decision is easy to picture. If the provider declined the payment, we can release the headphones. If it approved the payment and the reply got lost, someone may already be counting on that last pair.

ResultFlow is a TypeScript library I built on top of neverthrow for composing workflows that can fail. If your functions already return neverthrow’s Result or ResultAsync, you can use them directly in a flow. ResultFlow lets you decide which steps to retry, where to set a timeout, and when to run the workflow. Calling .run() returns a Promise that resolves to a regular neverthrow Result.

In this checkout, the interesting question is which steps a retry repeats. If a payment request times out, we can retry it with the same order ID. If saving the order fails because another worker updated it, we already have the payment approval. We only need to repeat the database work.

Start with the checkout 

import { ResultFlow } from '@youldali/result-flow';
import { err, ok, type Result } from 'neverthrow';

type CheckoutStatus = 'confirmed' | 'pending';

function checkoutFlow(orderId: string): ResultFlow<CheckoutStatus, CheckoutError> {
  return ResultFlow.from(() => reserveStock(orderId))
    .chain(reservation => paymentFlow(orderId, reservation))
    .tap(status => console.info('Checkout status', { orderId, status }))
    .ifFailure(failure => console.error('Checkout failed', { orderId, failure }));
}

checkoutFlow(orderId) builds the workflow. Passing () => reserveStock(orderId) keeps the inventory call lazy. The shop only reserves the headphones when the flow runs.

From there, .chain() passes the reservation to paymentFlow. If the headphones are already out of stock, checkout skips payment and .ifFailure() logs the typed failure. The same callback also logs unexpected exceptions. The inventory, payment, and database functions in this example belong to the application.

What happens if the payment times out? 

function paymentFlow(
  orderId: string,
  reservation: Reservation,
): ResultFlow<CheckoutStatus, CheckoutError> {
  // The provider uses orderId as the idempotency key, so retries
  // refer to the same payment authorization.
  return ResultFlow.from(() => authorizePayment(orderId))
    .timeout({ ms: 5_000, onTimeout: () => 'payment-timeout' as const })
    .retryPolicy({
      maxRetries: 2,
      condition: error => error === 'payment-timeout',
    })
    .chain(authorization => confirmOrderFlow(orderId, authorization))
    .map<CheckoutStatus>(() => 'confirmed')
    .orElse(async (error): Promise<Result<CheckoutStatus, CheckoutError>> => {
      switch (error) {
        case 'payment-declined':
          await releaseStock(reservation.id);
          return err(error);

        case 'payment-timeout': {
          // Keep the stock reserved and queue a job to check
          // the existing payment with the provider.
          const scheduled = await schedulePaymentCheck(orderId, reservation.id);
          if (scheduled.isErr()) return err(scheduled.error);

          return ok('pending');
        }

        default:
          return err(error);
      }
    });
}

Suppose the provider approves the first request, but its reply gets lost. After five seconds, .timeout() produces a 'payment-timeout' error and .retryPolicy() makes another request. Both requests carry the same orderId as their idempotency key, so the provider can return the existing authorization. Because .timeout() comes before .retryPolicy(), each request gets its own five-second deadline.

A decline takes a shorter path. Only timeouts qualify for a payment retry, so 'payment-declined' reaches .orElse() immediately. We release the headphones, then return the decline. Here releaseStock returns Promise<void>. If it rejects, .ifFailure() logs the exception and .run() rejects with it.

If all three requests time out, we still don’t know whether the provider approved the payment. schedulePaymentCheck queues a job to look up the existing payment later. In the meantime, the shop holds the reservation. Returning ok('pending') means the follow-up was successfully queued. If queuing fails, the caller gets that error instead.

What if payment succeeds but saving the order fails?

Suppose we load version 12 of the order. Before we save the confirmation, another worker updates the delivery instructions and saves version 13. The database rejects our stale write. What should we repeat?

function confirmOrderFlow(
  orderId: string,
  authorization: Authorization,
): ResultFlow<Order, ConfirmationError> {
  return ResultFlow.from(() => loadOrder(orderId))
    .chain(order => applyConfirmation(order, authorization))
    .chain(order => saveOrder(order))
    .retryPolicy({
      maxRetries: 2,
      condition: error => error === 'version-conflict',
    });
}

The retry starts at loadOrder. We load version 13, apply the payment approval we already received, and try the save again. This preserves the updated delivery instructions. If the other worker cancelled the order, applyConfirmation can return a different error and the retry stops.

The retry happens entirely inside confirmOrderFlow. By the time this function runs, authorizePayment has already succeeded. A database conflict can make us read and write the order again, but it never sends another request to the payment provider.

Run it 

const result = await checkoutFlow('order-123').run();

result is a neverthrow Result<CheckoutStatus, CheckoutError>. An Ok('confirmed') means the order confirmation was saved. An Ok('pending') means the shop is holding the headphones and has queued a payment check. A typed failure reaches the caller as an Err.

So when do we put the last pair back on sale? When the provider tells us it declined the payment. Five seconds of silence gives us a reason to retry. If the retries run out, we keep the headphones reserved until we know what happened.

ResultFlow on GitHub

title: A month of selling tools to AI agents: 350,000 requests, 28 paying wallets, $0.95
description:
Everyone says AI agents will pay for APIs per call. So I built two services they can pay without an account and watched what happened for a month.

The setup: a crypto market data API (prices, funding rates, liquidations, whale orders) and an "Agent Toolbox" of 30 everyday tools: web page to Markdown, structured extraction with a checked quote per field, screenshots, speech to text with subtitles, text to speech, image understanding and OCR, image generation, Base and Ethereum on-chain data, DNS, WHOIS and company records. Agents pay per call with x402 (USDC on Base) or MPP, or with a prepaid API key. The same tools are on RapidAPI, the Apify Store and a remote MCP server. Everything runs on Cloudflare Workers, so the running cost is close to zero.

Here is the first month, straight from my dashboard.

What Count
Requests 350,107
Shown a price (HTTP 402) and left 315,583
Refused (wrong method or address) 30,612
Paid x402 calls from outside wallets 165
Paying wallets 28
Wallets that came back and paid again 7
Revenue (USDC on Base, outside wallets only) $0.95
AI inference bill $0

1. Most traffic is the ecosystem indexing itself. About 320 different MCP clients connected to each server, around 14,000 connections each: uptime monitors, registries and scanners. Being listed everywhere works. Being used is another thing.

2. A 402 is not a lead. 315,583 price quotes turned into 165 paid calls. Most clients that ask for a price are checking that the paywall works, not shopping.

3. The real customers buy one thing, again and again. Seven wallets came back and paid again. One paid for speech to text 63 times in a single week. Most of the others were indexers paying each route once.

4. Agent search wants usage before it lists you. My services were registered on x402scan and passed validation, yet never appeared in agentcash search. A maintainer's reply to another seller explains why: resources need some usage through trusted sources, such as the agentcash client, before search shows them. New sellers start invisible.

5. Your payment middleware can fail where you can't see it. The x402 library starts up by asking the facilitator which payment kinds it supports. When that failed, every paid route answered 500, the 402 price quote included, and the log lost the error message. I now run start-up myself, retry it, keep the last good answer, and send 503 with Retry-After so agents try again.

6. Models disappear under you. Cloudflare retired the Qwen3 model behind one of my routes on 20 November. The route now runs its successor; a small probe script tests replacement models against the live binding in a minute.

7. The cost side is not the problem. AI usage stayed inside Cloudflare's free daily allowance, so the inference bill was $0. I can afford to wait for demand.

What I changed. Simple lookups now cost $0.001. Failed calls are free everywhere. There is a free allowance for extraction (20 a day per IP), and six new tools: text to speech, image understanding with OCR, and on-chain data for Base and Ethereum.

What I'd like to know. If you run an agent that pays for tools, what does it actually buy, and how did it find the seller?

Try it:

  • Agent Toolbox (x402, OpenAPI, llms.txt): agent-toolbox.zafermemon87.workers.dev
  • Remote MCP server, nothing to install: https://agent-toolbox.zafermemon87.workers.dev/mcp
  • Free extraction: POST https://agent-toolbox.zafermemon87.workers.dev/free/extract

title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
description:
arXiv:2611.23508v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

title: Reject Duplicate JSON Keys Before Mapping a Stock Update
description:
A JSON object can contain the same property name twice. Python's default decoder retains the last value, so an upstream ambiguity can disappear before a stock update reaches schema validation.

Reject duplicates while pairs are still visible

Use object_pairs_hook to inspect each object's ordered key-value pairs. The hook below rejects an exact repeated key, including inside nested objects. It preserves arrays and permits the same key in separate objects.

import json

def unique_object(pairs):
    result = {}
    for key, value in pairs:
        if key in result:
            raise ValueError("duplicate JSON key: " + key)
        result[key] = value
    return result

def read_update(text):
    return json.loads(text, object_pairs_hook=unique_object)

assert json.loads('{"quantity":2,"quantity":9}') == {"quantity":9}
assert read_update('{"sku":"A","quantity":2}') == {"sku":"A","quantity":2}
assert read_update('[{"sku":"A"},{"sku":"B"}]')[1]['sku'] == 'B'
assert read_update('{"SKU":1,"sku":2}') == {"SKU":1,"sku":2}
for text in ['{"quantity":2,"quantity":9}', '{"item":{"sku":"A","sku":"B"}}', r'{"a":1,"\u0061":2}']:
    try:
        read_update(text)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError("duplicate accepted")
print("7 checks passed")

Why this belongs before mapping

A Shopify 3PL adapter may receive a quantity update before shopify fulfillment work is prepared. If two quantity properties disagree, choosing the last one silently is an accidental policy. Rejecting the ambiguous object gives the sender a specific correction to make.

The same issue can occur in a drop shipping file handover or a china fulfillment stock feed. A china 3PL mapping layer should receive one unambiguous value before deciding its business meaning. International Fulfillment for Folligen is used here only as a hypothetical enquiry label for such a data handover, not a customer relationship or a tested integration.

Checks and limits

The example exercises seven assertions or rejection cases: default last-value behavior, a normal object, separate objects in an array, case-distinct keys, top-level duplication, nested duplication and an escaped spelling of the same key. Run it locally with Python; no store, warehouse or API is contacted.

This is an exact decoded-key rule. Case normalization, required fields, numeric ranges, non-standard number constants, document size and nesting limits require separate validation. The hook does not make arbitrary JSON safe or authorize a stock change.

Python's JSON documentation describes object_pairs_hook and the default handling of repeated names. For operational context, the integration overview describes the handover questions; this example is an isolated parser check.

title: How to get every job from a company's careers page as JSON (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and 7 more)
description:
If you are building a job board, a hiring-signal tool for sales, or a "tell me when Company X posts a data role" alert, you do not need to scrape LinkedIn or fight anti-bot walls. Most companies run their careers page on an applicant tracking system (ATS), and every major ATS publishes the open jobs through a public feed that the careers page itself reads.

Here is how to use those feeds directly, what breaks when you do it at scale, and a shortcut if you would rather not maintain ten parsers.

Step 1: find out which ATS the company uses

Open the company's careers page and click any job. The link usually gives it away:

If the job link goes to The ATS is Company identifier
boards.greenhouse.io/airbnb/... Greenhouse airbnb
jobs.lever.co/spotify/... Lever spotify
jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp/... Ashby ramp
jobs.smartrecruiters.com/BoschGroup/... SmartRecruiters BoschGroup
apply.workable.com/huggingface/... Workable huggingface

If the job opens on the company's own domain, view the page source and search for greenhouse, lever, ashby, workable or smartrecruiters: embedded boards load a script that contains the identifier.

Step 2: call the feed 

import requests

def greenhouse(company):
    r = requests.get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{company}/jobs", params={"content": "true"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j["location"]["name"], "url": j["absolute_url"],
             "department": ", ".join(d["name"] for d in j.get("departments", []))} for j in r.json()["jobs"]]

def lever(company):
    r = requests.get(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{company}", params={"mode": "json"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return [{"title": j["text"], "location": j["categories"].get("location"), "url": j["hostedUrl"],
             "team": j["categories"].get("team")} for j in r.json()]

def ashby(company):
    r = requests.get(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{company}", params={"includeCompensation": "true"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j.get("location"), "url": j.get("jobUrl"),
             "salary": (j.get("compensation") or {}).get("compensationTierSummary")} for j in r.json()["jobs"]]

print(len(greenhouse("airbnb")), "Airbnb jobs")
print(len(lever("spotify")), "Spotify jobs")
print(len(ashby("ramp")), "Ramp jobs")

That is enough for a weekend project. A November 2026 run returned about 200 jobs for Airbnb, 90 for Spotify and 180 for Ramp, each in under a second.

The feed URLs for all ten ATS (including Workable, Recruitee, Personio, Teamtailor, Gem and Breezy HR), with what each returns, are in this reference repo: ats-job-feeds.

Step 3: what breaks at scale

Once you follow a few hundred companies, the work moves from fetching to normalising:

  • Ten formats. Greenhouse and Ashby return JSON objects, Lever a JSON array, Personio XML, Teamtailor RSS. Dates come as ISO strings, epoch milliseconds or RFC 822.
  • Locations and remote work. "Remote (US)", "Hybrid - London", a list of offices, or a separate workplaceType field, depending on the ATS.
  • Salary. Ashby gives a structured range for about half of jobs; Lever only when the employer fills it in; Greenhouse not at all in the public feed. When pay is written in the description, you need text parsing or an LLM to get numbers out.
  • Paging. SmartRecruiters returns 100 postings per page; large employers have thousands.
  • Only new jobs. For alerts you have to remember which IDs you already sent, per company and per filter set.
  • Identifiers that are not the company name. Ubisoft2 on SmartRecruiters, case-sensitive slugs on Lever.

The shortcut

I got tired of maintaining this and packaged it as an Apify Actor: Company Careers Jobs API. You paste careers pages, board URLs or plain company names; it finds the ATS, reads the public feed and returns one format for ten ATS (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, SmartRecruiters, Workable, Recruitee, Personio, Teamtailor, Gem, Breezy HR). It has an "only new jobs" mode for scheduled runs and optional AI fields (visa sponsorship with the quote, normalised salary, seniority, skills).

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("sandy_cornfield/company-jobs-api").call(run_input={
    "companies": ["https://www.figma.com/careers/", "lever:spotify", "ashby:ramp"],
    "keywords": ["engineer"],
    "onlyNew": True,
})
for job in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(job["companySlug"], "|", job["title"], "|", job["workplaceType"], "|", job["url"])

It costs $2 per 1,000 jobs, with no monthly fee. If you only need one ATS, there are single-ATS versions for Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby.

Disclosure: I built those Actors. The feeds in steps 1 and 2 are free to use on their own; be polite with them (cache, a few requests per second at most).

title: Temporal Extrapolation of Elastic Seismic Wave Propagation in Layered Media Using Neural Operators
description:
arXiv:2611.25130v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal prediction of seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval represented in training remains challenging for neural operator models. This study develops a coupled neural operator framework for stress-conditioned temporal prediction in layered elastic media. A time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (TI-DeepONet) advances the velocity field through an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) scheme, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a residual correction to the predicted spatial field. The two components are trained jointly in a predictor-corrector configuration. Prediction is initialized with reference velocity fields at the first two time levels and proceeds autoregressively, with reference stress fields and prescribed excitation supplied throughout rollout, including beyond the training interval. Four cases consider horizontally polarized shear (SH) waves in four-layer soil columns with fixed total depths of 50 and 280 m, excited by third-order Gaussian-derivative (DOG3) wavelets with central frequencies between 0.5 and 6 Hz. Layer thicknesses and shear-wave velocities vary across profiles. Evaluations on test profiles extend beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration. The predictions reproduce principal velocity arrivals and depth-dependent response patterns, with accuracy varying across profiles. Across the four cases, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) range from 0.53% to 2.31% over the full evaluation windows and from 0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals. Both metrics use each profile's peak absolute reference velocity over the full evaluation window as the normalizer. These results demonstrate temporal velocity prediction under reference-stress conditioning for the tested configurations; autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

title: Mask Reveal Code: the small motion details that make it feel right
description:
Four digits, and the cells become one solid panel.

A code field where four digits trigger a panel that opens across the cells from left to right with a confirmation word. A wrong code shakes the row and clears it.

The trick

The panel is a veil clipped with inset(0 100% 0 0), and opening it is just animating that clip to 0.

Motion goes through one small go() helper on the Web Animations API, which sets durations to 1ms for reduced motion.

The shake is six translateX keyframes of 8 then 4 pixels, which decays like a real shake.

.veil{position:absolute;inset:0;background:var(--fx-on);color:var(--fx-on-ink);display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;gap:8px;font-weight:600;font-size:16px;clip-path:inset(0 100% 0 0);pointer-events:none;z-index:2}
const shake=el=>go(el,[{transform:'translateX(0)'},{transform:'translateX(-8px)'},{transform:'translateX(8px)'},{transform:'translateX(-4px)'},{transform:'translateX(4px)'},{transform:'translateX(0)'}],

Where I'd use it

Verification and 2FA screens

Each cell is a real input under the veil, so the field keeps its normal keyboard and autofill behavior.

The prompt for this one is free: uimotion.app.

title: How to Find and Highlight Text in a PDF with Java
description:
When you review a purchase agreement, the phrase “payment terms” might appear in the main contract and again in an addendum. A Java program can tell you which pages to check, pinpoint each match on the page, and save a highlighted copy to share with a reviewer.

The examples below use the same three-page PDF. You can run each one on its own, depending on whether you need page numbers, coordinates, or a marked-up document.

Set Up the Maven Project

Add this repository and dependency to your project's pom.xml.

<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>com.e-iceblue</id>
        <url>https://repo.e-iceblue.com/nexus/content/groups/public/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>e-iceblue</groupId>
        <artifactId>spire.pdf</artifactId>
        <version>12.10.3</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Prepare a Sample PDF

Save a searchable PDF as purchase-agreement.pdf in the program's working directory. To reproduce the examples, put the following text on three separate pages and export the document as a PDF.

Page Sample text
1 Payment terms: invoices are due within 30 days of receipt. Any change to the payment terms must be agreed in writing.
2 The supplier must deliver the equipment by the agreed date.
3 Payment terms in the signed addendum take precedence.

All three examples use TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase, so both “Payment terms” and “payment terms” match.

Find the Pages That Contain a Keyword

To see which pages mention the phrase, create a PdfTextFinder for each page and call find(). The size of the result tells you how many matches that page contains. The program skips pages with zero matches and adds 1 to the zero-based page index before printing it.

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFinder;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.TextFindParameter;

import java.util.EnumSet;

public class FindPdfKeywordPages {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String keyword = "payment terms";

        PdfDocument document = new PdfDocument();
        try {
            document.loadFromFile("purchase-agreement.pdf");
            int totalMatches = 0;

            for (int i = 0; i < document.getPages().getCount(); i++) {
                PdfTextFinder finder = new PdfTextFinder(document.getPages().get(i));
                finder.getOptions().setTextFindParameter(EnumSet.of(TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase));
                int matches = finder.find(keyword).size();

                if (matches > 0) {
                    System.out.printf("Page %d: %d%n", i + 1, matches);
                    totalMatches += matches;
                }
            }

            System.out.printf("Total matches for \"%s\": %d%n", keyword, totalMatches);
        } finally {
            document.dispose();
        }
    }
}

For the sample agreement, the console output looks like this.

Page 1: 2
Page 3: 1
Total matches for "payment terms": 3

Get the Page Coordinates of Each Match

Each match comes back as a PdfTextFragment. Its getPositions() method returns an array of points. A match that spans multiple lines can return more than one point, so the code prints every point for that match.

Coordinates are measured in points (pt) from the top-left corner of the page. The x-coordinate increases to the right, and the y-coordinate increases down the page.

import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFinder;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFragment;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.TextFindParameter;

import java.awt.geom.Point2D;
import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.Locale;

public class GetPdfKeywordPositions {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String keyword = "payment terms";

        PdfDocument document = new PdfDocument();
        try {
            document.loadFromFile("purchase-agreement.pdf");

            for (int i = 0; i < document.getPages().getCount(); i++) {
                PdfTextFinder finder = new PdfTextFinder(document.getPages().get(i));
                finder.getOptions().setTextFindParameter(EnumSet.of(TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase));
                int matchNumber = 0;

                for (PdfTextFragment match : finder.find(keyword)) {
                    matchNumber++;
                    for (Point2D position : match.getPositions()) {
                        System.out.printf(Locale.ROOT,
                                "Page %d, match %d: x=%.2f pt, y=%.2f pt%n",
                                i + 1, matchNumber, position.getX(), position.getY());
                    }
                }
            }
        } finally {
            document.dispose();
        }
    }
}

Here are the coordinates from the sample PDF. The values will vary with the layout of your file.

Page 1, match 1: x=72.00 pt, y=72.29 pt
Page 1, match 2: x=172.07 pt, y=96.29 pt
Page 3, match 1: x=72.00 pt, y=72.29 pt

Highlight All Matches in the PDF

Search each page as before, then call highLight(Color.YELLOW) on every match. Once all pages have been processed, save the document to a new file so you have a separate copy for review.

import com.spire.pdf.FileFormat;
import com.spire.pdf.PdfDocument;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFinder;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.PdfTextFragment;
import com.spire.pdf.texts.TextFindParameter;

import java.awt.Color;
import java.util.EnumSet;

public class HighlightPdfKeywords {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String keyword = "payment terms";

        PdfDocument document = new PdfDocument();
        try {
            document.loadFromFile("purchase-agreement.pdf");

            for (int i = 0; i < document.getPages().getCount(); i++) {
                PdfTextFinder finder = new PdfTextFinder(document.getPages().get(i));
                finder.getOptions().setTextFindParameter(EnumSet.of(TextFindParameter.IgnoreCase));

                for (PdfTextFragment match : finder.find(keyword)) {
                    match.highLight(Color.YELLOW);
                }
            }

            document.saveToFile("purchase-agreement-highlighted.pdf", FileFormat.PDF);
        } finally {
            document.dispose();
        }
    }
}

Open purchase-agreement-highlighted.pdf to see two yellow highlights on page 1 and one on page 3.

Common Issues

Why does the search miss text I can see on the page?

Try copying the phrase from your PDF viewer into a plain-text editor. If the page is an image-only scan, run OCR first to create a searchable text layer. If you can copy the text, check for extra spaces or line breaks in the copied phrase.

Why do the page numbers differ from the ones printed in the PDF?

The program counts from the first page in the file. If a cover page comes before the main text, the page labeled “1” in the footer may be page 2 in the search results.

Can I remove the highlights from the PDF viewer's comments panel?

highLight() writes the highlight into the page content. To give reviewers control over individual highlights in the comments panel, create PDF highlight annotations.

title: Attention Is Not Relevance: Challenging the Causality of Attention in Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2611.24051v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.

title: What Does a Java Developer Do in a Company? A Complete CTO Guide
description:
Java remains an important technology for building enterprise applications, backend systems, financial platforms, business software, and large-scale digital services. Many companies use Java because of its mature ecosystem, strong tooling, portability, and ability to support complex application requirements.

However, hiring a Java developer involves more than finding someone who can write Java code. Companies need professionals who understand application architecture, databases, APIs, security, testing, deployment, and long-term software maintenance.

For CTOs and engineering managers, understanding a Java developer's responsibilities helps define job roles, build effective development teams, and make better technology decisions.

This guide explains what Java developers do in a company, the skills they need, how they contribute to business projects, and when organizations should hire them.

1. What Is a Java Developer?

A Java developer is a software engineer who uses the Java programming language and its ecosystem to design, develop, test, deploy, and maintain software applications.

Depending on the company and project, a Java developer may work on:

  • Enterprise applications.
  • Backend services and APIs.
  • E-commerce platforms.
  • Banking and financial systems.
  • Customer management platforms.
  • SaaS applications.
  • Microservices architectures.
  • Internal business applications.

Java developers work with other professionals, including frontend developers, database administrators, QA engineers, DevOps engineers, software architects, and product managers.

Their responsibilities vary according to experience, project complexity, and organizational structure.

2. What Does a Java Developer Do in a Company?

A Java developer contributes throughout the software development lifecycle, from understanding business requirements to maintaining production applications.

A. Develop Backend Applications

One of the primary responsibilities is building backend functionality.

Java developers implement the business logic that powers applications, including:

  • User registration and authentication.
  • Order and transaction processing.
  • Payment workflows.
  • Business rules and validations.
  • Data processing.
  • Reporting functionality.
  • Customer account management.

For example, an e-commerce application may use Java backend services to process orders, calculate prices, manage inventory, and communicate with payment providers.

B. Build APIs and Integrations

Modern business applications frequently communicate with external systems and frontend applications.

Java developers build and maintain APIs that allow different services to exchange information.

Typical responsibilities include:

  • Developing RESTful APIs.
  • Integrating third-party services.
  • Implementing authentication and authorization.
  • Validating incoming requests.
  • Handling errors and API responses.
  • Maintaining API documentation.
  • Supporting communication between microservices.

Frameworks such as Spring Boot are commonly used to develop Java-based APIs and backend services.

C. Design and Manage Database Operations

Java developers frequently work with relational and NoSQL databases to store and retrieve application data.

Their responsibilities may include:

  • Designing database interactions.
  • Writing SQL queries.
  • Implementing data access layers.
  • Managing transactions.
  • Optimizing database performance.
  • Handling data validation and consistency.
  • Integrating applications with database systems.

Common database technologies include PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Database, and MongoDB.

Java developers may also use technologies such as Hibernate and Spring Data JPA to simplify database operations.

D. Implement Application Security

Security is an essential responsibility, especially when applications process financial, customer, or business information.

Java developers should understand and implement:

  • Secure authentication.
  • Role-based access control.
  • Input validation.
  • Secure session management.
  • Password hashing.
  • Protection against SQL injection.
  • Secure API communication.
  • Dependency vulnerability management.

Spring Security is commonly used to implement authentication and authorization in Java applications.

Security responsibilities should also involve code reviews, testing, infrastructure teams, and organizational security policies.

E. Write and Maintain Application Tests

Java developers are responsible for ensuring that application functionality works as expected.

Testing activities include:

  • Unit testing.
  • Integration testing.
  • API testing.
  • Regression testing.
  • Debugging and defect resolution.
  • Performance testing where required.

Popular Java testing tools include JUnit, Mockito, and Testcontainers.

Automated testing helps teams identify problems earlier and reduces the risk of introducing defects during application updates.

F. Maintain and Improve Existing Applications

Java development does not end after an application is launched.

Developers regularly work on:

  • Fixing production bugs.
  • Improving application performance.
  • Updating dependencies.
  • Refactoring outdated code.
  • Resolving security vulnerabilities.
  • Adding new business features.
  • Supporting application upgrades.

For established enterprise systems, maintaining existing functionality can be just as important as developing new features.

3. Java Technologies and Tools Developers Commonly Use

A Java developer's technology stack depends on the application architecture and project requirements.

Technology Category Common Tools and Technologies
Programming language Java
Backend frameworks Spring Boot, Spring MVC, Jakarta EE
ORM and data access Hibernate, Spring Data JPA
Databases PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, MongoDB
API development REST, OpenAPI, Swagger
Testing JUnit, Mockito, Testcontainers
Build tools Maven, Gradle
Version control Git, GitHub, GitLab
Messaging Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ
Containers Docker, Kubernetes
CI/CD Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI
Monitoring Prometheus, Grafana, OpenTelemetry

CTOs should evaluate whether candidates understand how these tools work together rather than judging technical ability by the number of technologies listed on a résumé.

4. Different Types of Java Developers in a Company

Not every Java developer performs the same responsibilities. Companies should align hiring decisions with project requirements.

Junior Java Developer

Typically works on smaller development tasks, bug fixes, basic APIs, unit tests, and database operations under senior guidance.

Mid-Level Java Developer

Handles independent feature development, API integrations, database operations, debugging, and application maintenance.

Senior Java Developer

Takes responsibility for complex features, code quality, technical decisions, performance improvements, and mentoring junior developers.

Java Technical Lead

Coordinates development activities, reviews architecture and implementation decisions, supports team members, and ensures technical delivery aligns with project goals.

Java Architect

Designs application architecture, evaluates technology choices, defines integration patterns, and addresses scalability, reliability, and security requirements.

5. Java Developer vs Backend Developer: What Is the Difference?

A Java developer is a software developer who specializes in Java and its ecosystem. A backend developer is a broader role focused on server-side application development.

A backend developer may work with Java, Python, Node.js, PHP, .NET, or other technologies.

A Java developer typically specializes in:

  • Java programming.
  • JVM-based application development.
  • Java frameworks and libraries.
  • Java application performance.
  • Java-specific testing and deployment practices.

The roles can overlap significantly. In many companies, a Java developer is effectively a backend developer specializing in Java.

6. How Java Developers Work With Other Teams

Software development requires collaboration across multiple functions.

A Java developer commonly works with:

  • Frontend developers: To connect user interfaces with backend APIs.
  • UI/UX designers: To understand application workflows and requirements.
  • Database administrators: To coordinate database design and performance.
  • QA engineers: To identify and resolve application defects.
  • DevOps engineers: To automate builds, deployments, and infrastructure operations.
  • Product managers: To understand business requirements and prioritize features.
  • Technical architects: To align implementation with application architecture.

Effective collaboration helps reduce integration problems and improves delivery quality.

7. When Should a Company Hire a Java Developer?

Hiring a Java developer makes sense when an organization has specific technical requirements that align with Java's strengths.

Consider hiring one when:

  • Building enterprise backend applications.
  • Developing complex business systems.
  • Creating scalable REST APIs and microservices.
  • Modernizing existing Java applications.
  • Integrating databases and external services.
  • Maintaining applications built on Java technologies.
  • Developing transaction-heavy systems.
  • Supporting long-term enterprise software projects.

However, Java is not automatically the right choice for every project. CTOs should evaluate application requirements, existing infrastructure, team expertise, performance needs, and maintenance costs before selecting a technology.

8. How CTOs Should Evaluate a Java Developer

A strong hiring process should assess practical engineering ability rather than focusing only on theoretical knowledge.

Evaluate candidates across these areas:

  • Core Java: Object-oriented programming, collections, exception handling, concurrency, and JVM fundamentals.
  • Framework knowledge: Practical experience with Spring Boot, Spring MVC, and Spring Security.
  • Database skills: SQL, transaction management, indexing, and ORM technologies.
  • API development: REST design, validation, authentication, and error handling.
  • Testing: Unit testing, integration testing, and debugging.
  • Architecture: Understanding of layered architecture, microservices, and design patterns.
  • Security: Secure coding practices and vulnerability awareness.
  • Collaboration: Git workflows, code reviews, documentation, and teamwork.

Use practical assignments based on realistic business scenarios. For example, ask candidates to design a simple order-management API with database integration, validation, authentication, and automated tests.

This provides a better understanding of how they approach real development challenges.

9. Java Developer Performance: What Should CTOs Measure?

Developer performance should not be measured only by the number of lines of code or completed tasks.

Useful indicators include:

  • Quality and maintainability of delivered code.
  • Reliability of implemented features.
  • Defect rates and production issues.
  • Effectiveness of automated tests.
  • Ability to resolve technical problems.
  • Collaboration with other team members.
  • Contribution to documentation and knowledge sharing.
  • Delivery against agreed project objectives.

Use these indicators alongside team-level delivery metrics. Avoid encouraging rushed development at the expense of code quality and long-term maintainability.

10. Common Mistakes Companies Make When Hiring Java Developers

Companies can make costly hiring decisions when they focus too narrowly on technical keywords.

Avoid these common mistakes:

  • Hiring based only on years of Java experience.
  • Ignoring practical coding and problem-solving ability.
  • Overlooking database and API knowledge.
  • Not evaluating security awareness.
  • Confusing framework familiarity with architecture expertise.
  • Expecting junior developers to independently handle complex systems.
  • Ignoring communication and collaboration skills.
  • Failing to assess long-term maintenance capabilities.

A clear job description and structured technical evaluation help companies select developers who match their actual engineering needs.

Conclusion

Java developers play an important role in building and maintaining business applications. Their responsibilities extend beyond writing code to include backend development, API integration, database management, application security, testing, performance optimization, and ongoing maintenance.

For CTOs and engineering managers, understanding these responsibilities helps create appropriate job descriptions, evaluate candidates, and build effective development teams.

The right Java developer should combine strong programming fundamentals with practical problem-solving, security awareness, collaboration, and an understanding of business requirements.

Ultimately, successful Java development depends not just on the programming language, but on how effectively developers use it to deliver reliable, maintainable, and scalable software.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What does a Java developer do in a company?

A Java developer designs, develops, tests, and maintains software applications using Java. Responsibilities commonly include backend development, API creation, database integration, security implementation, debugging, and application maintenance.

2. Is Java mainly used for backend development?

Java is widely used for backend development, enterprise applications, APIs, and distributed systems. It can also be used in other environments, but its enterprise and server-side ecosystem is particularly well established.

3. Which framework should a Java developer know?

Spring Boot is one of the most widely used frameworks for modern Java backend development. Depending on the project, developers may also work with Spring MVC, Spring Security, Hibernate, Jakarta EE, and other libraries.

4. What skills should a Java developer have?

Important skills include Core Java, object-oriented programming, data structures, SQL, Spring Boot, REST APIs, database integration, testing, debugging, security practices, and Git.

5. What is the difference between a junior and senior Java developer?

Junior developers generally work on smaller tasks with guidance, while senior developers handle complex features, technical decisions, performance improvements, code reviews, and mentoring.

6. Do Java developers need to know SQL?

Yes. Most enterprise Java applications interact with databases. Developers should understand SQL queries, joins, indexes, transactions, and database performance fundamentals.

7. Is Spring Boot necessary for Java developers?

Spring Boot is not mandatory for every Java role, but it is highly valuable for developers working on modern backend applications and REST APIs. Many enterprise teams use it to simplify application configuration and development.

8. Can Java developers work on microservices?

Yes. Java developers commonly build microservices using Spring Boot and related technologies. They may also work with API gateways, messaging systems, containers, service discovery, and distributed monitoring tools.

9. What should a CTO ask during a Java developer interview?

CTOs should evaluate Core Java, Spring Boot, database knowledge, API design, testing, security, architecture, debugging, and practical problem-solving. Realistic coding exercises are useful for assessing implementation skills.

10. When should a company hire a Java developer?

A company should consider hiring a Java developer when it needs enterprise backend development, complex business applications, scalable APIs, Java application modernization, database integrations, or ongoing maintenance of existing Java systems.

title: Find It in Thirty Seconds: A Naming Scheme for Cross-Cloud Network Resources That Works During an Incident
description:
During an incident, nobody searches by architecture diagram. They search by name. A gateway called gw-prod-2 in one cloud, a route table called main in another, and a firewall policy copied from a tutorial in a third will each make sense to the person who created them and to nobody else on the call. By the time the team has opened three consoles and translated three local naming habits, the outage has had a head start.

Naming feels like housekeeping until the estate spans AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle at once. Then it becomes part of the incident response system itself. A good scheme lets any engineer, in any cloud, answer three questions from a name alone: what is this, where does it live, and what depends on it.

Why local naming habits break across clouds

Each cloud encourages a different default. Resource groups imply one grouping in Azure, projects imply another in Google Cloud, and accounts and VPCs carve AWS differently again. Teams working inside a single cloud lean on that surrounding context, so their names can be short and vague without immediate cost.

That context disappears at the cloud boundary. A private link, a transit hub, or a shared egress point belongs to two clouds at once, so neither side's local context explains it. The result is predictable: duplicate names for different things, different names for the same logical path, and no reliable way to search the whole estate for every piece of one flow.

The fix is not a longer name. It is a shared grammar that travels across providers.

Build the name from fixed fields, in a fixed order

A workable pattern uses the same fields, in the same order, for every network resource in every cloud:

  1. Purpose first. Start with what the resource does, not who made it: mesh, egress, inspect, dns, ai, or data. During an incident, people filter by function before anything else.
  2. Scope second. Name the boundary it serves: a region pair, a shared services scope, or a single environment such as prod, stage, or dev. Never rely on the account or subscription name to supply this, because shared resources sit above any one account.
  3. Endpoint or peer third, for connecting resources. A link name should say both sides, in a consistent order, for example by alphabetical cloud name, so the same link is never named differently from the other end.
  4. Sequence last, and only when needed. A number should distinguish parallel instances of the same thing, not encode history. If a name needs a date, a ticket number, or a person's initials to make sense, the scheme is already leaking.

Keep the character set boring: lowercase, hyphens, no underscores where a provider treats them inconsistently, and no abbreviations that only one team understands. Write the grammar down in one page, with two or three worked examples per resource type, and treat that page as part of the network design, not as wiki trivia.

Names carry identity, tags carry everything else

A common failure is stuffing the name with facts that change: owner, cost centre, project, review date. Names are hard to change safely once dependencies, alerts, and runbooks point at them, so they should hold only facts that stay true for the life of the resource.

Put the changeable facts in tags or labels, applied the same way in every cloud:

  • Owner: the team accountable for the resource, not an individual.
  • Flow or service: the named business or platform flow this resource serves, so every piece of one path can be pulled up together.
  • Criticality: whether an outage here is an incident or an inconvenience.
  • Review or expiry date: essential for temporary links, test peerings, and exception rules that otherwise become permanent by neglect.

The discipline that matters is consistency of keys. If one cloud says owner, another says Owner, and a third says team, estate wide reporting quietly fails. Define the key set once, in lowercase, and enforce it in the provisioning code for all clouds.

Enforce the scheme where resources are created

A naming standard that lives only in a document will drift within a quarter. Enforce it at creation time:

  • Provide the pattern as a module or template in the infrastructure code, so the easiest way to create a gateway, route table, or policy is the compliant way.
  • Validate names in the pipeline with a simple pattern check, and reject creations that fall outside it. A short delay at provisioning time is cheaper than a confusing estate at incident time.
  • Audit existing resources on a schedule and report drift by team, not as blame, but as a list to fix during normal work. Drift reports that only appear during audits tend to be ignored; small, regular reports get cleared.

Leave a deliberate escape hatch for genuine exceptions, recorded as a tag with a reason and a review date. A scheme with no exceptions invites quiet workarounds. A scheme with recorded exceptions stays honest.

Renaming an existing estate without breaking it

Most estates cannot be renamed in one pass, and should not try. Renaming a resource that alerts, dashboards, and firewall rules reference can cause the very outage the scheme is meant to shorten.

Instead, run both systems for a while. Add the compliant tags and a compliant alias or description to existing resources first, so search by the new grammar finds old resources immediately. Apply the naming pattern to everything new from a set date. Then rename in place only where the provider allows it without recreation, and schedule recreation based renames alongside other planned changes to that resource, never as a standalone project. Within a few normal change cycles, the estate converges without a flag day.

Measure convergence simply: the share of network resources that match the pattern, reported per cloud. When that number stalls, the remaining exceptions are usually the interesting ones, and they deserve a direct conversation rather than another reminder.

The design point

A naming scheme is not decoration. In a multi-cloud estate it is how an engineer finds the right gateway, route table, and policy in thirty seconds, under pressure, in a cloud they did not build. Purpose, scope, peer, and sequence in the name; owner, flow, criticality, and review date in the tags; enforcement in the provisioning path; and a patient migration for everything already running.

That kind of consistent platform engineering across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle estates is part of the work described at CloudVerg, where VergForge covers platform engineering and VergMesh covers multi-cloud networking, alongside zero-trust security through VergShield and SOC 2 readiness support.

The test of a scheme is simple. Hand a new engineer a name from a cloud they have never opened, and see whether they can say what it does, where it sits, and what it serves. If they can, the scheme is working.

title: StyleQoRA: Quality-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation for Few-Shot Multi-Style Editing
description:
arXiv:2511.11236v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In recent years, image editing has garnered growing attention. However, general image editing models often fail to produce satisfactory results when confronted with new styles. The challenge lies in how to effectively fine-tune general image editing models to new styles using only a limited amount of paired data and a minimum number of parameters. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel few-shot multi-style editing framework. For this task, we construct a benchmark dataset that encompasses five distinct styles. Correspondingly, we propose Quality-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation for few-shot multi-style editing (StyleQoRA). Our StyleQoRA can automatically determine the optimal rank for each layer through a novel approach that estimates the importance score of each single-rank component using an image quality metric. To balance specialization and knowledge sharing, we design a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LoRA with hybrid routing in our StyleQoRA, consisting of style-specific routing to prevent cross-style confusion and style-shared routing to capture common transformation patterns. Additionally, we explore the optimal location to insert LoRA within the Diffusion in Transformer (DiT) model and integrate adversarial learning and flow matching to guide the diffusion training process. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches with significantly fewer LoRA parameters. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/cao-cong/FSMSE.
