title: When the Cloud Goes Down: Why Infrastructure Reliability Matters More Than Ever
description:
We live in a world where almost everything depends on cloud infrastructure.

From social media platforms and online banking to e-commerce websites, AI applications, and enterprise software, millions of services rely on cloud computing every single day.

We often hear companies say that their applications are hosted on AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud. We assume that because these platforms are operated by major technology companies, everything will always work perfectly.

But what happens when the cloud goes down?

A single infrastructure failure can affect thousands of applications, interrupt business operations, prevent users from accessing important services, and cause significant financial losses.

This raises an important question:

Are our applications really reliable, or are we simply trusting the cloud to never fail?

  1. What Happens During a Cloud Outage?

A cloud outage occurs when a cloud service or part of its infrastructure becomes unavailable or experiences serious performance problems.

Some common causes include:

Network configuration errors.

Hardware failures.

Database disruptions.

Software bugs and deployment mistakes.

DNS resolution problems.

Power and cooling failures.

Unexpected traffic spikes.

Consider a simple example.

Imagine an online shopping application hosted on a cloud platform.

A customer opens the application, searches for a product, adds it to the cart, and tries to make a payment.

But suddenly, the cloud service responsible for handling application requests becomes unavailable.

What happens next?

Customers cannot access the website.

Payments may fail or remain pending.

Orders cannot be processed.

Customer support receives complaints.

The company may lose revenue.

The interesting thing is that the shopping application itself might not contain any bugs. The problem could be somewhere in the infrastructure supporting it.

  1. The Hidden Problem: Everything Depends on Everything

Modern applications are not usually built as one independent system.

They depend on multiple services working together.

For example, a typical web application might depend on:

Frontend application.

Backend API.

Database.

Authentication service.

Cloud storage.

DNS provider.

Payment gateway.

External APIs.

Even if seven services are working perfectly, one critical dependency failing can make the entire application unusable.

This is called a Single Point of Failure (SPOF).

For example:

A backend application might run across multiple servers, but if all servers depend on one database instance and that database fails, the application may still stop working.

Having multiple servers does not automatically mean having a highly available system.

  1. Why Cloud Providers Cannot Guarantee Zero Downtime

Cloud providers invest heavily in infrastructure reliability, monitoring, security, and disaster recovery.

However, no infrastructure is completely immune to failure.

Even major cloud platforms can experience:

Regional service disruptions.

Network failures.

Storage problems.

Configuration errors.

Service dependencies becoming unavailable.

The important lesson is that cloud computing does not eliminate infrastructure risk.

It changes how we manage that risk.

Instead of maintaining every physical server ourselves, we depend on cloud providers while remaining responsible for how our applications are designed and deployed.

Moving an application to the cloud is not the same as making it reliable.

  1. How Can We Build Applications That Survive Failures?

This is where good system architecture and DevOps practices become important.

Here are some approaches engineers can implement.

A. Multi-Region Deployment

Instead of running an application in only one geographical region, deploy it across multiple regions.

If one region becomes unavailable, traffic can potentially be redirected to another healthy region.

Example:

Primary deployment: Mumbai.

Secondary deployment: Singapore.

This can improve availability, although data replication, consistency, latency, and failover must also be carefully managed.

B. Database Backups and Replication

Your database contains some of the most important information in your application.

Regular backups help recover data after accidental deletion, corruption, or infrastructure failures.

Replication maintains copies of data across different database servers.

However, replication is not a complete replacement for backups. Accidental deletions and corrupted data can also be replicated.

A reliable strategy needs both.

C. Load Balancing

A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple application servers.

If one server becomes unhealthy, the load balancer can stop sending traffic to it and use healthy instances.

This helps prevent a single application server from becoming a bottleneck.

D. Monitoring and Alerting

Engineers should know when something goes wrong before customers start reporting problems.

Monitoring tools such as:

Prometheus

Grafana

AWS CloudWatch

Datadog

can help monitor CPU usage, memory, network traffic, application errors, and service availability.

Alerts help engineering teams respond quickly when problems occur.

E. Disaster Recovery Planning

A disaster recovery plan explains how an organization will restore its services after a major failure.

It should define two important concepts:

RTO (Recovery Time Objective): How quickly should the service be restored?

RPO (Recovery Point Objective): How much data loss, measured in time, can the business tolerate?

For example:

If a business has an RTO of 30 minutes, it aims to restore the affected service within 30 minutes.

If its RPO is 5 minutes, it aims to limit data loss to the equivalent of five minutes of data changes.

These targets should be tested rather than simply documented.

  1. Is Multi-Cloud the Solution?

One approach companies consider is multi-cloud architecture.

This means using more than one cloud provider, such as AWS and Google Cloud, instead of depending entirely on one provider.

Potential benefits:

Reduced dependence on one cloud provider.

Additional deployment options.

More flexibility in infrastructure decisions.

Alternative recovery environments.

But multi-cloud also introduces challenges:

Higher operational complexity.

More infrastructure costs.

Difficult data synchronization.

Different security and monitoring configurations.

More complicated deployment processes.

Therefore, multi-cloud is not automatically the best solution for every organization.

Sometimes, a well-designed architecture within a single cloud provider is more practical and reliable.

The goal should not be to use as many cloud providers as possible.

The goal should be to eliminate unnecessary dependencies and prepare for failures.

  1. What Can Developers Learn From This?

Infrastructure reliability is not only the responsibility of DevOps engineers.

Developers also need to think about failure while writing application code.

For example:

What happens if an external API does not respond?

What if a database connection is lost?

Can the application retry failed requests safely?

What happens if a user submits a payment twice?

Can the system handle sudden traffic increases?

Can the application continue operating if a non-critical service becomes unavailable?

Developers can implement retry mechanisms, timeouts, circuit breakers, graceful degradation, and idempotent operations to improve application resilience.

A good application is not one that assumes everything will work.

It is one that knows how to respond when something fails.

  1. My Final Thoughts

Cloud computing has transformed the technology industry.

It has made it easier for startups, developers, and enterprises to build and deploy applications without maintaining their own physical data centers.

But as our dependence on cloud infrastructure increases, reliability becomes even more important.

We should stop thinking only about how quickly we can deploy applications and start thinking about how well those applications can survive failures.

Because in real-world software engineering, failures are not always avoidable.

What matters is how prepared your system is when they happen.

Let's Discuss!

I would love to hear what other developers and DevOps engineers think.

Should companies depend entirely on a single cloud provider?

Is multi-cloud architecture worth the additional cost and complexity?

Should every production application have a disaster recovery strategy?

What is more important: preventing failures or recovering quickly from them?

Share your experiences and thoughts in the comments!

title: MosaicLeaks: Privacy Risks in Querying-in-the-Open for Deep Research Agents
description:
arXiv:2605.30727v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep research agents increasingly combine private local documents with external tools like web retrieval, creating a privacy risk: an agent's external queries may leak sensitive information from its local context. This risk is amplified by the mosaic effect, where individual queries may appear harmless but become revealing in aggregate. We introduce MosaicLeaks, a benchmark of 1,001 multi-hop deep research tasks that chain private enterprise documents and a public web corpus, forcing agents to make external queries that depend on local information. We evaluate leakage with an adversary LLM that observes only the agent's external queries and attempts to infer private information at three levels: the agent's research intent, answers to specific private questions and verifiable claims about the enterprise documents. We find that models across families and sizes frequently leak at all three levels, that zero-shot privacy prompting has inconsistent effects across models and that reinforcement learning for task performance alone worsens leakage. To address this, we propose Privacy-Aware Deep Research (PA-DR), an RL framework that combines situational rewards for task success with a learned privacy classifier to provide dense credit assignment over both per-query and mosaic-level leakage. Training Qwen3-4B-Instruct with PA-DR improves accuracy from 48.7% to 58.1% and reduces Privacy Leakage from 34.0% to 6.5%.

title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
description:
arXiv:2611.23925v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

title: What happens when an offline POS sale syncs twice?
description:
A cashier completes a sale while the connection is down. Later, the server saves it, but the response never reaches the device. The app retries. Without a way to recognize the original request, the second attempt can create a second receipt and deduct stock again.

Give each sale a stable ID

Generate a client sale ID when checkout starts. Save it with the completed sale and the pending sync entry in one local transaction. Keep that same ID through retries and app restarts.

Make the server retry-safe

Use a unique database constraint scoped to the store and client sale ID. Commit the sale and its stock movements together. When the same ID arrives with the same payload, return the existing receipt. If the payload differs, return a conflict so the app can surface it for review.

Test the lost acknowledgement

  1. Complete a sale offline.
  2. Reconnect and let the server commit it, then simulate a dropped response.
  3. Restart the app and retry the pending sale.
  4. Verify that the receipt number is unchanged and inventory moved exactly once.

Treat a timeout as an unknown outcome. A stable ID gives the client a way to recover the receipt without guessing what happened.

— Programmings 360

title: Designing a city game for people who will only give it three minutes
description:
A lot of people will try a city scavenger hunt for about three minutes. Not because they hate it - because they are standing in a street with a coffee in one hand, a phone in the other, and somewhere else to be.

Design for those three minutes and the rest follows. Here is what we have learned about them.

The first glance is doing most of the work

When somebody opens the app, they are not reading. They are glancing at a phone screen while walking, in poor light, possibly with a backpack in the way.

That means the very first thing on the screen has to say what is happening. Not a slogan, not a logo animation - the actual instruction for the first stop. If the first thing they see is an explanation, they will read it later, and later never comes.

The same reasoning applies to the first photograph. It has to look like something they might find, because the first stop sets the expectation for every stop after it. Give somebody an opening shot that is unusual, and they will spend the rest of the hunt looking for unusual things that are not there.

The first "not quite" is the tone

The moment that matters most is the first time the app says the photograph is not right. It is going to happen, and it will happen within the first two minutes for most people.

If that message feels like a failure, the hunt is over. If it feels like a nudge - look again, you are close - then it becomes the normal texture of playing. The person is not failing a test, they are looking at a street and being asked to look slightly harder, and the wording has to say that.

This is the same reason the stops are written the way they are. "The blue door with the number on it" gives you something to look for. "The building" does not.

One stop at a time

It is tempting to show the whole route on a map, every stop at once, so the player can see the shape of the thing.

Resist it. A list of eight pins on a map tells somebody they have eight errands. What we want is a person walking and looking, which is a completely different posture, and the moment you show the whole route you have turned a walk into a checklist. Keep the route present but keep the next stop the loudest thing on the screen.

Three minutes in, they should be walking

Here is the test we apply: three minutes after opening the app, is somebody actually moving through a street, and are they looking at things rather than at the phone?

If the answer is no, the problem is almost always that the first stop is too far away, or too ambiguous to attempt, or too easy to pass by. Fix the first stop and the first three minutes take care of themselves.

We wrote up the flow in more detail, with screenshots, on our docs page: pinghunt.com/docs. And the short version of how it works is here: pinghunt.com/how-it-works.

The general rule, if you are building something like this: the first thirty seconds decide whether the next thirty minutes exist. Spend them accordingly.

title: Measuring “haunted” agent behavior: what two weeks of controlled experiments actually showed
description:
I’ve been focused on personal development for the past couple of months and haven’t posted much. Starting again.

Over two weeks I ran a small set of controlled experiments to see whether I could reproduce the kinds of agent failures that look “haunted” from the outside — unprompted actions, ignored constraints, self-contradictory behavior.

I treated it as a measurement exercise rather than a demo:

  • Pre-registered designs and decision rules
  • Positive controls in every experiment
  • Fake tools only (no real accounts or side effects)
  • Explicit limits on what any result can claim

What I tested

G1 – Ambiguous tool output
Gave agents odd or incomplete tool results with no instruction to act.

Counted destructive actions.

Result: Almost no destructive behavior. The main signal was extra diagnostic reads.

Task type (summarize vs operate) appeared to be a stronger gate than the ambiguous signals themselves.

I parked further expansion per the pre-registered rule.

H1 – Context compression and forgotten rules (first design)
Hypothesis: when an agent compacts context, an early user constraint (“don’t delete until I confirm”) might be dropped.

First design failed to test the hypothesis at all.

The models finished the task in 3–4 steps by reading everything in parallel, so compression never triggered (0/19).

Positive control (no rule) did produce deletions.

I closed this design as “not testable this way” instead of trying to rescue it after seeing data.

H1 – Second design (scripted long history)
Forced a single summary compression on a long scripted history (~21–22k tokens) and measured whether the model still respected the rule.

Result (gpt-4.1-mini):

  • No rule (positive control): 16/20 deleted
  • Full history + rule: 0/20
  • Summarized (two different prompts) + rule: 0/20

No effect observed. Floor effect is real here — with a 0/20 baseline I would have needed multiple violations to detect anything meaningful.

What actually broke (my harness, not the agents)

These are more useful than the hypothesis results:

  • A test accidentally issued 315 paid calls ($0.81). Paid calls are now refused by default.
  • I initially counted read-only queries as mutations.
  • One task wording made a model invent a non-existent path.
  • A thinking-enabled model burned its entire output budget on reasoning and returned empty summaries (16/16 in one pilot). The pre-registered gate stopped that arm.
  • Compaction trigger lagged one step behind the context it was supposed to watch.
  • One decision rule had a logic error (treated low baseline as a problem). Fixed before use.

Every one of these was caught by a pilot or positive control before the main runs.

Limits

  • Fake tools only
  • Small models
  • Single task family
  • One successful model on the second H1 design
  • 4 repeats per history are not independent
  • Keyword checks for “rule survived” missed most paraphrases

I am not claiming anything about real products or real incidents.

These are observations inside one harness with explicit controls and limits.

I’ll publish the more interesting individual failure modes separately.

Happy to share the pre-registration tags and harness details if useful.

title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23810v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
description:
arXiv:2611.24969v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

title: Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI Compromise: What Supply-Chain Attacks Teach About Agent Dependency Security
description:
Microsoft's Agent Framework package on PyPI was compromised on November 17, 2026. Two malicious versions (1.26.1 and 1.26.2) shipped with credential-stealing code that executed during Python startup, before any explicit import. The framework sees roughly 200,000 monthly downloads and is used to build and coordinate AI agents in production workflows.

This is the first major supply-chain attack targeting an agent orchestration framework. The incident exposes the security boundary between agent code and its runtime dependencies, and the verification gaps that exist when you run pip install in a production environment.

Attack Surface: PyPI as Agent Infrastructure

Agent frameworks sit at a privileged layer. They orchestrate tool calls, manage state, and handle credentials for external APIs. When you install an agent framework from PyPI, you're trusting that package with:

  • Cloud provider credentials (AWS, Azure, GCP)
  • API keys for LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere)
  • Database connection strings
  • Internal service tokens

The compromised Agent Framework versions exploited this trust by injecting a credential stealer into the package's __init__.py file. The malware executed automatically during Python's import machinery, even if the developer never explicitly imported the framework in their code.

Execution Flow of the Compromise

  1. Developer runs pip install agent-framework==1.26.1
  2. PyPI serves the compromised package
  3. Python's site-packages directory receives the malicious code
  4. On next Python startup, the malicious __init__.py executes
  5. Credential stealer scans environment variables, config files, and cloud credential stores
  6. Exfiltration occurs before the agent framework is ever imported

The attack bypassed the usual "import equals trust" model. The malicious code ran as part of Python's startup sequence, not as a result of explicit developer action.

Dependency Verification Gaps

PyPI has no mandatory code-signing or provenance verification. When you install a package, you're trusting:

  • The package name matches the intended project
  • The maintainer account hasn't been compromised
  • The package contents match the source repository
  • No malicious code was injected during the build or upload process

None of these assumptions are verified by default. The compromised Agent Framework versions retained their dependency on the legitimate agent-framework-core package, allowing the framework to function normally while the malware operated in the background.

What PyPI Does Not Verify

Security Control Current State Impact on Agent Frameworks
Code signing Optional, rarely enforced No cryptographic proof of author identity
Provenance attestation Not required Can't verify package was built from declared source
Dependency pinning Developer responsibility Transitive dependencies can introduce malicious code
Runtime sandboxing Not provided Packages execute with full Python interpreter privileges
Credential access control Not scoped Packages can access any credential the Python process can reach

Security Boundaries in Agent Orchestration

Agent frameworks typically require elevated permissions because they need to:

  • Execute arbitrary tool calls (API requests, database queries, file operations)
  • Manage long-running state across multiple LLM calls
  • Handle retries and error recovery with access to sensitive context
  • Coordinate between multiple agents with different permission scopes

When you install an agent framework as a PyPI dependency, you're collapsing the security boundary between orchestration logic and runtime execution. The framework code runs in the same process as your application, with the same permissions. A compromised package can access everything.

Where the Boundary Should Sit

In a secure agent architecture, the security boundary should exist between:

  1. Orchestration layer: Manages agent state, routes requests, enforces policies
  2. Execution layer: Runs tool calls in isolated environments with scoped credentials
  3. Credential layer: Provides time-limited, least-privilege tokens to execution environments

When you install an agent framework from PyPI, all three layers collapse into a single process with a single set of credentials. A compromised package can access everything.

Mitigation Strategies

Package Verification

Use package verification tools that check cryptographic signatures and provenance:

# requirements.txt with hash verification
agent-framework==1.26.0 \
    --hash=sha256:abcd1234...

# Or use pip-audit to scan for known vulnerabilities
pip-audit --requirement requirements.txt

This doesn't prevent zero-day supply-chain attacks, but it ensures you're installing the exact package version you intended.

Dependency Pinning and Vendoring

Pin all dependencies, including transitive ones, and vendor critical packages:

# Generate a complete lock file
pip-compile requirements.in --generate-hashes

# Vendor the agent framework
pip download agent-framework==1.26.0 --dest ./vendor
pip install --no-index --find-links ./vendor agent-framework

Vendoring gives you a local copy to audit before deployment. It also protects against package removal or compromise after your initial install.

Runtime Isolation

Run agent frameworks in isolated environments with scoped credentials:

import subprocess
import os

# Insecure pattern: Framework runs in main process with full credentials
# from agent_framework import Agent
# agent = Agent()  # Has access to all environment variables

# Recommended pattern: Framework runs in subprocess with scoped credentials
scoped_token = os.environ.get('SCOPED_OPENAI_KEY', '')
result = subprocess.run(
    ['python', '-m', 'agent_framework', 'run', '--task', 'task_123'],
    env={'OPENAI_API_KEY': scoped_token, 'PATH': os.environ['PATH']},
    capture_output=True,
    text=True
)
print(result.stdout)

This limits the blast radius if the framework is compromised. The subprocess can only access the credentials you explicitly pass to it.

Credential Scoping

Use short-lived, least-privilege credentials for agent execution:

  • AWS: Use STS AssumeRole with session policies
  • Azure: Use managed identities with time-limited tokens
  • GCP: Use Workload Identity with scoped service accounts
  • API keys: Generate per-task tokens with limited permissions

Never pass long-lived credentials to agent frameworks. If the framework is compromised, the attacker gets only the scoped token, not your root credentials.

Observability and Detection

Monitor for signs of supply-chain compromise:

  • Unexpected network connections: Agent frameworks should only connect to declared endpoints
  • Credential access patterns: Alert on reads from credential stores during package installation
  • File system modifications: Watch for writes to unexpected locations during pip install
  • Process spawning: Flag subprocesses launched during package installation

Use runtime security tools to detect these behaviors. For example, monitor Python processes for unexpected network activity:

# Example detection pattern using psutil
import psutil

def detect_suspicious_connections():
    for proc in psutil.process_iter(['pid', 'name', 'connections']):
        if proc.info['name'] == 'python':
            for conn in proc.info['connections'] or []:
                if conn.status == 'ESTABLISHED':
                    # Alert if connection is not to known endpoints
                    allowed_hosts = ['api.openai.com', 'api.anthropic.com']
                    if conn.raddr.ip not in allowed_hosts:
                        print(f"Suspicious connection: {proc.info['pid']} -> {conn.raddr}")

Technical Verdict

Use agent frameworks from PyPI when:

  • You're prototyping and can tolerate the risk
  • You vendor and audit all dependencies before production deployment
  • You run frameworks in isolated environments with scoped credentials
  • You have runtime monitoring to detect unexpected behavior

Avoid PyPI dependencies for agent frameworks when:

  • You're handling high-value credentials or sensitive data
  • You can't vendor and audit dependencies
  • You're running in a shared environment with other workloads
  • You lack runtime isolation and monitoring capabilities

The Microsoft Agent Framework compromise demonstrates that agent infrastructure is now a high-value supply-chain target. The attack surface is larger than traditional libraries because agent frameworks require elevated permissions by design. Treat agent framework dependencies as privileged code and apply the same security controls you'd use for authentication libraries or database drivers.

Source Links

  • Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI package compromised to steal credentials
  • Hacker News Discussion

title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
description:
arXiv:2611.25004v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback
description:
arXiv:2611.25005v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.

title: A Known-Data Check of Red and White Wine Domain Transfer
description:
A known-data check of red and white wine domain transfer

A model that looks useful on its own training source can still make worse per-record choices than a constant once it crosses to another source. I used the UCI Wine Quality files to make that gap visible with two small regressors, one trained on red wine records and one on white. The target is the sensory quality score from the source. This article records the saved run from November 4, 2026; publishing the article adds no new training.

The source files contain 1,599 red rows and 4,898 white rows, 6,497 in total. The UCI page summary of 4,898 instances describes white only. Each row has 11 physicochemical inputs and an ordered quality score from 0 to 10. The source names state that the score is the median of at least three expert evaluations. Individual chemistry units are not supplied in the files, so I keep the numeric scales as they appear. Treating that ordered score as an equally spaced number for MAE and MSE is a modeling assumption, not evidence that the score sits on an interval scale.

Before training, I assigned each record a role using only its 11 canonical feature values. I decimal-normalized the tokens, joined them, hashed the prefixed key with SHA-256, and used the integer modulo 10. Values 0 through 5 became a fit pool, 6 and 7 became a validation pool, and 8 and 9 became test. The same feature vector receives the same initial role in both colors, and quality and color are excluded from the key. That produces 5,318 unique groups among 6,497 rows and 1,179 duplicate-excess rows. Two exact input vectors appear in both colors. Exact vector identity is a duplicate control, not a producer or subject ID, and it does not prove that repeated rows are independent samples. Duplicate rows still enter the batch arithmetic, so they contribute repeated weight. Whether those repeated rows are ultimately independent measurements does not change that computational weighting.

The red source had 923 fit-pool rows, 335 validation-pool rows, and 341 test rows. The white source had 2,939 fit-pool candidates and 977 validation-pool candidates. I sampled 923 fit rows and 335 validation rows from white, leaving 2,016 fit candidates and 642 validation candidates unused. Tests were never downsampled, so the frozen test set is the full 341 red rows plus 982 white rows, 1,323 cases in total. Those same 1,323 cases are reused across three seeds in the paired comparison below.

Each source fit has 923 rows, 100 epochs, and batch size 64, giving 1,500 updates and 92,300 row visits per fit. The network is 11 inputs, 24 tanh units, and one linear output, 313 parameters. Seeds 17, 41, and 73 run for each source, giving six saved models. One initial parameter set per seed is shared between the red and white fits, three sets total; each set holds W1, b1, W2, and b2. Because each domain has its own train-only normalizer, a shared set does not necessarily define the same function on raw input scale. Validation and test rows never enter the normalizer statistics.

Checkpoint selection used each model's own 335-row validation set. I picked the earliest epoch with the strictly lowest MAE among all 100 checkpoints. Selected epochs were 31, 78, and 31 for red, and 52, 39, and 39 for white. Cross-domain evaluation never used the target color's validation set. An in-domain model's own source is also its target source, so that model did see the target-source validation set.

The aggregate MAE numbers are arithmetic means over three seeds, not ensembles and not confidence intervals.

Test domain Red-trained White-trained Red fit mean White fit mean Cases per seed
Red 0.476144 0.746975 0.647566 0.636872 341
White 0.649987 0.586350 0.748883 0.674610 982

The source-matched model has the lower mean error on both targets. The negative result sits inside that summary: the white-trained network is worse on the red holdout than its own fit-mean constant, 0.746975 versus 0.636872. Per seed, the three white-to-red MAE values are 0.657548, 0.732750, and 0.850627, each above that constant. The red-trained network beats the red constant on red, and the white-trained network beats the white constant on white. This is a specific cross-domain failure, not a statement that every neural model loses to every constant. The numbers also do not say that the white-trained model mostly emits its white training center, or that it learned no joint relation. They record that the aggregate error is worse than ignoring the inputs and returning the white fit mean.

The per-case view shows how much an average hides. Across 3,969 same-seed, same-case paired comparisons, the in-domain model had the larger absolute error in 1,585 pairs. By target domain, 321 of 1,023 red-target pairs and 1,264 of 2,946 white-target pairs went against the in-domain model. A negative value in the paired difference means the in-domain model was worse. These counts reuse the same 1,323 cases over three seeds. They are descriptive repetition, not 3,969 independent cases, and I did not run a significance test. The target-domain split is reported, but the denominators differ, and the repeated cases mean I cannot infer from those totals that one target domain explains the failures.

The fixed default case is red:0002. I selected it before any current-model test prediction as the lowest red test source ordinal. At seed 17, the red-trained model predicts 5.365765 and the white-trained model predicts 4.872778 for a true score of 5. The cross-domain model has the smaller error. I keep this case as a negative, not as a selected winner.

Figure: the actual study.png at 2015 by 1271 pixels, with all 600 own-source validation MAE points, the four seed-mean MAE bars and analytic fit-mean diamonds, and the full paired difference distributions. It is a descriptive known-data contrast, not a training-loss plot, screenshot, or causal diagram.

Equal rows, equal updates, and paired initial sets are computation controls. They do not isolate a source shift. The red fit pool contains all 923 red fit candidates. The white fit pool samples 923 from 2,939 white fit candidates. Train-only normalizers differ between the two pools. Feature support, quality distribution, own validation selection, and duplicate weighting differ at the same time. The source label is not the only thing that changes. A difference between the two training-pool feature means only shows that the pools differ. It does not prove that the white-to-red failure comes from a wrong center, a missing chemical relation, or another single mechanism.

Before assigning a mechanism, I would need separate runs that actually change the sampled training records under stated controls. One candidate would match the two pools by quality counts and overlapping feature support, keeping each domain's own normalizer and validation split, then check whether the white-to-red network still loses to its fit mean. Another would reweight duplicate rows down and see whether the headline errors move. Neither is part of this frozen run. The current result is a known-data descriptive comparison with the failures retained.

The fixed repository includes PROTOCOL.md, evaluation-001/results.json, and evaluation-001/paired-comparisons.json. Downloading only the static app page does not give you the complete set of research files. From the project root, after obtaining the fixed checkout at commit 2431a336acc4cef56f12b22a90bc77baed8c6863, the following Python 3 standard-library command recounts the headline numbers and the worse-pair split. It opens the two JSON files read-only. It does not download anything, install anything, fit anything, or write anything.

python3 - <<'PY'
import json, collections
r = json.load(open("evaluation-001/results.json"))
p = json.load(open("evaluation-001/paired-comparisons.json"))
for d in r["descriptive_seed_metric_means_not_ensemble"]:
    print("neural", d["target_domain"], d["trained_domain"], "mae", d["arithmetic_mean_seed_mae"])
for b in r["all_mean_baselines"]:
    print("mean", b["trained_domain"], "->", b["target_domain"], "mae", b["mae"])
c = collections.Counter((x["target_domain"], x["in_domain_worse"]) for x in p)
print("worse_split", "red", c[("red", True)], "white", c[("white", True)], "total", r["in_domain_worse_pairs"])
print("reuse_check", r["paired_rows"], "==", 3, "*", r["test_cases"], ":", r["paired_rows"] == 3 * r["test_cases"])
PY

The official space and the static demo load six saved forward models and two analytic constants. The demo is static, with no external API or browser storage. Edits entered in the page live in browser memory, so a refresh discards them. A deliberate export writes all eleven inputs, the six model outputs, the two mean baselines, normalizers, source matches, and provenance to a local JSON file; the file stays where the reader saves it. I state this so no one trusts unsaved work to survive. Input range checks are marginal bounds, not joint chemical support. An exact feature-key match is numeric consistency, not measurement provenance. Outputs are unrounded and unclipped, with no calibrated uncertainty or probability.

The original red and white CSV files and the derived weights, figures, and results retain attribution to Cortez, Cerdeira, Almeida, Matos, and Reis, UCI 186, DOI 10.24432/C56S3T, under CC BY 4.0. My code and documents are Apache 2.0. That split is recorded in NOTICE and LICENSES.md. The 2009 paper is cited as metadata; I did not read its full text, did not reproduce its model or scores, and did not use its results as my own. No tasting, health, certification, or future-vintage claim follows from this experiment.

title: Accord: Universal Online Metric Localization and Dense Mapping from one Camera and an IMU
description:
arXiv:2611.25279v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community

title: Active Learning For Contextual Linear Optimization: A Margin-Based Approach
description:
arXiv:2305.06584v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We develop the first active learning method for contextual linear optimization. Specifically, we introduce a label acquisition algorithm that sequentially decides whether to request the ``labels'' of feature samples arriving in an unlabeled data stream, where the labels correspond to the objective coefficients in the linear optimization problem. The label acquisition rule is guided by the decision loss induced by the predicted coefficients, known as the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss. Motivated by the structure of the SPO loss, our algorithm uses the distance to degeneracy as a margin-based criterion for label acquisition. The algorithm processes incoming feature samples in batches, acquiring within each batch only the labels of samples whose distance to degeneracy falls below a rejection threshold. We derive non-asymptotic bounds for direct SPO-loss minimization over a general hypothesis class and for surrogate-loss minimization over a linear prediction class. These bounds demonstrate that, under certain natural conditions, our margin-based active learning algorithm requires fewer labels than supervised learning to achieve the same excess population risk for the chosen training loss. We provide concrete examples in which these conditions hold under continuous (sub-)Gaussian noise. Finally, we present numerical evidence demonstrating the practical value of our approach in applications such as personalized pricing and shortest-path problems.

title: Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
description:
arXiv:2611.25191v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: LLM judges serve as rewards where no answer key exists, in the hope that their knowledge passes to the trained model. In 814 RL runs that teach 7-8B models to answer closed-book questions or abstain, we ask what passes. What a grader knows about single answers stays home. A wrong answer that a judge rewards is memorised for that one question. A model trained with the answer key, or with a far stronger judge, chooses which new questions to answer no better than the untrained model does by sampling 32 answers and abstaining where they disagree; the grader's knowledge adds about one corrected answer per hundred questions. What a grader believes about a kind of question travels. A judge that rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal. Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves the refusal from 5% to 90%, even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key; at that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals. The capitals are not forgotten: with "I don't know" blocked, the model answers 94% of them correctly. The grader therefore needs no knowledge of its own: rewarding the model for giving the answer that most of its own untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, earns the answer key's reward and keeps the category.

title: Making a Trino lake as fast as a SQL database
description:
Photo by Joshua Kettle on Unsplash

Moving analytics data from a SQL database to a lake usually comes with a quiet assumption: you will pay for cheap, unlimited storage with slower answers. I tested that assumption end to end, with an AI agent that answers business questions over synced SaaS data, and the result surprised me. With four fixes, full answers on the lake took the same time as on the database. The biggest fix had nothing to do with Trino's speed.

The setup, in one breath

The data is CRM and accounting records, copied by a managed ingestion service into Iceberg tables on Azure storage (ADLS). Iceberg is an open table format: plain files plus a small "description file" per table saying which files make up the table right now. A hosted Polaris catalog keeps the list of where each table's description lives. Trino is the query engine that reads all of it. The comparison point is the same data in Azure SQL.

The agent doesn't run one query per answer. It runs five to seven: it lists tables, reads column names, samples a few values, then asks the real question. That detail turned out to matter more than anything else.

Out of the box, the lake lost badly

A small question touching four tables took about 2 seconds in Trino, against about 0.1 seconds in the database. A big accounting question that combines 25 tables took about 30 seconds, against about 6.

I expected the time to be in reading data. It wasn't. Trino splits its own work into stages, and most of the time sat in "analysis", the step before any data is read.

The catalog was the bottleneck

Trino asks the catalog about every table, in every query, with no memory between queries. Each ask is a network call. Our catalog sat in one region and the engine in another, so each lookup cost about half a second. Twenty-five tables, twenty-five calls, about 13 seconds of waiting before the engine did anything useful.

Think of a delivery driver who phones head office for the address of every stop, every single day, even though the addresses never changed.

The fix was to give the driver a notebook. Trino supports an Iceberg catalog stored in a plain Postgres database (the JDBC catalog in Trino's docs). "Registering" a table there is just writing one row: its name and the location of its current description file, which I read from the table's own $metadata_log_entries. No data is copied. Nothing is written to the lake.


Before and after: the engine stops phoning the catalog and reads a local address book instead.

The result was the clearest number of the whole project. Analysis on the 25-table question went from about 13 seconds to 0.8. On the small question it went from 1.5 seconds to 0.17. Answers were byte-for-byte identical.

The price is a job you now own. Every time new data lands, the notebook has to be updated with each table's new description file, or the engine reads yesterday's data.

What didn't help

A newer Trino setting, snapshot-loading-mode=REFS, asks the catalog for a shorter answer that leaves out old table history. Someone on another catalog measured a 6x faster lookup with it, but their tables had about 9,000 old versions. Mine had one. I tried it anyway: no gain. The time was the trip, not the size of the reply.

Trino's metadata cache was already on, and it caches description files, not the catalog lookup. Rewriting or compacting the source tables was off the table too, since the ingestion service owns them and would undo it on the next sync.

Precompute the heavy questions

Removing the lookups took the big accounting question from about 30 seconds to about 17. What remained was real work: about 8 seconds planning a query with hundreds of stages, and about 8 seconds running it.

So I stopped doing that work at question time. The accounting "model" (the recipe that turns 25 raw tables into one clean ledger) runs once after each sync and saves its result as a single table. A question like "income in March" then reads one small table instead of rebuilding the ledger.


The heavy combining happens once per data refresh, not once per question.

I tried the ready table in three places: in Trino's memory, in Postgres, and as an Iceberg table on the lake itself. All three answered in about 0.15 to 0.3 seconds, against about 6 seconds in the SQL database. Writing it to the lake took about 30 seconds. Writing it into Postgres took about 90, because rows go in one by one.

That last point matters if you worried, like I did, that precompute means "we're back to a database." The data stays in the lake. Postgres only holds pointers, and you can rebuild it from the catalog at any time.

Distance, twice

The engine first ran on a VM on the US west coast, with the data on the east coast. A single round trip across the country took 65 to 100 milliseconds, and each catalog call needed several. Moving the engine east cut a call from 0.21 to 0.40 seconds down to 0.06 to 0.16, and small questions got about twice as fast again, landing around half a second.

Then I made the mistake that taught me the most. I timed full answers with the app on my laptop.

Full answers on the lake averaged 53.7 seconds. On the SQL database, 44.3. Same correct answers, nine seconds worse. The engine was fine; the app was talking to it five to seven times per answer, across the internet, several round trips each time.

When I ran the app on the same machine as the engine, the lake averaged 42.5 seconds. Inside the noise of the database's 44.3.


Same engine, same questions. Only the app's location changed.

About 40 seconds of every answer is the AI thinking, on either system, and it swings by five seconds from run to run. Per-query benchmarks hid that. If you are timing a database for an agent, time the whole answer, and put the app where it will live in production.

The cache that worked and didn't matter

An answer cache in the app, keyed on the exact SQL text, did what it promised. A repeated 18-second question came back in under a millisecond, and by the third question in a session only the real query reached the engine.

It saved about a second per answer. I've seen caching cut query latency by 60% on a high-traffic payment system before, where queries were the whole cost. Here the AI is the whole cost, so the same trick barely registered. Worth keeping, not worth leading with.

Two other engines

StarRocks read the same catalog and the same storage with the VM's managed identity (the machine's own Azure login, no passwords) on the first try (its Azure auth docs cover it), and gave identical answers. With none of the fixes above, small questions took 0.4 to 0.7 seconds and the big accounting questions 7 to 10. That is faster than plain Trino out of the box, likely because it keeps table information between queries and shares repeated query blocks instead of planning each copy. The catch is a different SQL dialect, so every query the agent writes would need porting.

Apache Doris connected to the catalog and listed every table, then failed on the first read. Its Azure storage docs list account-key access only, and I wasn't going to hand a query engine a key to the whole storage account. If you use managed identities on Azure, check this before anything else.

What I'd tell you before you start

Profile the step before the data. On a lake, the slow part is often looking things up, not reading. Keep a local copy of the catalog's answers, precompute the few heavy models, and put the engine and the app next to the data. Then time whole answers, not queries.

The lake was never slow. It was asking for directions.

title: AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner Badge - How to Earn It
description:
A beginner's guide to earning the free AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner badge on AWS Skill Builder, with steps, benefits and next steps.

tags: aws, cloud, beginners, learning

vishalcloudjourney

Learning cloud from videos and notes alone can feel dry. AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner on AWS Skill Builder takes a different route: you learn AWS by playing a game. I earned the AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner (Trained) badge, and in this post I'll cover what it is, how to earn it, its advantages, and how it can help you grow.

What Is AWS Cloud Quest?

AWS Cloud Quest is a 3D, role-based learning game on AWS Skill Builder. You play through a virtual city and solve problems using AWS services. Each assignment teaches a concept and then asks you to apply it.

The Cloud Practitioner role is aimed at beginners and needs no prior cloud experience.

Topics You Practice

The badge grounds you in foundational concepts like compute, storage, networking and security. Assignments include areas such as core security concepts, file systems in the cloud, a first NoSQL database, auto-healing and scaling applications, and highly available web applications. Services you work with include EC2, S3, VPC, RDS, DynamoDB and IAM.

How to Earn the Badge

Step 1: Create a free account. Register for a free AWS Skill Builder account. You may also be asked to set up an AWS Builder ID.

Step 2: Find Cloud Quest. Go to Skill Builder, search for Cloud Quest, and open AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner.

Step 3: Choose the free role. During the onboarding tutorial you pick a role. Choose Cloud Practitioner, which is the free one.

Step 4: Complete every assignment. The Cloud Practitioner course has 12 free hands-on assignments. To earn the official badge, you complete every assignment in the role.

Step 5: Claim and share your badge. Badges are shareable on Credly and on your Skills Profile. Add yours to LinkedIn, your resume and your portfolio.

Good to Know

  • It's free. Cloud Practitioner is one of the free roles.
  • The labs are real AWS work. They are done in the AWS console, so you build real things.
  • It is a training badge, not the certification. The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification requires passing the official exam.
  • Requirements can change. Check the official Skill Builder page for the latest details.

My badge: View on Credly

Advantages of Earning This Badge

  1. Hands-on experience, not just theory. You practice building real solutions instead of only watching videos.
  2. Free to start. Anyone can begin without paying.
  3. Beginner-friendly. Each assignment explains the concept first, then lets you apply it.
  4. Official, shareable proof. Easy to add to LinkedIn, your resume and your portfolio.
  5. Builds core knowledge. You touch compute, storage, networking, databases, security and scaling, the foundations of almost every AWS role.
  6. Supports certification prep. It prepares you for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner exam.
  7. Keeps you motivated. The game format makes it easier to stay consistent than passive learning.
  8. Stands out as a student. It shows initiative and real learning, which helps with internships, cloud clubs and community programs.

How This Badge Helps You Grow

A badge is a starting point, not the finish line.

  1. Build confidence. Finishing real labs proves to yourself that you can work with AWS.
  2. Take the next learning steps. Try the AWS Cloud Essentials Knowledge Badge, the free AWS Cloud Quest: Generative AI Practitioner, and the AWS Well-Architected basics.
  3. Prepare for certification. Use the badge as a base, then move on to exam prep for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02).
  4. Create your own projects. Set up a billing alarm, host a static site on S3, or launch an EC2 instance, then write about it.
  5. Share your journey. Posting on AWS Builder Center, dev.to and LinkedIn builds your portfolio and helps other beginners.
  6. Join the community. Engage with AWS communities, student groups and programs like AWS Community Builders.
  7. Grow toward a career. These skills lead naturally toward roles like cloud support, DevOps and cloud engineering, one step at a time.

Tips for Beginners

  • Don't rush. Read each explanation before starting the lab.
  • Take short notes on each service as you meet it.
  • Retry a lab if you get stuck. Repetition helps.
  • Connect each service to a real example, like S3 for file storage.
  • Pair it with the official Cloud Practitioner Essentials course for a fuller picture.

Key Takeaways

  • Cloud Quest turns AWS learning into a hands-on game, and the Cloud Practitioner role is free.
  • Complete all assignments to earn an official, shareable badge.
  • The badge shows hands-on training, and it is a strong first step toward the certification.
  • Badge by badge, lab by lab, that's how you grow. Keep learning, keep building, keep sharing.

  • dev.to: @vishal_patil_aws
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
  • Portfolio: vishalpatil-devops-aws.github.io/portfolio

title: Anthropic estreia na Nasdaq e fecha avaliada em US$ 1,76 trilhão
description:
Estreia termina acima do preço da oferta

Segundo a AOL, a Anthropic estreou na Nasdaq em 19 de novembro de 2026, e suas ações fecharam o primeiro pregão a US$ 97,17. O preço ficou US$ 14,17, ou 17,07%, acima dos US$ 83 definidos na oferta pública inicial (IPO), levando o valor de mercado da empresa a aproximadamente US$ 1,76 trilhão no fechamento.

Os papéis abriram a US$ 111,50, alta de 34,3% sobre o preço do IPO, e chegaram a US$ 115,10 durante o pregão, avanço de 38,7%. Depois recuaram, caindo abaixo de US$ 100 antes de encerrar a sessão acima do valor inicial da oferta.

Oferta reúne US$ 81,3 bilhões

O preço de US$ 83 por ação correspondia a uma avaliação de cerca de US$ 1,5 trilhão, considerando a diluição completa. A oferta somou US$ 81,3 bilhões, incluindo aproximadamente US$ 2 bilhões em ações vendidas por acionistas existentes; uma colocação privada concomitante de US$ 26 bilhões elevou o valor combinado das operações a US$ 107,3 bilhões.

A AOL classificou a operação como a maior oferta pública já registrada, acima do recorde anterior atribuído à listagem da SpaceX na Nasdaq, em junho, que levantou US$ 75 bilhões. No pico intradiário, a capitalização implícita da Anthropic chegou a cerca de US$ 2,09 trilhões, antes de recuar com a queda das ações.

Investidores passam a comprar ações diretamente

A abertura de capital oferece aos investidores uma forma direta de comprar ações de uma das empresas que desenvolvem modelos avançados de inteligência artificial. Até então, a exposição nos mercados públicos à expansão da IA se concentrava principalmente em fornecedores de chips, computação em nuvem e infraestrutura de data centers, como Nvidia e CoreWeave.

A avaliação elevada também coloca em foco a capacidade de converter avanços em IA em receitas e lucros sustentáveis. Entre os custos que investidores acompanharão estão computação, pesquisa e desenvolvimento; a trajetória das ações nas próximas semanas também pode influenciar outras empresas privadas do setor que avaliam abrir capital.

Expansão de infraestrutura e custos da IA

Fundada em 2021 em San Francisco por Dario e Daniela Amodei e outros ex-funcionários da OpenAI, a Anthropic desenvolve a família de modelos Claude, concorrente do ChatGPT. No registro do IPO, a empresa informou que pretende usar parte dos recursos para ampliar sua capacidade de computação e sua infraestrutura.

Essa expansão pode sustentar ferramentas de IA usadas em escrita, pesquisa, programação e produtividade no trabalho, mas também exige grande capacidade computacional e energia. O crescimento de data centers pode pressionar o fornecimento de eletricidade e comunidades próximas, enquanto investidores avaliam os custos, os riscos de regulação mais rigorosa e os efeitos da tecnologia sobre o emprego.

title: Agenvoy@v1.3.18-v1.3.19
description:
Agenvoy

v1.3.17 -> v1.3.19

Summary

  • v1.3.18 Adds a human-assisted step for pages that block automated access: a challenge cannot be avoided, but the content is still needed, so Agenvoy asks the user to complete the check in a browser window. Interactive prompts across every interface now follow the configured reply language, since a prompt exists to be understood by the person answering it.
  • v1.3.19 This hotfix extends manual human verification to page downloads with a session-scoped cache so users are not re-prompted across requests. It also skips interactive prompts in headless Linux environments and delegates shared browser checks upstream.

翻譯

title: CAIMS: Scalable Cross-Array In-Memory Search
description:
arXiv:2611.25141v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Search, especially top-k similarity search, plays a vital role in many applications, but its performance can be severely limited by memory access overhead. In-memory search (IMS), an alternative to CPU/GPU-based approaches, exploits massive parallelism within a content-addressable memory (CAM) array to perform search in situ and provides both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, the capacity of a single CAM array is often insufficient for modern workloads, requiring data to be distributed across multiple arrays. Deploying scalable top-k similarity search across multiple CAM arrays poses a fundamental problem that existing designs fail to address: how to accurately and efficiently reduce local binary match results to global top-k results. This work introduces CAIMS, a cross-array IMS framework that is agnostic to memory technologies and applications, enabling scalable and efficient top-k similarity search while preserving accuracy. To enable accurate top-k result reduction, CAIMS leverages the existing threshold match functionality with a combined offline and online parameter selection approach to transform local binary match results that lack globally comparable similarity information into global coarse-grained similarity scores. To further improve efficiency, CAIMS conducts hierarchical reduction and transfers only the selection results and necessary control signals with lightweight local peripherals. Implemented on a 3D NAND Flash model and demonstrated using the retrieval phase of retrieval-augmented generation, CAIMS improves throughput by up to $22.3\times/10.1\times$ and energy efficiency by $426.6\times/23.7\times$ compared to the server-class CPU baseline and prior 3D NAND Flash accelerators, respectively, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

title: One VAST MediaFile must satisfy the player requirements together.
description:
A tag can offer one rendition with the desired dimensions and another with a supported codec, while neither rendition meets the player's complete requirements. An incorrectly grouped validation check can combine their properties into a fictional playable file.

This is a logical error before it is a video problem. The question is whether one candidate satisfies all required predicates, not whether each predicate is satisfied somewhere in the list.

A useful selection report keeps each MediaFile intact, explains its failed conditions and distinguishes declared compatibility from observed decoding.

Write the destination policy explicitly

Start with a named player profile and the properties that matter for that deployment. They may include delivery type, container, codec, dimensions and bitrate. Preserve the profile version with the result.

Avoid a generic CTV-compatible boolean unless your application defines exactly which environment and requirements it represents. Different destinations can support different combinations, and a declaration that works on one player is not evidence about another.

The policy below is synthetic: minimum 1280 by 720, an application codec label of h264 and a positive bitrate no greater than 3000 kilobits per second. These are example thresholds, not universal VAST or CTV requirements.

The objects model already parsed and normalized declarations. They do not reproduce the full MediaFile schema.

Apply every predicate to the same candidate

Run this complete program with Node.js:

import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

const files = [
  { id: 'large-hevc', width: 1920, height: 1080, codec: 'hevc', bitrateKbps: 2500 },
  { id: 'small-h264', width: 640, height: 360, codec: 'h264', bitrateKbps: 700 }
];

const misleading = files.some(f => f.width >= 1280 && f.height >= 720) &&
  files.some(f => f.codec === 'h264') &&
  files.some(f => f.bitrateKbps > 0 && f.bitrateKbps <= 3000);

function failures(file) {
  const issues = [];
  if (!Number.isFinite(file.width) || !Number.isFinite(file.height) ||
      file.width < 1280 || file.height < 720) issues.push('dimensions');
  if (file.codec !== 'h264') issues.push('codec');
  if (!Number.isFinite(file.bitrateKbps) ||
      file.bitrateKbps <= 0 || file.bitrateKbps > 3000) issues.push('bitrate');
  return issues;
}

assert.equal(misleading, true);
assert.deepEqual(files.filter(f => failures(f).length === 0), []);
assert.deepEqual(failures(files[0]), ['codec']);
assert.deepEqual(failures(files[1]), ['dimensions']);

const usableDeclaration = {
  id: 'large-h264', width: 1280, height: 720,
  codec: 'h264', bitrateKbps: 1800
};
assert.deepEqual(failures(usableDeclaration), []);
assert.deepEqual(failures({ ...usableDeclaration, bitrateKbps: undefined }),
  ['bitrate']);
assert.deepEqual(failures({ ...usableDeclaration, bitrateKbps: 3001 }),
  ['bitrate']);

The first expression returns true even though neither original candidate passes. The corrected filter keeps the predicates together and returns no eligible candidate until a suitable declaration is supplied.

The diagnostic function is useful beyond this test. It can explain why each candidate was excluded instead of returning one unexplained false result for the entire tag.

Make missing metadata visible

A missing bitrate is not a measured zero. A missing codec declaration is not evidence of your preferred codec. Decide whether incomplete metadata should reject the candidate, require probing or produce an unknown result under the selected profile.

Keep that policy separate from parsing. First establish what the document declares and whether its types are valid. Then apply destination-specific requirements.

Preserve units in normalized field names. The example uses bitrateKbps to avoid comparing a kilobit value with a threshold measured in bits per second. Similar mistakes can occur when a probe result and an XML declaration use different representations.

Test exact boundaries as well as obvious failures. A candidate at the minimum dimensions or maximum allowed bitrate should exercise the policy's intended inclusive or exclusive comparison.

Select a candidate before claiming playback support

Several candidates may satisfy the declaration policy. Define how the player or integration chooses among them and record which one it selected in the test run.

A deterministic test should retain that candidate's URL, declaration and content identity when available. Otherwise a later run might choose a different rendition and make a regression appear intermittent.

If selection uses estimated bandwidth or device capabilities, preserve those inputs too. A selection algorithm cannot be reproduced from the MediaFile list alone when its other inputs change between runs.

Do not assume the highest resolution is always the intended choice. Use the destination's real selection rules and the network conditions relevant to the test.

Verify the resource behind the declaration

A declared MIME type, codec or dimension is an input to selection. It is not a probe of the media bytes returned by the URL.

After selecting a candidate, check the retrieval result and inspect the actual container, codec, dimensions and other properties required by your acceptance plan. Record when the resource was fetched because the content behind a stable URL can change.

Then exercise the selected rendition on the destination player. A resource can be retrievable and structurally consistent while decoding still fails in a specific runtime.

Keep declared, probed and observed values separate in the report. If the probe disagrees with the declaration, show that disagreement rather than replacing the declaration with the probe value and losing evidence of the original problem.

Give the creative team a specific repair

When no candidate qualifies, provide one row per candidate with the failed predicates. The report should make it clear whether a missing rendition would close the gap or whether all files share a common defect.

For the synthetic example, the team can see that the large file fails the codec requirement while the supported-codec file fails the dimensions requirement. That is more actionable than a message saying the tag has no playable media.

After a replacement is supplied, rerun the same profile and preserve the newly selected candidate. Also repeat the runtime test if the acceptance claim includes playback.

I maintain VASTlint. The VAST tester helps inspect the tag and its media choices. Keep your destination policy and selected-rendition observation with that result so every compatibility claim refers to one actual candidate.

Sources

  • VAST 4.3, MediaFiles and MediaFile

Technical sources checked October 25, 2026. Drafted with AI; examples are synthetic unless explicitly stated otherwise.
