title: Natural Language Processing: An Applied Research Practicum From Classical Text Processing to Multimodal and Agentic Systems
description:
arXiv:2605.03799v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: This preprint presents a systematic, research-oriented guide to modern natural language processing, covering the full NLP pipeline from tokenisation, text normalisation, vector representations, and classical machine learning to transformer architectures, large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, preference-based alignment, and multimodal systems.
  The material comprises eighteen practical works combining theoretical foundations, reproducible implementation examples, detailed experimental procedures, evaluation metrics, and research-oriented assignments. Each work includes three structured core tasks and optional advanced investigations. Common requirements for reporting, data provenance, experimental evaluation, and reproducibility are established across the guide.
  Particular attention is devoted to low-resource and morphologically rich languages, including Tajik, Tatar, and Bashkir. The guide addresses subword tokenisation, cross-lingual transfer, machine translation, language model adaptation, and the evaluation of NLP systems under limited data and computational resources.
  Advanced topics include prompt engineering, reasoning strategies, multi-agent collaboration, model compression, efficient inference, AI safety, and LLMOps. A capstone project integrates methods from different chapters into the development and evaluation of domain-specific NLP systems.
  The guide is intended for senior undergraduate students, graduate students, researchers, and developers interested in implementing and critically evaluating NLP methods.

title: Our 38 pages are 253 phone screens tall, and the first link that can sell anything is either in the top tenth or the last eighth
description:
I counted the links to our download page a while ago: 109 of them across Notifio's 38 pages, 76 of them the nav and footer repeated, and none at all in the five guides.

Counting links tells you how many there are. It does not tell you where they are, and "where" is the only thing that matters on a page six screens long. So I loaded all 38 live pages at 390 by 844, the iPhone viewport, and measured the vertical position of everything.

253 screens 

pages                                38
total document height           213,900 px
                                  253.4 phone screens
median page                        6.69 screens
longest   /terms                  12.12 screens
shortest  /download                2.90 screens

The shortest page on the site is the one whose entire job is to get an installer onto your machine, and the longest is the terms of service. That is probably the correct order.

The footer is the same 596 pixels on every one of the 38 pages:

footer, total                    22,648 px   10.6% of every pixel on the site
footer, as a share of /download                     24.4%
footer, as a share of /guides                       19.4%
footer, as a share of /about                        18.3%
footer, as a share of /terms                         5.8%

footer text                       9,158 characters    4.7% of the site's words

A quarter of the download page is the footer. It takes up 10.6 per cent of the site's pixels to carry 4.7 per cent of its words, which is what a fourteen-link sitemap column does when the page above it is short.

Two strategies, nothing in between

For each page I took the first link in the body content (ignoring the nav and footer) pointing at either /download or /pricing, and measured how far down the document it sits.

                                          first CTA     as % of page
/                                            379 px          4.6%
/alerts/idealista                            479 px          8.0%
/alerts/rightmove                            517 px          8.4%
   ... 15 site pages, all between 8.0% and 9.6% ...
/alerts/facebook-marketplace                 529 px          9.6%
-----------------------------------------------------------------
/download                                  1,704 px         69.6%
/guides                                    2,261 px         73.5%
/compare                                   3,897 px         82.7%
/guides/rental-documents-checklist         4,234 px         83.8%
   ... 13 guide, compare and audience pages, 83.8% to 87.8% ...
/for/students                              5,877 px         87.8%
-----------------------------------------------------------------
/pricing  /help  /about  /terms  /privacy     none

Sixteen pages put a conversion link in the top tenth of the document. Fifteen put the first one past 82 per cent. Two sit in between and five have none at all. For a site that was built page by page with no plan about this, that is a remarkably clean split, and it is not a coincidence: it is two templates.

The fifteen site pages are built from the alert-page template, which opens with an h1, a standfirst and a pair of buttons. You hit "Download" after 0.57 screens.

The guides, the comparison pages and the audience pages are built from one shared article layout, which is breadcrumb, h1, standfirst, sections, FAQ, and then a call to action at the bottom. On those pages the reader scrolls between 5.0 and 7.0 screens before the page offers them anything to click that leads to a purchase.

/for/students          6.96 screens before the first CTA
/compare/visualping    6.85
/guides/rental-scams   6.58
/alerts (the hub)      6.05

What is selling during those seven screens

One thing, and I measured it too. The nav is fixed top-0 and never leaves:

nav height                        49 px
"Get Notifio" button          98 × 31 px   =  3,038 px²
390 × 844 viewport                           329,160 px²
share of the screen                               0.92%

colour     #737373 on #0a0a0a      4.18:1
font       13px, weight 600

For seven screens of a guide, the entire commercial surface of the website is 0.92 per cent of the viewport, drawn in grey at 4.18:1, which fails AA for 13 pixel text by a third of a point. The other two nav links, "Sites" and "Pricing", are the same colour at 29 pixels tall.

There is nothing wrong with the sticky nav as an idea. It is doing the job that the published 109-link count made look generous: 76 of those 109 links are this nav and this footer, and what the geometry shows is that on half the site they are not a supplement to an in-content CTA, they are the only one for several thousand pixels.

The scroll handler, since I was already in there

The nav restyles itself once, at 20 pixels of scroll:

const onScroll = () => setScrolled(window.scrollY > 20);
window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll, { passive: true });

Passive, which is right. It also calls setScrolled on every single scroll event, which over a 3,600 pixel wheel fling is 30 calls, 29 of them setting the same boolean. React bails out of re-rendering when the next state is identical, so this costs 30 function calls and no renders, and the honest summary is that it is fine and that a scrollY > 20 check is not worth an IntersectionObserver.

What it buys is the nav going from flush and transparent to a floating rounded card: pt-3 px-4, max-w-6xl, rounded-2xl, a #262626 border, bg-[#0f0f0f]/90 and backdrop-blur-xl, over a 300 millisecond transition. Measured after scrolling, the nav sits at top: 12px with a 16 pixel radius and blur(24px). It is the one piece of motion on the site that fires on every page, and it is also what makes the CTA legible, because grey text on a blurred panel reads better than grey text over whatever happened to scroll past.

What I am changing

  1. A mid-article CTA in the shared layout. The geometry says exactly where: the first CTA should not be 87 per cent down a 7 screen page. After the second section is roughly two screens in, which on these pages is where the reader has decided whether they believe the article.
  2. #a3a3a3 for the nav links. 7.85:1 instead of 4.18:1 on the only control that is on screen all of the time. It is the same fix as the one I wrote up yesterday for the footer links that only reach readable contrast on hover, and the same two tokens.
  3. One link on /help. It is 6.6 screens long, it is the page people land on when something is not working, and the body contains no link to either the download page or the pricing page.

All of it is measurable from a phone and a browser console: load any guide, run document.documentElement.scrollHeight / window.innerHeight, and then count how far you have to scroll before the page asks you for anything.

title: 3 Subtle Rust CLI & Parser Bugs I Hunted Today (Silent Zip Truncation, Kebab-Case Alias Collisions & Quiet stderr Suppression)
description:
While hunting open-source bounties across the Stellar / Soroban Rust CLI (stellar/stellar-cli) today, I ran into three deceptively subtle CLI and contract parser bugs that pass normal unit tests yet fail quietly in production.

If you build Rust CLIs with clap, parse JSON into typed contract ABIs, or design tool-call sandboxes for AI agents, these three patterns are worth auditing in your own codebase.

1. Silent .zip() Truncation on JSON Tuple-Struct Arrays

When parsing untyped JSON arrays into typed Rust tuple structs (like Soroban contract spec types), it is tempting to pair the incoming serde_json::Value::Array elements with the struct's field definitions using .iter().zip():

Value::Array(array) => {
    if array.len() != strukt.fields.len() {
        return Err(Error::InvalidValue(Some(Type::Udt(Udt {
            name: strukt.name.clone(),
        }))));
    }
    let fields: Result<Vec<_>, _> = array
        .iter()
        .zip(strukt.fields.iter())
        .map(|(val, field)| self.from_json(val, &field.value_type))
        .collect();
    // ...
}

The trap: Rust's Iterator::zip stops as soon as either iterator is exhausted. Without an explicit array.len() != strukt.fields.len() arity check before .zip():

  1. Passing extra elements ([10, 20] for a 1-field tuple struct) silently drops the trailing values and succeeds.
  2. Passing too few elements ([] for a 1-field tuple struct) yields an empty iterator, bypassing field validation and failing downstream in the XDR encoder with a cryptic error.

The fix: Always guard .zip() over external input with an explicit arity check before mapping.

2. Dynamic clap Kebab-Case Alias Collisions

Many modern CLIs dynamically generate clap::Command subcommands at runtime from external schemas (e.g., smart contract methods, OpenAPI specs, or MCP tool definitions).

To make snake_case contract methods ergonomic on the command line, you might attach a kebab-case visible alias (hello_world -> --hello-world).

The trap: What happens when a contract defines both hello_world and hello-world, or a_b_c and a-b_c?

  • If the first function registers "hello-world" as a visible alias and the second function registers "hello-world" as its primary command name, clap panics at runtime with a duplicate subcommand/alias collision before --help can even render.

The fix: Run a two-pass pre-computation over the function list before building clap::Command nodes:

  1. Collect all canonical function names into a HashSet<String>.
  2. Count how many functions map to each kebab-case candidate kebab_name = name.replace('_', "-").
  3. Only attach .visible_alias(&kebab_name) when kebab_name != name, !canonical_names.contains(&kebab_name), and alias_counts[&kebab_name] == 1.

3. Macro-Generated --quiet Flags Swallowing Fatal stderr Errors

When writing a terminal printer helper in Rust, a macro often generates both informational (info, check, log) and error (error, errorln) helpers:

macro_rules! create_print_functions {
    ($name:ident, $name_ln:ident, $icon:expr) => {
        pub fn $name<T: Display + Sized>(&self, message: T) {
            if !self.quiet {
                eprint!(...);
            }
        }
    };
}

The trap: Gating error and errorln behind if !self.quiet violates POSIX CLI conventions. When a script runs a command with --quiet (or -q) and the command fails, it exits with code 1 and zero output on stderr, leaving CI pipelines completely blind to what failed.

The fix: Decouple error and errorln from the !self.quiet guard so --quiet only silences non-essential progress output while fatal diagnostics always reach stderr.

Grab Our Autonomous Engineering & Security Kits

I am documenting and packaging every security validation, AST parser, and multi-agent execution tool we build into zero-dependency developer kits:

  • AgentGuard Lite: Zero-Dependency Prompt & Tool-Call Firewall ($5 Starter Kit) — Fast Python AST & heuristic firewall for defending LLM tool calls against prompt injection, SSRF, and path traversal.
  • Autonomous Security & Bug Bounty Recon Kit ($19) — Automated CORS misconfiguration scanner, API shadow-route enumerator, and CVSS 3.1 / Bugcrowd VRT report generator.
  • Production Multi-Agent Architecture & Protocol Pack ($29) — Deterministic task-routing engine, SQLite WAL cross-agent memory bus, and sub-agent verification harness.

What's the nastiest silent truncation or CLI parser bug you've caught in production? Drop it in the comments!

title: Mastering Vue.js: A Comprehensive 101-Lesson Roadmap
description:
Most Vue tutorials stop at basic form binding. To build scalable, enterprise-grade applications, you need to understand the reactivity engine, compiler internals, and advanced architectural patterns.

I've been reviewing a 101-lesson curriculum that finally bridges the gap between "Hello World" and Senior Frontend Engineer status. Here is how the lessons are structured:

The Roadmap

  • Lessons 1–25: Foundations & Composition API Getting comfortable with the modern Vue 3 paradigm. This covers everything from project setup with Vite to ref/reactive rules, conditional rendering, and complex side-effect management.
  • Lessons 26–50: Component Architecture Moving into advanced reusability. You’ll cover lifecycle hooks, custom events, slot patterns, provide/inject for deep dependency injection, and extracting complex logic into custom composables.
  • Lessons 51–75: The Ecosystem (Pinia, Nuxt, & Testing) Integrating professional tooling. This section dives into Pinia state management, client-side routing, full-stack frameworks like Nuxt, and ensuring quality with Vitest and Playwright.
  • Lessons 76–101: Internals, Performance, & Vapor Mode The senior-level deep dive. Learn about the compiler, custom renderers, memory leak profiling, SSR/SSG mechanics, and the upcoming Vapor Mode architecture.

Why this matters

You can write code that "just works" without knowing how the VDOM patches, but you cannot optimize large-scale applications without it. This series moves past the syntax and gets into the engine room, teaching you how to debug hydration mismatches, handle memory leaks, and architect libraries.

Who this is for

  • Mid-level developers looking to solidify their understanding of the Composition API and Pinia.
  • Senior engineers transitioning from other frameworks (like React) who need a deep dive into Vue’s internal mechanics without the fluff.

title: Shopify Was Wrong and Right to Dump React Native
description:
In September Shopify announced it's moving every mobile app off React Native and rewriting them in Swift and Kotlin. Their reasoning fits in one sentence from the post: "building the same feature in Swift and Kotlin no longer carries the cost it used to." Agents write the second copy, so why share code at all?

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

React Native deserved to die. It's a heavyweight toolkit, and every heavyweight toolkit, from AWT to Xamarin.Forms, was eventually replaced by a lightweight one or by native code. Replacing it with two native codebases is wrong, because it takes the most expensive part of React Native, a separate platform per target, and doubles it. Code was never the cost. Platforms, testing and store churn are, and AI makes every one of them worse.

This isn't a post against AI. I use LLMs every day, and in the right setting they're superb. But they can't hold a Samsung phone, they don't know what Apple will announce next June, and they can't sign off on a release. Shopify's plan needs them to do all three.

TL;DR

  • React Native was designed to fail at the one thing you adopted it for. Its creators rejected write once, run anywhere in the launch announcement. In writing.
  • Your buttons belong to Samsung. Heavyweight toolkits hand your UI to the OS and the vendor skin, which is why Samsung's keyboard can hang your text field.
  • Not looking 100% native is a feature, and here's why. Lightweight toolkits ship the pixels you tested, and still embed a native map or web view when you need one.
  • Shopify's own post explains why its plan fails. Agents write code in seconds and need minutes to test it. Two codebases double the slow part.
  • "iOS and Android" is a lie. The web, the desktop, tablets, foldables, the watch, the car, TVs, consoles and embedded devices are all platforms too, and your developers end up as meat proxies between users and an LLM.
  • Meta gave up on a native WhatsApp desktop app. You have fewer engineers than Meta.
  • Testing is the real bill, and AI makes it bigger.
  • Apple broke apps with UIScene. Ours didn't notice.
  • A framework should beat the OS, not wrap it. Gantt charts, commerce with no commission, records as entities, every protection a bank app needs, built once, and a Base64 encoder nearly three times faster than Apple's.
  • One codebase pays double when it includes the server. Plus my generous offer of a PHP port.

Coming This Week

Before we proceed, here's a preview of this week on the blog:

  • Saturday, November 14: Calendars, Gantt Charts and Booking Apps Without Writing a Calendar. A scheduler, a Gantt chart with critical paths and resource leveling, Material 3 pickers and Slate, our appointment booking template.
  • Sunday, November 15: Subscriptions, Paywalls and a Customer Center, and We Don't Take a Cut. Offerings, experiments, refunds and invites across five stores.
  • Monday, November 16: Kafka Listeners, Mail and Live Streams in Your Backend, With Records as Entities. Spring-style messaging, transactional email, server-sent events, and an ORM that's ahead of JPA.
  • Tuesday, November 17: Ship Your Game on Steam, and Why the Art Matters More Than the Engine. Splat, a team paintball shooter, and the lesson it taught us.
  • Wednesday, November 18: Windows Kiosks and Command Line Tools, Built From Java. Windows IoT Enterprise as a target, and a console API for real terminal tools.
  • Thursday, November 19: Run an LLM and Whisper on the Phone, With No Server Bill. Local models through the same API as the cloud ones, so moving a feature onto the phone is a one line change.

Gantt with the critical path.
Booking in Slate.
Splat, in a match.

React Native was built to fail at write once, run anywhere

Nobody should be surprised that React Native didn't deliver one codebase. It never tried. When Facebook announced it in 2015 they wrote: "we're not chasing 'write once, run anywhere.'" They rejected it on purpose, and built a toolkit where platform code is part of the design. Then a decade of teams adopted it believing they'd get one codebase, and spent that decade writing platform code.

The reason is architectural. React Native is a heavyweight UI toolkit.

Heavyweight and lightweight

UI toolkits come in two families, and the split is older than smartphones.

A heavyweight toolkit maps each of your components to a widget the operating system owns. Your button is a UIButton on iOS and an android.widget.Button on Android. Java's AWT worked this way in 1995. So did SWT. Xamarin.Forms, .NET MAUI and React Native repeat it today.

A lightweight toolkit asks the OS for a surface and draws every pixel itself. Swing replaced AWT this way. Qt, Flutter and Codename One all draw their own UI.

Heavyweight has exactly one selling point: the widgets are the platform's, so they look the part for free. Everything else is a bill.

  • Many implementations of every widget. A text field on Android and a text field on iOS are different programs with different bugs, and it doesn't stop at two. Apple alone made everyone move from UIWebView to WKWebView, with different APIs and different behavior, and Android has gone through several generations of its own widgets. Each new target multiplies it again: a TV, a watch or a desktop brings its own set. The abstraction exposes only what all of them agree on, so anything interesting drops to platform code.
  • A bridge on every interaction. Layout, events and state cross from your code into the widget and back, on every frame.
  • Behavior you can't test in one place. The widget runs inside the OS, so it behaves according to the OS version, the vendor skin and whatever keyboard the user installed. A font that's a pixel taller on one vendor's build clips the bottom of your label. A minor OS update on one device family delivers focus and text events in a slightly different order, and a race that never happened before starts corrupting input on those phones only.

That last one is where the money burns. A controlled TextInput hangs on Samsung phones when the Samsung keyboard's Grammarly integration is on. Setting state on a controlled TextInput can duplicate its value. These are races between JavaScript, the bridge and a keyboard Samsung ships. You find them when a user with that phone and that keyboard complains, and you can't reproduce them on anything else.

Then the OS moves under you. When Apple shipped Liquid Glass, every app built with the new SDK got the redesigned system controls whether the team wanted them or not. Apple's escape hatch, the UIDesignRequiresCompatibility key, comes with a promise that it will be removed. And you have to know that key exists. Nobody tells you. With a heavyweight UI you don't just work for your boss. You work for Apple and Google too, reading their release notes and following their instructions every year to keep your own app looking like your own app.

Shopify's own numbers show what that bridge cost them. InfoQ reports cold start dropped 23% on iOS and 50% on Android after the rewrite, and crash-free sessions went from 99.5% to 99.95%. Those numbers are the price of heavyweight, finally itemized.

Lightweight is the architecture that works

A lightweight toolkit compiles the UI into your app. The pixels you tested are the pixels that ship, on every phone and every OS version, next year as well as today.

  • One implementation of each component. A bug fixed once is fixed everywhere.
  • No bridge. Drawing your own button needs no round trip into the OS.
  • Deterministic rendering. A screenshot test on a CI runner means something. Codename One's CI compares hundreds of screenshots on every commit across iOS, Android, desktop and the web.
  • Stability. An OS update can't restyle your app. A buggy vendor skin draws your app the way it draws any other surface.
  • Native where you want it. A lightweight UI can still mix in any native component as a peer. Google Maps, a platform web view, a camera preview, a payment sheet or a third party SDK's widget sits inside your layout like any other component. You choose native per component, instead of inheriting it for everything.

"It doesn't look 100% native." Correct. That's a feature. It's my app, not Apple's. Our Material 3 date picker is better than most native pickers I've used, and when I want it different I change CSS instead of waiting a year for a vendor to add a parameter.

Accessibility is the real question for any lightweight toolkit, because the OS can't read a button it didn't draw. A lightweight toolkit has to publish its components to VoiceOver and TalkBack itself. Codename One does, and keeps improving it. Ask every lightweight framework how it handles this. The answer separates the serious ones from the rest.

That last point deserves emphasis, because it's the answer to every "but I need the real thing" objection. In Codename One a PeerComponent places a native view inside the lightweight UI: Google Maps, an ad network's banner, a vendor's video player or chat widget, anything with a native view. It lays out, scrolls and layers with the surrounding components. Native becomes the escape hatch for the few components that need it. Heavyweight gets this backwards: native is the default, and consistency is what you claw back.

The old joke about Java was "write once, debug everywhere." It was coined when Java's UI was AWT, a heavyweight toolkit, and that's exactly what it described. Swing fixed it. The joke still describes every heavyweight toolkit: you pay for a platform per target, test per target, debug per target, and still have an abstraction in the way. Shopify paid native costs for a decade and got none of native's control. Now it will pay them twice.

Two codebases is the same mistake, twice

Shopify's own post explains why their cure fails:

"Agents can make code changes in seconds, but it takes them several minutes to test the output."

Writing code was never the expensive part, and AI made that obvious. Everything after the code is the cost, and a second codebase doubles all of it.

There are no "two platforms"

"iOS and Android" is a fiction. Start with the big ones: the web and the desktop, which the next section covers. Then the iPad, Android tablets and foldables, which need layouts that adapt instead of a stretched phone UI. A serious commerce app is also expected on the watch, in widgets, in Siri and in the car. Each is a platform with its own lifecycle and its own review rules, and each needs its own code in a native project.

Then there's everything beyond the phone, where the interesting products are being built: TVs, consoles, embedded devices and kiosks, AR and VR, and real-time systems on a factory floor. Two native mobile codebases reach none of them.

Every box has rules a model has to know and keep current. A GrapheneOS user reports that sign-in fails. Someone has to know that Google Play Services aren't there, find the library that assumed they were, test the fix on a phone they don't own, and feed all of it back to the agent. The agent writes the patch. The developer becomes a meat proxy between users and an LLM, and with two codebases they do it twice.

Skipping the niche platforms is a mistake too. People on GrapheneOS, a Linux desktop or an Amazon tablet have few choices. Show up for them early and they remember, and they tell everyone. They're the early adopters who carry a product across the chasm, and the chasm is where products die. That's why we support de-Googled Android officially.

The web and the desktop are the product now

WhatsApp belongs to Meta, one of the largest engineering organizations on earth. For years WhatsApp Web needed your phone online, because it was a mirror of the phone app. In 2025 Meta replaced the native Windows client with a wrapped web version. Meta couldn't keep a desktop client in step with its phone apps. Two native codebases won't either.

Picture a competitor with one codebase. They finish a feature and it ships on the phone, the tablet, the desktop, the web and the watch that same day. You finished the same feature in Swift, and you're still waiting for the Kotlin version, and when it lands it doesn't behave quite like the Swift one. The desktop and the web haven't started.

Testing is the bill

Shopify describes its review process for each change in the rewrite: tests, a visual comparison against the running app, two adversarial AI reviewers and a human approval. Per platform. Two codebases mean two test suites, two sets of screenshot baselines, two device farms and two release trains, and every native widget adds behavior only a physical device can verify.

Agents make the top half worse, not better. They produce more code per day, and every line of it lands in two pipelines that need devices and humans to sign off. The throughput limit was never typing. It's verification, and Shopify chose to verify everything twice.

The stores change the rules every year

The App Store and Play are where mobile projects lose weeks. Apple made UIScene lifecycle support mandatory and broke third-party plugins that hooked the app delegate. Codename One users got it as a build default: we turned ios.uiscene=true on by default after a month of testing, and nobody noticed. Same with the Xcode 26 migration, Google Play's 16 KB page requirement and every new target API level.

LLMs are trained on the past. Store requirements are announced for the future. The model writing your Swift today doesn't know next spring's privacy rule. A framework team that tracks those changes full-time and fixes them once for everyone matters more in the agent era.

A platform should give you more than the OS

A framework that wraps the OS hands you the lowest common denominator. A lightweight framework can ship what the OS doesn't have at all. Most of this week's release is exactly that:

  • A scheduler and a Gantt chart with resource leveling, plus Material 3 date and time pickers. Neither iOS nor Android ships a Gantt chart.
  • Subscriptions, paywalls and a customer center across Apple, Google, Amazon, Stripe and Paddle. We never touch your money, so there's no commission.
  • Crypto wallets for Ethereum, Bitcoin and Solana in the core.
  • An ORM that maps Java records as entities, which JPA still forbids.

Performance belongs here too. Codename One's Base64 on iOS uses a portable SIMD API we built into ParparVM, our ahead-of-time compiler, and it beats Apple's own implementation: 379 ms to encode against Apple's 1078 ms, 365 ms to decode against 713 ms.

Security is where this matters most. A financial app needs certificate pinning, passkeys, device keys, signed requests, screens hidden from screenshots and the app switcher, jailbreak and root detection, and obfuscation with string encryption. Each has a different pitfall on each platform, and most fail silently: the app works, it isn't protected. Two codebases means getting every one of them right twice. We built them once, and our Bastion bank template uses all of them in a working bank and exchange. Its Security Center shows which protections are live on that device and build, and a test fails the build if the screen ever claims more than the build delivers.

Bastion's Security Center.
Sign-in with passkeys and TOTP.

The full stack is where one codebase pays twice

Shopify's server is a separate world with separate teams. (If Ruby is what it takes to win them over, I'll consider a Ruby port. Probably.)

For everyone else, the phone app, the desktop app, the web app and the server in one Java project means one set of entity classes, one debugger session that follows a request from a tap to the database, and a compile error instead of a production incident when someone renames a field. When the system changes every week, seeing all of its state in one place is the difference between moving fast and guessing. Shopify now has three codebases that have to agree on every field.

// shared module: used by the app AND the server
@Entity
public class Order {
    @Id public long id;
    public String customer;
    public long totalCents;
}

// backend
@RestController
public class Orders {
    @PostMapping("/orders")
    public Order place(@RequestBody Order order) {
        return repository.save(order);
    }
}

More This Week

Calendars, Gantt charts and a booking app

Neither iOS nor Android ships a calendar view or a Gantt chart, so every business app ends up writing one. Codename One now has a Scheduler with day, week, month, agenda and per-resource views:

DefaultScheduleModel model = new DefaultScheduleModel();
model.addItem(new ScheduleItem("review", "Design review",
        TimeMath.at(today, 13 * 60, zone), TimeMath.at(today, 14 * 60 + 30, zone))
        .setDetail("Room 2"));
Scheduler scheduler = new Scheduler(model);
scheduler.setView(Scheduler.View.WEEK);

And a Gantt with dependencies, baselines, the critical path and resource leveling that tells you what moving people around costs before you apply it:

if (!ResourceLeveler.findOverallocations(project).isEmpty()) {
    LevelingResult proposal = ResourceLeveler.level(project);
    if (proposal.isChanged()) {
        proposal.apply();
    }
}

The week view.
The critical path.
After resource leveling.
The Material 3 date picker.

Slate, our booking template, is the same idea as a full product: clients, providers and an owner, with a slot engine that weighs rooms, buffers and travel time.

Download the Slate video.

Saturday's article covers both.

Commerce with no commission

Subscription platforms take a percentage of your revenue on top of what Apple and Google take. We never touch your money, so there's no commission. CommerceManager gives you entitlements, offerings, paywalls, experiments and a customer center across the App Store, Google Play, Amazon, Stripe and Paddle:

CommerceManager cm = CommerceManager.getInstance();
if (!cm.isEntitled("pro")) {
    Offering current = cm.getOfferings().getCurrent();
    Paywall.show(current, null);
}

Sunday's commerce article has refunds, retention offers, experiments, and invites.

Records as entities, Kafka and mail

JPA still forbids records as entities. Codename One's ORM maps them on the phone and the server, and generates a builder for each:

@Entity
public record Note(@Id long id, String title, int score, @Version long version) {}

Note saved = notes.save(NoteBuilder.create().title("Groceries").score(3).build());
Note changed = notes.save(NoteBuilder.of(saved).score(5).build());

The backend now talks to Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis Streams, SQS and Pub/Sub through one API. Spring's @KafkaListener and @RabbitListener work as written, and a message sent inside a transaction goes out only after the commit:

@MessageListener(value = "orders.placed", group = "shipping", concurrency = 4)
public void placed(Order order) {
    // ship it
}

Mail goes out through SMTP or SES from the same transactional outbox, and server-sent events stream with resume support. Monday's backend article walks through it.

Splat, and shipping games on Steam

Download the Splat video.

Splat is a first-person team paintball shooter: four against four, refereed by its own server, with fog, PBR materials, shadows and post processing on every GPU backend. It taught us that the art makes the game, not the engine.

Capture the flag.
The field from above.
The mission builder.

Games now ship to Steam from the build cloud, and Steam features come from portable code that does nothing on other platforms:

if (GameServices.isAvailable()) {             // true on Steam
    GameServices.unlockAchievement("FIRST_WIN");
    GameServices.writeSave("slot1", saveBytes);
}

Tuesday's article has all four videos, including the mission builder on the phone.

Windows kiosks and command line tools

One build hint turns an app into a locked down kiosk for Windows 10 and 11 IoT Enterprise, and mvn cn1:deploy-device installs it over SSH. Receipt printers and scales are a serial port away:

SerialPort printer = Hardware.getInstance()
        .openSerial("COM3", 9600, 8, SerialPort.PARITY_NONE, 1);

At the other end, the console API builds command line tools that compile to a native executable with no JVM:

Console.print(new Table("Service", "Status", "Replicas")
        .addRow("api", Console.style("running", Console.Style.GREEN), 3)
        .render());
String env = Prompt.select("Environment", Arrays.asList("staging", "production"));

Tables, progress and spinners.
Interactive prompts.

Wednesday's article has both.

An LLM on the phone

LlmClient.local runs a GGUF model through llama.cpp on the device, behind the same API as the cloud clients. JSON output is enforced with a grammar, so it always parses:

LlmClient client = LocalLlmClient.isSupported()
        ? LlmClient.local(modelPath)
        : LlmClient.ollama();          // desktop development
client.chat(ChatRequest.builder()
        .addMessage(ChatMessage.user("Name three primes"))
        .build()).ready(r -> Log.p(r.getText()));

A whisper cn1lib turns speech into text offline, so a voice memo becomes a summary without leaving the phone. Thursday's article shows how.

Fix the abstraction. Don't delete it.

React Native is a heavyweight toolkit, and heavyweight toolkits deserve to die. Shopify answered a bad abstraction with no abstraction, and signed up to pay for every platform, every test suite and every store rule twice, forever, on the theory that typing was the bottleneck. It never was.

If I were a Shopify competitor, I'd jump on this. When the leader zags, you zig. Pick up Codename One, KMP, Flutter or any other decent platform with one codebase, and put an agent to work on it. Every hour the agent spends goes into one product that ships everywhere, not into keeping two copies in step. By the time Shopify notices, you'll be so far ahead that catching up will take them years.

The answer to a bad abstraction is a good one: a lightweight UI you own, compiled to a native app, from one codebase, on every screen your users have.

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

title: Vercel Agent can now validate alerts before paging
description:
Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it.

To enable validation:

  1. Open a monitor’s notification settings and create or link a webhook destination for your paging system, such as incident.io.

  2. Select Critical Only next to that destination.

You can also configure notification destinations with the Vercel CLI using vercel monitors notifications. Add --critical-only when linking or updating a webhook destination.

Agent checks logs and metrics to assess impact. For example, it can identify health-check errors that don’t affect customers or confirm sustained 5xx errors affecting checkout requests. You can also add context to each monitor to guide Agent’s investigation.

Alert validation is available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus. Observability Plus includes ten Agent investigations per billing cycle, with additional investigations billed separately. Custom monitors cost $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Learn more in the alert webhook documentation.

title: I spent a week with Claude Code trying to squeeze more out of my memory tool's LongMemEval score. Almost nothing worked. Is it my code or the benchmark?
description:
I built a local-first memory for coding agents. It's a Rust binary and one SQLite file, using MiniLM embeddings plus BM25 keyword search, with no LLM in the retrieval path and no re-ranker.

On LongMemEval S (470 scored questions) it scores R@1 0.913 (429), R@5 0.987 (464) and R@10 0.996 (468).

I wanted more, mainly at R@1 and recall_all (every gold session in the top K). But all while preserving the strict rules of NO LLM, no re-ranker model and not tuning for the benchmark.

Claude Code did most of the legwork:

  • offline replays of chunk-score dumps
  • a DEV/TEST split by question-id hash
  • a "guard" suite (my coding eval plus probes against a snapshot of my real palace), so a benchmark gain couldn't quietly hurt real use

What we tried

Idea LongMemEval Real-palace guards
Fix two WordPiece tokenizer deviations 0 questions changed probes -1/200
Embed at MiniLM's trained 128 tokens, not 512 R@1 +1, recall_all@5 -7 probes 0.900 -> 0.875, fail
256 tokens +4/-4 at R@1 fail
Re-weight cosine vs BM25 (0.70 to 0.85), DEV only +/- 2 questions probes 0.885 -> 0.790, coding eval 0.922 -> 0.882
Count BM25 only when cosine > 0 <= 1 question probes -4 to -6 pts
RRF, min-max, z-score, saturating BM25 all within 3 questions of baseline n/a
Split two-part questions and merge best scores R@1 +2/-0 DEV, 0/0 TEST unchanged
Treat advice requests as preferences R@1 -5 n/a

The only clean win was 429 -> 431 at R@1. BEAM 100K is already 355/355 at R@5.

How I read it

  1. One question is 0.2%. Most "improvements" were 1 to 4 questions, moving in both directions.
  2. The right sessions are already in the top 30 for 469 of 470 questions. The losses come from ordering, not from failing to find them.
  3. Fusion is saturated: every way of combining cosine and BM25 lands within 3 questions of the others.
  4. Every LongMemEval gain cost my real-palace probes more than it gained.
  5. The leftover misses are reasoning, not retrieval: questions about dates and counting across sessions. The paper's own gains there come from an LLM, which I avoid on purpose.

So my answer is both, but mostly the benchmark. For a pure retriever, S is close to its ceiling. At R@1 I'm at the limit of a small embedding model plus BM25. The next real step is probably a local cross-encoder reranker, not more tuning.

The Claude Code part

The most useful thing it did was keep me honest. It flagged when a "win" was 2 questions, reported failed guards plainly, and stopped when I said "stop if we don't have clear wins". Nothing from the week shipped, and I think that's the right result.

Questions

  • At 98%+, is LongMemEval S still a useful signal for you, or have you moved to M, BEAM 1M or your own evals?
  • Has anyone gotten a real R@1 lift from a local cross-encoder on conversational memory without bad latency?
  • Is there a non-LLM trick for the date questions that I'm missing?

Repo, runner and per-question outputs: https://github.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs

title: Rust Rewrites, Faster LLMs, AI App Security, Video Clipping, and Blender MCP
description:
The latest developer-tool signal is clustering around five practical workflows: incremental Rust rewrites, local LLM performance tuning, AI-app security, self-hosted video clipping, and AI-controlled Blender scenes.

The GitHub star counts below are point-in-time signals from November 20, not proof that a tool is production-ready. The useful next step is to test each project against a small, measurable workload.

Rust Anything: incremental rewrites with behavior checks

What it is: Rust Anything is a workflow for converting existing software to Rust incrementally. It records the original program’s behavior, rewrites one component, and compares the Rust implementation against that recorded behavior before moving forward.

Why now: The project was created on November 16 and reached 5,188 GitHub stars by the November 20 signal—the strongest traction among the newly created tools in this report. That interest reflects a real problem: full rewrites often introduce subtle regressions in error handling, edge cases, or side effects.

Tutorial angle: Build a small CLI or HTTP service and use it to demonstrate the complete workflow:

  1. Record normal requests, malformed inputs, error responses, and other important behavior.
  2. Rewrite one bounded component in Rust.
  3. Run the parity check against the recorded baseline.
  4. Stop and roll back when the first mismatch appears.
  5. Expand the rewrite only after the component passes.

For a CLI, record stdout, stderr, exit codes, and file-system changes. For an HTTP service, include status codes, response bodies, headers, and side effects. That makes the tutorial useful beyond Rust: it demonstrates how to make behavior-preserving refactoring measurable.

Difficulty: Intermediate

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything.git && cd rust-anything && ls.

Inference Optimisation Skill: benchmark local LLM configurations

What it is: The Inference Optimisation Skill is an agent skill that searches for better local LLM serving configurations. It can tune decoding, speculative decoding, prefill behavior, KV-cache settings, startup time, and time to first token.

Why now: Created on November 16, the project accumulated 1,260 stars by November 20. Developers are running local models for coding, chat, and private workloads, but raw tokens-per-second numbers rarely explain why one configuration feels faster than another.

Tutorial angle: Start with a benchmark before allowing the optimizer to change anything. Measure:

  • Time to first token
  • Inter-token latency
  • Total generation throughput
  • Peak memory usage
  • Model startup time
  • Output correctness on a fixed prompt set

Keep the model, hardware, prompt set, context length, and sampling settings fixed. Run the optimization skill, compare the best configuration with your baseline, and then replay the prompts. A faster setup that produces different answers is not an optimization—it is a regression.

This separation is especially important for speculative decoding and cache changes. Both can improve latency while also changing the behavior you are trying to measure.

Difficulty: Intermediate

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/sybil-solutions/inference-optimisation-skill.git && cd inference-optimisation-skill && ls.

Lovable: test authorization in AI-built applications

What it is: Lovable is an AI application builder that generates web applications along with supporting code and data flows. The generated happy path can work quickly, but that does not prove that its access controls are correct.

Why now: A published security investigation reported exposed passport details and more than 200,000 private messages. The related Hacker News submission reached 1,007 points and 382 comments, showing strong developer interest in the gap between “the app works” and “the app is safe.”

Tutorial angle: Build a deliberately small two-user application using fake data only:

  1. Create users Alice and Bob.
  2. Give each user private records.
  3. Try to read or mutate the other user’s record by changing the object ID.
  4. Inspect the generated API routes, database queries, and storage permissions.
  5. Add server-side object-level authorization.
  6. Turn the failed cross-user request into a regression test.

The important check is that authorization runs on the server. Hiding a button in the interface does not prevent a direct API request. Also test both read and write operations; write authorization failures are just as serious as data leaks.

Difficulty: Intermediate

  • Start today: Open https://lovable.dev and create a throwaway two-user project populated only with fake records.

PeakCut: self-hosted AI video clipping

What it is: PeakCut is a self-hosted AI clipping tool for long videos and live streams. It supports a bring-your-own-key model-provider workflow rather than requiring users to send media to the tool’s own hosted backend.

Why now: The project was created on November 14 and gained 1,337 stars by November 20, making it one of the fastest-rising new content-processing repositories in the report. Turning hours of recordings into a short set of publishable clips is still a repetitive manual task.

Tutorial angle: Self-host PeakCut, configure a supported model provider, and process two different inputs:

  • A recorded long-form video
  • A live-stream recording

Record the selected start and end timestamps, then compare them with clips you would have chosen manually. Measure selection quality, processing time, and the amount of manual trimming required.

The privacy section should be precise. Self-hosting the application keeps media and project data under your control, but requests to a third-party AI provider may still disclose the relevant media or extracted content. Show exactly what leaves the machine and document the provider’s retention policy.

Difficulty: Beginner

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/haziqahmedqasmi/PeakCut.git && cd PeakCut && ls.

Blender AI MCP Add-on: give an AI client access to Blender

What it is: The Blender AI MCP Add-on combines a Blender add-on with an MCP server. Compatible AI clients can inspect a scene, manipulate objects, and work through visual chat and scene tools.

Why now: Created on November 19, the repository collected 526 stars within the November 20 signal. Unlike a chat-only assistant, an MCP-connected client can inspect the current Blender scene and perform operations that normally require clicking and menu navigation.

Tutorial angle: Install the add-on and MCP server, connect an AI client, and request one visible change—for example, moving or duplicating a cube. Save a “before” render, inspect the resulting scene, and save an “after” render. Then test the failure modes:

  • The client cannot reach the MCP server
  • Blender and the client use different configurations
  • The working directory or asset path is incorrect
  • The requested operation changes more objects than intended

Start with one deterministic scene containing only a few objects. Once that works, test a more complex scene with collections, materials, and external assets.

  • Start today: Run git clone https://github.com/bookwjitchieni1986/blender-ai-mcp-addon.git && cd blender-ai-mcp-addon && ls.

title: Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types
description:
arXiv:2611.25108v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) systems deployed in border control and airport surveillance are constrained by a critical assumption: subjects are captured at close range, typically under one meter. No existing benchmark systematically addresses multi-distance capture, diverse environmental conditions, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion-based attacks, leaving deployed models underprepared for real-world scenarios. We introduce a video-based PAD dataset of 374,000+ frames from 261 unique identities collected across five standoff distances (1 m-100 m) under indoor and outdoor conditions using a DSLR camera (C) and a mobile sensor (M), with three-class labels: live, spoof, and props (occlusions); models are trained and evaluated on video clips rather than single frames. We fine-tune and benchmark four CNN architectures: MobileNetV3, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50. The higher-resolution DSLR maintains near-perfect spoof classification rate across all distances, while the lower-resolution mobile sensor degrades sharply beyond 50 m, with props classification rate dropping to 55% at 75 m for MobileNetV3. EfficientNet achieves the best overall performance (98.48% accuracy, ACER 2.01%). Generalization tests on unseen attack datasets yield 89-94% accuracy, validating cross-domain robustness. These results establish capture distance and sensor resolution as critical but underexplored axes of PAD difficulty. The dataset will be publicly released under an End-User License Agreement to support reproducible long-range PAD research.

title: {\lambda}Split: Self-Supervised Content-Aware Spectral Unmixing for Fluorescence Microscopy
description:
arXiv:2603.23647v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In fluorescence microscopy, spectral unmixing aims to recover individual fluorophore concentrations from spectral images that capture mixed fluorophore emissions. Since classical methods operate pixel-wise and rely on least-squares fitting, their performance degrades with increasingly overlapping emission spectra and higher levels of noise, suggesting that a data-driven approach that can learn and utilize a structural prior might lead to improved results. Learning-based approaches for spectral imaging do exist, but they are either not optimized for microscopy data or are developed for very specific cases that are not applicable to fluorescence microscopy settings. To address this, we propose {\lambda}Split, a physics-informed deep generative model that learns a conditional distribution over concentration maps using a hierarchical Variational Autoencoder. A fully differentiable Spectral Mixer enforces consistency with the image formation process, while the learned structural priors enable state-of-the-art unmixing and implicit noise removal. We demonstrate {\lambda}Split on 3 real-world datasets that we synthetically cast into a total of 66 challenging spectral unmixing benchmarks. We compare our results against a total of 10 baseline methods, including classical methods and a range of learning-based methods. Our results consistently show competitive performance and improved robustness in high noise regimes, when spectra overlap considerably, or when the spectral dimensionality is lowered, making {\lambda}Split a new state-of-the-art for spectral unmixing of fluorescent microscopy data. Importantly, {\lambda}Split is compatible with spectral data produced by standard confocal microscopes, enabling immediate adoption without specialized hardware modifications.
