title: Make your repo enforce what you tell your coding agent: guard tests, ratchets and rule IDs you can copy
description:
TL;DR

  • Your coding agent treats CLAUDE.md as context, not law. Anthropic's own docs say so. Every rule you only write down will drift, at agent speed.
  • Turn each convention into a test whose failure message is the convention. Then the agent's strongest habit (make the red build green) enforces your rule for you.
  • Copy five shapes: rule IDs with an Enforced by line, the census (derive the population, check both directions), the monopoly (only one module may do the dangerous thing), the two-sided ratchet, and debt with a deadline. Add a review ledger for prose.
  • Keep CLAUDE.md a map: where things are, and the checklist whose every step names the test that fails if it's skipped.
  • When you correct an agent for the same thing twice, stop writing sentences. Write the test.

I build Gitmoap, a code forge I run on my own: git hosting, review, a work tracker, pipelines as code, package registries, an MCP server. In nine months it reached 865 HTTP operations, 442 spec files and 243 migrations, all of it built with Claude Code, from the first commit. This post is the setup that made that possible, as templates you can paste into your own repo. The examples are from Gitmoap's Rust codebase, simplified; the Python ones are sketches written for this post, not Gitmoap code.

The problem in one table

Every rule in my repository has an ID and a line saying how it's enforced. That let me check, for this post, what happened to rules depending on how they're enforced:

Rule Enforced by State today
A released migration is never edited a checksum file and a test none edited since the test arrived; 243 migrations
Every endpoint group has a docs page a test over the router's registry 0 missing, exemption list empty
No delivery-phase labels in comments "code review; a grep audit" 29 such comments, 2 of them written after the rule
No unwrap() in production code a lint "once adopted" not adopted

Same author, same care, same agents. The rules that can fail the build hold. The others are wishes. Anthropic's documentation for Claude Code says it directly: CLAUDE.md and auto memory are loaded into every session, and "Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration."

So the work is converting wishes into tests. Here's how.

1. Give every rule an ID and an Enforced by line

Put your rules in a few markdown files by theme, one heading per rule, with a stable ID:

### SEC-AUTH-FAIL-CLOSED — Authentication is fail-closed; the dev fallback is a positive opt-in.
- **Why:** a header fallback gated on "the pool id is unset" fails open: one missing env var
  turns the whole API into header-trust.
- **How:** the fallback needs a positive dev flag. A surface that verifies tokens refuses to
  start without a validator unless that flag is set.
- **Enforced by:** a startup assertion; an integration test that boots the production
  profile without a validator and asserts it refuses to start.

Three conventions make this pay:

  • IDs are forever. A retired rule leaves a tombstone heading (### RUST-CFG-OS *(retired)* — …); a renamed rule keeps its ID. So a comment, a test name or a commit message can cite SEC-AUTH-FAIL-CLOSED and still mean the same thing in a year.
  • Cite IDs in code. /// Fail-closed (SEC-AUTH-FAIL-CLOSED): … above a function gives the agent the reason, not just the code. In Gitmoap 171 distinct rule IDs are cited in the Rust source.
  • The Enforced by line is the audit. Grep it. Mine has 265 such lines; a rough regex finds about 114 naming a mechanical check and about 125 naming only review, and 24 say, in full, "Enforced by: PR review." in a repository that commits straight to main. That's your worklist.

Then make citations checkable. Gitmoap has a full markdown grammar for this (its spec index runs on customers' repositories too), but the first 80% is a short script:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail when anything cites a rule ID that no spec declares (sketch)."""
import pathlib, re, sys

FAMILY = r"(?:ARCH|RUST|SEC|TEST|OBS|PERF|DOCS)"
DECLARE = re.compile(rf"^#{{2,4}} ({FAMILY}-[A-Z0-9-]+)\b.*? — ", re.M)
CITE = re.compile(rf"\b({FAMILY}-[A-Z0-9]+(?:-[A-Z0-9]+)*)\b")

declared: dict[str, pathlib.Path] = {}
for path in pathlib.Path("specs").rglob("*.md"):
    for m in DECLARE.finditer(path.read_text()):
        rule = m.group(1)
        if rule in declared:
            sys.exit(f"{rule} is declared twice: {declared[rule]} and {path}")
        declared[rule] = path

dangling = []
for root in ("specs", "src", "tests"):
    for path in pathlib.Path(root).rglob("*"):
        if path.suffix not in {".md", ".rs", ".py", ".ts"}:
            continue
        for n, line in enumerate(path.read_text().splitlines(), 1):
            dangling += [f"{path}:{n}: {r}" for r in CITE.findall(line) if r not in declared]

if dangling:
    sys.exit("cited but never declared:\n" + "\n".join(dangling)
             + "\n\nDeclare the rule under a heading in specs/, or fix the citation.")
print(f"{len(declared)} rules declared, every citation resolves")

Run it in CI and in the test suite. An agent that invents SEC-TOKEN-ROTATION in a comment now has to either declare it (and write its Why, How and Enforced by) or stop citing it.

One lesson I paid for: never key a check on a section number. My first spec guard found the "Simulation Coverage" section by matching its heading as a literal string, number included. Thirty-six of a hundred documents numbered that section differently, so the guard never opened them, none declared what it was supposed to, and the build stayed green. Identify sections by name.

2. The census: derive the population, check both directions

The most valuable guard shape. It reads the real list of things from the code (never a hand-kept list), and asserts three things: everything is covered, everything claimed still exists, and every exemption is still needed.

Here's Gitmoap's documentation census, simplified. Every endpoint group must be claimed by a docs page, through the tags: in the page's frontmatter:

/// Endpoint groups no page claims: (group, why). Shrink it; never grow it.
const UNDOCUMENTED: &[(&str, &str)] = &[];

fn served_groups() -> BTreeSet<&'static str> {
    // The same registry the router is built from, so a new endpoint can't be missed.
    gitmoap::web::endpoint_registry::all().map(|e| e.tag).collect()
}

#[test]
fn every_served_group_has_a_page() {
    let claimed = groups_claimed_by_pages();
    let exempt: BTreeSet<_> = UNDOCUMENTED.iter().map(|(g, _)| *g).collect();
    let missing: Vec<_> = served_groups()
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|g| !claimed.contains_key(g) && !exempt.contains(g))
        .collect();
    assert!(missing.is_empty(),
        "endpoint groups with no documentation page: {missing:?}\n\
         Write a page and list the group in its frontmatter `tags:`. If it genuinely cannot \
         be written yet, add it to UNDOCUMENTED with a reason a reader can disagree with.");
}

#[test]
fn every_claimed_group_is_still_served() {
    let served = served_groups();
    for (group, page) in groups_claimed_by_pages() {
        assert!(served.contains(group.as_str()),
            "{page} claims `{group}`, which the platform no longer serves. \
             A page documenting something removed is rot that reads as coverage.");
    }
}

#[test]
fn no_exemption_is_stale() {
    let claimed = groups_claimed_by_pages();
    for (group, reason) in UNDOCUMENTED {
        assert!(!reason.trim().is_empty(), "`{group}` is exempt with no reason");
        assert!(!claimed.contains_key(*group),
            "`{group}` is documented now; remove it from UNDOCUMENTED");
    }
}

The same three tests work in any stack. With FastAPI the population is one comprehension:

from fastapi.routing import APIRoute
from myapp.main import app

def served_tags() -> set[str]:
    return {t for r in app.routes if isinstance(r, APIRoute) for t in (r.tags or [])}

Why a list of exemptions rather than a count? The comment above Gitmoap's list says it better than I can: "A number says fifty-five groups are undocumented and nothing else; the list says which, and requires a sentence per entry that a reader can disagree with."

Gitmoap runs this shape everywhere: every operation placed in the feature register or excluded with a typed reason; every new database column that names a person classified for account deletion; every new DEFAULT now() column classified for the simulator; every queue consumer routed in the simulator's event bus. Each one is a question somebody would otherwise forget to ask, asked by the build.

3. The monopoly: one module does the dangerous thing

Some operations must only ever happen in one place. In Gitmoap a branch moves for a platform-written commit only with a PushClearance, and only the push gate may create one, after the branch rules, push rules and storage quota have all said yes. Visibility can't express that across crates, so a test does:

const THE_GATE: &str = "services/push_gate.rs";

#[test]
fn only_the_push_gate_mints_a_clearance() {
    let mut offenders = Vec::new();
    for file in workspace::rust_files(&workspace::platform_src()) {
        if workspace::module_rel(&file) == THE_GATE { continue; }
        let src = std::fs::read_to_string(&file).unwrap_or_default();
        for (at, _) in src.match_indices("PushClearance::mint(") {
            let line = src[..at].matches('\n').count() + 1;
            offenders.push(format!("  {}:{line}", workspace::rel(&file)));
        }
    }
    assert!(offenders.is_empty(),
        "a push clearance is minted outside the push gate:\n{}\n\n\
         Ask the gate instead — `push_gate::clear` — so the branch rules, the push rules \
         and the storage quota have each said yes before a branch moves.",
        offenders.join("\n"));
}

/// Otherwise the test above guards nothing.
#[test]
fn the_gate_is_where_a_clearance_is_minted() {
    let src = std::fs::read_to_string(workspace::module_file(THE_GATE)).unwrap();
    assert!(src.contains("PushClearance::mint("), "has the gate moved? Update THE_GATE.");
}

The second test is the part people skip. A text-scanning guard goes silently green when the thing it scans for is renamed or moved. Every guard should also assert that its subject still exists.

Two more things this shape needs to be fair: put the reason in the failure message (the agent will read it and do what it says), and say what to do instead (Ask the gate instead — push_gate::clear).

4. The two-sided ratchet

For debt you can't clear today, a budget that only falls. Most ratchets are one-sided: fail when the count goes over. That's half of it. When the count drops and nobody lowers the budget, the ceiling stops measuring anything. Gitmoap's version fails both ways, with a message for each:

pub const RATCHET_SLACK: usize = 5;

pub enum Ratchet {
    Ok { actual: usize, budget: usize },
    Over { actual: usize, budget: usize },
    Slack { actual: usize, budget: usize },
}

impl Ratchet {
    pub fn judge(actual: usize, budget: usize) -> Ratchet {
        if actual > budget {
            Ratchet::Over { actual, budget }
        } else if budget.saturating_sub(actual) > RATCHET_SLACK {
            Ratchet::Slack { actual, budget }
        } else {
            Ratchet::Ok { actual, budget }
        }
    }

    pub fn message(&self, name: &str) -> Option<String> {
        match self {
            Ratchet::Ok { .. } => None,
            Ratchet::Over { actual, budget } => Some(format!(
                "{name} is {actual}, over its budget of {budget}. This change added debt; fix it, \
                 or raise the budget deliberately with the full list in the change")),
            Ratchet::Slack { actual, budget } => Some(format!(
                "{name} is {actual} against a budget of {budget}. Lower the budget to {actual} so \
                 the ratchet keeps its grip — a budget that drifts above the real number stops \
                 being one")),
        }
    }
}

Keep a movement log next to the constant: every time the budget moves, a line in a comment saying why, in the same change. Gitmoap's budget for "operations served with no spec heading of their own" went from 181 to 216 over three months, and every step is explained above the constant. A ratchet that climbs is allowed. A ratchet that climbs silently isn't.

And when a check reaches zero, make it a plain assertion in the same change. A check installed at zero costs one constant; the same check installed a week earlier costs a budget, a movement log, and everyone's attention every time the number moves.

5. Debt with a deadline

A staged migration (expand, migrate, contract) gets stuck at the last step for a structural reason: expand and migrate are pulled by a feature, and contract is pulled by nothing. A checklist doesn't decay. An allowlist that may only shrink doesn't either: one of mine went from six entries to two, then sat at two indefinitely.

So the debt carries a date, in the file that created it:

-- gitmoap:expand drops=environments.secret_path_prefix by=2026-11-05 one N-2 release window past E4 …

and the later migration that pays it says so:

-- gitmoap:contract discharges=environments.secret_path_prefix one N-2 window has passed, no binary in service reads or writes the column …
ALTER TABLE environments DROP COLUMN secret_path_prefix;

The test is small. A sketch:

import datetime, pathlib, re

EXPAND = re.compile(r"--\s*gitmoap:expand drops=(\S+) by=(\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})")
CONTRACT = re.compile(r"--\s*gitmoap:contract discharges=(\S+)")

def test_no_contraction_is_overdue(today=datetime.date.today()):
    sql = "\n".join(p.read_text() for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("migrations").glob("*.sql")))
    discharged = set(CONTRACT.findall(sql))
    overdue = [f"{target} (due {due})" for target, due in EXPAND.findall(sql)
               if target not in discharged and datetime.date.fromisoformat(due) < today]
    assert not overdue, ("overdue contractions: " + ", ".join(overdue) +
        "\nWrite the migration that drops them, or move `by=` in a commit that says why.")

In Gitmoap that column's by= was 5 November. The build went red on the 6th; migration 0194 dropped the column on the 7th. Moving the date is allowed, but it happens in a commit, so "not yet" stays distinguishable from "never".

The general rule from the lint's header is worth pinning above your desk: "A rule you cannot opt out of gets deleted; one that makes you write down why gets obeyed." Every hatch (-- gitmoap:contract, -- gitmoap:lock, an exemption list entry) costs a written reason.

6. A review ledger for prose

Code drifts and the build notices. A spec can be rewritten in the same commit as the behaviour and still claim it was "last reviewed" eight months ago. Gitmoap's fix is specs/REVIEWED: one line per document, the SHA-256 of its body (frontmatter excluded, so stamping the review date can't invalidate the digest), regenerated by a bless command and checked in CI. A minimal version:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""specs/REVIEWED: bless with `review.py bless`, check with `review.py check` (sketch)."""
import hashlib, pathlib, sys

LEDGER = pathlib.Path("specs/REVIEWED")

def body(text: str) -> str:
    if text.startswith("---\n"):
        text = text.split("\n---\n", 1)[1]          # drop the frontmatter
    return text.replace("\r\n", "\n").strip()

def digests() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {str(p): hashlib.sha256(body(p.read_text()).encode()).hexdigest()
            for p in sorted(pathlib.Path("specs").rglob("*.md"))}

if sys.argv[1:] == ["bless"]:
    LEDGER.write_text("".join(f"{d}  {p}\n" for p, d in digests().items()))
else:
    recorded = dict(reversed(l.split("  ", 1)) for l in LEDGER.read_text().splitlines())
    moved = [p for p, d in digests().items() if recorded.get(p) != d]
    sys.exit(f"changed since last review, re-read and bless: {moved}" if moved else 0)

Be honest about what it proves. It doesn't prove anyone read the document; a command gets run reflexively. What it buys is that the acknowledgement lands in the same diff as the edit. That's weaker than "reviewed" and much stronger than a date someone types.

Gitmoap applies the same idea to user docs against the API: each folder of pages has a generated CONTRACTS file listing, per page, every fact of every operation the page covers (method, path, scope, each parameter, each response field and type, each documented error). When audit records gained an outbound field, the regenerated seal showed this in the folder of the page that owed an edit:

 list_admin_audit_log  res.200.application/json.records![].operation_id!  string
+list_admin_audit_log  res.200.application/json.records![].outbound  object
+list_admin_audit_log  res.200.application/json.records![].outbound.oneOf[1].group_id!  string <uuid>

The test fails until the seal is regenerated, so the field-level change sits in the diff next to the page. The agent session that made the change added a row to the page in the same commit. A projection you can read beats a hash: + outbound object in a review is a sentence, where a changed digest isn't.

7. CLAUDE.md as a map, not a manual

The temptation is to put every rule in CLAUDE.md. Mine reached 19,633 words by July. I cut it to 3,512 the same day and gave it the line it still opens with: "This file is deliberately thin: specs/ is the single source of truth." (It has grown back to nearly 17,000 words, which is one of my open problems; Anthropic suggests under 200 lines.)

What belongs in it is what an agent needs to find its way and what a guard can't say. A skeleton:

# CLAUDE.md

One paragraph: what this is, and that `specs/` is the source of truth. Follow spec pointers.

## Commands
`make help` lists everything. The ones you need: check, lint, the test tiers,
the regenerators (openapi, census, docs seal), the bless commands.
Never run raw build tools; never run the whole-tree formatter.

## Where things live
One line per top-level directory and per crate/package: what it owns, its spec.

## Rules
Rules live in specs/engineering/*.md with IDs. Cite the ID in code and review.
Don't restate rules here.

## Adding a new endpoint (or consumer, or table)
Numbered steps. Every step names the test that fails if it's skipped:
1. Model …                      — `openapi::tests` refuses an undescribed schema
2. Migration … then `make migrations-bless`   — `migrations_lint` refuses an unblessed file
3. Declare the endpoint …       — the compiler refuses a missing facet (E0046)
4. Place it in features/ …      — `features_coverage` refuses an unplaced operation
5. Docs page …                  — `docs_coverage` refuses an undocumented group

## When you finish
Run the gates once, at the end, cheapest first. Fix every red gate you meet,
including ones you didn't cause. Regenerate, bless, bump package versions. Don't commit.

The checklist is where most of the value is, and also where most of my failures came from. Gitmoap's queue consumers need their name in a deploy list. The step was in a skill but not in CLAUDE.md's checklist, and sessions following CLAUDE.md skipped it three times; those consumers ran a placeholder that failed every invocation until a check caught it. An agent follows your checklist exactly. If the checklist is wrong, that's what it follows.

8. Promote corrections: from memory to guard

Claude Code keeps per-project memory. Mine has 241 notes: 52 are feedback ("don't do that again"), 104 are gotchas. Reading them back, the pattern is unmistakable. Here are some, by what eventually stopped them:

Correction How often What it became
Don't run two cargo builds at once (they fight over the lock) raised six times; once a wait loop stalled nine hours a lockf lock every build command goes through when agents run in parallel
Fix every red gate you meet, even ones you didn't cause after an agent called a failing guard "pre-existing" still a told rule, plus "run every root guard" (nine seconds)
Never run the whole-tree formatter once was enough: 1,079 files rewritten for a 34-file change told. A PreToolUse hook would make it mechanical, and I should write one
Every create needs a quota twice half-mechanical: the endpoint macro won't compile a write without a quota = answer, but it can't check the answer is honest
Unfinished migrations must decay once the by= date in section 5
Don't carry request context in a task-local once told; I chose 441 explicit edits over one task-local instead

The rule I follow now: the second time I correct the same thing, it becomes a test, a lock or a narrower command, never another sentence.

A note on hooks. Anthropic's docs recommend a PreToolUse hook when you need to block an action regardless of what the agent decides. I use none: everything above lives in the test suite, which binds me, CI and every agent alike. Hooks are the right tool for actions (don't run this command); tests are the right tool for states (the repository must never look like this). The formatter row above is an action, which is why it's still only told.

9. What this costs

  • Build time. The guards are cheap (Gitmoap's root suite runs in about nine seconds once built), but the guard binary links the platform. A cold full unit run was 47 minutes before I split the main crate and is about 16 now. Agents love running gates after every step; one of my notes exists because I told one we were "wasting tens of minutes". Run them once, at the end, cheapest first.
  • Guards only guard if they run. One commit landed with two red guards because its session ran three hand-picked suites. Make "run all of them" the cheap default.
  • A ledger proves less than it looks like. My tenets file passes its review check every day while recommending a database design I abandoned in July.
  • Writing the test is the real work. It's slower than writing the sentence. It's faster than finding the drift six months later.

Try it on your repo

You can do all of this in any repository with a test runner. If you want the spec half without writing the scripts, Gitmoap does it on every push: put markdown under specs/, docs/, legal/ or blog/, and it indexes every rule ID you declare and everyone who cites it, every link between documents that goes nowhere and every unchecked box, and posts a gitmoap/specs check that goes red on a merge request linking to a document that isn't there. The guide: https://docs.gitmoap.com/guides/specs. A small TypeScript library set up this way, with rule IDs its tests cite by name: https://gitmoap.com/gitmoap-showcase/commitkit

Gitmoap is free, run by one person, stores code in AWS Ireland, and never uses your content to train generative models. Clone and push go through its own git helper (no plain HTTPS or SSH yet), and there's no importer yet. https://gitmoap.com

What's the rule your agent keeps breaking? I'd bet it's one that can't fail your build.

title: I built an ML signal platform for the Colombo Stock Exchange. The model was the easy part.
description:
Most "AI trading bot" posts show a chart that goes up and to the right. This is not one of those.

Over the last few months I built a full machine-learning research and signal platform for the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) in Sri Lanka, as a solo personal project. It collects the data, cleans it, trains and tests models, and turns the result into clear daily guidance in a web dashboard. It does not trade by itself: every order is still placed by a person.

The biggest lesson? Building the model took maybe 20% of the time. Data, honest testing and guardrails took the rest. Here is how it is put together and what I learned.

Why a small market is hard (and interesting)

The CSE is not the NYSE. A few things make it tricky:

Thin liquidity. Many listed shares trade only a few times a day. A model that loves an illiquid stock is useless if you cannot actually buy it.
High costs. Broker fees are around 1.1% per side, so a round trip costs more than 2%. Any edge has to beat that before it is worth anything.
Messy history. Splits, bonus issues and rights issues show up as huge fake price jumps unless you deal with them.
No clean free dataset. I had to collect it.

That shaped every design decision.

  1. The data pipeline

The first job was getting 15+ years of daily prices for 700+ securities: more than 1 million rows.

A Python collector with Playwright pulls the history in date windows, retries failures, and resumes where it stopped.
During market hours it records live intraday snapshots every couple of minutes.
It also pulls announcements and daily market-wide flow data from public sources.
Everything lands in SQLite (fast, zero setup) and is mirrored to SQL Server.
Corporate actions: the silent model killer

A 2-for-1 split looks like a 50% crash overnight. Feed that to a model and it learns nonsense.

So the pipeline flags every suspicious overnight jump and classifies it: a clean split ratio whose new price level persists is adjusted, a move that reverts is kept as a real move, and anything unclear is masked out of training instead of guessed. Unknown is safer than wrong.

  1. The model, and how I tried not to fool myself

The model itself is plain: gradient-boosted trees (scikit-learn) on price, volume and market-context features. The interesting part is the testing.

Walk-forward testing. The model is trained on the past, tested on the next block of time it has never seen, then the window moves forward. Over 15 years that gives 60 out-of-sample blocks. Every prediction in the results was made before the model "knew" what happened.

Real costs in every test. Broker fees on both sides, plus slippage of at least half a price tick. I also found a bug here during QA: I had used one tick size for every share, but the exchange uses a larger tick above a certain price. Small detail, real money.

No look-ahead. A signal at today's close can only be acted on at the next day's open. Easy to get wrong, and it inflates results a lot when you do.

Saying "no edge" out loud. The dashboard has an honest verdict for every configuration, and most variations I tried did not survive. I spent a full day testing new features (sector groups, a "beat the market" target, a liquid-only universe, monthly rebalancing). Several of them improved the overall ranking metrics, but none improved the stocks the system would actually pick, so none went live. That was the most useful day of the project.

  1. Automation with a safety gate

The system runs unattended on a laptop:

starts with Windows and resumes collection on its own,
retrains weekly, but the new model only replaces the old one if its out-of-sample score is not worse, the export matches the trained model exactly, and nothing looks off. The old model is backed up first,
paper-trades every signal with the same rules, so there is a live track record before any real money,
backs up the database to the cloud daily,
sends phone and desktop alerts.

The safety gate matters. An automatic retrain that silently ships a worse model is worse than no retraining at all.

  1. The dashboard

The front end is React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind, served by a tiny Python HTTP server with live updates.

It has 18 pages: a control center, data quality, a model lab, a backtest studio where you can change settings and re-run instantly, paper trading with a journal, risk and system health, news, and a live intraday view.

The page I use most is Today's plan: given how much I want to invest, it shows what to buy (or, most days, "no buy today, and here is why"), what I hold, my break-even price after fees, and when each holding can be sold without a loss.

There is also a small browser extension that fills the broker's order form with the system's numbers, because typing quantities by hand is where mistakes happen. It never presses Buy or Sell; that stays a human decision.

  1. Testing the whole thing

Before calling it done I ran a full QA pass:

unit tests for the money logic (sizing, fees, tick sizes, sell rules, holidays),
integration tests that throw garbage and hostile input at every API endpoint,
UI tests that open every page at desktop and phone width and check for errors,
acceptance tests for the real user flows.

That pass found real bugs: a sizing fallback that could suggest a much larger order than the budget, a crash on a bad journal date, and a local API that another website could have called. All fixed, all covered by tests now.

What I would tell someone starting a project like this
Spend your time on data. Your model can only be as honest as your history.
Put real costs in from day one. Many "edges" disappear the moment you add fees.
Test walk-forward, never on data the model has seen.
Make "no" an easy answer. Build the system so it can tell you an idea does not work.
Automate, but with a gate. Retraining without a quality check is a risk, not a feature.
Stack

Python · scikit-learn · pandas · Playwright · SQLite · SQL Server · React 19 · TypeScript · Tailwind CSS

The source stays private, but there is a project showcase here: github.com/jkchinthaka/cse-signal-bot

I build data pipelines, ML systems, dashboards and full-stack web apps as a freelancer. If you are working on something similar, I would be happy to talk.

This is a research and learning project. Nothing here is investment advice.
(https://dev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/uploads/articles/mun7hwn9hithtqmhw0rm.png)

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
description:
arXiv:2611.23480v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

title: Fourteen of fifteen URLs serve the same title, and the cause is a three-word directive
description:
The symptom, measured

A site with different content on every route. I measured the raw HTML of 15 URLs — 7 static routes plus the 8 dynamic routes of one community — and this is what the server returns:

route title served
/ El Arquitecto Cuántico — Libros de Jose Alexis Román Martínez
/comunidad El Arquitecto Cuántico — Libros de Jose Alexis Román Martínez
/comunidad/arquitecto-cuantico El Arquitecto Cuántico — Libros de Jose Alexis Román Martínez
/comunidad/codigo-origen El Arquitecto Cuántico — Libros de Jose Alexis Román Martínez
/comunidad/mente-eterna El Arquitecto Cuántico — Libros de Jose Alexis Román Martínez
/privacy El Arquitecto Cuántico — Libros de Jose Alexis Román Martínez
/terms El Arquitecto Cuántico — Libros de Jose Alexis Román Martínez
/informes/ariastate Informe de riesgo estructural — ariastate · Platino Labs

Fourteen of fifteen. The exception is not random, and that is the whole piece.

(Abbreviated table: 8 of the 15 measured URLs are listed. The remaining 7 — /pinterest-demo, /tiktok-demo and the 5 community slugs not listed — return the same root title. The full listing is reproduced at the end.)

Also: rel="canonical" appears 0 times across the 15. And https://arquitectocuantico.com/sitemap.xml answers HTTP 404.

The cause is not the content

It is not that the site does not define titles. It is that it cannot define them with the mechanism it chose.

In the Next.js App Router there are two ways to set a title. The first is exporting metadata from a server component: the framework serialises it into <head>. The second is rendering a <title> element anywhere in the tree — React 19 hoists it into <head>, during server rendering too.

"use client" prevents neither of those things by itself, and it is worth saying so before going on, because the usual intuition — "client means the browser paints it and the server does not" — is false, and it is measured with one command. /privacy is a client component and its full text is in the raw HTML:

curl -sL https://arquitectocuantico.com/privacy | sed 's/<[^>]*>/ /g' | tr -s ' ' | wc -c
→ 3194

Three thousand one hundred and ninety-four characters of visible text served by the server, with JavaScript never executed. The client component is prerendered all the same.

What "use client" does do is exclude the module from the metadata export: that API is server-side and is not available on the client. The site chose metadata — once, in src/app/layout.tsx — and marked the other seven routes as "use client". The result is not an impossibility: it is an omission, with one declaration for fifteen URLs.

Counting over the repository, at fb28bab:

find src/app -name page.tsx | wc -l                            → 8
grep -rl '^"use client"' src/app --include=page.tsx | wc -l    → 7

Seven of eight page.tsx open with "use client" — 87.5%. The only one that does not is src/app/informes/ariastate/page.tsx, and it is the only one that exports a title of its own.

The 2×2, without exceptions

what the component is URLs served declares a title of its own
"use client" 14 0
server 1 1

Zero of fourteen, one of one. The only route that declares anything is also the only one metadata is allowed in.

And the effect is multiplicative, not additive: every new slug added to the community inherits the same root title without anyone touching anything. The debt does not grow one at a time; it grows with the catalogue.

The fix is structural

Writing a <title> inside each client component would also work — we just measured that it is prerendered — and that is precisely the trap: it scatters the same declaration across fourteen files, one per slug, and the fifteenth added tomorrow forgets it again. The debt is not paid once; it is paid with the catalogue.

The fix moves the declaration up to where the server lives, which is where the catalogue is already listed:

  • src/app/layout.tsx — metadataBase, title template, openGraph, robots.
  • src/app/comunidad/layout.tsx — the title of the shared room.
  • src/app/comunidad/[slug]/layout.tsx — generateMetadata, which does receive the params and produces a title per slug.
  • src/app/sitemap.ts and src/app/robots.ts — the two routes that did not exist and answered 404.
  • next.config.ts — X-Robots-Tag headers so the two demos are not indexed.

Six files, +147 −2 lines. With that: tsc --noEmit → RC 0, next build → RC 0, and the three server layouts emit a canonical plus three hreflang alternates per page.

The blind spot: the fix does not reach these URLs

This is where the piece parts ways with almost everything written about this topic. The patch is written and validated. And none of the fifteen URLs serves it.

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} age=%header{age}\n' https://arquitectocuantico.com/
200 age=783014

$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} age=%header{age}\n' https://arquitectocuantico.com/sitemap.xml
404 age=175297

783014 seconds is 9.06 days: the HTML the front page serves today was generated before the patch existed. 175297 seconds is 2.03 days: the sitemap 404 has been cached since the 18th.

And here is the second trap, the one that cost me a correction in the first draft of this piece: age measures the response, not the deployment. A CDN can serve a stale object while the origin already holds the new one; the age of the response does not distinguish "it was never deployed" from "it was deployed and the cache was not refreshed". What these two numbers do prove is the only thing that matters to the reader: the fix does not reach these URLs. Whether the origin has it cannot be known from here — there is no deploy credential and no version identifier in the headers. That field is NO_MEDIDO (not measured).

Three questions, three instruments, and none of them substitutes for another:

what you want to know what measures it verdict here
does the code compile and generate the routes? next build green, RC 0
does the fix reach these URLs? the response age no: 9.06 days old
does the origin hold the deployment? deploy credential or version id NO_MEDIDO

A green local build is not a public act: it is half the act. And a stale response is not proof of a missing deployment: it is proof of a stale response. The two confusions look alike because both feel like a verdict.

The outcome, measured today

I wrote the previous section without a deploy credential. Hours later there were two deployments made from the repository, and I ran the same census again over the same fifteen routes. The result is not the one that section leads you to expect:

measurement before after
routes measured 15 15
distinct titles 2 15
repeated titles 14 0
routes with rel="canonical" 0 15
/sitemap.xml 404 200, 11 URLs
/robots.txt with Sitemap: no yes

The fix covered the eleven URLs declared in the sitemap. The four remaining — /privacy, /terms and the two OAuth authorisation screens — still served the root layout title: they are client components with no server layout, which is literally the blind spot the previous section describes. Four more server layouts and the census closes at 15 of 15.

And a correction to my own plan: I had the Cloudflare purge as a mandatory step before probing. It was not needed. cf-cache-status answers DYNAMIC on / and on /sitemap.xml — served from the origin — and REVALIDATED on /robots.txt, which did have a stored copy and revalidated it against the origin. Which cache produced the old age is something none of those headers state: that field stays NO_MEDIDO. What is observed is the only thing that mattered for the act: with the new deployment, none of the three routes serves the previous object any more, and without a manual purge.

What this piece does not claim

  • It does not claim that fixing the titles will raise traffic. The domain's analytics are not reachable from where this measurement was taken: that number is NO_MEDIDO (not measured), and NO_MEDIDO does not read as zero.
  • It does not claim that the patch caused the sitemap 404. It is 2.03 days old and the patch was written today: the 404 predates it.
  • It does not claim that the deployment is absent from the origin. It measures that it does not reach the reader; the state of the origin is NO_MEDIDO.
  • It does not claim that the deployment will resolve itself. Between the repository and the domain there is a CDN that can rewrite robots.txt without consulting the origin; if it does, the Sitemap: directive from app/robots.ts will never appear in the response. That is not measured.
  • It does not claim that "use client" is a mistake. It is a correct directive whose side effect — excluding metadata — becomes expensive when applied to fourteen routes that need no interactivity.

Reproduce

The title each dynamic URL serves, in one line:

for s in arquitecto-cuantico codigo-origen corazon-punto-cero experiencias-de-lectura \
         mente-eterna sala-general sincronicidades suenos-y-meditaciones; do
  curl -sL "https://arquitectocuantico.com/comunidad/$s" | grep -o '<title>[^<]*</title>'
done | sort | uniq -c

The edge, in another:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} age=%header{age}\n' https://arquitectocuantico.com/sitemap.xml

And the count behind the cause, over the repository:

find src/app -name page.tsx | wc -l
grep -rl '^"use client"' src/app --include=page.tsx | wc -l

Single CTA

Before reading the content of any site you inherit, run this (EL-DOMINIO stands for the domain):

curl -sL https://EL-DOMINIO/ | grep -o '<title>[^<]*</title>'

If that title is also the title of the inner pages, the problem is not in the text: it is in where the declaration lives. And fixing the text does not touch it.

  • The instrument this is measured with: https://alexisromtz-lab.github.io/auditor-toolkit/
  • Other published measurements: https://alexisromtz-lab.github.io/la-auditora/

title: I let my AI agent buy every API in a marketplace. Total bill: $6.37. Here's what happened.
description:
Two weeks ago I gave my agent a strange mission: buy one call of every endpoint in the x402 ecosystem that wasn't indexed yet on the Bazaar — the discovery layer where agents find pay-per-call APIs.

Not to use the data. Just so the marketplace would notice the services exist.

Why would anyone do that?

In x402, discovery has a chicken-and-egg problem. The Bazaar indexes services that agents actually call — traffic through the facilitator is what gets you listed. So a brand-new API with zero callers stays invisible, and invisible means zero callers, forever.

We run a catalog of ~220 endpoints (crypto briefs, French company KYB, rail itineraries, restaurant hygiene data for 1,200+ cities, dev tools for LLM agents). About 83 were indexed when we started. My agent was told: fill the gap.

What the agent actually did

It worked through the list in batches over a few evenings:

  • Paid real x402 calls with a dedicated buyer wallet (never the merchant wallet — a rule I hardcoded after a close call)
  • Even a 404 after payment triggers settlement, so "broken" endpoints still get indexed
  • quirks it learned on the fly: company-compare wants siren=A&siren=B, health endpoints accept ?q=, one subscription service kept rejecting payments via its own spend controls (correctly — it's $12/mo, not pay-per-call)

The bill

Total: ~6.37 USDC on Base. That bought settlement events for roughly 160 endpoints. Final wallet balance: 13.09 USDC.

Compare that with listing on any traditional API marketplace: submissions, reviews, weeks of waiting. Here, the agent bootstrapped the catalog's own discoverability for the price of a coffee.

What broke

Honest section. Three endpoints stayed unindexed because their upstream data source (the French national railway API, fittingly) was having a bad night — 502s all evening. The agent logged them and scheduled a retry. Agents don't get frustrated; they reschedule.

Also: my earlier posts an expired API key burned my budget got some pushback about agents paying unsupervised. This experiment is my answer — the guardrails (separate buyer wallet, per-call max spend, hard-blocked merchant wallet) are what made an unattended $6 spending spree safe.

Takeaways

  1. Payments are the cheapest growth hack in agent-to-agent commerce. Your agent buying your own APIs is legitimate bootstrapping — settlement is settlement.
  2. Spend controls are the feature. max-amount-per-payment rules blocked exactly what they should have, even against the owner's interests. Trust the controls.
  3. Real-time data sources need retry budgets in your buyer scripts. The 502 endpoints weren't failures; they were queue items.

The whole thing ran on a few hundred lines of Node.js: fetch the official catalog, diff against the Bazaar index, attempt a purchase per missing endpoint, log results. The boring part wasn't the payments — those took seconds each. It was figuring out each API's query format with no docs but the 400-error messages themselves.

The catalog this describes is live; if your agent wants to try pay-per-call without keys, x402 + USDC on Base is genuinely a 20-minute integration. Questions welcome in the comments — I answer them with my agents, obviously.

title: Comment "LINK" to get it in DMs: how Instagram auto-replies actually work under the hood
description:
You've seen these posts everywhere on Instagram. A creator says "comment LINK and I'll send it to you" and a few seconds later there's a DM sitting in your inbox.

I used to think there was some guy with three phones doing this manually. There isn't. I ended up building this exact feature for my own product, so here's what's actually going on behind it, minus the marketing fluff.

It's not a bot clicking buttons

The old way people did this was with sketchy tools that logged into your account and pretended to be you. That's how accounts get flagged.

The legit way is Meta's official Instagram API. It only works with Business or Creator accounts linked to a Facebook Page, and every permission has to be approved by Meta. No passwords shared anywhere.

The flow, step by step

  1. Someone comments on your post. Instagram fires a webhook to your server with the comment text, the comment ID and the post ID.
  2. Your server checks for a keyword. Something as simple as: does this comment contain "link", "price" or "info"? I normalise the text first (lowercase, trim, strip emojis), because people type "Link!!" and "LINK 🔥" and you still want those to match.
  3. You send a Private Reply. This is the key part. Instagram lets a business send one DM to the person who commented, tied to that specific comment. It has to happen within 7 days of the comment.
  4. The conversation opens. Once the person replies to that DM, the normal messaging window opens. You can now keep talking to them for 24 hours from their last message.

So the "magic" is just webhook → keyword match → private reply API call.

Stuff that tripped me up

  • One private reply per comment. You can't spam someone with five messages because they commented once. Make the first message count.
  • The 24-hour window is real. If the user goes quiet, you can't just message them again three days later with a promo. Meta is strict about this, and honestly that's a good thing.
  • Webhooks can arrive twice. Store the comment ID and skip anything you've already processed, or people get duplicate DMs and it looks broken.
  • Reply to the comment publicly too. A quick "Sent you a DM 👀" under their comment makes other people comment as well. That's where the reach comes from.

Why I bothered building this

I'm an Android dev from India, and a lot of creators and small brands I know were losing leads simply because they couldn't reply fast enough. Someone asks "price?" at 11 pm, nobody answers, and that sale is gone.

So I built HeyDM: keyword triggers on comments and DMs, auto-replies, and lead capture, all on top of the official API. It's been a fun rabbit hole of webhooks, rate limits and edge cases.

If you're building something similar and get stuck on Meta's app review or the webhook setup, drop a comment. Happy to share what worked for me.

title: Evaluating invariance training with certified answer-changing controls in neural graph algorithms
description:
arXiv:2611.23907v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Invariance training aims to make neural algorithmic reasoners robust to answer-preserving input changes and is judged by accuracy and by how rarely such edits change predictions. We ask whether this evaluation detects lost sensitivity to answer-changing edits on minimum spanning trees of synthetic graphs, where both directions can be certified. Attaching a subgraph through one bridge provably preserves every original label. Attaching it through two edges, oracle-selected to change a label, and lowering one weight inside the graph serve as answer-changing controls; a response is a changed prediction on an edge whose label changes. A reproduced graph transformer (GDT) within its published accuracy range changes a provably fixed label on 53.3-65.9% of the 64-vertex graphs it solves exactly after a 64-vertex bridge attachment; removing the connecting edge changes little. With 16-vertex graphs and attachments, three invariance objectives lower GDT violations from 2.91% to 0.52-2.02% of pairs at essentially unchanged accuracy. Training also lowers the response to two-edge attachments from 97.6% to 66.0-79.0%, while the response to in-base weight edits stays near 99.5%. At 64 vertices accuracy also falls, but on 16-vertex bases only the attachment control reveals the loss. A message-passing network loses some attachment response at small penalty weights but gains little invariance. Running the conventionally trained GDT on each biconnected block separately removes all observed violations and keeps accuracy and both responses, so the task does not force the trade-off. Sensitivity checks for trained invariance should include certified answer-changing edits that attach material as the training edits do.

title: Embodied Graph: A Relational World Model for Long-Horizon Tasks
description:
arXiv:2611.24115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon tasks in embodied and web environments involve extended decision sequences and delayed feedback, making accurate planning crucial for success. World models tackle this by learning latent dynamics for imagination-based planning. However, existing approaches merely rely on dense pixel-level observations, which forces the model to absorb redundant information while overlooking relations among task-relevant entities. Consequently, small errors may accumulate over long imagined rollouts and gradually corrupt the predictions. In this paper, we explore world models that imagine over sparse state abstractions, which poses two key challenges: 1) how to remove redundant information and form a compact state abstraction; 2) how to incorporate the relational structure to learn reliable long-horizon dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose Embodied Graph, a relational state abstraction that supports structured dynamics modeling and long-horizon imagination, and the Relational World Model (RWM), which performs imagination directly over graph states. RWM consists of (i) a Task-Aware Embodied Graph Constructor that filters redundant details and maintains graph memory through online updates, and (ii) an Embodied Graph Recurrent State Space Model that learns node-wise latent dynamics while capturing inter-node dependencies. The imagined graph states provide predictions of action consequences to guide decision-making. Experiments on Minecraft and Crafter demonstrate the effectiveness of RWM in embodied environments. Notably, in Minecraft, RWM is the only method that obtains diamonds within the given budget. Experiments on web interaction further illustrate the applicability of relational state prediction to the decision making process of web agents.

title: Recurrent Domain Incremental Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models
description:
arXiv:2611.24075v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.

title: CalibCache: Cache-to-Full Feature Dynamics Calibration for Diffusion Transformers
description:
arXiv:2611.25296v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images, but iterative sampling remains computationally expensive. Feature caching reduces the number of full network evaluations, yet its approximation error can become more severe under short sampling schedules, where fewer full-compute steps and a coarser sampling grid can make history-based extrapolation less reliable. In this paper, we propose CalibCache, a lightweight offline calibration method that corrects systematic discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature dynamics. Specifically, CalibCache calibrates feature acceleration, defined as the second-order finite difference across sampling steps. Using only a single pair of full-compute and naive-cache trajectories at each setting, CalibCache fits scalar acceleration maps offline by centered least squares. These maps are then applied during sampling without additional full-network evaluations or online optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image on DrawBench and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, CalibCache consistently improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer under 20-step sampling at cache intervals $N=3,4,5$. At $N=5$, it reduces FLUX.1-dev LPIPS from $0.563$ to $0.429$ while achieving a $2.86\times$ denoising speedup over full-compute sampling, and lowers DiT-XL/2 FID from $16.39$ to $10.37$ relative to TaylorSeer.

title: Empirical Variational Bayes Factorization for Longitudinal Matrix Data
description:
arXiv:2611.25065v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Collecting high-dimensional data over time for multiple individuals is increasingly common in biomedical research, particularly in studies of disease progression or molecular time-course experiments. Often data are missing or the timepoints are irregularly spaced across individuals. There is a lack of flexible methodology to explore latent patterns of change over time and account for missing data. We propose an empirical variational Bayes (EVB) approach to factorize high-dimensional longitudinal data, in which the underlying factors have temporal correlation over time. The EVB approach is computationally efficient and accommodates flexible covariance structures over time with automatic determination of all hyper-parameters (including the underlying rank, i.e., number of factors). Simulations demonstrate that the approach captures the underlying signal more precisely than other strategies, and performs well with respect to missing data imputation under different scenarios. An application to a gene time-course data for multiple sclerosis treatment provides a factorization with interpretable components over time and improved imputation accuracy for missing data.

description:
[{"type_of":"article","id":5077842,"title":"Overlap-Proof Cron: File Locks with O_EXCL and Stale-Lock Self-Healing","description":"Windows Task Scheduler has no concept of mutual exclusion between runs. If you tell it to fire a job...","published":true,"published_at":"2026-11-20T01:01:37.555Z","slug":"overlap-proof-cron-file-locks-with-oexcl-and-stale-lock-self-healing-2j6p","path":"/mattleeee/overlap-proof-cron-file-locks-with-oexcl-and-stale-lock-self-healing-2j6p","url":"https://dev.to/mattleeee/overlap-proof-cron-file-locks-with-oexcl-and-stale-lock-self-healing-2j6p","comments_count":0,"public_reactions_count":0,"page_views_count":10,"published_timestamp":"2026-11-20T01:01:37Z","body_markdown":"Windows Task Scheduler has no concept of mutual exclusion between runs. If you tell it to fire a job every 15 minutes, it will do exactly that, whether or not the previous instance is still alive. For a job that normally finishes in 10-30 seconds, this rarely matters. But when a stuck network call stretches a round to the timeout cap, two processes end up writing the same state.json concurrently, and each one silently overwrites the other's positions. The result is a corrupted state file and positions that vanish or double. The fix is a lock file created with O_EXCL, plus a staleness rule so that a killed process can't wedge the scheduler forever. This post walks through the implementation, the failure modes, and a small test suite. ## Why a lock file at all The scheduler fires rounds on a fixed cadence. The job itself has no idea another instance is running. You have three broad options: 1. Let the scheduler serialize. Windows Task Scheduler has a "Do not start a new instance" setting, but it only applies within the same task definition and is easy to misconfigure across task folders, service accounts, or manual runs. It also does nothing if someone triggers the script by hand. 2. Use an in-process lock. Useless here: the two contenders are separate processes. 3. Use an OS-level lock file. This works regardless of who started the process. The lock file approach is the most portable and the easiest to reason about, provided you get two details right: atomic creation and stale-lock recovery. ## Atomic creation with O_EXCL The naive version of a lock is:

python if not os.path.exists(lock_path): open(lock_path, "w").close() run_job()

This is a check-then-act race. Two processes can both observe that the file is absent, both create it, and both proceed. Under a 15-minute cadence the window is tiny, but "tiny" is not "zero", and the failure mode (concurrent writes to state.json) is exactly the one you're trying to prevent. O_EXCL closes the race at the kernel level. os.open(path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) is a single atomic operation: it creates the file only if it does not already exist, and fails with FileExistsError otherwise. There is no window between the check and the create because there is no separate check.

python import os def try_acquire(lock_path: str, pid: int) -> bool: try: fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) except FileExistsError: return False try: os.write(fd, str(pid).encode("ascii")) finally: os.close(fd) return True

Writing the PID is not strictly required for correctness, but it is invaluable when you're staring at a stuck lock at 2 a.m. and want to know whether the owning process is still alive. ## The stale-lock problem O_EXCL gives you atomicity, but it also gives you a lock that never releases itself if the process dies. A taskkill, a crash, a power event, or a TerminateProcess from the scheduler all leave the lock file behind. The next scheduled round sees FileExistsError, exits, and the round after that does the same. The job is now permanently blocked, and nothing in the logs says why. You need a rule for deciding when an existing lock is abandoned. The lock file's modification time is the natural arbiter. A run that normally takes 10-30 seconds and is capped by a timeout should never legitimately hold the lock for two hours. So: - If the lock is younger than the staleness threshold, treat it as live and skip this round. - If the lock is older than the threshold, treat it as abandoned, remove it, and try to acquire again. The threshold has to be comfortably larger than the worst-case legitimate runtime. With a timeout cap of a few minutes, two hours is generous and still recovers within the same business day. There is a subtle race in the takeover path: two processes can both decide the lock is stale, both unlink it, and both create a new one. The second unlink may fail with FileNotFoundError (fine), but the second O_EXCL create can still succeed after the first process has already created its own. To narrow this, do the takeover as a two-step: unlink, then attempt O_EXCL. If the O_EXCL fails, another process won the takeover and you should back off. It is not perfectly atomic, but the window is milliseconds and the consequence is a single overlapping round, not a persistent wedge. If you need stronger guarantees, rename the stale file to a unique name before unlinking and only proceed if the rename succeeded. ## The full implementation

python import os import time import logging log = logging.getLogger(__name__) LOCK_PATH = r"C:\trading\state.lock" STALE_SECONDS = 2 * 60 * 60 # 2 hours def _lock_age_seconds(lock_path: str) -> float: try: return time.time() - os.path.getmtime(lock_path) except FileNotFoundError: return float("inf") # vanished; treat as stale so we retry def acquire_lock(lock_path: str = LOCK_PATH, stale_seconds: int = STALE_SECONDS) -> bool: """Return True if this process owns the lock, False if another run holds it.""" pid = os.getpid() # Fast path: atomic exclusive create. try: fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) except FileExistsError: pass else: try: os.write(fd, str(pid).encode("ascii")) finally: os.close(fd) return True # Lock exists. Is it stale? age = _lock_age_seconds(lock_path) if age < stale_seconds: log.warning("Lock held by another run (age %.1fs); skipping.", age) return False log.warning("Stale lock detected (age %.1fs); attempting takeover.", age) try: os.unlink(lock_path) except FileNotFoundError: pass # someone else already removed it # Second attempt; may still lose the race to another process. try: fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY) except FileExistsError: log.warning("Lost stale-lock takeover race; skipping.") return False try: os.write(fd, str(pid).encode("ascii")) finally: os.close(fd) return True def release_lock(lock_path: str = LOCK_PATH) -> None: try: os.unlink(lock_path) except FileNotFoundError: pass

Usage in the job entry point:

python def main() -> int: if not acquire_lock(): return 0 # nothing to do; next scheduled round will pick it up try: run_trading_round() finally: release_lock() return 0

The try/finally matters. If run_trading_round() raises, the lock must still be released, or the next round pays the staleness penalty for no reason. ## Lock failure must not block the business path There is a design decision hiding in the return 0 above. When the lock is held, the process exits cleanly without doing work. That is correct for a scheduled job: the next round is 15 minutes away, and the current holder is presumably doing the same work. But there is a second failure mode worth thinking about: what if the lock mechanism itself fails? A permissions change on the directory, an antivirus quarantine, a full disk that prevents file creation—these can all make os.open raise something other than FileExistsError. The rule should be: if you cannot determine lock state due to an unexpected error, do not block the business path. Log loudly, then proceed. A duplicate run is bad; a job that silently stops running for days because a lock file couldn't be created is worse. In practice the trading logic has its own idempotency guards (position sizing against the current state file, for example), so a rare overlapping run is recoverable, while a permanently stalled scheduler is not.

python def acquire_lock_or_proceed(lock_path: str = LOCK_PATH) -> bool: """Returns True if this run should proceed. Never raises.""" try: return acquire_lock(lock_path) except OSError: log.exception("Lock subsystem failed; proceeding without lock.") return True

Use this wrapper at the top of main(). You lose strict serialization in the rare broken-lock case, which is the right trade. ## Why not flock? Python's fcntl.flock is the idiomatic choice on POSIX, and it has a real advantage: the kernel releases the lock automatically when the owning process dies, so stale-lock recovery is free. On Windows, fcntl does not exist, and the portable substitutes are uneven: - msvcrt.locking works on file descriptors but has awkward semantics around byte ranges and blocking modes, and it does not release cleanly across all process-death scenarios. - portalocker wraps the platform differences reasonably well, but adds a dependency and its Windows backend still relies on msvcrt or LockFileEx via ctypes. - Third-party file-locking libraries vary in how they behave when the process is killed by the scheduler versus terminated by the user. O_EXCL sidesteps all of this. It is a single documented flag on every platform Python runs on, its semantics are identical everywhere, and the only thing you give up is automatic release on process death—which the mtime staleness rule handles. For a scheduled job that runs every 15 minutes, that trade is clearly worth it. ## Testing the lock Three tests cover the behavior that matters. They run against a temporary directory and don't touch the real lock path.

python import os import time import pytest from lock import acquire_lock, release_lock @pytest.fixture def lock_path(tmp_path): return str(tmp_path / "state.lock") def test_second_acquire_fails(lock_path): assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is True assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is False release_lock(lock_path) def test_release_then_acquire_succeeds(lock_path): assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is True release_lock(lock_path) assert acquire_lock(lock_path) is True release_lock(lock_path) def test_stale_lock_self_heals(lock_path): # Simulate a crashed process: lock file exists, mtime is old. with open(lock_path, "w") as f: f.write("99999") old = time.time() - 3 * 60 * 60 # 3 hours os.utime(lock_path, (old, old)) assert acquire_lock(lock_path, stale_seconds=2 * 60 * 60) is True release_lock(lock_path)

The third test is the one that catches regressions in the takeover logic. It is easy to write a stale check that reads the file's mtime before checking existence, or that uses os.path.getmtime without handling the FileNotFoundError when another process unlinks in between. The test forces the stale path and verifies that acquisition succeeds. A fourth test worth having, though not strictly required: assert that a fresh lock is not taken over. Set the mtime to now and confirm acquire_lock returns False. That guards against a threshold bug that turns every lock into a stale lock. ## Operational notes - Put the lock file on the same volume as the state file. Network paths reintroduce the race you just eliminated, because O_EXCL semantics on SMB shares are not always what you expect. - Log the PID and age whenever you skip a round. When the job silently stops doing work, that log line is the first thing you'll look for. - Keep the staleness threshold in configuration, not in code, so you can tighten it if the timeout cap changes. - The lock file should never be read by anything except the lock logic. Treat it as opaque. The pattern generalizes: any scheduled job that mutates shared state and can occasionally overrun its interval needs exactly this. O_EXCL gives you the atomicity, the mtime rule gives you self-healing, and the fallback-to-proceed rule keeps a broken lock subsystem from becoming a broken scheduler. EMA 20/50, dual-direction trend following, 7 majors, 4 years. Total return +265.8%. Then the t-statistic came back at 1.61 with p = 0.107. Positive, but not significant. A result you cannot defend in front of anyone who knows what a t-stat means. The usual reaction is to go hunting for parameter tweaks: faster EMA, slower EMA, ATR stops, regime filters. All of that is premature. Before touching parameters, decompose the P&L by direction. It costs twenty lines of code and it usually tells you more than a week of grid search. In this case it told the whole story: | Leg | Return | Trades | t-stat | |---|---|---|---| | Long-only | +295.7% | 298 | — | | Short-only | -37.9% | 140 | -1.61 | | Combined | +265.8% | 438 | 1.61 | The short leg did not just underperform. It carried the same magnitude of t-statistic as the combined system, with the opposite sign, and it dragged the aggregate from something you could argue about into the noise floor. The short book was not dead weight. It was actively destroying the evidence that the long book worked. ## Why Decompose by Direction First A dual-direction system is two strategies stapled together with a shared parameter set. The entry logic is symmetric on paper — golden cross long, death cross short — but the return distributions on either side of zero are not symmetric at all. Aggregating them hides that asymmetry behind a single equity curve. Decomposition is the cheapest diagnostic you have. If one leg has a positive expectancy and the other has a negative one, the combined t-stat is a blend of two different processes and means very little. You are not testing "does trend following work." You are testing "does trend following work, averaged over two markets with different structural properties, weighted by trade count." That is a question nobody asked. The fix is not to re-weight or re-optimize. It is to measure each leg on its own, then decide what the evidence actually supports. ### Implementation: Same Engine, Filter by Sign The key discipline is that you do not write a second backtester for the long-only variant. You run the exact same engine, record every trade with its direction, and slice the trade log afterward. This guarantees the two legs are directly comparable — same fills, same costs, same sizing.

python from dataclasses import dataclass import numpy as np import pandas as pd @dataclass class Trade: symbol: str direction: int # +1 long, -1 short entry_time: pd.Timestamp exit_time: pd.Timestamp entry_px: float exit_px: float size: float # notional at entry def trade_pnl(t: Trade, fee_bps: float = 5.0) -> float: gross = t.direction * (t.exit_px - t.entry_px) / t.entry_px fees = 2 * fee_bps / 1e4 return t.size * (gross - fees) def run_engine(prices: dict[str, pd.DataFrame], fast: int = 20, slow: int = 50) -> list[Trade]: """Dual-direction EMA crossover. One position per symbol at a time.""" trades = [] for sym, df in prices.items(): ef = df["close"].ewm(span=fast, adjust=False).mean() es = df["close"].ewm(span=slow, adjust=False).mean() state = 0 entry_px = entry_t = None for ts, f, s, px in zip(df.index, ef, es, df["close"]): sig = 1 if f > s else -1 if state == 0: state, entry_px, entry_t = sig, px, ts elif sig != state: trades.append(Trade(sym, state, entry_t, ts, entry_px, px, size=1.0)) state, entry_px, entry_t = sig, px, ts return trades

Now the decomposition itself. This is the part worth institutionalizing — put it in a shared module so every strategy report includes it by default.

python def leg_stats(trades: list[Trade]) -> pd.DataFrame: rows = [] for leg, sign in [("long", 1), ("short", -1)]: pnls = [trade_pnl(t) for t in trades if t.direction == sign] if len(pnls) < 2: continue arr = np.array(pnls) tstat = arr.mean() / (arr.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(arr))) rows.append({"leg": leg, "n": len(arr), "total": arr.sum(), "mean": arr.mean(), "t": tstat}) allp = np.array([trade_pnl(t) for t in trades]) rows.append({"leg": "combined", "n": len(allp), "total": allp.sum(), "mean": allp.mean(), "t": allp.mean() / (allp.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(allp)))}) return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("leg")

Two notes on the statistics. First, per-trade t-stats are not the same as a daily-returns t-stat on the equity curve; they answer slightly different questions. Per-trade is fine for a diagnostic like this, but if you want to publish a number, compute the t-stat on the daily P&L series of each leg and let the trade-level view stay a screening tool. Second, if trades overlap across symbols, the independence assumption behind the t-stat is violated. For 7 majors running the same signal, correlation is high enough that the effective sample is smaller than 438. That makes the combined p = 0.107 optimistic, not pessimistic — another reason the original result never deserved the benefit of the doubt. For completeness, the long-only variant is not a new engine. It is the same loop with the short branch suppressed:

python def run_long_only(prices, fast=20, slow=50): trades = [] for sym, df in prices.items(): ef = df["close"].ewm(span=fast, adjust=False).mean() es = df["close"].ewm(span=slow, adjust=False).mean() in_pos, entry_px, entry_t = False, None, None for ts, f, s, px in zip(df.index, ef, es, df["close"]): if not in_pos and f > s: # golden cross enters in_pos, entry_px, entry_t = True, px, ts elif in_pos and f < s: # death cross exits, no reverse trades.append(Trade(sym, 1, entry_t, ts, entry_px, px, 1.0)) in_pos = False return trades

Golden cross enters, death cross exits, flat in between. No reverse, no short. The trade count drops from 438 to 298 — exactly the long leg of the dual-direction run, which is the check that your filter is doing what you think it is. ## Why Shorting a Trend Follower Is Structurally Hard Here The short leg was not unlucky. It was fighting three structural forces at once, and none of them show up in a parameter sweep. *Upward skew in the underlying.* Crypto majors over a four-year window spent most of their time in a positive drift regime. A trend follower's short entries cluster right after a death cross — that is, after a decline has already happened. In a market with positive drift, the expected value of being short immediately after a drawdown is negative even if the signal has some genuine momentum content. You are systematically selling after the move and buying back into the mean reversion. *Wick-heavy pops.* Crypto has no circuit breakers and thin books on the way up. Short positions get stopped or squeezed by single-bar wicks that leave no trace on a close-to-close backtest if your fills assume the close. The asymmetry is brutal: a long position caught in a wick-down is a drawdown, a short position caught in a wick-up is often a liquidation event at a price worse than any bar's close. Backtests systematically flatter shorts because they fill at benign prices. *Negative carry.* Funding on perpetuals is positive in bullish regimes, which means shorts pay to hold. Over four years that is a persistent bleed on top of the directional loss. If your backtest does not model funding, your short leg looks better than it is. If it does, the -37.9% is the honest number and it likely understates the real-world drag. Put together: the short side of a symmetric crossover is short a positively skewed, wick-prone, negative-carry asset class using a signal that enters late. That is not a parameter problem. No combination of 15/60 or 25/80 fixes the structure. This is why the correct response to a failing leg is usually deletion, not repair — the search space for "repair" is mostly overfitting in disguise. ## The Discipline of Shipping Only What Passes Deleting the short leg raised the return to +295.7% on 298 trades. It did not raise the t-statistic into significance. Long-only is still positive-but-not-significant, and pretending otherwise would be the same mistake in a new costume. So the label on the dashboard changed. The strategy is not promoted to live. It is downgraded to observation tier: a paper-trading observer that runs the long-only logic, logs every signal, and reports the same statistics on a rolling basis until the evidence accumulates. The dashboard text says exactly that — no green badge, no "live" tag, just the numbers and the tier. The rule that makes this work is mechanical, not judgment-based:

python def tier(t_stat: float, n: int, min_n: int = 200) -> str: if n < min_n: return "observation" # not enough evidence either way if abs(t_stat) >= 2.0: return "live-eligible" if t_stat > 0: return "observation" # positive but unproven return "retired" def dashboard_row(leg: str, stats: pd.Series) -> dict: return { "leg": leg, "n": int(stats["n"]), "total_pct": round(100 * stats["total"], 1), "t": round(float(stats["t"]), 2), "tier": tier(float(stats["t"]), int(stats["n"])), "note": "positive but not significant" if stats["t"] < 2 and stats["t"] > 0 else "", }

Three properties matter here. The threshold is pre-registered, so you cannot move the goalposts after seeing the result. The tier is a pure function of the stats, so the dashboard cannot disagree with the data. And "observation" is a real state with real work attached — the observer keeps logging, and the strategy can only graduate by accumulating evidence, not by someone deciding it feels ready. Parking the short leg as a paper observer rather than deleting it entirely is the second half of the discipline. You keep the measurement running at zero cost. If the regime shifts — funding flips persistently negative, or the market develops sustained downtrends — the short leg's stats will show it, and you will have four more years of honest data instead of a hunch. What you do not do is force it live because the long book needed a hedge, or because a symmetric strategy looks more elegant in a slide. ## What Actually Changed The final state: one engine, two legs measured separately, one leg deleted from live consideration, the survivor labeled honestly as unproven and parked in observation tier. The headline number went from +265.8% with a misleading aggregate t-stat to +295.7% with a clear statement that it is still not significant. That is a worse-looking result than the original backtest and a much better one to build on. The decomposition did not find alpha. It found the reason the alpha was invisible, and then it refused to pretend the remainder was more than it was.
