title: Supportive Token Revealing for Fast Diffusion Language Model Decoding
description:
arXiv:2606.04236v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Discrete diffusion language models can generate text efficiently by updating multiple masked positions in parallel, but this parallelism introduces a quality-latency trade-off. Aggressive decoding may commit mutually dependent tokens too early, while conservative decoding requires many denoising steps. Existing methods address this tension by deciding which tokens are safe to reveal using confidence or dependency criteria. However, avoiding unsafe commits does not necessarily make the remaining masked sequence easy to decode, since uncertain tokens may depend on masked tokens, creating a bottleneck for denoising steps. We propose AXON, a training-free module that can be added on top of existing parallel decoding strategies for diffusion language models. Rather than replacing the base decoder, AXON monitors the remaining uncertain masked tokens and intervenes only when their current state suggests that additional context is needed. It then shifts the criterion from which tokens are safest to reveal to which confident reveals would best support later denoising. AXON selects anchors, confident masked tokens that uncertain positions attend to, using attention, uncertainty, and confidence signals. Experiments on reasoning and code-generation benchmarks across multiple diffusion language models show that AXON improves the quality-latency trade-off of existing parallel decoders, often reducing the number of function evaluations while maintaining or improving accuracy.

title: Goliat Cloud Inventory: recursos, suscripciones y costes de Azure en un solo panel
description:
Entender un entorno Azure exige relacionar varias piezas: qué recursos existen, a qué suscripción pertenecen, cómo están etiquetados y qué costes generan. Cuando la información queda repartida, responder una pregunta sencilla puede llevar más tiempo que la consulta técnica que hay detrás.

He creado Goliat Cloud Inventory para reunir esa exploración en un dashboard autoalojado. La aplicación combina un inventario consultable, análisis de costes y administración del colector, con una interfaz en español e inglés.

Web oficial y demo interactiva: Abrir la web de Goliat Cloud Inventory

Código en GitHub: Ver el repositorio de Goliat Cloud Inventory

El repositorio del producto incluye el panel, el backend, la Azure Function de recogida, la infraestructura y las guías para desplegarlo.

Captura real de la aplicación ejecutada en local. Los 214 recursos y las suscripciones que aparecen pertenecen al inventario ficticio de demostración.

Del inventario general al recurso concreto

El panel ofrece 73 vistas organizadas en 12 grupos de servicios. La visión general reúne indicadores y distribuciones; las categorías permiten profundizar en cómputo, contenedores, red, almacenamiento, bases de datos y otros servicios.

En las tablas puedes buscar, filtrar por suscripción y columna, agrupar, ordenar, paginar y exportar los datos. La búsqueda global permite localizar recursos por nombre, identificador o etiqueta, además de encontrar suscripciones y vistas del catálogo.

Un recorrido práctico podría ser:

  1. Abrir la visión general para conocer el volumen de recursos y la cobertura de etiquetas.
  2. Seleccionar una suscripción para limitar el análisis a un entorno.
  3. Buscar un recurso o una etiqueta de proyecto.
  4. Consultar su categoría y exportar el conjunto filtrado para revisarlo con el equipo.

La búsqueda trabaja sobre el inventario que ya se ha cargado. Cada interacción de la tabla no dispara una nueva recogida de Azure.

Cómo llega el inventario al panel

La arquitectura separa la recogida de recursos de su consulta:

Azure Resource Graph + Azure Resource Manager
                     ↓
             Azure Functions
                     ↓
         Snapshot JSON en Blob Storage
                     ↓
             Backend Next.js
                     ↓
                 PostgreSQL
                     ↓
           Dashboard de inventario

La Function recoge los datos y publica un snapshot. El backend lee ese documento, lo normaliza y lo importa en PostgreSQL. El navegador consulta al backend, que aplica el control de acceso.

Cada importación se ejecuta en una transacción. Si falla, se conserva el snapshot anterior; el mismo ETag del blob no se importa dos veces. Esto evita que un error de importación deje unas tablas con la nueva versión y otras con la anterior.

La actualización manual también coordina el trabajo entre usuarios y réplicas mediante un bloqueo compartido en PostgreSQL. Esto evita que dos personas inicien simultáneamente la misma operación desde el panel.

FinOps: consultar los costes con su contexto

La sección FinOps consulta Azure Cost Management desde el servidor. Permite elegir mes, suscripción, moneda y base de coste real o amortizado, y explorar la evolución diaria, la distribución del gasto y el detalle por recurso y servicio.

El inventario y los costes tienen recorridos distintos: los recursos proceden del snapshot importado, mientras que FinOps consulta la API de costes. El producto no mantiene un libro histórico de gastos en PostgreSQL.

Hay varios detalles que ayudan a interpretar los resultados:

  • Las monedas se mantienen separadas.
  • Los recursos eliminados y los cargos sin recurso conservan su importe.
  • Los resultados parciales y los errores de permisos se muestran de forma explícita.
  • La ausencia de datos no se presenta como un coste de cero.
  • La fecha de consulta no equivale al cierre de la factura; el mes abierto puede recibir ajustes.

La intención es facilitar la lectura y el análisis del gasto disponible. Esta versión no calcula previsiones ni recomendaciones automáticas de ahorro.

Administración del colector y de la actualización

La sección de administración reúne el estado y las métricas de la Function, información de salud de PostgreSQL y Blob Storage, y la comparación entre el inventario publicado y el importado.

También permite gestionar la programación del colector y las claves de etiquetas que se muestran como columnas. Esto ayuda a adaptar la vista a convenciones como proyecto, entorno o centro de coste.

Los diagramas de arquitectura están integrados en la aplicación y en la web del producto. Permiten seguir tanto el flujo de datos como el despliegue de referencia en Azure.

Identidad y permisos separados por responsabilidad

La aplicación admite autenticación con Microsoft Entra ID y un modo demo con usuario y contraseña. Las páginas y las APIs de datos comprueban el acceso en el servidor.

El colector utiliza permisos de lectura para consultar el inventario. La identidad del backend dispone de los permisos necesarios para leer el snapshot y, para FinOps, consultar los costes mediante Cost Management Reader en las suscripciones configuradas.

Las credenciales cloud y de PostgreSQL permanecen en el servidor y en el colector. El navegador recibe los datos que puede consultar, no las credenciales utilizadas para obtenerlos.

La administración requiere permisos adicionales definidos para sus operaciones. Separar esas responsabilidades permite revisar quién puede consultar, actualizar o administrar la instalación.

Probarlo con datos ficticios

La web de Goliat Cloud Inventory incluye una vista previa interactiva que funciona con datos ficticios y no consulta tu suscripción. Puedes explorar las vistas de inventario, FinOps y administración para conocer la interfaz.

Para probar la aplicación real en local necesitas Node.js y una base PostgreSQL vacía, siguiendo los requisitos del README. El recorrido de inicio es:

git clone https://github.com/danieljsaldana/goliat-cloud-inventory.git
cd goliat-cloud-inventory
npm ci
cp .env.example .env

# Configura PostgreSQL, el acceso demo y AUTH_SECRET en .env
# antes de ejecutar los siguientes comandos.
npm run db:init
npm run db:seed
npm run dev

La semilla incluye 214 recursos ficticios y permite probar el inventario sin credenciales de Azure. El análisis de costes de una suscripción real necesita su configuración y los permisos correspondientes.

Cuando quieras conectar un entorno real, la documentación explica el colector y el despliegue con Bicep y PowerShell: App Service, Azure Functions, Storage, PostgreSQL e identidades de Entra.

Dos herramientas con responsabilidades distintas

Goliat Nexus organiza una base de infraestructura y una aplicación de ejemplo. Cloud Inventory se centra en consultar recursos, suscripciones, etiquetas y costes.

Cada herramienta puede utilizarse de forma independiente. Inventory puede recoger los recursos de las suscripciones que configures, incluidas aquellas donde despliegues Nexus, siempre que tenga los permisos adecuados.

Enlaces oficiales de Goliat Cloud Inventory

  • Web oficial y demo interactiva.
  • GitHub: repositorio y código fuente.
  • README en español.
  • Wiki bilingüe.
  • Catálogo de servicios.
  • Guía de FinOps.

title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
description:
arXiv:2611.23990v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients. A falsifiable longitudinal evaluation would compare WRC-guided policies with strong version-aware baselines at matched coverage, utility, and review cost. This paper contributes a formalized problem statement, testable design obligations, and reporting protocol, not an implemented verifier, empirical superiority result, or proof of universal agent safety.

title: Think Multilingual, Not Harder: A Framework for Analyzing and Teaching Code-Switched Reasoning
description:
arXiv:2604.15490v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reasoning capabilities have enabled large language models to solve increasingly complex tasks. Interestingly, while reasoning models are often trained to generate monolingual text, these models have also been observed to code-switch (i.e., mix languages). Prior works have either viewed code-switching as an undesirable error, attempted to control code-switching through modifications to input prompts or the output decoding process, or focus on narrow subsets of languages, domains, tasks, and models. We address these gaps by introducing the first linguistically and behaviorally motivated fine-tuning framework for identifying beneficial code-switched reasoning behaviors in large language models and teaching these models to code-switch more effectively for reasoning. First, we create the Code-Switched Reasoning (CoRe) corpus, consisting of 7k reasoning traces from 15 models, 18 languages, 10 scripts, and diverse reasoning domains, providing insights into potentially helpful code-switching behaviors. Then, we expand CoRe into the Extended Code-Switched Reasoning corpus (EnCoRe) with 40 carefully curated datasets for training and evaluating six interventions on code-switching in reasoning across three models and seven languages, totaling 120 fine-tuning conditions. Across 80k+ reasoning traces from both language/culture-agnostic and -specific evaluations, English-dominated reasoning, semantically accurate code-switching, and a more even mix of languages are positively associated with correct answers, whereas dense switching is associated with incorrect answers. Moreover, we are able to elicit positive behaviors through fine-tuning tasks that do not directly demonstrate code-switching. Our work suggests that small but well-curated datasets can change how reasoning models code-switch, allowing us to reap the benefits of reasoning in the many languages that lack large-scale reasoning data.

title: LLM Model Fallback in TypeScript
description:
OpenAI returns a 503. Every LLM call in your app fails with it, and your users stare at a spinner while the status page catches up.

Model fallback is the fix everyone reaches for: if the primary model fails, send the call to a backup model on another provider. It sounds like a try/catch. In practice there are four details that decide whether it helps or makes things worse.

This post walks through those details and shows how to set up LLM fallback in TypeScript with VernLLM, using GPT-6.2 Sol as the primary and Gemini 4 Neon as the backup. No gateway, no proxy: it runs in your process.

Why a try/catch fallback is not enough 

try {
  return await openai.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-6.2-sol', messages });
} catch {
  return await gemini.models.generateContent({ model: 'gemini-4-neon', contents });
}

This is where most fallback code starts. It has four problems:

  1. It gives up on the primary too early. A single 503 is often a blip. You want a few retries with backoff on the primary before you switch providers.
  2. It falls over on everything. If the model returned JSON that fails your schema, or the user cancelled the request, a second provider will not fix it. You just pay twice.
  3. It breaks streaming. If the stream already sent half an answer, falling over splices a second model's output into text the user is reading.
  4. It hides who answered. Your metrics, costs and debugging all need to know which provider and model produced the response.

LLM fallback with VernLLM 

npm i vern-llm openai @google/genai

import OpenAI from 'openai';
import { GoogleGenAI } from '@google/genai';
import { VernLLM, metaRef } from 'vern-llm';
import { fromOpenAI, fromGemini } from 'vern-llm/adapters';

const llm = new VernLLM({
  client: fromOpenAI(new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY })),
  model: 'gpt-6.2-sol',
  name: 'openai',
  maxRetries: 2,

  fallback: [
    {
      client: fromGemini(new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY })),
      model: 'gemini-4-neon',
      name: 'gemini',
    },
  ],

  onEvent: (event) => {
    if (event.kind === 'fallback') console.warn(`fallback ${event.from} -> ${event.to}`);
  },
});

const meta = metaRef();
const summary = await llm.call({ userContent: 'Summarize the earnings call.', meta });

fallback is an ordered list. The order is the whole policy: VernLLM never reorders or scores targets behind your back, so the primary is always tried first.

Each target is independent. It gets its own retry loop, its own timeout, and its own circuit breaker and rate limiter if you configure them. Retry and timeout options a target leaves out inherit from the primary.

What a failover looks like

I ran this setup with a primary that always returns 503 and maxRetries: 2. The primary got 3 attempts, then the fallback event fired:

fallback openai -> gemini

and meta.current reported who answered:

{
  provider: 'gemini',
  model: 'gemini-4-neon',
  fallbackIndex: 0,     // -1 when the primary answers
  usedFallback: true,
  attempts: 1,
  position: 1
}

Your code gets a normal result. The outage shows up in your logs and metrics, not in front of your users.

When to fall back, and when to stop

After a target's own retries run out, VernLLM asks a policy whether to move to the next target. The default, defaultFallbackOn, moves on for failures a different provider can actually fix and stops for the rest:

Error Decision Why
5xx, timeout, network error next The provider is sick, another one may not be
circuit open next This target is known to be down, skip it right away
unsupported capability next Another adapter may support it
invalid JSON or schema validation stop Another model given the same prompt likely fails the same way
caller aborted stop The user cancelled, respect it
model refused stop Opt in with your own policy if you want another provider to try

In my run I also pointed the primary at a model that returned { "summary": 42 } against a Zod schema that wanted a string. The call stopped with a validation error and the backup received zero requests.

You can wrap the default instead of replacing it:

import { defaultFallbackOn } from 'vern-llm';

const llm = new VernLLM({
  // ...
  fallbackOn: (error, context) => {
    if (error.type === 'circuit_open' && context.isLastTarget) {
      alerting.page('every configured provider is unavailable');
    }
    return defaultFallbackOn(error, context);
  },
});

Streaming: fall back before the first chunk only

With stream: true, fallback applies when a stream fails to open: a 5xx or a timeout before the first chunk. Once a chunk has reached your user, a failure is final for that call. VernLLM will not splice a second model's answer into one the user already started reading.

Track fallback usage

onUsage reports provider and usedFallback on every successful call, so you can see how often you are running on the backup:

onUsage: (usage) => {
  metrics.increment('llm.call', { provider: usage.provider });
  if (usage.usedFallback) metrics.increment('llm.fallback_used', { provider: usage.provider });
},

Pick the order per call

targets chooses which targets to try for one call, and in what order:

await llm.call({ userContent: '...', targets: ['gemini', 'openai'] });

If you want the order chosen from health, latency or cost, the router extension does that as middleware. Core only runs the list it is given.

Wrap up

Model fallback is more than catching an error. Retry the primary first, fall over only for failures another provider can fix, never fall over mid stream, and always record who answered.

npm i vern-llm

Docs: Multi provider fallback

title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.25123v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.

title: Watermarks and Late Data Handling
description:
Navigating the Tides of Time: A Deep Dive into Watermarks and Late Data Handling

Hey there, fellow data adventurers! Ever felt like you're wrestling with a streaming pipeline, constantly trying to pin down when your data truly happened versus when it actually showed up? If so, you've probably bumped into the tricky world of late data and the elegant solutions that try to tame it: watermarks.

Think of it like this: you're expecting a package delivery. The shipping label says it left yesterday, but it only arrives today. Is it still "yesterday's" delivery, or is it "today's" problem? In the fast-paced realm of data streaming, this seemingly simple question can unravel your entire analysis if you're not prepared.

This article is your friendly guide to understanding watermarks and how they help us deal with those pesky late arrivals. We'll explore why they're essential, the magic they perform, and yes, even a few of their quirks. So, grab your favorite beverage, settle in, and let's dive into the fascinating currents of time-aware data processing!

Setting Sail: The "Why" Behind Watermarks and Late Data

Imagine a real-time dashboard showing you live sales figures for a coffee shop. Every time a customer buys a latte, that event should be processed and reflected on the dashboard. But what if the network hiccups for a few minutes? Or what if a point-of-sale system experiences a temporary glitch and sends its data a little later?

If your streaming application simply processes data as it arrives, those delayed latte sales might be attributed to the wrong time period. This can lead to:

  • Inaccurate aggregations: Your "sales today" might miss out on orders that arrived late.
  • Misleading insights: If you're calculating trends, late data can skew your results.
  • Incorrect state management: In systems that maintain state (like running totals), late data can cause inconsistencies.

Late data is essentially data that arrives after a certain threshold of "expected" time has passed. This "expected" time is often tied to the event time – the timestamp when the event actually occurred at its source.

This is where watermarks come to the rescue! They act as a mechanism to tell your streaming application, "Okay, I've seen enough data up to this point in event time. Anything arriving after this is likely to be late and should be handled accordingly."

Before We Dive In: Prerequisites for Understanding

To truly appreciate watermarks, a little foundational knowledge will go a long way. Don't worry, we're not talking about rocket science here.

  • Streaming Concepts: A basic understanding of stream processing, where data flows continuously rather than in batches, is helpful. Think of it as a river of data.
  • Event Time vs. Processing Time: This is crucial!
    • Event Time: The timestamp associated with when an event actually occurred at its source. (e.g., the time a customer clicked "buy" on an e-commerce site).
    • Processing Time: The timestamp associated with when an event is processed by your streaming application. (e.g., when your Flink job reads the event from Kafka).
    • The disconnect between these two is the root cause of late data issues.
  • Windowing: Most stream processing frameworks allow you to group data into time-based windows (e.g., a 5-minute window of sales data). Watermarks are intimately tied to how these windows are closed and finalized.

The Marvel of Watermarks: How They Work Their Magic

So, how does a watermark actually work? Think of it as a progress indicator for event time.

  1. Timestamp Assignment: Each event in your stream is tagged with an event timestamp. This is paramount. If your source doesn't provide event timestamps, you'll need to assign them.
  2. Watermark Generation: The streaming system (or your custom logic) observes the event timestamps arriving. It then generates a watermark. A watermark is simply a timestamp that indicates the maximum observed event time that the system is confident has been fully processed.
  3. The "Late" Threshold: A watermark is typically defined as current_event_time - allowed_lateness. The allowed_lateness is a configurable parameter that defines how much "fudge factor" you give to late data.
  4. Window Closing: When the watermark's timestamp surpasses the end of a specific event-time window, that window is considered "closed." This means the system can finalize any aggregations or computations for that window.
  5. Handling Late Data: Data arriving after a window has been closed due to a watermark is considered late. The system then has several options for handling it, which we'll discuss shortly.

The Key Idea: Watermarks allow your system to make progress on processing event time even if data arrives out of order or with delays. They provide a mechanism to reliably close windows and produce results.

A Practical Example: Flink's Watermark Strategy

Apache Flink is a popular stream processing framework, and it has excellent support for watermarks. Let's look at a simplified Flink example.

Suppose we have a stream of sensor readings with an event_timestamp field. We want to count the number of readings per minute.

// Assuming you have a DataStream of SensorReading objects
DataStream<SensorReading> sensorStream = ...;

// Assign event timestamps and generate watermarks
DataStream<SensorReading> timedStream = sensorStream
    .assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(
        WatermarkStrategy.<SensorReading>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(
            Duration.ofSeconds(5)) // Allow up to 5 seconds of lateness
        .withTimestampAssigner((event, timestamp) -> event.getEventTimestamp())
    );

// Group data into 1-minute tumbling windows and count
DataStream<Tuple2<Long, Long>> counts = timedStream
    .windowAll(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
    .aggregate(new CountAggregator());

// ... process 'counts' DataStream ...

// Example Aggregator
public static class CountAggregator implements AggregateFunction<SensorReading, Long, Long> {
    @Override
    public Long createAccumulator() {
        return 0L;
    }

    @Override
    public Long add(SensorReading value, Long accumulator) {
        return accumulator + 1;
    }

    @Override
    public Long getResult(Long accumulator) {
        return accumulator;
    }

    @Override
    public Long merge(Long a, Long b) {
        return a + b;
    }
}

// Assuming SensorReading class has getEventTimestamp() and other relevant fields
public static class SensorReading {
    private long eventTimestamp;
    // ... other fields ...

    public long getEventTimestamp() {
        return eventTimestamp;
    }
    // ... getters and setters ...
}

In this Flink example:

  • forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) tells Flink to assume that events are at most 5 seconds out of order. Flink will generate a watermark that lags behind the maximum observed event time by at most 5 seconds.
  • .withTimestampAssigner(...) tells Flink how to extract the event timestamp from each SensorReading object.
  • TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)) defines 1-minute windows based on event time.
  • When the watermark's timestamp passes the end of a 1-minute window (e.g., if the watermark reaches 10:01:00, the 10:00:00-10:01:00 window will be closed), Flink will emit the result of the aggregation for that window.
  • If a sensor reading with an event timestamp of 10:00:15 arrives after the watermark has passed 10:01:00, it will be considered late.

Advantages: Why We Love Watermarks

Watermarks aren't just a cool technical feature; they bring significant benefits to stream processing:

  • Correctness and Consistency: They ensure that your aggregations and computations are based on the correct event time, leading to accurate results even in the presence of delays.
  • Reliable Windowing: They provide a deterministic way to close event-time windows, allowing you to produce output that reflects the actual flow of events.
  • Handling Out-of-Order Data: They are a fundamental tool for dealing with data that doesn't arrive in its chronological event order.
  • Foundation for Advanced Features: Many sophisticated stream processing features, like session windows or complex event processing (CEP), rely on a robust watermark mechanism.
  • Tunable Lateness: The allowed_lateness parameter gives you control over how much late data you're willing to tolerate, balancing latency of results with completeness.

Disadvantages and Considerations: The Not-So-Sunny Side

While powerful, watermarks aren't a silver bullet, and they come with their own set of considerations:

  • Complexity: Implementing and understanding watermark strategies can be challenging, especially for complex scenarios.
  • Tuning allowed_lateness: Finding the right allowed_lateness value is crucial.
    • Too small: You might prematurely close windows and discard valid late data.
    • Too large: Your results will be delayed significantly, defeating the purpose of real-time processing.
  • Resource Consumption: Maintaining state for late data handling can increase memory and processing overhead.
  • Event Time vs. Watermark Drift: If your event timestamps are highly skewed or your system is under extreme load, the watermark might not accurately reflect the event time progress, leading to unexpected behavior.
  • Source Timestamp Quality: The effectiveness of watermarks heavily relies on the quality and accuracy of the event timestamps provided by your data sources. Garbage in, garbage out!

Features and Strategies: Different Flavors of Watermarks

There isn't a single "one-size-fits-all" watermark strategy. Stream processing frameworks offer various ways to generate and use watermarks:

1. Bounded Out-of-Orderness Watermarks

This is the most common type. It assumes that data is out of order by a certain, bounded amount.

  • How it works: The watermark lags behind the maximum observed event time by a configurable allowed_lateness.
  • Example (Flink): WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
  • Pros: Simple to configure, effective for many common use cases.
  • Cons: Requires careful tuning of allowed_lateness.

2. Monotonically Increasing Watermarks

In this scenario, event timestamps are guaranteed to be non-decreasing.

  • How it works: The watermark is simply the maximum event time seen so far.
  • Example (Flink): WatermarkStrategy.forMonotonousTimestamps()
  • Pros: Low latency results, minimal overhead.
  • Cons: Only applicable when event times are strictly ordered.

3. Periodic Watermarks

Watermarks are generated periodically based on the system's internal clock.

  • How it works: The system checks the maximum event time at regular intervals and generates a watermark.
  • Pros: Can be useful in custom watermark generation logic.
  • Cons: Less common as a standalone strategy in modern frameworks, often used as part of more complex custom implementations.

4. Custom Watermark Generators

For highly specific scenarios, you can implement your own watermark generation logic.

  • How it works: You write code that inspects incoming events, maintains internal state, and decides when to emit a watermark.
  • Example (Flink): Implementing the WatermarkGenerator interface.
  • Pros: Maximum flexibility to handle unique data patterns.
  • Cons: Requires significant development effort and deep understanding of the data.

Late Data Handling Strategies: What Happens to Those Stragglers?

Once a watermark signals that a window is closed, what do you do with the data that still trickles in? Here are the common approaches:

1. Discarding Late Data: The "Out of Sight, Out of Mind" Approach

  • What happens: Any data arriving after a window is closed is simply dropped.
  • When to use: When strict latency is paramount, and a small amount of potentially late data won't significantly impact your analysis. For example, real-time anomaly detection where the anomaly would have already occurred by the time the late data arrives.
  • Code Snippet (conceptual): Most frameworks handle this by default if no specific late data handling is configured.

2. Side Output (or Dead Letter Queue): The "Squirrel it Away" Approach

  • What happens: Late data is redirected to a separate stream or output sink for later inspection or processing. This is often called a "side output" in Flink or a "dead letter queue" in messaging systems.
  • When to use: When you want to capture all data, even if it's late, for debugging, auditing, or a secondary, less time-sensitive analysis.

  • Code Snippet (Flink concept):

    DataStream<SensorReading> lateSensorReadings = timedStream
    .windowAll(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Time.minutes(1)))
    .sideOutputLateData(new OutputTag<SensorReading>("late-readings") {})
    .aggregate(new CountAggregator());

// Access the late readings stream
DataStream<SensorReading> lateDataStream = lateSensorReadings.getSideOutput(new OutputTag<SensorReading>("late-readings") {});
// ... process lateDataStream ...

    Here, sideOutputLateData explicitly directs any data that arrives late for the window to a named OutputTag.

3. Updating Existing Results: The "Patch It Up" Approach

  • What happens: If your aggregation allows for updates (e.g., a running sum), late data can be used to correct or update the results of a previously closed window. This is more advanced and requires stateful aggregations that support incremental updates.
  • When to use: When you need highly accurate, finalized results that account for all data, even if it arrives late. This is common in financial reporting or scientific data analysis.
  • Code Snippet (conceptual): This would involve a more sophisticated AggregateFunction or ProcessFunction that can handle updates to existing window state.

4. Extending Windows: The "Give it More Time" Approach

  • What happens: Some frameworks allow you to configure a "grace period" or "lateness period" where windows can be re-opened or updated with late data even after their initial close time. This is closely related to the allowed_lateness in watermark generation but can sometimes offer more granular control.
  • When to use: When you want to ensure a certain level of data completeness without the explicit complexity of side outputs for every late record.
  • Code Snippet (conceptual): Frameworks like Flink have explicit configurations for handling late data within windows, often tied to the watermark strategy.

Conclusion: Mastering the Data Tides

Watermarks and late data handling are not just niche concepts; they are fundamental to building robust and reliable streaming applications. By understanding how watermarks work, you gain the power to:

  • Process data based on its actual occurrence time.
  • Ensure the accuracy of your real-time analytics.
  • Build systems that are resilient to network glitches and processing delays.

The journey through the tides of time in data streaming can be complex, but with the right tools and understanding, you can navigate it with confidence. Remember to always consider the trade-offs between latency, completeness, and complexity when choosing your watermark strategy and late data handling approach.

So, the next time you're building a streaming pipeline, don't let those late arrivals catch you off guard. Embrace the power of watermarks, and you'll be well on your way to taming the dynamic currents of your data! Happy streaming!

title: Container Security Fundamentals: What Compliance Certifications Actually Require (and What They Don't)
description:
Ask an enterprise IT buyer why they chose their cloud container platform and the answer is often a list of acronyms: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP, FIPS 140.

Those certifications matter. In most regulated industries, a platform without them is a non-starter.

But there is a misunderstanding that keeps catching engineering teams off guard:

A compliant cloud platform does not make your containerized application compliant.

A compliance badge confirms that the provider secured its data centers, hypervisors, and managed control plane during an audit window. It says nothing about the container image a developer shipped this morning that runs as root with a database password hardcoded in it. You can pass an audit in March and still fail an audit, or have an incident, by November.

The numbers suggest this gap is common. In Red Hat's 2024 State of Kubernetes Security survey of 600 DevOps, engineering, and security professionals, 40% reported a misconfiguration incident in the previous 12 months and 26% reported a failed audit, per ARMO's tabulation of the report data. An auditor's PDF does not patch a drifted worker node (one of the servers your containers run on) or block an unencrypted connection.

So what do the frameworks actually ask of you, and who owns each piece?

Who owns what: the three-layer model

Compliance obligations for containers split across three layers. The failures cluster in the middle one.

Layer 1: Infrastructure and managed control plane (provider owned)

This is the layer the certification badges actually describe. Your provider runs the data centers, the hypervisors, and the Kubernetes control plane. For SOC 2 and ISO 27001, they evidence that:

  • Physical access to hardware is logged and restricted.
  • Control plane data, including the etcd database that holds every cluster setting and secret, runs on provider-managed masters and is encrypted in transit and in backups. On IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service (the platform I work on), encrypting the live copy with your own key (IBM Key Protect) is an option you turn on yourself.
  • Customer environments are separated at the hypervisor.

Layer 2: Platform and cluster configuration (shared)

This is where audits most often go wrong, because the split is easy to misread. The provider hands you a hardened starting point. Keeping it hardened is your job:

  • Worker node patching. A published patch protects nothing until you apply it. IBM provides patched worker node images for IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service and Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Cloud, and you apply them by updating, reloading, or replacing your nodes. IBM's documentation suggests doing it monthly on IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service.
  • Benchmark alignment. Staying within the Center for Internet Security (CIS) Kubernetes and OpenShift benchmarks as configuration changes over time.
  • Cluster access. Least-privilege roles (RBAC) and service accounts with no more reach than they need.

Layer 3: Application and workload runtime (customer owned)

Whatever cloud you use, the workload is yours:

  • One compromised app shouldn't hand an attacker the machine underneath it, which means containers should run as a non-root user.
  • Known vulnerabilities in base images (the starting-point images containers are built from) and dependencies should be caught in the build pipeline, before they reach production.
  • A single compromised pod (the smallest unit that runs your containers) shouldn't be able to reach every other pod, which takes network policies that limit who can talk to whom.
  • Passwords and keys belong in a key management service, not in plaintext configuration files.

What the major frameworks look for in containers

Each framework views your container estate through a different lens. This matrix is my mapping of each framework onto Kubernetes controls, not a list the frameworks themselves prescribe:

Passing the annual audit with a folder of console screenshots is the easy part. Staying passed is the work.

Where compliance breaks down in practice

In the platform teams I talk to, failures rarely come from forgetting a regulation. They come from operational drift that nobody decided on.

1. Configuration drift and unpatched nodes

A cluster launched on January 1st may be fully hardened. Over the next six months, engineers ship emergency hotfixes, grant temporary full-admin access (cluster-admin) for troubleshooting, or switch off deploy-time safety checks to get a release out. Nobody plans to leave those in place. Without automated drift detection, the live cluster can wander away from the baseline you were audited against.

Even on IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service, you apply the worker patches yourself. A managed service shrinks your checklist. It doesn't empty it.

2. The default-root problem

Some popular public container images run as root out of the box. If an attacker breaks out of the container runtime through a flaw in the operating system kernel, root inside the container makes that escape far more damaging. PCI DSS requires application and system accounts to hold only the least privileges necessary (Requirement 7.2.5), so "it's just the image default" is a hard answer to defend.

3. Plaintext traffic between services

Teams often assume that a private network makes service-to-service traffic safe. The frameworks are less absolute than people think. As the rule stands today, HIPAA treats transmission encryption as an "addressable" safeguard: assess whether it's reasonable and appropriate, and if not, document why and use an equivalent alternative. PCI DSS requires strong cryptography for cardholder data crossing open, public networks. Neither spells out mutual TLS between pods (both sides of a connection verifying each other). But "it's inside our VPC" (our private cloud network) is an answer an auditor will ask you to defend, and plaintext HTTP carrying sensitive data is a tough one to defend.

The honest tradeoff: guardrails versus developer velocity

Here's the tension every platform leader runs into:

The stricter your enforcement, the more friction developers feel.

Strict enforcement breaks software you bought. Turn on Kubernetes' strictest built-in profile (the restricted Pod Security Standard), or OpenShift's equivalent rules (Security Context Constraints) that forbid root and privilege escalation, and some off-the-shelf vendor packages simply won't start. Friction is already the norm: Red Hat's survey found that 67% of respondents had delayed or slowed application development because of security concerns, and strict enforcement adds its own.

The team that gets hurt most is a small platform group supporting mostly vendor-packaged software. For them, strict enforcement from the first week mostly produces exemption tickets. Developers then wait days for approvals, or quietly spin up unmanaged clusters where nobody is watching.

The way out isn't weaker controls. Start in audit mode (Kubernetes' Pod Security Admission can warn and log without blocking), fix the worst offenders, then tighten. Pair that with paved paths: certified internal base images, pipeline scanning that catches misconfigurations before deployment, and self-service secrets management. The secure option has to be the easy one.

How the gap gets closed in practice

Capability matters more than brand here. Three kinds of capability help with parts of the gap, and each has open-source or other-cloud equivalents (policy engines such as Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper, which block or flag non-compliant configurations at deploy time, and other providers' security posture tools). On IBM Cloud, they look like this:

  1. Continuous posture checking. IBM Cloud Security and Compliance Center Workload Protection validates configurations against frameworks such as the IBM Cloud Framework for Financial Services, DORA, and NIST, and gives remediation instructions when a control fails. The Financial Services policy includes Kubernetes and Docker controls that run through an agent in your cluster. The frameworks it lists aren't SOC 2, PCI, or HIPAA, and IBM's documentation doesn't describe drift detection for it, so check what it covers before you rely on it.
  2. Hardened platform defaults. IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service ships worker nodes on an operating system image built to the CIS benchmarks, and IBM applies patch updates to the managed cluster master. That shrinks your starting gap; it does nothing about drift six months later.
  3. Hardware-enforced isolation, for a narrow set of workloads. IBM Cloud Confidential Containers use hardware-based memory encryption (Intel TDX) to protect data while it's in use. It is currently an experimental feature on Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Cloud, so treat it as something to evaluate, not something to build a compliance program on. Most workloads don't need it, and it won't fix a root container or a forgotten cluster-admin binding. It addresses a different threat.

The takeaway

A certified cloud gives you a secure foundation. Staying compliant on top of it takes continuous hygiene: drift detection, patched nodes, non-root containers, and paved paths that make the secure choice the easy one.

But you tell me: if you ran a live drift check on your "compliant" clusters today, how many would pass? And where do you think I've got the split wrong?

title: How to Search Tweets with twitter-api-v2 in Node.js (2026)
description:
Searching Tweets with twitter-api-v2

twitter-api-v2 is the most popular Node.js/TypeScript client for the X (Twitter) API, and searching recent tweets is one of the first things most developers reach for. It's also where people hit the most friction: the method returns a paginator, not a plain array, so getting to the actual tweets (tweets.data.data) and paging through results trips up newcomers constantly

This guide walks through searching tweets with twitter-api-v2 end to end: authenticating, calling client.v2.search(), reading the results correctly, paginating, the query operators worth knowing, and the rate-limit/cost realities. At the end we look at a simpler alternative for when the official API's setup and pricing are more than your project needs

Installing and Authenticating 

npm install twitter-api-v2

Recent tweet search is app-only, so all you need is a Bearer token from the X developer portal. No user OAuth flow required:

import { TwitterApi } from 'twitter-api-v2';

// App-only client from a Bearer token
const client = new TwitterApi(process.env.X_BEARER_TOKEN);

// Use the read-only sub-client for search/lookups
const roClient = client.readOnly;

Two things to know up front:

  • Recent search covers the last 7 days only. The full-archive endpoint requires an elevated (Pro/Enterprise or Academic) access level
  • Your access tier determines your rate limits and how many tweets you can pull per month

Your First Search: client.v2.search() 

const results = await roClient.v2.search('javascript lang:en -is:retweet', {
  'tweet.fields': ['created_at', 'public_metrics', 'author_id'],
  max_results: 100, // 10-100 per page
});

The first argument is your query string (operators covered below). The options object mirrors the API's query params: tweet.fields, user.fields, expansions, start_time, end_time, and max_results (capped at 100 per request)

Reading the Results: the tweets.data.data Gotcha

client.v2.search() does not return an array of tweets. It returns a TweetSearchRecentV2Paginator. There are three correct ways to read it, and mixing them up is the single most common source of confusion:

// 1. Recommended - .tweets is every tweet fetched so far, as a flat array
for (const tweet of results.tweets) {
  console.log(tweet.id, tweet.text);
}

// 2. The RAW current-page payload - this is where "tweets.data.data" comes from
console.log(results.data.data);  // TweetV2[] for the current page
console.log(results.data.meta);  // { result_count, newest_id, next_token, ... }

// 3. Async iterator - automatically pages through results (mind rate limits)
for await (const tweet of results) {
  console.log(tweet.text);
}

Why does results.data.data have a double .data? The paginator's .data property is the raw API response, shaped like { data: Tweet[], meta: {...}, includes: {...} }. So .data.data is the tweet array nested inside that response. Stick with results.tweets in application code, and reach for results.data.data only when you need the raw page exactly as the API returned it

Guard against empty results. When a search matches nothing, result_count is 0 and results.data.data can be undefined:

if (!results.meta.result_count) {
  console.log('No tweets matched.');
} else {
  for (const tweet of results.tweets) console.log(tweet.text);
}

Pagination: Getting More Than One Page

Each request returns at most 100 tweets. The paginator handles the rest for you:

// Fetch one more page and merge it into results.tweets
await results.fetchNext();

// Keep fetching until you have ~1000 tweets (or the pages run out)
await results.fetchLast(1000);

console.log('Collected ' + results.tweets.length + ' tweets');
console.log('Exhausted?', results.done);

The async iterator (for await ... of results) pages automatically. That's convenient, but it will happily burn through your rate limit on a broad query, so cap it yourself

Search Query Operators Worth Knowing

The query string is where most of the power lives:

Operator Matches
from:username Tweets from a specific account
to:username Replies directed at an account
#hashtag A hashtag
"exact phrase" An exact phrase
-keyword Excludes a keyword
lang:en A specific language
-is:retweet Excludes retweets
is:reply / -is:reply Only / no replies
has:media / has:links Tweets containing media / links
url:"github.com" Tweets linking a domain

Combine them freely: from:vitalikbuterin (ethereum OR rollup) -is:retweet has:links

Rate Limits and the Cost Problem

This is where teams get stuck. Recent search on the X API v2 is rate-limited per 15-minute window and capped by a monthly tweet-pull quota tied to your plan. In practice:

  • The Basic tier runs $200/month and still caps how many tweets you can retrieve
  • Recent search only reaches back 7 days; historical work needs the pricier full-archive access
  • Hitting the ceiling means 429 responses and building backoff, queueing, and quota tracking around them

For a detailed breakdown see our guides on X API pricing and rate limits

Other Recipes You Will Need Next

Search is rarely the only call. These are the four that follow it in almost every project

Pull a user's timeline 

const timeline = await roClient.v2.userTimeline('44196397', {
  max_results: 100,
  'tweet.fields': ['created_at', 'public_metrics'],
  exclude: ['retweets', 'replies'],
});

for (const tweet of timeline.tweets) console.log(tweet.text);

Note that userTimeline takes a numeric user id, not a handle. Resolving the handle first costs you an extra call

Resolve handles to ids 

const user = await roClient.v2.userByUsername('elonmusk', {
  'user.fields': ['public_metrics', 'created_at', 'description'],
});
console.log(user.data.id, user.data.public_metrics.followers_count);

// Up to 100 at once
const many = await roClient.v2.usersByUsernames(['elonmusk', 'vitalikbuterin']);

Read followers 

const followers = await roClient.v2.followers('44196397', {
  max_results: 1000,
  'user.fields': ['public_metrics'],
  asPaginator: true,
});

Followers is one of the tightest limits on the official API: 15 requests per 15 minutes on most tiers, so a 100k-follower account takes hours to page through

Filter by engagement, and why it silently fails

This is the trap that costs people the most time:

// Looks right. Does NOT work on API v2.
const results = await roClient.v2.search('solana min_faves:100');

min_faves:, min_retweets: and min_replies: work in the web search box but are silently ignored by API v2. No error, no warning, just unfiltered results. Your options are to filter client-side after fetching (paying for every tweet you throw away), or to use a provider whose search speaks the full web operator set

Common Errors and Fixes

  • 401 Unauthorized: bad or missing Bearer token, or your app lacks read access. Regenerate the token and double-check the project's permissions
  • 403 Forbidden: your access tier can't use this endpoint (recent search needs Basic+, full-archive needs Pro/Academic)
  • 429 Too Many Requests: you're rate-limited. Read the x-rate-limit-reset header and back off with jitter
  • results.data.data is undefined: the search matched nothing, so check results.meta.result_count before indexing

A Simpler Alternative: XCROP

If the developer-app setup, the 7-day window, and the $200/month floor are more than your project needs, XCROP exposes the same tweet-search capability behind a single API key. No OAuth app, no Bearer-token juggling, and credit-based pricing that costs a fraction of the official API

curl -X POST https://xcrop.io/api/v2/search \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer xc_live_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query": "javascript lang:en", "count": 100, "sort": "latest"}'

The response is plain JSON: a data array of tweets plus a meta object with the cursor, so there is no paginator and no .data.data to unwrap:

const res = await fetch('https://xcrop.io/api/v2/search', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Authorization': 'Bearer ' + process.env.XCROP_API_KEY,
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({ query: 'javascript lang:en', count: 100, sort: 'latest' }),
});

const { data } = await res.json();
for (const tweet of data) console.log(tweet.text);

You can sort by latest, engagement, or media, filter by min_likes / min_retweets / lang, and request up to 1,000 results in a single call. See every parameter in the interactive builder

Which Should You Use?

twitter-api-v2 (official) XCROP
Setup Developer app + Bearer token One API key
Auth OAuth / app-only token Bearer key in a header
Results shape Paginator (.tweets / .data.data) Plain JSON (data array + meta)
Search window 7 days (recent tier) Recent + trending coverage
Per-request cap 100 tweets Up to 1,000
Pricing From $200/mo (Basic) Free tier, then credit-based
Best for Deep X-native integrations Fast data pulls without the API-tier tax

If you're building a product deeply tied to the X platform, the official twitter-api-v2 library is the right tool. If you just need clean tweet data for a dashboard, a bot, research, or a side project, and you'd rather not wrestle with paginators, OAuth apps, and a $200/month minimum, XCROP gets you there in one curl

FAQ

What is tweets.data.data in twitter-api-v2?

It is the raw payload of the current page inside the paginator object. client.v2.search() returns a TweetSearchRecentV2Paginator, not an array: results.data is the API response and results.data.data is the TweetV2 array inside it. In application code you almost always want results.tweets instead, which flattens every page fetched so far

Why is data.data undefined after a search?

The search matched zero tweets. When nothing matches, result_count is 0 and results.data.data can be undefined, so check results.meta.result_count before you index into it

How far back can client.v2.search() go?

Seven days. Recent search only covers the last week; anything older needs full-archive search, which sits behind the Pro or Academic access tier

How many tweets can you get per call?

One hundred at most, set through max_results, then you paginate. Call results.fetchNext() for one more page or results.fetchLast(1000) to keep fetching toward a target count

Does twitter-api-v2 handle rate limits for you?

No. The library surfaces the rate-limit headers and throws on a 429, but the backoff is yours to write. Read x-rate-limit-reset and wait for the window rather than retrying immediately

Why does min_faves not work in API v2 search?

min_faves, min_retweets and min_replies work in the web search box but are silently ignored by API v2. There is no error, just unfiltered results, so you either filter client-side after fetching or use a provider whose search accepts the full web operator set

title: Stop migrating. Your Postgres is already the backend
description:
How to put a new, multi-role app on the database you already run, without a second copy or a migration plan. Then a 10-minute experiment to see whether you can break it.

Every "let's rebuild it" project has the same slide. Phase 1: migrate the data.

It always looks small on the slide. Then you meet the booking system that has written to that Postgres every day for six years. The nightly finance job that reads three of its tables. The POS terminals that will never write through your new API. Phase 1 becomes the whole project, and the new app ships two quarters late, if at all.

AI app builders tend to make this worse. They're good at greenfield. Ask Replit's Agent for persistence and it sets up a PostgreSQL database and creates the schema for you. That's ideal for a new idea. If you already have a database, the first thing the AI does is create the migration you were trying to avoid.

I'm a co-founder of Supero, and this is the problem we built it around. The question:

Can a brand-new app, with its own users and roles, run on the tables you already have, and leave them where they are?

Yes. The connection string is the easy part.

The 30-second version

  • Pick a mode per table, not per database. Copy the slow reference tables, read the busy ones live, and write through only where the new app owns the data.
  • Every request carries its own rules. The caller's tenant and the columns their role may use are compiled into the SQL before it reaches your database.
  • Your app code doesn't care. A live table answers the same API call as a native one.

Analysts got this years ago. Apps didn't.

Querying data where it lives is a solved problem if you're the one writing SQL:

  • Supabase Wrappers turn Stripe, ClickHouse, BigQuery or S3 into Postgres tables you can SELECT from, with no ETL in between.
  • Databricks Lakehouse Federation, announced in 2023, lets you discover, query and govern MySQL, PostgreSQL, Snowflake and others without moving or copying the data first.
  • Snowflake Secure Data Sharing gives a consumer live access, and no data is copied or moved between accounts.

All three are excellent, and they assume the caller is someone with credentials who writes SQL.

Now meet the person your app serves. Priya is a dispatcher. She opens the orders screen on her phone between two calls. She has no database role. She should see her company's orders and nobody else's. She can see status and total, but internal_margin is for managers only. The app writes the SQL on her behalf, thousands of times a day.

If every user of your app maps to a database role, Postgres column GRANTs and row-level security already handle this well. Priya doesn't, and neither do most app users. So the rules have to travel with her request.

Which tool for which job

These products overlap less than they seem. Each is the best fit for a different job:

Job Supabase Replit Databricks Snowflake Supero
New app, new database, fastest start Strong fit Strong fit Possible, inside a workspace Possible, inside an account Good fit: one prompt to a preview
Analysts querying data across systems Not the goal Not the goal Strong fit Strong fit Not the goal
App for your own users on a database you already run, rules on every request Possible, you build it Possible, you build it Not the goal: app viewers must be account users Not the goal: external viewers share one role Built for this
One shared database serving many customer orgs You write RLS per table You write it in app code Row policies, for platform users Row policies, for platform users Built in: tenant binding, deny by default (Pro)
Hidden columns that also can't be sorted, filtered or grouped by Per database role You build it Column masks, for platform users Masks apply in queries, for platform users Built in, per app role

Sources, checked 20 November 2026: Supabase column-level security, Supabase postgres_fdw, Replit authentication, Databricks app permissions, Databricks query federation, Snowflake external-viewer embedding, Snowflake column security.

Snowflake and Databricks enforce strong column and row rules, for people who have an identity in their platform. The gap Supero fills is the same rules for app users who don't, on a database that lives outside those platforms. And where they're ahead, they're well ahead: Supabase is open source with SOC 2 and HIPAA, Replit is the fastest route to a brand-new app, and Databricks and Snowflake are built for analytics at a scale Supero doesn't attempt.

If you're building an app for your own users on data you already run, that's the job Supero is built for.

One database, three decisions

The choice isn't "connect our database or don't." It's three questions, asked once per table:

Mode Reads come from Writes go to Use it for
sync A copy in the platform The copy, never your database Reference data you'd rather keep a copy of
live_read Your database, every request Refused with 403 Tables another system owns, like orders from the POS
live_readwrite Your database, every request Your database, in the same request Tables the new app owns (PostgreSQL, Supabase, MySQL)

One connector can mix all three. The connector config, trimmed:

{
  "source": { "plugin": "database",
              "config": { "db_type": "postgresql", "host": "db.internal.example",
                          "database": "operations", "username": "supero_connector",
                          "table_names": ["customers", "orders"], "ssl_mode": "require" } },
  "target": { "tables": [
    { "source": "customers", "schema": "customer_mirror", "mode": "sync" },
    { "source": "orders", "schema": "order_live", "mode": "live_read",
      "live": { "primary_key": ["order_id"],
                "columns": [ { "name": "order_id", "sql_type": "integer" },
                             { "name": "status", "sql_type": "varchar" },
                             { "name": "total", "sql_type": "numeric" },
                             { "name": "internal_margin", "sql_type": "numeric" } ],
                "field_map": { "order_id": "order_id", "status": "status",
                               "total": "total", "internal_margin": "internal_margin" },
                "tenant_binding": { "mode": "fixed", "tenant": "acme-ops" } } }
  ] }
}

columns matters: it is the allow-list of column names the planner will accept. If you'd rather not write it by hand, let discovery build the live block and then set only the tenant binding.

internal_margin is hidden from Priya by her role, not by the connector. Add it to the staff role's hidden_fields in its access rule, and managers still see it.

Your app reads order_live with the same endpoint and SDK as any other table:

import supero

org = supero.connect(domain_name="acme", api_key="ak_...", project="order-desk")
orders = org.crud.list("order_live", limit=20)   # rows come from your Postgres

A fixed binding is only for a table that holds one tenant's rows. If the table has an org_id-style column, Supero refuses the fixed binding unless you confirm the table holds one tenant's data. For one Postgres shared by many customer orgs, use a column binding, and every query gets a tenant predicate:

"tenant_binding": {
  "mode": "column", "tenant_field": "org_id",
  "tenant_value_map": { "acme": "42", "globex": "77" },
  "on_unmapped_tenant": "deny"
}

deny is the default. A tenant someone forgot to map gets a 403, never the whole table. (Apps with many tenants are on the Pro plan and above.)

The trip one request takes

Priya taps "Orders." Seven steps later she sees 20 rows. Three of them are where a homegrown pushdown usually leaks:

Scope the tenant. Her tenant becomes WHERE org_id = $1, with 42 bound as a parameter, never pasted into the string.

Guard the fields on the way in. Hiding internal_margin from the response is the easy half. If Priya could still filter on it or sort by it, she could binary-search every margin in the company without seeing one. So a field her role hides is refused as a filter, a sort key, an aggregate or a group-by, with a 400, before any SQL exists. For role-hidden fields the error is deliberately generic, because "that column is hidden" is itself a leak.

Compile from a closed list. Every column name is checked against that table's column list, then quoted. Every value is a bound parameter. One live query reads at most 10,000 rows by default, and when it hits the cap the response says so (source_meta.scan: "partial").

On a read, your database only ever receives a SELECT that was already safe to run. Supero also sets a 30-second statement_timeout on its own sessions and tags them application_name=supero-live-read/<connector id>, so your DBA can find them in pg_stat_activity.

Writes, when the app owns the table

live_readwrite sends inserts, updates and deletes to your database in the same request. A few rules hold it together:

  • The tenant column is set by Supero on insert and added to the WHERE on update and delete. A caller who tries to set it gets 403.
  • Primary keys can't be changed, and an update or delete that matches no row in the caller's tenant returns 404.
  • Each table needs a stable primary key. Tables with no key, or a timestamp in the key, are treated as event streams and stay read-only.
  • Engines: PostgreSQL (Supabase included) and MySQL accept live writes; Postgres is the one verified end to end. SQL Server reads live but refuses live writes with 501.

The 10-minute experiment

Reading about a guard is nice. Trying to beat it is better. You can start without a card, and connecting your AI needs no API key. Role and field rules are listed from the Pro plan up on the pricing page, so check your plan first.

1. Connect your AI. In a terminal, for Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http --scope user supero "https://mcp.supero.dev/mcp?features=core"

On claude.ai or ChatGPT, add https://mcp.supero.dev/mcp as a custom connector instead. You sign in through your browser.

2. Paste one prompt.

Build an order desk with Supero. Orders have order_id, customer, status,
total and internal_margin. Two roles: managers see internal_margin, staff
never do. Seed 30 realistic orders. Run build_verify, deploy a preview,
and give me the URL plus one manager and one staff login.

Previews last 30 minutes.

3. Try to break it. Sign in as staff and go hunting for the margin:

  • Filter on it with a range. Does the row count change?
  • Sort by it, ascending then descending. Are the two lists mirrors?
  • Ask for a count grouped by it.

If any of those tells you something about a column you can't see, that's a real bug, and I want to hear about it. A 400 every time means the guard is doing its job.

4. Point it at the real thing. Bringing your own database starts at the Basic plan. Create a connector with a least-privilege role and bind your orders table to the same object type in live_read. The app code doesn't change, as long as the field names match. A few query features, such as keyword search and range filters, return 501 on live tables, because they can't be pushed down faithfully yet.

CREATE ROLE supero_connector LOGIN PASSWORD '...';
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO supero_connector;
GRANT SELECT ON public.orders, public.customers TO supero_connector;
-- only for tables the app writes through:
-- GRANT INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON public.support_notes TO supero_connector;

Know this before you point it at production

  • Check the stamp, not the status. A live response carries a top-level access_mode of live-ro, live-rw or warehouse. If the platform can't resolve the connector binding for a caller, the read falls back to the empty local store and returns 200 with no rows. Monitor the stamp.
  • What Supero keeps. No row data for live tables, except the sample rows discovery reads to map columns and, for read-write tables, each row's primary key so records stay addressable.
  • Column tenant binding is set over the API. The console wizard saves a fixed binding and an empty hidden-fields list, so PUT both and read them back.
  • No conflict referee. With live_readwrite, both your app and the POS can change the same row. Supero doesn't arbitrate; reconciliation is yours. That's why orders stays live_read here.
  • Direct connections skip the rules. A BI tool logged straight into Postgres sees everything its own role allows. Supabase row-level security doesn't apply to the connector's login either, so scope that role tightly.
  • Engines differ. Warehouses (Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse, Fabric) are live and read-only, with results held in memory for up to 60 seconds. Oracle and MongoDB are sync-only for now, so ask us first.

When to copy instead

Live reads trade features for custody. Use sync for a table when you need keyword search, range filters, multi-field sorts or raw aggregation pipelines on it, or heavy queries you'd rather not run on your production primary. Simple stats, counts and distinct values still run in your database on live tables. Everything else can stay home.

The migration slide doesn't have to be Phase 1. For most tables it doesn't need to exist at all.

Try the experiment: supero.dev · How live reads and writes work: Connect your database · The security model: Live reads and writes: the security model

title: GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Sol in Kilo: The Great Pyramid Test
description:
From ancient wonders to artificial intelligence: we asked the latest Astra and Sol to build a pyramid

OpenAI just released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra is the new frontier model for the hardest projects. Sol is the fast, versatile model for everyday work.

We wanted to see the difference on a real task, not just on a chart. So we gave both models the same big prompt: build an interactive 3D scene where workers construct a pyramid, with boats bringing stones along a river. Then we put the results side by side.

This post covers what OpenAI announced, what we saw, and how you can run the same test yourself in Kilo Desktop, including on the ChatGPT plan you already pay for.

Meet Astra and Sol

Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Sol costs $2 and $10. Both are built to get better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you get more done within your usage limits.

These are standard API rates. Higher rates apply above 272K input tokens.

  • Astra's price dropped. Its input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra's, with a 60% discount on cached input.

  • Sol's price held. It keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's rates.

  • Where to find them. Both are in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users, and in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. Ultrafast is available for both at launch.

What OpenAI says they can do

The headline claim: Sol gets close to Astra at a fraction of the cost. On FrontierCode 2.0, which checks whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers' merge standards, Sol comes within 0.5 points of Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).

For Agents' Last Exam, OpenAI notes that its Fable 5.2 results leave out nine tasks that used a fallback model.

The AA-3D result is the one that made us curious. OpenAI says Astra and Sol can turn a written brief into an interactive browser experience, and that Astra builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming and 3D design. A pyramid-building scene is a good way to test that.

The test: build a pyramid

One of my colleagues, Marius Wichtner, built a pyramid benchmark for fun. It gives each model the same prompt and shows the finished apps side by side.

The prompt asks for a polished, interactive 3D scene of ancient Egyptian workers building a pyramid, with boats delivering materials along a river. Workers have to coordinate heavy loads. Boats have to dock, unload and keep materials flowing. The model picks the tech, the style and the building method.

We ran it with GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, both through Kilo. Both models chose Three.js, Vite and TypeScript, and both built a pyramid of 204 stones.

This is one run per model, so treat it as a first vibe look.

Astra looks like a film set. Sol looks like a strategy game.

Both models finished the job: 204 of 204 stones placed, all 8 courses built. The difference is in how they got there.

Astra pyramid building in progress

Sol pyramid building in progress

On looks alone, Astra wins clearly. Up close, the sledge, the ropes and the dock planks hold up. Sol's scene is simpler, but its panel tells you exactly what every crew is doing, which makes the work easy to follow.

That fits what OpenAI says about the two models: Astra for the work where quality matters most, Sol for everyday use. It is one run each, though. Run it a few times on your own tasks before you pick.

Run the test yourself in Kilo Desktop

Kilo Desktop is now generally available, and it is a good place for this kind of comparison. Every task gets its own session, and each session can run in its own git worktree, so two models never fight over the same files.

  1. Download Kilo Desktop and open an empty project.

  2. Start a session and give it its own git worktree. Pick GPT-6.2 Astra.

  3. Start a second session in a new worktree. Pick GPT-6.2 Sol.

  4. Paste the prompt below into both.

  5. When they finish, open each result in the built-in browser and compare.

Here is the prompt:

Build a polished, interactive 3D scene that simulates ancient Egyptian workers constructing a pyramid, supported by boats delivering materials along a river.

Choose the technical approach, visual style, layout, construction methods, and animation techniques yourself. Focus on meeting the requirements below rather than following a prescribed design.

Core Requirements

- Show construction from the beginning through to a finished, explorable pyramid.
- Workers must perform meaningful work and coordinate intelligently. Heavy loads should be handled collectively, with believable assignments and movement.
- Boats should travel convincingly, stop at suitable docking or anchor points, unload, and support a functional flow of materials to the builders.
- Include different useful wares, not only stones. Their delivery and use should matter to construction.
- Build the entrance, tunnels, and burial spaces as part of the simulation. Workers must construct them, rather than simply revealing a prebuilt interior.
- The finished pyramid should function as a believable virtual tomb with a connected, walkable interior.
- Draw inspiration from plausible ancient Egyptian engineering. Use judgment where historical methods are uncertain.

Experience and Quality

- Make the building, hauling, unloading, and underground work animations convincing, including when viewed up close.
- Different wares should have appropriate handling for their material, weight, and purpose. Avoid generic or cheap-looking motion, floating loads, unexplained transformations, and obvious clipping.
- Provide transparency and first-person buttons that remain available during construction.
- Transparency should make internal and underground work easy to inspect.
- First-person mode should offer a pleasant, responsive walking experience around accessible areas and through the finished interior.
- Keep the ordinary HUD minimal, retaining compact speed, reset, transparency, and first-person controls.
- Make underground information and navigation attractive and useful without cluttering the view.
- Ensure stable geometry and rendering, particularly inside the pyramid. Avoid flickering walls, visible gaps, and clunky movement.
- Use free tools and assets without requiring paid services.

Workflow and Delivery

- Build from scratch and stay in the current worktree.
- Implement and test the solution yourself, including the complete construction flow and exploration.
- Keep testing and iteration fast. Avoid endless analysis, repeated long benchmarks, or waiting through construction in real time for every check.
- Finish with a working application, start it, open the preview, and briefly report the results and any remaining limitations.

A few tips for a fair comparison:

  • Use the same Kilo Desktop version and settings for both models.

  • Run each model at least three times. One run can flatter or hurt either side.

  • Write down time and plan usage per run, so you can compare cost as well as looks.

  • Check the prompt's own requirements: boats docking, workers hauling together, a walkable interior, working transparency and first-person buttons.

Bring your ChatGPT plan to Kilo

You don't need an API key to try these models. With Sign in with ChatGPT, you pick "Continue with ChatGPT" in Kilo, and your requests draw on the Codex and ChatGPT Work usage included in your plan instead of per-token API billing.

  • Works across Kilo. Desktop, VS Code, JetBrains, the CLI, Cloud Agents, Code Reviews and the mobile app.

  • You stay in control. Per OpenAI, connecting an app adds no new allowance, and you can cap how much of your weekly plan Kilo uses in ChatGPT settings under Usage.

  • Your chats stay yours. Using your plan does not give Kilo access to your ChatGPT conversations or memories.

  • Switch freely. Use your plan's OpenAI models next to the 500+ models in the Kilo Gateway, from the same model picker.

For teams

Kilo now supports ChatGPT Business plans too. Admins enable "Use ChatGPT plan" for Kilo under Tenant settings, then External access in the OpenAI admin console, and can set a workspace-wide limit on how much of each member's included allowance approved services can use. Usage shows up in the OpenAI dashboard like any other connected app.

OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT docs list eligible plans (Go, Plus, Pro and Business) and the full admin steps.

Which one should you use?

Start with Sol for everyday work. It costs a quarter of Astra per token, and OpenAI's own FrontierCode result puts it within 0.5 points of Astra at about one-fifth the cost. Reach for Astra when quality matters most: 3D and visual work, long projects, and the hardest problems. In our pyramid test, that is where it pulled ahead.

The best answer depends on your tasks, and Kilo makes it easy to find out. Run both on the same job, compare the diffs, and keep the one you would merge. If you'd rather not choose, Auto Efficient picks the least expensive model proven capable of the task.

Download Kilo Desktop, connect your ChatGPT plan, and try the new Astra and Sol today. Then tell us what you build.
