title: Vite • seedcord v0.22.0
description:
With v0.22, we're bringing Vite to production builds too! seedcord dev was already using Vite, and now seedcord build does as well. With Vite 8 (Rolldown), this means faster builds and more consistency between development and production. Previously, production builds were transpiled with TypeScript and their aliases rewritten with tsc-alias.

To upgrade your bot, run your package manager's upgrade command:

pnpm update --latest seedcord @seedcord/http
bun update --latest seedcord @seedcord/http
npm install seedcord@latest @seedcord/http@latest
yarn upgrade --latest seedcord @seedcord/http

# Replace @seedcord/http with your transport, and update any Seedcord plugins you use.

New to seedcord? Scaffold your first bot with our create-seedcord CLI:

pnpm create seedcord@latest
bun create seedcord@latest
npm init seedcord@latest
yarn create seedcord@latest

Then head over to our first bot guide.

Curious what seedcord does and why? Start here!

Here are some things from this release we'd like to highlight:

Static builds with Vite & Vite plugin support

As mentioned above, this release features Vite builds for production (seedcord build). Before, only seedcord dev was using Vite, which meant we had two different build paths for dev and prod. As an additional pain point, the previous production build was more of a "transpilation": at runtime, your modules were still being dynamically read from the filesystem instead of statically imported.

By moving to Vite and unifying dev and build, we now have consistent parsing behaviour across dev and prod, as well as reduced complexity, and no more of that runtime module importing behaviour. Hooray for all!

Because we have now adopted Vite entirely, you can also use your own Vite plugins in the seedcord config file, like so:

import { defineConfig } from 'seedcord/config';
import { foo } from 'vite-plugin-foo';

export default defineConfig({
    // ...
    vitePlugins: () => [foo()]
});

Make sure that any environment-aware plugins target the seedcord environment, since that's the environment that seedcord is set up in.

You'll find more information about using Vite plugins, and when to use seedcord plugins vs Vite plugins, on this guide page.

This upgrade solves our bundling problems and lets us do something else that's pretty cool:

Edge bots

You can now write HTTP bots that run on the edge (Cloudflare Workers)! Previously, the option to run bots on Workers wasn't functional, and you only had the option to run it on a server runtime like Node. With this release, you can now write bots using seedcord that build as Cloudflare Workers. These bots use Discord's Interactions webhook capability to allow your bot to receive certain events as a webhook call to your bot instead of via the Gateway, and when you're done, you can deploy them to the Cloudflare Workers platform.

To get started, run either of these commands (depending on your package manager):

pnpm create seedcord
bun create seedcord
npm init seedcord
yarn create seedcord

Then select the HTTP bots option.

And finally select Cloudflare Workers.

Make sure to fill in the remaining details as requested, and then your bot should now be scaffolded.

Note: The runtime option will only appear for HTTP bots.

Now, cd into your project directory:

cd edge-bot # replace with your bot's directory

And run seedcord dev with your package manager. Your bot will now be running and ready for you to iterate on. Edit a relevant file, and your bot will have hot module replacement (HMR) activating to swap out the module you just edited, faster than you can blink!

In dev, the bot is running inside workerd, the same runtime used by Cloudflare Workers. This ensures there are few differences between your local testing and the production runtime. This is possible thanks to us moving to use Vite for both dev and build, allowing us to fully utilise the Vite Environment API. This system allows us to coordinate dev and build in a separate runtime like this and accurately map the seedcord application. Huge thanks to the Vite team for making this!

Before your first deploy, log in to Cloudflare and deploy your commands. The build reads their IDs from Discord:

pnpm exec cf auth login
pnpm exec seedcord commands deploy
pnpm build
pnpm exec cf deploy --prebuilt --secrets-file .secrets.env

Make sure DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN is available in your shell or .env when you build. For the first deploy, put every secret declared in cloudflare.config.ts in .secrets.env, not just the bot token. Keep that file out of git. After the first deploy, the scaffold's deploy script builds and deploys without the secrets file. With Bun, use bunx for each pnpm exec command and bun run build for pnpm build. And voila! Now you've got a seedcord edge bot deployed to Cloudflare.

Set Discord's Interactions Endpoint URL to your Worker URL in the developer portal.

Read up on this in the guide page.

Command management via CLI

If you've ever deployed any bot to Discord (not just seedcord ones), you'll know that command management is a bit of a pain. There's no way to delete your registered commands in Discord's developer portal, whether they're global or guild commands.

That pain is no more for seedcord bots! Starting with this version, the framework CLI now has a commands subcommand, which is your home for managing command deployments.

Running seedcord commands gives you the following options:

  • Deploy the commands in your code - seedcord will read your code, compile a list of commands, and deploy them according to how you configured your command (guild commands are deployed to a server of your choosing, global commands are deployed to the bot itself).
  • List the commands Discord has - Lists the commands your bot has deployed globally or in servers.
  • Delete guild commands that duplicate a global command - Removes guild commands that share a name with a global command.
  • Delete every command globally or in guilds - Deletes every command your bot has registered, globally and/or in guilds. This is very destructive. Make sure you've selected the right bot and, if applicable, the right guild!

Each of these can also be accessed with subcommands:

  • deploy [options]
  • list [options]
  • clean [options]
  • purge [options]

This allows you to have simplified command management while building and maintaining your bot with seedcord!

To learn more about the subcommands, visit this guide page.

Library mode

seedcord bots can be built (and published) as libraries! This allows you to write your bots using the framework, and export them for use as part of a larger application. This will be most useful to bots on HTTP transports, as you can easily integrate them into backend frameworks like Hono, H3, Elysia, or even full-stack frameworks like Nitro, TanStack Start, Astro, and more.

To build library bots, omit build.start from your seedcord config:

import { defineConfig } from 'seedcord/config';

export default defineConfig({
    root: './src',
    instance: './bot.ts'
    // do not set build.start
});

And now, your bot will be packaged as a library, ready for you to reuse it elsewhere.

To use library bots, simply import them from their bot entrypoint:

import bot from '@mypkg/bot'; // Change the entrypoint to your bot package entrypoint

HTTP bots comply with the export default { fetch } standard used by Cloudflare Workers, Bun, Hono, H3, Elysia, and more. This means that you can simply pass in one Request object and get the Response from the bot. In a Node server, call start() before passing requests to fetch(); on Workers, the first request starts the bot. The embedding guide has an example.

For Gateway bots, start them using the start method:

await bot.start();

Your bot can now be used like a library in another app.

See the guide to learn more. There's also a guide page on integrating with web servers.

Session lock files

Did you ever start a dev server and forget about it? Well, as a small new addition to this update, we've added a session lock file.

When you start a dev session, a lock file records the Discord application ID. If another dev session starts with the same application ID, the CLI shows the first session's folder, process id, start time, and lock file path. Press q in that session to stop it, or remove the lock if the session has already stopped.

This will not trigger if bots are using different applications, so it won't get in your way if you are developing several distinct bots.

Other fixes and improvements

  • ~40 bug fixes were included in this release
  • create-seedcord got a refreshed look, asks if you want to install dependencies and initialize a git repo, and comes with a sample uptime plugin.
  • The TUI is now more responsive for narrower screens (such as mobile or split screen on computers)
  • Certain layout and filter preferences for dev sessions are now saved across sessions.
  • The bot health check was revamped and now correctly says ready when the bot is actually ready for gateway and HTTP bots running on Node.

For the rest of the release information, read the release changelog.

Join our Discord server to chat with others about seedcord!

First posted on the seedcord blog.

title: What to do when you hit your Claude Code usage limit
description:
You're mid-task and Claude Code stops with You've hit your session limit. Here's what's going on, what you can do right now, and how to make the next window last longer.

1. Find out which limit you hit

On a Pro or Max plan, every request counts against two limits at once: a five-hour session limit and a weekly limit. Whichever runs out first stops you. Both are shared with claude.ai and Claude Desktop, so a long chat on the web leaves less for the terminal.

Run /usage to see both limits and when each one resets. The message also tells you which one you hit:

  • You've hit your session limit: the five-hour window. It resets in full five hours after your first message.
  • You've hit your weekly limit: resets at a fixed day and time on your account (Settings > Usage shows it).
  • You've hit your Opus limit / Sonnet limit: a model-specific cap. This is the only case where switching models gets you going again.

A 529 overloaded error isn't a usage limit at all. It means the servers are busy, so retry or switch models.

2. What you can do right now

Option How Cost
Wait Claude Code picks the task back up after the reset in interactive sessions (v2.1.234+) Nothing
Use a saved limit reset Settings > Usage on the web or in Claude Desktop, when Anthropic has given you one Nothing
Turn on usage credits /usage-credits opens Settings > Usage. Set a monthly cap API rates per turn
Use an API key Sign in with a Claude Console account Per token, billed apart from your plan
Upgrade Max or Ultra $100 or $200 a month as of November 2026. Weekly limits still apply

If you just need to finish one thing, usage credits with a low cap is the least painful. Every overflow turn bills at its model's API price, so leaving Opus on for a rename gets expensive.

3. Make the next window last

Most people burn their limit on the model, not the work. Claude Code's default model on Pro and Max is Opus 5.5, so every turn runs on Opus unless you change it: renames, commit messages and one-line fixes included. Anthropic's own cost guide says Sonnet handles most coding tasks well for less.

  • Make Sonnet your default: /model sonnet. Switch to /model opus when a task really needs it.
  • Or use opusplan: /model opusplan runs Opus while you plan and Sonnet while it executes (Shift+Tab cycles into plan mode).
  • Give subagents a smaller model: add model: haiku or model: sonnet to their frontmatter, or set CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL. Otherwise an Opus session runs Opus subagents.
  • /clear between unrelated tasks. Claude Code sends the whole conversation with every request, so a quick question at the end of a long session pays for all of it. /compact helps when you need to keep going, but the compaction itself is one big request.
  • Watch what runs while you're away: scheduled /loop tasks, subagents and agent teams all send their own requests. Agent teams can use about 7× the tokens of a normal session.
  • Keep usage on screen: /usage breaks recent usage down by skill, subagent, plugin and MCP server, and flags anything behind 10% or more of it.

The model swap is the big one. Moving routine turns off Opus stretches a plan much further than trimming context does.

4. Or let something pick the model for you

Switching models by hand works until you forget. I'm building AutoRouter, a Mac app that does it per turn: a router that lives inside all your coding agents and runs on the AI subscriptions you already pay for. In Claude Code you pick it with /model. Hard work goes to the strongest model your plans cover, and quick tasks go to the cheapest model that can handle them. Every turn shows which model ran, what it cost and why.

When one plan hits its limit, AutoRouter moves to the connected account with the most room left before it spends any credit. With Pro, turns keep going from its monthly included usage until your plan resets. It's free to start and runs on macOS 14 or later.

Quick checklist

  1. /usage: which limit, and when does it reset?
  2. Model-specific limit? Switch models. Session or weekly? Wait, use a saved reset, or turn on capped usage credits.
  3. Next session: /model sonnet (or opusplan), smaller models for subagents, /clear often.

For the same breakdown across every coding agent and plan, see AI coding usage limits, explained.

Disclosure: I'm a co-founder of AutoRouter.

title: MV-JEPA: Post-Training Video Encoders for Cross-View Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.25172v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: JEPA-based video encoders learn strong representations for video and image understanding through prediction in latent space. However, their standard pretraining predicts features within individual images or video clips, without explicitly exploiting paired camera views of the same object or moment. Consequently, the learned representations may not reliably support matching across different camera viewpoints. To solve this problem, we introduce multi-view predictive post-training to strengthen cross-view instance and temporal correspondence while retaining independent single-view inference. A shared encoder processes masked context views independently, and a training-time predictor jointly predicts latent tokens for masked context regions and a fully held-out view. We alternate cross-view prediction with single-view masked prediction on general image and video data to help retain the encoder's pretrained capabilities. After only 9,000 post-training updates on a single GPU, MV-JEPA improves cross-view instance retrieval and coarse cross-camera moment retrieval on various datasets, with further gains in zero-shot action-phase retrieval and frozen-feature classification on AE2. Frozen-probe evaluations further indicate that post-training largely preserves motion recognition, image recognition, and dense semantic segmentation performance on the evaluated benchmarks. Together, these results demonstrate that multi-view predictive post-training can strengthen instance and coarse temporal correspondence in JEPA video encoders without modifying the encoder architecture or single-view inference interface.

title: Fast Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty Quantification in Sparse AI Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.24159v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating how an AI system will perform on a new benchmark need not require another large model. We use public evaluation counts to choose a weak Beta prior, then update it exactly from at most 31 revealed outcomes. The predictor uses no item semantics, pretrained weights, or inference API. Its single online evaluation in the AIMS competition returned a team-reported Brier ALC of 0.188477, a 24.6% reduction from the constant-0.5 reference. The complete submission is 7,754 bytes; a server microbenchmark measures 12.71 microseconds per prediction with 31 matching labels. We describe how source evaluations are compressed into 301 prior means and show why a concentration of two lets new evidence rapidly determine the prediction. The resulting posterior gives exact uncertainty about the modelled success rate without numerical integration or neural inference. A public evaluation covers 79 system-benchmark pairs and eight seeds, reaching Brier ALC 0.200250 for the submitted method. Accompanying code and sufficient statistics reconstruct the fitted prior byte for byte and replay all 632 evaluation trajectories. The result demonstrates how much predictive value a compact Bayesian model can extract from sparse target feedback at very low online cost.

title: Our footer links brighten from 2.53:1 to 7.85:1 when you hover them, and a phone cannot hover
description:
I weighed every character on Notifio's site by its contrast ratio a few days ago, and the single worst thing in that measurement was the footer: the same 14-link column repeated on 38 pages, drawn in #525252 on #0a0a0a, which is 2.53:1 and fails AA at any size.

That post measured the colour. It did not look at what happens when you point at it. This one does, because the answer turned out to be the most interesting thing about the site's CSS.

#525252 on #0a0a0a      2.53:1    footer link, resting
#a3a3a3 on #0a0a0a      7.85:1    footer link, hovered

A footer link on this site goes from failing to comfortably passing when a pointer touches it. That is a 3.1x change in luminance contrast, triggered by an input device that nobody reading it on a phone has.

Every hover rule on the site

The whole stylesheet is 39,976 bytes and contains five media queries:

@media (min-width:40rem)    1     sm
@media (min-width:48rem)    1     md
@media (min-width:64rem)    1     lg
@media (hover:hover)        2

Those last two blocks are 649 bytes and hold every hover declaration on the site. All eleven of them, unminified:

@media (hover:hover){
  .hover\:border-\[\#2a2a2a\]:hover { border-color: #2a2a2a }
  .hover\:border-\[\#404040\]:hover { border-color: #404040 }
  .hover\:border-\[\#525252\]:hover { border-color: #525252 }
  .hover\:border-\[\#737373\]:hover { border-color: #737373 }
  .hover\:bg-\[\#0f0f0f\]:hover     { background-color: #0f0f0f }
  .hover\:bg-\[\#1e1e1e\]:hover     { background-color: #1e1e1e }
  .hover\:bg-\[\#141414\]:hover     { background-color: #141414 }
  .hover\:bg-\[\#e5e5e5\]:hover     { background-color: #e5e5e5 }
  .hover\:text-\[\#a3a3a3\]:hover   { color: #a3a3a3 }
  .hover\:text-\[\#fafafa\]:hover   { color: #fafafa }
}
@media (hover:hover){
  .group-hover\:text-\[\#fafafa\]:is(:where(.group):hover *) { color: #fafafa }
}

Border colour, background colour, text colour. Not one of them changes a text-decoration, a font-weight, a size or a position. The site's entire interactive vocabulary is "this thing changes colour".

Tailwind v4 is the reason they are inside a media query, and it is the right default: hover styles that stick to an element after a tap are a classic touch bug, so the generated CSS only applies them where the pointer can actually hover. I did not write that wrapper and I would not remove it. It does mean that on a phone, those 649 bytes are downloaded and never match anything.

Against the 1,091 links that are actually on the pages

I then walked every anchor on all 38 live pages and read its classes and computed styles.

anchors                              1,091
  footer                               532
  content                              348
  nav                                  211

carrying at least one hover token    1,048
  change colour only               1,048
  add an underline                       0
  change weight, size or position        0

carrying no hover response at all       43
  the nav wordmark, once per page        38
  the five cards on /guides               5

The 656 most common ones are hover:text-[#a3a3a3] on a base of #525252, which is the footer measurement above plus the citation links on the fifteen site pages.

And then there are the 43 with nothing. Thirty-eight of them are the wordmark in the nav, which is fine: it is a logo, it reads as a home link by convention. The other five are the five guide cards on the guides hub, and the reason that is worth a paragraph is what sits directly underneath them on the same page:

/guides, content links            hover classes
  "How fast do rental listings..."   none
  "How to be first to a new..."      none
  "What to write in your first..."   none
  "The documents to have ready..."   none
  "How to spot a rental scam..."     none
  "For students"                     hover:bg-[#0f0f0f]
  "For people relocating"            hover:bg-[#0f0f0f]
  "For Amsterdam"                    hover:bg-[#0f0f0f]
  "See pricing"                      hover:bg-[#e5e5e5]
  "Compare the alternatives"         hover:border + hover:text

Two card grids, one page, and only the lower one responds to a pointer. The sites hub and the comparison hub both give their cards hover:bg-[#0f0f0f] as well, so the five guide cards are the only clickable cards on the site that do nothing at all when you point at them.

What is left when hover is gone

So I asked the narrow version of the question: with no pointer, no hover and no colour perception, how do you know something is a link? The answer for a standalone link in a card or a list is position, which is legitimate. The answer for a link inside a sentence has to be an underline, because WCAG 1.4.1 requires a non-colour cue when a link sits in a block of text.

underlined anchors                              90 of 1,091
anchors inline in prose, next to other text     25
  of those, underlined                          25
  of those, the same colour as the text around   20

Twenty-five is a small number for a 38 page site, and it is the right number to care about: everything else on this site is a card, a nav item or a list row. All 25 of them are underlined, so the site passes the one rule most marketing sites fail. Twenty of the 25 are drawn in exactly the same colour as the sentence they sit in, which means the underline is not a decoration there, it is the entire signal. Delete underline from the shared class string and twenty links become invisible prose on the terms, the privacy policy and the about page.

Focus is the third cue, and the stylesheet has exactly two authored focus rules, both of them on the one email field in the app. Every link keeps Chrome's default focus ring, which is the only state cue on this site that works for a keyboard user and the reason the keyboard story is in better shape than the touch story.

The actual problem, stated plainly

Hover is an enhancement. It is not allowed to be the thing that makes text readable, and in our footer it is.

532 footer links
  resting:  #525252  2.53:1   fails AA for all text sizes
  hovered:  #a3a3a3  7.85:1   passes AAA
  on touch: no hover state exists

A reader on a phone gets the 2.53:1 version and has no way to reach the other one. The fix is one token: make #737373 (4.18:1) or #a3a3a3 the resting colour and let the hover go to #fafafa. That is the same number of CSS declarations, it costs nothing in bytes, and it moves the readable state from "if you have a mouse" to "always".

The two smaller ones while I am in there: give the five guide cards the hover:bg-[#0f0f0f] their sibling hubs already have, and keep the 25 prose underlines exactly where they are.

Everything above is measurable from outside. Open the footer of any page, compare it on a phone and on a laptop, and the difference you are looking at is 649 bytes of CSS that one of those two devices has decided not to use.

title: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler adds 589 new API actions and event bus targets
description:
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler expands its AWS SDK integrations with 589 new API actions across 81 AWS services, and adds templated targets for the enhanced EventBridge Custom event bus. You can now schedule direct invocations of a broader set of AWS services without writing custom integration code.

EventBridge Scheduler is a serverless scheduler that allows you to create, run, and manage billions of scheduled events and tasks across more than 270 AWS services, without provisioning or managing the underlying infrastructure. With a new templated target, you can schedule event delivery directly to the Custom event bus using its PutEvents or PutRawEvents API. The templated target also makes it easier to add metadata fields to each event. For example, you can send an event to your bus every night at midnight to start a reconciliation workflow, with no function in between to call the API.

The new API actions are available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon EventBridge Scheduler is available, subject to the availability of each target service in the Region. The templated targets for the Custom event bus are available in all AWS Regions where the enhanced Custom event bus is available. To learn more, see Using templated targets in EventBridge Scheduler and Using universal targets in EventBridge Scheduler in the Amazon EventBridge Scheduler User Guide. Install the Agent Toolkit for AWS to start building with your AI coding agent.

title: China-Linked Hackers Exploit Critical VMware vCenter Zero-Day to Gain Admin Access and Steal Data

title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.25003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

title: Social Identity Unlinking Under Abuse (Keeping Logistics Operators Signed In)
description:
Keep the existing identity attached until another working sign-in method has been confirmed, and make that check inseparable from removal. For a logistics application wiring Google and GitHub social sign-in, successful authentication through one provider doesn't justify letting a browser remove every other way back into the dispatcher account.

Short answer: list the account's identities before unlinking, verify that at least one usable method will remain, authorize the change against the signed-in account, and notify the user which methods remain afterward. Serialize competing changes to the same account. A count checked against an old snapshot cannot protect the last login method.

The request for a Node.js unlink example has a language-independent safety requirement: the server must preserve that invariant across the entire mutation. The Go examples below separate the decision from the transport so neither depends on guessed authentication response fields.

What page fired when a social identity disappeared?

Start the prospective postmortem with that question. A dashboard showing successful unlink requests says little about whether a dispatcher can sign in again before the next shift, and a successful session already open in a browser is poor evidence that the remaining Google or GitHub identity will work on the next login.

Consider a deliberately hypothetical account, dispatcher-42, with 2 attached identities: one Google identity and one GitHub identity. A legitimate operator wants to remove GitHub. An attacker with access to that operator's session could want the same mutation for a different reason, particularly if removing another method makes recovery harder. The unlink control therefore needs both authorization and a remaining-method check; a CAPTCHA alone cannot establish that the person requesting the change owns the account or can use the surviving identity.

Count usable methods.

An attached identity is a record, while a working login is an operational property that needs evidence. Before allowing this example's GitHub removal, require the operator to demonstrate access through the Google method that will remain, following a fresh authentication flow appropriate to the application's risk. Don't infer that access from a matching email address or a provider label supplied by the browser. This is an application policy recommendation, not a claim that every identity service exposes the same verification field.

The page should identify user impact: an account left without a usable sign-in method, or unexpected account changes that warrant investigation. Track rejected removal attempts separately so a bot cannot turn repeated clicks into an endless stream of urgent alerts. A notification that says only “security settings changed” also misses the useful information: which sign-in method still works, and what to do if the change was unexpected.

How can an account unlink a social identity and keep one login method?

Use the authenticated server-side account as the owner of the operation. Treat the identity selected in the UI as an untrusted target, require fresh authorization for this sensitive change, and apply the same per-account serialization to every code path that can alter login methods. Read the identity list inside that boundary, establish that the target belongs to the account, and check for a confirmed alternative before removing anything.

The dangerous interleaving is small: request A sees Google and GitHub, request B sees the same pair, then each removes a different identity. Both prechecks passed. The account has no remaining method. A lock scoped only to an individual HTTP handler, or a check performed after deletion, doesn't resolve that race across application instances.

For logistics operators, reject an unsafe change with a useful next step: confirm another login method and try again. Keep that interaction out of the dispatch workflow wherever possible; making account maintenance disruptive creates pressure to weaken the guard during a busy shift.

Here is a complete local Go program that demonstrates the guard and its refusal to remove the final method. Its fields are application-owned example data, not a vendor response schema. confirmed represents evidence established by trusted authentication code before this operation; never populate it directly from a request body.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "sync"
)

type identity struct {
    provider  string
    confirmed bool
}

type account struct {
    mu         sync.Mutex
    identities map[string]identity
}

func (a *account) unlink(target string) ([]string, error) {
    a.mu.Lock()
    defer a.mu.Unlock()

    if _, exists := a.identities[target]; !exists {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("identity is not attached to this account")
    }
    remaining := make([]string, 0, len(a.identities))
    for id, method := range a.identities {
        if id != target && method.confirmed {
            remaining = append(remaining, method.provider)
        }
    }
    if len(remaining) == 0 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("confirm another working login method first")
    }
    delete(a.identities, target)
    return remaining, nil
}

func main() {
    dispatcher := &account{
        identities: map[string]identity{
            "google-example": {provider: "Google", confirmed: true},
            "github-example": {provider: "GitHub", confirmed: true},
        },
    }
    remaining, err := dispatcher.unlink("github-example")
    fmt.Printf("remaining=%v error=%v\n", remaining, err)
    _, err = dispatcher.unlink("google-example")
    fmt.Printf("last-method attempt: %v\n", err)
}

The first operation returns Google as the remaining method. The second returns an error before deleting it. That refusal is the behavior to carry into a Node.js handler as well; changing the language doesn't change the ordering requirement.

This program deliberately has one account in one process. Its mutex doesn't coordinate multiple servers, its map isn't durable, and it doesn't implement OAuth, session validation, or notifications. In production, coordinate the authoritative identity mutation across all writers. If a remote provider owns identity state, a local database transaction alone cannot make that provider's removal atomic; assess the provider's concurrency guarantees and ensure every application removal passes through the same coordinator. Without that boundary, a clean unit test proves very little about the race that matters.

Choose the identity boundary before choosing the dashboard

The useful comparison is how much of the identity lifecycle the application must coordinate. None of the following choices removes the need to define what counts as a usable alternative or to authorize the unlink request.

Auth0 documents unlinking an identity from an account, making its account-linking model a relevant starting point when evaluating how a service handles linked social identities. Examine its primary and secondary identity semantics before mapping a dispatcher to them; a deletion primitive is only part of the application policy.

Firebase Authentication documents unlinking a provider from a user. That provider-oriented model is worth examining when Google and GitHub are the identities your application presents, but the UI still needs to explain what survives the change. Test the next sign-in rather than treating a successful unlink call as the acceptance criterion.

Amazon Cognito documents AdminDisableProviderForUser for disabling a provider relationship. Its administrative operation is a different integration surface from a client-facing unlink action, so assess where privileged authorization belongs and how your application maps the selected external identity. Don't make the browser responsible for that decision.

Infrai is another option for identity management and the follow-up email, offering a unified API across 295 routes and 20 modules through one REST API with no SDK required, one key and one bill. For this logistics workflow, adding a remaining-method notification extends the same contract instead of introducing another integration, credential to rotate, or invoice to reconcile. Public, keyless discovery supplies request and response schemas, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages; those help a team implementing the same policy in Node.js and Go avoid inventing adapter fields. The trade-off is application responsibility: a common transport contract does not replace the remaining-login policy or its concurrency boundary. Prefer an existing Auth0 integration if its identity model already meets the application's requirements and this change would otherwise require a migration.

The table compares integration boundaries rather than claiming that one product blocks more bots. Setup effort is a qualitative assessment for this unlink workflow, not a benchmark.

Option Integration surface Setup effort for this workflow Suitable context Main boundary to review
Auth0 Identity management API Map primary and secondary identities before authorizing removal An application already using its linked-account model Unlink semantics and the surviving account's access
Firebase Authentication Provider unlink operation through its SDK model Map the selected provider to the current user An application already managing social providers with Firebase Remaining-provider usability and sensitive-change authorization
Amazon Cognito Administrative provider-disabling API Put privileged execution behind application authorization A user pool already owning the application's identities Provider identifiers and the consequences of disabling a relationship

Choose on that boundary.

Existing ownership of the user record, the location of privileged credentials, and the ability to coordinate every removal matter more here than a polished settings screen. If the existing identity service already meets those requirements, keeping its identity model avoids a migration solely for an unlink button. These alternatives have different identity models; comparing them as interchangeable buttons hides exactly the distinction an incident responder needs to understand.

For a read-only transport check, this separate Go program lists the identities before any removal. Configure AUTH_API_ORIGIN with the service's documented HTTPS origin, without a trailing slash or version path, and set INFRAI_API_KEY and AUTH_USER_ID in a controlled server environment. The user ID must come from trusted account context. This inspection program prints the response, so keep its output out of shared logs. The intentionally unparsed response must be mapped using the discovered schema before connecting it to the guard above.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func run() error {
    origin := os.Getenv("AUTH_API_ORIGIN")
    key, user := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"), os.Getenv("AUTH_USER_ID")
    u, err := url.Parse(origin)
    if err != nil || u.Scheme != "https" || u.Host == "" ||
        u.User != nil || u.Path != "" || u.RawQuery != "" || u.Fragment != "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set AUTH_API_ORIGIN to the documented HTTPS origin")
    }
    if key == "" || user == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("set INFRAI_API_KEY and AUTH_USER_ID")
    }
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    path := strings.ReplaceAll("/v1/auth/identity/list/{user_id}", "{user_id}", url.PathEscape(user))
    endpoint := origin + path
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    return fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after %s seconds", retry)
                }
                if wait := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second; wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                wait := time.Until(date)
                if wait > 60*time.Second {
                    return fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after %s", retry)
                }
                if wait > delay {
                    delay = wait
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("identity listing returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("identity listing retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This GET performs no mutation. It uses an explicit method, server-held credentials, a 15-second request timeout, and at most 4 attempts that honor a valid Retry-After value or return control when the requested wait exceeds the 60-second local budget. Those are example limits, not service guarantees. A successful response is evidence that listing worked, not permission to remove an identity.

Verify the next login before closing the change

Use a staging dispatcher account with Google and GitHub attached, confirm the surviving Google method through trusted authentication code, remove GitHub, and then start a separate sign-in through Google. Check that it reaches the same application account. The still-open settings session is insufficient evidence.

Test the refusal path too.

With only Google remaining, attempt to remove it and verify that the identity is retained. Also exercise a missing target, an identity belonging to another account, an unconfirmed alternative, and two concurrent removals aimed at different identities. For the two-removal case, require at least one rejection and inspect the final authoritative identity state, rather than accepting two successful HTTP responses as evidence that the implementation behaved correctly.

For abuse resistance, include repeated removal attempts from a session that has not completed the required fresh authentication. The acceptance condition is that those attempts cannot mutate identity state. Rate-limit this sensitive action according to application risk, but keep authorization and the surviving-method guard in place; slowing an unauthorized operation doesn't make it authorized. OWASP's authentication guidance is the reference point for sensitive-change reauthentication, rather than a claim that any vendor automatically applies this exact policy.

After a confirmed removal, notify the user which login methods remain. Keep notification delivery separate from the success criterion for preserving access: an email reaching an inbox cannot establish that the surviving social identity signs in to the intended dispatcher account. Record the change and its outcome without copying credentials or authentication tokens into operational logs.

Roll back the release without weakening the guard

If verification fails, stop accepting new unlink operations while preserving ordinary sign-in. Keep the remaining-method requirement in the previous release as well; rolling back the interface must not reopen the final-identity deletion path.

A code rollback does not reattach an identity already removed. If an operator needs to restore a provider relationship, require the normal authenticated linking flow and proof of control, or follow the application's established recovery procedure when sign-in is unavailable. Don't reconstruct ownership from a matching email address or a support request alone.

The postmortem question is concrete: which page would tell the responder that a dispatcher cannot get back in? A dashboard full of successful removals still leaves that question unanswered.

References

  • OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
  • Auth0, Unlink User Accounts
  • Firebase Authentication, account linking and unlinking
  • Amazon Cognito, AdminDisableProviderForUser

title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2607.15277v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to perform a form of conditional inference. In-context learning is one implicit way to do this. The prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We use binary trees as an evaluation scaffold to recursively partition a population into increasingly fine-grained subpopulations. We then prompt LLMs with verbalized subpopulation descriptions in context, aggregate the resulting estimates back into population-level estimates, and compare them across partitions of varying granularity. Translating these comparisons into a benchmark score and evaluating frontier models across problem domains, we demonstrate widespread violations of basic consistency properties. An in-depth study of persona prompting further reveals a pattern we call the macro fallacy: estimates reconstructed from more fine-grained subpopulation responses are often better aligned with human reference data than direct population-level estimates. The effect persists across variations in partitioning, verbalization, and estimation task, suggesting that models possess relevant subpopulation knowledge but do not reliably propagate it into aggregate estimates. This gap establishes statistical self-consistency as an unsaturated, reference-free criterion for evaluating LLMs.

title: Why Android apps behave differently on x86 emulators: ARM translation and native libraries explained
description:
Updated November 2026

Android apps behave differently on x86 emulators because native code is compiled for one CPU architecture at a time. Kotlin and Java run on ART and don’t care. Native .so libraries do. An x86 emulator runs either the app’s x86 libraries, which ARM phones never use, or ARM libraries translated to x86 inside the app’s process. Testing on ARM hardware, physical or cloud-hosted, closes both gaps.

What are Android ABIs?

An ABI (application binary interface) is the contract between compiled code and the CPU and system it runs on. Android’s NDK docs describe one ABI per combination of CPU and instruction set. It covers the instruction set, calling conventions, the binary format (always ELF on Android) and endianness (always little-endian).

The NDK supports four ABIs today:

  • armeabi-v7a: 32-bit ARM, with Thumb-2 and Neon

  • arm64-v8a: 64-bit ARM (AArch64)

  • x86: 32-bit Intel and AMD

  • x86_64: 64-bit Intel and AMD

Older ABIs like armeabi and MIPS were removed in NDK r17.

Every device reports which ABIs it can run, primary first:

bash
adb shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist

The primary ABI matches the machine code of the system image itself. Any others listed are secondary ABIs the image also supports. That one line tells you more about a test device than its model name.

On the app side, native libraries live inside the APK at lib/<abi>/lib<name>.so. A “fat” APK carries a folder for each ABI it supports. Since an APK is a zip file, you can check this in seconds:

bash
unzip -l app.apk 'lib/*'

At install time, the package manager looks for libraries under the device’s primary ABI first. If it finds none, it tries the secondary ABIs. It copies the best match into the app’s native library directory and ignores the rest.

That detail drives most of what follows.

What happens when an ARM-only app runs on an x86 emulator?

It depends on the system image. On an image without ARM translation, an ARM-only app usually won’t install. On an image with translation, it installs and runs, with the ARM code translated to x86 inside the app’s process.

Here’s the background. In March 2020, Google announced Android 11 emulator system images for x86 that can run ARM binaries. Before that, you had two options for ARM-only apps on an x86 computer. You could use a full ARM emulation image, which Google describes as much slower, or test on a physical device.

How the translation works, per that Android Developers Blog post:

  • The whole system runs as x86, with normal hardware virtualization.
  • When an app’s process needs an ARM binary, only that binary is translated to x86, inside that process.
  • Everything else in the process, including ART and graphics libraries like libGLES and libvulkan, keeps running natively as x86.
  • The translator skips low-level, hardware-specific libraries to avoid a performance hit.

Two conditions matter for teams. The translation ships only on Google APIs and Play Store system images. It’s also licensed for development and debugging on your own machines, on-premises servers and cloud environments you procure yourself, not for commercial hosted services.

Without translation, the package manager finds no library folder matching any ABI on the image. You’ll usually see INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS and “Failed to extract native libraries” in the install output.

What if the APK also ships x86 libraries?

Then translation never happens, and that’s the trap worth knowing about. The emulator’s primary ABI is x86 or x86_64, so the package manager picks the x86 libraries first. Your test passes on code no ARM phone will ever run.

Usually that’s fine. The x86 and ARM builds come from the same source. But compiler flags, intrinsics, hand-written assembly and third-party SDKs can differ per ABI. A bug that lives only in the ARM build won’t show up on the emulator.

You can push the emulator toward the ARM build on a translation-capable image. Android’s docs describe forcing an ABI at install time on devices that support more than one:

bash
adb install --abi arm64-v8a app.apk

Now you’re testing the ARM library through the translator. That’s closer to what users run, but still not the same as ARM silicon.

On ARM hosts, the picture changes again. Google’s Apple silicon emulator preview ran ARM64 system images through ARM64 hardware virtualization, with no translation involved. Your library then runs as ARM code, but on a laptop CPU inside an emulator, not on a phone’s chipset and vendor build.

What did the test show?

[WRITER: one sentence on the setup. Suggested: “On [date], I installed three apps with native libraries on an x86_64 emulator ([image: API level, Google APIs or Play] on [host CPU]) and on an ARM device ([model, Android version, physical or cloud]).”]

*When is ARM hardware worth it for testing?
*
When native code is part of what you’re testing. If your app is pure Kotlin or Java and every dependency ships x86 builds, an emulator covers most of your day-to-day work. Once native libraries enter the picture, an ARM run before release earns its place.

It’s worth it when:

  • A dependency ships ARM only. Many third-party SDKs never build x86, so on the emulator you’re always testing through translation.
  • You ship x86 libraries too. The emulator runs those by default, so it never touches your ARM build.
  • Native code is performance-sensitive. Games, video, audio, image processing and crypto behave differently under translation, and frame timings on an x86 laptop say little about a phone.
  • Crash reports come only from ARM devices. Reproduce them where they happen.
  • It’s a release candidate. One pass on ARM hardware, the way users install from the store, catches packaging mistakes like a missing ABI folder.

Google’s own advice in the translation announcement points the same way. It still recommends publishing both x86 and ARM variants and treating translation as a testing convenience.

*Where do you get ARM devices?
*
Most teams mix these:

  • Physical phones. The real thing, with sensors, SIM and vendor builds. They need a desk, cables and someone to keep them charged.
  • Device farms. Services like Firebase Test Lab and BrowserStack host physical devices you test on per session. Good for broad coverage and CI. Devices reset between sessions.
  • Cloud phone providers. Persistent Android devices in a data centre that you keep and reach over the network. Multilogin, a cloud Android phone platform for multi-account management, is one example: each cloud phone runs on its own real ARM Android device. It offers 30+ device types across 12 brands, Android versions selectable per profile, APK upload and full ADB access, so the commands above work as-is. Its cloud phones can’t receive SMS or calls, and they need a reliable connection. GeeLark, DuoPlus and VMOS Cloud also offer cloud phones.
  • ARM hosts running ARM64 emulator images. No translation, but still an emulator, not a phone.

Whichever you pick, run getprop ro.product.cpu.abilist first. It’s the quickest way to know what you’re actually testing on.

FAQ

What’s the difference between ARM and x86 Android emulators?
An x86 emulator runs an x86 system image. ARM native libraries run there only through translation, and only on images that include it. An ARM64 image on an ARM host runs ARM code directly. Neither is a phone, but only the second runs your ARM libraries as ARM code.

Why does my app crash only on the emulator?
Check which library it loaded. If the APK has x86 libraries, the emulator runs those, so the crash may sit in your x86 build. If it’s ARM-only, the crash may come from code the translator handles differently. adb logcat -b crash -d shows the native stack, including the library path.

Do I need ARM hardware if my app is pure Kotlin or Java?
Rarely for day-to-day work, because ART runs your bytecode on any ABI. Check your dependencies with unzip -l app.apk 'lib/*'. If a lib/ folder shows up, you have native code after all.

Can I use the emulator’s ARM translation in a hosted testing service?
Not as a commercial service. Google’s announcement limits it to development and debugging on your own machines, on-premises servers and cloud environments you procure. It isn’t meant for providing commercial hosted services.

Is a cloud-hosted ARM device the same as a physical phone for testing?
For native code, it runs ARM binaries on ARM hardware, as a phone does. Other details depend on the provider, such as device models, Android versions, SIM and sensors. Multilogin’s cloud phones, for example, offer full ADB access but can’t receive SMS or calls.

title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
description:
arXiv:2611.23398v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever.
  To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

title: Training-Free Domain Generation for One-Shot Federated Learning with Server-Side Pre-trained Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2611.23908v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) has attracted increasing attention for its ability to substantially reduce communication overhead by limiting client-server interaction to a single communication round. Nevertheless, this limited interaction makes learning from heterogeneous client distributions challenging. Diffusion-based OSFL approaches seek to address this challenge by synthesizing data that approximate client distributions. However, existing diffusion-based approaches often impose substantial computational costs on clients and lack effective visual guidance to generate data aligned with client distributions. To address these limitations, we propose FedDoG, a training-free Domain Generation framework that leverages server-side pre-trained diffusion models to synthesize data aligned with client domains. FedDoG extracts compact domain representations using a frozen image encoder, substantially reducing client-side computational and communication costs. These representations are incorporated into the diffusion model through a pre-trained image-conditioning adapter, thereby providing explicit visual guidance for domain generation. To further improve the quality of synthetic data, FedDoG adapts the strength of visual conditioning according to domain concentration and filters generated samples based on class consistency and predictive entropy. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that FedDoG generates higher-quality synthetic images and outperforms existing OSFL baselines in classification accuracy. Meanwhile, FedDoG reduces client upload and computation time by 99.9% and 91.5%, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/YXTong17/FedDoG.

title: How to Verify AI-Generated Code With Evidence
description:
An AI coding agent says the change is complete. The tests pass. Is that enough to merge?

Not always. The code and its tests may share the same mistaken assumption. A unit test can pass while the feature fails when a real user follows the full workflow. A code review can miss a bug if the reviewer sees the same incomplete context that shaped the implementation.

On November 16, 2026, Addy Osmani described how the Claude Code team approaches this problem. He says about 90% of the team's code is written and reviewed by Claude. That figure comes from Anthropic, not an independent audit. The post's practical value is its verification design. Run the change. Use different checks. Keep each check separate from the change it judges. Measure whether the checks catch real defects.[1]

The same ideas apply to any coding agent. This article turns that account into a workflow you can adapt to an existing project. It does not claim that tests can prove software has no bugs. The goal is narrower: collect evidence that matches the change, then make the remaining uncertainty visible.

Start with the behavior, not the test command

A green test suite answers one question: the checks that ran passed. It does not answer whether the right checks ran or whether they cover the user's task.

Before asking an agent to change code, write down the behavior that must remain true. Keep it concrete. For a paginated endpoint, require no more than the requested number of parent records. Each record should include the expected child data. Also check that the database does not load every match into application memory. These are requirements to verify, not claims about a particular framework or database.

This short list gives the agent a target and gives the reviewer a basis for checking the result. It also makes a useful distinction: implementation evidence shows that the code changed as expected; behavior evidence shows that the running system still meets the requirement.

The Claude Code team's post makes running the application part of verification, not an optional final check. It describes project-specific instructions for starting the app and exercising a change before saving a commit (a snapshot of the code in version control). It also says failures that remain after three repair rounds are handed to a person.[1] The lesson is not that every team needs the same number of attempts. It is that an agent should not keep retrying indefinitely or label a change complete while a required check still fails.

Use tests that look at different failure modes

No single test type catches every class of defect. A reliable workflow uses checks that fail for different reasons.

End-to-end tests check a real path

An end-to-end (E2E) test drives the application through a user-visible flow. A test might create a record. Then it opens the detail page and changes a field. After a reload, it checks the new value.

This can catch failures isolated unit tests miss. The route may not be wired. A response shape can be wrong. A browser control may stay disabled. Data can disappear between layers. The Claude Code team's article recommends investing in E2E tests because they give an agent a running system to inspect and a clear result to act on.[1]

E2E tests cost more time and can fail for reasons outside the code under test. Keep a small, stable path for the behavior being changed. Make the failure useful: preserve the step that failed, the relevant output, and a screenshot or trace when the test environment supports them. A bare timeout gives less help than a report that says which action failed and what the page showed.

Property-based tests check rules across many inputs

A normal example-based test checks a few inputs chosen by a person. A property-based test states a rule, then uses a library to generate many inputs and look for a counterexample (an input that breaks the rule). The rule might say that encoding and then decoding a value returns the original value, or that an account balance never becomes negative.

The Claude Code post discusses round-trip encoding and invariants, which are conditions that must always hold. It also covers idempotency, where repeating an operation has no extra effect, and checking optimized code against a simpler reference implementation. Generated inputs can reveal edge cases that hand-picked tests miss.[1]

Property-based tests are useful when a rule has a broad input space. They are less useful when the requirement is vague or when a generated case cannot be interpreted. Start with a property that a product owner or maintainer can explain in one sentence. Keep the failing input when the library finds a counterexample; that input can become a regression test (a test that catches the same bug if it returns).

Differential tests compare old and new behavior

A differential test runs two implementations with the same inputs and compares their outputs. This helps during a migration or rewrite when the expected behavior should stay the same, even if the internals change.

For instance, a team could run a new parser and the existing parser against the same sample documents. If their outputs differ, the difference needs investigation. Some differences may be intended, so normalize irrelevant details and record approved changes rather than treating every mismatch as a bug. The Claude Code article recommends random inputs or a sample of production traffic for this kind of comparison.[1]

Differential testing has a boundary: the old system is a reference, not an infallible specification. If the old behavior contains a defect that the migration should fix, matching it would preserve the defect. Record which differences are expected and why.

Keep the verifier independent from the patch

A test can be green and still be weak if the code under review can rewrite the test or the rule that runs it. This is a problem of independence as well as test coverage.

The Claude Code team's article describes keeping review rules on the base branch (the target branch for a proposed change) rather than reading a modified copy from the proposal. It also says review results are tied to one commit. That stops a passing result from silently applying to newer code.[1] These controls make the evidence refer to the exact change that was checked.

A project can apply the same principle in simpler ways:

  • Keep required checks in continuous integration (CI) configuration or another trusted location.
  • Have the verifier report the commit identifier it checked.
  • Re-run checks after any code change.
  • Make changes to test rules visible to a human reviewer.
  • Do not let a code change weaken a failing assertion (the condition a test checks) just to make the suite pass.

For a new gate, start in observe mode if the system supports it. It logs which changes would have been blocked without stopping work. Review false alarms, adjust the rule, and enforce it after the check behaves as expected. The Claude Code team describes using this gradual rollout for its commit gate.[1]

This does not mean tests should never change alongside product code. New behavior often needs new tests. It means changes to the judging rules deserve separate scrutiny. When a passing code change removes a check or changes expected output, the reviewer should understand why the old expectation was wrong.

Turn incidents into checks that match the diff

A static checklist can become long enough that nobody uses it. The Claude Code team says it keeps a reliability list of 39 items. Each item has a trigger that can be recognized in a diff (the set of code changes), a check, and a link to the incident or pull request (a proposed code change for review) that motivated it. The agent checks the items whose triggers match the change, usually three to ten items, rather than applying the full list every time.[1]

A small project can use the same structure without copying that list. When a production bug or a review miss happens, record the code change that would have exposed it. Then write a check that runs only when a later diff touches the same behavior. For example, when session storage or message types change, check that older transcripts still work when a new field is missing. That example follows the Claude Code team's post.[1]

This keeps lessons close to the code that needs them. It also gives the reviewer a reason for each extra check. The list needs regular cleanup: remove outdated rules, merge duplicates, and confirm that each check still catches the failure it was added to detect.

For Claude Code users, skills can store reusable instructions for a procedure. Hooks can run defined actions at events such as a tool call or session end. The official skills documentation describes how Claude loads skills for relevant tasks. The hooks reference documents commands and HTTP calls. It also covers other hook types.[2][3] These features can help make checks repeatable, but they do not make a weak check reliable. The project still owns the test commands and their results.

Make failure behavior explicit

An agent needs a stopping rule. Without one, it may repeat a flaky test (one that passes or fails unpredictably). It may alter a timeout or keep editing until the failure disappears. It might do this without finding the cause.

The Claude Code team says it does not let Claude skip flaky tests or add sleeps. It also does not let it retry until a test passes. If it cannot identify the cause, the team removes the test and records why.[1] That is the team's process, not a universal rule that deleting a test is always correct. Another project may set a flaky test aside temporarily. It can record a bug report and block the affected release until the test is repaired.

A useful failure policy answers four questions:

  1. Which failures may the agent repair without approval?
  2. How many repair attempts are allowed before it stops?
  3. What evidence must it include when asking a person to decide?
  4. What happens to a flaky or unavailable check before merge?

If the agent changes a test, it should explain the old assertion. It should say why that assertion was wrong or incomplete. It should also show how the replacement catches the intended regression. A passing result alone cannot answer those questions.

Check whether the checks catch important bugs

A test suite can grow while its value stays unclear. Reviewers can also become noisy: they may report issues that are already present or miss defects that later force the team to undo a change.

The post points to a Code Review team's evaluation based on past incidents and changes later undone. It separates a tuning set (examples used to adjust the check) from a fixed test set (kept aside for evaluation). It compares findings with merged changes that have stayed stable to reduce false alarms. It also measures recall (the share of known defects found) at three stages: raw findings, findings after verification, and final review.[1]

A small team does not need to copy that evaluation system in full. Start by saving examples of defects that escaped review and changes that were incorrectly flagged. For each new check, ask:

  • Does it catch the intended failure in a known example?
  • Does it stay quiet on a similar change that is correct?
  • Is the result actionable, or does it only say that something looks suspicious?
  • Does the check still work after the surrounding code changes?

This shifts review from saying the agent found a bug to asking whether the finding matches a known failure mode and points to evidence. It also helps you decide whether to refine a check or remove one that creates noise.

A practical verification loop

For a small change, the workflow can be direct:

  1. State the expected behavior. Write a short acceptance condition before implementation.
  2. Ask the agent to inspect the relevant code and tests. Require it to identify the commands it plans to run.
  3. Make the smallest useful change. Keep unrelated formatting and cleanup out of the proposed change.
  4. Run focused checks first. Run the narrow test or property check tied to the change.
  5. Run the application path. Exercise the real user flow or the part of the service affected by the code change.
  6. Run broader checks before review. Build the app, run automated style checks, and run the relevant test suite.
  7. Inspect the diff and evidence. Confirm that tests were not weakened and that the reported results belong to the final commit.
  8. Stop on unresolved failures. Let a person decide when the failure is unexplained, flaky, or outside the agent's permission.

The sequence is the useful part. Define what done means and test at more than one level. Keep evidence tied to the final change. Make unresolved failures visible.

The point is evidence, not autonomy

More agents do not remove the need for engineering judgment. They increase the amount of work that can be proposed, which makes a clear verification process more important.

The Claude Code team's account offers a practical pattern. Run the change end to end. Add tests for broad input spaces or comparisons with old behavior. Keep review rules independent. Then evaluate whether checks catch the defects that matter. The account also shows a limit: the team escalates unresolved failures to a human.[1]

For any coding agent, the useful completion message is not simply "done." It should say what changed and which checks ran. It should report the results, note what was not checked, and say whether any failure remains. That gives a reviewer evidence to assess instead of asking the reviewer to trust the agent's summary.

Sources

[1] Addy Osmani, "How the Claude Code team thinks about verification" (November 16, 2026). The reported team practices and 90% figure are Anthropic's own account.

[2] Claude Code documentation: Skills.

[3] Claude Code documentation: Hooks.

title: Can you use AI on listing photos? The rules of 22 US MLSs (open data)
description:
Can you use AI on listing photos? It depends on your MLS, and the rules differ more than most agents expect. We read the photo and virtual staging rules of 22 US MLSs in October 2026 and put every rule, label and fine in an open dataset (mls-photo-rules.csv, CC BY 4.0), with a link to the source page on every row.

What we found

  • 8 of 22 mention AI by name. Seven treat an AI-edited photo like any other digitally altered or virtually staged photo; NorthstarMLS covers it in best-practice guidance, not in its rules.
  • 9 of 22 want the unaltered original in the listing next to the altered photo (for HAR, only when real property was changed).
  • 6 of 22 want the disclosure on the image itself as a watermark. Canopy MLS says disclosure only in captions or remarks is "NOT acceptable".
  • 2 of 22 (REcolorado, Doorify) need no disclosure label for virtual staging on the pages we read, but still ban edits that change the property.
  • Where the rules spell it out, the line is the same: no removing power lines, no adding views, lawns or pools, no changing the real estate. Brightness, colour, cropping and sharpening need no label (ARMLS, SFARMLS).

Where AI is named

MLS Region What they ask for
CRMLS California "AI Altered" or similar in the photo description, the original next to it. No AI landscaping. $250 after a warning
SDMLS San Diego "Digitally Altered" in the remarks plus the original's URL on the altered image
Bright MLS Mid-Atlantic Generative AI counts as virtual staging: disclosed in both Private and Public remarks
ARMLS Arizona Flexmls "Digitally Altered" watermark plus the original. $200 a violation from December 2026
MLSListings Bay Area "AI altered" is an accepted label; disclosed in public remarks; submit the original
SFARMLS San Francisco AI images showing things that don't exist need disclosure and the MLS watermark
Canopy MLS Charlotte Disclosure on the image, the original right before or after
NorthstarMLS Minnesota Best practice: disclose like staging, add an unaltered "before" image

Fines

The highest published amounts for photo breaches: Southeast Florida MLS $500 rising to $1,500, BeachesMLS $500 a photo, Stellar MLS $100 rising to $1,000 for staging breaches. MLS Now has scanned photos with an AI vision service since 2023, so a missed label is more likely to be caught than it used to be.

Query it 

import pandas as pd
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/October-ai-jpg/listing-photo-data/main/data/mls-photo-rules.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url)
ai = df[df["ai_alteration_rule"].notna()]
print(ai[["mls", "region", "ai_alteration_rule"]].to_string())

Caveats

  • Rules as published on 22 October 2026. Some MLSs keep the full policy behind a member login (NWMLS); those rows say so.
  • "Not addressed" means not on the pages we could read, not that anything goes. Check your own MLS before you upload.
  • This is not legal advice.

The same rules in words, with a checklist before you upload: AI photo editing and MLS rules, and every MLS in one table: MLS photo rules by MLS. The data is also on Hugging Face and Zenodo.

Disclosure: written with an AI agent for October, an iPhone app that guides you through the rooms and returns listing photos and a walkthrough video, with the rooms kept as they are.

title: Java4Shell ameaça servidores Minecraft em CPUs AVX-512 VBMI
description:
Falha no Java pode expor servidores Minecraft

A vulnerabilidade Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) afeta o decodificador Base64 do HotSpot, usado pelo OpenJDK em determinadas CPUs x86-64. O problema alcança as versões 17.0.6 e posteriores e as linhas 21 e 25 quando o processador oferece os recursos necessários. Servidores públicos de Minecraft recebem dados de qualquer pessoa que se conecta, o que torna importante verificar a JVM em execução.

A Red Hat atribuiu gravidade 9,8 à falha, enquanto a pontuação registrada pela CNA é 8,1. A correção depende da versão da JVM: os mínimos corrigidos são 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 e 25.0.5.1. Atualizar Paper ou plugins, sem atualizar o Java usado pelo processo do servidor, não resolve o problema.

Confira a CPU e a JVM ativa

O caminho vulnerável exige uma CPU x86-64 com AVX-512F, AVX-512BW, AVX-512 VBMI e BMI2. Xeons Intel Ice Lake ou mais recentes e processadores AMD Zen 4 ou posteriores, como Ryzen 7000 e 9000, podem atender aos critérios; máquinas ARM não executam esse caminho.

grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo; grep -oE '(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u

Se os quatro recursos aparecerem, confira a JVM do processo do servidor, não apenas o Java disponível no terminal: um serviço ou contêiner pode usar outra instalação. O exemplo abaixo consulta a versão e a configuração do HotSpot em um servidor Paper executado pelo usuário minecraft.

sudo -u minecraft jcmd $(pgrep -u minecraft -f paper.jar) VM.version
sudo -u minecraft jcmd $(pgrep -u minecraft -f paper.jar) VM.flags -all | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics

O utilitário jcmd vem com o JDK, não com o JRE, e deve ser executado pelo mesmo usuário do servidor. As versões do Minecraft 26.1 a 26.3 usam Java 25; as versões 1.20.5 a 1.21.11 usam Java 21; e as versões 1.18 a 1.20.4 usam Java 17. Lançamentos 1.17.1 e anteriores não são afetados.

Verifique o estado da distribuição ou imagem

Em 19 de novembro de 2026, o Ubuntu 24.04 já oferecia a versão corrigida 21.0.13.1+2. Builds disponíveis no Debian 12 e 13 e instaladores Temurin para Windows ainda estavam vulneráveis naquele levantamento; não havia uma build Temurin corrigida para Windows. A versão do Java fornecida pelo sistema, contêiner ou painel pode, portanto, mudar o resultado.

As imagens itzg/minecraft-server latest, java21 e java25 ainda usavam JDK Temurin vulnerável, mas incluíam a opção temporária de proteção por padrão. As tags stable e 2026.11.0-* também estavam vulneráveis e não incluíam essa opção na verificação. As imagens Pterodactyl yolks para Java 21 e 25 passaram a definir a opção no ponto de entrada em 17 de novembro; nós com imagens antigas em cache podem não recebê-la.

As imagens de contêiner citadas ainda não distribuíam um JDK corrigido. No Minecraft Launcher, a runtime Java 25 para versões 26.x estava corrigida no Linux e no macOS, mas não no Windows x64; as runtimes Java 21 e 17 ainda não tinham sido atualizadas. A checagem da build efetivamente usada ajuda a distinguir esses casos.

Atualize o OpenJDK no Ubuntu

No Ubuntu 24.04, a Canonical disponibilizou pacotes OpenJDK reconstruídos em 18 de novembro. A atualização pode reiniciar o serviço e desconectar jogadores: o needrestart pode reiniciar um serviço do systemd durante a instalação. Avise os jogadores e programe a mudança para um horário adequado.

sudo DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y --only-upgrade openjdk-21-jre-headless openjdk-21-jdk-headless

Depois da instalação, confirme a versão informada pela JVM que atende às conexões. Serviços iniciados fora do systemd, por exemplo em sessões screen ou tmux, podem continuar usando as bibliotecas antigas até que o processo seja reiniciado manualmente. Para Java 17 ou 25, use os pacotes correspondentes à linha necessária e confira a versão ativa.

Use a opção temporária se não puder atualizar

A opção -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics desativa o decodificador vulnerável e faz a JVM usar o decodificador Java padrão. Ela reduz a velocidade de decodificação Base64, efeito que não foi medido em um servidor de jogo, e só entra em vigor após reiniciar o processo.

Inclua a opção na linha de inicialização antes de -jar. No exemplo Linux usado para o servidor Paper, ela aparece entre as opções da JVM e o arquivo do servidor; em um arquivo Windows start.bat, deve ficar na mesma posição.

!/bin/sh

cd /opt/minecraft
exec java -Xms2G -Xmx2G -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics -jar paper.jar --nogui

Uma opção escrita incorretamente pode impedir a JVM de iniciar. Se ela ficar depois de -jar paper.jar, será enviada ao Paper, e não ao Java. Após o reinício, consulte a configuração da JVM em execução: UseBASE64Intrinsics deve aparecer como false. Não use -XX:UseAVX=2 como alternativa: ela desativa otimizações AVX-512 e pode impedir a inicialização da JVM em ARM.

Confira as tags Docker e a proteção efetiva
