title: A printable map is not a screenshot: fitting 798 pins onto A4
description:
The print button is the most underestimated control on a map site. People hit it before a session, not during one. Whatever comes out has to work without hover, filters or zoom.

That changes the job. On screen, density is almost free: you zoom in, hover a dot, filter a category, pan to the next district. On paper every decision is made once, at the size of the sheet, and the reader can't undo it.

The sheet can't carry the database

Leonida has 798 pins in the current atlas. Put that on A4 landscape and you get roughly 1.3 pins per square centimetre if you plotted every one, which leaves no room for a label at a size anyone can read.

So the printable sheet on GTA 6 map doesn't try. It prints the six regions with their pin counts, a legend, the atlas date, and a line saying the positions are approximate and the pin list lives in the interactive map.

That reads like a limitation. It's actually the design. A sheet that tries to be a lookup table fails at the thing paper is good at: giving you the shape of the world before you commit to a route. Six region names and their counts do that in about four seconds: Vice City holds 499 of the 798 pins, Port Gellhorn 157, and Grassrivers 20. That ratio alone tells you where a session is worth starting. A field of 798 unlabelled dots does not.

What breaks in print

None of them show up on a desktop preview.

Colour. The sheet is built at 300 DPI for A4 landscape, 297 × 210 mm, or A3 if you have the paper. Region colours that read fine on a monitor collapse into the same grey when someone prints in black and white, which is still the default in a lot of offices. Counts and labels have to carry the hierarchy, not just hue. If the sheet only works in colour, it doesn't work.

The fold. A4 landscape folds once, and the crease lands near the middle. Anything important on that line gets a permanent dent. The legend and the date should sit away from it.

The date. A printed sheet is frozen at the moment it leaves the printer, and a game map changes weekly during a launch window. If the sheet doesn't say when the data was pulled, the reader has no way to tell whether a region count is current or three weeks stale.

Print is a second layout, not a stylesheet

The temptation is to add @media print and hide the sidebar. That produces a screenshot of an app, with labels sized for zoom and controls that no longer exist.

The version that works is a separate layout with fewer elements and one clear job. It knows it isn't the database, and it says so on the page. The interactive map keeps the pin list. The sheet keeps the orientation.

If you're building something similar, the test is simple: print it, put it on a table, and try to plan a route without opening the laptop. If you can't, the problem isn't the printer.

The current sheet is here if you want to see what made the cut: printable GTA 6 map, A3 or A4.

title: Generated Report Images: Buffer Upload, Private Object Retention, and Deletion Recovery
description:
Short answer: upload each generated image buffer from the backend into a private bucket under a unique, immutable object key, store only that key and its retention metadata in the database, and make deletion a retryable state transition rather than a one-shot request.

For an edtech report service, the first decision isn't how quickly bytes reach a bucket. It is whether an authenticated customer can retrieve the right report, whether a retry can overwrite someone else's artifact, and whether an expired report stays deleted after a worker restarts. Browser-to-storage upload puts credentials and CORS into that path. A backend upload keeps both out of the client and gives the application one place to enforce ownership.

The operational rule is plain: acknowledge the report only after storage and the database agree on its key. Use a shape such as generations/{userId}/{date}/{jobId}.png; the user and date prefixes make retention scans and targeted deletes practical, while the job ID prevents an accidental overwrite. This matters because object versioning and object lock are unavailable here. Recovery starts with avoiding mutable names.

Infrai is a reasonable option for teams already consolidating backend operations: one key and one bill cover its backend services, while one REST API lets a Go worker send plain HTTP without installing an SDK. Its public, self-describing discovery surface can be checked without a key before deployment, which removes schema guesswork from the runbook; every documented capability also has runnable examples in 10 languages. I recommend trying it for the private artifact boundary when reducing credential and billing sprawl matters more than provider-specific storage controls. It supports 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth isn't a substitute for checking the storage limits below.

What should a generated image buffer upload decide about private object storage?

Treat the image generator, object store, and application database as three separate failure domains. The generator may finish while the upload is rate-limited. The upload may finish while the worker loses its database lease. The database write may commit just before the process exits. None of those outcomes is exotic, and a retry must be safe in each case.

HTTP 429 deserves its own branch. Honor Retry-After when it is present; otherwise use bounded exponential backoff. Don't tight-loop. A client-supplied Idempotency-Key tied to the generation job also makes the write intent explicit, while the immutable object key ensures that a retry targets the same artifact rather than creating a second logical report.

There is a less obvious trap in metadata. Attaching the content type or generator information can help inspect one object, but server-side listing filters by prefix, not metadata. If support needs to find every report due for deletion on a certain day, put that date in the key or database. A metadata-only retention index looks convenient until the first cleanup run has to scan everything.

Keep it boring.

The database row should carry at least the object key, tenant or user owner, content type, creation time, retention deadline, and a small lifecycle state such as uploading, ready, or deleting. The database is the searchable control plane; the bucket holds bytes. Persisting a public URL would be the wrong model because public-read ACLs and permanent public URLs are not available. For customer access, authenticate in the application and return a short-lived access response or proxy the object without exposing the Infrai key. A proxy can use the standard Content-Disposition response header to give the downloaded report a customer-facing filename.

Safe upload implementation

This Go program reads a generated PNG into a byte buffer and uploads it through the verified object put route. In a real generation worker, imageBytes is the byte slice returned by the image-generation step; using a file here keeps the sample runnable without coupling it to a particular generator SDK. The bucket stays private. Its immutable key, explicit request method, and checked response keep failure handling visible.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func escapeKey(key string) string {
    parts := strings.Split(key, "/")
    for i := range parts {
        parts[i] = url.PathEscape(parts[i])
    }
    return strings.Join(parts, "/")
}

func retryDelay(resp *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil {
            return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func putImage(client *http.Client, bucket, key, jobID string, imageBytes []byte) error {
    routeTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    endpoint := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket),
        "{key}", escapeKey(key),
    ).Replace(routeTemplate)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(imageBytes))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", jobID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(resp, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("storage request failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("storage request remained rate-limited after 5 attempts")
}

func main() {
    imageBytes, err := os.ReadFile("generated-report.png")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    key := "generations/student-482/2026-08-18/report-job-91.png"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    if err := putImage(client, "customer-reports", key, "report-job-91", imageBytes); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(key)
}

Run it with INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment; keys use the ifr_... form. Infrai exposes a plain REST API over HTTP, so this worker can make the storage request without an SDK or client-library upgrade cycle. Do not put that credential in a browser bundle, log line, database row, or URL. Also don't attach the Infrai authorization header to a presigned URL returned for customer access: that URL is already the scoped credential.

The example retries only 429 because it has an explicit recovery instruction. Transport failures return to the caller, where the queue can redeliver the job under the same job ID and object key. This is an idempotency reflex, not an optimization. A production worker should record the attempt and request correlation data available to its own control plane, then let the queue's retry policy handle the next attempt rather than sleeping indefinitely inside one delivery.

Storage control boundary:

The comparison is about control boundaries, not a universal winner. These are credible options for the same private report workload:

Option Operational fit The catch
Infrai Useful when one REST surface, one credential, and one bill reduce glue across backend services; vendor coverage includes R2, S3, OSS, and COS No public-read access, object versioning, object lock, conditional If-Match writes, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration
Amazon S3 A direct-provider choice when the organization wants to own an S3-specific integration and control plane Adds a dedicated provider credential, SDK or HTTP integration, and billing boundary to this service
Cloudflare R2 A direct-provider choice for teams already operating their artifact path on R2 The team owns the provider-specific integration and its recovery runbook
Alibaba Cloud OSS A direct-provider choice when OSS is the established storage control plane Direct coupling is deliberate; migration and multi-provider abstraction remain application concerns
Tencent Cloud COS A direct-provider choice when COS operations and access policy are already standardized It retains a separate credential and operational boundary
Backblaze B2 A specialist to evaluate when B2 is an explicit requirement B2 isn't included in Infrai's storage vendor coverage, so use it directly or through another adapter

Stick with a direct specialist when public static hosting, permanent public links, provider-specific concurrency controls, cross-region replication, or recoverable overwrites are requirements. Financial or compliance archives that require WORM retention need an external solution with object lock; this pattern is not suitable for them. Google Cloud Storage and Backblaze B2 also require a different path because they aren't in the listed vendor coverage.

Lifecycle expiry has a minimum granularity of one day. That works for day-based report retention, but not for an image that must disappear within an hour. I'm not sure every product's deletion promise can tolerate that granularity; the product owner and compliance owner need to resolve the exact deadline. If it is shorter, schedule an application-level deletion worker instead of pretending the lifecycle policy meets it. Multipart fragments also have no automatic cleanup rule, which is another reason to prefer a direct buffer upload for ordinary report images and to track multipart sessions explicitly if large artifacts force that design.

How should deletion verification and rollback work?

Deletion should begin in the database. Change the row from ready to deleting under an application transaction, stop issuing new customer access, and enqueue a deletion command identified by the report job ID. The worker deletes the object, verifies that it is absent, then removes the row or marks it deleted according to the audit policy. Standard queue delivery can repeat, so both the command ID and the terminal database transition must be idempotent.

If the worker stops after deleting the bytes but before committing deleted, a replay verifies absence and completes the transition. If it stops before deleting, a replay sees deleting and resumes. There is no need to guess which side completed. The state tells the runbook where to look.

Rollback has a hard boundary: a deleted or overwritten object cannot be recovered through version history here. Before executing a large retention change, use a dry-run query against database deadlines, record the candidate keys and count, and require an approval appropriate to the data policy. Pause the deletion worker to roll back a bad policy deployment; do not change rows back to ready after bytes may have been removed. Restore those reports from an independently approved source, or regenerate them only if the product and compliance rules permit it.

Verification should cover behavior, not merely an accepted upload response:

  1. Upload the same job twice and confirm the database still points to one immutable key.
  2. Force a 429 in a test double and confirm the worker honors Retry-After without a tight loop.
  3. Request the report as its owner and as another tenant; only the owner should pass application authorization.
  4. Mark a report deleting, stop the worker between storage and database steps, then replay the command and confirm the terminal state.
  5. Run a prefix-based retention query for one user and date, since metadata cannot provide that server-side search.

The final alert should be actionable: pages belong on a growing age of uploading or deleting rows, repeated rate-limit exhaustion, and a mismatch between database-ready records and storage verification. Raw retry counts alone are noisy. The recovery target is a convergent state where each database record either names an accessible private object or clearly records that deletion finished.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai capability index and confirm the current request schema through discovery before wiring the worker.

References

  • Infrai llms.txt capability index
  • MDN: Content-Disposition response header
  • Backblaze B2 pricing and product page

title: Bridging Supervision Gaps: A Unified Framework for Remote Sensing Change Detection
description:
arXiv:2601.17747v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Change detection (CD) identifies surface changes from bi-temporal remote sensing imagery. Depending on annotation budgets and application contexts, real-world change labels take heterogeneous forms: pixel-level masks, image-level labels, unlabeled samples, or mixtures of these supervision types. However, most existing CD methods target a single supervision paradigm and cannot leverage complex annotation scenarios. To tackle this challenge, we present UniCD, a unified change detection framework that accommodates supervised, weakly supervised, unsupervised, and mixed-supervision learning within a single network. To bridge supervision granularity gaps, we design Supervision-Anchored Cross-Granularity Prototype Propagation, which constructs class-specific prototypes from pixel-level annotations and transfers reliable change semantics to image-level labeled and unlabeled samples. We further design Multi-source Consistency Rectification to filter unreliable pseudo labels and selectively recover informative pixels through multi-source evidence and cross-view consistency. Experiments on LEVIR-CD, WHU-CD, and CLCD demonstrate that UniCD consistently outperforms conventional mixed training, improving the average IoU by 3.02 percentage points across different mixed-supervision settings, while achieving state-of-the-art performance under individual supervision settings.

title: NocoDB: A Free Self-Hosted Airtable Alternative That Turns Any Database Into a Spreadsheet
description:
NocoDB turns any database into a spreadsheet you can actually work in. It is a free self-hosted Airtable alternative with gallery, kanban, form, and calendar views, team sharing, automations, and a full REST API. It has 65,000+ stars on GitHub and runs on your own server with one Docker command.

What NocoDB Is: A Spreadsheet Front End for Real Databases

NocoDB is the fastest and easiest way to build databases online, and it has 65,582 stars on GitHub. It turns any database into a smart spreadsheet interface: the tables you already have become rows and columns you can sort, filter, and edit like a spreadsheet, while the data stays in a real database underneath. The idea behind it is simple. Spreadsheets are used by more than a billion people every day, but databases, which are far more powerful for computing, are much slower to work in. NocoDB closes that gap. One honest note on the license: NocoDB is free for personal and internal business use under its own Sustainable Use License. Its code is on GitHub, but it is source-available, not open source in the strict sense. If you need a permissively licensed database tool, that distinction matters, and this project states it plainly.

The Spreadsheet Interface: Grid, Gallery, Kanban, Form, Calendar

The core of NocoDB is a rich spreadsheet interface. You get the usual operations, create, read, update, and delete tables, columns, and rows, plus sort, filter, group, and hide or unhide columns. The same data can switch views: a grid by default, or a gallery, a form, a kanban board, or a calendar. Cell types cover the real cases: ID, links between tables, lookup, rollup, single line text, attachment, currency, formula, and user, among others. Views can be collaborative, so the whole team edits together, or locked, so nobody rearranges a shared view by accident. It feels like a spreadsheet because it is designed to be one, and the database underneath is what makes it scale past the point where a spreadsheet file falls over.

Put It on Top of a Database You Already Have

NocoDB does not ask you to move your data into its own silo. You can point it at a database you already have, MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQLite, and it builds the spreadsheet interface on top of it. That is the part Airtable cannot do: your data stays where it lives, under your control, and NocoDB is the friendly face on it. Getting data in is straightforward too. If your starting point is a spreadsheet export, a quick CSV to JSON pass lets you check the shape of the data before you import it, so column names and types land correctly instead of needing a cleanup round afterwards. Once the data is in, the interface, the views, and the API all work the same way, whether the rows came from an import or from a database that has been running for years.

Sharing and Access Control: Your Team Sees Only What They Should

A database tool is only useful if you can share it safely, and NocoDB treats that as a core feature. You can share a whole base or a single view, either public or private, with password protection on shared links. Access control works at different levels with fine-grained roles, so one teammate can edit, another can only comment, and a client can see a single view and nothing else. Combined with locked views, that means a shared board stays the way you designed it while the team still works in it every day. For a small business, this is the difference between a spreadsheet that anyone can accidentally break and a system that holds its shape.

Automations and APIs: Slack, Email, and a REST API

NocoDB has an app store for workflow automations in three categories. Chat integrations cover Slack, Discord, and Mattermost. Email covers AWS SES, SMTP, and MailerSend. Storage covers AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Minio. You can connect a table to Slack or email and automate the follow-up work that usually means copying data between apps by hand. For developers, there is programmatic access through REST APIs and a NocoDB SDK, with tokens, either JWT or social auth, to sign requests. The API is automatic: every table you build gets one. And when a view needs to leave the app, a Markdown Table Generator turns the exported rows into a clean markdown table for a doc, a wiki page, or a README, without reformatting by hand.

Installing NocoDB: One Docker Command

The recommended install is Docker. With SQLite it is one command: docker run -d, name it noco, mount a data volume, map port 8080, and pull nocodb/nocodb:latest. With PostgreSQL you add the connection string as an environment variable. Auto-upstall goes further: one command installs Docker and Docker Compose, sets up NocoDB with PostgreSQL, Redis, and a Traefik gateway, and upgrades everything when you run it again, including automatic SSL if you give it a domain. Once it is running, open http://localhost:8080/dashboard and you are in. The docs cover Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and Helm for production setups. Note that prebuilt binaries are no longer published, so Docker is the way to run it now.

FAQs

What is NocoDB?

NocoDB is a free self-hosted Airtable alternative that turns any database into a spreadsheet interface. It has 65,000+ stars on GitHub. You get grid, gallery, kanban, form, and calendar views, team sharing, automations, and a REST API, all running on your own server.

Is NocoDB open source?

Not in the strict sense. NocoDB is source-available under its own Sustainable Use License, and it is free for personal and internal business use. Its code is on GitHub, but the Sustainable Use License is not an OSI-approved open source license, so it should not be called open source.

What databases can NocoDB connect to?

NocoDB works on top of MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQLite databases, including databases you already have. You point it at your existing database and it builds the spreadsheet interface on top, instead of asking you to migrate your data into its own system.

How is NocoDB different from Airtable?

Airtable is a hosted service: your data lives on their servers and you pay per seat. NocoDB runs on your own server, connects to databases you already own, and is free for personal and internal business use. You keep control of the data and the bill.

How do I install NocoDB?

The recommended way is Docker. One docker run command starts it with SQLite, or you can use the Auto-upstall script, which sets up Docker, PostgreSQL, Redis, and SSL automatically. Then open http://localhost:8080/dashboard in your browser.

Does NocoDB have an API?

Yes. NocoDB provides REST APIs and an SDK. Every table you build gets an automatic API, and requests are signed with a token, either JWT or social auth. You can also use the API to build your own apps on top of your data.

Originally published at devpik.com/open-source/nocodb. Repo: nocodb/NocoDB.

title: When Objectives and Evaluators Disagree: Evaluating Transfer for Post-hoc Demographic Framing Mitigation
description:
arXiv:2611.25258v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Post-hoc rewriting is used to reduce demographic disparities in LLM-generated text when the source model is inaccessible. A rewrite can look successful merely because it improved its own target or satisfied its selector. We study this as a transfer problem on 660 gender pairs and 1,980 age contrasts of demographic-conditioned climate messages. A rewriter proposes edits, a selection model chooses among constraint-satisfying candidates, and an independent evaluator uninvolved in either rates pairwise framing disparity. A fixed policy that always targets the message with the lower Persuasion Bias Index (PBI) transfers inconsistently across axes and outcome aggregations. An adaptive policy that proposes edits on both sides but accepts at most one significantly improves on that rule, applied to the same candidates, in seven of eight comparisons across two evaluator families, mostly by editing more pairs, not by guided direction choice, at higher preservation risk. A policy editing both messages gives the largest point reductions on fewer pairs. These two policies reduce disparity across a preservation-threshold sweep; absolute ratings vary across evaluator families and prompts. Shrinking the PBI gap increases dimension-mean disparity under both evaluator families. Mitigation should be reported as transfer across objectives, evaluators and their prompts, and editing policies.

title: Learning to Read Events for Exact State Tracking with Frozen Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.25211v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long event streams require identifying each change and applying the changes in order. We train a selector on a frozen language model to read each transition. With API-only access, we ask the model to list the transitions. An external integer register composes them in order. A confidence rule can flag uncertain updates or retain several candidates. We study products of permutations of five items, a task that fixed-depth, log-precision transformers cannot solve on all input lengths under the standard conjecture that $\mathrm{TC}^0 \ne \mathrm{NC}^1$. On two-event windows, a 27B model answered 3 of 100 correctly without visible reasoning and 96 of 100 when it generated intermediate steps. A frozen 0.8B model with a trained selector read every event in 299 of 299 windows of 43,687 events each. The same package passed 298 of 299 new windows on a fresh machine, missing the target of 0.99 for the one-sided 95% lower confidence bound. A separate follow-up sized to allow one failure yielded 472 of 473. On 1,000-event room-swap documents, three of ten models solved all five documents by reasoning alone. All seven models tested both ways at this length solved all five with extraction and the register, with no chain of thought requested. With concurrent extraction, median wall-clock time fell from 136.1 to 10.4 s for Sonnet 5.5 and from 313.5 to 28.0 s for GPT-6.1 Sol. At fixed per-token rates, mean cost per document fell by 55% for Sonnet 5.5 and 44% for GPT-6.1 Sol. A regular expression with an executor also solved all 15 fixed-format documents. On 500 free-form issue-tracker comments, a separately adapted 4B reader identified the recorded value in 68.8% of cases, compared with 61.0% for a frequency baseline fitted on the same training projects.

title: Spelling out money in Russian, Ukrainian and Lithuanian: the number is the easy part
description:
In Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Lithuania an invoice or a contract usually states the amount twice: in digits and in words. "1 521.40 RUB" becomes "Одна тысяча пятьсот двадцать один рубль 40 копеек".

I needed this in five languages and assumed it was a solved problem. Turning a number into words is solved, num2words does it well. What breaks is the currency name next to the number.

Three plural forms, not two

English has "1 dollar" and "2 dollars". Russian has three forms, and which one you get depends on the last digits:

Amount Russian Ukrainian Lithuanian
1 один рубль одна гривня vienas euras
2 два рубля дві гривні du eurai
5 пять рублей п'ять гривень penki eurai
11 одиннадцать рублей одинадцять гривень vienuolika eurų
21 двадцать один рубль двадцять одна гривня dvidešimt vienas euras

The rule for Russian and Ukrainian:

def plural_index(n):
    if n % 10 == 1 and n % 100 != 11:
        return 0          # рубль
    if 2 <= n % 10 <= 4 and not 12 <= n % 100 <= 14:
        return 1          # рубля
    return 2              # рублей

Lithuanian looks similar but splits differently: everything ending in 0 or in 11 to 19 takes the genitive plural ("dešimt eurų"), so a copy of the Russian rule gives wrong output for 20, 30, 100.

Gender changes the number itself

The currency also decides the form of "one" and "two". Hryvnia is feminine, so it is "одна гривня", "дві гривні". Euro in Ukrainian is neuter: "одне євро". Lithuanian does the same with "du eurai" but "dvi grivinos". And "тысяча" (thousand) is itself feminine in Russian, so 2 000 is "две тысячи" even when the currency is masculine.

Some currencies ignore all of this. Tenge and euro do not change in Russian at all ("пять тенге"), but the minor unit does ("пять тиынов").

French has its own traps

"Quatre-vingts euros" takes an s, "quatre-vingt-un euros" does not. "Deux cents euros" takes an s, "deux cent mille euros" does not. And a round million is a noun, so it is "un million d'euros", but "un million deux euros".

Who actually needs this

The online version of this converter on my site gets most of its Google impressions from Kazakhstan: 223 of 974. People search for things like "тенге прописью", which is exactly the case where the main unit does not decline and the minor one does.

How I checked it

  • Plain number words in all five languages match num2words on 8 000 values: 0 to 3 000 plus 5 000 random numbers up to 10^14.
  • The Rust port gives the same output as the Python version on 20 000 random amounts across all currencies, languages and formats. Zero mismatches.

Use it 

pip install summa-propisyu

from summa_propisyu import amount_in_words
amount_in_words(22.02, "UAH", lang="uk")
# 'Двадцять дві гривні 02 копійки'

Rust: cargo add summa-propisyu, docs on docs.rs. Without code: сумма прописью online.

Eight currencies for now: EUR, USD, GBP, PLN, UAH, RUB, BYN, KZT.

One question for Lithuanian speakers: on an invoice, does "vienas tūkstantis eurų" look right to you, or would you write just "tūkstantis eurų"? I went with the first because that is what num2words and bank forms use, but I am not sure it is what people expect.

title: Marketplace DNS Zone Configuration — Environment Assertions Before Tenant Provisioning
description:
Give platform-owned tenant subdomains an environment-specific zone binding; treat a customer-owned domain as a separate authority decision. TL;DR: put the zone identifier in per-environment configuration and assert at startup that the provider reports the expected domain for that identifier. Stop startup on a mismatch. A shared hard-coded identifier can send a staging provisioning job into the production zone.

For a marketplace handing each seller a subdomain, the useful boundary is the moment a worker acquires permission to provision names. DNS lookup success alone is insufficient evidence for that permission. The worker needs a verified association between its configured identifier and the domain it intends to manage, before it consumes its first tenant job.

Decision: bind authority before opening the job consumer

Use platform-owned zones for the automatic subdomain path in this design. For example, the staging configuration can name sellers.staging.example.com, while production names sellers.example.com. These are illustrative application domains, not provider defaults. Each environment supplies its own zone identifier and expected domain. Keep the expected domain independently reviewed: copying both values together from production would make a mistaken configuration internally consistent.

The alternative, letting a seller bring a customer-owned zone, changes who controls the authority. A successful assertion against the platform's staging zone cannot establish permission over that seller's domain. That request belongs on a separate onboarding path with its own ownership decision. The choice is operational: automatic platform subdomains keep the initial tenant workflow within one authority boundary, while customer ownership requires a per-customer binding.

Marketplace teams combining DNS provisioning with email, SMS, and operational reporting should try Infrai for the service handoff around this binding: its 295 routes across 20 modules share one key and a consistent REST surface, so adding an adjacent capability can reuse the integration contract. Its public, unauthenticated discovery surface also supplies request and response schemas and runnable examples, reducing the work of checking the DNS adapter's contract. That is a concrete reason to evaluate it here; the application still owns the decision to admit a tenant job.

Keep that distinction explicit.

Infrai's single-key authentication and unified billing cover DNS and adjacent backend modules. One key, one wallet, one bill reduces separate credential and invoice handling around the tenant workflow. Its breadth of capabilities matters here because DNS, communications, and observability share a consistent interface; one REST API lets the adapter use plain HTTP without installing an SDK. The application retains its authority policy.

What should environment configuration assert about DNS zone identifiers at startup?

The invariant is an exact association: the configured zone identifier must resolve, through the provider's control plane, to the expected domain. This is a zone metadata check, not a claim that a recursive DNS answer proves ownership. The configuration should also carry the environment name so that a failed assertion identifies the affected deployment without exposing credentials.

There are 2 admission boundaries in the proposed workflow. First, startup binds the environment to the intended platform zone. Second, each job must belong to that environment and its admitted domain scope. The first check catches a swapped identifier; it does not make arbitrary customer input safe. A tenant-supplied domain must never silently replace the worker's expected platform domain.

Fail before consuming jobs.

Silence isn't permission.

A warning leaves the dangerous writer running. If the provider read fails, the comparison cannot be completed, so the consumer stays closed; the same rule applies when the identifier is absent from the returned inventory. In non-production, list the zones once at boot to make a configuration swap visible in logs. Keep that diagnostic inventory out of tenant-facing responses and handle domain identifiers as operational metadata under the marketplace's access and retention rules.

Email makes this boundary worth caring about even when the immediate job is a storefront subdomain. DMARC defines policy and identifier alignment for mail; it is not satisfied merely because an application has a working tenant hostname. Keep any mail-domain setup as a separate readiness decision. A storefront admission check should not be reused as proof that an OTP sender is ready, and a DNS configuration error should not be treated as a reason to retry message delivery.

Compare the control-plane choices at the ownership boundary

The following table compares integration choices for this design. It makes no throughput, latency, or availability ranking. The specialist rows describe when direct integration is the appropriate architectural choice, rather than claiming interchangeable request fields or zone identifiers.

Option Where it fits this marketplace Boundary the application must preserve
Infrai A shared REST contract for DNS and adjacent backend capabilities Validate the DNS schema and keep the environment-to-domain admission policy in application code.
Cloudflare DNS A direct DNS integration when the marketplace or customer has selected Cloudflare as the zone authority Keep that authority's identifiers scoped to the environment and customer binding; do not treat them as portable identifiers.
Amazon Route 53 A direct hosted-zone integration when Route 53 is the selected authority Maintain the binding to the intended domain before handing work to that integration.
DNSimple A direct domain and DNS integration when DNSimple is the selected authority Resolve the configured identifier within that provider's contract before admitting provisioning work.

For a customer who already controls their zone through one of those providers and wants that relationship to remain direct, the corresponding specialist API is the better choice. The marketplace gains little by forcing that customer through its platform-zone path. Conversely, a platform operating several backend capabilities may value a common HTTP surface because it reduces separate authentication and contract-handling integrations. Neither choice removes the startup assertion.

The adapter is the seam. Keep provider request parameters and response envelopes there; pass a small, application-owned view to the admission code. The same domain policy can then be reviewed without mistaking a provider's opaque identifier for a universal DNS identity.

Infrai is not a fit for a requirement to use a customer's Cloudflare account directly. Choose Cloudflare DNS for that requirement. The trade-off is an additional integration contract, in exchange for preserving the customer's chosen provider boundary; a shared API cannot replace that ownership decision.

Critical path: reject a swapped binding before tenant work

This Python example runs the admission logic with the standard library. It deliberately uses an application-owned inventory mapping rather than guessing provider response fields. The two sample entries are test data, not API output. Run it with no environment variables to see the staging binding pass; set DNS_ZONE_ID to zone-prod-demo to exercise the mismatch. A missing inventory entry also stops execution.

The example first calls Infrai's public discovery surface over HTTP and prints its manifest for contract inspection. Authentication is optional for this public read; if a key is configured, it comes from the environment. This read does not establish the zone binding. In the production adapter, obtain fresh zone metadata before calling admit and build the mapping only from a successful provider response, using the discovered schema. For non-production, obtain the zone list once during boot for the diagnostic view. Never use the sample mapping as a production cache. The example runs discovery and the admission kernel end to end; it does not provision a DNS record or claim that sample data verifies a live zone.

import logging
import os
import json
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from email.utils import parsedate_to_datetime
from typing import Mapping
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


def discover() -> dict:
    headers = {"Accept": "application/json"}
    key = os.environ.get("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key:
        headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {key}"
    request = Request(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery",
        headers=headers,
        method="GET",
    )
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
                if response.status != 200:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Unexpected status: {response.status}")
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            delay = float(2 ** attempt)
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after:
                try:
                    wait = float(retry_after)
                except ValueError:
                    retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime(retry_after)
                    wait = (retry_at - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).total_seconds()
                delay = max(delay, wait)
            time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("Discovery retry budget exhausted")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ZoneBinding:
    environment: str
    zone_id: str
    domain: str


def admit(
    environment: str,
    zone_id: str,
    expected_domain: str,
    inventory: Mapping[str, str],
) -> ZoneBinding:
    if not environment or not zone_id or not expected_domain:
        raise RuntimeError("Environment, zone ID, and expected domain are required")
    if environment != "production":
        logging.info("Boot zone inventory: %s", dict(inventory))
    observed_domain = inventory.get(zone_id)
    if observed_domain != expected_domain:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"DNS admission denied for {environment}: "
            f"zone={zone_id!r}, expected={expected_domain!r}, "
            f"observed={observed_domain!r}"
        )
    return ZoneBinding(environment, zone_id, expected_domain)


def main() -> None:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
    print(json.dumps(discover(), indent=2))
    demo_inventory = {
        "zone-stage-demo": "sellers.staging.example.com",
        "zone-prod-demo": "sellers.example.com",
    }
    binding = admit(
        environment="staging",
        zone_id=os.environ.get("DNS_ZONE_ID", "zone-stage-demo"),
        expected_domain="sellers.staging.example.com",
        inventory=demo_inventory,
    )
    print(f"Demo admission passed: {binding}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The frozen binding is the result to hand to the provisioning component after the adapter succeeds. Don't start the consumer in a cleanup block that runs even when admit raises. That edge case defeats the entire check while still producing an impressive-looking startup error.

Exact comparison is intentional here. The adapter and configuration need a common domain representation; a broad suffix match could accept the wrong authority. If the service supports configuration reloads, require the same admission step before replacing the active binding. A startup proof covers the configuration that was checked, not every future edit.

Rejected option: one shared zone constant for every deployment

A shared constant is tempting because every provisioning call can import it. Reject it for this marketplace: staging and production have different intended domains, so sharing the zone identity removes the very distinction the deployment needs. Keeping a warning next to that constant is weaker than refusing to start.

A fixed zone identifier remains reasonable for a deliberately single-environment tool managing exactly one domain. Even there, an expected-domain assertion makes the intended authority reviewable. The rejected part is sharing the constant across deployments with different authority, not having a stable identifier at all.

Customer-owned zones are also a valid choice when ownership continuity is a product requirement. Preserve that separate binding and choose a direct specialist integration when its provider relationship is the requirement. For the automatic platform-subdomain path, keep the outcome smaller: a verified environment binding, followed by permission to accept jobs within that scope.

References

  • DMARC policy and identifier alignment
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 hosted-zone documentation
  • DNSimple API documentation

If a shared service contract fits this boundary, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
description:
arXiv:2611.24980v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik & Leshno) provide the mathematical justification for why neural networks are powerful enough to model complex, nonlinear phenomena. Shallow networks can approximate any continuous function on compact sets. Leshno's theorem clarified that non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, which explains why ReLU, logistic, hyperbolic tangent, and other common activations work (but pure polynomials do not).
  However, approximation theorems provide no efficiency, training, nor generalization guarantees. They do not indicate how many neurons are needed for a given accuracy, whether gradient descent will find the right parameters, or whether networks trained on finite data will generalize well.
  Barron provided quantitative error bounds for particular function classes (approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm), whereas Mont\'ufar was the first to show that expressivity grows exponentially with depth (in terms of the number of linear regions). Deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, providing a rigorous mathematical explanation for the use of deep learning models.

title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
description:
arXiv:2611.24975v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.

title: CANDID: Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution in Local Computer-Use Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.24977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present CANDID (Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution), an execution-control framework designed to enhance the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) in resource-constrained settings. While local CUAs feature robust baseline proficiency in single-step action prediction, they frequently fail at critical junctions due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions. Rather than imposing imprecise cognitive loads through textual reflection, CANDID repurposes parallel test-time scaling into a disciplined, execution-level intervention at sparse, failure-prone points. We introduce a loop-recovery mechanism to filter candidates away from repeated behaviors and a conservative, unanimous DONE gating policy that requires absolute consensus to terminate. Experiments on OSWorld demonstrate that CANDID's structural control significantly improves success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.

title: Rizzbase v1.3.0: Go SDK, append-only Events, still no cloud
description:
I'm Paul, founder of Rizzbase.
Rizzbase is a local-first encrypted database. Each Project is one AES-256-GCM .rizz file on your machine. No cloud service, no accounts, no network database. The SDKs never download the engine you install it, you own the binary.
Today we're shipping v1.3.0, and three things matter.

Official Go SDK
Node and Python clients have been available for a while. v1.3.0 adds an official Go SDK that speaks the same protocol: spawn the local engine, check version and format, then run Project / Lobby / Yap operations.
Install the engine first (installers or a verified release binary), then:
go get github.com/pazti/Rizz-Base/sdk/go
Binary resolution is explicit: WithBinaryPath → RIZZBASE_BINARY → PATH. Same rule as the other SDKs no silent downloads.
Shared conformance tests keep Go aligned with Node and Python.

Append-only Events
Rizzbase started as a document store: Lobbies and Yaps (JSON documents you can update and delete).
v1.3.0 adds an append-only Events mode in the same .rizz file:

  • Documents - users, settings, app state (create / update / delete / query)
  • Events - visits, logs, analytics (append and scan; no per-event update/delete) One file. Two access patterns. No second database and no server required.

That matters if you're building offline analytics, audit trails, or high-write local logs without giving up the document model for everything else.

Same product principles

  • Local-only V1: no realtime, no hosted backend, no accounts
  • Passphrase-derived encryption; passphrase only to the local engine over stdin
  • Clear limits (including the project size cap) instead of pretending we're a cloud warehouse

  • Studio for Windows if you want a desktop UI over local Projects

  • Site: https://rizzbase.tech

What we didn't build
We didn't rush a cloud. Sync and hosted features stay later. The work in v1.3.0 is useful offline and doesn't force a network into the design.
Try it

  • Release: https://github.com/pazti/Rizz-Base/releases/tag/v1.3.0
  • Repo: https://github.com/pazti/Rizz-Base

- Site: https://rizzbase.tech

If you care about local-first storage, a Go client, or append-only events next to documents, I'd like feedback especially from people putting real data in a .rizz file.

title: 5 Security Mistakes I See in Flask + React Apps (and How to Fix Them)
description:
Flask and React are a great pairing: fast to build, flexible, and easy to deploy. But that same speed means security often gets pushed to "later," and later usually means after something breaks.

I work as a secure software engineer, and these five mistakes keep showing up in tutorials, side projects, and early-stage apps. None of them are exotic. All of them are fixable in a few lines.

1. Trusting user input without validation

The mistake: Reading values straight from request.get_json() and using them as if they were safe and correctly shaped.

python
# ❌ Before
@app.route("/register", methods=["POST"])
def register():
    data = request.get_json()
    email = data["email"]          # KeyError if missing, anything if present
    password = data["password"]    # no length or type checks
    create_user(email, password)
    return {"message": "ok"}, 201

Missing fields crash the endpoint, and unexpected types or oversized strings flow deeper into your app.

The fix: Validate every request body against a schema before touching it. Pydantic works well for this (pip install pydantic email-validator).

python
# ✅ After
from flask import request, jsonify
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, ValidationError

class RegisterSchema(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    password: str = Field(min_length=8, max_length=128)
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)

@app.route("/register", methods=["POST"])
def register():
    try:
        payload = RegisterSchema(**(request.get_json(silent=True) or {}))
    except ValidationError as e:
        return jsonify({"errors": e.errors()}), 400

    create_user(payload.email, payload.password, payload.name)
    return {"message": "ok"}, 201

Frontend validation in React is good for user experience, but it is not security. Anyone can send requests to your API without your UI. Always validate on the server.

2. Storing JWTs in localStorage

The mistake: Saving the access token where any JavaScript on the page can read it.

javascript
// ❌ Before
const { data } = await axios.post("/api/login", credentials);
localStorage.setItem("token", data.token);

axios.defaults.headers.common["Authorization"] = `Bearer ${data.token}`;

If an attacker lands a single XSS payload (a vulnerable dependency, an unsanitized dangerouslySetInnerHTML), they can read localStorage and steal the session.

The fix: Keep the token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so JavaScript cannot read it. With flask-jwt-extended:

python
# ✅ After (Flask)
from flask import jsonify
from flask_jwt_extended import (
    JWTManager, create_access_token, set_access_cookies
)

app.config["JWT_TOKEN_LOCATION"] = ["cookies"]
app.config["JWT_COOKIE_SECURE"] = True        # HTTPS only
app.config["JWT_COOKIE_SAMESITE"] = "Lax"
app.config["JWT_COOKIE_CSRF_PROTECT"] = True  # keep this on with cookies

jwt = JWTManager(app)

@app.route("/login", methods=["POST"])
def login():
    # ...verify credentials...
    token = create_access_token(identity=str(user.id))
    resp = jsonify({"message": "logged in"})
    set_access_cookies(resp, token)
    return resp
javascript
// ✅ After (React)
// Send cookies with every request. The token itself never touches JS.
axios.defaults.withCredentials = true;

Trade-off to know: cookies are automatically attached by the browser, which opens the door to CSRF. That's why JWT_COOKIE_CSRF_PROTECT stays on, and your React app sends the CSRF token (from the csrf_access_token cookie) in an X-CSRF-TOKEN header on state-changing requests.

3. A wide-open CORS configuration

The mistake: Making CORS errors disappear during development with CORS(app) and never tightening it.

python
# ❌ Before
from flask_cors import CORS
CORS(app)  # allows requests from any origin

Combined with cookie-based auth, an over-permissive policy lets other websites make requests to your API from a visitor's browser.

The fix: Allow only the origins you actually use, and be explicit about credentials.

python
# ✅ After
import os
from flask_cors import CORS

ALLOWED_ORIGINS = os.environ.get(
    "ALLOWED_ORIGINS", "http://localhost:5173"
).split(",")

CORS(
    app,
    origins=ALLOWED_ORIGINS,
    supports_credentials=True,
    methods=["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"],
    allow_headers=["Content-Type", "X-CSRF-TOKEN"],
)

Set ALLOWED_ORIGINS to your real production domain in your deployment environment, and never use * together with credentials.

4. Building SQL queries with string formatting

The mistake: Putting user input directly into a SQL string.

python
# ❌ Before
cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'")

If email is ' OR '1'='1, the query returns every user. With worse payloads, attackers can modify or delete data. SQL injection is decades old and still one of the most damaging bugs around.

The fix: Use parameterized queries so the database treats input as data, never as SQL.

python
# ✅ After (psycopg2 with PostgreSQL)
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))
python
# ✅ After (SQLAlchemy ORM)
user = User.query.filter_by(email=email).first()

# ✅ After (SQLAlchemy raw SQL, still safe with bound parameters)
from sqlalchemy import text
db.session.execute(
    text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email"),
    {"email": email},
)

The rule is simple: if user input is ever concatenated or f-string-ed into a query, stop and parameterize it.

5. Leaking secrets through .env files and frontend bundles

The mistake: Hardcoding secrets, committing .env to Git, or putting secrets in frontend environment variables.

python
# ❌ Before
app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = "supersecret123"
app.config["DATABASE_URL"] = "postgresql://admin:MyPassword@db.example.com/app"

bash
# ❌ Before: committed to the repo, and exposed to the browser
REACT_APP_STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...

Two things go wrong here. Anything committed to Git can live in history forever, even after you delete the file. And any variable prefixed with REACT_APP_ (or VITE_ in Vite) is bundled into your frontend code, so every visitor can read it.

The fix:

python
# ✅ After (Flask)
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()  # reads .env locally; in production use real environment variables

app.config["SECRET_KEY"] = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]
app.config["DATABASE_URL"] = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]

bash
# ✅ .gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

Commit a .env.example with placeholder values so teammates know what to set.
Keep secrets on the backend only. Frontend variables should hold public values, such as an API base URL.
If a secret was ever committed, rotate it. Deleting the file is not enough.
Add a scanner like gitleaks as a pre-commit hook or CI step to catch leaks early.

title: The Column I Appended Months Ago Costs Me the Whole File
description:
On 29 June 2026 I added incremental builds to this blog's publishing pipeline. The idea was plain: keep a digest of each article's source file in the database, compare on publish, skip re-rendering whatever has not changed. It took one line of schema change, and it still sits at line 44 of migrate-content.mjs:

try { db.exec('ALTER TABLE posts ADD COLUMN source_hash TEXT'); } catch { /* kolon var */ }

ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN puts the new column at the end of the table. I did not treat that as a decision at the time. Where SQLite put the column was not something I cared about; having the value there was enough.

Five months later, against last night's build, I ran the measurement on the query that reads it. SELECT id, source_hash FROM posts: 2,866 rows, a 287 KiB result set. The kernel's counter came back with 64.69 MiB. The entire database.

My first suspect was the query, so I looked at EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: SCAN posts. A full scan, yes — but a full scan means "visit every row", not "read every row in full". What was missing was not an index. What was missing was the decision I had made in June without noticing: where the column sits inside the record.

In this same database the query plans did not change after ANALYZE, and the question there was what the planner picks. Here the plan never changes. What changes is how many bytes the same plan costs.

The setup

The file under test is the blog's live content database: the 19 November 17:15 build, /opt/mustafaerbay/dist/content.db. 67,829,760 bytes, 16,560 pages at a 4 KiB page size, one table (posts), 1,433 Turkish and 1,433 English rows. PRAGMA auto_vacuum is zero and PRAGMA journal_mode is delete, so there is no WAL file beside it. Both of those matter later.

I did not write to the live file. Everything ran against a /tmp copy on the same server over a read-only connection. Warm timings came from Python's sqlite3 module on my Mac (SQLite 3.49.1) and from the pipeline's own driver on the server (better-sqlite3, SQLite 3.53.0).

For the cold runs I dropped the file's page cache with posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) and took the read_bytes delta from /proc/self/io. The kernel documentation defines that counter as an "attempt to count the number of bytes which this process really did cause to be fetched from the storage layer", counted "at the submit_bio() level"; its sibling rchar also counts reads served out of the page cache. The first was the one I wanted.

I owe you a warning here. POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED is a hint, not an order. The code in mm/fadvise.c returns zero to the caller even when pages are not dropped; a failure count is kept internally and never reported. So "I dropped the page cache" is, on its own, an assumption. My evidence that it actually happened is this: the same run repeated three times and returned a byte-identical number each time — the whole file. Had the cache survived, that number would have shrunk.

The table's column order, straight from pragma_table_info:

0  id              9  author         18 translated_from
1  url_slug       10  human          19 translated_to
2  lang           11  series         20 draft
3  title          12  cover_image    21 headings
4  description    13  cover_image_alt 22 body_html
5  category       14  reading_time   23 source_path
6  tags           15  word_count     24 rendered_at
7  publish_date   16  faq            25 source_hash
8  updated_date   17  social_media

body_html sits at number 22 and averages 19,034 bytes. The source_hash I appended in June is dead last, at 25.

Where the record ends

SQLite writes a row as a single record: a header carrying one varint per column, then the values back to back in column order. The file format document says "the values for each column in the record immediately follow the header", and adds that the order is the order of the columns in the table definition.

The interesting part starts the moment a record does not fit on its page. The bytes kept on the leaf page come out of four quantities; in the document's own letters: U is the usable page size, X = U-35, M = ((U-12)*32/255)-23 and K = M+((P-M)%(U-4)), with P the total record size. The rule is in the same place: "If P is greater than X then the number of bytes stored on the table b-tree leaf page is K if K is less or equal to X or M otherwise."

In this file U = 4,096 (no reserved space), so X = 4,061 and M = 489. The average record is 22,581 bytes, and 2,844 of the 2,866 rows overflow. Everything past the local part goes to overflow pages, which form a linked list: "the first four bytes of each overflow page are a big-endian integer which is the page number of the next page in the chain."

Now I know what sits at the end of that chain: the column ALTER TABLE put there. Reading source_hash means walking that row's entire chain.

One sentence in the document taught me something here. Explaining why the thresholds were picked as they were, it says the point is to keep enough of the payload on the b-tree page that "the record header can usually be accessed without consulting an overflow page." What is guaranteed is the header, not the values. I have worked with this format for years and had never read that sentence this way.

The local part is not 489 bytes

The K formula deserves attention, because I skipped over it on first reading. The local part is not fixed at M, at 489 bytes; K is computed per row and wanders between 489 and 4,061. I counted it across my own table: the local part runs from 489 bytes at the low end to 4,057 at the high end, with a median of 2,069. In 13.3% of rows (380 of them) K exceeds X, the rule falls back to M, and the local part really is 489 bytes. In the rest, far more than that stays on the page.

The practical consequence: there is no "past byte 489 you are in the chain" shortcut. A column ending at byte 489 is local in every row. A column at byte 2,000 is still local in half of them (51.7%). Past 4,061, in none.

How many pages a column position costs

I counted this one too. A script computes, per row, the header size, the ending byte offset of every column, and that row's K by the rules above, then totals the question "how many overflow pages must be walked to reach this column" across the table.

column position avg. end offset rows kept local overflow pages walked
title 3 221 B 2,866 0
tags 6 432 B 2,824 42
cover_image_alt 13 650 B 2,379 487
faq 16 1,628 B 1,671 1,195
headings 21 2,813 B 960 1,956
source_hash 25 22,581 B 22 14,384

That 14,384 stopped me, because it had turned up elsewhere: the dbstat virtual table counts exactly 14,384 overflow pages for posts. Record arithmetic on one side, SQLite's own page accounting on the other — two independent methods, one number. Reaching the last column means walking every overflow page the table has.

Of the file's 16,560 pages, 14,384 are overflow pages: 86.86%. I had been thinking of this file as "metadata plus bodies for 1,433 articles". It is almost entirely body chain, with metadata as a thin strip along the edge.

The table holds one more detail: source_hash stays local in 22 rows. I looked at which ones — eleven articles and their Turkish/English twins, all published between 25 March and 19 May 2026, with records from 2,148 to 4,027 bytes. The oldest and shortest posts on the blog. Their records stay under X, so they never overflow.

There could have been one more exemption, and there is not. The file format document notes that "a record might have fewer values than the number of columns": a column added by ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN is simply absent from older rows and comes back from the default when read, with the record body never touched. source_hash is exactly such a column. Hopeful, I checked: zero rows have a null value and every length is 40 characters. The pipeline rewrites every row at least once, so that exemption closed long ago.

The bill on a cold cache

The derived page counts come from a model. What does the kernel say?

Before each run I dropped the page cache, ran the query, and took the read_bytes delta. Beside it, the bytes the model predicts — leaf, interior and walked overflow pages:

column queried model (MiB) measured read_bytes (MiB)
title 7.79 10.96
tags 7.95 11.07
faq 12.46 14.75
headings 15.43 19.52
source_hash 63.98 64.69

Every measured row exceeds the model, as expected: read_bytes also counts the kernel's readahead, and a full scan is readahead's favourite pattern. What read_ahead_kb can get up to on this same machine has its own measurement. On the last row the gap narrows to 0.71 MiB, and that gap is exactly 182 pages: the index, schema and freelist pages the model leaves out. Nothing in the file goes unread.

The source_hash run repeated three times and came back byte-identical each time: 64.69 MiB. Wall clock wandered between 1.89 and 3.82 seconds; the server is not idle, so I draw no conclusion from the time. The bytes are the solid part.

The query delivers a 287 KiB result set, which makes the ratio 231x. Look only at the digest column — 112 KiB — and it is 592x, but the query also returns id, so the honest number is 231.

Does it really walk, in the code

That is the behaviour. I wanted the mechanism in the source. The accessPayload function in SQLite's btree.c reaches an offset beyond the local part of a record exactly this way: it takes the first overflow pointer from the cell, then advances through a while( nextPage ) loop, reading each page's own "next" pointer. The comment in that loop was the sentence I was after: "The only reason to read this page is to obtain the page number for the next page in the overflow chain. The page data is not required."

SQLite is not handing me body_html, not decoding it, not wanting it; it visits every page to ask "where is the next one" so it can step over 19 KB. The price of stepping over is fetching the page.

Two shortcuts exist, and neither works on this file — I have to write down why, because my first draft claimed flatly that there is no way to jump ahead, and that claim is false.

The first is the cursor cache. Once a row's chain has been walked, the page numbers live in a BtCursor.aOverflow array, and the function's header comment introduces it as a cache that "subsequent calls use ... to make seeking to the supplied offset more efficient". The cache is invalidated when the cursor moves. In a full scan the cursor moves at every row, so each of the 2,866 rows walks its chain from scratch.

The second is more interesting. The header comment on getOverflowPage says that where possible it "uses the auto-vacuum pointer-map data instead of reading the content of page ovfl" to find the next page: it guesses that the next page is ovfl+1, checks the guess against the pointer map, and on a hit never reads the overflow page at all. So SQLite does have a way to jump ahead — but only in auto-vacuum databases. In my file PRAGMA auto_vacuum is zero, there is no pointer map, and the shortcut is inoperative. The number I got is therefore this file's number, not a universal property of SQLite.

One more note: the file format document says nothing about this cost. It describes how a record is laid out, not what reaching a column costs.

Three layouts, all measured

I set up both fixes and put them through the same cold run. I also added a control, because my first comparison was flawed: it set a file that had grown over months against a freshly written one, and there was no telling how much of the gap came from the column moving and how much from the rewrite. The control is simple — VACUUM with the same column order.

layout cold read_bytes note
today's schema 64.69 MiB —
same order + VACUUM (control) 64.05 MiB the rewrite on its own changes nothing
body_html last 25.61 MiB 2.5x
covering index 0.41 MiB 158x

All four ran three times, and the byte figures repeated exactly. The control did its job: a fresh rewrite takes 64.69 down to 64.05, so the gain really does come from where the column sits.

The control had a side effect I was not looking for. The bytes did not move, but the wall clock did: 1.89 to 3.82 seconds on the aged copy, 0.26 to 0.40 seconds on the vacuumed one. Same page count, far quicker. Scattered chains must be defeating readahead. That is not what I set out to time, so I claim no factor for it, but it does mean a long-lived database can do worse than 231x on a cold cache, not better.

Why the covering index wins so completely: CREATE INDEX idx_hash ON posts(id, source_hash) holds both columns the query wants, so the table is never consulted. SQLite's optimization document describes the case: when every column to be fetched is already available in the index itself, "SQLite will use the values contained in the index and will never look up the original table row." The plan agrees: SCAN posts USING COVERING INDEX idx_hash. It costs 82 pages, 328 KiB — roughly five thousandths of the file. In exchange it creates a second b-tree to maintain on every publish; for 2,866 rows that is small, but it is not free.

Column order helped less than I expected, and the table says why: faq and headings still come before source_hash, and both run to kilobytes. "Put the big column last" is half a recipe here.

Two more options sit on the table, untested by me. The first is PRAGMA page_size: at 8 KiB, M = 1,003 and X = 8,157, so every record under 8,157 bytes stops overflowing altogether. The second is what production should actually do: move body_html into a separate table keyed by id. Metadata rows then stay narrow enough never to overflow, and this article's subject disappears.

Warm — the conditions the pipeline actually runs in — the same query against better-sqlite3 on the server takes 68.78 ms on today's schema and 3.89 ms with the covering index (median of seven runs). A factor of 17.7.

What the bill actually comes to

Here is the deflating part. How often does this query run? Counting the last seven days of deploy-only runs: three a day. On a warm cache the same chain walk bills me roughly 206 milliseconds a day. The 231-fold amplification is a cold-cache figure; if every deploy hit a cold cache it would come to 194 MiB of reads a day.

This is not a problem. The covering index is not going into the pipeline today, because changing a schema in the same breath as measuring it undercuts my trust in the measurement. It goes on the open list with its condition attached: the day a second full scan over metadata lands on this table — the search index or the newsletter query reading metadata per request — the index ships.

A small bill does not make the mechanism unimportant. In my pipeline this query runs three times a day; the same pattern running per request would be different arithmetic entirely. Three things are worth checking in your own schema.

Queries on the serving path come first. This blog's list query reads up to the draft column, position 20, which the model puts at 3,262 pages, or 12.74 MiB. It stays cheap because it is cached once per process lifetime — without that cache, every request would carry it.

Second, what drives the cost is row width, not row count. 2,866 rows is a small table; the bill here comes from the 22 KB average record. On a narrow table with a hundred thousand rows, this article's subject never surfaces.

Third, the places where the cache is absent: a network filesystem, a memory-capped container, a freshly started process. A warm cache hides this cost, and when whatever hides it goes away, the cost comes back.

Checklist

If you want to look at your own schema, the order is this:

  1. Get the ground truth with PRAGMA page_size, PRAGMA page_count and PRAGMA auto_vacuum. The last one matters: auto-vacuum on means the pointer-map shortcut is live.
  2. Run SELECT pagetype, count(*), sum(pgsize) FROM dbstat WHERE name='<table>' GROUP BY pagetype. Overflow pages in the tens of percent means wide records.
  3. Pull your column order from pragma_table_info, then compute K for your own average record size. Do not trust a "489 bytes" threshold; in my file the real median came out at 2,069.
  4. Do not estimate the cost. On Linux, posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED) plus /proc/self/io is a ten-line script; read read_bytes, not rchar, and repeat the run at least three times — the call can fail silently, and a repeated identical number is your only evidence that it did not.
  5. Before reaching for a fix, multiply unit cost by frequency. Mine came out at 206 ms/day, which is a sufficient answer for doing nothing today.

Closing

When I write SELECT id, source_hash FROM posts I think I am writing a narrow query. Two columns, both small, neither of them a body. What the measurement shows is that the width of a query is set not by the size of the columns you ask for but by where those columns sit inside the record. title is at byte 221; free. source_hash is at byte 22,581; the whole file.

The uncomfortable part is who wrote that cost. I wrote the query this week, but its price was set in June, when ALTER TABLE appended the column and I thought I was adding a column. Adding one to a schema always looks like cheap work; it returns in a second and nothing breaks. Nothing does break. But every new column lines up behind the ones before it, and that order becomes the read cost of a query somebody writes months later.

I could have caught this earlier. When four libraries were asked about mmap_size they gave two different answers — the same database, but not the same file: that snapshot was 52.2 MiB, 13,365 pages and 2,498 rows, where this one is 64.69 MiB, 16,560 pages and 2,866 rows. Do not line the two up and derive a growth rate from them; I am not doing that either. Two snapshots, nothing more. What they have in common is that both times the question went to the file itself. Database files hide nothing. It is just that nobody asks.

Official Sources

  • SQLite — Database File Format
  • SQLite — Query Planning (Covering Indexes)
  • SQLite — EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
  • SQLite source — src/btree.c
  • Linux kernel — proc filesystem documentation
  • Linux kernel source — mm/fadvise.c

title: A minimal probe of task modeling in language models
description:
arXiv:2605.02028v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Language models read long contexts and score well on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, but neither shows whether a model can do work whose next step depends on everything that came before, as a long-running agent must. We call this ability task modeling and propose counting identical items as its simplest test: every item adds to the total and no item records it. We define counting capacity (CC) as the sequence length up to which a model returns the exact count more often than not, and measure it for 205 models. Every resolved measurement loses count abruptly, at a median of 50 items and at most 627; across release years the median rose 1.6-fold while context windows grew about 80-fold. Changing the counted symbol or the delimiter moves a model's CC severalfold, yet the model accounts for about three quarters of the variance across 16 models and 11 encodings. Reasoning leaves the median CC unchanged across 77 matched pairs. In six open-weight models the count stays readable in early layers past the boundary but does not reach the output, and an activation edit that carries the count forward also carries the state of an object-tracking task. CC tracks the METR task horizon after controlling for general capability, and rises with capacity on grid-execution tasks and, with reasoning off, on object tracking. We do not show that counting is necessary or sufficient for long-horizon work; that remains a hypothesis, which this cheap measurement can test.

title: MUSE: A Full-Text Cross-Domain Knowledge Base of Scientific Problems, Solutions, and Rationales
description:
arXiv:2608.10974v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Scientific papers contain fine-grained records of problem solving: authors mention technical obstacles and methods that were used to address them, often along with reasoning on why those methods were chosen. We introduce MUSE (Mining Underlying Scientific Explanations), a full-text, multi-domain resource of scientific Problem-Solution-Rationale (P-S-R) triplets. We curate 579 expert-annotated full-text paragraphs, with a rich annotation schema covering salient problem, solution, and rationale spans, solves and rationale_of links and conceptual coreference. A modular extraction pipeline scales this annotation to build a high-quality knowledge base of 37K source-grounded P-S-R triplets. We evaluate the extraction components and include a preliminary experiment training a rationale-supervised LLM for scientific problem solving. Interestingly, we find that rationale supervision improves performance on complex, multi-constraint problems but can harm performance on simpler ones.
