title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
description:
arXiv:2611.25185v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.

title: @Data on a JPA Entity Gave Us a False `equals()` and 18,000 Duplicate Rows
description:
The nightly import had been running for months without a complaint. Then a report came back with customers listed twice, and a count of the staging table showed roughly 18,000 rows more than the source file contained. The import code had a deduplication step, it was three lines long, and it looked impossible to get wrong.

Set<Customer> toSave = new HashSet<>(existingCustomers);
toSave.addAll(importedCustomers);
customerDao.saveAll(toSave);

A HashSet deduplicates by equals and hashCode, and the entity had both, because it was annotated with Lombok's @Data. That is the part everyone trusted and nobody read.

@Data generates equals and hashCode from every field of the class, and on a JPA entity every field includes the primary key. A customer loaded from the database carried an id. The same customer parsed from the import file had not been persisted yet, so its id was null. Two objects describing the same person, with the same external reference and the same email, were not equal to each other, because one of them had an id and the other did not. The set kept both, saveAll inserted the second one, and the deduplication step had been quietly doing nothing for as long as the id had been part of the comparison.

The same generated method has a second failure mode that is easier to hit and harder to see. Because the id participates in hashCode, an entity's hash changes the moment it is persisted and the database assigns a value. An object placed in a HashSet before the flush lands in one bucket, and after the flush the set looks for it in another. The object is in the collection and the collection says it is not there. Any code that holds entities in a set or uses them as map keys across a flush boundary is exposed to this, and it fails intermittently, which is how it survives review.

The fix was to stop deriving identity from the database. The import records had a natural key already, a source system and an external id, unique by contract and never changed after creation, so equals and hashCode were written by hand against those two fields and nothing else. Identity became a property of the record rather than of its row, which means it is the same before the insert, after the insert and after a detached object is merged back.

@Override
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) {
        return true;
    }
    if (!(o instanceof Customer other)) {
        return false;
    }
    return sourceSystem == other.sourceSystem && externalId.equals(other.externalId);
}

@Override
public int hashCode() {
    return Objects.hash(sourceSystem, externalId);
}

When there is no natural key to lean on, the usual alternative is a UUID assigned in the constructor rather than by the database, which gives the same stability without requiring the business to supply one.

There is a smaller reason to keep @Data away from entities, and it shows up in logs rather than in data. The annotation also generates toString across all fields, including lazily loaded associations, so printing an entity can trigger a query per association, or a LazyInitializationException outside a session. The usual compromise, if Lombok is going to stay on the class, is @Getter and @Setter rather than @Data, with equals, hashCode and toString written.

The broader point is that an entity has two identities, the row it maps to and the thing it represents, and they are not available at the same moments in its lifecycle. A generated method cannot know which one you meant. Ours picked the row, in a set that was asking about the thing.

title: My permanent seller URL returned 530 while the tunnel was healthy
description:
The address buyers saw was the one I trusted most: the permanent workers.dev domain. It had been in the directory for weeks, it was the URL in my listings, and it was the one I used in payment challenges.

On the day I added a new endpoint, that address started returning an HTML error page. The tunnel behind it was still answering every request locally.

Deploy success, crawl failure

The deploy API returned HTTP 200 success=True. The worker version was created. The new endpoint answered 402 locally with and without parameters. The test suite passed 33 checks.

The directory said otherwise:

toolCount 43
routable false
health 0.6
routerDispatchReason crawl_failed
fallbackErrors:
  /openapi.json -> Unexpected token '<', "<!DOCTYPE "... is not valid JSON
  /agents.json  -> Unexpected token '<', "<!DOCTYPE "... is not valid JSON

The seller had 43 tools, not the 46 the live backend exposed. The crawler was reading HTML where JSON should have been.

The edge was not the backend

The live tunnel returned 200 for /review, 200 and 168 KB for /openapi.json, and 402 for the new endpoint. The local process was healthy.

The worker was deployed too. The Cloudflare API listed a new version. The failure was at the edge: the worker returned its own HTML failure page for the discovery documents. The crawler correctly refused to parse it, and the whole seller became non-routable.

That is why toolCount is not a health check. A cached count can survive after the documents stop parsing. The useful checks are the ones that read the same path a buyer reads:

  1. GET /review on the public seller URL, not the tunnel.
  2. GET /openapi.json and parse it as JSON, not just check the status code.
  3. POST /mcp with tools/list.
  4. The directory's fallbackErrors, toolCount, routable, and health.

A dead entry outranked the live one

While the permanent domain was serving HTML, the live tunnel was indexed as a separate seller. It had 46 tools, routable=true, and health=1. But the directory still put the dead permanent entry first for the buyer's query and the live tunnel second.

The rank was not a quality signal. The dead entry had the older registration and the exact name; the live entry had a newer registration. A buyer clicking the first result got an error page.

The fix was not another redeploy. It was to stop the dead entry from owning the buyer's phrase: re-register the old URL with a neutral legacy name that no longer matched the query, and point the stable seller URL at the live tunnel. The live entry moved to first.

The three-layer check

The permanent domain is not automatically the healthiest domain. It is only a name. The seller origin is the address that answers the buyer's path with the right status and the right body.

Keep three separate facts:

  • Tunnel health: the tunnel process is alive and the local path answers.
  • Edge health: the public host answers the buyer's discovery path with JSON or 402.
  • Directory health: the directory parses the seller and marks it routable.

Those three can disagree. A process check only proves the first. A deploy success only proves the second at upload time. Only the directory's routable and fallbackErrors prove the third.

The rule I use now: never let a permanent URL outrank a live seller just because it is older. If the permanent URL is broken, rename its directory entry so it stops matching the buyer's phrase, point the stable URL at the live origin, and keep the live origin registered until the permanent one passes the same probe.

The cost

The outage did not cost a server bill. It cost the only thing that matters: buyers who searched the exact phrase, found a seller, clicked, and got an error page. The backend was healthy the whole time. The seller was not.

The check that would have caught it in one minute was not a deploy log. It was a single request to the public URL, with the response body parsed as JSON. That is now the first check after every deploy, before any directory refresh.

The full evidence table, the exact directory fields, and the rename procedure are in the paid version: My permanent seller URL returned 530 while the tunnel was healthy.

title: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
description:
arXiv:2611.23855v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/

title: Effects or Effectiveness? What Really Makes a Website Successful
description:
Imagine two websites for companies offering the same service. One greets visitors with spectacular animation, full-screen video and an unusual menu. The other immediately explains what the business does, presents examples of its work and provides clear terms and a contact button. Which one is more effective?

You cannot answer from appearance alone. The first could communicate the brand beautifully and attract customers. The second could be fast but struggle because of an unconvincing offer or insufficient trust. The real question is how each design decision supports the visitor's task and the business outcome.

1. What businesses pay for when commissioning a website

A shop owner wants orders. A clinic wants to make appointments easier to book. An architect needs to demonstrate professional expertise and attract clients with an appropriate budget. An equipment manufacturer must make technical specifications available so potential partners can request a quotation.

Success differs between industries, but a website should support specific actions: finding information, evaluating an offer, choosing a product, booking an appointment or contacting the company. Design, content, imagery, speed and integrations contribute to that goal together.

Before development begins, define what a successful outcome means. For an online store it might be paid orders; for a service company, qualified enquiries; for a portfolio, interest from the right audience. An emotional impression matters, but it is not automatically equivalent to a sale.

2. Aesthetics matter, but they are not everything

Nielsen Norman Group describes the aesthetic-usability effect: people tend to perceive attractive interfaces as easier to use. Good design can create a positive first impression and encourage visitors to explore an offer.

The reverse side is that favourable reactions to appearance can mask usability difficulties. Someone may call a shop beautiful while struggling to find the correct size, shipping information or checkout button. This is why researchers recommend observing what people actually do, rather than relying only on their opinions about visual design.

Good web design includes typography, contrast, photography, information hierarchy, composition and intelligible interaction states. A restrained interface can look premium, and an expressive design can be easy to use. The number of decorative effects is not a quality metric in itself.

3. Clarity as a competitive advantage

In his ten usability heuristics, Jakob Nielsen emphasises understandable feedback, alignment with users' expectations and prioritisation of necessary information. The aesthetic and minimalist design principle does not require every website to look like an identical white page. It means that less important elements should not obscure essential ones.

The first screen of a commercial website should help visitors answer four questions:

  • What does the company do, and who is its offer for?
  • What benefits, conditions or prices are available?
  • Where can I view projects, products or services?
  • What should I do next?

Visitors should not have to decipher the designer's intentions. An unusual menu that takes time to discover may impress during a project presentation but cause difficulty for someone browsing on a phone while travelling.

Assess an effect according to its function in a particular user journey.

4. Speed and stability: what Google measures

Google explains in its Core Web Vitals documentation that three metrics help assess website experience. LCP describes how quickly the main content appears, INP measures responsiveness to interactions, and CLS measures unexpected layout shifts. The good-experience thresholds at the 75th percentile of real visits are LCP up to 2.5 seconds, INP up to 200 milliseconds and CLS no greater than 0.1.

These metrics reveal problems that a static design cannot show. Heavy video may delay the main content; excessive JavaScript can slow responses to clicks; an image without reserved dimensions can move the button a visitor is about to tap.

At the same time, Google explicitly explains that good Core Web Vitals do not guarantee top search rankings. A PageSpeed Insights score does not measure sales either. Distinguish Lighthouse laboratory tests, real-user measurements and business metrics.

5. Can speed influence sales?

There are concrete experiments as well as recommendations. In the Vodafone case study published on web.dev, the company compared two landing-page variants in an A/B test focused on performance. The variant with a 31% improvement in field-measured LCP recorded 8% more sales.

That is the result of a particular experiment, not a universal formula for every website. A shop with different customers, prices and traffic sources could see a different outcome. The case illustrates why performance deserves attention as a business issue, not merely a technical competition over scores.

6. What ecommerce research reveals

Baymard Institute researches shoppers' behaviour during checkout. Its cart-abandonment materials distinguish people who are simply not ready to purchase from difficulties that merchants can address. These include unexpected extra costs, complicated forms, mandatory account creation and unclear conditions.

If customers cannot understand shipping costs, return to their basket or complete a payment, even a beautiful catalogue cannot solve the underlying problem.

Instead of evaluating only the homepage, test the entire journey: product search, filters, variant selection, cart, address entry, delivery method, payment and confirmation. Repeat the test on mobile devices. Check what happens when an item becomes unavailable or a payment fails, not only when everything succeeds.

7. When animation is genuinely useful

In The Role of Animation and Motion in UX, Nielsen Norman Group considers movement a communication tool. It can draw attention to a change of state, show relationships between elements and help people understand the outcome of an action.

Useful examples include brief confirmation that a product has been added to a basket, smooth disclosure of information, a clear loading indicator or a transition between quotation calculator steps. On an architecture studio's website, a compelling presentation of visual material may actually help sell the service.

But visitors should not repeatedly wait for an effect to finish before accessing the menu or a form. If each paragraph appears only after a scripted delay, it becomes harder to scan a page quickly. Smooth interaction should not turn into waiting.

8. Animation, performance and accessibility

The technical guidance on animations and performance from web.dev recommends using transform and opacity where appropriate rather than properties that repeatedly require layout calculations or repainting. Even a carefully implemented effect still needs testing on actual devices.

Accessibility matters too. In WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.3.3, at level AAA, W3C describes allowing users to disable non-essential motion triggered by interaction. A separate Success Criterion 2.2.2, at level A, deals with automatically moving content, among other things: under specified conditions, content moving for over five seconds alongside other content needs a way to be paused, stopped or hidden.

Supporting the operating system's prefers-reduced-motion setting allows a website to adapt motion to individual preferences. Keyboard access, readable text, clearly labelled forms and sufficient contrast also matter. An expressive website should remain usable without its decorative animation.

9. How a business owner can assess website effectiveness

Clients do not need to become engineers. Agree on user journeys, acceptance criteria and ways to measure results.

  • Ask someone unfamiliar with the business to understand the offer and find relevant information.
  • Complete the primary journey on both a phone and a computer, including forms and payments.
  • Measure performance on the homepage, service pages and important shop pages.
  • Check accessibility, visual stability and the behaviour of integrations.
  • After launch, track relevant actions: enquiries, checkout starts, completed orders or bookings.

Evaluate effectiveness through concrete journeys and measurable results.

When comparing designs, change a limited number of elements and account for traffic sources, seasonality and the amount of evidence available. A high conversion rate across ten visits proves little. Sometimes interviewing a few actual customers and identifying an obvious obstacle is more useful than waiting months for a statistically convincing experiment.

10. CianBay Studio as a practical example

For our own CianBay Studio website, we chose a distinctive but restrained visual style. We focused on clear service descriptions, published starting prices, real projects, multilingual content and the blog. In our PageSpeed Insights laboratory checks, selected pages achieved performance scores of 96 or above. These are specific test results, which can change, rather than a promise of the same score for every visitor.

We could introduce more elaborate animation. Our priority, however, was to enable potential clients to find answers and understand the terms of cooperation. Another project, such as a premium brand or creative portfolio, may have different visual priorities.

Restraint is not a goal in itself. An effect that makes interaction easier, improves a product presentation or communicates the brand appropriately deserves consideration. If it causes delays or distracts from an important action, its implementation deserves reconsideration.

Frequently asked questions

Does a high PageSpeed score mean a website will succeed?

No. It is a useful technical indicator, but sales also depend on demand, pricing, the offer, trust, traffic and how easily customers can complete the desired action.

Should websites avoid animation entirely?

No. Animation can clarify interface actions and states, present products and express a brand. It should be implemented efficiently and accessibly.

What should come first when commissioning a website?

The needs of the business and its audience, clear design, reliable functionality, mobile usability, speed and agreed quality criteria. Evaluate visual decisions within that context.

A website that works for the business

The objective is not a website without animation or a maximum laboratory score. It is a website where the right audience can get information, make a choice and take the required action. That is the balance we seek when delivering business websites, WooCommerce stores and website performance optimisation.

Sources and further reading

  • Google Search Central: Core Web Vitals
  • Google Search Central: Page experience
  • Nielsen Norman Group: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect
  • Jakob Nielsen: 10 Usability Heuristics
  • Nielsen Norman Group: The Role of Animation and Motion in UX
  • Baymard Institute: Cart & Checkout Usability Research
  • web.dev: Vodafone case study
  • web.dev: Animations and performance
  • W3C: WCAG 2.2 Animation from Interactions
  • W3C: WCAG 2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide

title: eMondrian now speaks JSON: a REST API on your semantic model
description:
Until now, a program that wanted numbers from eMondrian had to speak XMLA: SOAP envelopes, XML answers, a client library that exists for few languages. Excel and Power BI do this for you. A Python script, a Node backend or an n8n workflow don't.

From Community 2026.11.20 eMondrian also answers over REST with JSON. Send an MDX or DAX query in a POST request and get rows back:

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' https://demo.emondrian.com/api/v1/query -d '{
  "catalog": "OnTime",
  "query": "SELECT {[Measures].[Flights], [Measures].[Avg Arr Delay]} ON 0, TopCount([Airline].[Airline].Members, 5, [Measures].[Flights]) ON 1 FROM [OnTime (attributes)] WHERE [Time].[2024]"
}'

{
  "columns": [
    { "name": "Airline", "kind": "member", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "Flights", "kind": "measure", "type": "number" },
    { "name": "Avg Arr Delay", "kind": "measure", "type": "number" }
  ],
  "rows": [
    { "Airline": "WN", "Flights": 1419419, "Avg Arr Delay": 12.13 },
    { "Airline": "DL", "Flights": 1009174, "Avg Arr Delay": 13.19 },
    { "Airline": "AA", "Flights": 984306, "Avg Arr Delay": 23.01 },
    { "Airline": "UA", "Flights": 760451, "Avg Arr Delay": 15.07 },
    { "Airline": "OO", "Flights": 744658, "Avg Arr Delay": 15.96 }
  ],
  "rowCount": 5,
  "truncated": false,
  "elapsedMs": 168
}

You can run this request yourself: it goes to our public demo, 182 million US flights in ClickHouse, open without sign-in. The answer took 168 ms.

What the API does

Request Answer
GET /api/v1/catalogs The catalogs, each with the cubes you may see
GET /api/v1/catalogs/{catalog}/cubes/{cube} Dimensions, hierarchies, levels and measures
POST /api/v1/query The result of an MDX or DAX query, as a table
GET /api/v1/openapi.json The OpenAPI 3 description
  • Read-only. It runs queries. It doesn't change models or write data back.
  • MDX and DAX. A DAX query comes back as the table it defines.
  • No licence key for the API itself. DAX queries need the DAX module, as everywhere.
  • The same security as XMLA. The same users, passwords and tokens, sent in the header, and every query runs with the caller's roles.

The full reference: REST API (JSON).

Why it matters: the model is now for every system

A semantic model defines your numbers once: what Revenue is, how Margin is calculated, which rows each customer may see. Excel, Power BI and AI agents already use it. Now everything else can, too, and gets the same numbers.

Here is what that opens up.

1. Your own HTML dashboard on governed data

With an AI agent anyone can build a dashboard page in their own design in minutes. The hard part is the data behind it: the agent writes the numbers into the file, or the page gets a database password.

With the REST API, the page's backend asks eMondrian for the data at each view:

// server side: the token stays on your server
const res = await fetch("https://bi.example.com/api/v1/query", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Authorization": `Bearer ${process.env.EMONDRIAN_TOKEN}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    catalog: "FoodMart",
    query: "SELECT {[Measures].[Unit Sales]} ON 0, NON EMPTY [Store].[Store State].Members ON 1 FROM [Sales]"
  })
});
const { rows } = await res.json();

The data is live, the file holds no numbers, and the database password stays in eMondrian. The measures are the model's: Unit Sales on the page is the same number as in Excel.

2. A customer portal where each customer sees only their rows

Give each customer an eMondrian user and a role. An administrator issues that user's personal token, on the page /account/tokens?user=acme-portal or from a script:

curl -u admin -H 'Content-Type: application/json' https://bi.example.com/account/api/tokens \
     -d '{"user": "acme-portal", "name": "Acme portal backend", "days": 90}'

The answer shows the token once. Your backend keeps it and calls the API with it, and the server filters the rows:

"rows": [ { "Store State": "OR", "Unit Sales": 67659 } ]

Same query, same code. With an administrator's token the answer has three states; with Acme's token, only Oregon. With rollupPolicy="partial" on the role's grant, totals count only the rows the role allows. The filter is not in your JavaScript, so nobody can remove it in the browser.

A user has one personal token, so give the portal a user of its own: revoking its token stops nothing else. To take access away, revoke the token or disable the user: the token stops working within 30 seconds.

3. Scripts and notebooks

A data scientist doesn't need an XMLA library to get the official numbers:

import os, requests, pandas as pd

r = requests.post(
    "https://bi.example.com/api/v1/query",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['EMONDRIAN_TOKEN']}"},
    json={"catalog": "FoodMart", "cube": "Sales",
          "query": 'EVALUATE SUMMARIZECOLUMNS(Store[Store State], "Unit Sales", [Unit Sales])'},
)
df = pd.DataFrame(r.json()["rows"])

A DAX query names the cube, and its columns are named as in the query: Store[Store State] and [Unit Sales]. The forecast in the notebook starts from the same Unit Sales as the board report.

4. Low-code tools and automations

n8n, Make, Retool, Zapier, a Power Automate flow: any tool that can send an HTTP request and read JSON can now query the model. A few ideas:

  • A morning KPI message in Slack or Teams: yesterday's sales against the same day last year.
  • An alert when a measure crosses a threshold: late deliveries above 5%, stock below a minimum.
  • An internal tool in Retool on the same measures as Power BI.

5. Exports to other systems

A scheduled job reads aggregates from the model and writes them where they are needed: a CRM field with each account's revenue, a planning sheet, a partner's file. The numbers in the export are the model's, not another SQL query that someone wrote once and nobody checks.

By default a request returns up to 10,000 rows; it can ask for up to 100,000 with maxRows. Both limits are server settings, and truncated says when rows were left out.

6. Services that AI agents write for you

An agent that writes code reads /api/v1/openapi.json, signed in with the service's credentials, and knows the whole API. It reads the cube's model from /api/v1/catalogs/{catalog}/cubes/{cube} and writes queries in business names: Unit Sales, Store State, not tables and joins. The service it writes runs as a user with a role, so it sees only what that user may see.

Security: the same as XMLA

Sign-in How
User name and password HTTP Basic
Personal token (emk_…) Authorization: Bearer emk_…
OAuth access token Authorization: Bearer <token>
  • A token goes in the header, where proxies and browser histories don't keep it. A token in the address is refused.
  • Every query runs with the caller's roles: row-level security, hidden measures, hidden cubes.
  • Every request through the gateway is a line in its access log, with the user and the sign-in method.
  • Pages on other sites can't call the API from a browser unless you list them in auth/identity.yml. A token in a web page can be read by anyone who opens it, so call eMondrian from your server where you can.

Try it

  1. Run the curl request above against the demo, or open https://demo.emondrian.com/api/v1/catalogs in a browser.
  2. On your own server: update to Community 2026.11.20.2 or later. The API is on at https://<your server>/api/v1.
  3. Create a personal token at /account/tokens, or have an administrator issue one for a program's own user, and call the API with it.

Read more: REST API (JSON) · Security · AI agents (MCP)

First published on docs.emondrian.com.

title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters
description:
arXiv:2611.25235v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

title: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
description:
arXiv:2611.23509v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

title: React UseCallBack Hook
description:
whenever a React component re-renders, the functions inside that component are normally recreated. To avoid unnecessary function reference changes, we can use useCallback.
useCallback is a React Hook that memoizes a function and returns the same function reference until its dependencies change.

import React, { useCallback, useState } from 'react'

function UseCallbackhook() {
    const[count,setCount] = useState(0);
    const[msg,setMsg] = useState("");
    function increase(){
        setCount(count+1);
    }
    // function fncallback(){
    //     console.log("hello world");
    // }
    const fncallback = useCallback(()=>{
        setMsg("hello world");
        console.log("hello world")
    },[]);
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>count : {count}</h1>
      <h1>message :{msg} </h1>
      <button onClick={increase}>+</button>
      <button onClick={fncallback}> show message</button>
    </div>
  )
}

export default UseCallbackhook

How does it work?
Initially, the component renders.
useCallback remembers the showMessage function reference.
When we click Increase, the count changes.
React re-renders the component.
Since the dependency array is empty, React returns the same function reference.

Advantages of useCallback

Helps avoid unnecessary function reference changes.
Useful when passing functions to memoized child components.
Helps optimize component rendering in suitable situations.
Useful when a function is a dependency of another Hook.

title: What real estate photo editing costs in 2026: open data from 27 services and apps
description:
Editing one real estate photo (bracket merge, straight verticals, bright windows) costs from $0.25 to $5 depending on who does it. We read the price pages of 27 photo editing services and apps made for listing photos in November 2026 and put every row in an open dataset (real-estate-photo-editing-prices.csv, CC BY 4.0).

What we found

  • $0.90: median price for one edited HDR photo across the 18 providers that publish a per-photo price.
  • $0.99 with human editors (11 services), $0.80 with AI tools (5 apps). The gap is small; turnaround is the bigger difference (seconds or minutes for AI, 12 to 48 hours for most human services).
  • $29 a month: median cheapest plan among the 9 tools with a monthly plan under $100.
  • 23 of 27 offer some free trial: a few free photos, a free first property or watermarked previews.

Per photo, cheapest first

Provider Type One HDR photo
Retouching Labs human editors $0.25
Imagen AI + human review $0.32
Real Estate Camera AI AI $0.50
Color Clipping human editors $0.70
Autoenhance.ai AI $0.75
BackOfficePro human editors $0.75
AutoHDR AI $0.80
Clipping World human editors $0.80
Smart Photo Editors human editors $0.80
Exposio AI $0.99
Visuals Clipping human editors $0.99
Phixer human editors $1.00

FixThePhoto human editors $1.50
Styldod human editors $1.50
PhotoUp human editors $1.88
Ovvy AI + human review $2.00
Bella Virtual human editors $5.00

What a listing costs

A typical listing uses 25 photos. At the median that is about $22 in editing, against a median of $225 for a photographer who shoots and edits a 1,500 to 3,000 sq ft home (see the photographer price data in the same repository). Editing only works if the photos you send in are good: level, from the right spots, with exposure brackets. That part is still on you.

Query it 

import pandas as pd
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/October-ai-jpg/listing-photo-data/main/data/real-estate-photo-editing-prices.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url)
print(df.groupby("type")["hdr_per_photo_usd"].median())

Caveats

  • Prices are what each provider publishes, read on 18 November 2026. Many are "from" prices, and bulk prices are lower.
  • Some providers publish only credits or plans; they are in the data with a plan price and no per-photo price.
  • Item removal, day-to-dusk and sky replacement are priced separately; the dataset has columns for each.

The ranking in words, with free trials and turnaround: the cheapest real estate photo editing. The data is also on Hugging Face and Zenodo.

Disclosure: written with an AI agent for October, an iPhone app that guides you to the right spots and returns finished listing photos and a walkthrough video. October is not in the price tables.

title: Zero-Shot Video Restoration and Enhancement with Assistance of Video Diffusion Models
description:
arXiv:2601.21922v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Although diffusion-based zero-shot image restoration and enhancement methods have achieved great success, applying them to video restoration or enhancement will lead to severe temporal flickering. In this paper, we propose to systematically utilize both homologous and heterogeneous video diffusion models to assist the image-based method in maintaining more temporal consistency for zero-shot video restoration and enhancement. We propose homologous latents fusion, heterogenous latents fusion, and a CoQ fusion ratio strategy to utilize both homologous and heterogenous text-to-video diffusion models to complement the image method. Moreover, we propose temporal-strengthening post-processing to utilize the image-to-video diffusion model to further improve temporal consistency. Our method is training-free and can be applied to any diffusion-based image restoration and enhancement methods. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.

title: aster - personal AI from scratch
description:
aster

A private, persistent mind written from scratch in Rust. No pretrained models, no external AI APIs. It learns only from what you teach it, shows its reasoning, and asks when it doesn't know.

  • No ChatGPT. No Claude. No Llama. No pretrained weights. No external AI APIs.
  • Every word it knows, every reply it gives, came from you teaching it, rating it, or handing it text to read.
  • It runs on your own machine (or your own server) and keeps everything in your own database.
  • It keeps running when you close the window. It has internal levels like energy and curiosity that rise and fall over time, and it'll ask you things on its own when it's idle.

aster is not a wrapper around an existing AI model. There's no API key for OpenAI, Anthropic, or anyone else, and there are no downloaded model files. The language model, the memory search, the reply scoring and the neural network are all written in Rust in this repo, and they all start empty.

clxrityy/aster

Why?

Almost every "AI" product right now is the same thing underneath: a giant model trained by a big company on a huge chunk of the internet, with an app on top. That works, but it means:

  • You don't know what it knows. It was trained on things you never saw.
  • You can't really teach it. You can prompt it, but it forgets when the chat ends, and its core never changes because of you.
  • It isn't yours. Your conversations go to someone else's servers, and the model can change or disappear any time.
  • It'll confidently make things up. It's built to always produce an answer.

I wanted the opposite. Something that starts out knowing nothing (or close to it), and grows only from what I give it. Something I can open up and see why it said what it said. Something that says "I don't know, what does that mean?" instead of guessing.

I wanted to see the full picture, hold the camera, and adjust the angle.

  • Read all about how it works and what it offers on the full blog
  • Developer documentation

What comes next with aster is up to you.

Thanks for checking my post out! ~

title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
description:
arXiv:2611.23700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
description:
arXiv:2611.25292v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.

title: Pragmatic zero-trust: what to ship in the first 90 days
description:
Zero-trust as a slide deck is overwhelming. Zero-trust as a 90-day delivery plan is achievable. The goal of the first quarter isn't a finished architecture — it's removing the three or four assumptions that, today, would let a single compromised laptop or credential cause a serious incident.

Days 0–30: identity is the perimeter

Consolidate workforce identity behind a single IdP (Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace). Enforce phishing-resistant MFA — WebAuthn or hardware keys, not SMS. Turn on conditional access policies that check device posture before granting access to sensitive apps.

On the workload side, remove long-lived AWS access keys. Issue short-lived credentials via IAM Identity Center for humans and IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) for workloads. The day you can prove no static AWS keys exist in your org is the day half of your worst-case incidents become impossible.

Days 30–60: networks stop trusting themselves

Replace the flat VPN with an identity-aware proxy or a zero-trust network access (ZTNA) product. Access decisions move from "are you on the network?" to "who are you, on what device, asking for what?".

Inside the cluster, enable default-deny NetworkPolicies and only open the flows you need. Most lateral-movement incidents we've investigated would have stopped at this step.

Days 60–90: detection that actually fires

Centralise logs in a SIEM your team will actually triage — small and well-tuned beats large and ignored. Wire up a handful of high-signal detections first: impossible-travel logins, new IAM principals created, root-account use, anomalous data egress. Each one should map to a runbook.

By day 90 you should be able to answer three questions in under five minutes: who is logged in where, what is running in production, and what did an attacker just touch? Everything else is iteration.

title: Amazon SQS Request/Reply Between Microservices: Setup, Reply Queues, and Idempotency
description:
TL;DR

  • Amazon SQS has no built-in request/reply, so a service that needs an answer from another service has to add a correlation identifier and a reply queue of its own, and has to handle duplicate delivery because standard queues deliver each message at least once.
  • Three SQS settings decide whether synchronous-style calls behave well: the visibility timeout (30 seconds by default, 12 hours at most), the dead-letter queue redrive policy, and the receive wait time (long polling allows up to 20 seconds).
  • Message bodies are capped at 1 MiB, FIFO queues deduplicate only inside a 5-minute window, and every consumer should be idempotent regardless of queue type.
  • The Graftcode Amazon SQS plugin carries a Graft call over SQS in two modes: request/reply (a per-client reply queue plus a correlation ID attribute) and one-way (no reply; the message is deleted after processing).
  • The plugin ships as a single shared library, works with standard and FIFO queues, and can be tried locally against LocalStack with a ready-made Docker sample so that calls can move onto SQS without hand-written producers and consumers.

Amazon SQS is often the first managed queue that a team on AWS reaches for. It decouples producers from consumers, absorbs traffic spikes, and keeps messages until a consumer deletes them. Most of the time, the interaction is fire-and-forget: a service drops a job on a queue and moves on. The harder case comes when the caller needs the result, such as a job-orchestration service that must read a score from a scoring service before deciding what to do next. SQS offers no response channel, so every team ends up building the same plumbing for correlation, reply routing, timeouts, and retries.

This piece walks through how request/reply works on top of SQS, which queue settings decide whether it behaves well, and where duplicate delivery and message size limits bite. It then shows how the Amazon SQS plugin for Graftcode carries a typed method call over the same queues, including the configuration for both modes, the IAM permissions each side needs, and a LocalStack setup for local development. A related plugin, Azure Service Bus, handles reply routing differently, and that difference helps explain a design choice.

How Request/Reply Works on Top of Amazon SQS

A queue is a one-directional channel. A producer sends a message, and a consumer receives and deletes it. To get an answer back, the caller needs a second channel in the opposite direction, and it needs a way to match each answer to its question. The usual pattern has three parts. The caller creates or owns a reply queue. Each request carries two pieces of metadata: a correlation ID that identifies the call and the reply queue address. The service that processes the request sends its response to that address and copies the correlation ID onto it.

On the caller's side, a receiver polls the reply queue and matches each incoming response to a waiting call by correlation ID. If no matching response arrives before a timeout, the call fails. Messages in SQS carry user-defined message attributes, which are the natural place for the correlation ID and the reply address, because they travel with the message without changing the body.

Everything else in the design follows from what SQS does and does not provide. It does not route a response to the right caller on its own. It does not guarantee a message is delivered only once on standard queues. It does not tell the sender whether processing succeeded. Each of those gaps becomes a setting or a design decision in the sections that follow.

Why Each Caller Needs Its Own Reply Queue

On brokers that can filter receives by a message property, several callers can share one reply queue, and each can pick out its own responses. SQS cannot filter a receive by message attribute. A consumer that receives a message that belongs to someone else would have to put it back, and SQS has no such operation. The practical result is that each client process owns a reply queue, and no two independent processes read from the same one.

This cost is easy to underestimate. A deployment with many short-lived client processes needs a reply queue lifecycle: create the queue, give the process permission to receive from it, and remove it when the process is gone. A fixed set of long-lived services needs one reply queue per service instance, created ahead of time. Either way, the number of reply queues grows with the number of callers, not with the number of services being called.

Other brokers distribute that cost differently. Azure Service Bus, for instance, uses sessions so many clients can safely share a single session-enabled reply queue. SQS has no equivalent, so the one-queue-per-client rule applies to every SQS-based design, whether it is hand-written or generated.

Delivery Guarantees, Visibility Timeouts, and Dead-Letter Queues

Standard SQS queues deliver each message at least once. According to the Amazon SQS developer guide on at-least-once delivery, a copy can occasionally be delivered again, and the guide advises designing applications to be idempotent, meaning they are not adversely affected by processing the same message more than once. For request/reply, this applies in both directions: a service may receive the same request twice, and a caller may receive the same response twice.

The visibility timeout controls how long a message stays hidden after a consumer receives it. The visibility timeout documentation gives a default of 30 seconds and a limit of 12 hours from when the message is first received. If processing finishes after the timeout expires, the message becomes visible again, and another attempt starts, even though the first one is still running. A timeout shorter than the slowest call directly causes duplicate work.

A dead-letter queue collects messages that keep failing. As described in the dead-letter queue documentation, the maxReceiveCount value in the redrive policy sets how many times a consumer can receive a message before SQS moves it to the dead-letter queue. Setting it to 1 sends a message there after a single failed attempt, so the guide recommends a value high enough to allow sensible retries. Without a dead-letter queue, a request that can never succeed returns to the queue indefinitely until it expires.

Standard Queues Versus FIFO Queues for Service Calls

FIFO queues add ordering and a deduplication feature that standard queues lack. The message deduplication documentation describes a 5-minute deduplication window in which only one message with a given deduplication ID is accepted and delivered. SQS keeps tracking that ID even after the original message has been received and deleted.

Two details limit how far this protection extends. The window is five minutes, so a retry that arrives later is treated as a new message. The protection also applies to sending, not to processing: if a consumer crashes after doing the work but before deleting the message, the message is received again and processed again. For service calls, FIFO reduces duplicate sends from client-side retries, and the receiving service still needs to tolerate a repeated request.

The choice between the two types usually comes down to whether the calls being made depend on ordering within a group. Standard queues are the simpler default for independent calls. FIFO queues fit calls that must be applied in sequence for the same entity. One consequence applies to any design that uses a single message group. The message group documentation states that messages within the same group are always processed one at a time, in strict order. A queue where every message shares one group ID therefore processes requests serially no matter how many consumers are attached, and parallelism comes from using several group IDs. Both queue types need idempotent handlers.

Message Size and Long Polling Limits to Plan Around

The maximum message size is 1,048,576 bytes (1 MiB), per Amazon SQS message quotas. The same page describes the SQS Extended Client Library for larger payloads, which stores the payload in Amazon S3 and sends a reference. A binary payload that is Base64-encoded before it is sent grows by roughly a third, so a body close to the limit before encoding will not fit after encoding. Large results are better returned as a reference to stored data than as a response body.

Receive behavior affects both latency and cost. With long polling, a receive request waits for a message to arrive before it returns, and the long polling documentation sets the maximum wait at 20 seconds. Long polling queries all SQS servers rather than a subset, reducing both empty responses and false empty responses, and returns messages as soon as they become available. A caller waiting on a reply queue benefits most, since a short-polling loop can miss a message that is already there.

Putting these pieces together by hand requires writing a producer, a consumer, a correlation table, timeout handling, a poller per reply queue, and the idempotency logic on both ends. The next section shows what that looks like when the call is generated from the service's public methods instead.

Carrying Graft Calls Over SQS with the Graftcode Plugin

Graftcode lets one service, the Caller, call another service's public methods through a generated, strongly typed interface called a Graft. The service that exposes those methods is the Receiver, and by default a Graft connects directly to the Receiver's Graftcode Gateway. Transport plugins offer a second path, in which the Graft call travels through a broker instead. The graftcode-extensions repository lists plugins for RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, Kafka, Amazon SQS, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub, and the SQS plugin's README describes both a request/reply mode and a one-way mode. The Gateway runs and hosts the Receiver service, consumes requests from the queue, invokes the method, and sends the result to the reply queue named in the request.

The plugin maps directly onto the design problems described above. For correlation, each request carries a GraftcodeCorrelationId message attribute. For reply routing, it carries a GraftcodeReplyTo attribute with the caller's reply queue URL, so there is no fixed reply queue, and each client names its own. A background receiver in the client dispatches replies by correlation ID, so several calls through one transport instance can run at the same time. Binary Graft payloads are Base64-encoded into the message body with a graftcode-base64: prefix, and bodies over 1 MiB after encoding are rejected.

Delivery follows the SQS rules. The Gateway deletes a request only after processing succeeds and, for request/reply, after the reply has been sent. If something fails, the message becomes visible again after the visibility timeout. It is received again, so the README tells users to make operations idempotent and to attach a dead-letter queue. The plugin works with standard and FIFO queues. When the queue URL ends in .fifo, it sets MessageGroupId (default graftcode, configurable with messageGroupId) and MessageDeduplicationId. FIFO requests reuse the correlation ID, so an SDK retry doesn't enqueue a second request. At the same time, reply sends use a new ID so a redelivered request can still publish a response inside the deduplication window.

Failures and concurrency follow from how the Gateway side is built. In the plugin source, a request whose processing fails, or whose reply cannot be sent, is simply left on the queue, so it returns after the visibility timeout and is processed again until it succeeds or lands in the dead-letter queue. On the client side, a response whose first byte is 255 is treated as an error: the remaining bytes become the message of a thrown exception, the same convention the Azure Service Bus plugin uses. A call that never receives a reply fails once rpcTimeoutMs expires. Each Gateway instance reads one message at a time and handles requests one after another, so throughput grows by running more Gateway instances against the same request queue. The visibility timeout is not extended while a request is being processed, which is another reason to set it above the slowest call.

The reply queue is not created by the plugin. The client config supplies its URL, and the queue has to exist before the first call, which is why the Docker sample runs an init job that creates graft-requests and graft-replies.

Configuration for the Gateway and the Client

The Gateway side is started with the plugin config file. Install the Gateway from a terminal (on Windows, iwr https://grft.dev/get | iex; on Linux and macOS, curl -fsSL https://grft.dev/get | sh), as a Docker image, or as a binary from the Gateway releases page. The plugin library comes from the extensions releases page, and gg looks for it next to the config file first, then in its working directory. The README's Windows example runs from the folder that contains gg.exe, the hosted module (netapp.dll), and SqsPlugin.dll:

.\\gg.exe netapp.dll \--config sqsplugin.json
The matching sqsplugin.json in the README targets LocalStack:

{
  "name": "SqsPlugin",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "endpointOverride": "http://localhost:4566",
  "accessKeyId": "test",
  "secretAccessKey": "test",
  "requestQueueUrl": "http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/graft-requests",
  "waitTimeSeconds": 10,
  "visibilityTimeoutSeconds": 60,
  "verifySsl": false
}

The name value is the library name without its extension, so it is SqsPlugin on Windows and libSqsPlugin on Linux and macOS. On AWS itself, the README says to omit endpointOverride, accessKeyId, secretAccessKey, and verifySsl, and the plugin then uses the AWS default credential chain. The Gateway needs only requestQueueUrl and does not need replyQueueUrl.

The client config has no runtime or host keys, because the plugin supplies the transport. Every client process needs its own replyQueueUrl:

{
  "configurations": {
    "graft.nuget.netapp": {
      "plugin": {
        "name": "SqsPlugin",
        "region": "us-east-1",
        "endpointOverride": "http://localhost:4566",
        "accessKeyId": "test",
        "secretAccessKey": "test",
        "requestQueueUrl": "http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/graft-requests",
        "replyQueueUrl": "http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/graft-replies",
        "rpcTimeoutMs": 30000,
        "waitTimeSeconds": 10,
        "visibilityTimeoutSeconds": 60,
        "verifySsl": false
      }
    }
  }
}

In C#, the README loads that config through the Hypertube SDK (Hypertube is Graftcode's runtime and protocol layer) and calls the hosted module:

using Hypertube.Netcore.Sdk;
using Hypertube.Netcore.Sdk.Configuration;

RuntimeBridge.AddConfig(ConfigPriority.User, configJsonOrPathToFile);
var rtmCtx = RuntimeBridge.InitializeRC("graft.nuget.netapp");
var result = rtmCtx.GetType("netapp.Calculator").CreateInstance()
    .InvokeInstanceMethod("Add", 1, 2).Execute().GetValue();

AddConfig accepts a JSON string, a file path, or the name of an environment variable holding either; the key under configurations must match the name passed to InitializeRC, and only one plugin config is loaded per process.

One-Way Calls and the Settings That Tune Both Modes

For methods that do not return a value, set oneWay to true on both the client and the Gateway. The client then sends without waiting; the message carries no GraftcodeReplyTo attribute, and the Gateway deletes the message after processing. The one-way client needs only the request queue:

{
  "name": "SqsPlugin",
  "region": "us-east-1",
  "endpointOverride": "http://localhost:4566",
  "accessKeyId": "test",
  "secretAccessKey": "test",
  "requestQueueUrl": "http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/graft-requests",
  "oneWay": true,
  "verifySsl": false
}

Four settings in the field reference map straight onto the SQS behavior covered earlier. rpcTimeoutMs (default 30000) is how long the client waits for a reply. waitTimeSeconds (default 1, range 1 to 20) is the long-poll duration. visibilityTimeoutSeconds (default 30, range 1 to 43200) is the per-receive visibility timeout, and it should be set above the longest call. messageGroupId sets the FIFO group. Raising rpcTimeoutMs for a slow method without raising the visibility timeout reproduces the duplicate-work problem from the earlier section, so the two values move together.

Local Development with LocalStack and the Sample Setup

The README's local setup uses LocalStack. From the sqs folder in the plugin sources, docker compose up -d starts LocalStack and creates the graft-requests and graft-replies queues. If the init hook did not run, the queues can be created with the AWS CLI by pointing --endpoint-url at http://localhost:4566.

One detail catches many first attempts: queue URLs in the config must be the URLs the broker returns, such as http://sqs.us-east-1.localhost.localstack.cloud:4566/000000000000/graft-requests, and not http://localhost:4566/.... The SDK endpoint, endpointOverride, stays http://localhost:4566 and is configured separately. An http:// prefix on endpointOverride selects plain HTTP, which is why the LocalStack examples also set verifySsl to false. A second pitfall is message size: some LocalStack versions and older queues still enforce 256 KiB rather than 1 MiB, so a large payload that fits on a current AWS queue can be rejected locally.

The repository also carries ready-made Docker samples. According to the samples README, the SQS sample publishes LocalStack on port 4566 and the Gateway on port 10304, with Graft Vision on port 10404. Running .\run.ps1 in the sample folder builds the images, and the first run downloads the latest Linux Gateway and the matching plugin release. For manual setups, use a plugin and a Gateway of matching versions, because plugin v1.2.0 introduced a new transport C ABI, so a plugin and a Gateway from different generations may not load together. Only the first of three Gateway servers publishes ports to the host. The other two are internal consumers that compete for the same queue, which shows how additional Gateway instances share the request load. The sqs-init service is a one-shot job that creates the queues and should end in Exited (0).

Permissions and Production Settings Checklist for AWS

A working local setup uses static test credentials, and none of that carries over to AWS. The README lists the permissions for each identity. The Gateway needs sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, and sqs:SendMessage on the request queue, plus sqs:SendMessage on reply queues. A client needs sqs:SendMessage on the request queue, plus sqs:ReceiveMessage and sqs:DeleteMessage on its own reply queue. Static test credentials belong to LocalStack only, and on AWS the default credential chain supplies identities.

The remaining items come from the earlier sections. The queue URLs should be the ones AWS returns. The visibility timeout should exceed the longest call. A dead-letter queue should be attached with a maxReceiveCount that allows enough retries. Each client process should have its own reply queue, and the handlers behind every exposed method should tolerate being called twice.

Where Should You Start with SQS and Graftcode

SQS gives a team on AWS durable queues with very little to operate, and request/reply over SQS comes down to a handful of decisions: a correlation ID and a reply address on each request, one reply queue per client process, a visibility timeout longer than the slowest call, a dead-letter queue for requests that never succeed, and idempotent handlers because delivery is at least once. The 1 MiB message limit and the 5-minute FIFO deduplication window set the outer edges of what a single call can carry and what duplicate protection to expect.

The Graftcode plugin applies those decisions through configuration instead of hand-written queue code. A good first step is the LocalStack sample in the graftcode-extensions repository: run one Gateway and one client in request/reply mode, then switch one method to oneWay and compare the behavior. The Graftcode website has the product overview and links to the documentation for the Gateway and Grafts.

FAQs

Is there an Amazon SNS plugin for Graftcode?

No. The graftcode-extensions repository lists plugins for RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, Kafka, Amazon SQS, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub, and the SQS plugin's README states that Amazon SNS is not involved. SNS can still sit in front of an SQS queue on the AWS side, because SNS can deliver a copy of each published message to every subscribed SQS queue. The plugin itself does not unwrap SNS envelopes. It decodes each message body as its own graftcode-base64: payload and reads Graftcode message attributes, so a message that arrives wrapped by an SNS subscription is not something the Gateway can process as a call.

Does the plugin require a FIFO queue?

No. The README states that both standard and FIFO queues are supported. A queue URL ending in .fifo makes the plugin send MessageGroupId (default graftcode) and MessageDeduplicationId with each message. Either queue type needs idempotent handlers, since a consumer that fails after doing the work still sees the message again. With the default group ID, all requests on a FIFO queue share one group and are processed one at a time, so throughput-sensitive services should use a standard queue or set messageGroupId deliberately.

Can several client processes share one reply queue?

No. SQS cannot filter receives by message attribute, so each client process needs its own replyQueueUrl, and independent processes must not share one. A single process can run many concurrent calls, because a background receiver dispatches replies by correlation ID.

What happens if a call takes longer than the visibility timeout?

The message becomes visible again and is received for another attempt, which can cause the same request to be processed twice. Set visibilityTimeoutSeconds above the longest call, and raise it together with rpcTimeoutMs when a method needs more time. The value can range from 1 to 43200 seconds in the plugin, which lines up with the 12-hour limit that SQS applies.

title: FACET - Facet Aware Contrastive Embeddings for Traits- Big Five Estimation from Life Narratives
description:
arXiv:2611.23560v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.
