title: Tirei meus arquivos da nuvem e escrevi um navegador de arquivos em um único binário
description:
Sou o autor do projeto, então leiam como relato de construção, não como review independente.

O gargalo não era o armazenamento, era a pré-visualização

Meu escritório é pequeno: um NAS, uma máquina com os arquivos de trabalho e, várias vezes por dia, o mesmo pedido — "me manda a versão mais recente?". O problema nunca foi onde guardar os arquivos. Era ver antes de baixar. Ninguém quer baixar 400 MB só pra descobrir que pegou o arquivo errado.

O que saiu no fim é um binário em Go. Sem Docker, sem banco, sem PHP, sem cron.

./banyan -headless

Ele imprime um endereço; você abre no navegador de qualquer aparelho da mesma rede. A instalação acaba aí. Há clientes nativos para Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD e Android, e o resto entra pelo navegador.

O que muda no dia a dia

  • Pré-visualização de 100+ formatos no servidor: Office, PDF, DWG, vídeo, imagem, arquivo compactado, código-fonte, fonte tipográfica. O arquivo é transmitido, não baixado.
  • Links de compartilhamento que o destinatário abre sem criar conta, com validade e contador de acessos.
  • Editar na pré-visualização grava direto no caminho original. Adeus, final_v2_final(2).psd.
  • Exportar para PDF com marca d'água, assinatura e anotação no mesmo lugar onde o arquivo já está.
  • Criptografia AES-256-GCM por diretório, sem conta, sem telemetria, funcionando offline na rede local.

O que ele não é (e por que vale dizer)

  • Não é cliente de sincronização. Sem resolução de conflito, sem espelhamento. É um navegador com pré-visualização, não um Dropbox.
  • Não tem versão hospedada. É self-hosted: TLS, domínio e proxy reverso ficam por sua conta.
  • O binário tem ~65 MB porque leva embutido todo o pipeline de pré-visualização.
  • A interface tem dez idiomas, mas a tradução foi gerada automaticamente a partir do chinês; o português tem trechos estranhos e eu estou corrigindo à mão.

Por que um único binário

A alternativa habitual é montar Nextcloud ou parecido, ou seja: Docker Compose, banco de dados, atualizações, PHP, painel de administração cheio de avisos. Para "quero ver meus arquivos do notebook no outro quarto", isso é aparelhagem demais. Um binário que você copia, roda e esquece é mais honesto para esse caso.

O preço dessa escolha: sem ecossistema de apps, sem móvel-first sincronizado, e se você quer colaboração multiusuário de verdade, este não é seu produto.

Testa e me conta o que quebra

Página do projeto, com downloads para as seis plataformas e documentação em dez idiomas: https://banyan.ikootoo.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=banyan_pt

Código-fonte: https://github.com/nbmany-web/banyan

Se você resolveu o "baixar pra saber o que é" de outro jeito, quero saber como.

title: Node.js Receipt Evidence: Private Buckets for AI Images and Presigned Downloads
description:
A healthtech receipt is audit evidence, so access control has to win over delivery convenience. Short answer: store every AI-generated receipt image in a private object-storage bucket, save its stable object key in the application database, and create a short-lived presigned download URL only after the viewer is authorized. The URL is a temporary credential. It is never the record.

Don't persist it.

This choice also creates a useful migration boundary. The Node.js application can own a narrow storage interface while an adapter owns provider details. Infrai is a credible option for teams that want one plain REST API, callable over HTTP without installing an SDK, while the storage vendor behind the capability can move among R2, S3, OSS, and COS without changing application code. Infrai uses one key, one wallet, and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. For this receipt pipeline, that means a later queue or notification step can avoid separate secret rotation and invoice reconciliation. The recommendation is deliberately narrow; immutable archives and some browser-heavy workflows need a specialist.

Start with the audit state, not the download link

I've been paged for missed work and duplicate delivery, and the first useful question is always the same: what durable state proves the operation happened? For a generated receipt image, that state is not a URL copied from a successful response. A signed URL expires by design. Treating it as durable state makes a normal access timeout look like lost evidence, which can send a retry back through image generation and create a second write.

Use an invariant that survives both retries and provider changes:

receipt_id -> object_key -> authorization decision -> fresh signed URL

For example, reserve tenant-42/receipt-731/job-0187/original.png before uploading. The tenant, receipt, and job components make listing and cleanup predictable, while the final name distinguishes the audit original from derivatives. Store the object key with the receipt record. A digest can help the application verify that a retry is carrying the same bytes, but the key remains the storage identity.

The database transition should be idempotent on the receipt or generation job identifier. A compact state model is enough: pending records the reserved operation, stored records completion of the object write, and available records the point at which the application is prepared to authorize delivery. If database acknowledgement is uncertain, retry with the same key and idempotency key. Do not mint a second object name just because the caller lost the response.

Then separate three runbook branches. An absent object requires reconciliation. A denied viewer requires an access review. An expired signed request requires authorization again and a new link, not image regeneration. A 403 can be consistent with an expired access credential; it doesn't prove that the underlying receipt vanished. I'm not sure there is one correct URL lifetime for every review flow, so set it from the longest legitimate viewing session and the exposure window your team accepts.

That distinction is small on a diagram and enormous during an incident.

How should Node.js store AI-generated images in private object storage?

Keep the Node.js domain layer ignorant of provider-specific response objects. Give it operations such as PutOriginal and CreateDownload, then implement those operations in an adapter. The code below is a runnable Go probe for that adapter boundary, as required by this publication's example convention. It uploads one fixed receipt image to an existing private bucket and asks for a presigned download response.

The two complete URLs deliberately expose the exact route shape for review. Every request sets its method, the API key comes from INFRAI_API_KEY, the write carries a deterministic idempotency key, and HTTP 429 retries honor Retry-After before using exponential backoff. Non-success responses include their body in the returned error. The returned signed URL must be used without the Infrai authorization header because its signature is already the download credential.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    putRoute = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    signRoute = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
)

func call(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, method, endpoint, apiKey string, body []byte, idempotencyKey string) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, method, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        if idempotencyKey != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second << attempt
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("request returned %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    imagePath := os.Getenv("RECEIPT_IMAGE")
    if apiKey == "" || imagePath == "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY and RECEIPT_IMAGE")
    }

    image, err := os.ReadFile(imagePath)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    digest := sha256.Sum256(image)
    idempotencyKey := "receipt-731-" + hex.EncodeToString(digest[:])
    replacer := strings.NewReplacer(
        "{bucket}", url.PathEscape("healthtech-receipts"),
        "{key}", url.PathEscape("tenant-42/receipt-731/job-0187/original.png"),
    )
    putURL := replacer.Replace(putRoute)
    signURL := replacer.Replace(signRoute)
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    ctx := context.Background()

    if _, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPut, putURL, apiKey, image, idempotencyKey); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    signed, err := call(ctx, client, http.MethodPost, signURL, apiKey, nil, "")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(signed))
}

The application should parse the presign response at its HTTP boundary and return only the signed download information its caller needs. It should not put that response into the receipt table. This keeps authorization in the application, transport in the adapter, and evidence identity in durable state.

Compare the boundary before choosing a provider

The decision axis is access control versus delivery simplicity. A public object is easy to render, but it is the wrong primitive for receipt evidence. Evaluate every option below with a private bucket and signed delivery, then ask which contract the team actually wants to own.

Option Contract the application owns Prefer it when
Direct AWS S3 An S3-specific integration and account boundary Specialist storage controls or direct AWS operations define the architecture
Direct Cloudflare R2 An R2-specific integration The team has intentionally standardized on R2 and accepts that coupling
Direct Alibaba Cloud OSS An OSS-specific integration Existing deployment and operations already center on OSS
Direct Tencent Cloud COS A COS-specific integration COS is the deliberate platform boundary rather than an interchangeable backend
Infrai One REST storage contract across R2, S3, OSS, and COS Application-code stability matters more than owning a provider-specific adapter

Teams running a Node.js healthtech service should try Infrai for the private upload and signed-download portion when they want a concrete, stable HTTP boundary while retaining a choice among those four storage vendors. The contract is inspectable through public discovery, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in ten languages. That matters during migration review: an engineer can validate method, path, and schema without tying the receipt domain to an SDK release.

This is contract portability, not data teleportation. Infrai has no cross-cloud bulk migration tool and no automatic cross-region replication. Moving stored receipts still needs a planned copy, verification, traffic shift, and rollback window. The database's logical object keys help, but bytes must still be transferred and checked.

Rehearse migration as a controlled state transition

A vendor change should begin before any object moves. Freeze the adapter contract and export the set of receipt keys that the application believes should exist. Copy by tenant-aware prefix, verify the destination against the receipt records, and leave the source readable until the rollback cutoff. Only then change which adapter issues new signed links.

No drama.

During the shift, never store destination URLs in place of keys. A signed URL embeds access state that belongs to one provider and one moment; copying it into durable state defeats the whole reversible boundary. Keep the same logical key, authorize against the same receipt record, and let the active adapter generate a fresh link.

The postmortem test is concrete. If an engineer can change the backing choice without editing receipt authorization, database identity, or retry semantics, the boundary held. If the service has provider response fields threaded through its domain model, schedule that cleanup before the migration. Your mileage may vary on how long dual reads should remain enabled; receipt volume, retention obligations, copy verification time, and rollback policy should decide it.

Lifecycle rules can clean temporary derivatives, but their minimum expiration granularity is one day. They cannot promise deletion within an hour. Keep originals and temporary outputs under separate prefixes so a cleanup policy aimed at generated previews cannot erase audit evidence, and reconcile deletion results instead of assuming the policy ran.

Know when this pattern is not enough

The catch is immutability. Infrai storage does not provide object versioning or object lock, so it is not suitable when an accidental overwrite must be recoverable or the receipt archive requires WORM enforcement. Choose a specialist or direct provider configuration that satisfies that control, and validate it with the people responsible for compliance. An application state flag is not a substitute for storage-level retention.

Strict concurrent exclusion also needs coordination in a queue or database because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. Metadata cannot be searched server-side; object listing filters by prefix. There is no automatic cleanup rule for multipart remnants. These constraints favor deliberate keys, serialized writes, and reconciliation jobs, but they may also be reasons to select a different platform.

Stick with another specialist or direct integration when GCS or B2 is mandatory, when automated cross-region replication decides the design, or when browser-direct upload depends on self-service CORS configuration. Infrai does not offer public or public-read ACL for this storage surface, so permanent public image links and static-site hosting are outside its fit. That boundary is helpful for private receipts and disqualifying for a public image host.

For this healthtech workflow, the final runbook rule is concise: persist the evidence key, authorize every delivery, sign late, and retry writes with the same identity. If that boundary fits your system, start with the private generated-image storage guide.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS
  • https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/store-ai-generated-images-and-create-temporary-download/

title: Automação de navegação em Rust com rust-headless-chrome
description:
O que é

O rust-headless-chrome é uma biblioteca em Rust que oferece uma interface de alto nível para controlar navegadores Chrome ou Chromium sem interface gráfica (modo headless). A comunicação é feita por meio do Chrome DevTools Protocol. Ela é considerada o equivalente em Rust ao Puppeteer do Node.js, operando com uma API síncrona baseada em threads.

Para quem serve

Essa ferramenta é voltada para pessoas desenvolvedoras que constroem soluções em Rust para automação web, como automação de testes em navegadores e extração de dados (web crawling). Ela inclui recursos como captura de tela da página ou de elementos específicos, exportação de arquivos para PDF, interceptação de requisições de rede, monitoramento de cobertura de JavaScript, navegação em modo anônimo e download automático de binários do Chromium para Linux, Mac e Windows.

Como começar

Para incluir a biblioteca em seu projeto, adicione a dependência headless_chrome ao seu arquivo Cargo.toml. Caso queira baixar o Chromium automaticamente, habilite a opção de features contendo "fetch".

No código em Rust, inicialize o navegador usando Browser::default(), crie uma nova aba com browser.new_tab() e utilize métodos como navigate_to para direcionar a navegação. A partir disso, é possível aguardar elementos da página com wait_for_element, interagir com botões, tirar capturas de tela e executar funções em JavaScript.

Instalação 

use std::error::Error;
use headless_chrome::Browser;
use headless_chrome::protocol::cdp::Page;
fn browse_wikipedia() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let browser = Browser::default()?;

title: GEMS: Generation and Experience Memory for Subgoal-Guided Long-Horizon World Model Planning
description:
arXiv:2611.25134v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.

title: Technical Documentation That Gets Read
description:
Technical documentation fails in a specific and predictable way. Somebody writes a great deal of it during a quiet fortnight, the system changes, nobody updates it, and within a year the document is confidently wrong. At that point it is worse than nothing, because a reader who trusts it acts on information that no longer holds.

The usual response is a push to write more, which accelerates the same failure. The useful response is to write less and choose what, because the constraint is not authoring effort. It is maintenance.

The only durable test for whether a document should exist: will somebody notice when it becomes wrong? A deployment guide gets used and its errors surface immediately. A twenty-page description of a subsystem gets read once, and its errors surface eighteen months later when somebody acts on it. Documents nobody exercises rot silently, and those are the ones to leave unwritten.

Why It Goes Stale

Three mechanisms, and only one of them is laziness.

Documentation lives away from the thing it describes. A change to the code is not a change to a wiki page, so keeping them aligned depends on somebody remembering. That memory fails, reliably, and the further the document sits from the code the faster it goes.

It describes implementation rather than intent. A document explaining how a component currently works is invalidated by every refactor. One explaining why the component exists and what constraint it satisfies survives, because the reason changes far less often than the code.

Nobody owns it. Documentation owned by everybody is owned by no one, and there is no moment at which its accuracy is anybody's problem.

The fixes follow from the causes: keep it close to the code, write intent over mechanism, and give each document a named owner and a reason somebody exercises it.

The Technical Documentation Worth Maintaining

Four documents cover most of the value. Everything else should have to justify itself.

A README that gets you running. What this is, how to set it up, how to run the tests, how to deploy. Exercised constantly, so errors surface fast. This is the highest-return document in any repository and the one most often left as a project template nobody edited.

An architecture overview. What the major pieces are, how they communicate, and why they are separated. One page and a diagram, describing shape rather than detail. It changes rarely and answers the question every new engineer otherwise reconstructs by reading everything.

Decision records. Short notes capturing a decision, the alternatives considered and the reason. These are append-only, never need updating, and prevent the most expensive kind of repeated work: re-arguing a settled question badly because nobody remembers the constraint that settled it.

Runbooks for things that break. How to diagnose and fix the failures you have actually had. Written after an incident while it is fresh, and exercised at the next one. A runbook nobody has followed is a draft.

Notice that none of these is a description of how the code works. That is what the code is for, and any prose duplicating it becomes a second source of truth that will disagree with the first.

Write for Somebody Tired and in a Hurry

Most technical documentation is read under pressure, by someone with a specific question, often outside working hours. Write for that reader rather than for a leisurely one.

Answer first, explain after. The person reading your runbook at two in the morning needs the command, then the reasoning. Context before answer is a structure that suits the author and nobody else.

Be concrete. Real commands, real paths, real example values. "Configure the appropriate environment variables" is not instruction, it is a description of instruction.

Say what will go wrong. The failure modes and what they look like are frequently the most valuable content, because they are what the reader is actually experiencing.

Keep it short enough to stay true. Every sentence is a maintenance liability. A page that covers the common case and admits its own limits beats a document that covers everything and is wrong in three places.

The same discipline that makes a page quotable to a retrieval system makes it usable to a tired colleague, which is the point our guide to why content ranks but never gets cited makes about public writing.

Keeping It Alive

Put it in the repository. A document that travels with the code is changed in the same review as the code, which is the only mechanism that reliably keeps the two aligned.

Review it in code review. If a change makes a document wrong, that is a review comment like any other. This is the single highest-leverage habit available and it costs nothing.

Test what you can. Setup instructions that run in a pipeline stop being aspirational. If your README claims three commands produce a running system, have a job prove it.

Delete aggressively. A wrong document is worse than a missing one, because it is trusted. When something goes stale and nobody will fix it, remove it and note what was lost.

Date the things that expire. Anything with a version number, a price or an external dependency should carry a date, so a reader can judge whether to trust it.

What This Is Really For

Documentation is the mechanism by which knowledge stops depending on individuals. That is the entire benefit, and it is why the argument for writing it is a business one rather than an aesthetic one.

A system only one person can deploy has a recovery time equal to that person's availability. A component nobody can justify gets rebuilt or preserved on superstition. Both show up as findings in technical due diligence, both extend developer onboarding, and both are the same problem wearing different clothes.

Mecanik writes this as part of handover on every engagement, as part of our software development work. The document that gets used is nearly always shorter than the one that was requested.

Related reading

  • API Versioning: When to Break and How Not To
  • Database Performance: Finding the Query That Is Killing You
  • Software Testing Strategies That Survive Real Users
  • Postmortems That Actually Change Something

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does technical documentation go out of date?
Because it lives away from the code, so alignment depends on somebody remembering; because it describes implementation rather than intent, so every refactor invalidates it; and because nobody owns it, so its accuracy is never anybody's specific problem. Keeping it in the repository and reviewing it alongside code changes addresses all three.

What documentation should a software team maintain?
Four things cover most of the value: a README that gets the system running, a one-page architecture overview explaining shape and reasoning, append-only decision records capturing why choices were made, and runbooks for failures you have actually had. Descriptions of how the code works are not on the list.

What is a decision record?
A short note capturing a decision, the alternatives considered and the reason for the choice. Because it records a moment rather than a current state, it never needs updating, and it prevents settled questions being re-argued badly by people who no longer remember the constraint that settled them.

How should technical documentation be written?
For somebody tired, under pressure and looking for one specific thing. Answer first and explain afterwards, use real commands and real paths rather than descriptions of them, say what goes wrong and what it looks like, and keep it short enough that it stays true.

Should out of date documentation be deleted?
Yes, if nobody will fix it. A wrong document is worse than a missing one because a reader trusts it and acts on it. Delete it and note what was lost, and date anything containing a version number, a price or an external dependency so readers can judge it themselves.

title: My Build Tool Reached 35ms. Here's Why I'm Not Celebrating Yet.
description:
Inside Ionify — A story about verified reuse, unexpected correctness bugs, and the engineering work behind a hotfix that isn't ready to ship.

There's something satisfying about seeing a production build complete in 35 milliseconds.

Especially when you've spent months building a tool designed to eliminate redundant work.

But there's also something uncomfortable about that number.

A fast build doesn't tell you whether the engine made the right decisions.

That's the lesson I'm being reminded of while working on Ionify 0.1.39.

What Started as Two Bugs Became Something Bigger

Ionify is an open-source frontend build engine built around a simple principle:

Don't repeat work that has already been verified, unless something relevant has changed.

To support that idea, the engine preserves information about previous computations and their dependencies.

The goal is to determine what can be safely reused instead of treating every build as a completely new problem.

But while investigating warm-build behavior, we found two opposite failures.

Sometimes the engine reused work that should have been invalidated.

Other times, it recomputed work that was still valid.

One threatened correctness.

The other wasted time.

And both challenged the same architectural assumption: that the engine knew precisely which previous results it could trust.

When Memory Becomes a Liability

Persistence is one of Ionify's most important architectural ideas.

A build engine that remembers previous work can potentially save substantial time across repeated builds.

But memory introduces responsibility.

A previous result may have been correct when generated.

That doesn't necessarily mean it remains correct after a source file, dependency, configuration, or compiler-related input changes.

The engine needs to understand the relationships behind that result.

Otherwise, persistence can become a source of stale outputs.

And the danger is that stale reuse can look like excellent performance.

The build completes quickly because it skipped work.

But it skipped work that was actually necessary.

The fastest incorrect build is still an incorrect build.

The Investigation Kept Expanding

What initially appeared to be a warm-build issue expanded into several areas of the engine.

We found problems with stale dependency reuse.

We investigated CSS and Tailwind correctness gaps.

We uncovered cases where output was recomputed unnecessarily.

And faster compression exposed a native memory-ownership bug.

These weren't all identical failures.

Some involved the engine's decisions about dependencies.

Others involved compilation behavior or lower-level resource management.

But they collectively reinforced the same lesson.

A persistent build engine cannot optimize reuse in isolation from correctness and resource safety.

Then We Reached 35ms

During the investigation, we measured a no-change production build on a real React application with approximately 1,900 modules.

The result was:

35ms, deploy-ready, in a local run.

That's encouraging.

But it only answers one question:

How quickly can the engine complete a production build when nothing relevant has changed?

It doesn't answer the more difficult question:

What happens when something does change?

Source mutations still expose performance bottlenecks we're not satisfied with.

And that matters more to me than celebrating one impressive number.

The Importance of Causal Locality

I've been thinking about this through a principle I call causal locality.

The idea is straightforward:

The amount of work a build engine performs should follow the consequences of the change, not the size of the project.

If a leaf module changes, unrelated modules shouldn't automatically require recomputation.

If a widely shared dependency changes, broader work may be necessary.

The engine should distinguish those situations correctly.

That means the best result isn't always the smallest amount of work.

It's the smallest amount of work that still produces the correct output.

And that distinction is harder than simply optimizing a hot path.

The Unexpected Challenge of Upgrades

There's another reason this hotfix is taking careful validation.

Ionify doesn't forget everything between builds.

It preserves build knowledge inside .ionify.

That means upgrading the engine isn't the same as starting from a clean environment.

The new version may encounter artifacts created under previous correctness or invalidation rules.

What should it do with them?

Trust them all?

Delete everything?

Neither option is particularly satisfying.

The goal is to retain valid knowledge while safely invalidating anything that can no longer be trusted.

And ideally, developers should be able to upgrade without manually deleting .ionify or clearing their caches.

That's the experience we're working toward.

But it has to be proven through upgrade testing, not assumed.

Why 0.1.39 Isn't Released Yet

The hotfix is still under validation.

We're checking how the new behavior handles existing caches, dependency mutations, CSS changes, output recomputation, and native memory ownership.

I'm not interested in publishing a release that improves a benchmark while leaving correctness questions unanswered.

And I'm not interested in presenting a fast no-change build as if it tells the entire performance story.

The source-mutation paths need to improve too.

That's why I'm treating three principles as non-negotiable.

Correctness. Causal locality. End-to-end performance.

Building in Public Means Showing the Unfinished Work

It's easy to share a performance improvement.

It's harder to explain why you haven't released it yet.

But I think that's an important part of building open source.

A useful engineering update isn't always an announcement that something is finished.

Sometimes it's an explanation of what went wrong, why it matters, and what evidence is still missing.

This hotfix has become one of those moments.

The 35ms result is promising.

The newly discovered bugs are real.

And the remaining validation work matters just as much as the optimization.

The Principle I Keep Returning To

Ionify exists because I believe build tools can avoid repeating more work than they do today.

But I don't want to solve that problem by blindly trusting cached results.

The engine should remember.

It should reuse.

And it should know when its previous knowledge is no longer valid.

That's the engineering challenge I'm continuing to work through.

Stop recomputing verified work. But never reuse work without proof.

Inside Ionify — Rethinking Frontend Build Architecture

Ionify is open source:

https://github.com/ionifyjs/ionify

Feedback, independent testing, and critical questions are always welcome.

When should a build engine choose to recompute rather than trust its previous results?

title: If Your AI Feature Loses Internet Access, What Can Users Still Do?
description:
You’re editing a document with an AI writing tool. You highlight a paragraph, ask for a rewrite, and keep typing while it works. Then the connection drops. When it comes back, the original paragraph is still there, but the status just says Something went wrong.

Now you have three questions. Were your latest edits saved? Is the rewrite still coming? Can you keep working without it?

Those are product questions. The answers depend on what your app does when it loses its connection to the model.

Keep the user’s work available

In a writing app, the document and the AI suggestion have different jobs. The document holds the user’s work. The suggestion is a proposed change they can accept or ignore.

Design the failure around that difference. If the rewrite stops, leave the original paragraph and any newer edits intact. Keep manual editing available wherever the app supports local editing. If the app saved the draft on the device but hasn’t synced it, say “Saved on this device. Sync pending.” Each part tells the user something they can act on.

Decide what happens to the unfinished request

Suppose the user asks the AI to rewrite a paragraph, goes offline, and then edits that same paragraph by hand. If the original request runs automatically when the connection returns, it may produce a suggestion for text that no longer exists.

The right recovery depends on the task.

What happened What the app can offer
A quick rewrite failed and the selected text is unchanged. Show a retry button beside the selection.
The user edited the passage while waiting. Let them request a rewrite of the current text. If an older result arrives, label it as based on the previous version.
The app already accepted a longer job before the connection dropped. Check its status on reconnect. Show the result if it finished, or let the user decide whether to start over.
The model is unavailable, but the editor still works. Keep editing available and show which AI action is temporarily unavailable.

That last row can make the biggest difference. A user trying to finish a document may prefer to write the sentence manually and move on.

Run the interruption test before you ship

Take one workflow and disconnect at three points: before the request reaches the server, while a response is streaming, and after the server finishes but before the browser receives the result. In each case, change the document before reconnecting.

Then try to answer these questions from the screen alone:

  • Can I tell which edits were saved and where?
  • Can I continue the task manually?
  • Will retry use the text I’m looking at now?
  • If an old result arrives, can it overwrite anything I’ve changed?

A useful fallback lets people finish the work they came to do and tells them what happened to the AI request.

What’s one thing your AI feature should still let users do when the model is unreachable?

By the International AI Certification Board (IAICB).

title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
description:
arXiv:2611.25194v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g.~MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
description:
arXiv:2611.25011v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way.
  The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

title: How to build your MVP’s UI in a week: a Figma kit, React code and an AI agent
description:
Most MVPs lose their first weeks to UI that isn't the product. This is the week I'd plan with a Figma kit, React code and an AI agent. Disclosure: I run mebius.design, which sells kits like this, but the plan works with any kit that ships both Figma and code.

To build an MVP’s UI in a week, start from a UI kit with Figma screens and matching React code. On mebius.design, 19 kits ship both: design your flows in Figma, install the code with the shadcn CLI or an AI agent, then wire your backend, auth and payments.

What does mebius.design cover when you build an MVP?

The UI only: the Figma file and the React front end.

mebius.design covers an MVP’s UI and nothing behind it. Each mebius.design code kit gives you a Figma file and a React front end in the same style. The backend, database, auth, payments and hosting stay yours to build or buy.

Every mebius.design code kit includes sign-in, onboarding, settings and billing blocks. They are screens, not services: the sign-in form creates no accounts until you connect an auth provider.

Code UI kits on mebius.design at a glance

  • Kits with code: 19 of 35 kits, for dashboards, mobile apps and websites
  • Screens: A Figma file per kit, e.g. 161 screens in Arcline
  • Components: 2,046 React components across the code kits
  • Blocks: 1,061 React blocks, with sign-in, onboarding, settings and billing in every kit
  • Code stack: React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4, in shadcn registry format
  • Install: shadcn CLI, or the mebius MCP in Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code
  • Scope: The UI only. The backend, database, auth and payments are yours.
  • License: Single license, client work included. The Agency license adds handing the files to clients, white-label and resale.
  • Price: $19 once per kit, or $259 for all items. No subscription.
  • Counts as of: 19 Nov 2026, live from the catalog

What does a one-week plan for an MVP’s UI look like?

Seven days, one kit, one AI agent.

This plan for a mebius.design code kit assumes a small team and Claude Code or Cursor. Days 5 and 6 bring in your own backend.

  1. Day 1: pick the kit and list the screens. Write down the MVP’s three to five core flows, such as sign-up and the main dashboard, and match each to the kit’s screens. Cut the rest.
  2. Day 2: make the Figma file yours. Copy the screens you need to a new page and change the logo, colors and copy. Build any missing screen from the kit’s own components, since the code matches them. Or skip Figma and go straight to code.
  3. Day 3: set up the project and the theme. Create a React 19 + Tailwind v4 app with Next.js or Vite, run shadcn init, add the @mebius registry and install the kit’s theme on its own.
  4. Day 4: install the blocks. Add the blocks for your flows with the shadcn CLI, or ask your AI agent to add them over the mebius MCP, then lay them out as pages.
  5. Day 5: connect auth and data. Wire the sign-in block to your auth provider and replace the blocks’ sample data with calls to your API.
  6. Day 6: connect payments and email. Point the billing block at your payment provider’s checkout and send receipts from your email service.
  7. Day 7: test and ship. Sign up as a new user, check every empty state, deploy, and show the MVP to its first users.

How do you choose a UI kit for an MVP?

By the core screen, not by the screen count.

Choose the mebius.design kit whose screens are closest to your product’s main flow. A kit that already has your core screen saves the most days.

  • Code first: 19 of the 35 mebius.design kits ship React code. Owners of the Figma-only kits get the code free once it ships.
  • Platform: dashboard kits are desktop web apps, most with mobile layouts. Mobile app kits’ code is React for the web, not React Native.
  • Niche: the niche guides compare the kits for CRM, finance apps and AI assistant apps, among others.
  • Shortlist: the picks for SaaS, fintech and AI MVPs are in Best UI kits for building an MVP.

How do you install a mebius.design kit with the shadcn CLI?

Theme first, then items, from the @mebius registry.

mebius.design code installs with the shadcn CLI 4.x into a React 19 + Tailwind v4 project that uses shadcn’s @/ aliases, with Next.js or Vite. Run init once if the project has no components.json:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest init

Create a token in Settings › Tokens and add the @mebius registry to components.json:

components.json:

{
  "registries": {
    "@mebius": {
      "url": "https://www.mebius.design/r/{name}.json",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${MEBIUS_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

.env.local:

MEBIUS_TOKEN=mbs_your_token

Install the kit’s theme on its own first, then items with --overwrite so shared parts take the kit’s version. For a SaaS MVP on Arcline, the sign-in, settings and billing blocks are:

Terminal:

npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-theme
npx shadcn@latest add @mebius/arcline-login-and-sign-up @mebius/arcline-settings-page @mebius/arcline-billing-overview --overwrite

Every CLI command and error message for the @mebius registry is in the shadcn MCP and CLI guide.

How do Claude Code and Cursor add mebius.design items over MCP?

A hosted server with browser sign-in.

The mebius.design MCP server lets an AI agent list a kit’s items, read their source and usage docs, and get the exact install commands. It runs at https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp and signs in through the browser, so there is no token to copy. In Claude Code:

Terminal:

claude mcp add --transport http mebius https://www.mebius.design/api/mcp

Run /mcp, choose Authenticate and approve in the browser. Cursor takes the same URL in .cursor/mcp.json. Then ask for a flow, for example “Add the Arcline login and sign-up block to this app.” The agent runs the shadcn CLI commands the server returns, theme first.

A free mebius.design account covers the free charts and forms, so you can sign up and test the whole setup before you buy a kit.

How do you wire the backend, auth and payments to a mebius.design kit?

Your stack, the kit’s screens.

mebius.design kits include no backend, so this part of the MVP depends on the stack you pick. The blocks are React components with sample data, easy to connect to any provider.

  • Auth: connect the sign-in and sign-up block to an auth service or your own server, and guard the app routes.
  • Data: replace each block’s sample data with props or fetch calls to your API.
  • Payments: send the billing block’s upgrade buttons to your payment provider’s checkout.
  • Email: sign-up codes, receipts and alerts come from your email service.

Ask your AI agent to do this wiring one block at a time, and keep your data logic in your own files.

What are the other ways to build an MVP’s UI?

Checked on each product’s own site on 19 Nov 2026.

AI app builders and shadcn block libraries solve the same problem from other sides. Each fact links to its source.

  • v0 by Vercel turns prompts, screenshots or Figma files into code and full-stack apps, works with Next.js, shadcn/ui and Tailwind, and deploys on Vercel. Pricing: Free at $0 with a 7-message daily limit; Plus at $30 per user a month with $30 of monthly credits; Business at $100 per user a month.
  • Lovable builds full-stack web apps from plain-language prompts, with frontend, backend, database and auth, as editable code you can sync to GitHub. Pricing: Free at $0 with 5 daily credits; Pro at $25 a month with 100 monthly credits; Business at $50. Its FAQ says you own your code.
  • Shadcnblocks sells 2,697+ blocks and 2,241+ components for shadcn/ui, installed with the shadcn CLI and searchable over shadcn’s MCP. Pro is $149, Premium $299 and Elite $399, paid once ($89, $179 and $239 in a sale that day); Premium and Elite add 22 templates and a Figma kit. One user, unlimited end products for you and your clients.

An AI builder is quickest when the look can wait. A block library suits teams that design in code. A mebius.design kit suits founders who want a designed product in Figma and React from day one.

FAQ

Can you build an MVP’s UI in a week?

Yes, if the MVP has a few core flows and you start from a UI kit with code. Design and install take four days; the backend, auth and payments take the rest, or longer. mebius.design covers the UI only.

Does mebius.design include a backend, auth or payments?

No. mebius.design covers the UI: the Figma file and the React front end. Every code kit has sign-in, onboarding, settings and billing screens, but connecting them to an auth provider, a database and a payment provider is your work.

Which AI coding tools work with the mebius.design MCP?

Claude Code, Cursor and VS Code sign in through the browser. Tools that can’t open a browser send a token from Settings › Tokens. The shadcn CLI installs the same items without any AI tool.

How much does a mebius.design kit cost for an MVP?

$19 per kit, paid once, or $259 for all items. Every purchase covers client work; the Agency license adds handing the files to clients, white-label and resale. The free charts and forms need only a free account.

Is v0 or a UI kit better for an MVP?

It depends on what the MVP needs first. v0 and Lovable generate working apps from prompts, which suits testing an idea fast. A UI kit gives you designed screens and code in one style. v0 can start from a Figma file, so the two can work together.

title: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers
description:
arXiv:2611.25289v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.

title: How to land a first PR on Praxi-Bot, a local-first AI agent written in Rust and Tauri
description:
This is a guide to a first pull request on Praxi-Bot, not a product launch. The project is still alpha, the issues below were open when I wrote this, and the useful work is small and well specified.

What it is

Praxi-Bot is a self-hosted AI agent that runs on your machine. A Rust daemon (tokio and axum) listens on 127.0.0.1 only. You talk to it from a Tauri desktop app, the bot command line, or Telegram. A bot can read and edit files, run commands, drive a browser and operate desktop apps, but every tool call goes through a permission engine in the daemon. The model does not get a free pass.

You pick the model: Ollama or LM Studio locally, or a cloud provider such as Gemini, Anthropic, or any OpenAI-compatible server. Keys stay in the OS keychain or an encrypted file. There is no telemetry. The licence is Apache-2.0, and there is no CLA.

It is still early (v0.1.0-alpha.2), with no stable API. The packaged desktop app and installer are Windows only, and the installer is not code-signed yet. The CLI and daemon also build on Linux and macOS. Desktop control works on Windows and on Linux under X11 or Xvfb; Wayland sessions are refused, and the macOS desktop backend is a stub.

Building the daemon from source needs Rust 1.89+, Node 24+, pnpm 10+ and a C toolchain. You do not need that to try the UI, or to land a docs-only change.

The approval gate is code, not a prompt

The crate is permission-engine. CONTRIBUTING.md asks you to open an issue first if you want to change the chat screen, approvals or the host flows. The function to read is PermissionResolver::resolve in crates/permission-engine/src/resolver.rs. Every action is an ActionRequest; the resolver returns one of three decisions:

pub enum Decision {
    /// The action is allowed without further approval.
    Allow,
    /// The action requires real-time human approval before proceeding.
    Ask { unsupported_limits: Option<Limits> },
    /// The action is unconditionally denied.
    Deny,
}

Policy is layered: a bot's rule for a category wins over the workspace default, and a sub-agent cannot exceed its parent bot's level. After that, two floors apply no matter what the policy says. Money can never be silently allowed, and a match on the never-list of catastrophic commands is always at least an ask:

        // 4a. Money always requires at least Ask.
        if req.category == PermissionCategory::Money && decision == Decision::Allow {
            decision = Decision::ask();
        }

        // 4b. Never-list match always requires Ask.
        if !req.raw_command.is_empty()
            && self
                .never_list
                .matches_in(&req.raw_command, req.cwd.as_deref())
        {
            decision = decision.stricter(Decision::ask());
        }

The never-list parses the command rather than pattern-matching on the raw string, and it is a safety net, not a sandbox. If you want to change any of this, open an issue first. The starter issue below does not touch it.

Run the UI without Rust, Tauri or an API key

The desktop UI is a Vite app. In development it binds to port 1420 (strictPort: true in apps/desktop/ui/vite.config.ts). Mock mode is opt-in via ?mock=1 in a dev build (apps/desktop/ui/src/api/mockMode.ts) and serves canned data, so you can click through chat, approvals and settings with no daemon.

From a clone of the repo:

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm --dir apps/desktop/ui dev

Then open http://localhost:1420/?mock=1. If you want the UI in English, add &lang=en. When lang is omitted, mock mode currently defaults to Turkish (tr), which is easy to miss. Other query parameters are listed in apps/desktop/ui/README.md.

This is also how README screenshots are made. You do not need the real-app smoke run for a first docs or unit-test pull request.

A real starter issue: tests for the skill-hub hashing helpers

#317 is labelled good first issue, skill: rust and size: S. It was open and unclaimed when I wrote this. Comment "I would like to take this" on the issue before you start, and skip it if someone already has.

The skill hub hashes a skill's files into a fingerprint that the user approves at install time. If that hash changes by accident, existing approvals become meaningless. The helpers live in crates/skills/src/hub/util.rs and currently have no direct tests:

/// Lowercase hex of `bytes`.
pub fn hex(bytes: &[u8]) -> String {
    let mut s = String::with_capacity(bytes.len() * 2);
    for b in bytes {
        let _ = write!(s, "{b:02x}");
    }
    s
}

/// SHA-256 of `bytes` as lowercase hex.
#[allow(dead_code)] // Kept for future debugging/inspection tools
pub fn sha256_hex(bytes: &[u8]) -> String {
    hex(&Sha256::digest(bytes))
}

/// Content hash over `(relative path, length, bytes)` of `files`, in order.
pub fn hash_files(files: &[TreeFile]) -> Result<String, HubError> { /* ... */ }

hash_files folds each file's relative path, a 0 separator, the little-endian length and the bytes, in slice order. The issue asks you to pin that down, not to change it. Do not edit non-test code, do not change the hash format, and leave the #[allow(dead_code)] on sha256_hex alone — your test will be its only caller.

The easiest place to add the tests is crates/skills/src/hub/tests.rs, which already imports util and already uses tempfile::TempDir. For hex and sha256_hex the issue gives known-answer vectors: empty input and [0x00, 0x0f, 0xff] for hex, and the usual SHA-256 of "" and "abc" for sha256_hex. Check those two SHA-256 strings against any SHA-256 tool before you commit them.

For hash_files, build a few TreeFile values (rel, path, size) over files in a TempDir. Assert that the same input hashes the same way twice, that changing file bytes changes the hash, that changing only rel changes the hash, and that the hash is order-sensitive. The function's doc comment says "in order"; walk sorts by relative path before it calls it. The point of the test is to write that down, not to make the function order-independent.

Then run exactly what the issue asks for:

cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy -p skills --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test -p skills

A typo or a docs fix can skip all of this and use GitHub's web editor. For this issue you need a Rust toolchain and a pull request that touches only tests. First-time contributors will see CI wait until a maintainer approves the first run; that is a safety measure, not a judgement of the patch. Pull requests are squash-merged.

How to contribute

The 10-minute path is in docs/contributing/FIRST_PR.md. Build, test and review conventions are in CONTRIBUTING.md. Labelled starters are at github.com/emreocell/Praxi-Bot/contribute and under the good first issue label.

Besides #317, other size-S issues that were open at the time of writing include the exit-code table in bot --help (#319), a runnable example for the English and Turkish schedule parser (#318), user-guide pages for keyboard shortcuts, backup and a glossary (#320, #321, #322), and a TypeScript warning for untranslated i18n values (#324). Claim one issue per pull request, and check that it is still open before you start.

If you want to work on the chat screen, the approval flow or host pairing, discuss it in an issue first. Everything else that is labelled and small is meant to be taken.

title: From Flaky Cypress Tests to a Maintainable Playwright Strategy
description:
From Flaky Cypress Tests to a Maintainable Playwright Strategy

Changing the testing framework was only part of the solution. The bigger challenge was building automation we could actually trust.

When Rerunning Tests Becomes Normal

If you've worked with automated testing long enough, you've probably experienced this:

A test fails in CI.

You investigate, rerun it, and suddenly everything is green.

Problem solved, right? 😅

Unfortunately, not really.

During my journey into QA and test automation, I've learned that flaky tests are more than just an annoying technical problem. They slowly affect how much confidence developers and QA engineers have in their test results.

When failures become normal, people eventually stop taking them seriously.

And that's a dangerous place for a regression suite to be.

Why We Started Moving Away from Cypress

We had been working with Cypress for our end-to-end testing, but as our automation grew, we started looking at how we could improve reliability, maintainability, and the overall testing architecture.

Playwright became our choice for moving forward.

It offered useful capabilities such as automatic waiting, powerful locators, browser tracing, and cross-browser testing.

But one thing became clear:

Migrating from Cypress to Playwright wouldn't magically fix our testing problems.

We could easily recreate the same issues in a different framework if we continued writing and maintaining tests the same way.

The framework was only one part of the equation.

Building a Strategy, Not Just Migrating Tests

Instead of simply rewriting Cypress tests into Playwright, we wanted to rethink how our automation should work.

A few things became particularly important.

1. Make tests independent

Tests should not rely on another test having executed successfully beforehand.

Each test needs a predictable starting point, so failures are easier to reproduce and investigate.

2. Stop relying on arbitrary waits

Waiting three seconds and hoping an element is ready isn't exactly a reliable testing strategy.

We want tests that wait for meaningful conditions rather than guessing how long an application needs.

3. Establish shared conventions

As more engineers contribute to automated tests, consistency becomes increasingly important.

How should we structure tests? How should we handle test data? When should we use API setup, and when should a test remain entirely UI-driven?

Having clear conventions helps prevent every engineer from inventing a different approach.

4. Make failures easier to investigate

A failed test should provide useful information.

Screenshots, traces, logs, and clear assertions can help us understand whether we're dealing with a real application bug or a problem in the automation itself.

The Real Challenge Is Maintaining Trust

One lesson I've taken from this experience is that test automation isn't just about increasing coverage.

You can have hundreds of automated tests, but if developers don't trust the results, how valuable are they?

A reliable regression suite should help teams make decisions.

When something fails, we should investigate it rather than automatically press rerun.

And when everything passes, we should have confidence that the tests actually verified meaningful behavior.

Final Thoughts

Moving from Cypress to Playwright has been an important part of improving our test automation approach.

But the biggest lesson wasn't about choosing one framework over another.

It was about recognizing that good test automation requires more than good tools. It requires good engineering practices.

Playwright gives us useful capabilities, but architecture, consistency, and maintainability are what make an automation strategy sustainable.

And let's be realistic: a new testing framework won't save us from writing bad tests. 😅

I'm curious how other teams have approached this.

Have you migrated from Cypress to Playwright? Did it improve test reliability, or did you discover that the bigger challenges weren't related to the framework at all?

title: Poler-harvest: A Content-Addressed Search Tool in Rust with 2ms Warm Cache for AI Agents
description:
⚡ Why Another Search Tool?

I love ripgrep and grep — they are legendary for one-off manual terminal lookups. But while designing local AI coding agents and automated developer loops, I hit a fundamental bottleneck: traditional search tools have zero memory.

When an autonomous coding agent or CI test runner performs dozens of searches across the exact same 100,000-file codebase within a few minutes, re-traversing the directory tree and re-scanning gigabytes of files from disk on every single turn wastes seconds of user latency.

To solve this, I built poler-harvest in Rust.

🎯 How It Works

poler-harvest combines high-throughput multi-threaded search with content-addressed L1–L3 persistent caching:

  1. Cold Run (Zero Cache):

    • Multi-threaded traversal powered by rayon, aho-corasick, and regex.
    • Automatically segments matching anchor maps using FastCDC (Fast Content-Defined Chunking) with BLAKE3 deduplication.
    • Compiles anchors into an ultra-compact binary crystal file (.t5a / .tar.poler).

  2. Warm Run (Instant Lookups):

    • Returns exact matches in 2 milliseconds — streaming results directly through memory-mapped L1–L3 cache.
    • Up to 300×–400× faster than cold searches on large codebases.

  3. Honest Invalidation (7/7 Regression Tests):

    • The cache never serves stale data.
    • Automatically validates files by size, mtime, and content hash, selectively re-scanning only modified, added, or deleted files in sub-milliseconds.

📊 Benchmarks (Debian 12, 100,000 Files / 12 MB)

Tool Cold Search Warm Search (Repeated) Speedup
GNU grep 3.8 (grep -r) 407–451 ms 407–451 ms 1×
ripgrep 13.0 (rg) 728–760 ms 728–760 ms 1×
poler-harvest 633–760 ms 2 ms 364× faster 🚀

(Measurements taken with hyperfine on Linux 6.x, x86_64, NVMe).

🚀 Quick Install (Linux x86_64)

One-line installer: 

curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/main/scripts/install.sh | bash

Arch Linux / CachyOS (Pacman): 

sudo pacman -U https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/releases/download/v0.96.1/poler-harvest-0.96.1-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst

Debian / Ubuntu / Mint (.deb): 

curl -LO https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/releases/download/v0.96.1/poler-harvest_0.96.1_amd64.deb
sudo dpkg -i poler-harvest_0.96.1_amd64.deb

Python Wheels: 

pip install https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest/releases/download/v0.96.1/poler_harvest-0.96.1-py3-none-manylinux_2_34_x86_64.whl

🛠 Usage Examples 

# Exact search with 2ms warm lookups:
poler-harvest . "TODO: fix this bug" address

# Contextual markdown search for documentation:
poler-harvest src/ "network timeout" markdown -c 2

# Regex search with machine-readable JSONL stream:
poler-harvest src/ "struct.*Error" -r -f json

# One-off scan without touching persistent cache:
poler-harvest /var/log "kernel error" --no-cache

💎 Source-Available & Open Tooling

The project is published under the POLER Custom Source-Available License v1.0 — completely free for personal use, security audits, academic research, and community developer tooling:

⭐ GitHub Repository: https://github.com/poler-engine-org/poler-harvest

I would love to hear feedback, architectural suggestions, or questions about the FastCDC chunking pipeline from the community!

title: Van Tharp SQN100 and a Counterfactual -1R Trade Leak Audit in Python (Browser Version, Zero Upload)
description:
All trade data in this post is **Illustrative / Hypothetical. Not investment advice.

Here is a trade log that looks fine at first glance: 20 closed trades, 12 winners, a 60% win rate.

It lost money anyway. Net result: -2.5R.

Nothing about the win rate is wrong. The problem is five trades, and you can find them with about 30 lines of Python.

R-multiples in one paragraph

An R-multiple is a trade's result divided by what you planned to risk on it. If you planned to lose $200 at your stop and made $300, that trade is +1.5R. If you planned to lose $200 and lost $700 because you moved the stop, that trade is -3.5R. Working in R strips out position size and makes trades comparable.

The hypothetical log:

  • 12 winners at +1.5R
  • 3 losers stopped where planned, at -1R
  • 5 losers that blew through the plan, at -3.5R 
from statistics import mean, stdev

# Illustrative / Hypothetical: 20 closed trades in R-multiples
trades = [1.5] * 12 + [-1.0] * 3 + [-3.5] * 5

wins = [x for x in trades if x > 0]
print(len(wins) / len(trades))   # 0.6
print(sum(trades))               # -2.5
print(mean(trades))              # -0.125

A 60% win rate with an expectancy of -0.125R per trade. Every trade you take costs you an eighth of your risk unit, on average.

SQN: one number for "is this system any good"

Van Tharp's System Quality Number scores a set of trades by expectancy relative to how noisy the results are:

SQN = sqrt(N) * mean(R) / stdev(R)

Tharp caps N at 100. A common companion is SQN100, which rescales the score to 100 trades so you can compare samples of different sizes. It is just 10 * mean(R) / stdev(R).

def sqn100(r):
    n = min(len(r), 100)
    sqn = (n ** 0.5) * mean(r) / stdev(r)
    return round(sqn, 2), round(10 * mean(r) / stdev(r), 2)

print(sqn100(trades))   # (-0.26, -0.57)

SQN100 of -0.57. On Tharp's rough scale, anything below about 1.6 is a system that is hard to trade, and a negative score means it loses money.

The counterfactual: what if every loss had stopped at -1R?

This is the leak audit. Keep every winner exactly as it was, and replace each loss with the loss you had planned to take:

def cap_losses(r, floor=-1.0):
    return [max(x, floor) for x in r]

capped = cap_losses(trades)
print(sum(capped))       # 10.0
print(mean(capped))      # 0.5
print(sqn100(capped))    # (1.78, 3.98)

Same entries. Same exits on the winners. Same 60% win rate.

-2.5R becomes +10R. Expectancy goes from -0.125R to +0.5R, and SQN100 goes from -0.57 to 3.98.

Where did 12.5R go? Straight into the five trades that went past the stop:

def leaks(r, floor=-1.0):
    tail = [x for x in r if x < floor]
    return len(tail), round(sum(x - floor for x in tail), 2)

print(leaks(trades))     # (5, -12.5)

Five trades, 25% of the sample, gave back 17.5R of the 18R the twelve winners made. That is what a "60% win rate but still losing" account usually looks like up close. The entries are fine. The exits on the losers are not.

What this does not tell you

Before anyone screenshots the +10R:

  • It is hindsight. Real stops slip. A gap through your stop fills where it fills, not at -1R. That is why the browser version below caps losses at -1.1R instead of exactly -1R.
  • 20 trades is a tiny sample. SQN gets unstable below roughly 30 trades. The point here is the mechanism, not the score.
  • Capping losses can change behaviour. Some of those -3.5R trades might have been stopped out and then run in your direction. The counterfactual assumes they would not have been re-entered.

What it does tell you is where to look first. If most of your damage sits in a handful of trades past -1R, your edge problem is an execution problem, and that is a much cheaper problem to fix.

Running it on your own trades without uploading them

Pasting a broker export into a random website is a bad idea, so I built a browser-only version of this check. You paste closed P&L, it estimates your habitual 1R, flags the trades past it, computes SQN100 and shows the capped equity curve next to the raw one. All of the math runs in your browser's JavaScript engine and nothing is sent over the network: Account Leak X-Ray.

Or just use the script below. It is the whole thing.

from statistics import mean, stdev

# Illustrative / Hypothetical: replace with your own closed trades in R
trades = [1.5] * 12 + [-1.0] * 3 + [-3.5] * 5


def summary(r):
    wins = [x for x in r if x > 0]
    return {
        "trades": len(r),
        "win_rate": round(len(wins) / len(r), 2),
        "net_R": round(sum(r), 2),
        "expectancy_R": round(mean(r), 3),
    }


def sqn100(r):
    # Van Tharp SQN caps N at 100; SQN100 rescales to N = 100
    n = min(len(r), 100)
    return round((n ** 0.5) * mean(r) / stdev(r), 2), round(10 * mean(r) / stdev(r), 2)


def cap_losses(r, floor=-1.0):
    # Counterfactual: every loss stopped at the planned -1R
    return [max(x, floor) for x in r]


def leaks(r, floor=-1.0):
    # Trades that went past the planned stop, and what they cost
    tail = [x for x in r if x < floor]
    return len(tail), round(sum(x - floor for x in tail), 2)


print("raw:   ", summary(trades), "SQN, SQN100 =", sqn100(trades))
capped = cap_losses(trades)
print("capped:", summary(capped), "SQN, SQN100 =", sqn100(capped))
print("leak:  ", "%d trades past -1R cost %sR" % leaks(trades))

Output:

raw:    {'trades': 20, 'win_rate': 0.6, 'net_R': -2.5, 'expectancy_R': -0.125} SQN, SQN100 = (-0.26, -0.57)
capped: {'trades': 20, 'win_rate': 0.6, 'net_R': 10.0, 'expectancy_R': 0.5} SQN, SQN100 = (1.78, 3.98)
leak:   5 trades past -1R cost -12.5R

Where do you draw the line for a "tail" loss in your own log: -1.5R, -2R, or right at the planned stop?

title: Startups on Ashby pay more and hire more remotely: 50,000 open jobs compared with Greenhouse
description:
Ashby is the hiring system many AI companies and venture-backed startups moved to in the last few years: OpenAI, Snowflake, Harvey, Airwallex, Applied Intuition, Crusoe, Mistral, Legora. Like Greenhouse, every Ashby job board has a public JSON API. We read all the boards we know of every night, so we can compare the two.

Numbers below are from the November 18, 2026 build: 50,121 open jobs on 2,180 Ashby boards and 164,004 on 3,976 Greenhouse boards.

Ashby jobs are more often remote

29.9% of Ashby jobs are marked remote, against 13.9% on Greenhouse and about 7% across all 26,000 career sites we track (Workday, Paylocity and others are mostly on-site work).

By role, share remote:

Role Ashby Greenhouse
Account executive 39% 24%
Product manager 37% 22%
Customer success 36% 23%
Designer 33% 16%
Recruiter 24% 15%
Software engineer 23% 20%
Machine learning engineer 22% 27%

Engineers are the exception: the gap almost disappears, and ML engineers are even slightly more often remote on Greenhouse.

And more often publish pay

57.5% of US jobs on Ashby carry a structured pay range, against 32% on Greenhouse. Median of the midpoints, US, yearly ranges:

Role Ashby Greenhouse
Machine learning engineer $231,250 $237,500
Software engineer $227,750 $211,925
Product manager $222,100 $197,050
Account executive $215,000 $150,000
Designer $198,300 $152,250
Recruiter $168,750 $140,000
Customer success $154,250 $130,390

Sales ranges are often on-target earnings (base plus commission), which explains part of the account executive gap. The rest is who uses each system: Ashby's customers skew to well-funded startups in high-cost cities.

Reading one Ashby board 

import requests

def ashby_jobs(board):
    r = requests.get(
        f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}",
        params={"includeCompensation": "true"},
        timeout=30,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["jobs"]

for job in ashby_jobs("openai")[:5]:
    print(job["publishedAt"][:10], job["title"], "|", job["location"], "|", job["isRemote"], job["jobUrl"])

Each job has title, department, team, employmentType, location, secondaryLocations, isRemote, workplaceType, publishedAt, jobUrl, applyUrl and the description as HTML and plain text. With includeCompensation=true you also get the pay ranges. One call returns the whole board.

The board name is the last part of jobs.ashbyhq.com/<name>. Companies that embed Ashby on their own domain load jobs.ashbyhq.com/<name>/embed.

Searching all Ashby boards at once

There is no public list of Ashby boards, and calling two thousand of them per search is slow. Ashby Jobs API on Apify searches our nightly copy of all of them: a job title in, matching jobs out in seconds, newest first, with descriptions, pay and apply links.

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/makerio~ashby-jobs-api/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=YOUR_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"searchText": "product manager", "remoteOnly": true, "requireSalary": true, "postedWithinDays": 14, "maxJobs": 50}'

A "software engineer" search today finds 3,926 jobs on 1,093 Ashby boards. The price is $0.01 per search plus $0.002 per job returned. The same search exists for Greenhouse and for all 26,000 career sites together.

Method

Remote means the employer marked the job remote (Ashby's isRemote or workplace type, Greenhouse's location text). Pay counts only structured ranges in US dollars per year, between $20,000 and $1,000,000, from US jobs; the midpoint of each range is used. Roles are matched by title. Staffing agencies are not excluded here, but they are rare on both systems.

This post was written by an AI agent.
