description:
arXiv:2611.24963v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run.
  In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens.
  Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale.
  These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.

title: Branch Caching After Step Distillation in Four- and Eight-Step Image Generators
description:
arXiv:2611.25248v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can a distilled image generator save time by reusing features between its few remaining denoising steps? We study a fixed branch cache that replaces selected attention and MLP evaluations while preserving the student's noise schedule. One full trajectory and one raw-cache trajectory from the same initial noise supply a scalar correction for each branch type and reuse position. At $1024^2$, one internal reuse reduces four-step Qwen-Image-Lightning denoising time from 1.279 to 0.977 seconds. Three reuses yield $1.51\times$ speedup on eight-step Lightning and $1.53\times$ on eight-step Hyper-FLUX. We evaluate image quality on all 200 DrawBench prompts. With the reuse positions held fixed, correction improves mean same-seed image fidelity over raw reuse by 0.66 and 0.87 dB on the two Lightning students. On Hyper-FLUX the PSNR difference is 0.01 dB, while LPIPS improves from 0.1625 to 0.1546. These results measure the effect of branch caching and correction while retaining each student's original sampling grid.

title: React, deeply · 3. Effects, honestly
description:
React, deeply · Chapter 3 of 12 · Web · new chapter every Monday night

By the end of this chapter: Identify the small number of cases useEffect is for, and the far larger number where it is the wrong tool.

The problem

Emma, a front-end engineer, is working on a real-time analytics dashboard with a two-month sprint deadline. The dashboard updates a table every second with live metrics from a WebSocket. After adding a "filter by region" feature, the dashboard started experiencing issues: the table lags by up to three seconds, the CPU usage on the user's laptop spikes to 90%, and the performance monitoring alert fires every time a user opens the page. The team cannot afford to roll back the feature, and the sprint deadline is only three days away. Emma needs to identify the cause of the problem and fix it quickly.

The issue seems to be related to the way the state is being updated and the effects that are being run after each update. Emma has been using useEffect to handle the side effects of updating the table, but she's not sure if she's using it correctly. She's also not sure if there are other factors contributing to the performance issues.

Emma's current implementation uses useEffect to fetch new data from the WebSocket and update the table every second. However, she's noticed that the useEffect hook is being run more frequently than expected, causing the CPU usage to spike. She's tried to optimize the code by using useCallback and useMemo, but the issue persists.

Before you start

To follow along with this chapter, you should have a good understanding of React's rendering and reconciliation process, as well as the different state mechanisms available in React, such as useState and useReducer. You should also have a basic understanding of how to use useEffect to handle side effects in your React components.

Make sure you have the following installed:

  • Node.js (version 16 or later)
  • npm (version 8 or later)
  • React (version 18 or later)
  • A code editor or IDE of your choice

You can verify that you have the correct versions installed by running the following commands in your terminal:

node -v
npm -v
npm ls react

Understanding useEffect

useEffect is a powerful hook in React that allows you to run side effects after rendering a component. However, it's often misused or overused, leading to performance issues like the one Emma is experiencing.

To understand how useEffect works, let's break down its signature:

useEffect(effect, dependencies)

The effect function is the code that will be run after rendering the component, and the dependencies array specifies which values the effect depends on. If any of the values in the dependencies array change, the effect will be re-run.

When to use useEffect

So, when should you use useEffect? Here are some scenarios where useEffect is the right tool for the job:

  • Fetching data from an API or WebSocket
  • Setting up event listeners or subscriptions
  • Updating the DOM directly (although this should be avoided whenever possible)

However, there are many cases where useEffect is not the right tool. For example:

  • Updating state based on user input
  • Running computations that don't have side effects
  • Handling errors or exceptions

In these cases, other hooks like useState, useReducer, or useCallback might be more suitable.

Build it

Let's take a look at Emma's code and see where she might be going wrong. Here's an example of her useEffect hook:

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

function Dashboard() {
  const [data, setData] = useState([]);
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState('all');

  useEffect(() => {
    const socket = new WebSocket('ws://example.com/data');
    socket.onmessage = (event) => {
      setData(JSON.parse(event.data));
    };
    return () => {
      socket.close();
    };
  }, [filter]);

  return (
    <table>
      {data.map((row) => (
        <tr key={row.id}>
          <td>{row.name}</td>
          <td>{row.value}</td>
        </tr>
      ))}
    </table>
  );
}

The problem with this code is that the useEffect hook is being run every time the filter state changes, which is causing the WebSocket connection to be reopened and closed repeatedly. This is likely causing the CPU usage to spike and the table to lag.

To fix this issue, Emma can use the useEffect hook with an empty dependencies array, like this:

useEffect(() => {
  const socket = new WebSocket('ws://example.com/data');
  socket.onmessage = (event) => {
    setData(JSON.parse(event.data));
  };
  return () => {
    socket.close();
  };
}, []);

This will ensure that the useEffect hook is only run once, when the component mounts, and not every time the filter state changes.

When this breaks

There are several ways that the useEffect hook can break, including:

  • Running the effect too frequently, causing performance issues
  • Failing to clean up after the effect, causing memory leaks
  • Not handling errors or exceptions properly

To avoid these issues, make sure to:

  • Use the useEffect hook with caution and only when necessary
  • Always clean up after the effect by returning a function from the useEffect hook
  • Handle errors and exceptions properly using try-catch blocks and error boundaries

What it costs

Using useEffect can come with a cost, including:

  • Performance issues if the effect is run too frequently
  • Memory leaks if the effect is not cleaned up properly
  • Complexity and debugging issues if the effect is not handled properly

To minimize these costs, make sure to:

  • Use the useEffect hook only when necessary
  • Optimize the effect to run as infrequently as possible
  • Use tools like the React DevTools to debug and optimize the effect

In the interview

When interviewing for a front-end engineering position, you may be asked questions about useEffect and how to use it properly. Here are some example questions and answers:

Q: What is useEffect and how does it work?
A: useEffect is a hook in React that allows you to run side effects after rendering a component. It takes two arguments: the effect function and the dependencies array. The effect function is run after rendering the component, and the dependencies array specifies which values the effect depends on.

Q: When should you use useEffect?
A: You should use useEffect when you need to run a side effect after rendering a component, such as fetching data from an API or setting up event listeners.

Q: What are some common mistakes people make when using useEffect?
A: Some common mistakes people make when using useEffect include running the effect too frequently, failing to clean up after the effect, and not handling errors or exceptions properly.

Your tasks

  1. Create a simple React component that uses useEffect to fetch data from an API and update the component's state.
  2. Optimize the component to run the effect as infrequently as possible.
  3. Use the React DevTools to debug and optimize the component.
  4. Write a test for the component to ensure it is working correctly.
  5. Refactor the component to use a different hook, such as useCallback or useMemo, to see if it improves performance.

Your tasks this week

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing
one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened:
tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions
that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.

title: CoRelate: Coordinated Human-Object Motion Synthesis through Interaction Relations
description:
arXiv:2611.25166v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Human-object motion synthesis requires coordinated human participation as objects move toward specified goals. However, reaching object targets does not ensure that contact is established and maintained, while adjustments that improve contact may interfere with task completion. We introduce CoRelate, a diffusion framework that coordinates full-body human-object motion through explicit interaction relations and task feedback for rigid and articulated objects. We represent intended participation through hand-part relations that specify the participating hand, its part-relative reference position, and participation interval. These relations serve both as generation conditions and as references for measuring interaction realization. At each denoising step, a temporal refiner trained jointly with the generator combines relation deviations, task residuals, and motion features from the current prediction to jointly update human and object motion across the sequence. After generation, temporal motion correction addresses remaining contact failures by optimizing local motion segments while preserving object trajectories and protected human motion. Experiments demonstrate improved object-goal satisfaction, contact F1, and complete interaction success over the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies support the benefits of relation conditioning and the complementary roles of task and relation feedback.

title: Beyond Restoration: Content-Degradation Factor Unfolding for Real-World Concealed Object Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2611.25239v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable visual perception under degradation requires distinguishing task-relevant content from degradation-induced variations, especially in concealed object segmentation (COS), where foreground cues are inherently weak. The central challenge is not merely improving visibility, but identifying reliable content evidence amid degradation-induced variations. RGB-space segmentation often entangles content and degradation cues, while restoration-based methods primarily focus on image recovery and task interaction. This motivates explicit factorization to distinguish content evidence from degradation effects and assess its reliability. Retinex provides a spatially aligned basis for this separation but remains illumination-centric. We therefore extend it to content-degradation formation with task-asymmetric factor roles. The Factor Unfolding Network (FUN) uses the content factor R as the sole source of direct semantic evidence for segmentation, while the degradation factor L captures degradation-related variations and generates a spatial reliability map to calibrate this evidence. A unified energy couples observation formation with reliability-weighted foreground-background separation, and its alternating updates yield a coarse-to-fine network without clean-image supervision. In this way, FUN factorizes degradation for perception rather than removing it. Extensive experiments across clean and degraded conditions and diverse segmentation tasks demonstrate robust performance and generalization. Code will be released.

title: Polar: A Benchmark for Evaluating Political Bias in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2606.12922v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Political bias in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly significant, but difficult to measure reproducibly across political and linguistic contexts. We introduce Polar, a 4,026-instance multiple-choice benchmark that measures political bias through option-level likelihoods rather than prompt-based generation. Polar covers two ideological axes and eight issue categories derived from the Manifesto Project, and evaluates models in parallel across U.S. and South Korean political contexts. Across 38 LLMs, measured bias varies systematically with political context, issue category, model group, and presentation language. All models lean left-progressive on U.S. political content, but show more centered and mixed patterns on South Korean content. Translation experiments further show that presentation language alone can shift measured bias. These findings highlight the need for multilingual and cross-contextual evaluation of political bias in LLMs.
  The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/mcrl/Polar) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/thunder-research-group/Polar).

title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
description:
arXiv:2611.25114v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.

title: Amazon VPC Lattice now supports CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources
description:
Amazon VPC Lattice now publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources. Resource owners — those who share resources via VPC Lattice — and resource consumers — those who access those shared resources — can now see TCP traffic to resources such as databases, clusters, and on-premises endpoints. Resource owners get metrics for resource gateways and resource configurations. Consumers get metrics for resource endpoints, service network endpoints, and service network VPC associations. Previously, resource access logs were the primary way to see this traffic, but they required additional processing and provided limited real-time visibility. Now you can monitor your layer-4 resources directly in CloudWatch.

With these metrics, you can proactively catch connectivity issues and optimize resource capacity. Capacity planning metrics — including bytes processed, new flows, and active flows — let resource owners monitor traffic per resource gateway and per resource configuration to track load on shared resources. Reliability metrics, such as dropped packets, help you detect problems early. Resource gateways also report port allocation errors, which show when a resource gateway needs more IPv4 addresses per network interface. Consumers can monitor traffic per resource endpoint, service network endpoint, or service network VPC association. They can set CloudWatch alarms for when new flows drop to zero or dropped packets increase, catching an unreachable resource before their applications do. Both owners and consumers can break metrics down by Availability Zone to isolate zonal issues or verify connections after configuration changes.

CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon VPC Lattice is available. For the list of Regions, see the Amazon VPC Lattice FAQs.

To learn more, see CloudWatch metrics for Amazon VPC Lattice in the Amazon VPC Lattice User Guide, or visit the Amazon VPC Lattice product page.

title: Why avatar image public URLs stop working with private object storage and signed URLs
description:
If you need an avatar to render for a signed-in user, use a short-lived signed GET URL and let the browser pull the object directly from storage. On a private bucket a permanent public link is not on the table — there is no public-read ACL to flip, public_url comes back null, and the only address you get is one that expires. That is the whole explanation for the symptom everyone reports first, where the image renders fine for an hour and then every request comes back 403.

Nothing is wrong with the storage. The link was never meant to outlive its signature.

An incident that starts in the wrong layer

The system I have in mind is a property-management SaaS. Every managed building gets its own key prefix inside one private bucket — staff and tenant avatars under avatars/, plus a nightly per-tenant backup archive under backups/ holding leases, inspection photos and countersigned PDFs. Two very different objects, one access model. The avatars are 40 KB each. The restore archives run to several GB, and on the day an operations manager asks to restore last Tuesday's snapshot, download throughput on that single object is the only number anybody cares about.

The avatar question and the restore design turn out to be the same decision.

The way it breaks is dull, which is why it keeps happening. An upload handler takes whatever URL the storage response hands back and writes it into users.avatar_url. For a while that column holds a signed link with an expiry and a signature sitting in the query string. Cached in the database, rendered in the portal, perfectly fine for an hour. Then 403 for every user at once, which is what makes a schema mistake look like an incident — the on-call engineer sees a wall of identical errors and starts checking the bucket instead of the column.

The invariant that falls out of it is short. A signed URL is a capability, not an address. Store the bucket and the key; mint the URL at render time.

Why does a public URL for an avatar image stop working on private object storage?

Because the object never had a public address to begin with. There is no public-read ACL to set on a private bucket, so public_url stays null and an anonymous browser has nothing to resolve. What the API gives you instead is a signed download URL — the object path, an expiry, and a signature computed over both. Storage verifies that signature on every GET. Once the clock passes expires_at the signature authorises nothing, and the request is refused. Expiry is the feature, not the side effect.

Storage backends differ in whether they will hand you a public address at all. S3 and Cloudflare R2 will if you configure them to; Cloudinary is public by default and treats access control as the opt-in; Infrai storage only serves private objects, which is exactly why public_url reads null there.

The second-order effects are where teams actually get hurt. A signed URL inside an <img src> is fine. The same string pasted into an email, picked up by a crawler, or cached by a CDN keyed on the full query is a small liability, because anyone holding it holds the object until it expires. And if you fetch the URL from JavaScript rather than letting the browser load it as an image, the storage origin has to allow your origin — an <img> tag skips the preflight entirely.

Two delivery options, and how they differ under load

Two shapes, and the difference is where the bytes go.

Shape one puts your application in the data path. The browser asks your handler for /files/:id, the handler checks the session, streams the object down, and the client never learns that storage exists. The invariant is that every byte transits your app, which makes your app the bill, the bottleneck and the failure domain. You get stable URLs, per-request authorisation, and an audit line for every byte.

Shape two keeps your application out of the data path. The handler checks the session, mints a signed URL, and answers with a 302 or a small JSON body the front end drops into an <img>. Here the invariant is that your app never touches object bytes, and the URL itself is the capability — TTL becomes your revocation window, so a 5-minute avatar link and a 15-minute restore link are two separate risk decisions you get to make on purpose.

On large-file throughput the two are not close, and that is what settles it for this workflow. Proxying a multi-GB restore archive through an application instance means a rolling deploy kills the transfer mid-stream, the load balancer's idle timeout becomes a hard ceiling on how big a snapshot you can ship, one tenant's restore competes with every other tenant's API traffic, and your memory graph starts tracking downloads. That is a bad postmortem to have to write. Shape two hands the bytes to storage, which is built to serve them and will happily do ranged requests and resumes, and shrinks your handler down to an authorisation check plus a Location header. The same shape is fine for a 40 KB avatar even though throughput is irrelevant there — one delivery path is less to operate than two.

Option Public object links Private delivery Fits when
Amazon S3 / MinIO bucket policy or CloudFront presigned GET and PUT you already own the IAM, lifecycle and replication story
Cloudflare R2 public bucket or custom domain presigned GET and PUT you want public assets and large downloads served from one place
Cloudinary public by design, with transforms signed delivery is opt-in profile images are meant to be seen by the open web
Infrai none, private objects only presign call with expires_seconds one key already covers the rest of your backend

If you're running an authenticated portal like this one and you don't want to hand-roll IAM policies and lifecycle rules before you can mint a single URL, Infrai storage is worth trying for the private-object half of the workflow — its API is self-describing, so one discovery call to GET /v1/discovery/storage.object.presign returns the request schema, the response shape and a runnable Go example, and wiring it up is reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That's also why Infrai earns a row above rather than a section of its own — one key and one consistent envelope cover storage alongside the scheduling and email work this portal already needs, so there's one integration to audit instead of three.

The code path that prevents the 403

Mint on demand, hand the URL to the browser, keep it out of your database. This is the whole preventative measure, in the boring form I'd actually put in a runbook.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

const apiBase = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type presignReq struct {
    Op             string `json:"op"`
    ExpiresSeconds int    `json:"expires_seconds"`
}

type presignResp struct {
    URL       string            `json:"url"`
    Method    string            `json:"method"`
    ExpiresAt time.Time         `json:"expires_at"`
    Headers   map[string]string `json:"headers"`
}

// signGet mints a short-lived download URL for one private object.
// The returned URL carries its own signature, so it is fetched WITHOUT
// the platform Authorization header.
func signGet(client *http.Client, bucket, key string, ttl time.Duration) (presignResp, error) {
    payload, err := json.Marshal(presignReq{Op: "get", ExpiresSeconds: int(ttl.Seconds())})
    if err != nil {
        return presignResp{}, err
    }
    endpoint := fmt.Sprintf("%s/storage/object/presign/%s/%s", apiBase, bucket, key)

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", endpoint, bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return presignResp{}, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return presignResp{}, err
        }
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusOK {
            var out presignResp
            if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &out); err != nil {
                return presignResp{}, err
            }
            return out, nil
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(backoff(attempt, res.Header.Get("Retry-After")))
            continue
        }
        return presignResp{}, fmt.Errorf("presign %s/%s: %d %s", bucket, key, res.StatusCode, string(body))
    }
    return presignResp{}, errors.New("presign: still rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func backoff(attempt int, retryAfter string) time.Duration {
    if secs, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && secs > 0 {
        return time.Duration(secs) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func main() {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

    avatar, err := signGet(client, "pm-tenant-4417", "avatars/u_8812.jpg", 5*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "avatar:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    // Serve as a 302 Location, or as JSON the front end drops into <img src>.
    fmt.Println(avatar.Method, avatar.URL, "good until", avatar.ExpiresAt.Format(time.RFC3339))

    archive, err := signGet(client, "pm-tenant-4417", "backups/2026-08-04.tar.zst", 15*time.Minute)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "archive:", err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(archive.Method, archive.URL, "good until", archive.ExpiresAt.Format(time.RFC3339))
}

Two details earn their keep. The 429 branch honours Retry-After instead of tight-looping, because a portal that re-renders an avatar grid will ask for forty URLs at once and a tight loop turns one slow response into an outbound flood. And every non-200 gets surfaced with its body attached, since a 4xx carries the reason and swallowing it is how you end up debugging the wrong layer at 2am.

Upload is the other half, and it's where I reach for an idempotency key rather than a retry counter. The platform convention here is an Idempotency-Key header with a 24-hour dedup window, so a client that retries a PUT after a network blip does not land the same lease PDF twice under two keys. Retry-safety you have to reason about is retry-safety you'll get wrong.

Where this breaks down: public profiles and retention rules

The catch is that all of this assumes every reader of the object is authenticated by you. If your product has public tenant profiles, listing photos or avatars that need to be crawlable, permanently addressable and cacheable by someone else's CDN, private-only storage is not suitable and no TTL setting will rescue it. Stick with a backend that serves public objects — R2 behind a custom domain, S3 with a bucket policy — or an image service like Cloudinary that treats public delivery and transforms as the product.

Two more boundaries before you commit. If your retention rules demand immutable copies of those lease PDFs, you want object versioning and object lock, which Infrai storage lacks, so S3 Object Lock or an equivalent WORM store is the honest pick for that slice. And if the restore path has to survive a regional failure without operator involvement, you need cross-region replication configured at the storage layer rather than a scheduled copy job you wrote yourself.

I'm not certain where the crossover sits for mid-sized objects. Somewhere between a 40 KB avatar and a 4 GB archive there's a range where proxying through your app is simpler and the throughput cost is noise, and I'd measure it on your own load balancer rather than trust a rule of thumb from an article. If the private-object boundary fits your system, the avatar case is written up in more detail at https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/storage/answers/why-avatar-image-public-url-not-working-private-object/ — start there, then decide which of the two shapes you want to run.

  • Amazon S3, sharing an object with a presigned URL — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation — https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • MinIO object storage documentation — https://min.io/docs/minio/linux/index.html

title: MAWAM: A Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Coordinated Manipulation
description:
arXiv:2611.25105v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Every move in a robot team changes the world in which its teammates must act. Coordinated manipulation therefore calls for predicting the team's actions together with the physical future they jointly create. We introduce MAWAM, a multi-agent world-action model that jointly generates each robot's future views and executable action chunks in a single sample. Built from a pretrained single-robot world-action backbone, MAWAM jointly denoises all robots' action and future-view tokens through cross-agent attention, while preserving a separate control interface for each robot. MAWAM achieves the highest success on all three real-robot tasks (laundry-bag collection, bath-towel folding, and umbrella handover), with 67.8% mean success, 18.9 percentage points above MA-VLA trained on the same demonstrations and cameras. In simulation, MAWAM reaches 90.3% mean success on eight tasks with teams of up to four arms. Ablations show that cross-agent attention and team-stage future-video supervision both improve coordinated control: without attention, a four-arm relay falls from 95.0% to 39.0%, and without this supervision, Place Food falls from 78.0% to 47.0%.

title: How to Scrape Job Listings from Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby Career Pages (Python and No-Code)
description:
If you want the open jobs of a list of companies (for a job board, market research, a recruiting tool or your own job search), you do not need to scrape HTML career pages one by one. Most companies host their career page on an applicant tracking system (ATS), and several of them publish the open jobs as public JSON.

This post shows the three easiest ones in Python, the catches you will hit after that, and a no-code option for when you need many companies and many systems.

Option 1: public job board APIs in Python

Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby each have a public, read-only endpoint per company. You only need the company's board name, which is usually in its careers URL (boards.greenhouse.io/stripe, jobs.lever.co/palantir, jobs.ashbyhq.com/ramp).

import json
import urllib.request


def get(url):
    # some job boards reject Python's default User-Agent, so send a normal one
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (job-list-script)"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
        return json.load(r)


def greenhouse(board):
    data = get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{board}/jobs")
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j["location"]["name"], "url": j["absolute_url"]}
            for j in data["jobs"]]


def lever(board):
    data = get(f"https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{board}?mode=json")
    return [{"title": j["text"], "location": j["categories"].get("location"), "url": j["hostedUrl"]}
            for j in data]


def ashby(board):
    data = get(f"https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{board}")
    return [{"title": j["title"], "location": j.get("location"), "url": j["jobUrl"]}
            for j in data["jobs"]]


for name, jobs in [("stripe", greenhouse("stripe")), ("palantir", lever("palantir")), ("ramp", ashby("ramp"))]:
    print(name, len(jobs), "open jobs, e.g.", jobs[0]["title"], "-", jobs[0]["location"])

That is enough for a handful of companies on these three systems. Things to know before you scale it:

  • Full descriptions are optional. Greenhouse returns them with ?content=true; Lever includes descriptionPlain; Ashby has descriptionPlain and, with ?includeCompensation=true, salary ranges when the company publishes them.
  • Every system has its own shape. Locations, departments, remote flags, dates and salaries live in different fields, so you will write a normalizer per system.
  • You first have to know which ATS a company uses. A list of company names does not tell you whether to call Greenhouse or Workday.
  • Workday is the hard one. Large companies often use Workday, which has no simple per-company feed: each company has its own tenant, data center number and site name, and the job list is a paged POST endpoint.
  • Monitoring needs state. To get "only jobs that are new since yesterday", you have to remember what you already saw.

Option 2: a ready-made Actor for many companies and systems

I packaged all of that as an Apify Actor: ATS Jobs Scraper. You paste company names, domains or careers URLs, and it finds the system behind each one (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Workable, SmartRecruiters, Recruitee, Personio and Breezy) and returns one clean row per job:

{
  "company": "Linear",
  "ats": "ashby",
  "title": "Senior / Staff Fullstack Engineer",
  "department": "Product",
  "team": "Engineering",
  "location": "Europe",
  "isRemote": true,
  "workplaceType": "remote",
  "employmentType": "Full-time",
  "salary": null,
  "url": "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/linear/d3bc1ced-3ce4-4086-a050-555055dbb1ff",
  "applyUrl": "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/linear/d3bc1ced-3ce4-4086-a050-555055dbb1ff/application",
  "descriptionText": "At Linear, we're building the product development system for teams and agents. ..."
}

On top of the script above it gives you:

  • Filters for title keywords (or keywords in the description), excluded words, locations, remote only, departments and "posted within the last N days"
  • Salary in one format (min, max, currency, interval) when the company publishes it
  • Return only new jobs: schedule it daily and each run returns only the jobs that earlier runs did not return
  • Export to JSON, CSV or Excel, or push results to Google Sheets, Slack or a webhook with Apify integrations

From code, use the Apify client:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("webobsidians/ats-jobs-scraper").call(
    run_input={"companies": ["stripe", "linear.app", "palantir"], "keywords": ["engineer"], "remoteOnly": True}
)
for job in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(job["company"], "|", job["title"], "|", job["location"], "|", job["url"])

It costs $1.00 per 1,000 jobs plus $0.00005 per run start, with platform usage included, and Apify's free plan includes monthly credit to try it.

Which one should you use?

  • A few companies on Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby: the Python script.
  • Many companies, Workday, a daily "new jobs" feed, or a spreadsheet for a non-developer: the Actor.

Either way, you are reading job posts that the companies publish for everyone, so keep request rates reasonable.

title: TALD: Transferability-Aware Logit Disentanglement for Cross-Modal Knowledge Distillation
description:
arXiv:2611.25126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cross-modal knowledge distillation can incur negative transfer when source-modality supervision conflicts with the target modality's discriminative characteristics. We propose TALD, a two-stage framework for Transferability-Aware Logit Disentanglement in class-aligned logit space. Guided by task-dependent self-benefiting and cross-modal exclusivity criteria, a Residual Disentangler decomposes logits from a teacher and an independently trained target-modality reference student into modality-general and modality-specific components. A Sample-Adaptive Modulator regulates decomposition constraints and sample-specific fusion weights. The learned modality-general components are then adaptively fused to supervise the final student. Across five benchmarks spanning vision, audio, and text, TALD achieves the largest mean accuracy gain and highest positive-transfer frequency among the compared methods. Across ten transfer directions with five runs each, TALD improves over training without distillation in 84% of evaluations, compared with at most 70% for the baselines, while offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We plan to release the code.

title: Designing for Wrong: The UX of AI That Is Sometimes Mistaken
description:
Every other piece of software you have ever shipped made a promise: press this button and the same correct thing happens every time. AI quietly breaks that promise, and most teams are still designing as if it had not. They wrap a probabilistic engine in an interface built for a deterministic one, and then they are surprised when users trust it too much, then too little, then not at all.

I have come to think the hardest part of shipping an AI product is not the model. It is the interface around it, because that interface has to do something no interface before it had to do: present output that is usually right and sometimes confidently wrong, to a human who has to decide, in the moment, whether to believe it. Get that wrong and it does not matter how good your model is. The product that earns durable trust is not the one with the best benchmark. It is the one whose design tells the user, truthfully and continuously, how much to rely on what they are looking at.

The assumption that quietly breaks

Classic product design rests on an assumption so deep we rarely name it: the system is correct, so the job of the interface is to make the correct thing easy to reach. Menus, forms, buttons, confirmations, all of it is choreography around a reliable engine. When something goes wrong it is an error, an exception, a state you handle and move on from. Correctness is the floor.

AI removes that floor. A language model returns an answer that is fluent, well-formatted, confident, and sometimes simply wrong, and critically it looks exactly the same whether it is right or wrong. There is no red underline, no stack trace, no obvious tell. If you design the interface the old way, treating every output as correct and polished, you have built a machine that launders uncertainty into false confidence. The better your visual design, the more convincing the wrong answers look. You have made the failure mode prettier.

So the first move is a mental one. Stop designing a tool that produces answers and start designing a tool that produces proposals of varying reliability, where conveying that reliability is a first-class part of the product, not a footnote.

Confidence is a design material

In a deterministic app, confidence is not a thing you design, because the answer is just correct. In an AI product, the system's confidence, and the gap between how confident it is and how confident it looks, is one of the most important materials you work with.

The failure to manage this is everywhere. A model returns a low-probability guess in the same crisp, authoritative typography it uses for a near-certain fact, and the user has no way to tell them apart. That is a design decision, even if nobody decided it. The fix is to treat confidence as something the interface expresses: hedge the uncertain answer in language and in visual weight, flag when the system is extrapolating beyond what it knows, distinguish a sourced fact from a plausible generation. This is not about plastering percentages everywhere, which users cannot interpret anyway. It is about the interface feeling appropriately sure when the system is sure, and appropriately tentative when it is not. A calibrated product feels truthful even when it is wrong, because it warned you. An uncalibrated one feels like a betrayal the first time its confident answer fails.

Make correction the main road, not the shoulder

Here is the assumption to design against: the user will need to change the output. Not occasionally, as an error case. Routinely, as the normal shape of the work. AI products are collaborative by nature, the human and the model converging on something good, and if your interface treats the model's first answer as a finished artifact with a tiny grudging edit button in the corner, you have designed for a world that does not exist.

The correction loop is the product. Editing, refining, regenerating, steering, giving feedback, undoing: these are not recovery paths, they are the main interaction, and they deserve the best real estate and the most design care. The question is not "how does the user accept the answer" but "how does the user quickly turn a 70% answer into a 100% one". A product that makes that cheap and obvious feels like a capable collaborator. A product that makes you copy the text out, fix it elsewhere, and paste it back feels like a demo that forgot real work exists. Most AI products are still demos in this specific way.

Design the failure, not only the success

Teams pour their design energy into the happy path, the moment the demo shines, and leave the unhappy paths as default states nobody owned. With AI, the unhappy paths are not rare, so this is backwards. The empty result, the low-confidence answer, the "I genuinely do not know", the request that falls outside what the system can do: these are frequent, and how you handle them is most of what determines whether users trust the product over time.

A system that can say "I am not sure about this" is more trustworthy than one that never does, even though it feels weaker in a demo. A graceful "I could not find a good answer, here is what I can tell you and here is how to get further" beats a confident fabrication every single time in the real world, because the fabrication is the thing that detonates trust. Designing the failure well means giving the model permission to be uncertain in the interface, and giving the user a real next step when it is. No dead ends. Every state, including the ones where the AI came up short, has a forward path.

Keep the human genuinely in control

There is a seductive failure mode where the interface is technically interactive but psychologically passive. The answer appears, polished and authoritative, with an implicit "approve" as the path of least resistance, and the human, busy and trusting, rubber-stamps it. This is automation bias, and a badly designed AI product manufactures it. You have put a human in the loop on the org chart while designing them out of it in practice.

The antidote is design that keeps the output a proposal and keeps disagreement cheap. Surface why the system produced this answer, so the human can actually evaluate it rather than just accept it. Make the uncertain parts visibly uncertain so attention goes where it should. Make editing and rejecting as easy as accepting, not a harder path that friction pushes people away from. Where the stakes are high, deliberately slow the human down at the decision point rather than letting them one-click through. The goal is a human who is actually exercising judgment, not one who has been smoothly led to agree. An AI product that quietly trains its users to stop thinking is a liability wearing the costume of a productivity tool.

Set expectations plainly at the door

Trust in an AI product is set early and hard, and the single most destructive thing you can do is let the first wrong answer arrive with no warning that it was possible. A user who was told, clearly, that the system is a capable assistant that is sometimes mistaken and should be checked will forgive an error and keep using it. A user who was given a flawless-looking magic box and then hit a confident falsehood will not come back, and no amount of later accuracy wins them back, because the wound was to trust, not to accuracy.

So onboarding is not a tutorial on where the buttons are. It is a frank briefing on what the system is good at, where it is weak, and how to use it well, including the uncomfortable parts. This feels like it undercuts the product, and it is the opposite. Calibrated expectations are what let a user integrate an imperfect tool into real work instead of bouncing off it at the first failure. You are not lowering their opinion of the product, you are making their reliance on it survivable.

Trust is the actual product

Step back and the thread connecting all of this is trust, and specifically calibrated trust: the user relying on the system exactly as much as it deserves, no more and no less. Too little and they ignore a tool that could help them. Too much and they get burned and then abandon it. The entire job of AI product design is to continuously calibrate that trust through the interface, so that reliance tracks reliability in real time.

This reframes what you are even building. The model is the engine, but the product is the trust relationship, and that relationship is made almost entirely of design decisions: how confidence is shown, how correction flows, how failure is handled, how control is preserved, how expectations are set. The teams that win the next few years of applied AI will not be the ones with a two-point benchmark lead. That lead is temporary and invisible to users anyway. They will be the ones whose products are trustworthy to use, where the interface is truthful about what is underneath it, and where a user can rely on the thing precisely because the design never pretended it was something it is not.

I am still refining my own version of this discipline, and I would value comparing notes. When you look at your AI product, does the interface make the user more calibrated about when to trust it, or does it just make the output look finished? Those are very different products, and only one of them keeps its users.

I write a field-note series on shipping AI that actually works in production. The original of this piece, and the rest, live on my LinkedIn. Originally published on LinkedIn.

title: How I Built a VS Code AI Coding Assistant That Runs Under 3.2K Tokens Per Request
description:
Most AI coding assistants feel heavy fast. Between injecting open tabs, large file trees, and dozens of tool schemas on every turn, a simple coding request can easily balloon to 30K–100K+ tokens—driving up latency and burning through API credits.

When I built Sidekick Code AI, I wanted to test the opposite approach: how useful can an in-editor coding assistant be if you keep context retrieval tight and predictable?

The Token & Latency Baseline

In recent trace runs (sidekick_cloud_chat_completion), a real code-generation turn used 3.13K total tokens and completed in ~2 seconds[cite: 2]:

  • Input: 2.75K tokens (88%) — system prompt, user request, and targeted local context[cite: 2]
  • Output: 383 tokens (12%) — focused code generation and next-step guidance[cite: 2]

For BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) workflows, keeping routine turns around ~3K tokens makes a big difference: on mid-tier models, a request costs under two cents, and on lightweight models it costs a fraction of a tenth of a cent.

3 Decisions That Kept Context Lean

1. Local Indexing Over Full-File Dumping

Instead of stuffing entire files or every open editor tab into the prompt by default, Sidekick indexes locally and pulls only the relevant snippets needed for the active request.

2. Minimal Prompt & Schema Overhead

Every unused tool definition or verbose system instruction gets tokenized on every single call. Keeping the base prompt compact prevents context bloat before the user even types a question.

3. Targeted, Incremental Edits

Rather than asking the model to rewrite large modules in one pass, prompts are structured to generate focused changes step by step—keeping output tokens low (~300–500 tokens) and latency around 2 seconds[cite: 2].

Try It in VS Code

If you prefer lightweight, BYOK tools and want to test it on a real repo, you can install Sidekick Code AI directly inside VS Code via Quick Open (Ctrl+P / Cmd+P):

ext install alidendenne.sidekick-code-ai

Or via terminal:

code --install-extension alidendenne.sidekick-code-ai

I'm actively refining the local indexing and context budgeting based on real developer workflows—if you try it out and hit any friction or edge cases, I'd genuinely appreciate your technical feedback in the comments.

title: RocketMQ-Rust vs. Apache RocketMQ 5.5.0: The Full Benchmark Overview
description:
AI disclosure: This article was generated from the project’s public benchmark report and pull requests. It does not report a new test run.

The November 2026 RocketMQ-Rust benchmark covers Broker sends, LitePull, message sizes from 128 B to 64 KiB, synchronous flush, Controller-mode replication, a Java client cross-check, and Proxy gRPC sends. At 1 KiB, synchronous sends reached 1.79× Java 5.5.0 throughput. Putting 256 asynchronous requests on one connection brought the ratio down to 0.96×. Here is the full matrix and where the bottlenecks moved.

1. Test setup

An Intel i7-11700K ran Docker Desktop on Windows with WSL 2 (Linux 6.18, 16 GB). The services and load generator were pinned to separate sets of eight logical CPUs. Traffic stayed on loopback; the store used the container filesystem. The Rust release-image setup used PGO and BOLT for the Broker and PGO for the Proxy. The Java side used the official 5.5.0 image with default OpenJDK 8 settings. Both Brokers used the same Rust load generator for the main comparison. The project warmed up fresh containers, rotated run order and reported medians of four to nine runs per cell, with zero reported failed sends. Displayed rates are rounded; ratios come from the report.

2. Broker sends and LitePull at 1 KiB

These measurements use one replica and asynchronous disk flush. A synchronous send means the client waits for one response before sending again. In the async rows, 4×64 means four connections with up to 64 requests outstanding on each.

Workload Java msg/s Rust msg/s Rust / Java CPU µs/msg (Java → Rust)
Sync send 2.3k 4.0k 1.79× 381 → 137
Async 1×256 116.6k 112.4k 0.96× 44.9 → 46.8
Async 4×64 115.9k 137.8k 1.19× 50.5 → 46.4
Async 16×16 100.9k 123.7k 1.23× 58.4 → 51.4
LitePull 107.7k 140.0k 1.30× 17.9 → 11.2

Synchronous send p50 fell from 0.43 to 0.24 ms. Broker CPU per message fell by about 64% for sync sends and 37% for LitePull. The one-connection throughput was measured after #12699; the corresponding CPU figure is from the earlier round. They are not values from the same run.

3. Message size sweep

Rust/Java throughput ratios for uncompressed payloads with one replica. The 1 KiB row is from a separate round from the main Broker table.

Payload Sync Async 1×256 Async 4×64
128 B 1.74× 1.14× 1.34×
1 KiB 1.72× 0.99× 1.16×
4 KiB 1.86× 1.21× 1.55×
64 KiB 2.14× 1.49× 1.34×

At 64 KiB on one asynchronous connection, Rust stored about 1.05 GB/s versus Java’s 0.70 GB/s. Across the three 64 KiB workloads, Rust Broker CPU per message was 14–37% of Java’s.

4. Synchronous flush and three replicas

1 KiB workload Java msg/s Rust msg/s Rust / Java
Sync flush · sync 0.7k 0.8k 1.15×
Sync flush · async 1×256 48.1k 46.3k 0.96×
Sync flush · async 4×64 46.2k 47.9k 1.04×
3 replicas · sync 1.3k 1.9k 1.39×
3 replicas · async 1×256 44.2k 63.2k 1.43×
3 replicas · async 4×64 53.7k 64.3k 1.20×

With synchronous flush, both Brokers waited for msync, about 2 ms per call on this machine. The three-replica run used one Controller-mode Broker group, two required in-sync replicas and asynchronous flush. Stopping both followers at the end of each run caused synchronous sends to the leader to fail, confirming that acknowledgements depended on replication. Total Broker CPU across all three replicas was 1,062/127/119 µs per message for Java and 748/96/94 for Rust in table order. The Broker processes and Controllers shared the same CPUs, so these are not cross-host replication capacity numbers.

5. Java client cross-check

With a Java 5.5.0 client and the same in-flight limits, sync throughput was still 1.47×, and the Rust Broker used 59% less CPU per message. The Java client limited async throughput on both Brokers. Server-side CPU nevertheless differed: Rust used 3.6% more at one connection and 11.5% and 23.2% less with four and sixteen client processes respectively. A throughput plateau is a reason to check the load generator before tuning the Broker.

6. Proxy gRPC sends

Cluster mode, one 1 KiB message per RPC. Java and Rust ran on the same host with the same settings but a day apart, not as paired A/B runs. The latency column reports Rust only.

Workload Java msg/s Rust msg/s Rust Proxy CPU µs/msg Rust p99
Sync 0.8k–0.9k 2.89k 184 0.49 ms
1×256 34.9k–35.4k 38.6k 97 20 ms
4×64 39.3k–39.7k 53.1k 82 10.5 ms
32×4 27.2k–28.4k 45.7k 91 6.5 ms

Two separate Rust-only A/B tests explain why tracking both CPU and latency matters. TCP_NODELAY on accepted sockets moved median p99 from 43.6 to 6.9 ms at 32×4. In the PGO A/B, CPU per message fell about 10% at 1×256 while p99 rose from roughly 14 to 20 ms. Neither experiment establishes a post-fix p99 advantage over Java.

7. Reproducing and extending the results

Use client-production-benchmark for Broker sends and LitePull and grpc_send_benchmark for Proxy sends. The full report has the exact sample commands. Record image digests, build flags, CPU placement, payload size, connections, in-flight limits, flush and replica settings. Keep every run’s JSON, throughput, error counts and tail latency. Repeat with independent load generators and Brokers before planning capacity.

The dedicated-host plan is the next step. The published report does not cover cross-host networking, long runs, failover, cold reads, Push/POP, filtering, many topics and queues, or Proxy consumption.

title: Handling Payment Fumbles: ACH Return Codes and Recovery Logic
description:
Handling Payment Fumbles: ACH Return Codes and Recovery Logic

When Payments Go Wrong: Learning from Failure

In fintech, a failed payout isn't just frustrating—it's a data point. Every ACH return carries a specific code that tells you why the transfer failed. Just like a football team must analyze every turnover, a payment system needs to decode each return and route around it. This article walks through real ACH return codes and how to build logic that doesn't let a single failure break your payout flow.

The ACH Return Code Playbook

The National Automated Clearing House Association (Nacha) defines 85 possible return codes (R01–R85). Each maps to a specific rejection reason. Here are the most common ones you'll encounter:

Code Meaning Reversible? Retry Strategy
R01 Insufficient funds No Retry after 2–5 days or flag for manual review
R03 No account/unable to locate No Route to alternate rail or request new bank details
R04 Invalid account number structure No Request corrected account info from customer
R10 Unauthorized by account holder No Contact customer; may indicate fraud or dispute
R29 Corporate account closed No Update customer records; request new account

R01 (Insufficient Funds) fires when the receiver's account balance can't cover the debit. This is temporary—retry logic works here. Implement exponential backoff: retry at 24 hours, then 48 hours, then escalate to dunning (send a notification asking the receiver to top up).

R03 (No Account) means the account doesn't exist or the routing number is wrong. This is permanent. Don't retry. Instead, flag the receiver's account for manual review and ask them to verify their banking details.

R10 (Unauthorized) suggests the account holder disputed the transaction or blocked ACH debits. This requires human intervention—reach out to the customer directly.

Building a Return Handler

Here's a concrete pattern for handling returns programmatically:

async function handleACHReturn(returnData) {
  const { payoutId, returnCode, receiverId } = returnData;

  const returnLogic = {
    'R01': async () => {
      // Insufficient funds: retry after 48 hours
      await scheduleRetry(payoutId, 48);
      await notifyReceiver(receiverId, 'Please ensure sufficient funds.');
    },
    'R03': async () => {
      // No account: flag for manual review
      await flagForReview(payoutId, 'Invalid account number');
      await requestBankingDetails(receiverId);
    },
    'R04': async () => {
      // Invalid account structure: request correction
      await requestBankingDetails(receiverId);
      await markPayoutFailed(payoutId);
    },
    'R10': async () => {
      // Unauthorized: escalate to support
      await escalateToSupport(payoutId, 'Unauthorized by account holder');
    },
  };

  const handler = returnLogic[returnCode];
  if (handler) {
    await handler();
  } else {
    // Unknown code: log and alert
    await logUnexpectedReturn(payoutId, returnCode);
  }
}

Routing Around Failures

When an ACH return is permanent (R03, R04, R10), don't retry the same rail. Instead, offer an alternate:

  1. Check for a secondary account on file. Many customers link both checking and savings accounts.
  2. Route to RTP (Real-Time Payments) if available. RTP settles in seconds and has lower return rates (~0.1% vs. ACH's ~1%).
  3. Fall back to Visa Direct for card-based payouts (higher cost, but 99%+ success rate). 
async function routeAroundReturn(payoutId, returnCode) {
  const isPermanent = ['R03', 'R04', 'R10', 'R29'].includes(returnCode);

  if (isPermanent) {
    const receiver = await getReceiver(payoutId);

    if (receiver.secondaryBankAccount) {
      return await retryWithAccount(payoutId, receiver.secondaryBankAccount);
    }

    if (receiver.cardOnFile) {
      return await routeToVisaDirect(payoutId, receiver.cardOnFile);
    }

    return await escalateToSupport(payoutId);
  }
}

Reconciliation and Timing

ACH returns arrive 2–5 business days after the original debit. During that window, your payout status should be "pending" or "processing," not "complete." Once a return lands, update your ledger immediately and trigger the appropriate handler.

Track return rates by code and receiver bank. If one bank consistently returns R01, consider requiring a

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.23410v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

title: Meta cria TLX para ampliar o controle de execução em GPUs com Triton
description:
A Meta desenvolveu o Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX) para dar aos engenheiros mais controle sobre a execução em GPUs, mantendo o modelo de programação do Triton. A extensão aproxima as abstrações de alto nível da linguagem do controle de baixo nível necessário para aproveitar recursos das arquiteturas modernas.

GPUs atuais oferecem recursos como especialização de warps, movimentação assíncrona de memória, memória de tensores e execução em nível de cluster. Esses recursos diferem do modelo tradicional do Triton, que simplifica a criação de kernels ao abstrair estruturas de execução de baixo nível, segundo os engenheiros da Meta.

Controle explícito de execução

Em um kernel moderno do FlashAttention, por exemplo, um grupo de warps pode emitir transferências de memória enquanto outro executa cálculos nos núcleos tensoriais. Um kernel GEMM para Blackwell pode coordenar vários grupos de warps, alocações de memória de tensores e recursos de cluster ao mesmo tempo.

Nesses casos, o desempenho depende também de como os grupos de execução cooperam. A Meta afirma que o uso desses recursos exigia grandes quantidades de código de orquestração específico para cada arquitetura, pois as abstrações do compilador Triton não ofereciam acesso direto a essas estruturas.

O modelo MIMW e os recursos do TLX

O TLX introduz o modelo de execução MIMW, de múltiplas instruções e múltiplos warps, que ocupa um espaço entre o controle por thread do CUDA e a abstração por bloco do Triton. A extensão amplia a linguagem em cinco áreas: orquestração de grupos de warps, sincronização, organização da memória, execução em clusters e disposição opcional dos dados.

Com essas funções, desenvolvedores podem continuar usando Python, ajuste automático de parâmetros e programação de tensores em blocos, mas acessar explicitamente estruturas de execução da GPU. A Meta apresenta esse equilíbrio como forma de combinar a produtividade do Triton com um controle mais próximo do oferecido pelo CUDA.

Uso em treinamento e inferência

A empresa afirma usar o TLX em produção há vários meses, em três cargas principais. No treinamento de modelos GEM em milhares de GPUs NVIDIA Blackwell, relata utilização de FLOPs do modelo (MFU) de 20% a 25% no fluxo completo e aceleração de até duas vezes na etapa de passagem direta (forward pass).

Na otimização de transmissão dentro do kernel para inferência de recomendação, a Meta relata aceleração de quatro vezes em uma GPU H100 para um kernel de compressão linear. Em modelos desenvolvidos em conjunto com essa otimização, a latência de redes com uso intensivo de computação caiu em até dois terços.

Em operações GEMM agrupadas e distribuídas para o pré-treinamento de grandes modelos de linguagem, a empresa relata ganhos de desempenho, confiabilidade e facilidade de manutenção em grandes conjuntos de GPUs durante períodos prolongados de treinamento.

Próximos passos

A Meta planeja ampliar o suporte do TLX para outras arquiteturas da NVIDIA, da AMD e para aceleradores personalizados. Também pretende automatizar a orquestração de grupos de warps por meio de abstrações de nível mais alto e integrar a extensão ao torch.compile. A InfoQ detalha a extensão e os resultados relatados pela empresa.

Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/meta-tlx-extensao-triton-controle-execucao-gpu/

title: BullMQ for Beginners: Background Jobs That Actually Scale
description:
Some work should not happen inside a web request. Sending a welcome email, generating a PDF, resizing an image, or processing a payment webhook — if any of these run slowly, your user waits. BullMQ solves this by moving the work into a queue backed by Redis, so your API can respond instantly and the heavy work happens in the background.

The pattern is simple: a producer adds jobs, workers process them.

import { Queue, Worker } from 'bullmq';

const emailQueue = new Queue('emails', {
  connection: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 },
});

// Producer: add a job from your API route
await emailQueue.add('welcome', { userId: 42, email: 'a@example.com' });

// Worker: process jobs somewhere else
const worker = new Worker('emails', async (job) => {
  await sendWelcomeEmail(job.data.email);
}, { connection: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 } });

BullMQ adds the features that make queues production-ready: automatic retries with backoff when a job fails, delayed jobs that run later, rate limiting, job priorities, and a dashboard to see what is stuck. If your email service is down, the job retries instead of disappearing.

One thing to know: BullMQ needs Redis. For a small side project that might be overkill — a simple in-process queue or a cron job may be enough. But once you have real users and real background work, a proper queue is the difference between an app that survives a traffic spike and one that falls over.

BullMQ is for Node.js developers whose apps do slow work — emails, file processing, notifications, webhooks — and want it done reliably in the background instead of inside the request.

title: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware
description:
arXiv:2611.25274v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

title: MotionGrounder: Grounded Multi-Object Motion Transfer via Diffusion Transformer
description:
arXiv:2604.00853v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Motion transfer enables controllable video generation by transferring temporal dynamics from a reference video to synthesize a new video conditioned on a target caption. However, existing Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based methods either transfer the motion of a single object or handle multiple objects without binding each object caption to its object, restricting fine-grained control in real-world scenes. In this work, we introduce MotionGrounder, a training-free DiT-based framework that is the first to jointly handle motion transfer and object grounding in multi-object scenes. Our Flow-based Motion Signal (FMS) in MotionGrounder provides a stable motion prior for target video generation, while our Object-Caption Alignment Loss (OCAL) grounds object captions to their corresponding spatial regions. We further propose two new metrics: the Object Grounding Score (OGS), which jointly evaluates (i) spatial alignment between source video objects and their generated counterparts and (ii) semantic consistency between each generated object and its target caption, and the Motion Grounding Score (MGS), which evaluates whether each object moves like its source object at the correct location. Our experiments show that MotionGrounder improves object grounding over recent baselines, with the advantage appearing once several objects are present, across quantitative, qualitative, and human evaluations.

title: A minus sign before an SCSS interpolation that Biome read as math
description:
Minus signs in SCSS are a little tricky. $a - $b is a subtraction, -$b is a negative value, and 1px 2px is a list. A formatter has to read every minus sign exactly the way Sass does, or it quietly changes your CSS.

That's what issue #12957 was about. The reporter had this:

$s: 8px;
.a {
  margin: -#{$s} -#{$s} -#{$s} auto;
}

and Biome formatted the value as -#{$s} - #{$s} - #{$s} auto. Looks like a spacing tweak. It isn't. The reporter checked with Dart Sass: the original compiles to margin: -8px -8px -8px auto;, the formatted file to margin: -8px-8px-8px auto;. That's invalid CSS, so the browser drops the whole declaration.

I picked it up, and the fix was merged in biomejs/biome#12983.

Why it happened

The formatter wasn't really the problem. It prints the tree the parser gives it. The SCSS parser decides what counts as a binary operator in crates/biome_css_parser/src/syntax/scss/expression/precedence.rs, and its scss_binary_precedence function took every - after a value as subtraction. So -#{$s} -#{$s} became "negative #{$s}, minus #{$s}". Once the tree says subtraction, the formatter prints spaces around the operator.

Sass reads it differently. A - written directly against #{ starts an interpolated identifier. With a space before it, that's simply the next item in the list. Only $a - #{$s}, with a space on both sides, subtracts.

The fix

Both parse_scss_binary_tail and is_at_scss_binary_operator go through scss_binary_precedence, so one check there covers both. I added a small helper:

/// Returns whether the current `-` starts the next item of a space-separated
/// list instead of subtracting: it follows whitespace and is written directly
/// against an interpolation.
///
/// Sass reads a `-` followed by `#{` as the start of an interpolated
/// identifier, so `-#{$s} -#{$s}` is a two-item list (`-8px -8px`), while
/// `$a - #{$b}` subtracts.
///
/// Docs: https://sass-lang.com/documentation/operators/numeric/#unary-operators
#[inline]
fn is_at_scss_negated_interpolation_list_item(p: &mut CssParser) -> bool {
    p.at(T![-])
        && (p.has_nth_preceding_whitespace(0) || p.has_nth_preceding_line_break(0))
        && is_nth_at_scss_interpolation(p, 1)
        && is_nth_source_tight(p, 1)
}

In words: a minus, with a space or a line break before it, followed by #{ with nothing in between. When that's true, it's not a binary operator:

if !p.at_ts(SCSS_BINARY_OPERATOR_TOKEN_SET) || is_at_scss_negated_interpolation_list_item(p) {
    return None;
}

I kept it narrow on purpose. It only looks at #{, so height: 1 -$s; still parses as a subtraction, same as before.

Tests, and two snapshots that moved

I added the same input as a parser spec and a formatter spec:

$s: 8px;

.a {
  margin: -#{$s} -#{$s} -#{$s} auto;
  padding: 1px -#{$s};
  width: $a - #{$s};
  height: 1 -$s;
  inset: -#{$s}
    -#{$s};
}

The formatter now leaves margin and padding as written, keeps $a - #{$s} as a subtraction, prints height as 1 - $s like it always did, and joins the two line inset into -#{$s} -#{$s}. Both specs fail without the parser change.

Two existing snapshots changed too. In the Prettier compatibility snapshot parens.scss, the line prop25-4 used to come out as #{$width} - #{$width} where Prettier keeps #{$width} -#{$width}. Now Biome matches Prettier on that pair.

The bigger one showed up when I ran the whole parser suite. The ok/scss/value/minus-operator.scss snapshot, a matrix of subtraction cases, had 17 cases recorded as subtractions, all of the same shape: a space before, the minus tight against #{, like 10 -#{10} and #{10} -#{10}. I checked them against Sass's own conformance tests in sass/sass-spec, and Sass's expected output keeps every one of them as separate values. So I updated that snapshot as well.

ematipico merged it on 6 November 2026, the same day I opened it, with no changes asked. Thanks!

What I'm keeping from this one

When a formatter changes what your code means, look at the parser first. The formatter here did exactly what the tree told it to.

The reporter's compiled output was the best part of the issue. -8px-8px-8px next to -8px -8px -8px made the bug obvious in one line.

And run the whole suite, not only your new tests. Those 17 cases sat in an existing snapshot.

Do you write negative interpolations like this in your SCSS, or do you wrap them in parentheses to be safe? I'd like to hear what your team does.
