title: Do Not Flatten the Clusters: Connecting Kubernetes Across Clouds Without Merging Their Trust Boundaries
description:
The fastest way to connect two Kubernetes clusters in different clouds is also the most dangerous way: join them into one flat network, share service discovery, and let any pod in one cluster reach any service in the other. It demos well. It also means a compromised workload in the least protected cluster now has a network path into every cluster, and an outage or a bad route in one place can spread to all of them.

Multi-cloud Kubernetes is common for ordinary reasons. One cloud hosts the GPU training cluster, another hosts the customer facing services, a third was inherited or chosen for a specific managed service. The clusters need to talk. They do not need to become one cluster, and they should not become one trust zone.

Start with the flows, not with connectivity

Before choosing any tool, list the actual cross-cluster flows. In most estates the real list is short:

  • A named service in cluster A calls a named service in cluster B, on a known port, for a known reason.
  • A data job reads from or writes to a store that happens to live near the other cluster.
  • Operators need logs, metrics, and traces from both clusters in one place.

That list is the design. If a flow is not on it, it should not work by default. Connectivity products and mesh tools make it easy to connect everything first and restrict later, but later rarely arrives. Start restricted, with the named flows working, and add flows deliberately as teams request them with an owner and a reason.

This also settles the addressing argument early. Pod and service address ranges often overlap between clusters, especially when each cluster was built from the same tutorial defaults. Overlap only matters for flows that actually cross. A gateway pattern, described below, avoids renumbering every cluster just so that two services can talk.

Connect services through gateways, not networks through tunnels

Treat each cluster as its own network domain, with its own pod ranges, service ranges, policies, and failure modes. Between domains, place an explicit crossing point:

  1. Each cluster exposes only the services that other clusters are allowed to use, through a dedicated gateway or egress and ingress pair, not through direct pod to pod routing.
  2. Traffic crosses the private cross-cloud path between those gateways, so the path can be measured, encrypted, and audited in one place.
  3. Inside the receiving cluster, the gateway hands traffic to the target service only. It does not become a general router into the pod network.

The cost is a small amount of extra latency and one more component to run. The gain is large: each cluster keeps its own addressing, its own network policy, and its own blast radius. A route leak, a misconfigured policy, or a noisy workload inside one cluster stays inside that cluster, because there is no flat network for it to leak across.

It also makes the cross-cloud path honest. When all cross-cluster traffic passes through known gateways, capacity, errors, and latency on that path can be measured per flow. When traffic can cross anywhere, nobody can say which flows depend on the link until the link fails.

Identity should cross, addresses should not be trusted

On a flat network, teams quietly start trusting source addresses: allow traffic from the other cluster range. That trust is misplaced. An address says where a packet came from, not which workload sent it or whether that workload was allowed to call this service.

Use workload identity at the gateway and at the receiving service:

  • Each calling service presents a verifiable identity, issued per cluster and rotated automatically, rather than a shared secret copied between clusters.
  • The receiving service authorises the calling identity for that specific operation, not the source network for all operations.
  • Identity mappings are written down per flow, matching the flow list from the first section, so a reviewer can check who can call what without reading packet rules.

This is where many multi-cloud designs quietly fail. The two clouds issue identity differently, so teams fall back to network rules because they work everywhere. Resist that fallback for cross-cluster calls. Network rules can stay as a second layer, limiting which gateways can talk, while identity decides which workloads can.

Keep discovery local, publish a small directory

Shared global service discovery sounds convenient and creates a hidden dependency: when discovery breaks or returns stale answers, calls fail across every cluster at once, and a service that was only meant to be local becomes reachable everywhere because it was registered globally.

A safer pattern is boring. Each cluster keeps its own local discovery for its own services. For the small set of cross-cluster services, publish a small, explicit directory: name, owning team, gateway address, port, and the identity allowed to call it. That directory can be configuration in the gateway or a simple internal record, as long as it is reviewed like code and changes to it are visible.

When a cross-cluster service moves, only its directory entry changes. When a team wants a new cross-cluster dependency, adding the entry is the review point. That friction is a feature. Cross-cluster dependencies are architectural decisions, not accidents of discovery.

Plan for one cluster to be down, or untrusted

Two failure questions should be answered before the design ships:

First, if one cluster is down, what should the other cluster do? With gateway connections and local discovery, the answer can be per flow: queue the work, serve a cached answer, or fail that one feature. On a flat joined network, the failure tends to be global and surprising, because timeouts and retries cross the boundary in ways nobody listed.

Second, if one cluster is compromised, what can an attacker reach? The honest answer should be: the gateway, and only the services and operations that gateway was allowed to present, with identities that the compromised cluster cannot mint for other clusters. Test this. From a test workload in one cluster, try to reach a service that is not on the flow list, a pod address directly, and the other cluster API. All three should fail, and the attempts should be visible in logs.

Retries deserve a specific mention here. A calling service that retries aggressively across a slow cross-cloud path can turn a small problem in one cluster into a load problem in both. Set retry budgets and timeouts for cross-cluster calls separately from local calls, and make them stricter, because the path is longer and the shared resource, the link, is smaller.

A practical rollout order

For an estate connecting clusters that already exist, this order works without a flag day:

  1. Inventory the flows that already cross informally, including scripts, jobs, and operator access, not just application calls.
  2. Stand up the gateways on the private path and route one low risk flow through them, measuring latency and errors against the old route.
  3. Add identity checks for that flow, then remove the old network level permission for it.
  4. Move remaining flows one at a time, deleting the broad rule that made the informal route work only after the last flow has moved.
  5. Run the down cluster and untrusted cluster tests, and record the results with the flow list.

Notice what is not in that list: renumbering clusters, replacing the container network, or adopting a single control plane for every cluster. Those may be worth doing for other reasons, but they are not prerequisites for safe cross-cluster traffic, and tying them together turns a bounded network project into an open ended platform rebuild.

The design point

Clusters in different clouds need to cooperate, not merge. Keep each cluster as its own domain, cross between domains only at gateways, authorise workloads by identity rather than by address, publish only the services that are genuinely shared, and test what happens when one side is down or untrusted.

That kind of bounded, private multi-cloud design across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Oracle estates is part of the work described at CloudVerg, where VergMesh covers multi-cloud networking and VergShield covers zero-trust security, alongside SOC 2 readiness support and managed services.

The test is simple. Pick any service in one cluster and ask what it can reach in the other, who approved that reach, and what happens if the other cluster disappears. If the team can answer from a short flow list, the clusters are connected well. If the answer is everything, they are not connected. They are flattened.

title: Your AI tool changed this week. Would your team know?
description:
Most teams version-pin their dependencies, read changelogs and get a pull request when a library bumps. Then they hand a chunk of their daily work to an AI service that can change under them with no version bump at all.

This week the Ada Lovelace Institute published a feature called Running up that bill? (Charlie Grossman, 16 November 2026). It catalogues how AI subscriptions have changed what they deliver while the price stayed put. It's written about consumer plans, but it says organisations on business plans "remain exposed to practices like plan repricing or changes to how usage is counted."

Here's the engineering version, and a small fix.

What the feature documents

Some of the examples from the past 15 months, as the feature reports them:

  • Anthropic cut Claude Code's weekly limits by 17% after a temporary increase.
  • A new Anthropic tokeniser produced up to 35% more tokens for the same text.
  • OpenAI cut the reasoning time behind GPT-5.2 Thinking's "standard" setting and kept the name.
  • OpenAI's GPT-5 router sent some requests to less capable model variants.
  • OpenAI acknowledged an issue that applied the wrong usage limits to 40,000 accounts.

It isn't only pricing games

Two older data points matter more to engineers, because they're about quality, not allowances.

In 2023, Chen, Zaharia and Zou compared the March and June versions of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. On identifying prime numbers, GPT-4 fell from 84% accuracy to 51%. GPT-3.5 improved on the same task. Their conclusion was that the same named service can change a lot in a short time and needs continuous monitoring.

In September 2025, Anthropic published a postmortem of three infrastructure bugs that intermittently degraded Claude's output between August and early September. At the worst hour, one routing bug hit 16% of Sonnet 4 requests. Anthropic said plainly these were bugs, not demand-based cuts. The bit I'd underline is its admission that "we relied too heavily on noisy evaluations."

If the provider's own evals missed it, "the model feels off today" in Slack is not a detection strategy.

My inference: treat the AI service like a dependency you can't pin

This is my mapping onto engineering work, not something the sources prescribe.

You probably can't pin a consumer chat plan. You can still do the three things you'd do for any upstream you don't control:

  1. Record the contract. Plan, model names, stated limits, reasoning setting, price. Write it down on the day you adopt the tool.
  2. Run a canary. A fixed set of your own tasks, run on a schedule, scored the same way every time.
  3. Keep a change log. One table where canary results and provider announcements sit side by side.

Build the canary set in an afternoon

  • Pick 10 to 20 tasks from real work: a function with existing unit tests, a SQL query with a known result set, a log excerpt with a known root cause, a diff with a known bug.
  • Prefer tasks with a mechanical pass mark. Tests pass, query matches, bug found. Skip anything that needs a long debate to grade.
  • Fix the prompt, settings and context. Store them in the repo next to the expected answers.
  • Run it weekly, same day, and record pass count, wall-clock time and tokens where the API reports them. The feature notes that API responses come back with a token count, which consumer web apps don't show.
  • Expect noise. The feature cites a 2026 study where the most expensive run of the same coding task typically used around twice the tokens of the cheapest. Look for a shift that holds across two runs, not one bad Tuesday.

If you're on the API, pin a dated model version where the provider offers one, and treat a version change like a dependency upgrade: run the canary before you switch.

The artefact: an AI service change log

Copy this into your repo as ai-service-log.md. The rows are labelled examples to show the shape. They are not measurements from the sources.

| Week | Tool / plan / model | Canary pass (of 20) | Median time | Tokens (API) | Provider change seen | Our change | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EXAMPLE 2026-W45 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 18 | 41s | 212k | None | None | Baseline recorded |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W46 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 18 | 44s | 260k | Changelog: new tokeniser | None | Watch token use, check allowance |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W47 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 14 | 63s | 255k | None found | Longer system prompt | Revert prompt, rerun before blaming vendor |
| EXAMPLE 2026-W48 | Assistant X, team plan, default model | 14 | 61s | 250k | None found | Prompt reverted | Raise ticket with vendor, attach W45 vs W48 |

Two columns do the real work. "Our change" stops you blaming the vendor for your own prompt edits. "Provider change seen" forces someone to actually read the changelog and status page each week.

What to ask before you renew

Take these to your next renewal:

  • How much notice do we get before models, limits, reasoning settings or usage counting change?
  • Can we export usage data per user and per request?
  • What credit applies if a bug drains our allowance?

Consumer plans give weak answers to all three, the feature argues. Business contracts are where you can get better ones.

Sources

  • Running up that bill?, Charlie Grossman, Ada Lovelace Institute, 16 November 2026.
  • How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?, Chen, Zaharia and Zou, arXiv, July 2023.
  • A postmortem of three recent issues, Anthropic, 17 September 2025.

Has your team ever caught an AI tool getting worse with actual numbers, or was it gut feel every time?

We build Nodus, so read this with that in mind. Every competitor number links to that company's own page, and every total is written out so you can redo it with the rates you see today.

What does Denvr Dataworks offer for training today?

Denvr sells GPU machines by the hour, on demand or reserved. Its pricing page lists an 8-GPU NVIDIA H100 SXM node at $3.00 per GPU-hour with 3,200 Gbps InfiniBand. On-demand instances are billed by the minute, and reserved contracts save up to 20% on multi-month or annual terms. The same page lists the A100 SXM 80 GB at $2.00, the GH200 at $3.87, Intel Gaudi 2 at $2.00, and the H200 SXM as reserved only.

Its homepage describes data centers in Canada and the USA, clusters of up to 1,024 GPUs, managed inference endpoints and shared NVMe storage. It also runs a startup program that starts with a $1,000 credit and goes up to $500,000 for eligible teams.

That is a solid offer for steady cluster work. The reasons people look elsewhere are usually the on-demand H100 rate, a wish to stop managing machines, or a job that must keep going when a machine disappears.

Billing unit Per minute Prepaid, with a spend cap per job Per second
Largest training setup Up to 1,024 GPUs Up to 8 nodes (Beta) 16 to 2,000+ GPUs
Recovery when a machine is lost Restores the job's saved state on new capacity

Prices checked November 20, 2026: Denvr pricing, Denvr homepage, Nodus pricing, Nodus multi-node docs, Nodus checkpoint docs, Together AI pricing, Runpod pricing, Lambda pricing and CoreWeave pricing. CoreWeave's figures are for its 8-GPU NVIDIA HGX H100 instance.

What does the same 72-hour, 8 x H100 run cost on each?

We priced one job everywhere: a fine-tune or continued-pretraining run on one 8 x H100 machine for 72 hours. That is 8 x 72 = 576 GPU-hours. Each total is 576 times the per-GPU rate, except CoreWeave, which prices the whole 8-GPU instance, so its total is 72 x $49.24.

Provider H100 rate 72 hours on 8 GPUs
Nodus $2.60/GPU-hr $1,497.60
Denvr Dataworks on-demand $3.00/GPU-hr $1,728.00
Together AI GPU Clusters on-demand $3.99/GPU-hr $2,298.24
Runpod Secure Cloud $4.39/GPU-hr $2,528.64
Lambda 8 x H100 instance $4.59/GPU-hr $2,643.84
CoreWeave on-demand $49.24/instance-hr $3,545.28

Same sources and check date as the first table. GPU compute only: storage and data transfer are not included for anyone.


At list prices the 72-hour run costs $230.40 less on Nodus than on Denvr, about 13% less.

Two cheaper tiers sit outside the chart because they are not on-demand. Together AI lists preemptible H100 at $1.99, which would make the job $1,146.24, and CoreWeave lists spot at $19.71 per instance-hour, which would make it $1,419.12. Both can beat Nodus on paper if your training code saves state often and you accept those providers' terms for interruptible capacity.

Is a Denvr reservation cheaper than paying on demand?

A reservation wins only if you keep the machine busy almost all the time. Denvr says reserved contracts save up to 20%, so the best case for the H100 is $3.00 x 0.8 = $2.40 per GPU-hour. That is below the $2.60 Nodus listing, and it is the one place in this comparison where Denvr's own price beats ours.

The catch is that a reservation bills every hour of the term. Take one 8 x H100 node for a 730-hour month. At the best-case discount the reservation costs 8 x $2.40 x 730 = $14,016 whether you use it or not.

Nodus on demand costs 8 x $2.60 = $20.80 for each hour you actually run. It stays cheaper until you use $14,016 / $20.80 = 673.8 hours, about 92% of the month. Denvr's own on-demand rate of $24.00 per node-hour crosses at 584 hours, which is 80%.

Hours used in the month Nodus on demand Denvr on demand Denvr reserved, best case
200 $4,160 $4,800 $14,016
400 $8,320 $9,600 $14,016
600 $12,480 $14,400 $14,016
730 $15,184 $17,520 $14,016

Rates from the Denvr pricing page and Nodus pricing page, checked November 20, 2026. The 20% is Denvr's stated maximum; your quoted discount may be smaller, which moves the crossover later.


A best-case Denvr reservation only pays off past about 674 busy hours a month, roughly 92% utilization.

Our decision rule from this math: reserve on Denvr if one node will run above about 92% of every month for the whole term. Below that, pay on demand. For the wider version of this tradeoff, see reserved vs on-demand GPUs.

Can you keep spending Denvr credits while you move to Nodus?

Yes, for single-node work. The Nodus cloud-accounts docs list Denvr among the providers you can connect, first to view your existing instances and then, as a separate Beta step, to run work in your own account. Denvr asks for an API key, the cluster your credits or quota are in (Msc1 or Hou1) and optionally a VPC.

Once you choose "Run work in my account" and set a spending limit, Nodus places your single-node Jobs in that account first. Denvr bills the machine and disk against your credits, and Nodus adds a route fee of $0.02 per device-hour. On the 72-hour job that is 576 x $0.02 = $11.52. Sandboxes and multi-node runs still use Nodus capacity.

This matters most if you joined Denvr's startup program. You can burn down the credit balance with the same job definitions you will use afterwards, instead of keeping two workflows. Check what you have connected with the command from the docs:

nodus get cloudaccounts

For other ways to stretch credits, see how startups get GPU credits.

What happens to a multi-day run when a machine fails?

On Nodus, the job comes back with its saved state. Your script writes weights, optimizer state and the step counter under /nodus/state. When the capacity under a job is reclaimed, the next attempt starts with that directory restored, as the checkpoint guide describes. The script must load what it saved, because a restored attempt starts your command from the beginning.

On a machine you hold yourself, at Denvr or any provider in the table, recovery is your job: notice the failure, start a new machine and relaunch from your last checkpoint. That is fine when you watch the run. It is costly over a weekend, because the idle hours before you notice are still billed.

Where is Denvr Dataworks the better choice?

Denvr is the better pick in several specific cases, and we would tell you to stay in them.

  • You need data to stay in Canada. Denvr runs sovereign Canadian infrastructure and supports Canadian organizations qualified for the ISED Canada AI Compute Access Fund. If residency is a hard requirement, that alone is a reason to stay.
  • You train across more than 64 GPUs. Denvr describes clusters up to 1,024 GPUs on 3,200 Gbps InfiniBand. Nodus multi-node training is in Beta with a ceiling of 8 nodes.
  • You will keep a reserved node above roughly 92% busy. At the best-case discount Denvr's $2.40 per GPU-hour beats our $2.60 listing.
  • You want Intel Gaudi 2 or NVIDIA GH200. Denvr lists both; the Nodus pricing page lists neither.
  • You want one vendor for the whole stack, including managed inference endpoints and shared NVMe storage next to the cluster.

If none of these apply and you mostly run single-node jobs of hours or days, the on-demand math points elsewhere.

How do you move a Denvr training job to Nodus?

Keep your training script and change how it is launched. Install the CLI and sign in, as the install docs show:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login

Then submit the run. This is the eight-GPU example from the nodus run reference, detached so it keeps going after you close the terminal. Raise --max-cost from the example's $40 to your budget; the 72-hour job above is $1,497.60 at list price.

nodus run --gpu H100:8 --max-cost 40 -d -- torchrun train.py

Point your checkpoint path at /nodus/state so a restored attempt can pick up where it stopped. If you are coming from another provider too, Runpod alternatives and SF Compute alternatives cover the same ground for those platforms.

FAQ

Is Denvr Dataworks cheaper than Lambda for H100s?

At on-demand list prices, yes. Denvr lists the H100 SXM at $3.00 per GPU-hour and Lambda lists its 8-GPU H100 instance at $4.59, so the 72-hour job is $1,728.00 against $2,643.84.

What is a cheaper alternative to Denvr for A100 training?

Nodus lists the A100 80 GB at $1.09 per GPU-hour against Denvr's $2.00 for the A100 SXM 80 GB. For 576 GPU-hours that is $627.84 on Nodus and $1,152.00 on Denvr.

Does Nodus charge extra when it runs jobs in my Denvr account?

Nodus adds a route fee of $0.02 per device-hour for GPU Jobs in your own account, and Denvr bills the machine and disk as usual. Your account spending limit uses Nodus's estimate of cloud costs, which can differ from Denvr's actual invoice.

Can I run multi-node training in my own Denvr account through Nodus?

Not today. Running in your own account covers Jobs, Workspaces and other single-node work; multi-node runs use Nodus capacity, up to 8 nodes in Beta.

Does Denvr bill by the second?

No. Denvr's pricing page says on-demand instances are billed by the minute. Runpod bills by the second, and Nodus enforces a dollar cap you set per job.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: Backports and Version Claims for CVE-2026-121810
description:
Backports and Version Claims for CVE-2026-121810

An NGINX version string is a starting clue, not a patch receipt. CVE-2026-121810 affects official Open Source releases 1.25.0 through 1.31.8, but distributions may retain an older-looking version while carrying a backported security fix. Container images may show the inverse: a current tag that still contains an old binary layer. Accurate assurance needs package and process evidence.

Vulnerability overview

F5 published CVE-2026-121810 on November 18, 2026. It is a use-after-free in HTTP/3 stream handling, CWE-416, with CVSS 3.1 score 8.1 and high attack complexity. The NGINX advisory labels it medium severity. The upstream fixes are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9; NGINX Plus branches include 37.0.0 before 37.0.8.1, 37.1.0 before 37.3.0.1, and R34 through R36.

No confirmed in-the-wild exploitation or KEV entry was reported in the public advisory material at publication.

Mechanism and exploitation conditions

HTTP/3 request streams are children of a QUIC connection and consume worker connection slots. During stream creation, NGINX protects the parent from drain by removing it from a reusable queue. The new stream is not in the parent's tree until after the slot allocation. An idle sibling can close during that interval, cause the shutdown check to miss the in-progress stream, and requeue the parent.

The request's upstream connect then allocates another slot and can drain the parent. NGINX frees the request pool while the connection routine still holds an upstream pointer. Xint demonstrated worker-privilege code execution using HTTP/3 proxying and a controlled listener. The vendor notes that more conditions must align than the version range alone.

Impact

The issue can crash or restart workers, interrupting service and obscuring the trigger in ordinary request logs. Successful exploitation can execute code with the worker's rights and expose backend paths or local configuration. The CVE does not itself establish root or control-plane compromise.

Affected products and scope

The affected scope is a vulnerable binary with HTTP/3 and an upstream proxy path. Backports can make a reported version safe, while an unpatched fork or stale container layer can keep it vulnerable. A fixed upstream version may also be present in an image that is not the process actually serving traffic.

For package assurance, record the full package version, vendor advisory, binary hash, container digest, and process start time. Inspect the effective configuration for QUIC listeners and upstream behavior. Verify IPv4 and IPv6 reachability separately.

Exposure context

The selected ZoomEye Search app="NGINX" returned 316,219,992 product fingerprints. The CVE Filter returned 0. Exposure is 316,219,992 under the maximum-count rule.

That figure is not a version report and cannot resolve backports. It is useful for identifying a large product surface, but remediation evidence must come from the owned package and running process.

Remediation and mitigations

Install a fixed package or vendor backport and restart or live-upgrade the executable. Verify that worker processes use the new binary, not merely that the package database changed. For containers, rebuild the image, pin the package layer, and confirm the digest that runs in production.

If a patch cannot be deployed immediately, disable HTTP/3 by removing QUIC listeners and setting http3 off. Clear Alt-Svc and verify the effective socket state. A firewall can reduce reachability, but it is a containment layer and may not cover every network path.

Document the advisory mapping and retain the exact evidence used to approve closure. Re-check after rollbacks, base-image refreshes, or configuration imports because these operations can reintroduce an old binary or listener. A version string without package and process proof should remain an open assurance question.

References

  • NGINX security advisories
  • NCSC advisory on F5 NGINX vulnerabilities
  • Red Hat CVE-2026-121810
  • Xint NGINX2Root technical analysis
  • NGINX 1.31.9 release note

title: AWS CloudFormation Service-Managed StackSets adds custom execution roles with nested stacks support
description:
AWS CloudFormation StackSets now supports custom execution roles for service-managed stack sets, which enables you to scope the permissions StackSets uses in each target AWS account. StackSets deploys the same infrastructure, such as networking and security settings, across thousands of accounts and Regions in one operation. With a custom execution role, you can also use nested stacks, macros, and transforms in service-managed stack sets, which allows you to deploy the reusable templates you use for individual stacks across your organization.

With a custom execution role, you define what StackSets can do in each account. By default, service-managed stack sets use a role in each account that can provision any resource in a template without additional setup, and that default remains available. Now, you can provide a template that defines an IAM role, called the execution role, and StackSets creates it in each account before deploying. For example, a stack set that creates Amazon S3 buckets can use an execution role limited to CloudFormation and Amazon S3 permissions. When you update the execution role template, StackSets updates the role in every account it deployed to.

To get started, choose Set execution role when you create a stack set in the CloudFormation console, or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit the documentation and the AWS DevOps Blog. This feature is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. Refer to the AWS Region table for details.

title: Pull-request-only preset now available for preview builds
description:
A new Ignored Build Step preset lets you skip preview builds for branches without an open pull request. Production deployments and previews for branches with open pull requests continue to build.

On GitHub and GitLab projects, skipped preview deployments are canceled before consuming any Build CPU Minutes.

To enable this, open your project’s Deployments > Configuration. Under Ignored Build Step, select Only build previews for pull requests from the Behavior menu and click Save.

Learn more in the Ignored Build Step documentation.

title: Python Number Programs: Spy Number, Perfect Number & Neon Number
description:
While learning Python, I started practising different number-based programs to improve my logical thinking and problem-solving skills.

In this blog, I'm going to explore three interesting number programs:

  1. Spy Number
  2. Perfect Number
  3. Neon Number

Let's understand each one with an example and Python code using while loops.

1. Spy Number

A Spy Number is a number where the sum of its digits is equal to the product of its digits.

Example: 1124

Digits: 1, 1, 2, 4

Sum of digits:

1 + 1 + 2 + 4 = 8

Product of digits:

1 × 1 × 2 × 4 = 8

Since both results are equal, 1124 is a Spy Number.

Python Code:

num = 1124
temp = num

total = 0
product = 1

while temp > 0:
    digit = temp % 10

    total += digit
    product *= digit

    temp //= 10

if total == product:
    print("Spy Number")
else:
    print("Not a Spy Number")

Output:

Spy Number

2. Perfect Number

A Perfect Number is a number whose sum of proper divisors is equal to the original number.

Example: 6

The proper divisors of 6 are:

1, 2, 3

Sum of divisors:

1 + 2 + 3 = 6

Since the sum is equal to the original number, 6 is a Perfect Number.

Python Code:

num = 6
i = 1
total = 0

while i < num//2:
    if num % i == 0:
        total += i

    i += 1

if total == num:
    print("Perfect Number")
else:
    print("Not a Perfect Number")

Output:

Perfect Number

3. Neon Number

A Neon Number is a number where the sum of the digits of its square is equal to the original number.

Example: 9

First, calculate the square:

9 × 9 = 81

Now calculate the sum of its digits:

8 + 1 = 9

Since the sum is equal to the original number, 9 is a Neon Number.

Python Code:

num = 9
square = num * num
total = 0

while square > 0:
    digit = square % 10

    total += digit
    square //= 10

if total == num:
    print("Neon Number")
else:
    print("Not a Neon Number")

Output:

Neon Number

title: Understanding the Java Developer Role: Backend Systems, APIs, and Cloud Operations
description:
Java has been a core enterprise language for decades, and it is still behind a large share of banking systems, e-commerce platforms, logistics software, telecom networks, and internal business applications. Yet "Java developer" is one of the most loosely used job titles in technology. In one company it means someone fixing a legacy monolith. In another it means someone designing cloud-native microservices, owning APIs, and being on call for production.

This guide clarifies what a Java developer actually does today, with a focus on three areas that define the role: backend systems, APIs, and cloud operations. It is useful for hiring managers writing job descriptions, SMB leaders deciding what to ask for, and developers mapping their own growth.

What a Java Developer Does

At its core, a Java developer designs, builds, tests, and maintains server-side software that runs on the Java Virtual Machine. That software typically handles business logic, data processing, integrations, and communication with other systems.

Day to day, the work usually includes:

  • Turning business requirements into working, maintainable code
  • Designing and building services and APIs
  • Working with databases and messaging systems
  • Writing automated tests and reviewing teammates' code
  • Diagnosing performance and reliability problems
  • Packaging, deploying, and monitoring applications
  • Collaborating with product owners, QA, operations, and security teams

The weight given to each activity varies by seniority and by how much the team practices DevOps. Modern Java roles increasingly include operational responsibility, which is why cloud skills now sit alongside language skills.

Part 1: Backend Systems

The Foundation

Backend work centers on the logic and data that users never see directly. A strong Java developer has solid command of:

  • Core Java: Object-oriented design, collections, generics, exceptions, streams, and the language features added in recent releases. Many teams run long-term support versions, so familiarity with current LTS versions and migration between them is valuable.
  • Concurrency: Threads, executors, synchronization, and the newer lightweight concurrency features. Concurrency bugs are among the hardest to diagnose, so depth here separates strong developers from average ones.
  • JVM understanding: Memory management, garbage collection behavior, profiling, and tuning. Production issues often come down to heap usage, thread contention, or slow startup.
  • Build and dependency tools: Maven or Gradle, dependency management, and reproducible builds.

Frameworks

Most Java backends use a framework to avoid reinventing common plumbing.

  • Spring and Spring Boot dominate enterprise work, covering dependency injection, web services, data access, security, and configuration.
  • Quarkus, Micronaut, and similar frameworks focus on fast startup and low memory use, suiting containers and serverless.
  • Jakarta EE underpins many established enterprise systems.

A good developer understands what the framework does under the hood, not just which annotation to add.

Data and Persistence

  • Relational databases and SQL: Schema design, indexing, query tuning, and transactions. Poor database design is a common root cause of slow applications.
  • ORM and data access: Hibernate and JPA, plus an awareness of their pitfalls, such as inefficient queries and lazy loading surprises.
  • NoSQL and caching: Document stores, key-value stores, and caches, used where they genuinely fit.
  • Messaging and streaming: Queues and event streaming platforms for asynchronous processing and decoupled services.
  • Migrations: Versioned schema changes that can be applied safely.

Architecture Patterns

  • Layered and modular monoliths, which remain a sensible choice for many teams
  • Microservices, with their benefits and operational costs
  • Event-driven architectures
  • Domain-driven design concepts for modeling complex business rules
  • Resilience patterns, such as retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, and idempotency

A mature developer chooses architecture based on the problem and the team, rather than following fashion. Microservices adopted without the operational maturity to run them often create more problems than they solve.

Quality Practices

  • Unit, integration, and contract testing
  • Test-driven or test-supported development where appropriate
  • Code review and static analysis
  • Clear logging and error handling
  • Documentation of decisions and interfaces

Part 2: APIs

APIs are how Java services talk to the outside world, and increasingly how most business capability is delivered.

Designing APIs

  • REST is the most common style, using resources, standard HTTP methods, and sensible status codes.
  • GraphQL suits clients that need flexible queries, though it adds complexity around performance and authorization.
  • gRPC and similar RPC approaches suit high-performance internal service communication.
  • Event-based and webhook interfaces support asynchronous integration.

Good API design emphasizes consistency, clear naming, versioning strategy, pagination, helpful error responses, and backward compatibility. An API is a contract. Breaking it breaks other people's systems.

Specification and Documentation

Developers should be comfortable defining APIs with a specification such as OpenAPI, generating documentation, and keeping the spec in sync with the code. Contract-first design helps teams agree on interfaces before implementation and supports automated testing.

Security

API security is a core part of the role, not a specialist add-on.

  • Authentication and authorization: OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, token handling, and permission checks on every request, including object-level authorization.
  • Input validation and output filtering, so only necessary data is returned
  • Rate limiting and abuse protection
  • Secrets management, keeping credentials out of code and configuration files
  • Dependency vulnerability management, since Java projects pull in many third-party libraries
  • Secure handling of personal and sensitive data

Broken authorization is among the most common and damaging API flaws, so developers should test it deliberately rather than assume the framework covers it.

Integration

  • Consuming third-party APIs safely, with timeouts, retries, and fallback behavior
  • Handling partial failures and unreliable networks
  • Mapping between external and internal data models
  • Working with legacy interfaces, such as SOAP, file-based exchanges, or message formats still common in enterprise settings

Performance and Reliability

  • Efficient serialization and payload sizes
  • Caching strategies
  • Asynchronous and non-blocking approaches where they make sense
  • Load testing and capacity planning
  • Observability for each endpoint, including latency, error rates, and traffic

Part 3: Cloud Operations

The modern Java developer is expected to understand where and how their code runs. The extent of operational ownership varies, but the trend is toward "you build it, you help run it."

Containers and Orchestration

  • Packaging applications as container images, with small, secure, reproducible builds
  • Understanding resource limits and how the JVM behaves inside containers
  • Working with Kubernetes or a managed container platform, at least at the level of deployments, configuration, health checks, and scaling
  • Alternatively, using serverless or platform-as-a-service offerings where appropriate

Cloud Platforms

Familiarity with at least one major cloud provider is valuable, including:

  • Compute options and when to use each
  • Managed databases, queues, caches, and storage
  • Identity and access management
  • Networking basics, such as private networks, load balancers, and DNS
  • Cost awareness, since poorly sized services quietly burn budget

CI/CD and Release Practices

  • Automated build, test, and deployment pipelines
  • Environment promotion, from development through staging to production
  • Feature flags, blue-green and canary releases, and rollback procedures
  • Infrastructure as code, using tools such as Terraform or provider-native options
  • Secure handling of build secrets and artifacts

Observability and Incident Response

  • Logging: Structured, searchable, and free of sensitive data
  • Metrics: Application, JVM, and business metrics with meaningful alerts
  • Tracing: Following requests across services
  • Dashboards and alerts that signal real problems without creating noise
  • Incident handling: Participating in on-call rotations, diagnosing production issues, writing postmortems, and fixing root causes

Security and Compliance in the Cloud

  • Least-privilege access for services and people
  • Scanning of code, dependencies, and images
  • Patching of base images and runtime versions
  • Encryption in transit and at rest
  • Awareness of data residency and privacy obligations

Cost and Capacity

Developers who understand how their design choices affect cloud bills, such as chatty service calls, oversized instances, or unbounded logging, deliver more value than those who treat infrastructure as someone else's problem.

Skills by Seniority

Junior developer. Solid core Java, basic Spring usage, SQL, version control, unit testing, and the ability to implement well-defined tasks with guidance. Learning how production systems run.

Mid-level developer. Independent delivery of features end to end, good API design, database performance awareness, containerization, CI/CD use, and the ability to debug production issues.

Senior developer. Architectural judgment, mentoring, cross-team design, performance and reliability ownership, security awareness, and the ability to weigh trade-offs and communicate them to non-technical stakeholders.

Staff, principal, or tech lead. Setting technical direction, standards, and strategy across teams, managing technical debt, and aligning engineering decisions with business goals.

Titles vary between companies, so judge by demonstrated responsibility rather than label.

Soft Skills That Matter

  • Clear written and verbal communication
  • Ability to clarify ambiguous requirements
  • Collaboration across product, QA, operations, and security
  • Ownership of outcomes, not just tasks
  • Willingness to learn as the ecosystem evolves
  • Pragmatism in choosing simple solutions

For Hiring Managers: Writing a Realistic Role

  • Separate must-have from nice-to-have. Few people are experts in every framework, cloud, and tool listed in a typical job posting.
  • Describe the actual work. Legacy maintenance, greenfield development, API platform work, and operations-heavy roles attract different people.
  • State on-call expectations honestly.
  • Specify the stack in use, including Java version, frameworks, databases, cloud provider, and deployment approach.
  • Assess through realistic exercises, such as designing an API, reviewing code, or debugging a scenario, rather than trivia.
  • Test for operational awareness if the role includes production ownership.
  • Consider growth potential. A strong developer with a related stack can often learn your tools faster than a weaker one who ticks every keyword.

Interview Areas Worth Probing

  1. Explaining a past system they built, including trade-offs and mistakes
  2. Designing a simple API with attention to errors, versioning, and security
  3. Diagnosing a slow endpoint or a memory problem
  4. Handling a failing downstream dependency
  5. Describing how their code gets from commit to production
  6. Reviewing code for readability, correctness, and security issues

For Developers: Growing in the Role

  • Master the fundamentals. Language, concurrency, SQL, and the JVM pay dividends for years.
  • Learn to read production. Logs, metrics, and traces teach more than documentation.
  • Understand the platform you deploy to, even if you do not run it.
  • Study API design and security. These skills are in demand and transferable.
  • Keep current with Java releases and ecosystem changes.
  • Practice communicating trade-offs, since senior roles depend on it.
  • Contribute to quality, through tests, reviews, documentation, and mentoring.

Common Misconceptions

  • "Java is outdated." The language and platform continue to evolve, with regular releases and active ecosystems.
  • "A Java developer only writes code." Modern roles include design, testing, deployment, and often operations.
  • "Knowing Spring is enough." Frameworks change, but fundamentals persist.
  • "Microservices are always better." They add operational overhead that not every team can justify.
  • "Cloud means no operations." Managed services reduce work but do not remove responsibility for reliability, cost, and security.

Conclusion

The Java developer role today spans three connected responsibilities: building reliable backend systems, designing and securing APIs, and understanding how software behaves in cloud environments. Strong developers combine language depth with sound architecture, careful attention to data and security, and a practical grasp of deployment and operations.

For organizations, the best results come from describing the role honestly, assessing realistic skills, and valuing judgment over keyword matching. For developers, the path forward is to deepen fundamentals while widening your view from code to production. Either way, the role rewards people who build software that works not only on a laptop, but reliably, securely, and economically in the real world.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

1. What does a Java backend developer do?
A Java backend developer builds the server-side logic and data handling behind applications. This includes designing services and APIs, working with databases and messaging systems, writing tests, and diagnosing performance issues. Many roles also include deploying, monitoring, and supporting the software in production.

2. What skills should a Java developer have for API work?
Key skills include REST design, specification with OpenAPI, versioning, error handling, and pagination. Security matters just as much, including OAuth 2.0, authorization checks, input validation, and rate limiting. Developers should also handle integration with third-party systems safely, using timeouts, retries, and sensible fallbacks.

3. Do Java developers need cloud and DevOps skills?
Increasingly, yes. Many teams expect developers to package applications in containers, work with CI/CD pipelines, understand a major cloud platform, and use logging, metrics, and tracing to support production. The depth varies by company, so clarify expectations in the job description.

4. Is Spring Boot required for Java backend roles?
It is the most common framework in enterprise Java, so many roles list it. Alternatives such as Quarkus, Micronaut, and Jakarta EE are also used. A developer with strong fundamentals can usually learn a new framework quickly, so focus on understanding over memorizing one tool.

5. How should I evaluate a Java developer in an interview?
Use realistic exercises, such as designing a small API, reviewing code, or diagnosing a performance or reliability scenario. Ask candidates to explain past systems, trade-offs, and mistakes. For roles with operational responsibility, probe how they deploy, monitor, and troubleshoot production services.

title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration
description:
arXiv:2611.25214v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs.

title: LongBEL: Long-Context and Document-Consistent Biomedical Entity Linking
description:
arXiv:2605.13451v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Biomedical entity linking maps textual mentions to concepts in structured knowledge bases such as UMLS or SNOMED CT. Most existing systems link each mention independently, using only the mention or its surrounding sentence. This ignores dependencies between mentions in the same document and can lead to inconsistent predictions, especially when the same concept appears under different surface forms. We introduce LongBEL, a document-level generative framework that combines full-document context with a memory of previous predictions. To make this memory robust, LongBEL is trained with cross-validated predictions rather than gold labels, reducing the mismatch between training and inference and limiting cascading errors. Experiments on five biomedical benchmarks across English, French, and Spanish show that LongBEL improves over sentence-level generative baselines, with the largest gains on datasets where concepts frequently recur within documents. An ensemble of local, global, and memory-based variants achieves the best results across all benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the largest gains occur on recurring concepts, suggesting that LongBEL mainly improves document-level consistency rather than isolated mention disambiguation.

title: Export Mailchimp Data with the API: A Node.js Script
description:
Export your Mailchimp data with the API and you get something the dashboard export doesn't give you: a repeatable, scriptable backup you can run whenever you like and feed straight into another system. With Bending Spoons agreeing on November 19, 2026 to buy Mailchimp from Intuit (closing is expected in early 2027), plenty of teams want a complete copy of their data on their own disk. Nothing has changed yet. This is just good practice.

This guide walks through a single Node.js script that:

  1. lists every audience in the account,
  2. exports every contact in each audience, by status (subscribed, unsubscribed, cleaned and the rest), with merge fields and tags,
  3. saves the HTML of every sent campaign, and
  4. optionally loads your subscribed contacts into Cresca, an AI email marketing and transactional email platform, through its contacts API.

Mailchimp API details below come from Mailchimp's developer documentation, checked on November 20, 2026. For the business side of the deal, see Bending Spoons acquires Mailchimp: what it means for you.

What the Mailchimp API export covers (and what it doesn't)

Data API Dashboard export
Contacts with status, merge fields and tags Yes: GET /lists/{list_id}/members Yes, one CSV per status
Merge field definitions Yes: GET /lists/{list_id}/merge-fields Column headers only
Sent campaign HTML Yes: GET /campaigns/{campaign_id}/content Yes, in the account data export
Template HTML No documented endpoint returns full template HTML Custom-coded templates only, or the account data export
Open and click history Reports endpoints Campaign report exports

For templates, use the dashboard: Account, Settings, Manage my data, Export Data puts the HTML of your templates in a Templates folder. You can run that export once every 24 hours.

Step 1: Get a Mailchimp API key and your server prefix

In Mailchimp, open your profile, then Extras and API keys, and create a key. A Mailchimp API key has full access to the account and doesn't expire, so treat it like a password, keep it in an environment variable and delete it when you're done.

The key ends in a dash and your data centre, for example -us6. That suffix is the server prefix in the API URL: https://us6.api.mailchimp.com/3.0.

Authentication is HTTP Basic, with any string as the username and the API key as the password. Bearer tokens work too.

export MAILCHIMP_API_KEY="your-key-us6"
# Optional, for step 5:
export CRESCA_API_KEY="cr_live_..."

Step 2: A small Mailchimp API client with pagination

Mailchimp's list endpoints return at most 1,000 items per call. You page through them with count and offset, and each response includes total_items. The API allows 10 simultaneous connections per user and returns 429 TooManyRequests above that. This script makes one request at a time, so it stays well under the limit, and it retries on 429 just in case.

// export-mailchimp.mjs (Node.js 18 or later, no dependencies)
import { mkdir, writeFile, appendFile } from 'node:fs/promises';

const KEY = process.env.MAILCHIMP_API_KEY;
if (!KEY || !KEY.includes('-')) throw new Error('Set MAILCHIMP_API_KEY (it ends in -usN)');
const SERVER = KEY.split('-').pop();                 // e.g. "us6"
const BASE = `https://${SERVER}.api.mailchimp.com/3.0`;
const AUTH = 'Basic ' + Buffer.from(`export:${KEY}`).toString('base64');
const OUT = './mailchimp-export';
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

async function mc(path, params = {}) {
  const url = new URL(BASE + path);
  for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(params)) url.searchParams.set(k, String(v));
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: AUTH } });
    if (res.status === 429 && attempt <= 5) { await sleep(attempt * 2000); continue; }
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Mailchimp ${res.status} on ${path}: ${await res.text()}`);
    return res.json();
  }
}

// Yields every item of a paginated collection, 1,000 at a time.
async function* all(path, key, params = {}) {
  const count = 1000;
  for (let offset = 0; ; offset += count) {
    const page = await mc(path, { ...params, count, offset });
    yield* page[key];
    if (offset + count >= page.total_items) return;
  }
}

Step 3: Export every contact, by status

A full backup needs more than your subscribers. The unsubscribed and cleaned contacts are your record of who must not get marketing email again, so the script exports every status Mailchimp documents for this endpoint. Each audience gets a JSON Lines file with the complete member objects, so nothing is lost, plus a simple CSV of subscribed contacts for importing elsewhere.

const STATUSES = ['subscribed', 'unsubscribed', 'cleaned', 'pending', 'transactional', 'archived'];
const slug = (s) => s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, '');
const csvCell = (v) => `"${String(v ?? '').replace(/"/g, '""')}"`;

async function exportAudiences() {
  await mkdir(`${OUT}/audiences`, { recursive: true });
  const subscribedByAudience = {};

  for await (const list of all('/lists', 'lists')) {
    const name = slug(list.name) || list.id;
    const dir = `${OUT}/audiences/${name}`;
    await mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });

    // Merge field definitions (FNAME, LNAME, and your custom fields)
    const fields = [];
    for await (const f of all(`/lists/${list.id}/merge-fields`, 'merge_fields')) fields.push(f);
    await writeFile(`${dir}/merge-fields.json`, JSON.stringify(fields, null, 2));

    const subscribed = [];
    for (const status of STATUSES) {
      const file = `${dir}/${status}.jsonl`;
      await writeFile(file, '');
      let n = 0;
      for await (const m of all(`/lists/${list.id}/members`, 'members', { status })) {
        await appendFile(file, JSON.stringify(m) + '\n');
        n++;
        if (status === 'subscribed') {
          subscribed.push({
            email: m.email_address,
            first_name: m.merge_fields?.FNAME || '',
            last_name: m.merge_fields?.LNAME || '',
            tags: (m.tags || []).map((t) => t.name).join('|'),
          });
        }
      }
      console.log(`${list.name}: ${n} ${status}`);
    }

    const header = 'email,first_name,last_name,tags';
    const rows = subscribed.map((r) => [r.email, r.first_name, r.last_name, r.tags].map(csvCell).join(','));
    await writeFile(`${dir}/subscribed.csv`, [header, ...rows].join('\n'));
    subscribedByAudience[list.name] = subscribed;
  }
  return subscribedByAudience;
}

On a very large audience (hundreds of thousands of contacts), consider Mailchimp's batch operations endpoint (POST /batches) instead. A batched GET without a count pages through the whole collection on Mailchimp's side, and you download the results as a gzipped tar file.

Step 4: Save the HTML of every sent campaign

GET /campaigns lists campaigns, and GET /campaigns/{campaign_id}/content returns the campaign's html and plain_text. That gives you a permanent archive of every email you've sent, including the drag-and-drop designs you can't export as templates.

async function exportCampaigns() {
  await mkdir(`${OUT}/campaigns`, { recursive: true });
  let n = 0;
  for await (const c of all('/campaigns', 'campaigns', { status: 'sent' })) {
    const content = await mc(`/campaigns/${c.id}/content`);
    const date = (c.send_time || '').slice(0, 10) || 'unsent';
    const base = `${OUT}/campaigns/${date}-${slug(c.settings?.subject_line || c.id)}-${c.id}`;
    if (content.html) await writeFile(`${base}.html`, content.html);
    if (content.plain_text) await writeFile(`${base}.txt`, content.plain_text);
    n++;
  }
  console.log(`Saved ${n} sent campaigns`);
}

Step 5: Load your subscribers into Cresca (optional)

If you want to try a different tool while your Mailchimp account keeps running, the same script can load your subscribed contacts into Cresca. Cresca's POST /contacts endpoint takes up to 1,000 contacts per request, creates the list if it doesn't exist, and never duplicates a contact. Imports are limited to 120 requests per 15 minutes, which is up to 120,000 contacts.

Only subscribed contacts are sent. Unsubscribed and cleaned addresses stay in your backup, where they belong.

const CRESCA = 'https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1';

async function importToCresca(listName, contacts) {
  for (let i = 0; i < contacts.length; i += 1000) {
    const chunk = contacts.slice(i, i + 1000).map((c) => ({
      email: c.email,
      ...(c.first_name && { first_name: c.first_name }),
      ...(c.last_name && { last_name: c.last_name }),
    }));
    const res = await fetch(`${CRESCA}/contacts`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ list_name: listName, contacts: chunk }),
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Cresca ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);
    const { summary } = await res.json();
    console.log(`${listName}: +${summary.created} new, ${summary.updated} updated, ${summary.rejected} rejected`);
  }
}

// Run everything
const audiences = await exportAudiences();
await exportCampaigns();
if (process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY) {
  for (const [name, contacts] of Object.entries(audiences)) {
    await importToCresca(`${name} (from Mailchimp)`, contacts);
  }
}
console.log(`Done. Files are in ${OUT}`);

Run it:

node export-mailchimp.mjs

You end up with a folder like this:

mailchimp-export/
  audiences/
    newsletter/
      merge-fields.json
      subscribed.jsonl
      unsubscribed.jsonl
      cleaned.jsonl
      pending.jsonl
      transactional.jsonl
      archived.jsonl
      subscribed.csv
  campaigns/
    2026-11-14-black-friday-early-access-abc123.html
    2026-11-14-black-friday-early-access-abc123.txt

To get a Cresca API key, create a free account (30 days, 250 contacts, 1,000 emails, no credit card) and create a key with full access. The add contacts API reference has the full request and response format. Cresca's contacts API stores email, first name and last name. Your other Mailchimp merge fields stay in the JSON backup.

Step 6: Send your first campaign from Cresca

Once the import finishes, your Mailchimp audience is waiting in Cresca. Here's how to send to it, from sign-up to report:

1. Verify your sending domain

Open Sending Domains, add your domain and add the DNS records Cresca shows (ownership, DKIM and MAIL FROM/SPF), each with a copy button. When the domain shows as Verified, add your sender address.

2. Find your imported list

Open Contacts, then Contact Lists. The script named each list after its Mailchimp audience, with "(from Mailchimp)" at the end.

Contact Lists in Cresca (sample data).

3. Describe the email to Cresca AI

Open Templates and type a brief in the Message Cresca AI box, for example "Welcome email for new subscribers with the code HELLO10 for 10% off". The AI agent designs the whole email in your brand, and you can refine it in the same conversation or in the editor.

Cresca AI designing a welcome email from one brief (sample brand).

4. Create the campaign

In Campaigns, choose New Campaign. Pick your sender, the template and the imported list, then send now or schedule it.

Scheduling a campaign in Cresca (sample data).

5. Check the results

on the dashboard or in Delivery logs: deliveries, bounces, complaints and unsubscribes. Hard bounces and complaints are suppressed automatically.

What to do with the backup

  • Store it somewhere safe and private. It contains personal data, so treat it under the same privacy rules as your live list.
  • Re-run it before any big change, such as a plan change, a migration or the deal closing.
  • Keep the unsubscribed and cleaned files for as long as you keep sending email. They're how you avoid emailing people who opted out.
  • Delete the API key when you're finished, because Mailchimp keys never expire on their own.

Why developers like Cresca

If your product sends both marketing and transactional email, Cresca puts them in one account, on your own domain:

  • a REST API for transactional email at https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1, included on every plan, with templates, batches of up to 100 emails, scheduled sends and idempotency keys;
  • an AI agent that designs your marketing campaigns from a one-line brief, so nobody on the team has to hand-code newsletter HTML;
  • guided SPF and DKIM setup, one-click unsubscribe and automatic bounce and complaint suppression.

Email automation workflows are launching soon in Cresca. Campaigns, the AI agent and the transactional API are available today. Start with the quickstart, or try Cresca free for 30 days.

FAQ

Can I export Mailchimp contacts with the API?

Yes. GET /lists/{list_id}/members returns up to 1,000 contacts per call with count and offset for paging, and a status filter for subscribed, unsubscribed, cleaned, pending, transactional and archived contacts.

Does the Mailchimp API export templates?

No documented endpoint returns a template's full HTML. GET /templates/{template_id}/default-content returns only the editable sections. Use the account data export, which includes template HTML files, or export custom-coded templates from the dashboard.

What are the Mailchimp API rate limits?

Mailchimp allows 10 simultaneous connections per user and times out calls after 120 seconds. Going over the connection limit returns a 429 error.

Is my Mailchimp data changing because of the Bending Spoons acquisition?

No change has been announced. The deal is expected to close in early 2027, and neither company has said anything about plans, prices or data. A backup simply means you have a complete copy whatever happens.

title: Space-X: Self-Evolving Spatial Agents Weaving Clues into Evidence Chains
description:
arXiv:2611.24004v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Spatial reasoning connects visual observations, geometric estimates, and linguistic decisions into a coherent derivation. Yet tool-augmented agents often acquire evidence without clear targets, combine outputs under inconsistent object or reference-frame semantics, and misjudge evidence sufficiency. Thus, more tools or calls do not reliably improve reasoning. We introduce Space-X, a spatial-reasoning framework that self-evolves toward complete, continuous evidence-chain construction. An Execution Agent acquires, associates, and judges evidence per problem using role-specific memory. A Control Agent diagnoses evidence-chain breaks from execution traces and jointly revises tools, interfaces, skills, memory organization, and decision rules. This loop co-evolves capability and evidence use: evidence needs guide capability development; usable results guide actions. Across multiple benchmarks, Space-X yields gains with four base models. Relative to baselines, GPT-6-sol improves answer accuracy on ViewSpatial and MMSI by 50.39% and 23.07%, respectively; Gemini-3.8-Flash gains 47.50% and 25.22% on these benchmarks. This provides a unified route from fragmented spatial clues to traceable, derivable answers.

title: Executive Summary: Engineering Safe Database Fallback During Cache Failure
description:
Overview

A cache outage is not merely a latency issue; it is a massive load-transfer event. If a system natively routes all traffic to the database when a cache (like Redis) fails, the database will instantly become overwhelmed, turning a partial outage into a complete systemic failure. This document outlines the engineering principles required to safely manage database fallback through bounded concurrency, graceful degradation, and controlled recovery.

The Core Problem: The Load-Transfer Illusion

  • Asymmetric Capacity: Redis is designed to absorb massive, repeated read demand. The primary database is sized for writes, ingestion, and complex queries, not cache-level throughput.
  • The "Retry Storm": When Redis fails or slows down, naive fallback mechanisms dump 100% of the read load onto the database, compounded by users and automated clients aggressively retrying their delayed requests.
  • The Objective: Fallback must be treated as a scarce emergency resource. The goal is to preserve critical business functions (like active threat containment) while protecting the database, not to artificially maintain 100% feature availability.

Key Principles for Safe Database Fallback

1. Endpoint Classification and Graceful Degradation

  • Not all functions deserve emergency database access.
  • Critical endpoints (e.g., active incident status) receive reserved fallback capacity.
  • Important endpoints serve bounded stale data.
  • Deferrable endpoints (e.g., historical exports) fail fast (HTTP 503) to preserve resources.

2. Stale-While-Revalidate (The Safest Fallback)

  • The most efficient fallback query is the one that isn't executed.
  • Serve slightly expired data from a local, in-memory cache (like Caffeine) during transient Redis outages, explicitly labeling the data's age for the user so trust is maintained.

3. Bounded Fallback Concurrency (Bulkheads)

  • Implement strict concurrency limits (e.g., using semaphores). If the database can only safely handle 20 emergency read queries per second without disrupting core writes, any requests beyond that limit must be immediately rejected or served stale data.

4. Single-Flight Coordination

  • To prevent "cache stampedes" on missing popular keys, use single-flight controls. Only one request is allowed to execute the heavy database query, while simultaneous requests wait briefly to share the calculated result.

5. Prioritizing Authoritative Writes

  • During an outage, writing new security alerts and logging containment actions is more important than rendering monitoring dashboards. Read fallbacks must use isolated resource pools to prevent starving database writes.

Fast Detection and Controlled Recovery

  • Circuit Breakers: Use short timeouts and circuit breakers (e.g., Resilience4j) to detect Redis degradation instantly. Waiting seconds for a timeout consumes application threads and worsens the outage.
  • Controlled Rewarming: When Redis recovers, do not immediately dump all read traffic back to an empty cache. Systematically warm up high-value keys first to prevent a "cold-cache storm" against the database.
  • Observability: Monitor fallback permits in use, rejected emergency requests, and specific data freshness metrics, rather than relying solely on binary Redis process health checks.

title: Calibrated Decision Rewards: Training Language Models with a Judge That Knows How Sure It Is
description:
arXiv:2611.25135v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can only teach a language model what its reward can recognize. Answer checkers are exact but need a reference answer; learned reward models and LLM judges work everywhere, but their scores are not probabilities. We study RLCDR (Reinforcement Learning from Calibrated Decision Rewards). An LLM converted into a decision model answers a typed question about a response ("is the final answer correct?", "which step is the first error?") with a probability distribution, read in one forward pass, debiased over option orders and calibrated with about a hundred labels. Training Qwen3-1.7B with GRPO on MATH, this reference-free reward raises MATH500 accuracy from 72.2% to 76.8% (+4.65 points, p < 1e-4), matching training on the answer key (76.9%), while a random reward gains only +0.65. The gain grows with difficulty, from 44.8% to 51.7% on the hardest level. On the policy's own changing samples the reward stays calibrated: its expected calibration error is half that of a softmax judge on the same 27B backbone (0.074 vs. 0.141), and it shows no sign of reward hacking. Without step training, the same model finds the first wrong step better than a dedicated 7B process reward model (ProcessBench F1 0.772 vs. 0.722, 20/20 splits). We also map where the approach stops being enough: trained only on problems the base model mostly fails, the reference-free reward still improves the policy (+1.9 MATH500 points, p = 0.03) but trails the answer key, because its probabilities become overconfident on that distribution. We state six hypotheses in advance and test each with a control designed to falsify it.
