title: async/await in practice: async code that reads like normal code
description:
This code looks right. It runs, it throws nothing, and the logs come out:

console.log("before");
[10, 20, 30].forEach(async (ms) => {
  await wait(ms);
  console.log("inside:", ms);
});
console.log("after");

before
after
inside: 10
inside: 20
inside: 30

And it's broken. forEach doesn't wait for async callbacks, so the code after it runs before the loop, and there's no way to know when the whole thing finished. No error, no warning: just a wrong order that in production becomes a response sent too early.

async/await solves the underlying problem — writing async code without chains of then — but it brings traps of its own. This lesson is about the three that hurt most.

An async function always returns a promise

async doesn't make a function magic: it changes its return type.

async function f() {
  return 1;
}

const p = f();
console.log(p);
console.log(p instanceof Promise);
p.then((value) => console.log("inside:", value));

Promise { 1 }
true
inside: 1

Whatever you return comes out as a promise. Return a value and the promise is fulfilled with it; throw and it's rejected. Which explains why .then works on an async function: it's just another promise.

await doesn't block, it suspends

The usual confusion is thinking await freezes the program. It freezes nothing: it suspends the current function and hands control back to whoever called it.

async function f() {
  console.log("a");
  await null;
  console.log("b");
}

f();
console.log("c");

a
c
b

await null isn't waiting for anything — null isn't a promise — and it suspends anyway. c runs before b because b sits in a microtask, which you already know from the event loop lesson.

If you come from Python, the syntax will feel familiar to the point of suspicion: async def, await, same shape. The difference isn't in the code, it's in the runtime. Python needs an event loop you start explicitly; Node already has one running. An await in Python without a loop is an error; in Node it's a Tuesday.

Sequential or parallel

This is where your endpoint takes 300 ms or 900. Three independent operations, 300 each:

const t0 = Date.now();
const [x, y, z] = await Promise.all([wait(300, "x"), wait(300, "y"), wait(300, "z")]);
console.log("parallel:", Date.now() - t0, "ms", x, y, z);

const t1 = Date.now();
const a = await wait(300, "x");
const b = await wait(300, "y");
const d = await wait(300, "z");
console.log("sequential:", Date.now() - t1, "ms", a, b, d);

parallel: 301 ms x y z
sequential: 901 ms x y z

The rule is easy to state and easy to forget: if an operation doesn't need the previous result, don't wait for it. Three awaits in a row mean "one after another", even when all three were independent.

And the detail that makes it pleasant: you can destructure the array Promise.all returns on the same line.

Top-level await, with small print

In an ES module you can use await at the top level, without wrapping it in a function:

const x = await Promise.resolve(1);
console.log(x);

1

But only in a module. The same code in a CommonJS file doesn't start:

const x = await Promise.resolve(1);
console.log(x);

SyntaxError: await is only valid in async functions and the top level bodies of modules

The message says it all. If your file is .js with "type": "commonjs", or .cjs, wrap the code in an async function and call it. Same reason import used to fail back in the modules lesson.

try/catch: the clean pattern

With async/await, error handling goes back to what it was before promises: try, catch, finally.

const fails = () => Promise.reject(new Error("the database is not answering"));

async function save() {
  try {
    await fails();
    console.log("this should not run");
  } catch (error) {
    console.log("recovered:", error.message);
  } finally {
    console.log("closing the transaction");
  }
  console.log("the function is still alive");
}
await save();

recovered: the database is not answering
closing the transaction
the function is still alive

await turns a rejection into an ordinary exception, and from there the catch you already knew works. No chained .catch, no error callbacks: the code reads top to bottom.

return await, or the catch that doesn't catch

There's a two-word difference that changes behaviour, and it's best seen by running it:

async function withoutAwait() {
  try {
    return Promise.reject(new Error("boom"));
  } catch (error) {
    return "caught: " + error.message;
  }
}

try {
  console.log("without await →", await withoutAwait());
} catch (error) {
  console.log("without await escaped:", error.message);
}

async function withAwait() {
  try {
    return await Promise.reject(new Error("boom"));
  } catch (error) {
    return "caught: " + error.message;
  }
}
console.log("with await →", await withAwait());

without await escaped: boom
with await → caught: boom

In the first one, return hands back the rejected promise without unwrapping it, so the inner catch never sees it and the error escapes to the caller. In the second, await unwraps it inside the try and the catch collects it.

The rule, with its exception: plain return is usually fine and return await is noise. The exception is exactly this one — when you return from inside a try that wants to catch the error — and then return await isn't optional.

When you forget the await

A rejection with no catch isn't a warning: it's an exception nobody collects, and Node won't let it slide.

async function save() {
  const result = Promise.reject(new Error("I forgot the await"));
  console.log("carried on without waiting");
}
save();

carried on without waiting
file:///tmp/l6/e.mjs:2
  const result = Promise.reject(new Error("I forgot the await"));
                                ^

Error: I forgot the await

And the process exits with code 1. The rest of the trace is the stack, which is beside the point here; what matters is that the rejected promise had nobody looking at it, and Node decided to stop pretending everything was fine.

It feels harsh. It's correct: an async error that gets ignored is an error that shows up later, somewhere else, in another shape — half a transaction, an incomplete record. Failing fast where the failure happened is cheaper than debugging its consequences.

The last resort: unhandledRejection

If you want to hear about those cases without the process dying at three in the morning, there's a global handler:

process.on("unhandledRejection", (error) => {
  console.log("last resort:", error.message);
});

async function save() {
  Promise.reject(new Error("I forgot the await"));
  console.log("carried on without waiting");
}
save();

carried on without waiting
last resort: I forgot the await

The process survives. Which is exactly why it should be used with care: it's a net, not a cushion. If the handler prints and moves on, you end up with a service that ignores its own failures and answers as if nothing happened. Its place is observability — telling someone who needs to know — not absolution.

Loops: for...of yes, forEach no

Back to the code from the start, now with the correct alternative. First the one that fails:

console.log("before");
[10, 20, 30].forEach(async (ms) => {
  await wait(ms);
  console.log("inside:", ms);
});
console.log("after");

before
after
inside: 10
inside: 20
inside: 30

And now the one that works:

console.log("before");
for (const ms of [10, 20, 30]) {
  await wait(ms);
  console.log("inside:", ms);
}
console.log("after");

before
inside: 10
inside: 20
inside: 30
after

for...of runs one iteration after another, and await works because you're genuinely inside an async function. forEach doesn't: it calls your callback, ignores what it returns and carries on. There's no way to await the whole loop, not even by putting await in front of it.

And if the order doesn't matter and you want parallelism, it's neither of those: it's Promise.all with a map.

const results = await Promise.all([10, 20, 30].map((ms) => wait(ms, ms)));
console.log("all at once:", results);

all at once: [ 10, 20, 30 ]

Three shapes, three behaviours: forEach doesn't wait, for...of waits in series, map with Promise.all waits in parallel.

And outside loops it's the same story

forEach isn't the only one ignoring what an async callback returns. setTimeout, an event handler, a server.on(...): none of them waits for your promise. If that promise rejects, nobody collects it.

setTimeout(async () => {
  throw new Error("nobody collects this");
}, 10);

Error: nobody collects this

And the process exits with code 1. The exception isn't seen by an outer try/catch or by setTimeout: it's an orphaned promise. When you write an async handler for an API that doesn't await callbacks, error handling is yours, inside the handler, always.

A timeout with Promise.race

Last piece: cutting off something that takes too long. Promise.race returns the first promise to settle, either way, and that's how you build a time limit.

const withTimeout = (promise, ms) => Promise.race([promise, wait(ms).then(() => Promise.reject(new Error("timeout")))]);

try {
  console.log(
    "slow:",
    await withTimeout(
      wait(500).then(() => "data"),
      100,
    ),
  );
} catch (error) {
  console.log("slow →", error.message);
}

try {
  console.log(
    "fast:",
    await withTimeout(
      wait(10).then(() => "data"),
      100,
    ),
  );
} catch (error) {
  console.log("fast →", error.message);
}

slow → timeout
fast: data

Whoever gets there first wins: if the data lands in 10 ms you get the data; if it takes 500 and the limit is 100, you get the timeout.

Mind what this doesn't do: it doesn't cancel the slow operation. The request is still alive in the background, burning a connection and memory; you've only stopped waiting for it. Real cancellation is a different thing, and it has a name.

Cancelling for real: AbortSignal

The standard way to interrupt something in JavaScript is an AbortController and its signal. The controller aborts; the signal is passed to the operation, which must have agreed to listen.

import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

const control = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => control.abort(), 100);
const start = Date.now();

try {
  await sleep(1000, "done", { signal: control.signal });
  console.log("this should not run");
} catch (error) {
  console.log("aborted after", Date.now() - start, "ms ·", error.name);
}

aborted after 102 ms · AbortError

A hundred milliseconds in, the one-second timer stops waiting. The operation isn't cancelled by magic: the node:timers/promises API knows how to read { signal } and cuts out when the signal fires. If the API doesn't accept a signal, there's no cancellation, only patience.

For the most common case — a time limit — there's a shortcut that saves you the controller:

import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

try {
  await sleep(1000, "done", { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(100) });
} catch (error) {
  console.log("built-in timeout ·", error.name);
}

built-in timeout · AbortError

And a third piece that saves manual checks: signal.throwIfAborted() throws the abort reason if it has already fired, carrying whatever reason you gave it. This is how file reads, fetch, streams and the in-flight work of a graceful shutdown get cancelled: the AbortController is passed down the stack and every layer checks its signal.

Common problems

The process dies with Error: ... and code 1 when I didn't throw anything

A rejection with no catch and no await. Look for the promise you created and never waited for: it's almost always a missing await.

forEach with async doesn't wait

That's what forEach does: it ignores the value the callback returns. Switch to for...of for series, or map with Promise.all for parallel.

My endpoint takes the sum of three calls

You're waiting for them one after another. If they're independent, they go in Promise.all.

Top-level await doesn't work in my file

It isn't an ES module. "type": "module" in package.json, a .mjs extension, or wrap it in an async function.

I added an unhandledRejection and now I don't see the errors

You're using it as a cushion. The handler should alert, not silence.

What you take from this lesson

  • An async function always returns a promise, carrying either the value or the error.
  • await suspends the current function, not the program.
  • If two operations are independent, they go in Promise.all: 300 ms, not 900.
  • Top-level await only exists in ES modules.
  • try/catch/finally is the error pattern again, with no chains of catch.
  • Forgetting an await kills the process, and rightly so: the error can't be lost.
  • unhandledRejection is an observability net, not forgiveness.
  • forEach doesn't wait; for...of waits in series; map with Promise.all in parallel.
  • Promise.race gives you a timeout, but it cancels nothing.

You can now write async code that reads. What's missing is the ground it lives on: the objects and modules Node gives you to talk to the system. The first is process, and with it the globals, the standard library and the pieces that are there without you importing them.

Never stop coding!

title: NestJS for ASP.NET Core developers: a TypeScript backend that will feel familiar
description:
If your team writes ASP.NET Core and is about to build something in TypeScript (a service next to a frontend that's already in TypeScript, a backend for a product that's leaving .NET, or just a team that wants one language), the Node.js world can look like a pile of small libraries you're expected to assemble yourself. Express, a validation library, a DI container someone picked, a folder structure someone invented. Coming from a framework where dotnet new webapi gives you DI, configuration, logging, validation and a request pipeline out of the box, that's a step back, and it's a fair objection.

Nest is the framework that takes those decisions for you. It has a DI container with lifetimes, attribute-style routing, a pipeline of middleware and filters, typed configuration, and first-party packages for authentication, authorization, background jobs, health checks and OpenAPI. Most of what you know carries over.

This post is the tour I'd give a .NET team on day one: the tools, the structure, each ASP.NET Core feature and its Nest counterpart with code on both sides, how it ships, and the differences that will actually bite.

The short version

ASP.NET Core Nest
dotnet new webapi, NuGet nest new, npm
builder.Services.AddScoped<T>() @Injectable() classes, listed in a module
AddSingleton(sp => ...) a factory provider (useFactory)
Keyed services an injection token and @Inject()
Singleton, scoped, transient Scope.DEFAULT, Scope.REQUEST, Scope.TRANSIENT
[ApiController], [HttpGet] @Controller(), @Get()
Middleware (app.Use()) middleware
Authorization, action and exception filters guards, interceptors, exception filters
Data Annotations, FluentValidation a validation pipe, with class-validator or Zod
Authentication handlers, Identity @nestjs/authentication
Policies, IAuthorizationService @nestjs/authorization
appsettings.json, IOptions<T> @nestjs/config
EF Core TypeORM (@nestjs/typeorm) or Drizzle (@nestjs/drizzle)
BackgroundService, Hangfire lifecycle hooks, @nestjs/schedule, @nestjs/bullmq
MediatR notifications @nestjs/event-emitter
IHttpClientFactory, Polly @nestjs/http-client, @nestjs/resilience
Health checks @nestjs/terminus
ILogger<T> Logger from @nestjs/common
Swashbuckle, NSwag @nestjs/swagger
SignalR WebSocket gateways
WebApplicationFactory<T> @nestjs/testing with Supertest

Every row has its own section below. The docs have the same mapping as a reference page, with a link to the full chapter for each row: Coming from ASP.NET Core.

Your tools, translated

Before any code, here's what replaces the things around it:

.NET world Nest world
The .NET SDK and runtime Node.js (a current LTS release)
dotnet CLI the nest CLI, plus npm
NuGet, .csproj npm, package.json
dotnet new webapi npx @nestjs/cli new
dotnet watch npm run start:dev, which restarts on every save
dotnet build, dotnet publish npm run build (the TypeScript compiler, or SWC for speed), a dist/ folder plus node_modules
Roslyn tsc
xUnit and Moq Vitest, with its own mocks
Visual Studio, Rider VS Code, or WebStorm
A solution with several projects a Nest workspace: nest generate app and nest generate library

npm run start:debug starts the app with the Node inspector attached, and both editors above attach a debugger to it, breakpoints and all.

Project layout

nest new orders-api gives you a small src/ folder and asks two questions: ES modules or CommonJS (ESM is the default, with Vitest; CommonJS uses Jest), and whether to set up NestJS Observe for monitoring. As the app grows, the convention is one folder per feature, each with its module, and tests next to the code they test rather than in a separate test project:

src/
  main.ts                    # Program.cs
  app.module.ts              # the root module
  orders/
    orders.module.ts         # what AddOrders() would register
    orders.controller.ts
    orders.controller.spec.ts
    orders.service.ts
    order.entity.ts
    create-order.dto.ts
  payments/
    payments.module.ts
    ...
test/
  app.e2e-spec.ts            # end-to-end tests

nest g resource orders generates the orders/ folder above with CRUD routes filled in, which is the fastest way to see the structure with your own names in it.

Program.cs registers services and builds the pipeline:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddControllers();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrdersService, OrdersService>();

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();

In Nest, services are registered in modules, and main.ts only creates the app from the root module:

async function bootstrap() {
  const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule);
  await app.listen(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
}
await bootstrap();

Services are providers, and modules own them

A service in both:

public class OrdersService : IOrdersService
{
    private readonly OrdersRepository _ordersRepository;

    public OrdersService(OrdersRepository ordersRepository)
    {
        _ordersRepository = ordersRepository;
    }
}

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly ordersRepository: OrdersRepository) {}
}

Constructor injection, and private readonly works like a C# primary constructor. Where ASP.NET Core registers everything on one IServiceCollection, Nest registers providers in modules:

@Module({
  controllers: [OrdersController],
  providers: [OrdersService, OrdersRepository],
  exports: [OrdersService],
})
export class OrdersModule {}

Think of a module as the AddOrders() extension method you'd write for a feature, with one addition: what it doesn't export stays private. OrdersRepository above can't be injected anywhere outside OrdersModule. In a large .NET solution you'd get that with separate projects and internal. Here the container enforces it, and you can read what a feature exposes from one file. A module that needs OrdersService adds OrdersModule to its imports.

If a dependency can't be resolved, the app fails at startup with an error naming the class, the missing dependency and the module.

Factories and library registrations

A registration that builds the instance itself, like AddSingleton(sp => new S3Client(...)), becomes a factory provider. inject lists what gets passed to the factory, in order, and the factory can be async:

@Module({
  providers: [
    {
      provide: S3Client,
      useFactory: (config: ConfigService) =>
        new S3Client({ region: config.getOrThrow<string>('AWS_REGION') }),
      inject: [ConfigService],
    },
  ],
  exports: [S3Client],
})
export class StorageModule {}

Libraries that you'd register with an AddXyz() extension method ship as modules you import and configure: ConfigModule.forRoot(), TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync(), ScheduleModule.forRoot().

Interfaces and keyed services

AddScoped<IOrdersService, OrdersService>() is the first thing that has no direct translation. TypeScript interfaces are erased when the code compiles, so there's nothing left for the container to look up. Use an abstract class as the contract: it exists at runtime, so it doubles as the injection token.

export abstract class PaymentGateway {
  abstract charge(orderId: string, amountInCents: number): Promise<void>;
}

@Module({
  providers: [{ provide: PaymentGateway, useClass: StripePaymentGateway }],
  exports: [PaymentGateway],
})
export class PaymentsModule {}

// anywhere that imports PaymentsModule
constructor(private readonly paymentGateway: PaymentGateway) {}

Keyed services, AddKeyedSingleton() with [FromKeyedServices("primary")], become a string or Symbol token and @Inject(TOKEN) on the parameter.

Lifetimes: the default is different

Nest has the same three lifetimes, under different names:

ASP.NET Core Nest
AddSingleton() Scope.DEFAULT, the default
AddScoped() Scope.REQUEST
AddTransient() Scope.TRANSIENT

The difference is the habit around them. In ASP.NET Core, scoped is everywhere, mostly because DbContext is scoped. In Nest, providers are singletons unless you say otherwise, and that's right for almost all of them. ORM clients are singletons holding a connection pool, so there's no per-request context to scope.

And request scope behaves differently. ASP.NET Core's scope validation, on by default in Development, rejects a scoped service injected into a singleton as a captive dependency. Nest instead makes the singleton request-scoped too, along with everything up to the controller, and rebuilds that chain on every request. It works, but it's slower and rarely what you meant. When you need the current user or tenant deep in a service, read it from AsyncLocalStorage, which flows through await the way AsyncLocal<T> does, instead of reaching for an IHttpContextAccessor equivalent.

IHostedService.StartAsync() and StopAsync() have counterparts too: any provider can implement onApplicationBootstrap() and onApplicationShutdown().

Controllers 

[ApiController]
[Route("orders")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IOrdersService _ordersService;

    public OrdersController(IOrdersService ordersService)
    {
        _ordersService = ordersService;
    }

    [HttpGet]
    public Task<List<Order>> FindAll([FromQuery] int page = 0) => _ordersService.FindAllAsync(page);

    [HttpGet("{id}")]
    public async Task<ActionResult<Order>> FindOne(string id)
    {
        var order = await _ordersService.FindOneAsync(id);
        return order is null ? NotFound() : order;
    }

    [HttpPost]
    public async Task<ActionResult<Order>> Create(CreateOrderRequest request)
    {
        var order = await _ordersService.CreateAsync(request);
        return CreatedAtAction(nameof(FindOne), new { id = order.Id }, order);
    }

    [HttpDelete("{id}")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Remove(string id)
    {
        await _ordersService.RemoveAsync(id);
        return NoContent();
    }
}

@Controller('orders')
export class OrdersController {
  constructor(private readonly ordersService: OrdersService) {}

  @Get()
  findAll(@Query('page', new ParseIntPipe({ optional: true })) page = 0) {
    return this.ordersService.findAll(page);
  }

  @Get(':id')
  async findOne(@Param('id') id: string) {
    const order = await this.ordersService.findOne(id);
    if (!order) {
      throw new NotFoundException();
    }
    return order;
  }

  @Post()
  create(@Body() dto: CreateOrderDto) {
    return this.ordersService.create(dto);
  }

  @Delete(':id')
  @HttpCode(204)
  remove(@Param('id') id: string) {
    return this.ordersService.remove(id);
  }
}

Small things:

  • Route parameters are :id.
  • Every parameter says where it comes from (@Body(), @Query(), @Param(), @Headers()), so there are no binding source conventions to remember.
  • Query and path parameters arrive as strings. ParseIntPipe converts and validates one, and answers 400 for ?page=abc.
  • There's no ActionResult<T>. You return the body and throw NotFoundException, ConflictException and friends for error statuses.
  • A POST answers 201 by default and @HttpCode() changes any status. There's no CreatedAtAction(): set a Location header with @Header() when you need one.
  • Handlers return Promises, your Task, and Nest serializes the result as JSON. Property names are whatever they are in your TypeScript, which is camelCase by convention, so there's no naming policy to configure.

Minimal APIs

There's no app.MapGet("/orders/{id}", ...) style in Nest. The smallest Nest app is still a controller and a module, and nest new orders-api --minimal puts them in a single file, src/main.ts. It grows into the layout above by moving things out of that file, not by rewriting them.

Middleware and filters

The pipeline maps closely. Middleware runs first, then four kinds of components around the handler:

ASP.NET Core Nest When it runs
Middleware (app.Use()) Middleware before routing, with the raw request
Authorization filters, [Authorize] Guards after routing: may the handler run?
Action, result and endpoint filters Interceptors around the handler, with its result
Model binding and validation Pipes on each argument
Exception filters, IExceptionHandler Exception filters when anything above throws

Like filters, each can be bound to one handler, a controller or the whole app.

Middleware looks almost the same. A correlation id, in both:

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    var id = context.Request.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"].FirstOrDefault() ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString();
    context.Response.Headers["X-Correlation-Id"] = id;
    await next();
});

export function correlationId(req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) {
  const id = req.header('x-correlation-id') ?? randomUUID();
  res.setHeader('x-correlation-id', id);
  next();
}

// main.ts
app.use(correlationId);

For middleware that needs injected services or only some routes, write a class implementing NestMiddleware and apply it in a module's configure() with consumer.apply(...).forRoutes(...).

An interceptor is an IAsyncActionFilter, with next.handle() in place of await next():

@Injectable()
export class TimingInterceptor implements NestInterceptor {
  private readonly logger = new Logger(TimingInterceptor.name);

  intercept(context: ExecutionContext, next: CallHandler): Observable<unknown> {
    const started = performance.now();
    const handler = `${context.getClass().name}.${context.getHandler().name}`;
    return next
      .handle()
      .pipe(tap(() => this.logger.log(`${handler} took ${Math.round(performance.now() - started)} ms`)));
  }
}

next.handle() returns an RxJS stream of the handler's result, which the interceptor can transform before it goes out, the way a result filter would.

Exception filters and problem details

An IExceptionHandler:

public class OrderNotFoundHandler : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(HttpContext context, Exception exception, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (exception is not OrderNotFoundException) return false;
        context.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status404NotFound;
        await context.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(
            new ProblemDetails { Status = 404, Title = "Not Found", Detail = exception.Message }, ct);
        return true;
    }
}

In Nest, @Catch() says which exception types a filter handles, so there's no type check to write:

@Catch(OrderNotFoundError)
export class OrderNotFoundFilter implements ExceptionFilter {
  constructor(private readonly httpAdapterHost: HttpAdapterHost) {}

  catch(exception: OrderNotFoundError, host: ArgumentsHost) {
    const { httpAdapter } = this.httpAdapterHost;
    const response = host.switchToHttp().getResponse();
    httpAdapter.setHeader(response, 'Content-Type', 'application/problem+json');
    httpAdapter.reply(
      response,
      { type: 'about:blank', title: 'Not Found', status: 404, detail: exception.message },
      404,
    );
  }
}

Register it app-wide as a provider in the root module, { provide: APP_FILTER, useClass: OrderNotFoundFilter }, and it can inject other providers. Exceptions nobody handles become a 500 with a generic body, and the stack trace goes to the log, not to the client.

One thing to know if your clients parse problem details: Nest's own error responses, validation errors included, are not RFC 9457 problem details out of the box. They're plain JSON objects with a statusCode and a message. If you need problem details everywhere, one catch-all filter like the one above does it.

Validation is explicit, and that's the first gotcha

[ApiController] validates models before your action runs, with rules from Data Annotations:

public record CreateOrderRequest(
    [Required] string CustomerId,
    [Required, MinLength(1)] List<OrderItem> Items,
    [MaxLength(500)] string? Note);

In Nest, a global pipe does that job. With classes, it's class-validator decorators and ValidationPipe:

export class CreateOrderDto {
  @IsString()
  @IsNotEmpty()
  customerId: string;

  @ArrayNotEmpty()
  @ValidateNested({ each: true })
  @Type(() => OrderItemDto)
  items: OrderItemDto[];

  @IsOptional()
  @MaxLength(500)
  note?: string;
}

app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));

whitelist drops fields the DTO doesn't declare, and transform turns the body into an actual CreateOrderDto instance.

If you like FluentValidation's rules-in-code style better, Nest 12 takes a Zod (or any Standard Schema) schema per parameter, and the parameter's type is inferred from it:

export const createOrderSchema = z.object({
  customerId: z.string().min(1),
  items: z.array(z.object({ productId: z.string(), quantity: z.int().positive() })).min(1),
  note: z.string().max(500).optional(),
});
export type CreateOrderDto = z.infer<typeof createOrderSchema>;

@Post()
create(@Body({ schema: createOrderSchema }) dto: CreateOrderDto) {
  return this.ordersService.create(dto);
}

Here's the gotcha. System.Text.Json creates the type your action declares, so a body is at least the right shape. TypeScript types are erased when the code compiles. Without a pipe, @Body() dto: CreateOrderDto is whatever JSON the client sent. Register a validation pipe globally on day one and you never think about it again. Forget it and the compiler won't warn you.

Identity and policies

@nestjs/authentication closes every route the moment you register it, like a fallback policy that requires an authenticated user, and @Public() is your [AllowAnonymous]:

[ApiController]
[Authorize]
[Route("me")]
public class MeController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult Me() => Ok(new { Id = User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier) });
}

@Controller('me')
export class MeController {
  @Get()
  me(@CurrentUser() user: User) {
    return user;
  }
}

Where ASP.NET Core has authentication handlers, the package has credential providers: one reads the session cookie, another a bearer token, another an API key, and each loads the user through your code. The user is your own object, rather than a ClaimsPrincipal you dig claims out of. It covers much of what Identity and its endpoints do: sign-up, password hashing, server-side sessions, email verification and password reset links, TOTP two-factor, OpenID Connect sign-in, access and refresh tokens and API keys. The state lives in your database through a store you write against documented interfaces, not through a fixed EF schema.

Authorization will feel natural if you use policies. @nestjs/authorization puts them in classes, and the check on a route is type-checked against the class, so a misspelled ability doesn't compile:

[HttpPost]
[Authorize(Policy = "Staff")]
public Task<Product> Create(CreateProductRequest request) => _productsService.CreateAsync(request);

@Policy()
export class ProductPolicy {
  create(user: User | null) {
    return !!user?.roles.includes('staff');
  }
}

// in the controller
@Post()
@Can(ProductPolicy, 'create')
create(@Body() dto: CreateProductDto) { ... }

Resource-based authorization, AuthorizeAsync(User, resource, policy), is authorizationService.authorize(ProductPolicy, 'view', user, product) in a service. And the guard denies by default, so a route that declares no check is closed.

Configuration and options

appsettings.json, the per-environment files and environment variables become .env files and environment variables through @nestjs/config. Real environment variables win over the files, as they do in .NET:

{
  "Orders": {
    "PageSize": 20,
    "PaymentsUrl": "https://payments.example.com"
  }
}

@Module({
  imports: [
    ConfigModule.forRoot({
      isGlobal: true,
      envFilePath: [`.env.${process.env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development'}`, '.env'],
      validationSchema: z.object({
        ORDERS_PAGE_SIZE: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(20),
        PAYMENTS_URL: z.url(),
      }),
      load: [ordersConfig],
    }),
  ],
})
export class AppModule {}

NODE_ENV plays the role of ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT, and the first file in envFilePath that defines a variable wins, so .env.production overrides .env the way appsettings.Production.json overrides appsettings.json. The schema is your ValidateOnStart(): a missing or malformed variable stops the app at startup instead of failing the first request that reads it. Keep secrets out of committed files, the way you'd use user secrets locally and a vault in production.

configuration["Orders:PageSize"] becomes config.get('ORDERS_PAGE_SIZE'), or getOrThrow() for a value that must be there. IOptions<OrdersOptions> becomes a registerAs() namespace, injected with its type:

export default registerAs('orders', () => ({
  pageSize: Number(process.env.ORDERS_PAGE_SIZE ?? 20),
  paymentsUrl: process.env.PAYMENTS_URL!,
}));

// in a service
constructor(@Inject(ordersConfig.KEY) private readonly config: ConfigType<typeof ordersConfig>) {}

EF Core becomes TypeORM (or Drizzle)

There's no EF Core in Node, and I won't pretend otherwise: nothing matches LINQ. TypeORM is the closest in shape, with entity classes, a repository per entity in place of a DbSet<T>, and migrations:

public class Order
{
    public Guid Id { get; set; }
    public required string CustomerId { get; set; }
    public OrderStatus Status { get; set; }
}

@Entity('orders')
export class Order {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')
  id: string;

  @Column()
  customerId: string;

  @Column({ type: 'varchar', default: 'pending' })
  status: 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped';
}

@Module({
  imports: [TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Order])],
  providers: [OrdersService],
  controllers: [OrdersController],
})
export class OrdersModule {}

@Injectable()
export class OrdersService {
  constructor(@InjectRepository(Order) private readonly orders: Repository<Order>) {}

  findPending(customerId: string) {
    return this.orders.findBy({ customerId, status: 'pending' });
  }
}

orders.Where(o => o.CustomerId == id && o.Status == OrderStatus.Pending) becomes findBy() with an object of conditions, and anything bigger goes through the query builder. There's no SaveChanges() sweeping up tracked changes: save(), insert() and update() write when you call them. Transactions are a callback that commits when it resolves and rolls back when it throws, where you'd write a using var transaction block with CommitAsync():

return this.dataSource.transaction(async (manager) => {
  const order = await manager.save(Order, { customerId: dto.customerId });
  await manager.insert(OrderItem, dto.items.map((item) => ({ ...item, orderId: order.id })));
  return order;
});

@InjectRepository(Order) names the entity for the same reason interfaces don't work as tokens: Repository<Order> and Repository<Customer> are the same class at runtime.

The alternatives: MikroORM is the closest in behavior, with a unit of work and an identity map like EF's change tracking, and its em.flush() is the one that works like SaveChanges(). Drizzle (@nestjs/drizzle, the other first-party option) is the one I'd point a Dapper fan to: typed SQL, inferred result types, no entities. Prisma and Mongoose work too. dotnet ef migrations becomes the ORM's own migration tool, run as a separate step before the new version starts.

Background work

A BackgroundService splits into three tools, depending on what it does.

Work on a timer becomes @Cron() from @nestjs/schedule:

public class InvoiceExportService : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromHours(1));
        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            // ...
        }
    }
}

@Injectable()
export class InvoiceJobs {
  @Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_HOUR)
  @OnOneInstance({ key: 'invoices:export' })
  async exportInvoices() {
    // ...
  }
}

A Nest cron job runs on every replica, just like a hosted service does. @OnOneInstance() from @nestjs/locks takes a lease in a store every instance shares, so the job runs on one of them, the way you'd use a Hangfire recurring job or a distributed lock.

Work handed off by a request (send this email, build that report) goes on a queue with @nestjs/bullmq, with retries and delays, which is what Hangfire's background jobs give you. And startup or shutdown work goes in the onApplicationBootstrap() and onApplicationShutdown() hooks from earlier.

In-process events, the job MediatR notifications often do, come from @nestjs/event-emitter:

// publishing
constructor(private readonly events: EventEmitter2) {}
this.events.emit('order.created', new OrderCreatedEvent(order.id));

// handling, in any provider
@OnEvent('order.created')
handleOrderCreated(event: OrderCreatedEvent) { ... }

And if you use MediatR for commands and queries, @nestjs/cqrs has command and query buses with handlers in the same style.

Calling other services

IHttpClientFactory with typed clients becomes HttpClient from @nestjs/http-client, built on Node's own fetch. Each upstream service gets a named client with its base URL and timeout:

@Module({
  imports: [HttpClientModule.register({ name: 'payments', baseUrl: process.env.PAYMENTS_URL, timeout: '5s' })],
  providers: [PaymentsClient],
})
export class PaymentsModule {}

@Injectable()
export class PaymentsClient {
  constructor(@InjectHttpClient('payments') private readonly http: HttpClient) {}

  async getStatus(orderId: string) {
    const { data } = await this.http.get<PaymentStatus>(`/payments/${orderId}`);
    return data;
  }
}

Polly's timeouts, retries and circuit breakers become @nestjs/resilience. Like a named resilience pipeline, you describe each dependency once as a preset, and routes opt in with a decorator:

ResilienceModule.forRoot({
  presets: {
    carrier: {
      timeout: '2s',
      retry: { attempts: 2 },
      circuitBreaker: { failureRateThreshold: 50, minimumCalls: 10, openDuration: '30s' },
    },
  },
}),

// in a controller
@Get('quotes')
@Resilience('carrier')
getQuotes(@Query('orderId') orderId: string, @Signal() signal: AbortSignal) {
  return this.shippingService.getQuotes(orderId, signal);
}

@Signal() injects an AbortSignal, the JavaScript CancellationToken, which fires when the attempt times out. Pass it to the HTTP call and the request is actually cancelled. Retries only apply to safe methods like GET by default, so a retried POST never charges a card twice. Inside services, where decorators don't apply, the same presets are available as policy objects.

Health, logs and OpenAPI

AddHealthChecks() and MapHealthChecks() become a controller using @nestjs/terminus, with separate liveness and readiness checks:

@Public()
@Controller('health')
export class HealthController {
  constructor(
    private readonly health: HealthCheckService,
    private readonly db: TypeOrmHealthIndicator,
  ) {}

  @Get('live')
  @HealthCheck()
  live() {
    return this.health.check([]);
  }

  @Get('ready')
  @HealthCheck()
  ready() {
    return this.health.check([() => this.db.pingCheck('database')]);
  }
}

(@Public() because @nestjs/authentication closes every route, and probes don't sign in.)

ILogger<OrdersService> becomes private readonly logger = new Logger(OrdersService.name). The built-in ConsoleLogger writes JSON with json: true, and if you're used to Serilog, pino plugs in the same way. For the traces, errors and metrics Application Insights gives many .NET teams, nest new offers to set up NestJS Observe, which reports requests, jobs and errors in terms of your controllers and providers.

Swashbuckle and NSwag become @nestjs/swagger:

const config = new DocumentBuilder().setTitle('Orders API').setVersion('1.0').build();
SwaggerModule.setup('api', app, () => SwaggerModule.createDocument(app, config));

Swagger UI is at /api. Swashbuckle gets your types by reflection. TypeScript has no runtime types to reflect on, so @nestjs/swagger comes with a compiler plugin that reads property types and optionality from your DTOs at build time, and you don't put @ApiProperty() on every field. Zod schemas describe the document too.

SignalR becomes a gateway

Real-time endpoints are gateways, on Socket.IO or plain WebSockets, using the same providers, guards and pipes as controllers:

@WebSocketGateway()
export class OrdersGateway {
  @SubscribeMessage('track')
  track(@MessageBody() orderId: string) {
    return { event: 'status', data: { orderId, status: 'shipped' } };
  }
}

A hub method becomes a @SubscribeMessage() handler. It's not wire-compatible with SignalR clients, so the browser side switches to a Socket.IO or WebSocket client. For services talking to each other, @nestjs/microservices has transports for gRPC, Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, Redis and MQTT.

Testing

WebApplicationFactory<Program> becomes a testing module, and the HttpClient it creates becomes Supertest:

public class OrdersTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory) : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task ReturnsAnOrder()
    {
        var client = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(builder => builder.ConfigureTestServices(services =>
            services.AddSingleton<IOrdersService>(new FakeOrdersService()))).CreateClient();

        var order = await client.GetFromJsonAsync<Order>("/orders/42");
        Assert.Equal("42", order!.Id);
    }
}

describe('Orders', () => {
  let app: INestApplication;

  beforeAll(async () => {
    const moduleRef = await Test.createTestingModule({ imports: [AppModule] })
      .overrideProvider(OrdersService)
      .useValue(new FakeOrdersService())
      .compile();
    app = moduleRef.createNestApplication();
    await app.init();
  });

  afterAll(() => app.close());

  it('returns an order', async () => {
    const response = await request(app.getHttpServer()).get('/orders/42').expect(200);
    expect(response.body.id).toBe('42');
  });
});

overrideProvider() is your ConfigureTestServices(). A testing module can also hold just the parts a test needs, say one controller and a fake service, which runs faster and needs no database. And for a plain unit test you need no framework at all: a provider is a class, so new OrdersService(fakeRepository) works.

Shipping it

dotnet publish gives you a folder or an image. A Nest service ships as compiled JavaScript plus its node_modules, almost always in a container. A production Dockerfile, built in one stage and run in another:

FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:24-slim
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "--enable-source-maps", "dist/main.js"]

Three things to check that the .NET host handled for you:

  • Shutdown hooks. The .NET host stops hosted services on SIGTERM without being asked. Nest runs onModuleDestroy() and onApplicationShutdown() only after app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts.
  • The process gets the signal. Use the exec form, CMD ["node", ...], not npm start, which doesn't reliably forward signals to Node.
  • Memory. Set Node's heap limit with --max-old-space-size, below the container's memory limit, so running out of memory is a JavaScript error with a stack trace instead of a silent OOMKilled.

Moving over without a rewrite

You don't have to move an ASP.NET Core codebase to Nest to start using Nest. The pattern I'd recommend:

  • Start with a new service, not a port. The next service you need gets written in Nest, behind the same gateway or reverse proxy (YARP works fine for this), using the same database conventions and the same auth (a guard can verify the JWTs your .NET services already issue, for example with @nestjs/jwt).
  • Share the contract, not the code. Swashbuckle or NSwag already publish an OpenAPI document for your .NET services, and NSwag can generate a TypeScript client from it. The other way round, @nestjs/swagger publishes one for the Nest service.
  • Move existing endpoints only when you'd rewrite them anyway. A route that's being redesigned can move to the Nest service behind the proxy, one path at a time.

What's actually different

The syntax takes a week. These take longer, so I'd rather you hear them from me than find them in production.

async/await looks identical, and the runtime isn't. I/O behaves the same: while a request awaits the database, others run. But ASP.NET Core runs continuations on a thread pool, and Node.js runs all of your JavaScript on one thread. CPU-heavy work in a handler, like hashing a big file or a long synchronous loop, stalls every other request in the process, and there's no Task.Run() to push it aside. Move it to a queue or a worker thread, and scale with more processes or containers. If your service is mostly computation, .NET is the better runtime, and I'd tell anyone that. On the bright side, there's no SynchronizationContext and no ConfigureAwait(false) to think about.

No cancellation token unless you ask. ASP.NET Core binds RequestAborted to a CancellationToken parameter. Nest handlers get nothing by default. The JavaScript equivalent is an AbortSignal, and the HTTP client, fetch() and @nestjs/resilience all take one.

Types are a compile-time check. Interfaces and generic type arguments don't exist at runtime, which is why injection uses abstract classes or tokens, and why a request body, a database row or a message from another service is only as typed as the code that validated it. There's no reflection to fall back on.

Decorators are functions, not attributes. An attribute is passive metadata read by reflection. A decorator runs when the class is defined, and that's how Nest records what it reads at startup. In practice you'll rarely notice, but it explains why decorators can take arbitrary expressions.

Numbers are doubles. There's no decimal. Keep money in integer cents, or use a decimal library and the database's numeric type, which most drivers return as a string.

No LINQ. Array methods (filter, map, reduce) cover in-memory queries, and query builders cover the database, but nothing composes over both like IQueryable does.

ES modules. A new project imports local files with a .js extension, even from .ts files, because that's the name of the compiled file. It looks wrong for about a day.

When I'd stay on .NET

To be fair to .NET: if you have a large ASP.NET Core codebase that works, a rewrite to get TypeScript is rarely worth it. If the work is CPU-bound or leans on EF Core's LINQ for complex queries, stay, or put the TypeScript service next to it rather than in place of it.

Nest is a good fit when the new thing is a new service, when the people building it also write the TypeScript frontend, or when you want one language from the browser to the database without giving up the structure you're used to.

Getting started 

npx @nestjs/cli new orders-api
cd orders-api
npm run start:dev

Then nest g resource orders, and you have a module, controller, service, DTOs and tests to compare against the ASP.NET Core version in your head. The Coming from ASP.NET Core page in the docs keeps this mapping as a reference, with a link from each row to its full chapter.

If something there doesn't match how you'd do it in .NET, tell me. It's written for you, and it's easy to fix.

Coming from Java instead? Here's the same tour for Spring Boot: NestJS for Spring Boot developers.

title: Require the agent to leave existing data-analytics attributes alone
description:
The PR restyles a checkout button. It also removes data-analytics="checkout-submit" and renames data-cta="upgrade" to data-cta="upgrade-button" “to be clearer.” Nothing in the UI tests fails. A week later the funnel report is empty, because the collector still looks for the old names.

I’ve started treating analytics and experiment attributes as a contract, the same way I treat test IDs. A visual change is not a tracking-plan change. If the ticket is not about analytics, those attributes stay.

Why the attributes disappear

The model sees data-* hooks as optional decoration. It will “clean up” anything that is not a class or a handler, or it will rename them to match the new component name. Unlike a broken test id, a missing data-analytics attribute often has no CI check. The damage is delayed and silent.

Renames are as bad as deletions. Downstream dashboards, GTM triggers, and experiment buckets are not in the repo. Grep in the frontend will not find them.

A simple analytics-attribute policy

  • Existing data-analytics, data-cta, data-track, data-experiment, and similar hooks stay as they are
  • A rename or removal is its own PR, with an analytics owner in the review
  • New attributes are fine when the ticket adds a new event, using the existing naming scheme
  • Do not invent a second tracking prop (onTrack, a wrapper track()) when the hook already exists on the element

If the design system Button already forwards a trackingId or spreads data attributes, use that API. Do not drop the attribute because the new styled button “looks cleaner.”

What to put in the prompt 

Do not remove or rename existing data-analytics, data-cta, data-track, or data-experiment attributes.
A visual or copy change is not a tracking-plan change.
If a new event is required, add a new attribute using the existing naming scheme, and mention it in the PR.
Do not invent a parallel tracking helper.

In review, diff only the attribute lines: rg -n 'data-(analytics|cta|track|experiment|amp)'. Unexpected deletions or renames are a send-back, even if the screenshot looks right.

Reject / send back

Reject

  • A restyle that drops a tracking attribute
  • A “clearer” rename of an existing event name
  • A new trackClick() wrapper that replaces the attribute
  • Moving the attribute to a parent so the collector no longer sees the click target

Accept

  • A UI change that leaves the existing attributes untouched
  • A new attribute for a genuinely new event, documented in the PR
  • A dedicated analytics PR that updates the attribute and the tracking plan together

title: How we verify a PHP to Java migration: responses, DB writes and outgoing calls
description:
TL;DR. A PHP-to-Java cutover is only as good as the comparison you run before it. I record real traffic against the PHP application — HTTP responses, every database change, and every outgoing API call — then replay those journeys against the Java version in a sandbox with the clock, timezone, sql_mode and charset pinned. I compare all three channels, because a matching response can still hide a destructive write. Before any Java number means anything, the PHP application has to reproduce its own recording, at 99.5% or better. And the checker itself has to be tested: a harness that never contradicts you is not a harness.

I spend a lot of time on PHP-to-Java migrations thinking about a question that looks simple: how do you know the new system behaves like the old one?

The usual answers are a test suite, a QA pass, and a staging week where people click around. Those are useful. They are also incomplete. Legacy PHP applications accumulate behaviour that nobody wrote down: a side-effecting delete, a rounding rule, a call to another system that only happens on one path. If you only compare the HTTP response, you will miss the part that actually costs money.

So I do three things. I record real user journeys against the PHP application. I replay them against the Java 21 / Spring Boot version in a deterministic sandbox. And I compare the HTTP response, every database write, and every outgoing API call. Cutover stays blocked until they match.

This is the method, including the parts that failed.

HTTP agreement is not behavioural agreement

The example I keep coming back to is a delete.

I migrated a delete endpoint. The Java version returned the same HTTP status as the PHP version and followed the same redirect. On the response alone, the two systems agreed. The database write did not. The migrated delete also removed the client's invoices and payments.

That is the kind of bug a browser test can walk past, because the page looks fine. It is also the kind of bug that would have shown up in production as missing financial records. The only reason it was caught before cutover is that the comparison included database writes, not just the response.

The same process has also caught a missing login check, data visible across tenants, and a skipped cashback payout. Some of what it found was not introduced by the migration at all: it was already wrong in the original PHP. That is useful too. If you are going to move a system, you should know which defects you are carrying with you.

Record real traffic, not the paths you remembered to test

I do not start with invented test cases. I record real traffic against the PHP application: the HTTP responses, every database change, and every outgoing API call.

Recorded journeys have a bias of their own, which I will come back to. But they have a property that a handwritten suite often lacks. They include the awkward paths people actually take: the retries, the empty submits, the deletes, the odd query parameters. Those are the places where PHP and Java tend to drift.

The recording is the fixture. Everything after it — replay, comparison, the decision to allow cutover — is only as strong as what was captured.

Replay in a sandbox that does not invent differences

A comparison is only useful if a mismatch means a real behavioural difference, not an environmental one.

I replay the same journeys against the Java version in a sandbox where the clock, the timezone, sql_mode and the charset are pinned. If the PHP ran in a particular timezone or wrote datetimes a particular way, the Java side has to do the same, or the diff fills up with noise. The same is true of MySQL sql_mode and charset. A string that was legal on one side and truncated on the other is a real difference. A timestamp that is "wrong" because the clock moved is not.

The point of pinning the environment is not to make the systems look the same. It is to make sure that when they look different, the difference is in the application.

Compare all three channels

Each channel catches something the others miss.

Responses tell you about status codes, redirects, headers and body content. They miss silent writes. A 200 and a clean redirect can sit on top of a delete that went too far, or an update that never happened.

Database writes tell you about inserts, updates and deletes, including the ones that were not supposed to happen. They miss calls that never touch your database: a request to another service, a webhook, a payment or notification call.

Outgoing API calls tell you about those outward effects. A matching page that sent a different payload, or failed to send one, is still a failed migration. The other system will notice even if your UI does not.

The delete I mentioned earlier is the simplest illustration: identical HTTP response, identical redirect, and a write that would have removed invoices and payments. If we had only compared the response, we would have shipped it.

The PHP application has to match itself first

Before any Java number means anything, the PHP application has to match itself. I replay the recorded journeys against the same PHP system that produced them. I want that self-comparison at 99.5% or better. If the original system cannot reproduce its own recording, you are not measuring a migration. You are measuring a flaky harness.

I learned this the slow way. I once spent two days chasing differences that looked like migration bugs. They were leftover probe rows that only one side could see. The Java was not wrong. The fixtures were dirty. Until the PHP side could replay cleanly against its own recording, every Java mismatch was a waste of time.

This step is unglamorous, and I would not skip it again. It is also the step that makes the later numbers honest. A 100% match against a recording the PHP application itself cannot reproduce is not a result. It is a measurement error.

Then test the checker

A harness that never contradicts you is not a harness. I plant deliberate bugs in the Java and measure how many the checker actually catches.

The self-test catch rates so far are 57.14% on WA Blast Pro wave 1, and 35.89% on InvoicePlane wave 1. Those are not comfortable numbers, and I publish them next to the parity figures for that reason. 100% parity means every recorded fixture matched. It does not mean the checker would catch every possible bug.

The pattern in what it catches, and what it misses, has been consistent. Lost writes and missing escaping are always caught. NULLs and .00 amounts are missed, because the recordings never produce them. That is a coverage problem, not a comparison problem. If a journey never writes a NULL, the checker has no opportunity to notice that the Java side would handle a NULL differently. The same is true of a .00 amount that never appears in real traffic. The planted-bug tests showed that gap clearly. Closing it means changing what gets recorded, or adding cases the live traffic does not provide, not pretending the three-way comparison is complete.

I would rather have a checker with a published miss rate than one that only ever agrees with me.

What the benchmarks actually show

The numbers below are from two benchmarks, not from paid client work. I want to be clear about that. This is early. These results are from systems we already had in hand.

  • WA Blast Pro, my own production multi-tenant WhatsApp SaaS, written in plain PHP.
  • InvoicePlane, a public open-source invoicing application on CodeIgniter 3, written by other people.

Together that is 858 fixtures, at 100% parity, after hand fixes. First-pass parity, before those fixes, was 82% on one wave, with 9.7 hand fixes per 1,000 PHP lines. The generator is not the judge. Replay closes the gap, and engineers still fix things. The gate tells them where.

The bugs I listed earlier — the over-broad delete, the missing login check, the cross-tenant data, the skipped cashback payout, and defects already in the original PHP — came out of this process. Some of them would have been serious in production. Catching them on a benchmark is not the same as catching them on a client's system, but it is why I trust the three-way comparison more than a green HTTP diff.

What this covers today

The method is in use today for plain PHP and CodeIgniter 3. Laravel is next, as a source. I am not going to pretend the Laravel path is ready.

I also will not pretend that recorded-journey comparison is a complete substitute for a thoughtful review of the Java. Parity tells you the new system behaves like the old one on the journeys you recorded. It does not tell you whether the Java is well structured, whether the transaction boundaries are right, or whether it will hold up at a volume the recordings never reached. Those are separate questions, and they still need an engineer.

The honest sequence, as I now run it, is narrow. Make the PHP application match its own recording. Replay the same journeys against Java in a pinned sandbox. Compare responses, database writes and outgoing calls. Test the checker with planted bugs, and treat the miss rate as part of the result. Keep cutover blocked until the recorded journeys match. Then, separately, read the Java.

If you are planning a move

I am building this work as MigrateForge, at migrateforge.com. If you are planning a move from PHP to Java 21 / Spring Boot and you want to talk about how you will verify it, I am happy to compare notes.

#MigrateForge
