title: Next.js `revalidatePath` vs `revalidateTag` in 2026: Choosing the Right Cache Invalidation Primitive at Scale
description:
Next.js revalidatePath vs revalidateTag in 2026: Choosing the Right Cache Invalidation Primitive at Scale

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

The Cache Invalidation Primitive You're Probably Using Wrong

Most Next.js developers reach for revalidatePath when a mutation happens. It is familiar, straightforward, and works immediately in development. The function invalidates everything under a path, ensuring users see fresh data after an update. This approach breaks down in production when applications scale beyond a single container or when cache entries multiply across dozens of routes.

The problem manifests when a product price changes. The developer calls revalidatePath('/products'), expecting the product list to refresh. The homepage also displays featured products, so they add revalidatePath('/'). The search page shows products too, so another call goes in. Within weeks, every mutation triggers a cascade of path invalidations, wiping caches that have nothing to do with the actual change.

Problem diagram showing revalidatePath invalidating unrelated cached data

Teams discover months later that a user profile update invalidates the product catalog because both routes sit under the same path prefix. Cache hit rates drop. Response times climb. Developers start questioning whether caching provides any benefit at all.

The solution requires understanding that Next.js offers two distinct primitives with fundamentally different invalidation semantics. revalidateTag targets specific cache entries by tag, leaving unrelated data intact. revalidatePath wipes everything under a URL path, regardless of whether the underlying data changed.

Solution diagram showing revalidateTag surgically invalidating only tagged data

This distinction determines whether a caching strategy scales or collapses under real traffic. The choice between these primitives shapes cache efficiency, deployment complexity, and the ability to reason about invalidation across a growing application.

Key Takeaways

  • revalidatePath invalidates all cached data under a URL path, often clearing unrelated entries and reducing cache hit rates in complex applications.
  • revalidateTag targets specific cache entries by tag, allowing surgical invalidation that preserves unrelated cached data.
  • Path-based invalidation requires no tagging infrastructure but becomes unmaintainable as applications grow and routes share data.
  • Multi-container deployments expose coordination failures with both primitives when using Next.js's default in-memory cache, requiring external cache adapters.
  • The correct primitive depends on data granularity, mutation patterns, and whether the application runs on a single instance or distributed infrastructure.

Understanding revalidatePath: Broad Strokes Invalidation

revalidatePath invalidates every cache entry associated with a URL path. When a Server Action or Route Handler calls revalidatePath('/products'), Next.js marks all cached data for that route as stale. The next request triggers fresh data fetches for the entire page, regardless of which specific piece of data changed.

This primitive exists for scenarios where precise tagging is impractical or impossible. A content management system might store dozens of content types across a single route. A dashboard might aggregate data from fifteen different sources. Tracking which tags to invalidate for each mutation becomes error-prone when the page composition changes frequently.

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateProduct(productId: string, data: ProductData) {
  await db.product.update({
    where: { id: productId },
    data
  })

  // Invalidates all cached data for /products and its dynamic segments
  revalidatePath('/products')
}

The function accepts a second parameter controlling the scope. Setting it to 'page' invalidates only the exact path. Setting it to 'layout' invalidates the path and all nested routes. The default behavior matches 'page' in Next.js 15.3 as documented in the official revalidation guide.

Diagram showing revalidatePath invalidation scope through route hierarchy

The primitive works immediately in single-container deployments where all requests hit the same process. In-memory cache entries disappear synchronously when revalidatePath executes. Developers see instant feedback during local development and staging environments running on single instances.

The limitation surfaces when multiple routes depend on the same data but sit under different paths. A product appears on the homepage, search results, category pages, and its detail page. Invalidating the product requires calling revalidatePath for every path, or accepting stale data until the next scheduled revalidation.

Teams often solve this by calling revalidatePath('/') to invalidate the entire site. This approach sacrifices all caching benefits to avoid tracking which paths need invalidation. Response times climb as every page regenerates from scratch after any mutation.

Understanding revalidateTag: Surgical Cache Busting

revalidateTag invalidates cache entries that explicitly opt into a tag. Functions using the use cache directive call cacheTag('tag-name') to register their cache entry with one or more tags. Later mutations call revalidateTag('tag-name') to invalidate all entries with that tag, regardless of which routes or components created them.

This primitive scales to applications where many routes share the same underlying data. A product detail component might appear on five different pages. Tagging its cache entry with product:${id} allows a single revalidateTag call to invalidate the product everywhere it appears.

import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function getProduct(id: string) {
  'use cache'
  cacheTag(`product:${id}`)

  return db.product.findUnique({
    where: { id }
  })
}

The tagging happens inside the cached function, not at the call site. This decouples cache invalidation from route structure. Components consume getProduct without knowing or caring about tags. Only the data layer manages cache semantics.

import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateProduct(productId: string, data: ProductData) {
  await db.product.update({
    where: { id: productId },
    data
  })

  // Invalidates the product everywhere it appears
  revalidateTag(`product:${productId}`)
}

The Next.js revalidation documentation recommends passing 'max' as the second argument to revalidateTag. This sets the stale-while-revalidate window to its longest duration, allowing stale content to serve while fresh data generates in the background. Users see instant responses while cache entries refresh asynchronously.

Diagram showing revalidateTag invalidating only tagged entries across routes

The tradeoff appears in infrastructure requirements. Tag-based invalidation requires a shared cache store in multi-container deployments. The default in-memory cache cannot coordinate tags across processes. Next.js 15.3 provides unstable_cache with pluggable backends, but custom cache adapters remain necessary for production distributed systems.

Tag naming conventions matter at scale. Prefixing tags by entity type prevents collisions. product:123 and category:123 represent different entities despite sharing an ID. Including version numbers in tags like api:v2:product:123 allows gradual cache migration during API changes.

The primitive also supports cache entry hierarchies. A product page might tag its cache with both product:123 and category:electronics. Invalidating category:electronics refreshes all products in that category without knowing their individual IDs. This pattern reduces coordination complexity when relationships change.

Direct Comparison: When Each Primitive Wins in Production

The choice between revalidatePath and revalidateTag determines cache efficiency and maintenance burden. Each primitive excels in specific scenarios while creating problems in others.

Aspect revalidatePath revalidateTag
Invalidation scope URL path and optionally nested routes Specific tagged cache entries only
Infrastructure requirement None (works with in-memory cache) Shared cache store for multi-container setups
Setup complexity Zero (immediate use) Requires tagging cached functions
Cache hit rate Drops as routes share data Remains high with proper tagging
Maintenance Simple initially, unmaintainable at scale Requires discipline but scales linearly
Cross-route invalidation Requires multiple calls or broad invalidation Single call affects all tagged entries

Path-based invalidation wins when routes operate independently. An admin dashboard with dedicated data for each page benefits from path invalidation. Each route fetches distinct data that never appears elsewhere. Invalidating /admin/users affects nothing else. No tagging infrastructure provides value here.

Comparison diagram showing when path invalidation works versus when tags work

Tag-based invalidation becomes essential when data appears across many routes. E-commerce applications display products on listing pages, detail pages, search results, recommendations, and cart summaries. A price change must invalidate the product everywhere. Tracking which paths contain which products quickly becomes impossible.

The difference compounds in applications with dynamic routes. A blog with /posts/[slug] might have thousands of post pages. Invalidating a single post requires either calling revalidatePath with the exact slug or invalidating the entire posts section. Tags allow revalidateTag('post:abc123') to target exactly one post regardless of its URL.

Mutation patterns influence the decision. Applications with frequent broad updates favor path invalidation. A stock market dashboard might refresh all displayed stocks every few seconds. Invalidating /dashboard once beats invalidating dozens of individual stock tags. The cache lifetime matters more than granular invalidation here.

Applications with infrequent, targeted mutations favor tags. A content management system might publish one article per day. Invalidating only that article's cache entries preserves every other cached page. Cache hit rates stay high even with daily updates.

Deployment architecture forces the decision in multi-container environments. Teams running on serverless platforms or container orchestrators must implement external cache coordination regardless of primitive choice. At that point, tag-based invalidation provides strictly more power for the same infrastructure cost.

Multi-container deployment diagram showing cache coordination challenges

The primitives combine in mature applications. Core shared data uses tags for surgical invalidation. Peripheral features with isolated data use paths. A product catalog relies on revalidateTag('product:*') while an admin settings panel uses revalidatePath('/admin/settings').

Real-World Code: Implementing Both With unstable_cache

Production applications require explicit cache control beyond Next.js automatic caching. The unstable_cache function provides programmatic cache management with support for both revalidation primitives. Despite its name, the API has remained stable since Next.js 14.0 as covered in Next.js caching patterns.

import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache'

// Tag-based approach for shared data
export const getCachedProduct = unstable_cache(
  async (id: string) => {
    return db.product.findUnique({
      where: { id },
      include: {
        category: true,
        reviews: {
          take: 5,
          orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }
        }
      }
    })
  },
  ['product'],
  {
    tags: ['products', 'product:${id}'],
    revalidate: 3600
  }
)

// Path-based approach for isolated data
export const getCachedUserSettings = unstable_cache(
  async (userId: string) => {
    return db.userSettings.findUnique({
      where: { userId }
    })
  },
  ['user-settings'],
  {
    revalidate: 300
  }
)

The third parameter to unstable_cache accepts a tags array. These tags enable surgical invalidation through revalidateTag. The function also accepts a revalidate number setting time-based expiration. Combining both strategies provides defense in depth: tags for immediate invalidation, time-based revalidation as a safety net.

Server Actions coordinate cache invalidation with data mutations. The Next.js revalidation guide documents two timing options: revalidateTag for stale-while-revalidate semantics and updateTag for immediate expiration. Most applications prefer revalidateTag with its 'max' stale window.

'use server'

import { revalidateTag, revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function updateProduct(
  id: string,
  data: ProductUpdateInput
) {
  const product = await db.product.update({
    where: { id },
    data
  })

  // Tag-based invalidation for shared product data
  revalidateTag(`product:${id}`, 'max')
  revalidateTag('products', 'max')

  // Path-based invalidation for product detail page if needed
  // revalidatePath(`/products/${product.slug}`)

  return product
}

export async function updateUserSettings(
  userId: string,
  settings: UserSettingsInput
) {
  await db.userSettings.update({
    where: { userId },
    data: settings
  })

  // Path-based invalidation for isolated settings page
  revalidatePath(`/users/${userId}/settings`)
}

The pattern separates concerns effectively. Data fetching functions declare their cache behavior through tags and expiration. Server Actions handle mutations and trigger invalidation. Components simply consume the cached functions without knowing cache semantics exist.

Teams often create cache utilities to standardize tagging conventions and prevent duplicate cache keys:

// lib/cache-utils.ts
import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache'

export function createProductCache<T>(
  fn: (id: string) => Promise<T>,
  cacheKey: string
) {
  return unstable_cache(
    fn,
    [cacheKey],
    {
      tags: ['products'],
      revalidate: 3600
    }
  )
}

export function withProductTag(id: string) {
  return [`product:${id}`, 'products']
}

// Usage in data layer
export const getCachedProduct = createProductCache(
  async (id: string) => {
    return db.product.findUnique({ where: { id } })
  },
  'product-detail'
)

This abstraction prevents tag typos and ensures consistent cache lifetimes across related functions. The utilities also provide a single place to change cache configuration when requirements evolve.

The key insight appears in production debugging. When a cache entry does not invalidate as expected, developers need to verify three things: the tags in unstable_cache match the tags in revalidateTag, the cache key remains consistent across calls, and the revalidation actually executes in the deployed environment.

Multi-Container Deployments: The Distributed Cache Problem

The revalidation primitives fail silently in distributed deployments when relying on Next.js default in-memory caching. A user updates a product on container A. The Server Action calls revalidateTag and invalidates the in-memory cache on container A. Container B still serves stale product data because its cache never received the invalidation signal.

This failure mode is subtle because it works perfectly during development. Local development runs a single Next.js process where all invalidations happen in the same memory space. Staging environments often use single containers for cost reasons, hiding the problem until production deploys multiple instances.

The failure compounds with load balancer behavior. Modern load balancers distribute requests across containers for fault tolerance and performance. A user might see fresh data on one request and stale data on the next, depending on which container handles the request. This creates a trust problem where users question whether their updates actually saved.

Diagram showing distributed cache invalidation failure across containers

The solution requires an external cache store that all containers share. Redis provides the standard choice for session stores and distributed caches. The Next.js runtime caching considerations document that serverless environments may not persist cache entries across invocations, requiring external storage for reliability.

Teams running on platforms like Google Cloud Run or AWS Lambda encounter this problem immediately. Each function invocation potentially runs in a fresh container with empty cache. The Payload CMS discussion on cache invalidation shows real production teams discovering this after deployment when users report seeing stale content.

Custom cache adapters bridge Next.js cache APIs to external stores. The adapter intercepts revalidateTag and revalidatePath calls, translating them to cache operations in Redis or another shared store:

// lib/cache-adapter.ts
import { Redis } from 'ioredis'

const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL)

export async function revalidateTagInRedis(tag: string) {
  const keys = await redis.smembers(`tag:${tag}`)

  if (keys.length > 0) {
    await redis.del(...keys)
    await redis.del(`tag:${tag}`)
  }
}

export async function setCacheWithTag(
  key: string,
  value: unknown,
  tags: string[],
  ttl: number
) {
  await redis.setex(key, ttl, JSON.stringify(value))

  for (const tag of tags) {
    await redis.sadd(`tag:${tag}`, key)
  }
}

This implementation stores cache entries in Redis with standard expiration. Each tag maintains a Redis set containing all cache keys associated with that tag. Invalidating a tag looks up the set, deletes all associated keys, and removes the set itself.

The distributed coordination problem affects both primitives equally. revalidatePath and revalidateTag both require synchronization across containers. Path invalidation might seem simpler because it avoids tagging infrastructure, but the fundamental coordination challenge remains identical.

Teams sometimes attempt to solve this by broadcasting invalidation events through message queues or pub/sub systems. Each container subscribes to an invalidation channel and clears its local cache when messages arrive. This approach introduces race conditions and partial failure modes that make cache behavior unpredictable.

The correct solution accepts that distributed caching requires shared storage. Using Redis or another external cache eliminates the coordination problem entirely. All containers read and write the same cache store, so invalidation becomes instantaneous across the deployment.

Distributed cache architecture diagram showing Redis coordination

Serverless platforms often provide managed cache services that integrate with application code. Vercel's native edge caching handles this automatically for applications deployed on their platform. Teams deploying elsewhere must implement cache adapters manually or choose managed services that provide Next.js-compatible cache backends.

The infrastructure tradeoff becomes clear: single-container deployments avoid external cache dependencies at the cost of limited scalability. Multi-container deployments require shared cache stores but support horizontal scaling and fault tolerance. The revalidation primitive choice matters less than the cache storage architecture at this scale.

Decision Framework: Choosing the Right Primitive at Scale

The decision between revalidatePath and revalidateTag depends on data sharing patterns, mutation frequency, and deployment constraints. A systematic framework prevents premature optimization while identifying genuine scaling bottlenecks.

Start by mapping which routes share data. Applications where most data appears on a single route favor path invalidation. A landing page builder might have dedicated data for each page URL. Invalidating /pages/homepage never affects /pages/pricing. The routes share no data, so tags provide no benefit.

Applications where data appears across many routes require tags. E-commerce catalogs display products on listing pages, detail pages, search results, cart views, and recommendation widgets. Invalidating a product means invalidating entries across all these routes. Tracking paths becomes impossible while tagging the product once handles every location.

Decision framework flowchart for choosing revalidation primitive

Mutation patterns influence granularity requirements. Applications with bulk updates might invalidate entire sections. A news aggregator might refresh all articles in a category when the feed updates. Invalidating the category path once beats invalidating hundreds of individual article tags.

Applications with targeted mutations benefit from precise invalidation. A project management tool updates one task at a time. Invalidating only that task's cache entries keeps every other cached task fresh. Cache hit rates stay high even with constant updates.

Deployment architecture often makes the decision. Teams running on managed platforms with built-in distributed caching can use tags freely. The platform handles coordination across containers. Teams running on traditional infrastructure must weigh external cache implementation cost against path invalidation maintainability problems.

The framework suggests starting with path invalidation during early development. Routes typically contain isolated data while teams validate product direction. As applications mature and routes begin sharing data, migrate to tag-based invalidation. This evolution matches natural application growth.

Teams tracking cache hit rates gain concrete data for decisions. If path invalidation maintains hit rates above 80%, tags might be premature. If hit rates drop below 50% despite proper cache lifetimes, path invalidation likely invalidates too broadly. The metrics reveal whether the current approach scales.

The Next.js caching mental model provides context for how these primitives fit into the broader caching system. Revalidation represents only one part of cache strategy. Time-based expiration, stale-while-revalidate semantics, and cache warming also affect overall performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should teams use revalidatePath instead of revalidateTag?

Use revalidatePath when routes operate independently with dedicated data, such as admin dashboards where each page manages distinct resources. The primitive also works well during early development before data sharing patterns emerge. Teams should migrate to tags once multiple routes begin displaying the same underlying data.

How do revalidateTag and updateTag differ in production?

revalidateTag uses stale-while-revalidate semantics where old content serves while fresh content generates in the background. updateTag immediately expires cache entries, ensuring users see updated data on the next request. Use updateTag only in Server Actions where read-your-own-writes matters, such as after creating a new resource that must appear in a list immediately.

Can applications mix revalidatePath and revalidateTag in the same codebase?

Applications frequently combine both primitives. Core shared entities like products or users use tags for surgical invalidation. Peripheral features with isolated data like settings pages use path invalidation. The combination reduces maintenance burden while preserving cache efficiency where it matters most.

What happens to cache entries when neither primitive is called?

Cache entries remain valid until their time-based expiration triggers. The Next.js revalidation documentation explains that cacheLife profiles set expiration windows from 1 second to 1 year depending on data volatility. Entries expire and regenerate automatically even without explicit invalidation.

How do distributed deployments coordinate cache invalidation?

Distributed deployments require external cache stores like Redis or managed services that synchronize cache state across containers. Next.js default in-memory cache cannot coordinate across processes, causing silent failures where some containers serve stale data. Teams must implement custom cache adapters or use platforms with built-in distributed caching.

Building Maintainable Cache Invalidation Strategies

The difference between revalidatePath and revalidateTag determines whether cache invalidation remains manageable as applications grow. Path invalidation works immediately but collapses when routes share data. Tag invalidation requires upfront tagging discipline but scales linearly with application complexity.

Teams should start with concrete metrics. Track cache hit rates, response times, and invalidation frequency. Applications maintaining high hit rates with path invalidation should keep using it until metrics suggest otherwise. Applications with declining cache effectiveness need surgical tag-based invalidation.

The infrastructure decision matters more than the primitive choice at scale. Distributed deployments require external cache coordination regardless of invalidation strategy. Teams should implement shared cache storage early if multi-container deployment is planned. The Next.js 15 caching changes provide context for how the caching system evolved to handle these distributed scenarios.

The correct approach combines both primitives based on data sharing patterns. Tag shared entities for surgical invalidation. Use paths for isolated features. Measure cache performance to validate the strategy. Build external cache infrastructure before scaling beyond single containers.

title: Building Tenant-Isolated RAG with Spring Boot: Preventing Cross-Tenant Data Leakage
description:
Introduction

A multi-tenant SaaS application may have hundreds or thousands of organizations using the same AI infrastructure.

Each organization has its own documents, policies, customer records, and knowledge base.

A shared RAG pipeline can make this architecture cost-effective, but it also introduces a serious security risk.

Imagine Organization A asks:

"Summarize our customer incidents from last quarter."

The vector database retrieves relevant documents.

One of the results belongs to Organization B.

The LLM receives the document and may incorporate its contents into the response.

The application may have authenticated the user correctly. The database may be encrypted. The REST APIs may have authorization checks.

But the retrieval pipeline has violated tenant isolation.

In this article, we'll build the foundation of a tenant-aware RAG retrieval gateway using Java and Spring Boot.

The focus is not simply adding a tenant ID to a vector record. We want to enforce tenant identity throughout the retrieval lifecycle.

1. Reference architecture

Our implementation will use the following components:

  • Java 17.
  • Spring Boot.
  • PostgreSQL for application metadata.
  • A vector database such as Pinecone, Qdrant, or pgvector.
  • An embedding model.
  • An LLM for response generation.

The architecture:

             AUTHENTICATED USER
                     |
                     v
              SPRING BOOT API
                     |
                     v
             TENANT RESOLVER
                     |
                     v
             TENANT CONTEXT
                     |
                     v
              RAG SERVICE
                     |
                     v
            VECTOR RETRIEVAL
                     |
              TENANT FILTER
                     |
                     v
           RESOURCE AUTHORIZATION
                     |
                     v
                 RERANKER
                     |
                     v
             CONTEXT BUILDER
                     |
                     v
                    LLM
                     |
                     v
              RESPONSE VALIDATOR
                     |
                     v
                   USER

The important design decision is that the LLM does not determine tenant identity.

Tenant identity comes from the authenticated application context.

2. Project structure

A simple project structure:

tenant-aware-rag/
|
+-- controller/
|   +-- RagController.java
|
+-- security/
|   +-- TenantContext.java
|   +-- TenantResolver.java
|
+-- retrieval/
|   +-- VectorSearchService.java
|   +-- RetrievalFilter.java
|   +-- RetrievedDocument.java
|
+-- authorization/
|   +-- DocumentAuthorizationService.java
|
+-- service/
|   +-- RagService.java
|   +-- ContextBuilder.java
|
+-- cache/
|   +-- RagCacheService.java
|
+-- model/
|   +-- RagRequest.java
|   +-- RagResponse.java
|
+-- repository/
|   +-- DocumentMetadataRepository.java

3. Define the tenant context

First, define the trusted execution context.

public record TenantContext(
    String tenantId,
    String userId,
    Set<String> permissions
) {}

The tenant ID must come from authenticated application identity.

Do not accept a tenant ID supplied by the LLM as an authorization input.

For example, a request may contain:

{
  "question": "Summarize the incident reports"
}

The application resolves the tenant using the authenticated principal.

@Component
public class TenantResolver {

    public TenantContext resolve(Authentication authentication) {

        if (authentication == null ||
                !authentication.isAuthenticated()) {
            throw new AccessDeniedException(
                "Authentication required"
            );
        }

        String userId = authentication.getName();

        // Resolve this mapping from a trusted identity/tenant service.
        String tenantId = resolveTenantForUser(userId);

        return new TenantContext(
            tenantId,
            userId,
            Set.of("DOCUMENT_READ")
        );
    }

    private String resolveTenantForUser(String userId) {
        // Replace with a trusted identity provider or tenant repository.
        throw new UnsupportedOperationException(
            "Implement tenant lookup"
        );
    }
}

This is a design skeleton. In production, the resolver should support users belonging to multiple organizations, tenant membership status, and permission changes.

4. Store tenant metadata with every chunk

A document may be split into hundreds of chunks.

Every chunk needs tenant ownership and document-level metadata.

Example vector record:

{
  "id": "chunk-1001",
  "values": [0.12, 0.34, 0.56],
  "metadata": {
    "tenant_id": "tenant-a",
    "document_id": "doc-1001",
    "classification": "internal",
    "source": "incident-report.pdf",
    "chunk_number": 1
  }
}

Do not store tenant ownership only on the original document.

When chunks become independently retrievable objects, ownership and authorization metadata must be available at the chunk level.

Also validate tenant ownership during ingestion. Never trust tenant metadata extracted from a document or supplied by a client.

5. Define the retrieval contract

Create a normalized retrieval request:

public record RetrievalRequest(
    String tenantId,
    String userId,
    List<String> permittedDocumentIds,
    String query,
    int topK
) {}

The tenantId and permissions should come from the trusted execution context.

The model must not be able to override them.

Define the result:

public record RetrievedDocument(
    String chunkId,
    String documentId,
    String tenantId,
    String content,
    double score
) {}

And the service contract:

public interface VectorSearchService {

    List<RetrievedDocument> search(
        RetrievalRequest request
    );
}

6. Enforce tenant filters during vector retrieval

The exact query syntax depends on the vector database.

Conceptually, the query should look like:

{
  "vector": [0.12, 0.34, 0.56],
  "topK": 10,
  "filter": {
    "tenant_id": {
      "$eq": "tenant-a"
    }
  }
}

For a database supporting SQL-based vector search, the equivalent idea might be:

SELECT
    chunk_id,
    document_id,
    tenant_id,
    content,
    embedding <=> :query_embedding AS distance
FROM document_chunks
WHERE tenant_id = :tenant_id
ORDER BY embedding <=> :query_embedding
LIMIT :top_k;

The tenant filter must be applied as part of candidate selection.

Do not perform global vector search and rely exclusively on filtering results afterward.

A production implementation must also validate document-level permissions. Tenant equality does not automatically mean every user within that tenant can access every document.

7. Add a second authorization check

Tenant filtering protects organizational boundaries.

However, users within an organization may have different permissions.

For example:

  • Finance users can access financial documents.
  • HR users can access HR documents.
  • Support users can access support documentation.

Define an authorization service:

public interface DocumentAuthorizationService {

    boolean canRead(
        String userId,
        String tenantId,
        String documentId
    );
}

Validate the documents returned by vector search:

@Service
public class RetrievalAuthorizationService {

    private final DocumentAuthorizationService authorization;

    public RetrievalAuthorizationService(
            DocumentAuthorizationService authorization) {
        this.authorization = authorization;
    }

    public List<RetrievedDocument> filterAuthorized(
            TenantContext context,
            List<RetrievedDocument> documents) {

        return documents.stream()
            .filter(document ->
                context.tenantId().equals(document.tenantId())
            )
            .filter(document ->
                authorization.canRead(
                    context.userId(),
                    context.tenantId(),
                    document.documentId()
                )
            )
            .toList();
    }
}

This second check is defense in depth.

The vector database filter limits the candidate set, while the authorization service verifies the user's actual resource permissions.

The check should use current authorization data, not permissions inferred by the LLM.

8. Build the RAG service

Now combine the retrieval and authorization steps.

@Service
public class RagService {

    private final VectorSearchService vectorSearch;
    private final RetrievalAuthorizationService authorization;
    private final EmbeddingService embeddingService;
    private final LlmService llmService;

    public RagService(
            VectorSearchService vectorSearch,
            RetrievalAuthorizationService authorization,
            EmbeddingService embeddingService,
            LlmService llmService) {

        this.vectorSearch = vectorSearch;
        this.authorization = authorization;
        this.embeddingService = embeddingService;
        this.llmService = llmService;
    }

    public String answer(
            TenantContext context,
            String question) {

        float[] embedding =
            embeddingService.embed(question);

        RetrievalRequest request = new RetrievalRequest(
            context.tenantId(),
            context.userId(),
            List.of(),
            question,
            10
        );

        List<RetrievedDocument> candidates =
            vectorSearch.search(request);

        List<RetrievedDocument> authorized =
            authorization.filterAuthorized(
                context,
                candidates
            );

        String prompt = buildContext(
            question,
            authorized
        );

        return llmService.generate(prompt);
    }
}

This is an illustrative service skeleton. The embedding is shown to establish the flow; the vector adapter must actually use it in its search request.

The context builder should include only authorized documents.

If a document fails authorization, it must never be sent to the reranker or LLM.

9. Prevent semantic cache leakage

Caching is another area where multi-tenant RAG systems can fail.

Suppose two tenants ask semantically similar questions.

If the cache uses only the normalized question, the second tenant may receive an answer generated from the first tenant's documents.

A cache key should include the effective authorization context.

For example:

public String buildCacheKey(
        TenantContext context,
        String normalizedQuery,
        String modelVersion,
        String retrievalVersion) {

    String rawKey = String.join(
        "|",
        context.tenantId(),
        context.userId(),
        String.join(",", context.permissions().stream().sorted().toList()),
        normalizedQuery,
        modelVersion,
        retrievalVersion
    );

    return sha256(rawKey);
}

This is a starting point. For a production system, represent the effective authorization scope using a stable permission-scope identifier or version rather than relying only on a simple permission list.

Also consider:

  • Permission changes.
  • Document updates and deletion.
  • Tenant membership changes.
  • Model and prompt versions.
  • Retrieval configuration changes.
  • Cache expiration and invalidation.

Never reuse a cached answer without confirming that the current caller is still authorized to access its underlying source information.

10. Add integration tests for tenant isolation

This is where the architecture becomes meaningful.

Create two tenants:

Tenant A
  document-a1
  document-a2

Tenant B
  document-b1
  document-b2

Now test the retrieval boundaries.

@Test
void shouldNeverReturnDocumentsFromAnotherTenant() {

    TenantContext tenantA = new TenantContext(
        "tenant-a",
        "user-a",
        Set.of("DOCUMENT_READ")
    );

    List<RetrievedDocument> documents = List.of(
        new RetrievedDocument(
            "chunk-a1",
            "document-a1",
            "tenant-a",
            "Tenant A incident report",
            0.91
        ),
        new RetrievedDocument(
            "chunk-b1",
            "document-b1",
            "tenant-b",
            "Tenant B confidential report",
            0.95
        )
    );

    List<RetrievedDocument> result =
        authorization.filterAuthorized(
            tenantA,
            documents
        );

    assertTrue(
        result.stream().allMatch(
            doc -> doc.tenantId().equals("tenant-a")
        )
    );
}

This tests the authorization filter, but it is not enough.

Add integration tests that inspect the actual vector query and verify that the tenant filter is applied before candidate retrieval.

Also test:

  1. Missing tenant context.
  2. Forged tenant IDs in user input.
  3. Unauthorized documents within the same tenant.
  4. Cross-tenant semantic cache hits.
  5. Permission revocation after a cache entry is created.
  6. Unauthorized document IDs reaching the reranker.
  7. Unauthorized content reaching the LLM.
  8. Cross-tenant citations in the final response.

The most important assertion is:

No unauthorized document should enter the model's context window.

11. Production hardening

Before deploying this architecture, address several additional concerns.

Ingestion security

  • Derive tenant ownership from trusted application identity.
  • Validate ownership before processing files.
  • Preserve tenant metadata through chunking.
  • Prevent document ID collisions.
  • Securely delete all associated chunks when documents are removed.

Retrieval security

  • Apply filters during candidate generation.
  • Validate document-level permissions.
  • Restrict access to vector database credentials.
  • Avoid exposing raw vector queries to the LLM.
  • Ensure reranking receives only authorized candidates.

Cache security

  • Scope cache entries to effective authorization context.
  • Invalidate after permission changes.
  • Avoid caching sensitive responses globally.
  • Include retrieval and model versions where relevant.

Operational security

  • Record retrieval and authorization decisions.
  • Monitor cross-tenant access attempts.
  • Avoid logging confidential document content.
  • Fail closed when tenant context or authorization services are unavailable.
  • Test isolation continuously.

Conclusion

Multi-tenant RAG is not simply a vector database configuration problem.

It is an end-to-end authorization problem.

A secure implementation must preserve tenant identity from ingestion through retrieval, reranking, caching, and final generation.

Traditional application security protects the API.

Enterprise AI security must also protect the information entering the model's context.

The context window is part of the security boundary.

If unauthorized information reaches it, the architecture has already failed.

About the Author

I'm Ashwin Giridharan, a Cloud & Enterprise Solutions Architect focused on building scalable systems and exploring the architecture of AI.

My interests include enterprise architecture, cloud platforms, distributed systems, Generative AI, LLMs, RAG, Agentic AI, and taking AI solutions from experimentation to production.

I share practical insights, technical explorations, and lessons learned while building and understanding modern technology systems.

title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
description:
arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
description:
arXiv:2611.23910v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

title: JSONB performance: declare access patterns to PostgreSQL query planner
description:
A common drawback of storing data in JSON fields is limited planner visibility: the optimizer doesn't automatically inspect documents, so selectivity estimates for JSON (or JSONB or BSON) predicates are often weak when useful statistics aren’t available. That’s expected—if you choose JSON to avoid defining the full application schema in the database upfront, the database can’t infer everything about those fields.

But this isn’t an all-or-nothing tradeoff. Even in MongoDB, you still declare part of the schema in practice—especially filter fields—through indexes. PostgreSQL, gives you two levers:

  • expression indexes (which provide both access paths and statistics)
  • extended statistics (which improve estimates even without adding an index).

I'm using an example from an old article by Dan Robinson on the Heap blog: When To Avoid JSONB In A PostgreSQL Schema. At the time, PostgreSQL 9.4 didn't support extended statistics, but expression indexes could have solved this (example on db<>fiddle), avoiding the expensive nested-loop join and producing good cardinality estimates.

I've run the following in a lab:


CREATE TABLE measurements (tick BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, record JSONB NOT NULL)
;
INSERT INTO measurements (record)
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
  'value_1', trunc(2 * random())::int,
  'value_2', trunc(2 * random())::int,
  'value_3', trunc(2 * random())::int,
  'scientist_id', trunc(10000 * random() + 1)::bigint
)
FROM generate_series(1, 100000)
;
CREATE TABLE scientist_labs (scientist_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, lab_name TEXT NOT NULL)
;
INSERT INTO scientist_labs (scientist_id, lab_name)
SELECT i,(ARRAY['California Scientific','Industrial Labs','Western Science People'])[(i % 3) + 1]
FROM generate_series(1, 10000) AS i
;
VACUUM (ANALYZE) measurements
;
VACUUM (ANALYZE) scientist_labs
;

Get the execution plan for this query:

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT s.lab_name, COUNT( * )
FROM (
  SELECT (record ->> 'scientist_id')::BIGINT AS scientist_id
  FROM measurements
  WHERE (record ->> 'value_1')::INT = 0
    AND (record ->> 'value_2')::INT = 0
    AND (record ->> 'value_3')::INT = 0
) AS m
JOIN scientist_labs AS s
  ON s.scientist_id = m.scientist_id
GROUP BY s.lab_name
ORDER BY s.lab_name
;

The estimated cardinality for "measurements" after the filter is rows=1, which is why PostgreSQL chooses a Nested Loop. However, the actual row count is rows=12518.00, so "scientist_labs" is accessed loops=12518 times:

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   Group Key: s.lab_name
   Buffers: shared hit=39186
   ->  Sort  (cost=5827.32..5827.33 rows=1 width=20) (actual time=139.215..150.787 rows=12518.00 loops=1)
         Sort Key: s.lab_name
         Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 645kB
         Buffers: shared hit=39186
         ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.29..5827.31 rows=1 width=20) (actual time=0.156..126.483 rows=12518.00 loops=1)
               Buffers: shared hit=39186
               ->  Seq Scan on measurements  (cost=0.00..5819.00 rows=1 width=105) (actual time=0.029..60.878 rows=12518.00 loops=1)
                     Filter: ((((record ->> 'value_1'::text))::integer = 0) AND (((record ->> 'value_2'::text))::integer = 0) AND (((record ->> 'value_3'::text))::integer = 0))
                     Rows Removed by Filter: 87482
                     Buffers: shared hit=1819
               ->  Index Scan using scientist_labs_pkey on scientist_labs s  (cost=0.29..8.31 rows=1 width=28) (actual time=0.002..0.002 rows=1.00 loops=12518)
                     Index Cond: (scientist_id = ((measurements.record ->> 'scientist_id'::text))::bigint)
                     Index Searches: 12518
                     Buffers: shared hit=37367

(19 rows)

Compare the Planned rows with the actual rows:

This is not optimal but easily fixed by indexing the fields used to filter:

CREATE INDEX measurements_value_1_idx ON measurements (
 ((record ->> 'value_1')::INT)
);
CREATE INDEX measurements_value_2_idx ON measurements (
 ((record ->> 'value_2')::INT)
);
CREATE INDEX measurements_value_3_idx ON measurements (
 ((record ->> 'value_3')::INT)
);
ANALYZE measurements;

We index an expression to retrieve its value by using the full path, and specify the data type the filter uses. This is like declaring part of the schema for the "schemaless" datatype—the parts correspond to the access pattern.

ANALYZE also gathers statistics about the index keys for the query planner, which uses them for the query:

(34 rows)

The estimated cardinality of "measurements" (rows=12538) is close to the actual count (rows=12518), so the query planner chooses a Hash Join and reads "scientist_labs" only once.

The query planner estimates the predicate’s overall cardinality by multiplying the selectivity of each field. This works here because the fields are uncorrelated. Three separate indexes offer flexibility when queries don’t filter on all three fields, but require a bitmap combination. If the fields always appear together in the filter, a compound index would be better:

CREATE INDEX measurements_value_123_idx ON measurements (
 ((record ->> 'value_1')::INT)
 ,
 ((record ->> 'value_2')::INT)
 ,
 ((record ->> 'value_3')::INT)
);
ANALYZE measurements;

The query planner prefers this index, and it still estimates cardinality correctly: rows=12564 for rows=12518.00:

CREATE STATISTICS measurements_values_stats (mcv, dependencies)
ON ((record ->> 'value_1')::INT)

The estimated rows=12450 is close to the real value rows=12518.00.

JSON columns in a relational database don’t force an all-or-nothing choice between flexibility and performance. PostgreSQL can inspect JSONB contents: for top-level fields—or nested fields accessible without traversing an array—you can create B-tree expression indexes that provide both an access path and the statistics the planner needs to estimate cardinality accurately. When you need better estimates without index overhead, or when predicates involve correlated fields, extended statistics on expressions (PostgreSQL 14+) let you specify exactly which field combinations the planner should understand. In practice, efficient applications use both approaches: keep flexible schema details known only to the application, and declare the fields that drive access patterns to the database through indexes, statistics, or both.

title: I gave Claude Code and Codex one landing page. Here’s the handoff I’d use.
description:
The fastest way to get two coding agents to do the same work twice is to give them the same vague brief in two separate chats.

The second agent starts from scratch. It can’t see why the first agent made a recommendation, which screenshot backs it up, or what you already decided not to change. You end up copying context between chats and reviewing two versions of the same work.

As a marketing engineer, I’d rather give Claude Code and Codex different jobs on the same task. One finds the problem. The other makes the fix. I decide whether it’s ready to ship.

One page, one problem

Say we’re reviewing a SaaS landing page. At a viewport width of 390 px, the hero’s two buttons wrap, and the primary CTA drops below the first screen. That’s an illustrative example, but it’s the kind of issue I’d hand off. “Improve the landing page” is too broad. “Keep the primary CTA visible on mobile without changing approved copy” gives both agents a clear finish line.

The handoff I’d put in the task

Goal: Keep the primary CTA visible at 390 px.
Sources: Staging URL, hero component, approved positioning brief.

Claude Code: Reproduce the issue. Leave a screenshot, point to the
relevant component, and explain the smallest change you’d try.

Codex: Use that evidence to make the change on a branch.
Leave the diff, a before/after screenshot at 390 px, and a note
on what you checked on desktop.

Constraints: Keep the approved copy and analytics event names.
Do not deploy.

Done when: The primary CTA is visible on mobile, there’s no
horizontal overflow, and the desktop layout still works.

How I’d set it up in ActVox

I’d connect both agents to the same Space over MCP, give them separate @handles, and enable Read and edit so they can take assignments. I’d leave sharing and publishing off for this exercise. Claude Code takes the first assignment. Codex gets the second on the same task, blocked until the first is complete. If Codex doesn’t pick it up, I’d prompt it to check its ActVox inbox before creating another task.

One setup caveat: ActVox’s guide confirms native MCP reads for Claude Code but doesn’t confirm production writes through that route. It documents a CLI fallback if a write doesn’t land. Full setup and commands.

What I’d actually review

I’d open the before/after screenshots and the diff side by side. If the button is visible but the click event changed, I’d return the task with that specific note. If the evidence matches the brief, I’d accept it. Deploying is a separate decision.

The part worth copying is the handoff itself: pass the evidence, the constraints, and the definition of done. That gives the next agent something to work from and gives you something to review besides a green checkmark.

If you’re running multi-agent workflows, what’s the one piece of evidence you always ask the second agent to return?

title: Never lazy-load your LCP image: the fetchpriority, preload and srcset checklist
description:
A Core Web Vitals tip: never lazy-load the image that decides your LCP (Largest Contentful Paint). Give it fetchpriority="high", leave loading out, and add a preload only when the HTML can't show the image.

The 2025 Web Almanac still finds 16–17% of pages lazy-loading their LCP image. Only 17% of mobile pages with an image LCP use fetchpriority="high".

What each attribute actually does

  • loading="lazy": the download waits for layout. On a hero, that wait is pure delay.
  • loading="eager": the default. Writing it changes nothing.
  • fetchpriority="high": the request starts at High instead of Low. Google Flights went from 2.6 s to 1.9 s LCP with it (web.dev).
  • lazy + high: still waits for layout. The delay stays.

When you need a preload

Only when the preload scanner can't see the image:

  • a CSS background-image hero
  • an image a script inserts
  • a JS-built slider

Put fetchpriority="high" on the preload too. Match imagesrcset and imagesizes to the element exactly, or the browser downloads twice.

Then cut the bytes

Same hero photo, 1920 px wide, our engine at Auto quality:

  • JPEG: 140.3 KB
  • WebP: 85.5 KB
  • AVIF: 69.3 KB

A phone that shows the hero at 400 CSS px on a 2x screen needs 800 px. That file is 35.2 KB. srcset + a real sizes value gets it there. Note that sizes="auto" only works with lazy images, so your LCP image needs a real value.

The markup 

<img
  src="/img/hero-1280.jpg"
  srcset="/img/hero-800.jpg 800w, /img/hero-1280.jpg 1280w, /img/hero-1920.jpg 1920w"
  sizes="100vw"
  width="1920" height="1076"
  alt="..."
  fetchpriority="high">

Wrap it in <picture> with an AVIF <source> first, then WebP.

What does your LCP breakdown look like? I'm curious which sub-part hurts most on real sites: load delay or load duration.

Full write-up with every byte count: https://blinkimg.com/blog/image-optimization?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=lcp-checklist

title: Run a Go + SvelteKit online store on your laptop with one docker compose
description:
GoCommerce is an MIT-licensed commerce engine written in Go: products, variants, inventory, carts, checkout, orders, payments and fulfilment over one PostgreSQL database, with an admin panel built into the binary. Svelte Commerce is the SvelteKit storefront that sells from it. This walkthrough runs both, plus Postgres, Meilisearch and Caddy, on your own machine, and ends with a working shop at https://acme.shops.localhost.

You need Docker with Compose v2 and Git. Nothing else: Go and Node run inside the images.

1. Get the code 

git clone https://github.com/itswadesh/gocommerce
cd gocommerce
cp .env.example .env

2. Fill in .env for a local trial

Open .env and set these. Everything else can stay empty.

POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<openssl rand -hex 24>
GOCOMMERCE_ADMIN_TOKEN=<openssl rand -hex 32>
GOCOMMERCE_ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com
GOCOMMERCE_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a password for the panel>
MEILI_MASTER_KEY=<openssl rand -hex 24>

ADMIN_DOMAIN=admin.localhost
GOCOMMERCE_PANEL_URL=https://admin.localhost
GOCOMMERCE_BASE_DOMAIN=shops.localhost
CADDY_GLOBAL_OPTIONS=local_certs

*.localhost names point at your own machine in current browsers, so no DNS is needed. local_certs makes Caddy issue certificates from its own local authority instead of asking Let's Encrypt, which can't reach your laptop. COMPOSE_PROFILES=proxy is already on in the example, which is what starts Caddy. If ports 80 or 443 are taken, set HTTP_PORT and HTTPS_PORT and add the port to the addresses below.

Leave out MEILI_MASTER_KEY and the engine still runs, just without search, but the Meilisearch container will keep restarting: in production mode it refuses to start without a key.

3. Start it 

docker compose up -d --build

The first build takes a few minutes: it compiles the engine and builds the storefront from the svelte-commerce repository. docker compose ps should then show postgres, meilisearch, gocommerce, storefront and caddy running. The engine logs a line like:

gocommerce listening addr=0.0.0.0:8080 version=1.2.0 modules=65 routes=728

4. Open a store

One install hosts many stores. Make the first one:

docker compose exec gocommerce /gocommerce store create acme "Acme Store"

Then open:

  • https://acme.shops.localhost, the storefront for the store you just made.
  • https://admin.localhost, the admin panel. Sign in with the email and password from .env.

Your browser will warn about the certificate the first time, because it comes from Caddy's local authority. That is expected for a local trial.

What's in the box

The compose file installs every module, and each one sits idle until you configure it: payments (Stripe, Razorpay, Cashfree and others), shipping (Shiprocket, Shippo and others), email and WhatsApp notifications, invoices, B2B company accounts, a CMS, and an MCP server. In code, each is an ordinary Go package under ext/. They change the core only through its services, never by writing its tables, so an order's state change and its event commit in the same transaction.

If you'd rather embed the engine in your own Go program than run the binary:

go get github.com/misiki-in/gocommerce/core@latest

A store is then a main() that passes the integrations it wants to gocommerce.New(...). The README has the full example.

Clean up 

docker compose down -v

-v also deletes the database and media volumes.

The engine and the storefront are free to self-host under the MIT licence. If you'd rather not run servers, ShopNx is the hosted version for Indian sellers, and it is free.

title: AI Coding Agent Feature Flags: Ship Faster Without Letting Agents Launch Too Much
description:
An AI coding agent can finish a feature before a reviewer has time to decide whether anyone should see it. That is useful right up until a generated checkout path, data mutation, or expensive model call reaches every customer at once.

The answer is not to slow every change with a long approval queue. It is to separate deployment from release. A well-designed feature flag lets a team merge and deploy a small, tested change while a person still controls who receives it, how quickly exposure grows, and how to stop it.

This guide shows how to give coding agents a safe feature-flag contract. It is aimed at small product teams that use agents to implement customer-facing changes and need a release process that remains understandable under pressure.

Why coding agents make release control more important

Agents make the batch size problem visible. A developer who hand-writes a change usually pauses at several points: while reading the code, waiting for tests, asking a question, or switching tasks. An agent can create the API route, UI branch, migration, analytics event, and test updates in one session.

That speed is not a reason to distrust generated code. It is a reason to keep the decision to expose a new behavior outside the code-generation loop.

Treat a temporary release flag as a small operational contract:

Field Why it matters
Key Gives code, dashboards, and incident notes one stable name.
Owner Makes one person or team accountable for the rollout and cleanup.
Default Defines safe behavior when the flag service is unavailable.
Scope States exactly which user, tenant, or environment can receive it.
Expiry Turns cleanup into scheduled work, not a vague intention.
Metrics Tells the operator what must remain healthy before expansion.

The important distinction is between a release flag and a kill switch. A release flag starts off and is gradually enabled for a new capability. A kill switch normally stays on and quickly disables an existing risky dependency or path. Do not use one flag for both jobs; their defaults, owners, and retirement rules are different.

Decide whether a flag is the right control

Flags add branches. Every branch increases the number of states tests and humans must reason about. Before asking an agent to add one, use this decision rule:

  1. Split the change if it can be delivered as a harmless smaller slice.
  2. Use a release flag when code is safe to deploy but not safe to expose widely.
  3. Use a kill switch for a dependency or behavior that may need immediate containment.
  4. Do not hide a schema-incompatible migration behind a flag. First make the database change compatible with both application versions.
  5. Do not use a flag as authorization. A feature being enabled does not mean a user has permission to perform an action.

For example, a new AI-generated account-summary panel is a good release-flag candidate. It changes customer-visible behavior, can increase model spend, and may need evaluation with real production-shaped data. A new permission check is not: it must be correct for every request before deployment.

Give the agent a flag contract before it writes code

An instruction such as “put new UI behind a flag” is too vague. It leaves the agent to choose a key, a default, a targeting rule, and whether the old path is still tested. Put a compact contract in the repository instructions that every coding agent reads.

## Release-flag contract
- Any customer-visible behavior change needs a release plan before implementation.
- Temporary flags use: rel_<area>_<capability>.
- The code default must be false for a new release flag.
- Include owner, ticket, expiry date, and rollback metric in the flag metadata.
- Keep evaluation at the boundary; do not scatter the same check through components.
- Add tests for both enabled and disabled behavior.
- Agents may create local or test-environment flags, but may not increase production exposure.
- Every flag PR includes a removal issue and the expected permanent state.

This does not require a particular flag service. The contract can work with a database table, a configuration provider, or a dedicated SDK. What matters is that the feature definition is reviewable and the production control is not silently granted to an agent.

Keep evaluation at a boundary

Evaluate once near the request boundary, turn the result into an explicit capability, and pass it into the feature. That makes tests simple and prevents different parts of the page from disagreeing.

type ReleaseAccess = {
  accountId: string;
  isSummaryV2Enabled: boolean;
};

export async function accountPage(request: Request) {
  const account = await requireAccount(request);
  const isEnabled = await flags.isEnabled("rel_summary_v2", {
    accountId: account.id,
    plan: account.plan,
  });

  const access: ReleaseAccess = {
    accountId: account.id,
    isSummaryV2Enabled: isEnabled,
  };

  return renderAccountPage(access);
}

Avoid checking flags.isEnabled() again inside a background job, a component, and an API endpoint. Mid-request changes can produce confusing partial states. Instead, persist the evaluated variant with the job when consistency matters, and make idempotency independent of the flag value.

Design a rollout plan the agent cannot improvise

Before a PR is opened, write the rollout card. It is short enough to live in the pull request description, but concrete enough for someone on call to use.

Flag: rel_summary_v2
Type: temporary release flag
Owner: billing-platform
Default: off
Audience: internal accounts -> 5 named design partners -> 5% eligible accounts
Success: no increase in summary error rate; median response under 2 seconds
Stop: disable if request failures exceed baseline by 1 percentage point
Expiry: remove by 2026-12-18; permanent state: on

Notice that “enable for 5%” is not a plan by itself. A safe plan names the eligible population, the measurement window, the stop condition, and the next decision owner. For a feature that triggers model calls, include a cost guardrail too: for example, no more than a set amount of incremental cost per completed task. This protects against a rollout that looks healthy in errors but quietly harms margin.

Target identities, not random requests

Use a stable identifier such as account ID for percentage rollouts. Random-per-request assignment lets one customer see two versions of the same workflow, making bug reports impossible to interpret. Exclude internal support accounts unless they are intentionally used for testing, and never place sensitive eligibility attributes directly in browser-visible flag payloads.

For multi-tenant products, tenant targeting is often safer than user targeting. It keeps an entire customer workspace on one behavior and makes support, audit logs, and rollback clearer.

Test both paths and the transitions between them

“The flag is off by default” is not a test. An agent-created change must prove three things:

  1. The off path preserves the existing behavior.
  2. The on path works with representative authorization, data, and failure cases.
  3. Changing the flag does not duplicate a side effect or leave a workflow half complete.

Here is a small deterministic test seam:

it("keeps the existing summary when the release is disabled", async () => {
  const page = await renderAccountPage({
    accountId: "acct_1",
    isSummaryV2Enabled: false,
  });

  expect(page.getByText("Account activity")).toBeVisible();
  expect(page.queryByText("AI account summary")).toBeNull();
});

it("shows the guarded summary when the release is enabled", async () => {
  const page = await renderAccountPage({
    accountId: "acct_1",
    isSummaryV2Enabled: true,
  });

  expect(page.getByText("AI account summary")).toBeVisible();
});

For background work, test the transition explicitly. Suppose enabling a flag starts a document enrichment job. The job should have an idempotency key based on the document and intended operation, not on “flag is currently true.” Otherwise a rollback and retry can create duplicate writes.

Also test the failure mode of the flag dependency. Most customer-facing release flags should fail closed: if the flag provider is unavailable, new behavior stays off. A kill switch that protects a risky provider may need the opposite design. Document the choice; do not inherit it accidentally from an SDK default.

Build observability around decisions, not prompts

During a rollout, log the release decision as a structured event. You need to answer: which variant did this account receive, when did it change, and did it correlate with a bad outcome?

{
  "event": "release_flag_evaluated",
  "flag": "rel_summary_v2",
  "variant": "on",
  "account_id": "acct_42",
  "rule": "design-partners",
  "request_id": "req_8f3",
  "config_version": "2026-11-20T09:15Z"
}

Do not put raw prompts, account secrets, or full model outputs in this event. Link the event to a privacy-reviewed trace ID if deeper debugging is needed. Pair decision telemetry with product metrics: successful task completion, latency, error class, support contacts, and cost per completed task. A rollout dashboard should make it easy to compare the flagged cohort with a comparable control group.

Keep production control human-owned

An agent can propose a rollout card, generate tests, create a flag definition, and summarize metrics. It should not silently raise production exposure. That boundary matters even for a trusted repository agent because flag changes alter live behavior without requiring a deploy.

Use a small permission model:

Action Agent Human reviewer On-call operator
Add code and a local flag Yes Reviews —
Create staging targeting Yes, logged Reviews —
Enable internal production cohort Propose only Approves Can execute
Increase customer exposure No Approves plan Executes
Disable a release flag No — Yes
Remove stale code Propose PR Reviews —

The fastest safe action should be disabling a risky rollout. Make that path independent of the agent, the deployment pipeline, and a database migration. Record who changed the flag and why, but do not make an incident responder wait for a meeting to use a kill switch.

Make removal part of “done”

Temporary flags become expensive when their expiry is optional. They leave dead code, multiply test combinations, and make the next coding agent less certain which path is real.

At creation time, create the removal work item and choose one of three final states:

  • Permanent on: remove the old path and the flag after the rollout.
  • Permanent off: remove the new path and the flag.
  • Operational kill switch: keep it, but label it as permanent, assign an owner, and review it like production configuration.

Your CI can help. Fail or warn when a temporary flag is past its expiry, has no owner, or is referenced in code but absent from the registry. A weekly report of expiring flags is useful, but a pull request that includes the removal plan is better: it connects the operational promise to the exact branches that must disappear.

A practical pull-request checklist

Before merging an AI-generated customer-facing change, verify:

  • [ ] The release flag has a key, owner, safe default, scope, expiry, and final state.
  • [ ] Authorization is enforced separately from the flag.
  • [ ] The off, on, and side-effect transition paths have deterministic tests.
  • [ ] The schema and API remain compatible for both variants.
  • [ ] Percentage targeting uses a stable tenant or account identity.
  • [ ] The rollout card names success metrics, a stop condition, and an operator.
  • [ ] Production exposure changes require a human action and an audit event.
  • [ ] Decision telemetry avoids prompts, secrets, and unnecessary personal data.
  • [ ] A removal issue exists before the feature is merged.

The goal is not to place every line of generated code behind a toggle. It is to use a small number of well-owned release controls where speed creates a real blast radius. When deployment and exposure are separate, coding agents can move quickly while the team keeps the final production decision legible, reversible, and human-owned.

FAQ

Should every AI-generated change use a feature flag?

No. Use flags for customer-visible or operationally risky behavior that is safe to deploy but needs controlled exposure. Small internal refactors and changes that must be universally correct, such as authorization fixes, should not gain an unnecessary branch.

What is the safest default for a new release flag?

For most new customer-facing behavior, default to off if the flag service cannot be reached. This preserves the known path during a dependency failure. Document exceptions, especially for protective kill switches, where the safe fallback may be different.

Can an AI coding agent turn on a production feature flag?

It can prepare the configuration and recommend a staged plan, but a human-owned production control should execute increases in exposure. Flag changes can affect live users without a deployment, so they deserve audit logs and clear authority.

How do feature flags affect testing for coding agents?

Test both values and any state transition that can cause a side effect. Pass the resolved variant into application code rather than mocking a remote SDK throughout the test suite; that keeps tests deterministic and makes the behavior explicit.

How long should a temporary release flag live?

Set an expiry when it is created, usually tied to the planned rollout window. The correct duration depends on risk and traffic, but the flag should have a named owner and a scheduled decision to remove code, not simply stay until someone notices it.

Are feature flags a replacement for permissions or approval gates?

No. A flag decides whether a released capability is available to an audience. Authorization decides whether a specific user may take an action. Approval gates decide whether a risky action should proceed in a given context. Keep those controls separate.

title: Glassmorphism in CSS: how it works + a free live generator
description:
Glassmorphism is the frosted glass look you see on Apple's interfaces, in Windows, and on half of the landing pages on Dribbble: a translucent card that blurs whatever is behind it, with a thin bright edge that catches the light.

It looks expensive, but in CSS it comes down to four properties. This guide explains each one, gives you a copy-paste class, covers the mistakes that make glass look like grey plastic, and links to a free live generator where you can tune every value with sliders and copy the result.

👉 Open the live glassmorphism generator: drag the sliders, watch the card change, press Get the CSS.

The four ingredients of glass

Real frosted glass does four things to the light that passes through it. Each one maps to a line of CSS.

1. A faint tint

Glass is never fully clear. A white background at 10–20% opacity gives it body:

background: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.14);

Go above about 30% and it stops looking like glass and starts looking like a white card.

2. Blur what's behind it

This is the heart of the effect. backdrop-filter applies a filter to everything behind the element, not to the element itself:

backdrop-filter: blur(18px);
-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(18px); /* Safari */

Between 10px and 24px looks like frosted glass. Under 6px it just looks smudged.

3. Boost the saturation

Blurring washes colours out. Real glass doesn't. Add saturate() in the same filter and the colours behind the card come back to life:

backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(160%);

This one line is the difference between "nice" and "wow". Most tutorials skip it.

4. A lit edge

Light catches the edge of a pane of glass. A thin, semi-transparent white border plus a 1px inner highlight on top sells the thickness:

border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 0.28);
box-shadow:
  0 30px 60px -20px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55),     /* lifts it off the page */
  inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.38);   /* light on the top edge */

The complete class

Put the four together and you have a reusable glass panel:

.glass {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / 0.14);
  backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(160%);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(160%);
  border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 0.28);
  border-radius: 22px;
  box-shadow:
    0 30px 60px -20px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.55),
    inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 0.38);
  color: #fff;
}

Want different values? Don't guess and refresh. Tune them live in the generator: blur, saturation, tint, edge light, corner radius and colours are all sliders, and Get the CSS gives you this exact rule with your numbers.

Why your glass looks like grey plastic

If you copied a glass class and it looks flat, it's almost always one of these.

There's nothing behind it. Blur only shows when there is something to blur. On a flat background, glass is just a grey box. Put colourful shapes, a photo or a gradient behind it. In the generator, three blurred circles drift behind the card for exactly this reason.

The tint is too strong. Above roughly 0.3 opacity the background wins and the blur disappears. Start at 0.1 and go up slowly.

You forgot saturation. Blur alone desaturates. Add saturate(140%–180%).

No edge. Without the thin white border the card has no thickness and melts into the background.

Dark text on a busy background. Glass changes as things move behind it, so text needs contrast everywhere. White text with a soft shadow, or a slightly stronger tint behind long text, keeps it readable.

Browser support and performance

backdrop-filter works in every current browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox (since version 103) and Safari (keep the -webkit- prefix for older iOS versions).

It isn't free, though. The browser has to re-blur everything behind the element whenever something under it moves. A few glass panels are fine. Dozens of large, overlapping ones on an animated page will cost frames, especially on low-end phones. Two tips:

  • Keep blurred areas small and few. Use glass for cards, navbars and dialogs, not whole page sections.
  • If you need a fallback for very old browsers, give the element a stronger solid tint first, then add the blur inside @supports (backdrop-filter: blur(1px)) { … }.

Accessibility

Glass is decoration, so make sure it doesn't cost readability:

  • Check text contrast against the busiest part of what can sit behind the card, not the calmest.
  • Respect prefers-reduced-transparency where it's supported, and fall back to a solid background: 
@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .glass { background: rgb(30 30 36 / 0.95); backdrop-filter: none; }
}

Try it yourself

Reading about blur values only goes so far. The fastest way to get a feel for glassmorphism is to drag the sliders and watch:

  1. Open the glassmorphism generator and move the Blur, Saturation and Glass tint sliders.
  2. Press Get the CSS to copy your version.
  3. Want to keep it, change the background or build your own card on top? Remix it on Devlyo: you get your own editable copy that runs live, and you can share it with a link.

Devlyo is a place for developers to share code that actually runs: live components, shaders and Three.js demos with sliders anyone can play with. If you build a glass effect of your own, post it there, and the best ones get featured.
