title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
description:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: Your SSH debug log is truncating the server's offer
description:
My SSH probe was reporting algorithm names that do not exist. The last entry in a server's list came back as …@openqu, cut off mid-word. The server was my own test box running an Open Quantum Safe build of OpenSSH, which offers 71 key exchange algorithms. My tool was reading that list from ssh -vv, and ssh -vv had quietly stopped printing it.

The cause is a fixed 1,024-byte buffer in OpenSSH's logging code. It truncates any log line longer than that, with no marker that anything is missing. This post shows where it happens in the source, who it affects, and how to read the server's list directly from the wire in about 20 lines of Python.

This is part 2 of a series on building pqc-probe. Part 1: Which post-quantum key exchanges does a server actually support?

Where the server's list shows up

Before any encryption starts, an SSH server sends its proposal: the key exchange algorithms, host key types, ciphers and MACs it accepts, each as a comma-separated list. Run the client with -vv and OpenSSH prints them:

debug2: peer server KEXINIT proposal
debug2: KEX algorithms: mlkem768x25519-sha256,sntrup761x25519-sha512,curve25519-sha256,...
debug2: host key algorithms: ssh-ed25519,ecdsa-sha2-nistp256,...

If the client and server share no key exchange algorithm, the connection fails with the server's list in the error instead:

Unable to negotiate with 192.0.2.10 port 2222: no matching key exchange method found. Their offer: ...

Both lines are easy to grep, and every OpenSSH client produces them, so scraping them is the obvious way to learn what a server offers. That is what my first version of pqc-probe did.

The cause: a 1,024-byte buffer

Every OpenSSH log message, debug or error, goes through one function, do_log in log.c. It formats the message into a fixed buffer on the stack:

#define MSGBUFSIZ 1024
...
    char msgbuf[MSGBUFSIZ];
...
    vsnprintf(msgbuf, sizeof(msgbuf), fmt, args);

vsnprintf never writes past the buffer. When the formatted text is longer, it keeps the first 1,023 bytes plus the terminating zero and drops the rest. Nothing is added to show the line was cut. That is safe, standard C, and exactly the right behaviour for a logger. It just means a log line is not a container for arbitrary-length data.

The server's list reaches that buffer from two places:

  • kex.c, line 198 prints each list with debug2("%s: %s", proposal_names[i], proposal[i]).
  • packet.c, line 2115 builds the "Unable to negotiate … Their offer: %s" error.

The buffer itself is at log.c, lines 327–392. Links point to OpenSSH portable as of 18 November 2026.

Who hits it

Stock OpenSSH servers do not. I measured the default lists compiled into OpenSSH portable: the server's key exchange list is 183 bytes and the longest default list, host key algorithms, is 605 bytes. Both fit with room to spare.

Post-quantum experiments do. The OQS fork of OpenSSH adds dozens of hybrid key exchanges with long names such as ecdh-nistp521-frodokem-1344-shaker2-sha512@openquantumsafe.org. Its default server list is 45 names and 1,577 bytes. As a debug2 line, OpenSSH keeps 1,023 of its 1,601 bytes, and the last name printed is ecdh-nis. My test server, configured with 71 names, lost even more.

So anything that learns a server's algorithms by scraping ssh -vv gets a silently incomplete answer from exactly the servers it most wants to inspect. That includes inventory scripts, compliance checks and scanners. In the fork's default list the classical algorithms come first, so the cut falls on the post-quantum ones: 26 names survive, and the 19 lost include every ML-KEM and sntrup761 variant at the end of the list.

The fix: read the packet yourself

The server's proposal is the first packet it sends, and it travels before any encryption, so you can read it with a plain TCP socket. RFC 4253 defines every byte:

  1. Both sides send an identification line such as SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_10.0. A server may send other text lines first (section 4.2), so skip lines until one starts with SSH-.
  2. The server then sends a binary packet (section 6) whose payload is SSH_MSG_KEXINIT (section 7.1).
Bytes Field
4 packet_length
1 padding_length
1 message type, 20 = SSH_MSG_KEXINIT
16 random cookie
4 + n kex_algorithms: length, then the comma-separated names
… nine more lists: host keys, ciphers, MACs, compression, languages (each in both directions where it applies)
1 + 4 first_kex_packet_follows, reserved

That is all it takes:

import socket, struct, sys

host = sys.argv[1]
port = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 22
sock = socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=10)
f = sock.makefile("rb")

line = f.readline(8192)            # servers may send text lines before their banner
while not line.startswith(b"SSH-"):
    if not line:
        sys.exit("connection closed before the SSH banner")
    line = f.readline(8192)
print("server:", line.decode(errors="replace").strip())
sock.sendall(b"SSH-2.0-kexinit-peek\r\n")

length, padding = struct.unpack(">IB", f.read(5))   # binary packet header
payload = f.read(length - 1 - padding)
if payload[0] != 20:
    sys.exit(f"first packet is message {payload[0]}, not KEXINIT (20)")
size = struct.unpack(">I", payload[17:21])[0]       # skip type byte + 16-byte cookie
names = payload[21:21 + size].decode().split(",")
print(f"kex_algorithms: {len(names)} names, {size} bytes")
print("\n".join(names))

Run it as python3 kexinit_peek.py example.com 22. Against a test server configured with the OQS fork's default list, it prints all 45 names, including the ones ssh -vv dropped:

server: SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_10.4
kex_algorithms: 45 names, 1577 bytes
curve25519-sha256
...
mlkem1024-sha384
mlkem1024nistp384-sha384
sntrup761-sha512

Against github.com, a typical production server, the whole list is 249 bytes, well inside the limit (the banner is GitHub's deliberately randomised one):

$ python3 kexinit_peek.py github.com
server: SSH-2.0-bdb6c72c
kex_algorithms: 10 names, 249 bytes
mlkem768x25519-sha256
sntrup761x25519-sha512
sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com
curve25519-sha256
curve25519-sha256@libssh.org
ecdh-sha2-nistp256
ecdh-sha2-nistp384
ecdh-sha2-nistp521
diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256
kex-strict-s-v00@openssh.com

It only reads; it never completes a key exchange or logs in, and the server simply sees a client that disconnected early. Run it against servers you are responsible for.

How pqc-probe does it

pqc-probe's reader is the same idea with the edges filed down, in kexinit.rs. A tool that connects to arbitrary servers has to assume some of them are hostile, so every length is bounded and checked:

  • packets larger than 35,000 bytes are refused (the size RFC 4253 requires implementations to handle);
  • at most 32 text lines and 8 KB are accepted before the banner;
  • a length field that points past the end of the packet is an error, not a crash.

The parsing step reads like the Python, with every slice checked:

let rest = p.get(17..).ok_or("payload shorter than type + cookie")?;
let len_bytes: [u8; 4] = rest
    .get(..4)
    .ok_or("missing kex_algorithms length")?
    .try_into()
    .map_err(|_| "bad length field")?;
let len = u32::from_be_bytes(len_bytes) as usize;
let end = 4usize
    .checked_add(len)
    .ok_or("kex_algorithms length overflow")?;
let body = rest
    .get(4..end)
    .ok_or_else(|| format!("kex_algorithms claims {len} bytes but the packet ends first"))?;

A regression test pins the bug down: it builds a packet with 60 names, more than 2,000 bytes, and checks that all 60 come back, the last one intact. If the scraping approach ever crept back, that test would fail.

One more lesson came with it. My old code treated an empty or unreadable offer as "the server offers nothing", and then reported that both clients "negotiate identically", which was technically true and completely wrong. An offer that cannot be read is now an error with a reason, never an empty success.

Debug output is not an interface

Nothing here is a bug in OpenSSH. A logger with a fixed buffer is sensible design, and nobody promised that ssh -vv would print every byte the server sent. The mistake was mine: I used human-facing diagnostics as a data source.

If you parse a tool's debug output anywhere in your own scripts, two questions are worth asking:

  • Can the value be longer than a log line? Algorithm lists, certificate chains and headers usually can.
  • Would you notice if it were cut? Truncation by vsnprintf leaves no marker, so a short answer looks like a complete one.

When the honest answer is "maybe" and "no", go to the source of the data instead. For SSH, the server's proposal is right there in the first packet, unencrypted, and the format has not changed since 2006.

Next in the series: probing SSH without getting penalised, or how OpenSSH 9.8's PerSourcePenalties turned real support into false negatives.

title: Cloud Storage for Storing User Uploads in Node.js — Edtech Restore Integrity
description:
Short answer: choose the object store that fits your existing identity, deployment, and data-residency controls, then make restore integrity the application contract. For an edtech platform storing user documents, the important comparison is not which service can accept an upload. All three can do that. The useful question is whether a Node.js backup pipeline can prove that a selected tenant snapshot is complete, unchanged, and safe to restore.

That shifts the decision axis from delivery convenience to recovery evidence. Keep the manifest in a database, keep the document bytes in object storage, and make every restore verify the relationship between them. A five-minute signed request can move bytes; it cannot prove that the manifest and the bytes belong to the same backup.

The bytes are only half the backup.

Choice Pick this when Restore-integrity trade-off
Amazon S3 Your platform already has AWS identity, lifecycle, and audit conventions Mature policy controls are useful, but the application still has to bind object keys to a snapshot manifest
Azure Blob Storage Your deployment and operator identity are centered on Azure and Microsoft Entra ID Shared identity conventions simplify operations; delegated SAS access still needs narrow scope and expiry
Google Cloud Storage Your services and IAM controls already run in Google Cloud Signed URLs make a simple transfer boundary; manifest validation and restore authorization remain application work
Provider-neutral adapter You expect multiple backends or a future migration More contract tests and adapter code, with less provider detail in the restore workflow

The table is a selection aid, not a ranking. Pick this way: use the first three choices when the surrounding platform already gives one of them strong operational ownership. Use the adapter when portability is a requirement you will test, not merely a sentence in an architecture diagram.

How should cloud storage handle user uploads and tenant restores?

The restore target is a snapshot, not a URL. A snapshot record should bind an immutable tenant ID and snapshot ID to an object key, byte length, checksum, schema version, creation time, and state. The manifest can then answer a precise question: “Which exact set of objects did this backup claim to contain?”

Here is the diagram in words: backup job -> manifest row -> object upload -> checksum verification -> sealed snapshot -> restore request -> second verification. The arrows matter. If a job marks the snapshot ready before the object and its checksum are recorded, the restore worker has no reliable stopping point. In a two-tenant fixture, that means a missing object for tenant A can look like a valid restore while tenant B's complete snapshot remains untouched; the state label alone cannot tell those cases apart.

I would use a small state machine such as writing, ready, restoring, and failed. ready means the manifest is durable and every listed object has passed the checks the application requires. It does not mean the provider has validated your business data. That distinction keeps an apparently successful upload from becoming a misleading backup status.

Four states. One useful boundary.

The providers expose different names for similar primitives. Amazon S3 presigned URLs inherit the permissions of the principal that created them. Azure describes SAS as delegated, time-limited access. Google Cloud Storage signed URLs provide time-limited access to a specific resource. Those are useful delivery mechanisms, but each is a bearer credential. A restore worker should therefore load the snapshot by ID, check tenant and state, and validate the downloaded bytes before writing anything back. A 300-second link can be appropriate for a browser action; it is not evidence that the restore itself is correct.

How should a Node.js restore boundary preserve that proof?

Put provider details behind an adapter, but keep integrity decisions above it. The controller should not accept an arbitrary client-supplied object key. It should accept a snapshot ID, authorize that ID for the tenant, and pass the stored key to the adapter. This is one extra lookup. It buys a stable audit subject and makes a guessed key irrelevant.

The adapter below returns bytes and metadata rather than a vendor SDK object. The checksum algorithm is an explicit part of the contract, so a future backend cannot quietly change what “verified” means.

type Snapshot = {
  tenantId: string;
  snapshotId: string;
  objectKey: string;
  expectedBytes: number;
  checksum: string;
  state: "writing" | "ready" | "restoring" | "failed";
};

type StoredObject = {
  body: AsyncIterable<Uint8Array>;
  bytes: number;
  checksum: string;
};

type ObjectStore = {
  read(key: string): Promise<StoredObject>;
};

async function readVerifiedSnapshot(
  tenantId: string,
  snapshotId: string,
  snapshots: { findById(id: string): Promise<Snapshot | null> },
  store: ObjectStore,
): Promise<StoredObject> {
  const snapshot = await snapshots.findById(snapshotId);

  if (!snapshot || snapshot.tenantId !== tenantId || snapshot.state !== "ready") {
    throw new Error("Snapshot is unavailable");
  }

  const object = await store.read(snapshot.objectKey);

  if (object.bytes !== snapshot.expectedBytes || object.checksum !== snapshot.checksum) {
    throw new Error("Snapshot verification failed");
  }

  return object;
}

In production, the comparison must use the checksum representation and algorithm defined by your manifest contract. Also decide whether verification happens while streaming into a temporary restore area or before any durable write. A temporary area is safer for partial downloads; it costs extra storage and cleanup work. That is a real trade-off, unlike a promise that one provider API will make an application-level restore atomic. The temporary approach adds one cleanup job and one more state transition, but it prevents a half-downloaded document from becoming the new source of truth.

When is delivery simplicity the right trade?

Direct browser uploads are attractive because the application does not proxy every document. A presigned S3 request, an Azure SAS request, or a Google Cloud Storage signed request can serve that transfer boundary. The common contract should still specify object key, method, content type, maximum expected size, and expiration. Do not expose provider policy JSON or SDK response objects to the rest of the application.

For a restore, the balance is different. A short-lived download request may be fine for a browser preview. A server-side restore usually needs a stream, checksum calculation, and state transition that the application can observe. The simple path is not always the smallest path: passing a URL to a worker is easy, while proving what the worker downloaded requires metadata, verification, and a retry policy.

Use one adapter per backend and run the same contract tests against each one. Test two tenants, two snapshots, a missing object, a changed checksum, an expired delegated request, and a retry after a partial restore. The negative case is the sharpest: tenant A must not restore tenant B's snapshot even when A knows B's snapshot ID or object name.

How do observability and migration change the choice?

Logs should identify the request ID, tenant ID, snapshot ID, backend label, operation, outcome, byte count when available, and duration. They should never contain document content or a signed URL query string. If object keys include user-provided names, hash or redact them before logging.

Metrics should distinguish upload failure, verification failure, authorization denial, restore duration, and cleanup failure. Break those measurements down by backend and tenant cohort. One global success rate can hide a single school whose restore jobs are consistently incomplete.

For migration, export the manifest format before moving bytes. Copy objects, verify their byte counts and checksums, then switch new writes and record the backend in the snapshot row. Keep the old backend readable until the retention window and a restore rehearsal have passed. That is more work than changing one SDK import, but it gives the team evidence that the move preserved recoverability.

Limits of this comparison

Object storage does not define your recovery point objective, restore ordering, legal hold, encryption-key ownership, or application-level consistency. A successful object download does not prove that a database backup and document manifest represent the same point in time. Record a manifest, validate checksums, and make the restore operation idempotent where possible.

The practical rule is narrow: choose the backend that matches your existing platform controls, then standardize the manifest, state machine, adapter contract, and observability above it. In an edtech system, recovery evidence is the product requirement. Upload delivery is only one step.

References

The provider-specific credential claims and the provider comparison are grounded in the public documentation below. The manifest, state-machine, testing, and observability guidance is provider-neutral engineering practice.

Sources

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/iam

title: Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer for Minimax Model Estimation in MDPs
description:
arXiv:2611.25160v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study active exploration for minimax transition estimation in unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). Frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer~\citep{gu2026kappa} addresses this problem through a parameterized family of exploration objectives, but requires confidence-bound constructions and joint optimization over plausible transition kernels and occupancy measures, introducing a computational burden that limits its practical applicability. We develop Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer, which simplifies this procedure by placing Dirichlet priors on the transition distributions. Under the posterior mean estimator, the posterior expected squared $\ell_2$ error equals the total posterior variance, providing a closed-form exploration signal. The algorithm plans under the posterior mean model, eliminating confidence-set optimization. Under the stated assumptions, this simpler planning procedure retains the $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/3})$ surrogate convergence rate of frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer. We further bound the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experiments on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi demonstrate lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than the tested baselines.

title: DEO: Training-Free Direct Embedding Optimization for Negation-Aware Retrieval
description:
arXiv:2603.09185v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have enabled diverse retrieval methods. However, existing retrieval methods often fail to accurately retrieve results for negation and exclusion queries. To address this limitation, prior approaches rely on embedding adaptation or fine-tuning, which introduce additional computational cost and deployment complexity. We propose Direct Embedding Optimization (DEO), a training-free method for negation-aware text and multimodal retrieval. DEO decomposes queries into positive and negative components and optimizes the query embedding with a contrastive objective. Without additional training data or model updates, DEO outperforms baselines on NegConstraint, with gains of +0.0738 nDCG@10 and +0.1028 MAP@100, while improving Recall@5 by +6\% over OpenAI CLIP in multimodal retrieval. These results demonstrate the practicality of DEO for negation- and exclusion-aware retrieval in real-world settings.

title: I Tested the Entire Prisma Platform on My Project: The Good, What Broke, and the Cloud Bill
description:
A few months ago, I wrote an article titled “I Reduced Prisma Database Operations by 60% Without Upgrading My Database”. In that post, I shared how profiling slow queries with EXPLAIN ANALYZE helped us cut database operations on my project, Sellary (sellary.in)—a digital commerce platform for Indian creators.

Shortly after publishing it, Martin Janse van Rensburg from the Prisma team reached out with an intriguing challenge:

"Since you already use Prisma ORM, would you be up for a follow-up running Sellary on the whole Prisma platform, adding Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute, with an AI agent doing the setup?"

Martin offered two months of trial credits and asked for an honest, unfiltered take: setup experience, developer experience, latency, pricing, and what broke along the way.

As a solo developer running an independent project, my rule is simple: you never risk customer data or production uptime on an infrastructure experiment. Sellary currently runs in production on Next.js 16 (App Router), Prisma ORM 6, and Supabase Postgres with Vercel hosting—and our hosting bill is currently $0/month.

So we established a strict ground rule: Zero risk to production. To us, "zero risk" meant far more than just creating a git branch. We set three strict rules to keep our production data 100% safe:

  • 1. Completely Separate Database Credentials:

    The staging application only ever connected to a freshly provisioned Prisma Postgres database in Singapore (sellary-staging-db). Production Supabase connection strings (SUPABASE_DATABASE_URL / SUPABASE_DIRECT_URL) were never injected into the experiment's GitHub Secrets or staging environment. If a query went rogue, it had zero network access to production tables.

  • 2. Sandbox External Services:

    Sellary handles real money via Razorpay. For staging, payment gateways were strictly bound to test-mode keys (rzp_test_...), and webhook secrets were dummy-scoped. A complete checkout could be executed in staging without touching live payment rails or triggering creator payouts.

  • 3. Using Dummy Secrets in GitHub Actions:

    Next.js App Router analyzes routes at build time. To prevent production secrets from being needed on GitHub Actions runners (or logged in build traces), we injected mock credentials and used SKIP_ENV_VALIDATION=1 during the CI build step, keeping production secrets completely air-gapped from the build pipeline.

We created an isolated staging lab on a dedicated git branch (experiment/prisma-infrastructure), equipped an AI coding agent with official Prisma skills, and evaluated whether Prisma Postgres and Prisma Compute could run Sellary end-to-end.

Here is an honest breakdown of what worked, the friction points we hit, and the economics.

1. Tackling Schema Drift: Migrating to Prisma Postgres

Sellary isn't a simple demo app. Our database schema contains 36 models, 28 enums, and over 1,400 lines in schema.prisma, alongside raw SQL queries with PostgreSQL-specific features like FILTER (WHERE ...) and ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.

Because the project had evolved rapidly during early development, our migration history was behind our schema. If we had naively run prisma migrate deploy against a clean database, 32 out of our 36 tables would have been completely missing.

Rather than trying to guess, we used Prisma's migration engine to generate a clean baseline SQL script:

npx prisma migrate diff --from-empty --to-schema-datamodel prisma/schema.prisma --script > prisma/baseline.sql

The Windows Catch: If you run this in PowerShell on Windows, default redirection emits UTF-8 with a Byte Order Mark (EF BB BF). PostgreSQL's query engine rejects this with a syntax error at byte 0. We stripped the BOM using an explicit UTF-8 encoding stream before applying it.

Once applied to our Singapore staging database (ap-southeast-1), we verified parity:

npx prisma migrate diff --from-schema-datamodel prisma/schema.prisma --to-url "$DATABASE_URL"
# Output: No difference detected.

All 36 models, indexes, and relations mapped cleanly with zero application query rewrites.

2. Deploying Next.js 16 on Prisma Compute

Prisma Compute runs containerized workloads powered by Bun. We configured Next.js 16 for standalone output (output: 'standalone' in next.config.ts) and defined our micro-container service using Prisma Composer in service.ts and module.ts:

import nextjs from '@prisma/composer/nextjs';
import { compute } from '@prisma/composer-prisma-cloud';

export default compute({
  name: 'web',
  deps: {},
  build: nextjs({ module: import.meta.url, appDir: '.' }),
});

We then set up GitHub Actions using prisma/cloud-deploy-action@v1 to build and deploy on every push to our staging branch.

That is where we encountered the real-world friction.

3. The 3 Real Integration Friction Points (And How We Solved Them)

When bridging bleeding-edge developer tools with an existing codebase, edge cases happen. Here are the three specific hurdles we encountered:

Friction 1: The Prisma ORM 6 vs. Prisma 8 Compute CLI Collision

  • The Problem: Sellary uses Prisma ORM 6.19.1 for queries, but Prisma Compute deployment requires the Prisma 8 CLI (prisma deploy module.ts). In GitHub Actions, prisma/cloud-deploy-action checks if node_modules/.bin/prisma exists. Because npm ci installs Prisma 6, the action executed the local binary—which lacks the deploy verb—causing the CI runner to halt.
  • The Workaround: We chained our Next.js build and binary cleanup inside the workflow's build-command: 
  build-command: >-
    npm run build &&
    rm -f node_modules/.bin/prisma node_modules/.bin/prisma.cmd

Next.js builds cleanly with Prisma 6, unlinks the local binary, and allows the deployment step to fall back to the bundled Prisma 8 Compute CLI via Bunx.

Friction 2: The $prismaConfig: 1 Marker Trap

  • The Problem: The Prisma 8 CLI validates prisma.config.ts by checking for an internal marker: value["$prismaConfig"] === 1. In a hybrid repo on Prisma 6, importing definePrismaConfig from @prisma/cli-engine breaks local commands like npx prisma generate.
  • The Workaround: We created a lightweight inline helper in prisma.config.ts: 
  function definePrismaConfig<T extends Record<string, any>>(config: T) {
    return Object.freeze({ ...config, $prismaConfig: 1 });
  }

  const isComposerCommand =
    process.argv.some((arg) => arg === 'deploy' || arg === 'dev') ||
    Boolean(process.env.PRISMA_COMPOSER || process.env.PRISMA_DEPLOY);

  export default isComposerCommand
    ? definePrismaConfig({
        composer: composer({
          extensions: [prismaCloud({ region: 'ap-southeast-1' }), nodeBuild(), nextjsBuild()],
          state: prismaState(),
        }),
      })
    : {};

Standard ORM commands receive {} (so Prisma 6's strict validator doesn't crash), while Compute commands get the valid marker.

Friction 3: Static Build Evaluation vs. Secrets

  • The Problem: Next.js App Router evaluates route modules during next build static page generation. Missing live staging secrets in the build runner halted CI.
  • The Workaround: We passed SKIP_ENV_VALIDATION=1, converted SDK constructors to lazy getters, and wrapped static ISR queries in build fallbacks.

4. Verified Performance & The Live Creator Flow

Once deployed to our staging URL in Singapore (sin.prisma.build), we ran a complete acceptance test:

  1. User Registration: Created a new account via email/password credentials → persisted into the User model on Prisma Postgres.
  2. Session Cookie: Issued and verified the sellary_sid JWT cookie through Edge middleware.
  3. Creator Flow: Created a test digital product (₹10), verifying database persistence in the Product table.
  4. Dynamic SSR Storefront: Requested the live SSR product page (/product/test) to verify that the page loads real data from the database properly on Prisma Compute.

The Numbers:

  • Container Server-Ready Log: 138ms observed in Bun container startup logs.
  • Dynamic SSR Product Page Latency: ~742ms (single measurement) warm roundtrip from India to Singapore (including TLS handshake, Next.js server-side rendering, and live database queries).
  • Database Write Latency: 749ms (single measurement) roundtrip on POST /api/v1/ping with prisma.creatorProfile.updateMany.

Everything functioned smoothly with zero application query modifications.

5. The Solo Developer's Math: Supabase vs. Prisma Platform

Now, let's talk about the cloud bill and Prisma's pricing structure.

Prisma offers a Free plan ($0/month) that includes 200,000 database operations, 2 GB of storage, and 1,000,000 Compute requests a month with no credit card required. For teams needing more capacity and backups, the Starter plan costs $10.00 / month and includes custom spend limits.

The Starter plan features:

  • 1,000,000 Database Operations
  • 5,000,000 Compute Requests (5M)
  • 10 GiB Database Storage

The Catch for Independent Projects:

Additional database operations on paid plans cost $8.00 per 1,000,000 operations.

In my previous article, I showed how eliminating N+1 queries cut our operations by 60%. In an operations-metered cloud model, query optimization is directly linked to your cloud bill.

If you have 24/7 background crons (e.g., an analytics flush running every 15 minutes = 2,880 runs/month, or hourly settlement tasks), unbatched queries can chew through your operation allowance before real users even visit your site.

This naturally brings up the concern of surprise bills. Fortunately, every paid plan allows you to set a hard spend limit in the Prisma Console. You choose the exact ceiling, and your monthly bill cannot exceed that number. This completely eliminates the fear of runaway overage charges.

Still, on Supabase Free, database operations are unmetered (pooled and connection-throttled), and Vercel Hobby covers our frontend traffic with zero overage risk. For an independent project funded out of pocket, $0/month with zero surprise bill risk remains our baseline.

Conclusion & Final Takeaway

Testing Prisma Compute and Prisma Postgres gave us high confidence that the unified Prisma platform can run a real, full-stack Next.js 16 application end-to-end. The branch-bound database isolation and fast container initialization are fantastic for staging workflows.

Our Path Forward:

  1. Production stays on Supabase + Vercel: Our production stack is stable, battle-tested, and costs us $0. Keeping project expenses at zero is a top priority.
  2. Staging stays on Prisma for ongoing evaluation: We are keeping our staging lab active on Prisma throughout our 2-month trial (and exploring whether their $0 Free tier can host our preview branches afterward) to continue benchmarking performance as the platform matures.

Suggestions for the Prisma Team:

  • Add CLI priority flags in prisma/cloud-deploy-action to prevent local Prisma 6 binaries from preempting Compute CLI 8.
  • Allow install-command: none to cleanly skip dependency installation.
  • Standardize hybrid configuration documentation for teams coexisting on Prisma 6 ORM.

Huge thanks to Martin Janse van Rensburg and the Prisma team for providing trial credits, asking for an unfiltered evaluation, and supporting builders.

title: Are Vision Foundation Models Foundational for Electron Microscopy Image Segmentation?
description:
arXiv:2602.08505v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Although vision foundation models (VFMs) are increasingly reused for biomedical image analysis, it remains unclear whether the latent representations they provide are general enough to support effective transfer and reuse across heterogeneous microscopy image datasets. Here, we study this question for the problem of mitochondria segmentation in electron microscopy (EM) images, using two popular public EM datasets (Lucchi++ and VNC) and three recent representative VFMs (DINOv2, DINOv3, and OpenCLIP). We evaluate two practical model adaptation regimes: a frozen-backbone setting in which only a lightweight segmentation head is trained on top of the VFM, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) in which the VFM is fine-tuned in a targeted manner to a specific dataset. Across all backbones, we observe that training on a single EM dataset yields good segmentation performance (quantified as foreground Intersection-over-Union), and that LoRA consistently improves in-domain performance. In contrast, training on multiple EM datasets leads to severe performance degradation for all models considered, with only marginal gains from PEFT. Exploration of the latent representation space through various techniques (PCA, Fr\'echet Dinov2 distance, and linear probes) reveals a pronounced and persistent domain mismatch between the two considered EM datasets in spite of their visual similarity, which is consistent with the observed failure of paired training. These results suggest that, while VFMs can deliver competitive results for EM segmentation within a single domain under lightweight adaptation, current PEFT strategies are insufficient to obtain a single robust model across heterogeneous EM datasets without additional domain-alignment mechanisms.

title: Stop Removing Stopwords: How an Inherited Preprocessing Default Distorts Legal Text-as-Data
description:
arXiv:2609.19153v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Empirical legal scholarship increasingly treats judicial text as data, and much of it still runs on sparse, interpretable pipelines -- TF-IDF features and linear classifiers -- because the textual feature is often the object of study rather than a means to prediction. Yet these pipelines inherit preprocessing defaults from mid-century information retrieval that were never validated against classification accuracy. The most entrenched of these is stopword removal. This study introduces an exhaustive single word ablation that measures the effect of a preprocessing step directly against the downstream objective, and applies it to stopword removal as the hardest case to dislodge. Matching Supreme Court Database labels to Caselaw Access Project opinion texts, the study examines two binary tasks that bracket F1 headroom, ideological direction (no-removal baseline F1 ~0.68) and constitutional versus non-constitutional law type (~0.92), across 7,668 and 7,001 opinions. For each task, the ablation removes each of about 18,500 candidate words in turn, and a task-specific stoplist is built from the measurements. Common generic stoplists fall below the no-removal baseline in all twelve held-out tests. The task-specific stoplists move held-out F1 by +0.0023 (95% CI [-0.0124, +0.0170]) on ideology and by +0.0001 ([-0.0082, +0.0085]) on law type. Neither task shows a detectable benefit from removal, and supplemental analysis finds that word-level statistics predict removal effects poorly, because true removal effects differ by less than the measurement can register, leaving little to predict. The method generalizes to any inherited preprocessing default; the result is a caution specific to interpretable legal text-as-data, where a step that reshapes which features a model sees can distort the doctrinal and ideological signal the research is meant to recover. The burden of proof sits with removal.

title: When Is an AI System Ready for Production? Five Engineering Approaches
description:
A coding assistant can pass its automated tests while skipping part of the original requirement. A document assistant can produce a convincing summary and quietly invent a detail. Both failures came up in GeekyAnts’ account of evaluating AI systems before release, alongside a clinical education example in which the system missed critical errors.

Each case exposes a different gap in the test suite. The coding assistant needed a check against the original requirements. The document assistant needed a check against its source material. The clinical education system needed a way to flag critical misses even when its overall score looked acceptable.

What belongs in an AI release gate?

Start with a small set of representative cases labeled by people who understand the workflow. For a support assistant, that might include a straightforward question, a policy exception, an ambiguous request, and a case that requires escalation. Each example should spell out what an acceptable response must contain and which errors should block release.

A practical evaluation suite can cover five areas:

  • Task completion. Did the system satisfy every requirement, including edge cases?
  • Grounding. Can factual claims be traced to the supplied source or an authorized record?
  • Privacy and fairness. Does the system respect access permissions, and does quality hold across relevant user groups?
  • Latency and cost. Does the complete workflow stay within its limits, including retries and tool calls?
  • Release approval. Are failures, fixes, retest results, and the approval recorded together?

Repeated runs matter because a single pass can hide inconsistent behavior. If a prompt change fixes a missed escalation, the team can rerun that case alongside previously passing cases. The fix is easier to review when the original failure, acceptance criterion, and retest result are all visible.

How five companies approach production readiness

1. Task-level evaluation and human sign-off

GeekyAnts describes assigning acceptance thresholds to individual tasks and testing against expert-labeled examples. Its process covers unsupported answers, privacy, bias, response time, and cost per call. Failed checks are rerun after changes, and a human reviewer signs off before release. The release record captures what was tested, what failed, and who approved it.

The company illustrates the process in How GeekyAnts Evaluates AI Systems for Production Readiness.

2. Repeatable evaluation for variable outputs

Thoughtworks’ guidance starts with a problem familiar to developers working with LLMs. The same input can produce several acceptable answers. A support response can vary in wording while still citing the correct policy, preserving its exceptions, and handling escalation correctly. Evaluating each of those behaviors gives the team a repeatable check that can survive changes to the model or prompt. Thoughtworks’ guide to evaluating an LLM system

3. Monitoring after deployment

IBM’s watsonx.governance documents evaluation metrics, model factsheets, and monitoring for signals such as drift and latency. This addresses a question that release tests leave open. What happens when live inputs start to differ from the cases used during development? A recorded baseline gives teams something to compare against when quality declines after a rollout. IBM’s model governance documentation

4. Testing the full multi-agent workflow

Accenture’s Distiller framework includes agent orchestration, evaluation, and observability. The combination matters when one agent’s output becomes another agent’s input. A retrieval agent might find the right record, while the drafting agent receives an incomplete version of it. An end-to-end evaluation can expose the failed handoff and show what each agent received before the workflow produced its final answer. Accenture’s Distiller framework overview

5. Checking permissions before an agent acts

Deloitte describes evaluating an agent’s proposed actions against policy before execution. For example, an agent may accurately summarize a claim and recommend a status change while still requiring approval to update the underlying record. The test should verify what the system actually did when authorization was missing, including whether it stopped or requested review. Deloitte’s framework for governing agent actions

What evidence would justify a release?

One useful exercise is to trace a single failed case through the workflow. What did the system do? Which criterion did it violate? What changed? Which cases were rerun, and who approved the release? That record gives the next engineer enough context to reproduce the decision when another prompt, model, or tool changes.

title: Does AI Assistance Preserve or Collapse Disagreement? A Study of Pre-Annotations in Ambiguous Video Labeling
description:
arXiv:2510.21798v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI-generated Pre-Annotations can accelerate video labeling, but they may also anchor annotators to model priors and suppress disagreement that is valuable for pluralistic dataset construction. We study this tradeoff in ambiguous temporal video annotation, where annotators choose event boundaries and assign context-dependent labels such as "normal" or "abnormal." We introduce a controlled audit protocol that separates annotation cost, consensus alignment, inter-annotator consistency, temporal-boundary variation, semantic-label variation, latent-space standardization, and edit behavior.
  In a counterbalanced pilot study with 18 annotators and 180 annotation sessions, a fixed CLIP-based Pre-Annotation engine reduced mean annotation time by 23.11%; 72% of annotators were faster with assistance, with a median per-annotator gain of 35%. Assistance increased inter-annotator consistency and CLIP-space standardization, while semantic-label entropy changed only slightly in aggregate. A six-annotator human consensus diagnostic showed comparable alignment across conditions (AMI $\approx 0.64$ in both conditions), but this diagnostic is self-including and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as independent evidence that model influence is absent. Overall, the results suggest that Pre-Annotations acted mainly as editable temporal scaffolds in this pilot setting, while leaving open the possibility of subtler semantic anchoring effects. We contribute an audit framework and anonymized interaction traces for studying when AI-assisted annotation preserves, reshapes, or collapses human disagreement.

title: RHEL, Ubuntu & AlmaLinux Fleet Automation with Ansible
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our Global DNS Propagation Checker & SSL Health Auditor, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

This comprehensive guide delivers an enterprise-level analysis of systems engineering across RHEL, Ubuntu, and AlmaLinux platforms. Learn how to architect, harden, and optimize mixed Linux fleets through kernel parameter tuning, storage engine configuration, and security subsystem management.

Architectural Divergence: Kernel Upstream Cadence and ABI Guarantees

Administering heterogeneous enterprise Linux clusters across Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL), AlmaLinux, and Ubuntu Server requires an understanding of their fundamental kernel engineering methodologies. RHEL and its binary-compatible downstream counterpart, AlmaLinux, operate on an Enterprise Application Binary Interface (kABI) stabilization model. RHEL 9 standardizes on kernel 5.14, heavily backporting thousands of patches from upstreams up through 6.x without modifying internal symbol checksums. This guarantees that out-of-tree kernel modules, specialized storage drivers, and proprietary fabric interconnects execute reliably across minor point releases (e.g, 9.2 to 9.4).

Ubuntu Server LTS (Long Term Support) executes an entirely different strategy. Canonical decouples the base system from long-term kernel freezes via Hardware Enablement (HWE) stacks. While Ubuntu 22.04 LTS initially shipped with kernel 5.15, its HWE updates rolling kernels from subsequent interim releases—transitioning through 6.2, 6.5, and 6.8. This exposes infrastructure to newer schedulers, updated eBPF hook mechanics, and early driver support, but breaks raw kABI stability. Systems engineers must evaluate whether their workload relies on hyper-stable hardware interfaces (favoring RHEL and AlmaLinux) or requires newer networking primitives like io_uring feature updates, advanced WireGuard optimizations, or cutting-edge cgroup v2 accounting enhancements available in Ubuntu LTS.

The AlmaLinux Redirection: ABI vs. Source-for-Source Compatibility

Following Red Hat's June 2023 distribution model shift that restricted public CentOS Stream source RPMs, AlmaLinux formally abandoned byte-for-byte 1:1 bug-for-bug compatibility with RHEL. Instead, the AlmaLinux engineering team transitioned to Application Binary Interface (ABI) compatibility. AlmaLinux sources patches through CentOS Stream, upstream kernel.org trees, and internal builds, targeting full binary parity at the user-space and kABI level. In testing, production binaries linked against glibc 2.34 on RHEL 9 function identically on AlmaLinux 9 without re-compilation. However, systems administrators must verify low-level kernel driver modules (KMODs) via modinfo and nm -u to confirm symbol CRC alignment across AlmaLinux and upstream RHEL kernels.

Package Management Engines: DNF/Libsolv vs. APT/Dpkg Internals

The operational divide between RPM-based distributions (RHEL, AlmaLinux) and Debian-based systems (Ubuntu) manifests centrally within their package dependency resolution engines. DNF5 and legacy DNF4 utilize libsolv, an SAT-solver algorithm originally developed by openSUSE. Libsolv converts package dependency graphs into Boolean satisfiability problems, delivering deterministic resolution even in complex multilib (x86_64 and i686) environments. Ubuntu leverages apt on top of dpkg, utilizing heuristic dependency parsing via an internal directed acyclic graph (DAG).

Repository Metadata Synchronization and Overhead

Under heavy automated fleet provisioning, repository metadata synchronization differences introduce measurable operational overhead. DNF consumes significantly more CPU cycles and RAM when downloading and decompressing repodata XML files (primary, filelists, and updateinfo) compared to APT's compressed Packages.xz indexes.

# Optimize DNF repository caching on RHEL/AlmaLinux
echo "fastestmirror=True" >> /etc/dnf/dnf.conf
echo "max_parallel_downloads=10" >> /etc/dnf/dnf.conf
echo "keepcache=True" >> /etc/dnf/dnf.conf
echo "metadata_expire=6h" >> /etc/dnf/dnf.conf

# Optimize APT performance on Ubuntu
cat  /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99tuning
Acquire::Queue-Mode "host";
Acquire::http::Pipeline-Depth "10";
APT::Acquire::Retries "3";
EOF

In continuous deployment environments deploying hundreds of ephemeral nodes simultaneously, unoptimized DNF processes can consume up to 800MB of resident memory during transactions, compared to 150MB for APT. Mitigate this in production by provisioning local repository mirrors (using reposync and apt-mirror) paired with local proxy caches.

Mandatory Access Control: SELinux Architecture vs. AppArmor Profiles

Security architectures diverge sharply between RHEL/AlmaLinux and Ubuntu. The Enterprise Linux family enforces Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) by default, while Ubuntu implements AppArmor. Both are Linux Security Modules (LSM), but their security models, enforcement overhead, and administrative maintenance models are entirely distinct.

SELinux: Type Enforcement and Object Labeling

SELinux relies on Type Enforcement (TE), Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), and Multi-Level Security (MLS). Every kernel object (inodes, memory pages, network sockets) carries a full security context consisting of user:role:type:level. The Linux kernel queries the Access Vector Cache (AVC) before permitting syscall operations.

# Inspect and debug SELinux policy violations
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_rw_content_t "/var/www/data(/.*)?"
restorecon -Rv /var/www/data

# Real-time policy compilation from AVC denials
ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2allow -M custom_workload
semodule -i custom_workload.pp

The administrative burden of SELinux requires explicit inode relabeling after non-standard storage mounts, alongside operational knowledge of boolean flags (e.g, setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect 1). However, SELinux prevents exploitation vectors that path-based access control cannot mitigate, such as directory traversal attacks relying on hardlink manipulation.

AppArmor: Path-Based Enforcement

AppArmor relies on absolute filesystem path tracking rather than inode extended attributes (xattrs). Profiles reside in /etc/apparmor.d/ as human-readable rule sets. Path-based enforcement eliminates the operational headache of relabeling filesystems during migration or backup restoration.

# Enforce and troubleshoot AppArmor profiles on Ubuntu
aa-status
aa-enforce /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.nginx

# Parse denials from audit framework
aa-logprof

The critical vulnerability in AppArmor's architecture lies in path aliasing. If a binary resolves an inode through alternative bind mounts, chroot boundaries, or specific namespace shifts, AppArmor can fail open if the rule does not account for the alternate path. For container workloads running beneath Podman or Docker, SELinux dynamically isolates container processes using Type Enforcement Multi-Category Security (MCS) labels (e.g, system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c123,c456), providing vastly superior kernel-level container breakout containment compared to standard static AppArmor base profiles.

Storage Subsystems and Filesystem Performance: XFS vs. Ext4

Filesystem selection dictates I/O latency, concurrency under multi-threaded direct I/O (DIO), and filesystem expansion capabilities across distributions.

Property RHEL & AlmaLinux Default: XFS Ubuntu Server Default: Ext4
Maximum Filesystem Size 1024 TiB (v5 superblock) 1 EiB
Maximum File Size 8 EiB 16 TiB
Online Expansion Supported (xfs_growfs) Supported (resize2fs)
Online Reduction Not Supported (Requires reformat) Supported (Unmounted only)
Internal Metadata Scaling Allocation Groups (Independent locks) Block Groups (Global locks on allocation)
Direct I/O Concurrent Write High (Parallel allocation per AG) Moderate (Thread serialization on inode lock)

RHEL and AlmaLinux standardize on XFS. Built specifically for high-concurrency enterprise workloads, XFS divides the filesystem into Allocation Groups (AGs), each managing its own free space and inode allocations independently. This design prevents lock contention when high-core servers write concurrently across NVMe arrays. However, XFS cannot be shrunk, which introduces operational constraints when resizing partitioned virtual disks.

Ubuntu defaults to Ext4. Ext4 is resilient on single-disk instances, handles sub-gigabyte allocations with lower metadata overhead, and supports offline shrinking. However, Ext4 suffers from centralized inode serialization bottlenecks during parallel Direct I/O writes, making it less optimal than XFS for enterprise database backends (PostgreSQL, Oracle, or high-throughput Kafka storage logs).

# High-throughput XFS mount options for database storage
mkfs.xfs -f -d agcount=16 -b size=4096 /dev/nvme0n1
mount -o noatime,nodiratime,logbufs=8,logbsize=256k,allocsize=64M /dev/nvme0n1 /mnt/nvme-pool

# Optimal Ext4 mount options for low-latency writes
mkfs.ext4 -E lazy_itable_init=0,lazy_journal_init=0 -O mmp /dev/nvme1n1
mount -o noatime,commit=60,data=writeback /dev/nvme1n1 /mnt/ext4-pool

Kernel Space Optimization: Network Stacks, Virtual Memory, and eBPF

Systems engineers deploying across both families must implement unified kernel tuning parameters via /etc/sysctl.d/99-enterprise-tuning.conf to maintain consistent operational baselines across environments.

Memory Management and Dirty Pages

Enterprise Linux distributions often default to conservative memory management configurations that yield catastrophic performance regressions under heavy write workloads. When vm.dirty_ratio is left at the stock 20% or 30%, a server with 512GB of RAM will buffer up to 150GB of dirty data before blocking threads to flush via pdflush/flushers. This induces multi-second storage pauses (I/O freezes).

# /etc/sysctl.d/99-enterprise-tuning.conf

# Avoid long I/O writeout stalls on large memory systems
vm.dirty_background_bytes = 268435456
vm.dirty_bytes = 1073741824
vm.swappiness = 10
vm.vfs_cache_pressure = 50

# Network Stack Latency & Buffer Allocations (100GbE NICs)
net.core.somaxconn = 8192
net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 16384
net.core.rmem_max = 67108864
net.core.wmem_max = 67108864
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 87380 67108864
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 65536 67108864
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = bbr
net.core.default_qdisc = fq
net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle = 0
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1

eBPF Tracing Differences

Tracing network operations and thread context switches via eBPF requires explicit distribution parity. On RHEL and AlmaLinux 9, compile eBPF programs against the BPF Type Format (BTF) exported via /sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux, standard in production kernels. On Ubuntu, ensure the linux-tools-$(uname -r) and linux-headers-$(uname -r) match your current HWE kernel deployment precisely, as dynamic kernel updates can decouple running kernel headers from the installed toolchains, breaking dynamic BPF compilation scripts (e.g, BCC tools, bpftrace) during active triage scenarios.

Operational Parity and Automation Runbook

Running a unified operational infrastructure spanning both RHEL/AlmaLinux and Ubuntu requires standardizing on systemd cgroup v2 resource limits and maintaining consistent patch management lifecycles.

Systemd Resource Limiting (cgroup v2)

Both distributions now operate fully within the unified cgroup v2 hierarchy. Rather than deploying divergent PAM limits (limits.conf), systems administrators should enforce CPU, memory, and task isolation natively at the systemd service or slice tier.

# /etc/systemd/system/production-workload.service.d/override.conf
[Service]
# Memory bounds
MemoryHigh=28G
MemoryMax=32G
MemorySwapMax=0

# CPU priority and hard bandwidth limit
CPUWeight=200
CPUQuota=800%

# Process containment
TasksMax=10000
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
PrivateTmp=true

Automated Patching Strategies

Patch lifecycles require strict automation to mitigate CVE exposure without inducing uncoordinated downtime.

  • Ubuntu: Leverage unattended-upgrades. Configure /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades to enforce reboot blackouts and restrict automated application to security repos: "${distro_id}:${distro_codename}-security";.
  • RHEL & AlmaLinux: Utilize dnf-automatic. Edit /etc/dnf/automatic.conf to execute upgrade_type = security with apply_updates = yes, and activate the systemd timer via systemctl enable --now dnf-automatic.timer.

By defining explicit boundaries between the packaging layer, filesystem architecture, and LSM controls, administrators can operate unified RHEL, Ubuntu, and AlmaLinux compute nodes with high performance, hardened boundaries, and predictable execution.

title: Periodic and Harmonic Periodic RoPE for Length Extrapolation in LLMs
description:
arXiv:2605.27980v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The ability to process long contexts is crucial for large language models (LLMs) to perform long-horizon tasks. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) gives every token a new rotation angle, so a model eventually meets angles it never saw in training, i.e., position exhaustion. We propose Periodic RoPE (P-RoPE), a positional encoding mechanism that operates in conjunction with sliding window attention. It repeats the first sliding-window-size \(W\) angles of the RoPE table, so the model needs only \(W\) distinct angles. P-RoPE works but introduces a wrap error at the window boundary. We further propose Harmonic Periodic RoPE (HP-RoPE), which removes the error by choosing frequencies that complete whole turns in \(W\) tokens. We compare models that share the same architecture, data, and schedule and differ only in the window-layer position encoding: standard RoPE, P-RoPE, and HP-RoPE. The results show that P-RoPE and HP-RoPE keep perplexity nearly flat from the training length \(768\) to \(16\)k, while RoPE, NTK, and YaRN rise. In a format-free Passkey test at \(16\)k, they remain at \(99\)--\(100\%\), against \(11\)--\(37\%\) for those RoPE interpolations. The code is available at \href{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}{https://github.com/Cominder/miniwin}.

title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
description:
arXiv:2611.25086v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely.We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

title: Stability Bands for Feature Attribution: The Core, the Nucleolus and the Bargaining Set of Explained-Variance Games
description:
arXiv:2611.25238v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation. We study feature attribution through the core, the nucleolus and the bargaining set of an explained-variance game, in which the worth of a set of features is the variance of the model's predictions that those features generate. For every feature we report a stability band (its range of shares over the core, or over the least core when the core is empty), with the nucleolus as distinguished point and a certificate that the allocation admits no justified objection. Three results organise the approach. First, for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, with pairwise Harsanyi dividends $2\beta_i\beta_j\sigma_{ij}$, so multicollinearity is what creates coalitional structure. Second, in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, the (least) core is point-symmetric around it, and the core is non-empty if and only if every cut of the interaction graph has non-negative weight. The Shapley value thus always lies in the prebargaining set, and stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. Third, for convex games the bands have a closed form and any allocation can be certified with one minimum cut. In a hedonic price model, the usual mean-SHAP explanation admits a justified objection by the coalition {Ratings, ROM, Battery}. In a gradient-boosting forecaster of retail orders the exact game has an empty core and strong higher-order interactions; the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares, and sparse third-order surrogates recover it where pairwise ones cannot.

title: Quantifying Cultural-Psychological Constructs in Four Centuries of Ottoman Court Registers
description:
arXiv:2611.24981v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Populations vary along cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor. But how can these dimensions be studied in historical societies for which conventional psychological data are unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational text-analytic framework for quantifying psychological constructs in 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513-1911 CE. We develop sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language and extend a theory-driven, text-analytic pipeline to capture cultural variation along the dimensions of individualism, collectivism, and honor in this historical corpus. We evaluate our models through multiple methods: document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and validation against expert annotations. Our adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) achieved a Recall@1 of .843 on the test set for document retrieval, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 for semantic textual similarity (meaning the best answer usually appeared as a top result), and classified questionnaire items with 89.58\% accuracy. Document-level performance varied across constructs and methods. Qualitative analysis further showed that high scores reflected historically specific legal and institutional patterns. We publicly release the models, construct representations, scoring pipeline, as well as an interactive web interface to support transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analyses of Ottoman Turkish court records spanning approximately four centuries. These computational tools enable the study of psychological variation across centuries of cultural and institutional change in a diverse empire.

title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
description:
arXiv:2611.24039v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.

title: One stack trace, 40 billed log entries: the logging cost most teams miss
description:
Most log platforms treat each line of stdout as a separate log entry. So one plain-text Java stack trace arrives as 40 or more entries: each one billed, most with no level or timestamp, and impossible to search as a single error. Python tracebacks, Node errors and .NET exceptions have the same problem.

It rarely shows up as a line item. It just makes the bill bigger and outages harder to debug.

How to tell if it's happening to you

Search your logs for entries that start with:

  • whitespace or a tab
  • at (Java and .NET frames)
  • Caused by: or ... N more
  • Traceback (most recent call last)

Another sign: your platform reports far more "errors" than your application actually threw. If a single failed request produces dozens of error entries, you're paying for line splitting.

Fix 1 (best): structured logging

Have the logger serialize the exception into one field of one JSON line:

{"level":"ERROR","message":"payment failed",
 "error.type":"java.net.SocketTimeoutException",
 "error.stack":"java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out\n\tat ...",
 "order_id":"8812"}

One error, one entry, fully searchable. It fixes levels, timestamps and request context at the same time. Every major language has a JSON encoder for its standard logger: Logback or Log4j2 for Java, pino or winston for Node, python-json-logger or structlog for Python, Serilog for .NET.

Fix 2 (stopgap): join the lines in the collector

When you can't change the application yet, have the log shipper stitch multi-line events back together before they're sent. With Fluent Bit:

[FILTER]
    Name                  multiline
    Match                 kube.*
    multiline.key_content log
    multiline.parser      java, python, go

The CloudWatch agent and Google's Ops Agent have equivalent multi-line settings. It's a stopgap because the joined entry is still unstructured text, but it stops the per-line billing today.

Bonus: AWS log groups that never expire

While you're looking at logging costs: CloudWatch log groups never expire by default. Any group nobody configured keeps growing forever. This lists every group with no retention set:

aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].logGroupName' --output text

Then set one, for example 30 days:

aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name <name> --retention-in-days 30

For comparison, Google Cloud's _Default bucket keeps logs for 30 days unless you change it, and Azure Log Analytics defaults to 30 days for most tables.

The short version

  1. Search for stack-trace fragments to see how much of your volume is split lines.
  2. Switch to JSON logging where you can.
  3. Join lines in the collector where you can't yet.
  4. Put a retention policy on every log group.
